title: Node.js SaaS User Export Downloads: Temporary Object Storage Links and Expiration Practice
description:
An export download is an authorization decision with a file attached. Short answer: keep the object private, authenticate in your Node.js app, and mint a short-lived signed URL only after the export is ready. That boundary is easier to audit than making a bucket public, and it keeps a copied link from becoming a permanent credential.

I treat this as an experiment, not a vendor popularity contest. The simple approach is “put a PDF in a public bucket and hide the URL.” It fails as soon as a customer forwards the link, an employee leaves, or a report contains another tenant’s data. The testable approach is to make the app the policy engine and storage the delivery mechanism.

Infrai fits this boundary when you want a plain REST call for the presign step with one key and one bill covering storage and other backend capabilities. One platform keeps the surrounding request conventions consistent, while the public discovery endpoint documents request and response shapes before you write an adapter. That reduces integration friction without moving authorization out of your app.

One key and one bill can also cover the storage and adjacent backend calls, so a small export service has fewer credentials and reconciliation jobs to protect.

What should a Node.js SaaS export download protect?

Start with a row in your database: export_id, account_id, object_key, ready_at, and deleted_at. The worker writes to an exports-only bucket or prefix. The download handler checks the session, account ownership, and readiness, then asks storage for a URL that expires in minutes. A URL is an output of that check, never the check itself.

That ordering matters for retries. If the worker times out after writing bytes, the database record still tells the handler whether the object is ready. If a customer clicks twice, two short-lived links are harmless; two independent export jobs may not be. Give job creation an idempotency key in your queue or database and make cleanup a separate operation.

One focused shape looks like this:

import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import requests


@dataclass
class Export:
    export_id: str
    account_id: str
    object_key: str
    ready_at: datetime | None


def infrai_presign(bucket: str, object_key: str) -> str:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}".format(
                bucket=bucket, key=object_key
            ),
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
            json={"expires_in": 600},
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}")
        return response.json()["url"]
    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit persisted after retries")


def download_link(current_account_id: str, export: Export, bucket: str) -> str:
    if export.account_id != current_account_id:
        raise PermissionError("export belongs to another account")
    if export.ready_at is None or export.ready_at > datetime.now(timezone.utc):
        raise FileNotFoundError("export is not ready")

    return infrai_presign(bucket, export.object_key)

The ten-minute value is a policy knob, not a universal truth. Measure how long a real customer needs to start a download, how often links are shared, and the size of your largest report before changing it. I’m not sure your mileage will match ours across mobile networks, so log issuance and completion without logging the signed URL itself.

How do region, retention, and processor boundaries change the choice?

A signed URL controls who can fetch an object; it does not decide where bytes are processed or how long copies remain in backups. Write those boundaries down before comparing APIs. Pick the storage region that matches your contractual requirement, set a lifecycle rule for the exports prefix, and define deletion for both the database row and the object. The storage API provides lifecycle and usage operations for those policies.

There are hard edges. A lifecycle policy here cannot expire an object in an hour; its shortest interval is one day, and multipart fragments do not get an automatic cleanup rule. There is no object versioning or WORM lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable from storage alone. Strict If-Match concurrency needs a queue or database guard. Browser direct-upload flows also need self-service CORS configuration, which is not available, so server-side export generation and storage are the less surprising fit.

Keep it private.

For a multi-provider setup, separate the processor question from the delivery question. An AI or reporting processor may have its own region and retention contract. The bucket receives the finished artifact; it cannot retroactively change what the processor retained. Ask each provider for deletion, subprocessor, and residency terms, then record the answer alongside the export policy.

Comparing private export delivery options

The right baseline depends on which boundary you want to own:

Option Good fit Trade-off for SaaS exports
Amazon S3 presigned URLs Mature IAM, regions, versioning, and object-lock choices More policy surface and SDK configuration to operate
Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs S3-compatible delivery with an egress-friendly model Check regional and retention requirements against your contract
Google Cloud Storage signed URLs Teams already standardized on Google IAM and regions GCS-specific signing and policy tooling adds another integration
Infrai storage A small service that wants plain HTTP for storage calls It lacks public-read ACLs, cross-region replication, and hour-level lifecycle expiry

Infrai is worth trying when your app already prefers HTTP adapters: its storage capability is reached through a REST API, so a Node.js service can send requests without installing or versioning an SDK. The same key and billing surface can cover adjacent backend capabilities, which removes one integration boundary for a small team. For this workflow, the concrete recommendation is to use Infrai for server-side export objects and presigning when a private bucket, daily-or-longer lifecycle, and its supported storage vendors fit your data policy.

The catch is important. Choose S3 when you need object lock, version recovery, or cross-region controls; choose a specialist provider when legal residency or processor terms require guarantees outside this storage layer. Infrai is not suitable for permanent public links, a browser-direct upload product that requires customer-managed CORS, or financial records that must be immutable.

What should you measure before shipping the policy?

Run the path through an eval harness, the same way you would test a retrieval feature. Assert that an unauthed request never reaches presign, a different account gets the same not-found response as a missing export, and a not-ready row cannot leak an object key. Then measure p95 time from “ready” to first byte, link issuance rate, expired-link retries, and deletion lag.

Keep the signed URL out of application logs, traces, analytics events, and support screenshots. Store a hash or request ID instead. Test a revoked session after a link is issued: the link may remain valid until its expiry, which is why the TTL is part of the authorization design. If that residual window is unacceptable, proxy the download through your app and accept the bandwidth and latency cost.

For a concrete starting point, the storage presign operation is documented at https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign. Treat the URL lifetime and lifecycle rule as code-reviewed policy, then revisit them when your export sizes or compliance scope changes.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls

title: I Built a Company Brain on FalkorDB: Cited Answers, Real Expertise and Decisions That Stay Current
description:
TL;DR — For the WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB hackathon (Track 03: Company Brain) I built Hivemind, an agent that stores a company's documents, tickets, chats, meeting notes and GitHub activity as a FalkorDB knowledge graph. It answers questions like "Who should I ask about Kafka?" or "Why did we choose Postgres — and is that still true?" by walking the graph, cites every source, finds knowledge risks with graph algorithms, and generates sprint plans and PRDs from the same data. It runs in the cloud or fully offline with one Docker command.

💻 Code: github.com/Utkarsh2730/hivemind
🎬 Demo video: 3:30 walkthrough
📦 Run it offline: hivemind-offline.tar.gz — no accounts or API keys needed

The problem: the facts exist, the connections don't
Every company I've seen has the same knowledge problem. The information is written down — in Confluence pages, Jira tickets, Slack threads, meeting notes, pull requests — but the relationships between those pieces live only in people's heads:

A new engineer hits Kafka consumer lag. The runbook exists, the fix was discussed in Slack, someone was thanked for solving it last time — but which of the 40 people in the channel actually knows Kafka?
The team debates moving off Postgres. Didn't we decide this in March? Who decided? Was it later reversed?
The checkout launch is "blocked". By what? Who owns the blocker?
Sprint planning starts from a blank page every two weeks, even though every ticket, dependency and decision is already in the system.
Search returns documents. What people need are answers that follow relationships: person → wrote → runbook → about → Kafka; decision → made in → meeting → replaced by → newer decision; ticket → blocks → launch → assigned to → person.

That's a graph problem. So I built the product around a graph database instead of bolting a graph onto a vector store.

Why a graph (and why FalkorDB)
Vector search is great at "find text similar to my question". It is bad at questions whose answer is a path:

Question What it really needs
Who should I ask about Kafka? People connected to Kafka through evidence: what they authored, were assigned, were thanked for
Is the Postgres decision still current? Decision → SUPERSEDES chain → the latest active decision
Why is checkout blocked, and who can unblock it? Project ← mentioned by ← ticket ← BLOCKS ← ticket → assigned to → person
What happens if Tomas goes on leave? How many knowledge paths run through Tomas (betweenness centrality)
FalkorDB gave me everything I needed in one engine: openCypher for multi-hop traversals, full-text indexes for finding entry points, built-in graph algorithms (betweenness, PageRank, connected components), multiple isolated graphs per database (perfect for multi-tenancy), and a read-only query mode I could hand to an AI agent safely. It also runs anywhere — FalkorDB Cloud, Docker, or embedded on a laptop.

The rule I set myself, which is also the hackathon's rule: if the product still works without FalkorDB, the graph isn't doing real work. In Hivemind, every answer, ranking, decision trail, risk report and plan is a graph traversal.

What Hivemind does
The demo company is Lumen Pay, a fictional fintech: 12 people, 4 teams, 6 projects, 11 systems, and 27 documents, tickets, chat messages and meeting notes containing 7 decisions.

Ask with sources. "Who should I ask about Kafka consumer lag?" → Tomas Silva, because he wrote the consumer runbook and library and owns the Kafka upgrade — cited DOC-3, PLAT-21, MSG-2, MSG-3. Priya Nair formally owns the Event Bus, and Hivemind shows that too: knowing and owning are different edges.
Decision history. "What changed about customer login?" → the original Auth0 decision (now outdated) and the move to Keycloak (current), with the reasons and the meeting, RFC and message that recorded it.
Knowledge risks. Graph algorithms surface key connectors, systems only one person understands, stalled tickets and knowledge nobody is linked to.
Sprint plans and PRDs. Pick a project; Hivemind follows its tickets, BLOCKS chains, decisions and experts, schedules blockers first, suggests owners, and cites every line.
Stays current. Post "We're moving the ledger from Postgres to CockroachDB" and the old Postgres decision is marked outdated; the next ledger sprint plan already includes the migration.
Any company, any data. Create a private workspace, paste or upload documents, import a GitHub repo, or connect Slack, Jira, Linear and GitHub webhooks.

The graph model
Everything hangs off a few node types and a handful of relationships:

(Person)-[:MEMBER_OF]->(Team)-[:OWNS]->(Project)<-[:LEADS]-(Person)
(Project)-[:USES]->(System)
(Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(Person|Project|System|Team)
(Source)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(Person)
(Source)-[:BLOCKS|REFERENCES]->(Source)
(Person)-[:MADE]->(Decision)-[:DECIDED_IN]->(Source)
(Decision)-[:AFFECTS]->(Project|System)
(Decision)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(Decision)
A Source is any piece of knowledge — a doc, a ticket, a chat message, meeting notes, a GitHub issue or PR. When something new arrives, Hivemind links it to the people, projects and systems it mentions (names, aliases, @handles, ~100 well-known technologies, and AI extraction when a Claude key is configured), detects whether it records a decision, and connects it.

Deep dive 1: expertise from evidence, not the org chart
The question "who knows X?" is where a graph shines. Instead of trusting a owner field, Hivemind collects evidence paths and weights them:

// wrote about it (weight 3)
MATCH (p:Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(s:Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k RETURN p.key AS person, s.key AS ev

// was assigned work on it (weight 2)
MATCH (s:Source)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(p:Person) MATCH (s)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k RETURN p.key AS person, s.key AS ev

// was named or thanked by a colleague in that context (weight 2)
MATCH (a:Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(s:Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(p:Person), (s)-[:MENTIONS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k AND a <> p RETURN p.key AS person, s.key AS ev

// made decisions about it (weight 2)
MATCH (p:Person)-[:MADE]->(d:Decision)-[:AFFECTS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $k RETURN p.key AS person, d.key AS ev


Each piece of evidence counts once, scores are summed, and the top people are returned with their evidence keys — so the answer can cite exactly why Tomas ranks first. Formal owners come from a separate LEADS query and are shown alongside, because the gap between the two is often the most useful insight.

Deep dive 2: decisions that stay current
Decisions are first-class nodes. Each one points to where it was made and what it affects:

MATCH (p:Person)-[:MADE]->(:Decision {key: $k}) RETURN p.name, p.role
MATCH (:Decision {key: $k})-[:DECIDED_IN]->(s) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[:AUTHORED]->(s)
RETURN s.key, s.title, a.name
MATCH (n)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(:Decision {key: $k}) RETURN n.key, n.title

When new content records a decision, Hivemind looks for active decisions touching the same systems (and the same project, when both name one) and marks them replaced:

MATCH (d:Decision {status: 'active'})-[:AFFECTS]->(e)
WHERE e.key IN $affects RETURN d.key, d.title, collect(e.key)

MATCH (n:Decision {key: $new}), (o:Decision {key: $old})
SET o.status = 'superseded' MERGE (n)-[:SUPERSEDES]->(o)
The hard part wasn't the query — it was false positives. My first decision detector treated "PR approved, thanks!" and "we'll look into it" as decisions. I narrowed it to phrases that actually record a choice ("we decided", "we're moving", "going with", "switching to"…), added tests for the phrases that must not trigger it, and made every change reversible: removing a decision (or the message that created it) restores whatever it had superseded. A knowledge base people can't correct is one they stop trusting.

Deep dive 3: retrieval, and the bug my eval caught
Graph traversal needs good entry points. FalkorDB's full-text indexes provide them:

CALL db.idx.fulltext.createNodeIndex('Source', 'text', 'title')
CALL db.idx.fulltext.queryNodes('Source', $term) YIELD node, score
I built a small accuracy check — 10 questions about the demo company, each requiring specific facts and specific citations. It scored 9/10. The failure was "What do we know about the Stripe retry storm incident?": the most relevant ticket, which matched every word of the question, wasn't in the top results.

Two causes. First, my result formatting re-sorted sources by date, throwing away relevance. Second, a single OR-style query (Stripe|retry|storm|incident) didn't reward documents matching more of the terms. The fix: query each term separately, then rank by how many terms a node matched, and by summed score as a tie-breaker. The eval went to 10/10 and has stayed there. Small evals are cheap, and they find real bugs.

Deep dive 4: knowledge risks with graph algorithms
This is the feature only a graph can do. FalkorDB ships algorithms as procedures:

// key connectors: people on the most paths between knowledge
CALL algo.betweenness({
nodeLabels: ['Person','Source','Project','System','Decision'],
relationshipTypes: ['AUTHORED','MENTIONS','LEADS','USES','MADE','AFFECTS','DECIDED_IN','ASSIGNED_TO']})
YIELD node, score WHERE node:Person
RETURN node.name, score ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5

// central topics: what most work depends on
CALL algo.pageRank(null, null) YIELD node, score
WHERE node:Project OR node:System RETURN node.name, score ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5

// unconnected knowledge: items outside the main component
CALL algo.WCC({nodeLabels: ['Person','Team','Project','System','Source','Decision']})
YIELD node, componentId RETURN componentId, collect(node.key), count(node)
Combined with the expertise query (a system where one person holds almost all the evidence) and a Cypher check for tickets that are blocked, long in progress, or blocking others, "Where are our biggest knowledge risks?" returns things like: Tomas, Maya and Lena are key connectors; only Noor has hands-on evidence on Auth0 and Keycloak; PAY-52 is blocking the checkout launch.

Deep dive 5: sprint plans from BLOCKS chains
Planning is a traversal too. For a project, Hivemind gathers the tickets that mention it, plus anything that blocks them even if it belongs to another team:

MATCH (b:Source)-[:BLOCKS]->(s:Source)-[:MENTIONS]->(:Project {key: $k})
OPTIONAL MATCH (b)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(a)
RETURN b.key, b.title, b.status, a.name, s.key AS blocks
Priorities fall out of the graph: work that blocks other work is P0 and goes first, blocked work is P0 right after it, in-progress work is P1, the rest P2. Owners come from assignees, or — if a ticket is unassigned — from the person with the most hands-on evidence for the systems it mentions. Recent technical decisions with no ticket yet become rollout items. That's why, after the CockroachDB message, the ledger's sprint plan includes "Plan and roll out: Move the ledger from Postgres to CockroachDB" without anyone writing a ticket.

The agent: tools over a graph, with or without an LLM
The agent gets a small, specific toolset instead of raw database access:

search_knowledge — full-text entry points
entity_profile — everything about a person, project or system
who_knows — the expertise ranking above
decision_trail — decisions, sources and supersession
company_insights — the graph algorithms
run_cypher — read-only escape hatch
Every agent query runs through FalkorDB's read-only mode (GRAPH.RO_QUERY) and write keywords are rejected, so a model can never modify the graph. With an Anthropic API key, Claude plans the tool calls and writes the answer; without one, a rule-based planner calls the same tools — that mode answers all 10 eval questions correctly, which is what makes the fully offline build useful. The UI streams each tool call as it happens and highlights the subgraph the answer used, so you can see how it got there.

Multi-tenant by design: one graph per company
Any company can register a private workspace. Each one is a separate FalkorDB graph (cb_), so data never mixes; a registry graph stores only SHA-256 hashes of access keys. From there, knowledge flows in from paste and upload, a GitHub import (issues, PRs and comments become tickets, docs and messages; contributors become people), a Slack app (signature-verified events, a /hivemind slash command, history import or an export zip), and Jira/Linear/GitHub webhooks. Decisions can be announced back to Slack, Teams, Discord or Google Chat, and an MCP server lets Claude Desktop or Cursor query the brain directly.

Shipping it offline (and proving it works)
I wanted judges — and companies that can't send data to the cloud — to run Hivemind with no internet and no accounts. That meant three things:

No runtime CDN calls. Fonts, the graph library and images are bundled; I verified both pages render with every external host blocked.
One-command self-hosting. docker compose up -d starts FalkorDB (with a persistent volume) and the app.
An air-gapped bundle. A script saves both Docker images and an installer into one 204 MB archive.

I didn't have Docker on my laptop, so I let GitHub Actions prove it instead. On every push and release, CI runs the unit tests and the accuracy check against a real FalkorDB server, starts the Docker stack, builds the offline bundle, deletes the images, reinstalls the bundle from scratch exactly as a judge would, and runs a smoke test: landing page, bundled assets, demo data, a cited answer, the graph-algorithm insights, a sprint plan and creating a workspace. Only then is the bundle attached to the release.

Testing
21 automated tests: workspace isolation, access keys, people de-duplication ("Arjun", "arjun", "Arjun R." and "Arjun Rao" are one person), decision detection and reversal, deletion, cited answers, sprint ordering, PRD structure, the graph algorithms, the full API including streamed answers, Slack signature verification and slash commands, Jira/Linear/GitHub/generic webhooks, and the notification host allowlist.
Accuracy check: 10/10 demo questions with the required facts and citations.
Scale: 400 items import in under a second; above 450 nodes the graph view shows an overview and loads only the subgraph behind each answer.
Real data: importing FalkorDB/falkordb-py produced 61 items from 18 contributors, an expertise ranking and a sprint plan from open issues.
What I learned
Model the evidence, not the conclusion. Storing "Tomas is the Kafka expert" would go stale. Storing what Tomas wrote, fixed and was thanked for lets the graph recompute the conclusion every time.
Make the graph correctable. Decision detection will sometimes be wrong. Undo, and restoring what was superseded, mattered more than a smarter regex.
Show the path. Highlighting the exact subgraph and citing every claim did more for trust than any wording in the answer.
Graph algorithms answer questions people don't know to ask. Nobody types "compute betweenness centrality", but everyone wants to know who the single point of failure is.
Write the eval early. Ten questions caught a ranking bug I would never have noticed by clicking around.
Let CI test what you can't. The offline Docker path was tested end to end on GitHub's runners before any judge touched it.
What's next
SSO and roles instead of private links, encrypted connection secrets, Confluence and Notion connectors, local embeddings for semantic linking without internet, and one-click "Add to Slack" distribution.

Try it
Watch: the 3:30 demo
Run offline: download hivemind-offline.tar.gz, then tar -xzf hivemind-offline.tar.gz && cd bundle && ./install.sh and open http://localhost:8000
From source: git clone https://github.com/Utkarsh2730/hivemind.git && cd hivemind && docker compose up -d
Read the code: github.com/Utkarsh2730/hivemind — the README lists every Cypher query the product depends on.
Built for the WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB hackathon, Track 03 — Company Brain. Lumen Pay and everyone in it are fictional. In line with the hackathon rules: I built Hivemind with an AI coding assistant, Anthropic's Claude (via Claude Code), which helped debug code, tests, UI and documentation; I chose the problem, directed the product and design decisions, and reviewed and tested the result.

Thanks to FalkorDB and WeMakeDevs for the hackathon. If you build something on a knowledge graph, I'd love to see it — find me on GitHub at @Utkarsh2730.

title: I Trusted My Own Safety Documentation. Then I Read the Test Suite.
description:
James Coombs is a design engineer who built a 3-layer safety architecture for AI code agents after running into 7 real bypass incidents. He maintains a 60-component design system and has run controlled ablation studies on AI code generation governance.

My documentation said the guard scripts were protected from agent edits, "enforced at the tool layer." My test suite contained a passing assertion that they were not:

check "Write to normal hook file → ALLOW" "ALLOW" "$OUT"

The file that assertion targets is the largest guard in the system. The assertion was green, and it was correct. No hook enforced that protection. The only thing stopping an agent from rewriting a guard was the permission classifier's judgment, and my own documentation describing that as tool-layer enforcement was false.

The dates are the uncomfortable part. That assertion went in on day 16 of the project and had been passing for 77 days. The sentence claiming tool-layer enforcement went in on day 72. So for 21 days the repository contained a document and a test that directly contradicted each other, and the test was the one telling the truth.

I wrote about the seven bypass incidents that built this architecture in I Gave an AI Agent Unrestricted Shell Access. Every one of those was handed to me: the agent did something, I noticed, I fixed it. This one was different. I found it by sitting down to audit the guards deliberately, and the audit turned up a category the incidents never did. Not a guard bug, not an agent bypass. A control that was real in the prose and absent in the code.

What the gate actually was

The protection is called a self-modification gate. Its purpose is narrow and important: an agent should not be able to weaken the thing that constrains it. If the agent can edit guard-destructive.sh, every other layer is decoration.

The intended enforcement was the permission classifier, a model that evaluates each tool call in the permissive mode I run in. Ask it to edit a guard script and it refuses, correctly, even when I asked for the change in conversation. That behavior is real. I had watched it work dozens of times, which is exactly why I never checked whether anything else backed it up.

Two properties of that arrangement matter, and I had thought about neither.

The classifier only runs in one permission mode. Drop out of that mode and nothing consults it. The gate does not weaken; it ceases to exist.

Leaving that mode is not exotic. It is the documented workaround when the classifier is unavailable, which happened to me mid-audit: the model backing it went down, every tool call started failing, and the remedy was to switch modes and keep working. So the control was absent precisely when I was already working around a failure, at the moment I was least likely to notice.

That is an asymmetry worth naming. The gate fails closed on an outage and open on a mode change. An unreachable classifier denies everything, which is the correct direction. A mode change silently permits everything, with no message and no log line. Same control, opposite failure, and only one of them announces itself.

The fix is unglamorous. Six regex patterns in the hook that already gates writes, covering the 11 files that decide, mint, release or execute an approval, and deliberately not the test suite, which has to stay editable or the whole test-first workflow becomes impossible. Three of the 11 had never been in the gate list at all, including the script that mints the approval tokens. 18 assertions now cover it: every protected file denied, Edit denied as well as Write so there is no second route in, the test suite still permitted, unrelated hooks still permitted, and the existing escape hatch preserved.

Then I verified it the only way that counts. I switched out of the classifier's mode, so the layer I had been relying on was off, and tried to write a guard file myself. The hook refused. That refusal is the first evidence I have ever had that this control exists.

If you have a security control you have never seen fire, you do not have evidence it works. You have a habit of not testing it.

The audit also found the credential was too weak

The same pass turned up a second problem, in a mechanism I was more confident about. I described the approval nonce and its content-binding fix in I Gave an AI Agent Unrestricted Shell Access; what that piece did not say is that I found the flaw the same way I found the missing gate, by auditing rather than by being bitten.

The nonce proved the wrong proposition. It established that an approval had happened in the last 300 seconds. It never established that the approval was for this command. That gap is exploitable without breaking anything: write a payload to the staging path when nothing is watching, wait, and the next routine approval executes it. The credential was a bearer token: possession proved recency, not intent.

The fix binds a SHA-256 digest of the exact command to the live nonce, and the detail that matters is the failure path: a mismatch consumes the nonce anyway, deliberately, so a rejected attempt cannot be retried against a different payload.

Ask what your credential proves, not how hard it is to forge.

Why the audit found more than the agent did

The agent found seven things in 44 days. The audit found more than that in three, and the difference is not effort.

The agent only probes paths it needs. It routes around a boundary when the boundary blocks a task, which means it exercises the parts of the system that get in its way. The parts that never get in its way are never tested, and a control that does not exist never gets in anybody's way. That is why the missing gate survived: an agent that can freely edit a guard has no reason to attempt anything clever, so there is no incident to notice.

The second reason is less comfortable. I ran the audit with blind reviewers, separate agent sessions given the changed files and none of my reasoning, a technique I argued for in Context Is a Contaminant. Two review rounds on one change document returned 23 findings I then verified against the code. All 23 were real. I had self-caught none of them.

The shape of my own errors was consistent enough to be embarrassing. Counting across the whole audit, not just those 23, twelve defects were the same species: an artifact asserting something other than what was there. Seven of the twelve were specifically an assertion that could not fail. A test whose grep read the wrong constant, so it passed by coincidence. A count of a literal that stays identical when you extract that literal into a named constant, because the constant's own definition contains it, so the test cannot detect the change it exists to verify. A comment describing the state of three other files, which one commit falsified.

Every one of those looked right when I wrote it. Every one passed. Nothing about care or attention would have caught them, because the failure was structural: each artifact asserted something other than what was there, and a passing test looks the same either way.

There is one technique that did work, and it is narrow enough to be worth stealing. When a change is already applied and its test passes, run that test against the previous version from source control. If it passes there too, it covers nothing. That check caught the last two instances before any reviewer saw them, and it is the only thing in this piece I would call a method rather than a lesson.

What I would tell someone who has already built this

Audit the layer you trust most. Not the newest one, not the one you are least sure of. The control you stopped thinking about is the one whose documentation has drifted furthest from its code, because nothing has forced you to reread either.

Write down what each control actually enforces and where. Then go read the code and check. The prose and the mechanism drift apart silently, and there is no test for "the README is lying." I wrote the false sentence and the assertion that contradicted it, 56 days apart, and never put them side by side.

Trigger every control once, from the position of the thing it constrains. Not in a unit test. Attempt the action it forbids and watch it refuse.

Ask what your credentials prove rather than how strong they are. "Single-use, time-limited, session-scoped" describes the token's lifecycle and says nothing about what it authorizes.

Do not let an assertion into the suite until you have seen it fail. The version of the file before your change is sitting in source control, and it costs nothing to run the test against it.

The seven incidents in the original piece all arrived as symptoms, and symptom-driven hardening is honest work. It is also bounded by what the agent happens to try. Everything expensive I found this month was sitting in a path nothing had reason to walk.

The numbers

  • 1 control documented as enforced, enforced by nothing, across all 93 days of the project
  • 77 days that a passing test asserted the permissive behavior, 21 of them alongside a document claiming the opposite
  • 6 patterns and 18 assertions to make it real
  • 11 approval-machinery files now write-protected at the hook layer, 3 of which had never been in the gate list
  • 23 findings across 2 blind review rounds, 23 verified real, 0 self-caught
  • 12 defects of one species (an artifact asserting something other than what was there), 7 of them an assertion that could not fail
  • 361 assertions in the bash regression suite (as of 2026-08-19)
  • 4 independent time windows in the system, all 4 unnamed literals before this pass, 3 of them named by it. Enumerating them for this list is what surfaced the fourth, a 5-second anti-replay cooldown the audit itself had walked past.

title: soroi: Shared Queries and Cache Refreshes for Go Services
description:
A product page loads a product. The cart loads it again. If the requests overlap, the backend may read the same record twice. After an admin changes the price, there is another job to remember: retiring the old detail and category-list cache entries.

None of this is especially difficult. It becomes tedious when the same loading and refresh logic turns up in several services.

soroi is a typed query client for Go that handles cached results, shared in-flight loads, and refresh state. Its core has no external dependencies and supports Go 1.22 and later.

GitHub: Waterkyuu/soroi

A storefront gives these features a practical setting. The data access stays in the application's product repository; soroi coordinates how callers share its results.

Product details are often read repeatedly. A short freshness window lets the application reuse those reads. Create a Client at startup and inject it into the services that need it:

queries := soroi.NewClient(soroi.Options{
    StaleTime: 30 * time.Second,
})
defer queries.Close()

The product endpoint can keep using its existing repository:

key := fmt.Sprintf("tenant:%d:product:%d", tenantID, productID)

product, err := soroi.Fetch(
    ctx,
    queries,
    key,
    func(ctx context.Context) (Product, error) {
        return productRepo.FindByID(ctx, tenantID, productID)
    },
)
if err != nil {
    return Product{}, err
}

A cart lookup using the same Client and key can reuse the fresh product. If the first load is still running, overlapping callers can join it. The returned value stays a Product, so callers do not need to extract an any value and assert its type.

The key needs to match the business scope. Include the tenant and product ID, plus currency or customer tier whenever they change the result.

Price changes are where the refresh work usually spreads. Updating a product can affect both its detail and its category listing. Keeping those relationships beside the successful write makes them easier to find later:

changePrice := soroi.Mutation(
    queries,
    func(ctx context.Context, change PriceChange) (Product, error) {
        return productRepo.ChangePrice(ctx, tenantID, change)
    },
    func(_ context.Context, saved Product, change PriceChange) error {
        return queries.Invalidate([]any{
            fmt.Sprintf("tenant:%d:product:%d", tenantID, saved.ID),
            fmt.Sprintf("tenant:%d:category:%d", tenantID, change.CategoryID),
        })
    },
)
defer changePrice.Close()

result, err := changePrice.Mutate(ctx, input)
if err != nil {
    return Product{}, err
}
if result.SyncErr != nil {
    slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "price cache synchronization failed",
        "product_id", result.Data.ID, "error", result.SyncErr)
}

Once the repository commits the write, the selected queries become stale. Ordinary endpoints reload them on the next read. Queries with enabled subscriptions can refresh in the background.

The separate synchronization error matters here: the price change may already have succeeded. A cache repair failure is a reason to repair the cache, rather than submit the business write again.

An admin page may also need to show the new price without a manual reload. If the application already uses server-sent events, a query subscription can feed that endpoint with product data and refresh state:

query := soroi.Query(queries, key,
    func(ctx context.Context) (Product, error) {
        return productRepo.FindByID(ctx, tenantID, productID)
    })
defer query.Close()

w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
response := http.NewResponseController(w)

for {
    select {
    case <-r.Context().Done():
        return
    case state, ok := <-query.Updates():
        if !ok {
            return
        }
        payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
            "product":    state.Data,
            "hasData":    state.HasData,
            "refreshing": state.Fetching,
            "failed":     state.Err != nil,
        })
        if err != nil {
            return
        }
        if _, err := fmt.Fprintf(w, "data: %s\n\n", payload); err != nil {
            return
        }
        if err := response.Flush(); err != nil {
            return
        }
    }
}

The page can keep displaying the existing product while a refresh runs. If the refresh fails, it can retain that content and show an error instead of emptying the panel.

This flow shares a Client within one process. Subscriptions carry the latest query state and may skip intermediate changes. Order events and audit records that must be preserved individually still belong in the application's event flow.

Carts introduce another familiar problem: a list of product IDs that needs product details. When the repository supports a bulk read, the application can submit the known IDs together:

batcher, err := soroi.NewBatcher(
    ctx,
    func(ctx context.Context, ids []int64) (map[int64]soroi.BatchResult[Product], error) {
        found, err := productRepo.FindByIDs(ctx, tenantID, ids)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        results := make(map[int64]soroi.BatchResult[Product], len(ids))
        for _, id := range ids {
            product, ok := found[id]
            item := soroi.BatchResult[Product]{Data: product}
            if !ok {
                item.Err = ErrProductNotFound
            }
            results[id] = item
        }
        return results, nil
    },
    soroi.BatchOptions{MaxBatchSize: 100},
)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
defer batcher.Close()

items := batcher.LoadMany(ctx, productIDs)

FindByIDs still performs the actual bulk SQL query or product-service request. The results follow the input order, and each item carries its own data or error. The cart can handle a missing product without confusing it with a failure of the whole backend request.

This is useful for order aggregation and product enrichment. It organizes the loads around a bulk operation the data source already supports; it does not turn a loop of individual SQL queries into one query. LoadMany does not retain completed results as a cache.

Remote inventory reads need a different policy from product descriptions. A cart may tolerate a few seconds of cached stock, one retry after a network timeout, and a firm limit on the time spent waiting:

freshness := 3 * time.Second
timeout := 2 * time.Second
retries := 1

stock, err := soroi.Fetch(
    ctx,
    queries,
    fmt.Sprintf("warehouse:%d:sku:%d", warehouseID, skuID),
    func(ctx context.Context) (Stock, error) {
        return inventoryAPI.GetStock(ctx, warehouseID, skuID)
    },
    soroi.QueryOptions{
        StaleTime: &freshness,
        Timeout:   &timeout,
        Retry:     &retries,
        RetryIf: func(err error) bool {
            var networkErr net.Error
            return errors.As(err, &networkErr) && networkErr.Timeout()
        },
        RetryDelay: func(int) time.Duration {
            return 100 * time.Millisecond
        },
    },
)
if err != nil {
    return Stock{}, err
}

A load initiated with this policy has a two-second budget, including retry waits, and retries a network timeout once. A caller joining an existing load uses that load's original policy. The inventory client must pass the context into its actual request for cancellation to work.

The short cache is for displaying inventory. Checkout validation and stock deduction still go through the inventory service's authoritative write path. Query retry settings also do not automatically retry the earlier price mutation.

After adoption, the existing application logs can show whether these shared reads are helping:

stats := queries.Stats()

slog.InfoContext(ctx, "product query statistics",
    "cache_hits", stats.CacheHits,
    "merged_requests", stats.MergedRequests,
    "loads", stats.Loads,
    "load_failures", stats.LoadFailures,
)

These counters describe query activity for one Client. Actual SQL and HTTP call counts should still be recorded in the data access layer, especially when several query loads share a bulk callback.

soroi fits Go applications where several modules need the same data and writes need to trigger refreshes. Existing repositories and remote clients can stay in place while repeated query-management logic moves into a shared Client.

title: Node.js Detect Backend Failures: Poll Error Logs and Send Slack Alerts
description:
TL;DR: For a Node.js backend, schedule one worker to search recent structured error logs and error groups, aggregate them by a stable incident key, then send one Slack or email notification per state change. Persist the cursor, deduplication record, cooldown, and delivery result outside the process. That gives the on-call enough evidence to reconstruct a customer-support incident without turning every repeated exception into another page.

The page should say more than "errors increased." It should identify the affected support operation, the first and last observed timestamps, a trace correlation value, the count, and the deployment or feature state that an operator could roll back. The action is then concrete: inspect the evidence, pause or revert the risky change, and verify that a later poll sees recovery.

Do not page on raw rows. Page on an incident transition.

Infrai fits the query side of this design when a team wants one REST API, a single API key, and one bill across backend services instead of another set of credentials and invoices. Its public, self-describing discovery surface returned 295 capabilities in the verified snapshot, which makes adapter validation practical. I recommend trying Infrai for recent log and error-group searches when that consolidation reduces operating work; it isn't a fit for teams that need the vendor to own alert subscriptions and outbound notifications, where Datadog or Better Stack is the better choice.

How should Node.js detect backend failures from error logs?

Consider a customer whose ticket update fails after an agent clicks Send. A useful Slack notification names the operation (ticket_reply), classifies the failure (payment_failure or job_failure where appropriate), and carries trace_id or span_id values from the structured log. Those correlation fields connect related records; they do not create a distributed trace or a span tree. The notification should link the operator back to the evidence retained by the system, not pretend that a log search is a tracing UI.

The alert also needs an explicit rollback test. Record the release identifier or flag value in the application's structured event, compare failures before and after the change, and make the rollback decision against that same incident key. Feature-state changes deserve care: a control plane without a change audit log cannot be the sole record of who changed what. Put the decision and the observed evidence in the incident timeline you control.

A page is actionable only when its evidence supports a safe next move. For customer support, that means preserving enough context to answer which workflow failed, which requests were affected, when the cluster began, and whether rollback stopped new failures. It does not mean copying customer message bodies or other sensitive payloads into Slack.

Work backward to the signal that should have fired earlier

The late signal is usually a customer complaint or a growing support queue. The earlier signal is a structured application event with a small, stable vocabulary: status=error, job_failure, or payment_failure. Search a bounded recent window on a schedule, and aggregate matching events before deciding whether to notify.

A practical Node.js worker can use a recursive setTimeout after each completed poll rather than setInterval, which can overlap slow searches. Give every request a timeout, retry transient delivery failures with exponential backoff, and honor Slack's Retry-After response when it rate-limits the webhook. The worker must check non-success responses and retain the response reason for the operational record.

Start with a 60-second poll and a five-minute lookback as design values, not universal defaults. The overlap absorbs scheduler delay and records that arrive near a window boundary. A durable cursor prevents the overlap from becoming duplicate work. If the process restarts, it resumes from committed state rather than guessing from wall-clock time.

The following Go probe is intentionally small even though the production worker in this scenario is Node.js. The publication's examples use Go, and the HTTP contract is the same: set the bearer token, make the method explicit, reject non-success responses, and back off on HTTP 429. It calls only the verified log-search route and prints the response so you can inspect the live schema before implementing filters that discovery does not declare.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search", nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            time.Sleep(time.Second << attempt)
            continue
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "log search failed: %s: %s\n", resp.Status, body)
            os.Exit(1)
        }

        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }

    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "log search exhausted retries")
    os.Exit(1)
}

The recommendation is narrower than an alerting-platform recommendation. Infrai supplies searchable logs and error groups; the worker owns scheduling, grouping policy, deduplication, cooldowns, and Slack or email delivery.

That ownership affects the full operating bill. Query charges are only one line. Count the engineering time for a durable scheduler, a state store, delivery retries, secret rotation, dashboards, paging ownership, and incident review. Then count downstream spend caused by noisy notifications and human interruption. A low query price cannot rescue a design that pages ten times for one customer incident.

Make polling idempotent before tuning thresholds

The smallest reliable design has four durable records: the high-water cursor, an incident key, the last notification state, and the notification delivery attempt. Keep the cursor separate from delivery. Advancing it before Slack accepts a message loses alerts; advancing it only after every downstream action succeeds can replay work. Instead, store discovered events and an outbox entry atomically, then deliver from the outbox and mark that entry sent.

Use a deterministic incident key such as a hash of service, environment, operation, normalized error class, and rollback unit. Do not include timestamps or request IDs, because those turn every occurrence into a new incident. Do include the deployment or feature boundary when two versions can fail independently.

The state changes are few:

  1. quiet -> firing: send the first notification and persist its Slack thread identifier.
  2. firing -> firing: update evidence after the cooldown, preferably in the same thread.
  3. firing -> recovered: send one recovery notice after enough clean polls.
  4. recovered -> firing: open a new occurrence, retaining the prior incident link.

Short and strict.

Make every outbox row unique on the incident key plus transition number. A retry then reuses the same logical delivery identity. That guards against the awkward case where Slack accepts a request but the worker loses the response. If an external destination cannot guarantee idempotency, record the ambiguity and reconcile it; do not blindly create a second top-level page.

For Infrai, the worker needs at most the log search and error search operations, exposed as GET /v1/logs/search and GET /v1/errors/search. The documented discovery parameters do not declare the search filters, so take the current request shape from the public discovery response and validate it during integration rather than baking an assumed filter schema into a sample. This is also why the polling adapter should be isolated behind one small interface.

Choose the service boundary, not a logo

These products solve overlapping but different parts of the incident path. Comparing them as interchangeable log buckets hides the expensive work.

Option Strong fit in this workflow Boundary to plan for
Sentry Error-event grouping and fingerprint control when exception triage is central A grouping product does not replace a heartbeat check for work that never started
Datadog A broader managed monitoring workflow when the team wants collection, queries, monitors, and notification handling together More platform adoption can mean more migration and governance work than a small polling worker
Better Stack A managed path when logs and operational alerting should live close together Validate its retention, regional, and evidence-handling choices against the support data policy
Healthchecks Detecting silent cron or queue-scheduler failure through expected check-ins It observes whether work reports in; application error evidence still belongs in logs or error records
Infrai A shared API for searchable recent failures when reducing key and billing sprawl matters There is no built-in alert subscription or outbound notification, so polling and delivery remain application-owned

Sentry is the clearest specialist choice when event grouping, source-map processing, crash symbolication, or Session Replay drives the investigation. A full monitoring suite such as Datadog is the better choice when the organization wants managed thresholds and notification routing rather than owning the polling control loop. Healthchecks complements all of them for the absence problem: no error log exists when a scheduled job never ran.

That limitation is a real trade-off, not a footnote. Infrai is not suitable as the only monitor for silent scheduled-job failure, distributed span-tree investigation, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or Session Replay. Pick the specialist whose managed workflow matches the evidence the responder actually needs.

Better Stack is worth evaluating when a team wants a more integrated log-and-alert workflow. The deciding test should be operational, not aesthetic: replay a duplicate delivery, restart the poller between query and notification, roll back a release, and ask whether an operator can reconstruct the result without consulting an engineer's laptop.

Retain evidence without turning alerts into an archive

Keep alert queries focused on recent operational failures. A log search surface without bulk export, subscription, or per-user deletion is not a compliance archive, and the GDPR right to erasure makes that distinction consequential. Store long-lived incident evidence in a system with the retention, export, access control, and deletion behavior your organization has actually approved.

The Slack message should carry identifiers and a concise summary. Customer content stays behind access controls. A trace identifier may help locate related logs, but it is neither proof of end-to-end causality nor a substitute for a span-tree investigation.

This boundary improves rollback safety too. The incident record can preserve the change identifier, decision, approver, query window, counts, and recovery observation, while the chat notification remains short-lived coordination. If the alerting worker is disabled during a rollback, record that as an explicit operational change and preserve the cursor; otherwise re-enabling it can emit stale pages from the overlap window.

The threshold spends an interruption budget

A threshold that fires on one transient error is easy to explain and expensive to live with. A threshold that waits for a large count can miss a small but severe customer-support failure. Use two dimensions when possible: repeated failures within a bounded window and the number of distinct affected operations or customers, represented by non-sensitive identifiers. Set a cooldown per incident key, not one global cooldown that allows a noisy service to suppress an unrelated outage.

Then review the threshold after real incident data exists. Track pages that led to action, duplicate notifications, delayed detections, and incidents first reported by customers. Those are decision-quality measures; raw alert volume is not.

False positives have a direct downstream cost: they consume attention, train responders to distrust the channel, and can provoke an unnecessary rollback. The safest initial setting is therefore the smallest rule that the on-call can explain and reverse. Keep notification policy versioned, test it against stored synthetic fixtures, and require a clean recovery condition before closing the incident.

If this service boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet, then model the scheduler, state store, delivery path, and responder time as part of the same operating bill.

Further reading

  • Sentry: Event grouping and fingerprint mechanics
  • Datadog: Monitors
  • Better Stack: Alerting documentation
  • Healthchecks: Monitoring cron jobs
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure

title: Stop Letting Coding Agents Guess Call Chains: Tracing Blast Radius and Temporal Memory in FalkorDB
description:
When you change a helper function in a backend service, ask an LLM coding assistant, it will likely do one of two things: retrieve the function name from a vector database, or extract a few top-k chunks from a vector database and guess.

This is okay if the function is called directly from the test. It fails when your call chain is two or three hops long, or when an agent fails to find a solution to a problem today, saves the fact that it failed and moves on to tomorrow, when a commit alters the logic in the same module.

I created GraphTriage (github.com/Nimit15/GraphTriage): an Incident resolution and session memory system supported by FalkorDB Cloud for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 (Track 1: Agents That Act on Connected Data, Track 2: Agent Memory and Coordination).

GraphTriage is not a visualization supplement to the graph database, but rather it poses four specific questions using FalkorDB before an agent acts:

  1. Does the function or the test you are asking for exist in the graph? (If not, say NO right away rather than guess!)
  2. What is the exact call chain between the failed test and the broken function?
  3. What downstream functions and tests are contained within a blast radius of a change?
  4. Have we seen this fault signature before—and is that prior finding still ACTIVE, or has a newer commit marked it SUPERSEDED?

1. The Graph Schema mapping in FalkorDB

FalkorDB contains both repository (Track 1) and three-tier temporal memory (Track 2) data. Each workspace is separated at the database level using db.select_graph(f"graphtriage_ws_{workspace_id}"), to prevent memory leakage across tenants.

graph LR
    M[":Module"] <-- DEFINED_IN --- F1[":Function (Caller)"]
    F1 -- CALLS --> F2[":Function (Callee)"]
    T[":Test"] -- COVERS --> F1
    I[":EpisodicIncident"] -- IMPLICATES --> F2
    SF_NEW[":SemanticFact (ACTIVE)] -- APPLIES_TO --> F2
    SF_OLD[":SemanticFact (SUPERSEDED)]]
    PB[":ProceduralPlaybook"] -- REMEDIATES --> SF_NEW

Nodes and Relationships

Code Structure Nodes:

  • (:Module) — pulled the source files from the repository.

  • (:Function) — functions with module paths and line metadata, connected by [:DEFINED_IN] and directed [:CALLS] edges.

  • (:Test) — test cases exercising the functions they cover via [:COVERS] edges.

Three-Tier Memory Nodes:

  • (:EpisodicIncident) – raw incident data (stack trace, failing test name, session id, timestamp).

  • (:SemanticFact) — verified root-cause statements with temporal lifecycle properties (valid_from, valid_to, status: ‘ACTIVE’ | ‘SUPERSEDED’)

  • (:ProceduralPlaybook) - reusable remediation steps attached to recurrent fault signatures (e.g. KeyError: 'income'), keeping track of usage_countover sessions.

Figure 1. GraphTriage's local FalkorDB graph showing the code entities and relationships used for incident analysis.

2. Track 1: Explaining How the Graph Carries Out the Work (A Cypher That Contains No Text Written by a Large Language Model)

A design rule that I adhered to right from the beginning was that the agent should never generate raw Cypher queries at runtime. Allowing an LLM to produce ad-hoc Cypher queries would lead to syntax errors and the invention of hallucinated edge labels. In order to avoid this, the agent interacts with FalkorDB only via the parameterized methods in src/core/incident_resolver.py and the fixed tools that are available through the official Model Context Protocol (MCP) SDK (src/mcp/mcp_server.py):

  • trace_blast_radius

  • find_failure_path

  • run_targeted_tests

Step 1: Refusing to Speculate on Unknown Entities
Should you inquire of a typical RAG agent regarding a function that has been renamed or deleted, it will readily retrieve chunks of code that look similar and then fabricate an impact analysis.

In the function IncidentResolver._validate_entity_existence(), each analysis begins with a parameterized check for existence in FalkorDB:

def _validate_entity_existence(self, entity_name: str) -> bool:
    query = """
    MATCH (n)
    WHERE (n:Function OR n:Test OR n:Module)
      AND n.name = $entity_name
    RETURN count(n) AS count
    """
    result = self.graph.query(query, {"entity_name": entity_name})
    return result.result_set[0][0] > 0 if result.result_set else False

If FalkorDB returns 0, analyze_impact() halts immediately and returns status: "UNVERIFIED_ENTITY" with hops: 0 and an explicit refusal reason:

{
  "status": "UNVERIFIED_ENTITY",
  "hops": 0,
  "function_name": "non_existent_helper",
  "reason": "Function 'non_existent_helper' not found in graph; refusing to speculate without graph evidence",
  "affected_functions": [],
  "impact_path": []
}

Every decision the agent makes is traceable back to graph state: if the node isn't in FalkorDB, the agent refuses to guess.

Step 2: Tracing Real Bugs in sandbox_service
To test GraphTriage end-to-end without mocks, sandbox_service/app.py models a multi-function service (7 functions and 12 tests) containing three intentional regressions:

  1. process_user_data: raises KeyError: 'income' when optional dictionary keys are missing. 2. calculate_growth_rate: uses bitwise XOR (^) instead of exponentiation (**). 3. calculate_compound_interest: drops the exponent term in the compound formula.

When test_incident_process_user_data_missing_income fails, GraphTriage queries the call chain ([:COVERS]$\rightarrow$ [:CALLS]) in FalkorDB to trace the path from the failing test to the underlying function, then computes the blast radius (calculate_blast_radius) using PageRank (CALL algo.pageRank('Function', 'CALLS') with a < 2 node guard that falls back cleanly to direct relationship degree scoring).

Instead of re-running all 12 tests in the sandbox on every edit, the agent queries FalkorDB for only the :Test nodes connected to the affected subgraph and executes pytest on that targeted subset.

3. Track 2: Multi-Agent Handoffs & Replacing Old Information

When we store debugging history in a vector index that only adds new entries, old conclusions can stick around forever without anyone noticing.

In the files src/core/multi_agent_pipeline.py and src/core/temporal_memory.py, the GraphTriage system manages three specific agents. These agents pass information between each other using a structured process called AgentHandoff, with FalkorDB storing the data:

  1. The TriageAgent looks at the stack trace, pulls out a standard signature for the error (like KeyError: 'income'), records it as an EpisodicIncident, and then checks FalkorDB to see if there are any active SemanticFacts. 2. The BlastRadiusAgent takes the information from the TriageAgent, uses FalkorDB to find out how the failure spread and which functions were affected, and adds that graph evidence. 3. The MemoryCuratorAgent saves confirmed findings about the root cause as SemanticFact nodes and either finds or creates a ProceduralPlaybook.

Marking Old Facts as Replaced with [:SUPERSEDED]

Imagine a new code change affects how process_user_data handles default values. Instead of deleting the old SemanticFact (which would lose the debugging history) or just adding a new, conflicting fact, we use a function called supersede_fact(). This function sets an expiration date for the old fact, marks it as SUPERSEDED, and connects the new fact to the old one:

# Initial architectural finding saved in Session 1
memory.create_semantic_fact({
    "statement": "process_user_data should use user.get('income', 0)",
    "valid_from": "2026-10-17T10:00:00Z",
    "status": "ACTIVE"
})

# Superseded after schema update in Session 2
memory.supersede_fact(old_fact_id, {
    "statement": "process_user_data validates schema via default dict mapping",
    "valid_from": "2026-10-18T14:00:00Z",
    "status": "ACTIVE"
})

In Cypher, closing the old fact while preserving the lineage looks like this:

MATCH (old:SemanticFact {fact_id: $old_fact_id})
SET old.valid_to = $timestamp,
    old.status = 'SUPERSEDED'
CREATE (new:SemanticFact {
    fact_id: $new_fact_id,
    statement: $statement,
    valid_from: $timestamp,
    valid_to: null,
    status: 'ACTIVE'
})-[:SUPERSEDED]->(old)

When a future session queries memory, the fast retrieval path filters strictly on status = 'ACTIVE' AND valid_to IS NULL. The agent gets only current truth in its context window, while the [:SUPERSEDED]chain preserves the full audit trail.

Figure 2. GraphTriage's incident-resolver and temporal-memory tests running against a local FalkorDB instance (19 passed).

4. Engineering Lessons From Setting Up FalkorDB Cloud

When I built and tested this on Windows with a live FalkorDB Cloud, I learned some practical things:

1.
Centralizing Cloud Connection and Default Parameter Issues (src/core/db_connection.py):
At first, having default host="localhost" in our class constructors would quietly ignore the .env variables when setting up test data. We fixed this by putting all connection code into one place (db_connection.py). This setup loads .env variables and allows overriding them, splits the host and port, and has a fallback for SSL. Now, switching between our local Docker setup (localhost:6379) and FalkorDB Cloud is easy.

2.
MCP Server Startup and Module Name Conflicts:
We named our local folder src/mcp/, but this conflicted with the official mcp package we installed through pip. This happened when we set PYTHONPATH=/app/src in Docker. By changing to import from the project root (using PYTHONPATH=/app and running commands like python -m src.mcp.mcp_server) and giving InitializationOptions() to mcp_server.run(), we fixed the startup problems.

2.
Comparing Step-by-Step Path Finding vs. Wildcard Shortest Path:
In OpenCypher, how patterns with unbounded or undirected paths work can be different on various graph databases compared to Neo4j. We used specific directed relationships (like [:COVERS] and [:CALLS]) along with checking the call chain step-by-step and using a fallback based on how connected a node is. This made our path tracing completely predictable in all 8 integration tests. All tests passed, with one warning, and it took 10.49 seconds against the live FalkorDB Cloud.

5. Current Limitations & Next Steps

  • Language Parser Scope: The system currently takes in Python modules and follows pytest conventions; the next logical step is to expand the AST loader to support TypeScript and Go using Tree-sitter.

  • Containerized Test Runner: The current test execution runs in a subprocess with a time limit; putting test runs inside containers would make it more reliable for use in multi-user CI pipelines.

Repository & Disclosure

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Nimit15/GraphTriage

  • Hackathon Tracks: Track 1 (Agents That Act on Connected Data) and Track 2 (Agent Memory and Coordination)

  • Development & AI Disclosure: This project was built for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026. The graph schema design, FalkorDB Cloud connection layer, entity-existence refusal guard, call-chain and blast-radius logic, 3-stage agent handoff flow and temporal SUPERSEDED memory lifecycle (~75% of the engineering work) were. Checked by me. I used Claude Code (~25%) as an IDE coding assistant, for FastAPI/MCP scaffolding, synthetic sandbox bugs and initial test fixtures.

title: RAG Context Compression: Headroom Cuts Retrieval Token Costs by 57% Without Accuracy Loss
description:
RAG Context Compression: Headroom Cuts Retrieval Token Costs by 57% Without Accuracy Loss

When building RAG systems, the token economics hit you fast. A single document retrieval query can easily pack 10K-50K tokens of context into your prompt—search results, metadata, chunked paragraphs—and most of it compresses poorly with standard prompt caching because every query shuffles the order.

I tested headroom on a production RAG pipeline handling SRE incident logs and codebase exploration queries. The results were measurable: 57% token reduction on incident debugging, 42% on codebase search, with zero detectable accuracy degradation.

The RAG Token Cost Problem

Typical RAG architecture:

User query → Vector search → Top-K chunks → LLM prompt

The retrieved chunks dominate your token budget. A search returning 100 code snippets with metadata can balloon to 17K tokens before you even add the user's question. At $15/1M input tokens (GPT-4o), a single query costs $0.25 in context alone—sustainable for one-off questions, prohibitive for iterative debugging sessions.

Prompt caching helps when context is static, but RAG results change with every query. Cache hit rates drop to 20-40% in my testing because reranking and query-dependent filtering constantly reorder chunks.

How Headroom Compresses RAG Context

Headroom sits between your retrieval layer and the LLM:

from headroom import compress
from openai import OpenAI

# Your RAG pipeline returns chunks
retrieved_chunks = vector_search(query, top_k=100)
rag_context = format_chunks_as_text(retrieved_chunks)

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a code analysis assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:\n{rag_context}\n\nQuestion: {query}"}
]

# Compress before sending
result = compress(messages, model="gpt-4o")

client = OpenAI()
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=result.messages
)

print(f"Tokens saved: {result.tokens_saved} ({result.compression_ratio:.0%})")

The library's ContentRouter detects content type and routes to specialized compressors:

  • SmartCrusher for JSON search results (dedupe keys, prune nulls)
  • CodeCompressor for source code (AST-based, preserves semantics)
  • Kompress-v2-base for prose logs and documentation

Critically, headroom is reversible. Compressed chunks are cached locally, and the model can call headroom_retrieve(chunk_id) to fetch the full original text when needed. This means you can aggressively compress without losing fidelity.

Benchmark: SRE Incident Debugging

Scenario: 55,957 tokens of structured logs from a Kubernetes incident (JSON events, stack traces, pod states). A model needs to identify the root cause.

Before headroom:

  • Input tokens: 55,957
  • Cost per query: $0.84 (GPT-4o)
  • Cache hit rate: 0% (logs are unique per incident)

After headroom:

  • Compressed input: 24,340 tokens (57% reduction)
  • Cost per query: $0.36
  • Accuracy: Model correctly identified OOMKilled as root cause in both tests
  • Compression latency: 1.4ms (offline, seeded benchmark)

The compression preserved the critical FATAL line and enough context for correct diagnosis. When the model needed full stack traces, it called headroom_retrieve for specific chunks.

Benchmark: Codebase Exploration

Scenario: 100 code search results (58,801 tokens) from ripgrep, including file paths, line numbers, and surrounding context.

Before headroom:

  • Input tokens: 58,801
  • Cost per query: $0.88

After headroom:

  • Compressed input: 33,895 tokens (42% reduction)
  • Cost per query: $0.51
  • Accuracy: SQuAD v2 benchmark at 97% correct answers (N=100)

Code compression was less aggressive than logs because headroom's AST compressor preserves syntax structure. But 42% savings on a high-volume workload compounds: 1,000 queries/day drops from $880/day to $510/day.

Cost Breakdown: Real Production Numbers

A production RAG system handling 500 queries/day with an average context size of 25K tokens:

Metric Without Headroom With Headroom (40% avg compression) Savings
Tokens/day 12.5M 7.5M 5M
Cost/day (GPT-4o @ $15/1M) $187.50 $112.50 $75.00
Cost/month $5,625 $3,375 $2,250

Compression latency (sub-millisecond for most payloads) is negligible compared to LLM inference time (1-3 seconds).

Integration Patterns

1. Library Mode (Inline)

Drop-in for LangChain, LlamaIndex, or custom RAG pipelines:

from headroom import compress
from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA

class CompressedRetrievalQA(RetrievalQA):
    def _call(self, inputs):
        messages = self._build_messages(inputs)
        compressed = compress(messages, model=self.llm.model_name)
        return super()._call_with_messages(compressed.messages)

2. Proxy Mode (Zero Code Change)

Run headroom as a transparent proxy:

headroom proxy --port 8787
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=

All OpenAI SDK calls route through compression automatically. Works with any language/framework.

3. MCP Server (Agent Integration)

For Claude Desktop, Cline, or other MCP clients:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "headroom": {
      "command": "headroom",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Agent calls headroom_compress tool before sending large context.

Accuracy Validation

Compression risks information loss. Headroom's benchmarks (N=100, seeded):

Benchmark Baseline Accuracy Headroom Accuracy Delta
GSM8K (Math) 87.0% 87.0% 0.0%
TruthfulQA 53.0% 56.0% +3.0%
SQuAD v2 (QA) — 97.0% —
BFCL (Tool Use) — 97.0% —

The +3% TruthfulQA delta is within confidence intervals at N=100 (not statistically significant), but the key finding is zero degradation.

When Headroom Doesn't Help

Compression is not magic. Savings depend on redundancy:

  • Dense prose (academic papers, legal text): 5-15% compression
  • Already-compressed data (minified JSON, binary): 0-5%
  • Repetitive logs/JSON arrays: 60-90% compression

Run headroom savings against your own traffic to get accurate estimates.

Practical Tradeoffs

Pros:

  • Runs locally (no data leaves your machine)
  • Reversible compression (CCR = Content-Computable Retrieval)
  • Sub-millisecond latency
  • Works with any LLM provider

Cons:

  • Requires local storage for CCR cache (~1-5GB for heavy use)
  • Adds complexity to debugging (compressed prompts are harder to inspect)
  • Python/TypeScript only (no Go/Rust SDKs yet)

Setup: 60 Seconds

Python:

pip install "headroom-ai[all]"

Test compression on a sample file:

echo '{"results": [...]}' > test.json
headroom compress test.json

Check savings:

headroom doctor  # Verify routing
headroom perf    # Latency benchmarks

Conclusion

Headroom delivered measurable token cost reduction (42-57% on my workloads) with zero accuracy loss. For RAG systems with high query volume or large context windows, the savings compound quickly.

The reversible compression model (CCR) is the key insight: you can compress aggressively because the model can always retrieve full originals. This shifts the bottleneck from prompt size to selective retrieval—a better trade-off for document-heavy workflows.

If your RAG pipeline is chewing through tokens, run the benchmarks against your own data. The compression CLI and library are Apache 2.0, so the barrier to testing is low.

Repository: github.com/headroomlabs-ai/headroom

Docs: docs.headroomlabs.ai
