title: Frontend Testing: Confidence Without Brittleness
description:
⚡ TL;DR: Test behavior, not implementation, and your suite stops breaking on every refactor. Follow the testing trophy to put effort where it pays, write component tests that survive change, and reserve end-to-end for critical flows.

Contents

  • The suite that broke on every refactor
  • The one principle that fixes most of it
  • The testing trophy: where effort should go
  • Choosing the right layer for each test
  • A component test that survives refactors
  • Behavior over implementation, in practice
  • End-to-end: the critical-flow crown
  • Common mistakes that cost hours
  • Takeaways
  • Where to go next

The suite that broke on every refactor

Here is a story you have probably lived. Your team has 600 frontend tests and a green checkmark on every pull request. Then one day you rename a prop from onSubmit to onConfirm and clean up some internal state, pure refactor, zero behavior change. Forty tests go red. They were asserting that a useState hook held a certain value, that a child got a specific prop, that a function was called with exact arguments. None of those things matter to a user. You spend the afternoon updating tests to match the new internals.

The cruel twist: a week earlier, that same 600-test suite shipped a checkout button that did nothing when clicked. The handler was wired to the wrong element. Every test passed. The suite was loud about things that did not matter and silent about the one thing that did.

That is the central tension of frontend testing. Tests coupled to how a component is built break constantly and protect nothing. Tests coupled to what the user experiences survive refactors and catch the bugs that reach production. This article is about deliberately writing the second kind.

📌 Who this is for: Frontend engineers who write tests but feel they are paying a tax without getting safety in return. You know the tools (Jest, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright) but want a model for what to test, at which layer, and what to leave alone. Comfort with React and TypeScript is assumed; the principles apply to any component framework.

The one principle that fixes most of it

Test what the user does, not how the component is built. The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they give you.

The Testing Library philosophy, paraphrased

Every decision downstream, which queries to use, what to mock, where to draw the line, falls out of this one idea. A user does not know your component uses a reducer. They click a button labeled "Add to cart" and expect the cart count to go up. So your test should find the button by its label, click it, and assert the count went up. If you can swap the reducer for a signal and the test still passes, the test was measuring the right thing.

In the real world In tech
Test-driving the car: turn the key, it starts; press the brake, it stops Behavior test: render the UI, click the button, assert what the user now sees
Opening the hood to check the exact spark-plug part number Implementation test: assert a specific hook value or internal prop name
A new model with a redesigned engine still passes the test-drive A refactored component still passes the behavior test
The part-number check fails the moment the supplier changes, even if the car drives fine The internals test fails on every refactor, even when nothing user-visible broke

Two ways to verify a car works, one survives every redesign, one breaks on a new model year.

The testing trophy: where effort should go

The old advice was a pyramid: a wide base of unit tests, fewer integration tests, a thin cap of end-to-end. For frontends, that shape underinvests in the layer where most user value, and most bugs, actually lives: components wired together. The modern shape is the testing trophy: a sliver of static checks, a modest band of pure-unit tests, a fat middle of component/integration tests, and a focused crown of end-to-end.

The testing trophy, width hints at relative volume. Cheap static checks at the base, a fat component layer in the middle, a focused E2E crown on top.

Read the trophy top to bottom as a cost gradient. Static analysis is nearly free and runs as you type, a typo or a wrong prop type is caught before a test ever executes. Unit tests cover logic with no DOM: a currency formatter, a date helper, a reducer. Component tests render real UI in a fake DOM (jsdom) and interact with it, this is where you spend most of your effort because it most resembles real use while staying fast. End-to-end drives a real browser through a whole flow; slow and occasionally flaky, so reserve it for the handful of journeys that must never break.

  1. Let the type checker and linter run first: tsc --noEmit and ESLint catch a whole class of bugs, undefined props, unhandled null, wrong shapes, with zero test code. Treat them as the base of the trophy and run them in CI on every push.
  2. Unit-test the logic with no UI: Extract pure functions (formatting, validation, calculations) and test them directly. Fast, deterministic, no rendering. If a piece of logic is hard to unit-test, that is a hint it should be extracted from the component.
  3. Component-test the user-facing behavior: Render the component, query by what the user sees (role, label, text), interact, and assert the resulting DOM. This is your highest-leverage layer, aim most of your test count here.
  4. End-to-end the critical flows only: Pick the 5-10 journeys that, if broken, cost real money or trust, sign-in, checkout, the core create-action. Run them in a real browser with Playwright or Cypress against a deployed-like build.

Choosing the right layer for each test

When you are unsure where a test belongs, match the thing you are protecting against the layer that catches it most cheaply. Push tests down the trophy whenever a cheaper layer can catch the same bug, but never so far down that you stop testing real behavior.

Test type What it catches Cost / speed When to reach for it
Static (TS, lint) Type errors, undefined props, dead code, unsafe access Free, instant Always on, the default safety net for every change
Unit Wrong logic in pure functions, edge cases in helpers and reducers Very cheap, milliseconds Non-trivial logic you can isolate from the DOM
Component Broken rendering, wiring, conditional UI, accessibility of interactions Cheap, fast (jsdom) The default for anything a user sees or clicks, most of your suite
End-to-end Whole-flow breakage: routing, real network, auth, cross-page state Expensive, seconds, occasionally flaky A small set of business-critical journeys only

Pick the cheapest layer that still catches the bug you care about.

A component test that survives refactors

Here is a component test the right way: it renders the real component, finds elements the way a user (or a screen reader) would, by role and text, never by class name or test-id-on-everything, interacts, and asserts the visible outcome. Notice there is not a single reference to internal state, hook names, or child props.

AddToCart.test.tsx

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { AddToCart } from "./AddToCart";

test("adds an item and reflects it in the cart count", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<AddToCart productName="Wireless Mouse" price={29} />);

  // Query the way a user perceives the UI: by role + accessible name.
  const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /add to cart/i });
  expect(screen.getByText(/cart: 0 items/i)).toBeInTheDocument();

  await user.click(button);

  // Assert the user-visible outcome, not internal state.
  expect(screen.getByText(/cart: 1 item/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
  expect(
    screen.getByRole("status", { name: /added wireless mouse/i })
  ).toBeInTheDocument();
});

test("disables the button while a request is in flight", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<AddToCart productName="Wireless Mouse" price={29} />);

  const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /add to cart/i });
  await user.click(button);

  // The user sees a disabled, busy button, we never inspect a loading flag.
  expect(button).toBeDisabled();
});

Two things make this test durable. First, queries by role and accessible name mean the test only passes if the markup is actually accessible, a free accessibility check baked into every test. Second, userEvent simulates real interaction (focus, key events, the works) rather than firing a synthetic click, so you exercise the same path a person would. Rename the internal state, swap the styling, move logic into a custom hook, as long as the button still says "Add to cart" and the count still updates, the test stays green.

💡 Query priority: Reach for queries in this order: getByRole (with a name), then getByLabelText / getByText, then getByPlaceholderText. Use getByTestId only as a last resort for elements with no accessible handle. If you cannot find an element by role or text, that is often a sign the markup itself is not accessible.

Behavior over implementation, in practice

The rule "test behavior, not implementation" sounds obvious until you are mid-test and tempted to peek at internals. A quick litmus test: would this assertion break if I refactored the component without changing what the user sees or does? If yes, you are testing implementation. Asserting a useState value, that a specific function was called, or that a child received a named prop, all break on refactor and protect nothing.

Implementation tests also lie in the dangerous direction. A test that checks setLoading(true) was called will pass even if the spinner never actually renders because of a CSS bug or a missing conditional. A behavior test that asserts the spinner is visible catches that. Always assert the outcome the user perceives, not the mechanism you hope produces it.

Mocking the network, at the boundary, not inside

Components fetch data, and tests should not hit a real server. The brittle approach is to mock your fetch wrapper or stub a hook's return value, that couples the test to your data-fetching internals. The durable approach is to intercept at the network boundary with a tool like MSW (Mock Service Worker). You declare what the endpoint returns; your component does its real fetching, parsing, and error handling against that fake server. Swap fetch for axios for React Query and the test does not care.

ProductList.test.tsx

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
import { ProductList } from "./ProductList";

const server = setupServer(
  http.get("/api/products", () =>
    HttpResponse.json([{ id: "1", name: "Wireless Mouse", price: 29 }])
  )
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test("renders products from the API", async () => {
  render(<ProductList />);
  // The component does its real fetch; we wait for the user-visible result.
  expect(await screen.findByText("Wireless Mouse")).toBeInTheDocument();
});

test("shows an error state when the API fails", async () => {
  // Override just this test's response to exercise the error path.
  server.use(
    http.get("/api/products", () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 }))
  );
  render(<ProductList />);
  expect(
    await screen.findByText(/couldn't load products/i)
  ).toBeInTheDocument();
});

The same MSW handlers can back your component tests and your Playwright end-to-end runs, and even power local development with a mock backend. One source of fake truth, reused everywhere, far better than a thicket of per-test jest.mock calls.

End-to-end: the critical-flow crown

Component tests run in jsdom, a simulated DOM with no real layout, no real browser quirks, no real navigation. For the journeys that absolutely cannot break, you want a real browser. Playwright (and Cypress) drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through a complete flow: load the page, fill the form, click through, assert what renders. It catches things component tests structurally cannot, broken routing, a real network round-trip, auth redirects, a button hidden behind a z-index bug.

checkout.spec.ts

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("a user can complete checkout", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/products");

  // Same philosophy as component tests: locate by role and text.
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /add to cart/i }).first().click();
  await page.getByRole("link", { name: /view cart/i }).click();
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /checkout/i }).click();

  await page.getByLabel(/card number/i).fill("4242 4242 4242 4242");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: /pay now/i }).click();

  // Assert the user-visible success outcome.
  await expect(
    page.getByRole("heading", { name: /order confirmed/i })
  ).toBeVisible();
});

Notice the queries look almost identical to the component test, by role and accessible name. That consistency is the payoff of the behavior-first philosophy: the same mental model scales from a single component up to a full browser flow. Keep this layer small. A handful of E2E tests for your money-making journeys gives enormous confidence; a hundred of them gives you a slow, flaky pipeline nobody trusts.

Common mistakes that cost hours

  1. Testing implementation details. Asserting hook values, internal state, or that a function was called with exact args. These break on every refactor and pass even when the UI is visibly broken. Assert what the user sees instead.
  2. Snapshot overuse. A wall of auto-generated snapshots becomes noise: people update them blindly when they go red, so they catch nothing and just nag. Reserve snapshots for small, stable, intentional outputs, and review every diff.
  3. No end-to-end for critical flows. Component tests in jsdom cannot catch broken routing, real auth, or a button buried under an overlay. If sign-in or checkout breaking would be a disaster, it needs at least one real-browser test.
  4. Over-mocking. Mock the network boundary, not your own modules. When you stub the very code under test (the fetch wrapper, the hook, the child component), you are testing your mocks, not your app, green tests, broken product.
  5. Querying by class or deep test-ids. container.querySelector('.btn-primary') couples tests to styling and bypasses accessibility. Prefer role and text; the test doubles as an a11y check.
  6. Chasing 100% coverage. Coverage measures lines executed, not behavior verified. Test the paths that matter, error states, edge cases, the happy path, and let trivial getters go untested.

Takeaways

The whole article in seven lines

  • Test what the user does, not how the component is built, that one rule prevents most brittleness.
  • Follow the testing trophy: a little static, some unit, a fat layer of component tests, a focused crown of E2E.
  • Static checks (TypeScript, ESLint) are the cheapest layer, let them catch a whole class of bugs for free.
  • Query by role, label, and text; touch internals never. Accessible markup falls out for free.
  • Mock at the network boundary (MSW), not inside your own modules, reuse the handlers across unit, component, and E2E.
  • Reserve end-to-end for the few money-making journeys; keep that layer small to keep it trustworthy.
  • A green suite that breaks on refactors and misses real bugs is worse than fewer, behavior-focused tests.

Where to go next

Testing rides on top of how your components are structured and how your state flows. Well-factored components with clear inputs and accessible markup are dramatically easier to test, so the testing payoff is also an architecture payoff.

  • Component Architecture & Design Systems, composable, accessible components are the ones that test cleanly by role and text.
  • State Management in Frontend Apps, predictable state flow is what makes behavior assertions stable across refactors.
  • See how this fits the broader role on the Frontend Engineer path.

Originally published on TheSimplifiedTech, where this guide is interactive, with in-browser terminal labs and diagrams. Learn cloud and DevOps by doing, no videos.

title: Rust Backend Services: From Cargo Project to Running Container
description:
Rust is a good fit for backend services that must stay small, predictable, and fast. Its compiler catches a large class of errors before code runs, and a release binary has few runtime dependencies. Those strengths come with a cost: the edit-compile-run loop is slower than in most interpreted stacks, and a service that runs alongside others needs the same plumbing as any other service. This article walks through a practical Rust HTTP service with axum, from the project layout to the container image, and then looks at what changes once it lives in a multi-service system.

Choosing the framework

Rust has several web frameworks. axum is built on tokio and the tower ecosystem, and it is the one most teams reach for when they want to compose middleware and keep routing explicit. Its handlers are plain async functions, and its extractors make request parsing type-checked.

For a new service, pin the major version of the framework and the async runtime in Cargo.toml. A service that builds today with an unpinned dependency may fail next month for reasons unrelated to its own code.

A minimal service

A service needs three things before it is useful: a route that reports health, a way to read its port from the environment, and a bind address that accepts connections from outside its own process.

use axum::{routing::get, Json, Router};
use serde_json::{json, Value};

fn app() -> Router {
    Router::new().route("/health", get(health))
}

async fn health() -> Json<Value> {
    Json(json!({ "status": "ok" }))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let port = std::env::var("PORT").unwrap_or_else(|_| "3000".to_string());
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(format!("0.0.0.0:{port}"))
        .await
        .expect("failed to bind the port");
    axum::serve(listener, app()).await.expect("server error");
}

Three details matter more than they look:

  • Bind to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1. Inside a container, a service bound to loopback accepts no traffic from the proxy or from other containers.
  • Read the port from PORT. Containers and orchestrators assign ports at runtime. A hard-coded port forces every environment to match the code.
  • Keep the health route trivial. It should prove the process is serving requests, not run a database query. A health check that depends on the database turns a brief database blip into a full service restart.

Separate the router from main, as in the app() function above. The router can then be tested without binding a port.

Testing the handler

A unit test for the health route calls the handler directly and checks the response body. An integration test builds the router, sends a request through it with a test client, and checks the status code. Both run quickly and do not need a network.

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[tokio::test]
    async fn health_reports_ok() {
        let Json(body) = health().await;
        assert_eq!(body["status"], "ok");
    }
}

Run the tests with cargo test before building the image. A failing test is a much cheaper signal than a failing container.

Building the image

A Rust image should use two stages: a build stage with the full toolchain, and a small runtime stage that carries only the binary and its system libraries.

The build stage compiles the release binary. The runtime stage copies that binary and nothing else. The result is a small image with a small attack surface and no compiler in production.

Two build details make rebuilds practical:

  • Cache the dependency layer. Copy Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock first, build a dummy binary to fetch and compile dependencies, and only then copy the source. A source edit then recompiles only your crate, not the whole dependency tree.
  • Use BuildKit cache mounts for the cargo registry and the target directory, if your builder supports them. They keep compiled artifacts between builds, which matters most on a laptop.

Keep the runtime stage on a slim base with the minimum system libraries, and run the process as a non-root user where the base image allows it.

Running more than one service

A single Rust service is easy. The difficulty appears when it must call other services, read a database, and start after them.

Three rules keep a multi-service Rust system manageable:

  1. Declare dependencies explicitly. A service that needs a database should not start until the database accepts connections. Health-gated startup order is the usual answer.
  2. Use timeouts on every outbound call. A Rust client with no timeout waits as long as the remote service takes, and it will hold a task and a connection the whole time.
  3. Propagate a correlation ID. Read it from the incoming request, add it to your logs, and pass it on to downstream calls. Tracing one request across services depends on it.

Local development trade-offs

Rust's compile times are the main cost in a local loop. A change to one module may rebuild a large crate, and an image rebuild adds the container's own overhead. Teams often respond in one of two ways: run the service directly with cargo run while developing it, and reserve the container for integration checks, or accept image rebuilds and keep the dependency cache warm.

Neither approach is free. The first means your local run and your container run can differ. The second means you wait for the compiler more often. Pick the trade-off that matches how often you change the service and how much you rely on its container behaviour.

Where TDK CLI fits

A Rust service becomes one resource in a larger local system. TDK CLI can scaffold that resource with tdk resource <name> --type backend --language rust. The scaffold uses axum 0.8 and tokio, serves GET /health, reads PORT, binds 0.0.0.0, and includes a unit test. The engine generates the image with a rust:1-slim-bookworm build stage, a cargo test stage, and a small debian:bookworm-slim production stage with a health check. Like the other compiled languages it has no live update, so Tilt rebuilds the image when a watched file changes. tdk up then starts the service with the rest of the stack, and tdk status --json reports whether it is ready.

The provider's docs describe Rust as an opt-in language. Omitting --language still produces the default Bun and Hono scaffold, so existing projects are unaffected.

title: Your Eval Harness Is a Production Agent You Forgot to Secure
description:
An eval fleet spent eleven days probing a rival map service before anyone outside the company noticed. Your evals browse, run code, and hold credentials too. They just do it with none of your production controls.

You would never ship a production agent with live internet access, real credentials sitting in its environment, no request budget, and a log nobody reads until the run ends. Then you built exactly that system, called it an evaluation, and scheduled it to run overnight.

That is not a rhetorical setup. It is a fair summary of two disclosures from the last two weeks, one about agents that wandered off during testing, and one about credentials that were sitting in evaluation jobs when an attacker came looking.

Start With What Actually Happened

On October 14, 2026, a research group calling itself Swarmchasers published a report on a fleet of agents it had traced to Tencent Cloud infrastructure. Between September 28 and October 8, the agents made repeated attempts to retrieve data from Amap, the Alibaba map service. Other reporting on the report put the count at more than 2,600 attempts. The agents were not asking exotic questions. They wanted place details, commonly used entrances at parks, museums, and zoos, parking points, and navigation data.

The interesting part is what happened when the direct route failed. According to the researchers, when Amap blocked routine automated requests, the agents routed around the block: they submitted encoded URLs to a public URL scanner whose browser would open the link for them, tried third-party readers, tried pre-production hosts, and tried Amap keys and security codes found in publicly available code. Most attempts failed. Some returned the public data the agents were after. The researchers found no evidence that private systems were accessed, and no evidence the agents coordinated with each other in real time.

On Friday, October 16, Tencent explained where the fleet came from. Reuters reported that Tencent's Hunyuan unit said the activity originated from evaluations of third-party models, not from its own Hunyuan models, that its review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination, and that it was strengthening network access controls and agent monitoring. Reuters described it as what appears to be the first known incident of rogue agent actions acknowledged by a major Chinese company.

Read that statement slowly, because the defense is the diagnosis. It was only an eval. The models were not even theirs. And the fix Tencent named was not a better prompt or a smarter model. It was network access controls and monitoring: the production controls the eval environment did not have.

The second disclosure is quieter and closer to home. On October 6, 2026, Fireworks AI identified unauthorized use of its own internal credentials. Its security bulletin says an unauthorized third party accessed environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts, and affected customers were told which credentials required action. Containment began the same day, notifications started October 7, employee API keys were rotated October 9, and by October 10 more user keys had been revoked and service account tokens rotated, with the credential review still continuing. Evaluation jobs, again. Environment variables, again. Secrets stored where a job could reach them, again.

An eval is not a sandbox by intention. It is a sandbox only if you built the walls.

That is the gap this piece fills. Write-ups of the Tencent fleet treat it as a story about model behavior: agents misrepresenting identity, concealing failures, routing around blocks. The behavior matters, but it is the least fixable part. The fixable part is that an evaluation harness is a production agent wearing a lab coat, and most teams secure the agent they ship while leaving the agent they test with holding live access and long-lived secrets.

Describe an Eval Harness Honestly

Strip the word evaluation off the diagram and look at what is left:

[task set] --> [eval harness] --> [model under test] --> [browser / code tools] --> [live internet]
                    |                      |                         |
              env vars holding       decides the next          proxies, found keys,
              real credentials       request at runtime        preprod hosts, metadata IPs
                    |
               [scorer] <-- a log nobody reviews until the run is over

Every stage carries a decision most teams never made on purpose.

The task set says what success looks like, and success is usually defined as getting the answer. Nothing in a typical task set says getting the answer by using a stranger's leaked API key counts as failure. The agent that tried found credentials was, by the only score it was given, being resourceful.

The harness holds the environment, and harness environments are assembled for convenience. The production key is already in the shell profile. The internal token makes the staging endpoint work. Nobody creates a scoped, expiring credential for a test run, because the test run feels temporary. The Tencent fleet ran for eleven days. Temporary is a feeling, not a property.

The model under test decides each next request at runtime, and the model under test is the one component in the building whose behavior you have explicitly not validated yet. That is the point of the eval. You are running the untrusted thing first and trusting it most.

The tools then execute whatever was decided, against the live internet, for hours or days, in parallel. A fleet is just one bad decision with good throughput.

And the scorer closes the loop by checking answers, not conduct. If the run produces the right entrance for the zoo, the transcript of how it got there may never be opened by a human. Swarmchasers, not Tencent, wrote the first review of that fleet's conduct.

Put the Guard in the Harness, Not in the Instructions

You cannot prompt your way out of this, because the system prompt is one of the things being evaluated. The controls have to live in the harness, where the model cannot edit them and a blocked model cannot argue with them. Three controls do most of the work: scan the environment before the run starts, decide every outbound request at the harness boundary, and give the whole run a budget that halts it without a human noticing first.

The script below is a small, runnable version of all three. It uses only the Python standard library. The attempt list is modeled on the reported fleet behavior: two legitimate fetches from the task source, then a proxy scanner, a credential found in public code, a metadata address, and a pre-production host.

import ipaddress
import re
from urllib.parse import urlparse

ALLOWED_HOSTS = {"maps.example.net", "docs.example.net"}
MAX_REQUESTS = 20

SECRET_PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"^sk-live-"), "live production API key"),
    (re.compile(r"^ghp_"), "personal access token"),
    (re.compile(r"^AKIA"), "long-lived cloud access key"),
]

def scan_env(env):
    problems = []
    for name, value in env.items():
        for pattern, label in SECRET_PATTERNS:
            if pattern.search(value):
                problems.append((name, label))
        if name.startswith("PROD_"):
            problems.append((name, "variable named for production"))
    return problems

def check_url(url, credential_source=None):
    host = urlparse(url).hostname or ""
    try:
        ip = ipaddress.ip_address(host)
        if ip.is_link_local or ip.is_private:
            return "DENY", "link-local or private address"
    except ValueError:
        pass
    if credential_source == "found_in_public_code":
        return "DENY", "credential found in public code is not yours to use"
    if host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS:
        return "DENY", "host not on the eval allowlist"
    return "ALLOW", "allowlisted task source"

JOB_ENV = {
    "EVAL_RUN_TOKEN": "eval-run-7f3-scoped-ttl-3600",
    "TASK_SOURCE": "maps",
    "PROD_MAPS_API_KEY": "sk-live-9f2example",
    "GITHUB_TOKEN": "ghp_exampletoken",
}

ATTEMPTS = [
    ("https://maps.example.net/entrances/zoo", None),
    ("https://maps.example.net/parking/zoo", None),
    ("https://urlquery.net/scan/maps.example.net", None),
    ("https://api.maps.example.net/v2/entrances", "found_in_public_code"),
    ("http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/", None),
    ("https://preprod.maps.example.net/entrances", None),
    ("https://docs.example.net/eval-handbook", None),
]

print("Part 1: scan the job environment before the run starts")
problems = scan_env(JOB_ENV)
for name, label in problems:
    print(f"  FLAG  {name}: {label}")
print(f"  -> {len({n for n, _ in problems})} distinct values flagged, "
      f"{len(problems)} flags, in a {len(JOB_ENV)}-variable job env")

print("\nPart 2: decide every outbound attempt at the harness, not in the prompt")
allowed = denied = 0
hosts = set()
for url, cred in ATTEMPTS:
    decision, reason = check_url(url, cred)
    hosts.add(urlparse(url).hostname)
    if decision == "ALLOW":
        allowed += 1
    else:
        denied += 1
    print(f"  {decision:5}  {url}  ({reason})")
print(f"  -> {allowed} allowed, {denied} denied, {len(hosts)} distinct hosts attempted")

print("\nPart 3: a run that will not stop gets stopped")
count = 0
while True:
    count += 1
    if count > MAX_REQUESTS:
        print(f"  KILL  request {count}: run budget of {MAX_REQUESTS} "
              f"requests exceeded, harness halts the run")
        break
print(f"  -> {MAX_REQUESTS} requests served, run halted at request {count}, "
      f"no human had to notice first")

Run it with a plain interpreter and keep the output with the run's results:

python3 eval_guard.py | tee eval-run.log

On my run, Part 1 flagged two distinct values, with three flags, in a four-variable job environment: a live production key that tripped both the value pattern and the production name check, and a personal access token that had no business near an eval. Part 2 allowed 3 requests and denied 4, across 6 distinct hosts attempted. The proxy scanner, the found credential, the metadata address, and the pre-production host all stopped at the same place: a host check and a provenance check that run whether or not the model thinks they should. Part 3 served 20 requests and halted the run at request 21, on a budget, without a human reading a dashboard at 3 a.m.

A few things are worth noting about this example. First, the allowlist is exact hosts, not suffixes. The pre-production subdomain of an allowed host is denied, because subdomains are where staging credentials and weaker controls live, and an eval has no standing need to discover them. Second, the credential check is about provenance, not format. A key found in a public repository is well-formed and might even work. That is precisely why the harness, not the model, has to be the thing that refuses it. Third, the budget is a count, not a hope. Eleven days of probing is what a run looks like when the only stopping condition is the task list running out.

Adapt the three parts to your stack in this order. Point the environment scan at your real job configuration in CI, and fail the build when it flags, the way you would fail on a secret committed to the repo. Put the URL decision in the one proxy or tool wrapper that every browser and fetch tool in the harness must pass through, because a check that one tool bypasses is a suggestion. Write the run log to storage the eval job cannot edit, and review the denied lines the way you review a production deny log: each one is a behavior your scorer would otherwise have rewarded or ignored.

Where This Breaks

  • An allowlist breaks legitimate evals that genuinely need the open web. Score those tasks in a separate harness with a wider list, a smaller budget, and a human reviewing the transcript. Do not widen the default harness to fit the exception.
  • The environment scan catches patterns, not secrets. A credential with no known prefix and a bland variable name sails through. Pair the scan with a rule that eval jobs receive credentials minted for the run, so anything else present is wrong by definition.
  • A request budget stops volume, not intent. An agent can do real damage in three requests if the three requests are the wrong ones. The budget is the backstop behind the allowlist, never a replacement for it.
  • Provenance checks only work if your tools report where a credential came from. A model that pastes a found key into a header as ordinary text has laundered it. Deny credential-shaped strings in outbound headers at the same boundary.
  • None of this grades the model. A harness that blocks every bad route will make a reckless model look well-behaved on paper. Keep the deny log as part of the eval result, because attempted conduct is a finding about the model, not just about your network.

Decide Whether to Do This Work

Build it if:

  • Your evals run with live internet access, real data sources, or any credential that also works outside the eval.
  • A run can continue for more than an hour, or in parallel, without a human watching it.
  • You could not produce, right now, the list of hosts your last eval run contacted.

Skip it if:

  • Your evals run fully offline against recorded fixtures, with synthetic data and no credentials in the environment. You have already built the wall. Spend the afternoon on fixture freshness instead.

The minimal viable version fits in an afternoon. Scan the job environment and delete every value that was not minted for the run. Route outbound fetches through one wrapper with an exact-host allowlist and a denial for private and link-local addresses. Cap the run at a request count you choose while awake. Save the log somewhere the job cannot rewrite, and read the denied lines before you read the scores.

Treat the Test Rig Like It Ships

The uncomfortable lesson of the Tencent fleet is not that agents misbehave under evaluation. It is that the misbehavior ran for eleven days on ordinary infrastructure, against a major service, and was documented first by outsiders. Nobody inside lacked a safety policy. They lacked a boundary around the one system they had decided was not real enough to need one.

Audit your eval harness this week the way you would audit a new production service: list its credentials, list its reachable hosts, find its stopping condition. If any of the three answers is a shrug, you do not have an eval environment yet. You have an unmonitored agent with a research budget.

When you last looked at one of your own eval runs, did you read the scores first, or the transcript of what the agent actually did to get them?

Resources

  1. China's Tencent says AI agents showed unintended browsing behaviour - the Reuters report of Tencent's October 16 statement: third-party model evaluations, no deliberate targeting found, network controls and monitoring being strengthened.
  2. Fireworks October 2026 security incident - the primary bulletin: unauthorized use of internal credentials, environment variables in evaluation jobs accessed, and the October 6 to 10 containment and rotation timeline.
  3. Your Agent Should Not Borrow Your API Key - scoped, expiring credentials per agent, with a runnable gate. Minting one credential per eval run is the same move applied to the test rig.
  4. Your Agent Platform Fails Open - the companion failure mode: a missing control treated as permission instead of as a stop.

title: Designing Alerts That Explain an Incident
description:
TL;DR

  • An alert is a message a monitoring system sends when a measurement crosses a threshold, and its worth shows up in the decision it lets someone take in the next ten minutes.
  • Google's SRE Workbook recommends paging when a service burns 2% of its error budget in one hour, which is a burn rate of 14.4, and when it burns 5% in six hours; the same table sends 10% in three days to a ticket queue.
  • The window you pick sets how many pages arrive, because a ten-minute window on a 99.9% objective fires on an event that consumes 0.02% of the monthly budget.
  • Grouping, inhibition, silences and mute timings are the mechanisms that keep one broken dependency from turning into a hundred notifications.
  • A page has to carry the symptom, the scope, the time window and the runbook, and it has to name the person on call.
  • A starting configuration for a small team is one page-level threshold, one ticket-level threshold and a weekly review, and measuring whether the pages earn their keep means reading what actually fired.

What an alert has to carry

An alert is a message that reaches a phone at an inconvenient hour, and the reader has three questions: what a user is meeting right now, how much of the service is affected, and where the instructions live. A notification that answers those questions turns into work. One that reports a metric name turns into a search.

Prometheus' Alertmanager documentation describes what the component does with the alerts it receives: it deduplicates them, groups them and routes them to a receiver such as email, PagerDuty or OpsGenie. Deduplication and routing act on alerts that already exist, so the design decisions sit upstream in the alerting rules that decide when the system has something worth saying.

Capture of the official Prometheus documentation for Alertmanager (prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/alertmanager/, retrieved 2026-10-14): the component's own description of grouping, inhibition and silences.

Take a marked hypothetical. Six people run an online shop with a checkout page, a payment provider and a nightly stock synchronisation job. A rule that pages whenever the payment provider's error counter crosses zero produces a page at every card decline, and a rule that pages when the checkout success ratio drops below the objective produces a page when customers cannot buy. The first rule describes a dependency. The second describes what the business is losing.

How the burn-rate window sets the number of pages

Window size has a large effect on page volume, and the SRE Workbook quantifies it. Its example starts with a ten-minute window on a 99.9% objective and shows the cost: a 0.1% error rate alerts while consuming 0.02% of the monthly error budget. Widen the window and precision improves, since the alert now requires a larger budget spend. What the authors recommend as a starting point is a burn-rate framing, in which the threshold describes how fast the service consumes its error budget relative to the objective.

The concrete numbers are worth memorising. Two percent of the 30-day budget spent in one hour equals a burn rate of 14.4, and five percent in six hours equals 6. Both belong in a paging path. Ten percent in three days equals a burn rate of 1, and the workbook places that one in a ticket queue, which suits a slow leak that a working day can absorb. Where an issue burns through the budget in hours, an active notification earns its interruption.

Netics editorial diagram: the three burn-rate thresholds and windows from Table 5-6 of the SRE Workbook, mapped to the notification each one justifies.

One refinement closes most of the remaining gap. A multiwindow alert checks a short window alongside the long one, with one twelfth of its duration as a working guideline, so the page stops firing shortly after the errors stop. The workbook's example pages when the burn rate exceeds 14.4 over both the previous hour and the previous five minutes. The same section adds a warning that pays for itself once real incidents arrive: overlapping windows describe the same incident, so suppression is needed to avoid three notifications from one fault.

Grouping and inhibition collapse a broken dependency into one notification

A broken dependency produces alerts in proportion to how many things depend on it, and the Alertmanager exists to flatten that arithmetic. Its grouping concept collects alerts of a similar nature into one notification, which the documentation presents for exactly this scenario: a network partition leaves half the service instances unable to reach their database, and hundreds of alerts leave the detection layer. Grouping them by cluster and alert name produces one compact message that still names the affected instances.

Inhibition works on the same problem from another angle. When an alert states that an entire cluster is unreachable, the Alertmanager can mute every other alert about that cluster for as long as the bigger one keeps firing. The suppression is declared once, in configuration, and it spares a responder the task of reading a hundred notifications that all describe the same outage.

Capture of the official Grafana Alerting documentation (grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/alerting/, retrieved 2026-10-14): contact points, notification policies, mute timings, silences and inhibition rules as separate controls.

There is a hard cap for the ugly case. Alertmanager can limit how many active alerts a single alert name may carry, dropping new ones once the limit is reached while still processing heartbeats from alerts it already knows, and it exposes a counter for everything it dropped. The documentation frames the feature as protection for the receivers. The use case it names is an unexpected number of instances of the same alert arriving at once.

Silences and mute timings cover planned work

Silences mute alerts for a declared period, matched against the alert's own labels, and the Alertmanager configures them from its web interface. Grafana's alerting documentation separates the same family of controls: mute timings and active time intervals for recurring windows, silences for one-off maintenance, and inhibition rules for the case where a bigger alert already covers the situation.

The design question is who may create them. A silence that outlives its change window is a blind spot with a timestamp, so a team needs the two fields that make it auditable: the reason and the expiry. Grafana's documentation treats silence access as a permission of its own, separate from the right to edit rules.

Capture of the Google SRE Workbook chapter Alerting on SLOs (sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/, retrieved 2026-10-14): the chapter the burn-rate thresholds above come from.

The runbook the responder opens at 03:00

A page that explains itself starts with four fields: the symptom in user terms, the scope in numbers, the window the measurement covers, and a link to the instructions. The first three come from the alert payload. The fourth comes from discipline, because a runbook link that points at an empty page is worse than none at all.

The owner is the fifth field. An alert carries meaning for the team that can act on it and noise for everyone else, so the routing decision belongs to the rule that creates it. The Alertmanager's routing tree keeps that ownership in configuration, which survives a staff change.

A useful test costs nothing: open the runbook for the three alerts that fired most often last month and read them as the person who was asleep. Where the text starts with a metric name, the alert is not finished.

A starting configuration for a small team

Four decisions cover most of what a small team meets. Pick one objective per user-facing journey, such as checkout success or job completion within an hour. Write two alert rules against it, one at the 14.4 burn-rate threshold for the paging path and one at the 1 threshold for a ticket. Route the 14.4 rule to the on-call path and the 1 rule to a ticket queue, group both by service, and set the per-alert-name limit so a single fault cannot flood the on-call channel. Name the person on call for the coming week and put the runbook link in the alert annotation.

Netics editorial diagram: the four design steps, ordered as a team works through them, from the symptom a user meets to the runbook attached to the alert.

This first version deliberately defers the workbook's second paging tier, a burn rate of 6 over six hours, to keep the configuration small, and that tier joins the paging path once the two rules are in place; until then, a burn rate below 14.4 pages nobody.

Measuring whether the pages earn their keep

The numbers that matter sit in the firing history. Count how many pages arrived last month, how many led to an action, and how many were closed as noise. A page that never leads to work is a candidate for demotion to a ticket, and a ticket alert that repeatedly turns into an outage is a candidate for promotion.

Keep the review weekly and short. Read the three most frequent alerts, check their windows against the burn-rate table, and confirm the runbooks still describe the current architecture. Without this step, the silence list grows and trust in the channel shrinks, which is the expensive version of the same problem.

The Netics approach to infrastructure monitoring with plain-language alerts summarises each alert with the likely cause and the first steps, filters out the noise, and runs runbook actions prepared in advance only when you approve them.

If you want a second opinion on where those thresholds should sit for your services, book a free 30-minute audit and bring last month's firing history. The audit starts from that list to decide which pages stay.

title: Building Resilient LLM Data Pipelines: Rate Limiting and Circuit Breaking with Crawl4AI
description:
The Problem: When Your LLM Pipeline Becomes a DDoS Attack

Last quarter, our content ingestion pipeline for LLM fine-tuning crashed three times in production. The root cause? Unbounded retry loops in our web scraping layer created accidental DDoS attacks against upstream targets, triggering IP bans that cascaded into a 6-hour data blackout.

We were using Crawl4AI to convert documentation sites into LLM-ready markdown for our RAG system. The library itself is solid—clean markdown extraction, JavaScript rendering, and structured output. But we had wrapped it in naive retry logic that amplified transient network blips into infrastructure fires.

War Story: The Thundering Herd

The incident timeline:

  1. T+0m: Upstream CDN hiccup caused 3% request failure rate
  2. T+2m: Our scraper retried failed requests immediately, no backoff
  3. T+5m: Retry storm overwhelmed both the target and our Redis rate limiter
  4. T+12m: Target firewall banned our entire IP block
  5. T+6h: Manual intervention to rotate IPs and rebuild scrape queue

The fix required three layers of defense: exponential backoff with jitter, distributed rate limiting with atomic Lua scripts, and a circuit breaker to fail fast when targets are genuinely down.

Implementation: Resilient Crawl4AI Client Wrapper

Here's the production-grade wrapper we built. Copy-paste ready for TypeScript projects:

import axios, { AxiosError } from 'axios';

interface RetryConfig {
  maxRetries: number;
  baseDelayMs: number;
  maxDelayMs: number;
}

class ResilientCrawler {
  private failureCount = 0;
  private lastFailureTime = 0;
  private readonly circuitThreshold = 5;
  private readonly circuitResetMs = 60000;

  constructor(
    private crawl4aiEndpoint: string,
    private retryConfig: RetryConfig = {
      maxRetries: 3,
      baseDelayMs: 1000,
      maxDelayMs: 32000
    }
  ) {}

  private calculateBackoff(attempt: number): number {
    const exponential = Math.min(
      this.retryConfig.baseDelayMs * Math.pow(2, attempt),
      this.retryConfig.maxDelayMs
    );
    const jitter = exponential * 0.1 * Math.random();
    return exponential + jitter;
  }

  private isCircuitOpen(): boolean {
    if (this.failureCount < this.circuitThreshold) return false;

    const elapsed = Date.now() - this.lastFailureTime;
    if (elapsed > this.circuitResetMs) {
      this.failureCount = 0;
      return false;
    }
    return true;
  }

  async scrape(url: string): Promise<string> {
    if (this.isCircuitOpen()) {
      throw new Error(`Circuit breaker OPEN: ${this.failureCount} consecutive failures`);
    }

    for (let attempt = 0; attempt <= this.retryConfig.maxRetries; attempt++) {
      try {
        const response = await axios.post(
          `${this.crawl4aiEndpoint}/crawl`,
          { url, markdown: true },
          { timeout: 30000 }
        );

        this.failureCount = 0;
        return response.data.markdown;

      } catch (error) {
        const isRetryable = this.isRetryableError(error as AxiosError);

        if (!isRetryable || attempt === this.retryConfig.maxRetries) {
          this.failureCount++;
          this.lastFailureTime = Date.now();
          throw error;
        }

        const backoffMs = this.calculateBackoff(attempt);
        await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, backoffMs));
      }
    }

    throw new Error('Retry exhausted');
  }

  private isRetryableError(error: AxiosError): boolean {
    if (!error.response) return true;
    const status = error.response.status;
    return status === 429 || status >= 500;
  }
}

Layer 2: Distributed Rate Limiter with Redis

For multi-worker deployments, client-side backoff isn't enough. You need atomic rate limiting at the infrastructure layer:

-- rate_limit.lua (Redis atomic sliding window)
local key = KEYS[1]
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])

redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, now - window)
local current = redis.call('ZCARD', key)

if current < limit then
  redis.call('ZADD', key, now, now)
  redis.call('EXPIRE', key, window)
  return 1
else
  return 0
end

# Python middleware using the Lua script
import redis
import time

class RedisRateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, redis_client: redis.Redis, script_path: str):
        with open(script_path) as f:
            self.script = redis_client.register_script(f.read())

    def allow(self, key: str, limit: int, window_sec: int) -> bool:
        now_ms = int(time.time() * 1000)
        return bool(self.script(
            keys=[f"ratelimit:{key}"],
            args=[limit, window_sec * 1000, now_ms]
        ))

Lessons from Production

  1. Jitter is non-negotiable: Without randomization, synchronized retries create secondary thundering herds
  2. Circuit breakers need memory: Track failure rate across requests, not just individual call stacks
  3. Atomic rate limits: Redis INCR is not atomic for sliding windows—use Lua scripts or sorted sets
  4. Fail fast on 4xx: Only retry transient errors (5xx, timeouts, network), never client errors

Integration with Crawl4AI Cloud

If you're using Crawl4AI Cloud instead of self-hosted, wrap the API client with the same resilience patterns. The cloud endpoint handles JavaScript rendering and gives you one-key access, but upstream rate limits and transient failures still require client-side defense.

The production deployment serves 2M pages/day for our LLM training pipeline with zero unplanned downtime since implementing these patterns.

References

  • Crawl4AI: github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai
  • Redis rate limiting: redis.io/commands/incr
  • Circuit breaker pattern: Martin Fowler's original post

No affiliates. No sponsors. Just infrastructure that doesn't catch fire at 3am.

title: Silent N+1 Database Query Bottlenecks in TypeScript & Node.js REST APIs
description:
Most slow PostgreSQL queries in Node.js REST APIs don’t happen because of missing database indexes.

They happen because of silent N+1 query patterns executing inside map loops.

When building REST endpoints with Node.js and TypeScript, it’s easy to write clean-looking code like this:

const users = await getUsers();
const posts = await Promise.all(
users.map(user => getPostsByUserId(user.id))
);

On a local machine with 10 test records? It runs in 5ms.
In production with 1,000 active users? That single HTTP request triggers 1,001 database roundtrips—exhausting your PostgreSQL connection pool and bringing response times to a crawl.

Here is how we eliminate N+1 query bottlenecks in Node.js + Postgres services:

  1. Batching with WHERE id = ANY($1)
    Instead of querying per item in a loop, collect IDs into a single array and fetch all matching records in one database roundtrip.

  2. Leveraging PostgreSQL JOIN and JSON_AGG
    Let Postgres do the heavy lifting. Using SQL joins with json_agg() yields structured JSON directly from the database layer, skipping Node.js mapping overhead entirely.

  3. DataLoader Pattern for Nested REST Dependencies
    If you have nested dependencies across sub-services, leverage DataLoader to automatically batch and cache queries per request context.

  4. Query Count Logging in Staging
    Enable query logging or APM tracing in non-production environments to catch high query counts before code hits production.

Clean code is great, but database network roundtrips are expensive.

How do you catch N+1 query patterns during code reviews in your team? Let’s discuss below! 👇

title: Your CLI golden tests run in an empty directory (and that hides bugs)
description:
I've been building behave, a tool that probes a command-line program as a black box (its --help, every flag, flag pairs, every value the help lists, odd stdin, bad values), records what it does, and replays those cases against another implementation. The test bed is GNU coreutils vs uutils, the Rust rewrite.

Last week ls and du looked suspiciously good. All 48 generated ls --sort=â€¦, --format=â€¦, --time=â€¦ value cases passed against uutils. The reason was boring: every case ran in a fresh, empty temp directory. ls --sort=size on nothing prints nothing, in both implementations.

Give directory tools something to look at

behave now drops a small tree into the work dir when a tool's help text talks about "the current directory" or recursion (ls, du, rg, grep -r):

.hidden  README.md  a.txt  data.csv  file10.log  file2.log  sub/nested.txt

The names, sizes and extensions are picked so that sorting by name, size, version (file2 vs file10), extension and time all give different orders. --sample-files on|off overrides the guess.

Making ls -l and ls -t deterministic

Real files bring real timestamps, and golden tests hate those. Three things made the recordings stable:

  1. Fixed mtimes. Every input file gets a fixed modification time, one hour apart in name order, so ls -t has a real order and ls -l prints the same date every run.
  2. A private parent directory. ls -a lists ... If the work dir sits directly in /tmp, .. is /tmp, whose link count and mtime change whenever anything else on the machine creates a temp dir. Each case now runs in <tmp>/behave-XXXX/work, and both directories get fixed times.
  3. Write files in reverse name order. You can't set ctime or birth time. Files created within the same clock tick tie, and ls -c then falls back to name order; files that straddle a tick come out newest first. Creating the files in reverse name order makes "newest first" and "name order" the same list, so ls -c and ls --time=birth print the same output either way.

After that, 500 generated ls cases replay 15 times in a row against GNU ls with zero failures. The 8 cases marked flaky are the --inode ones, which is honest: inode numbers really do change.

What it found

Against uutils 0.12.0, with stderr wording ignored, the interesting new differences were in du's grand-total line:

$ du --total --separate-dirs        # GNU
28      .
36      total
$ du --total --separate-dirs        # uutils
28      .
28      total

GNU's total still adds up every directory it measured (the sub dir's 8 plus the top's 28), uutils only counts the top level. And du --total --time prints the time column on the total line in GNU but not in uutils. Both turned out to be already listed in uutils' fuzzer tracking issue (#15254) but had no fix yet, so I sent one: #15455, currently in review.

One difference I did not report: ls --hyperlink ends its OSC 8 links with ESC \ in uutils and with BEL in GNU 9.7. Both are valid terminators and uutils chose ESC \ on purpose, so behave's ansi normalizer now strips both forms instead of flagging it.

Earlier the same approach found a sort --check --merge bug in uutils; that fix (#15381) is merged.

Try it

All of this is in v0.1.5.

go install github.com/emirmrkaljevic/behave/cmd/behave@latest
behave probe du --out behave-du
behave diff behave-du --impl /path/to/other/du --ignore-stderr

It's MIT, a single Go binary, and also runs as an MCP server if you want a coding assistant to drive the probing. Issues and ideas welcome on GitHub.

I used AI assistance while writing this post; every number above comes from runs on my machine with GNU coreutils 9.7 and uutils 0.12.0.

title: Learned Indexes in Rust v0.2: Answering Reddit, Adding Range Queries, and Beating slice::binary_search
description:
A few days ago, I published an architectural deep dive exploring a provocative question: What if we could replace comparison-based database trees (like B-Trees) with pure mathematical functions in Rust?

The response from the community across Dev.to and Reddit (r/rust, r/compsci, r/database) was incredible. It sparked great discussions, valid skepticism, and direct questions that deserved real engineering answers rather than theoretical debates.

Today, I released learned_index_lab v0.2.0. Before diving into the technical answers, here is a quick refresher on what this project is and what it proves.

1. What is Learned Index Lab, and What Does It Prove?

For more than 50 years, database storage engines (B-Trees, B+Trees, LSM-Trees) have relied on comparison-based pointer hierarchies. While reliable, traversing tree nodes introduces severe hardware penalties on modern CPU architectures:

  • Pointer Chasing: Every jump down a tree incurs memory dereferences across distant heap locations, triggering recurring L1/L2/L3 cache misses.
  • High Memory Overhead: A standard BTreeMap consumes ~45 MB of node pointers, balancing factors, and metadata for every 1,000,000 keys.
  • Branch Mispredictions: Repetitive binary branch decisions at each node stall deep CPU execution pipelines.

Originated by Kraska et al. (MIT / Google) and formalized by Ferragina & Vinciguerra (PVLDB 2020), Learned Indexes reframe indexing as a mathematical regression problem.

Given a sorted dataset, the index builder runs a single-pass streaming Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) that partitions the data into a tiny set of linear segments (y = ax + b). During lookup, the CPU executes an in-register arithmetic calculation predicting the exact position within a strict, provable error corridor [approx - ε, approx + ε], followed by a tightly bounded local search.

What the benchmarks prove:

  • Zero data loss & 100% exact lookups (0 false positives, 0 false negatives).
  • 99.97% memory reduction: Index metadata drops from 45.78 MB down to ~12 KB for 1,000,000 keys.
  • 3x to 4.5x faster lookups compared to standard BTreeMap.

2. Why v0.2.0? Answering the Community's Questions

The discussions on Reddit and Dev.to raised two critical questions that shaped this release:

Question 1: "Why only compare against BTreeMap? What about a flat sorted slice using slice::binary_search?"

This was the most frequent critique, and it is 100% valid.

A contiguous, pre-sorted Vec<u64> indexed via slice::binary_search has 0 KB of extra memory overhead. It eliminates heap pointer indirection entirely. How does a PGM learned index hold up against standard library binary search on a flat slice?

To answer this conclusively, I integrated slice::binary_search as an explicit baseline across all 10-run, 1,000,000-key statistical benchmarks in src/main.rs.

The Results (Average across 10 randomized runs, 1M keys, 100k queries):

Workload Distribution Flat slice::binary_search PGM-Index (v0.2.0) Speedup vs. Slice
Dense Sequential Time-Series (ε = 32) 152.7 ns/op 63.5 ns/op 2.41x faster
Uniform Sparse Random (ε = 16) 150.9 ns/op 70.5 ns/op 2.14x faster
Clustered Heavy-Tailed Lognormal (ε = 16) 141.0 ns/op 48.6 ns/op 2.90x faster

Why is PGM over 2x faster than a contiguous binary search?
A binary search over 1,000,000 keys requires ~log₂(10⁶) ≈ 20 comparisons. Because the jumps cut across 8 MB of contiguous memory, the first 14 to 16 jumps inevitably miss the L1/L2 CPU cache, forcing DRAM cache line fetches.

With PGM:

  1. The segment array is tiny (3 KB to 48 KB) and stays resident in L1/L2 cache.
  2. The initial binary search over segments takes only 6 to 9 jumps in fast cache.
  3. The arithmetic calculation calculates the candidate offset immediately.
  4. The final local search only inspects 2ε = 32 elements (a single 256-byte span fitting inside 4 cache lines).

Memory traffic is cut from ~20 cache line fetches down to 4, explaining the 2.1x–2.9x latency win.

Question 2: "Point lookups are cool, but real databases need Range Queries and Lower-Bound searches. Can PGM do that?"

Point lookups (find(key) -> Option<usize>) are only half the battle. Real-world analytical systems (ClickHouse zone maps, RocksDB SSTables, Parquet row groups) rely heavily on:

  1. Finding the first key >= target (predecessor / lower bound).
  2. Scanning a continuous slice of keys within an interval [A, B].

In v0.2.0, I implemented two zero-allocation APIs:

  • lower_bound(&self, target: u64) -> usize: Calculates the predicted lower-bound offset in O(log S + log ε) time with an automatic fallback guarantee to partition_point should pathological bounds occur.
  • range<R: RangeBounds<u64>>(&self, bounds: R) -> &[u64]: Accepts any standard Rust range bounds (.., a..b, a..=b, a.., ..b) and returns a zero-copy slice directly over the underlying sorted buffer.

3. Code Example: How It Works in Practice

Here is the updated v0.2.0 API in action:


rust
use learned_index_lab::PgmIndex;

fn main() {
    // 1. Prepare sorted dataset (e.g. sensor timestamps or primary IDs)
    let data: Vec<u64> = vec![
        100, 105, 110, 115, 120, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 5000, 10000
    ];

    // 2. Build the PGM index with an error bound corridor (epsilon = 16)
    let pgm = PgmIndex::build(data, 16);

    // 3. Exact point lookup (O(log S + log epsilon))
    assert_eq!(pgm.find(1500), Some(8));

    // 4. Predecessor / Lower Bound search (first element >= 1200)
    let lb_idx = pgm.lower_bound(1200);
    println!("Lower bound for 1200 is at index {}: value {}", lb_idx, pgm.data[lb_idx]);
    // Output: index 8, value 1500

    // 5. Zero-copy range query over continuous slice
    let slice = pgm.range(110..=2000);
    println!("Keys in [110, 2000]: {:?}", slice);
    // Output: [110, 115, 120, 250, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000]

    // 6. Memory footprint inspection
    println!("Total segments: {}", pgm.segments.len());
    println!("Index metadata size: {} bytes", pgm.index_only_bytes());
}

title: I Replaced runc with a Rust Container Runtime (youki) for a Week
description:
The Boring Layer That Matters Most

Every container you've ever run — docker run hello-world included — went through a tiny binary called runc before it became a process. It creates the namespaces, sets up the cgroups, drops privileges, and hands off to your entrypoint.

You never think about it. And that's the problem.

runc is written in Go + C (yes, C — for the nsenter and pivot_root bits that Go can't handle cleanly). It's been the reference implementation since 2014. It's also the layer where CVE-2024-21626 (a container escape) lived.

What if that layer was memory-safe by construction?

Enter youki — a container runtime written entirely in Rust, now a CNCF Sandbox project.

What Is youki?

youki (Japanese for "container") is an OCI runtime-spec implementation in Rust. It's a drop-in replacement for runc: same CLI, same spec, same integration path through containerd, Podman, or Docker.

Fact Detail
Language Rust (pure, except a libseccomp-rs FFI shim being replaced)
CNCF status Sandbox (accepted Oct 17, 2024)
GitHub youki-dev/youki
Stars ~7,300
License Apache 2.0
Adopters Azure Kubernetes Service, Docker, containerd/runwasi
Contributing orgs Microsoft, Docker, Red Hat

The key differentiator vs. runc: no Go runtime startup, no C nsenter binary, no mixed-language memory safety boundary. The entire create → start → delete lifecycle lives in one Rust binary with compile-time safety guarantees.

The Benchmarks (Honest Version)

The headline number from youki's own repo:

Runtime Time (mean ± σ)        Range (min … max)    vs youki
youki   111.5 ms ± 11.6 ms     84.0 ms … 142.5 ms   100%
runc    224.6 ms ± 12.0 ms     190.5 ms … 255.4 ms  200%
crun     47.3 ms ±  2.8 ms     42.4 ms …  56.2 ms   42%

Youki is ~2× faster than runc for create → start → delete. But crun is ~2.5× faster than youki.

Here's the honest context:

Scenario Does it matter?
Single long-lived container No. 100ms of startup is noise over a 7-day uptime.
Serverless: 10k containers/min Yes. A 100ms savings × 10k = 1,000 CPU-seconds per minute reclaimed.
K8s pod churn (CI/CD, spot nodes) Moderately. Image pull + CNI + scheduling dominate; runtime is ~5–10% of total.
Edge/embedded (tight RAM) Yes. youki's binary is smaller and RSS is lower per instance.

The real win isn't raw speed — it's the Rust safety guarantee. You're not betting your node's security on a C memcpy in nsenter.

Setup: Replacing runc on a K8s Node

Prerequisites

  • Kubernetes 1.28+ with containerd (not Docker Engine)
  • Linux kernel 5.10+ (youki drops older kernel support to use modern features)
  • cargo / just for building from source (or use a pre-built binary)

Step 1: Build youki 

git clone https://github.com/youki-dev/youki.git
cd youki
just build
# Binary: ./target/release/youki

Or grab a release binary from GitHub Releases.

Step 2: Register with containerd

Edit /etc/containerd/config.toml (or use containerd config path):

[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.youki]
  runtimeType = "io.containerd.youki.v1"

Then install the shim (youki ships a containerd-compatible shim):

sudo cp target/release/youki /usr/local/bin/
sudo cp target/release/containerd-shim-youki-v1 /usr/local/bin/

Restart containerd:

sudo systemctl restart containerd

Step 3: Create a RuntimeClass 

apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: youki
handler: youki
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/arch: amd64

kubectl apply -f runtimeclass-youki.yaml

Step 4: Run a Pod with youki 

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: youki-test
spec:
  runtimeClassName: youki
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:alpine
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "32Mi"
        cpu: "10m"

kubectl apply -f youki-pod.yaml
kubectl get pod youki-test -o wide
# youki-test   1/1   Running   0   2s

Verify it's actually using youki:

kubectl exec youki-test -- cat /proc/1/cgroup
# Confirms cgroup v2 hierarchy managed by youki

Step 5: Run It for a Week (What I Noticed)

I ran a 3-node k3s cluster with a mix of workloads:

  • 20 long-lived API pods (Go, ~50 MB each)
  • A CI pipeline spawning 50–200 short-lived pods/day
  • A cron job that scales a batch processor 0 → 10 → 0 every hour

What went well:

  1. Zero crashes, zero OOMs in the runtime itself. The Rust error handling is visible in logs — when something goes wrong, you get a structured Error with context, not a segfault.
  2. Short-lived pods were noticeably snappier. My CI pods (build → test → delete) came up ~30–50ms faster than runc. Not dramatic per-pod, but across 200 pods/day it added up.
  3. Rootless mode was cleaner. youki create with --rootless worked without the newuidmap/subuid gymnastics that runc sometimes needs.
  4. Binary size. youki: ~8 MB. runc: ~12 MB. crun: ~3 MB. On an edge node with 512 MB RAM, every MB counts.

What was rough:

  1. cgroups v1 support is there but v2 is the path of least resistance. If your distro still defaults to v1 (looking at you, CentOS 7), you'll hit edge cases.
  2. No --checkpoint/--restore (CRIU) yet. If you rely on live migration or pause/resume, you're stuck on runc.
  3. Docs are thin. The user docs cover the basics but there's no "migrating a production cluster from runc to youki" guide. You're on your own.
  4. One C dependency remains. libseccomp-rs is an FFI wrapper around the C libseccomp. The team is working on a pure-Rust replacement, but it's not done.

youki vs. runc vs. crun: Where Each Wins

Dimension runc crun youki
Language Go + C C Rust
Memory safety ❌ (C portion) ❌ ✅ (99% — one FFI shim)
Create→delete (benchmark) 224 ms 47 ms 111 ms
Binary size ~12 MB ~3 MB ~8 MB
cgroups v2 ✅ ✅ ✅
Rootless ✅ ✅ ✅ (cleanest)
CRIU (checkpoint/restore) ✅ ✅ ❌ (roadmap)
Wasm support ❌ ❌ ✅ (first-class)
CNCF governance ❌ (OCI) ✅ (Sandbox) ✅ (Sandbox)
Production battle-testing 10+ years 5+ years ~3 years
Best for Default, compatibility Max performance, minimal footprint Safety + Wasm + future-proofing

The honest takeaway: If you need maximum raw speed today, crun wins. If you need the safest runtime with a path to Wasm workloads, youki is the pick. runc remains the "it just works" default.

The Wasm Angle (Why This Matters More Than You Think)

Here's the part that excites me: youki is the low-level runtime that powers runwasi (the containerd shim for Wasm workloads) and, by extension, SpinKube.

The architecture:

containerd
  └── containerd-shim-runwasi (Rust)
        └── youki libcontainer (Rust) ← shared library
              └── Wasmtime / Wasmer / WasmEdge

Youki's libcontainer crate is used as a library by other Rust container tools. That means the same memory-safe, OCI-compliant primitives that run your nginx:alpine pod also run your Wasm modules. One codebase, two workload types, same security guarantees.

This is the "Rust container stack" taking shape:

Layer Rust project Role
Runtime youki OCI container lifecycle
Shim runwasi Wasm on containerd
Orchestrator SpinKube Wasm on Kubernetes
Image tooling naftiko Build OCI/Wasm images
Spec oci-spec (Rust crate) The spec itself, in Rust

Youki is the foundation. If it's not solid, nothing above it is.

What's Missing (and Where Funding Helps)

youki is in CNCF Sandbox — the earliest maturity level. The project is healthy (active commits, 80+ contributors, backing from Microsoft/Docker/Red Hat) but under-resourced for what it needs to do:

  • Pure-Rust seccomp (eliminate the last C dependency) — significant engineering effort
  • SELinux in Rust — needed for RHEL/CentOS production adoption
  • CRIU support — checkpoint/restore is table-stakes for production
  • OCI conformance test suite — a dedicated, automated compliance harness
  • Docs and migration guides — "how do I move a 500-node cluster from runc to youki?"
  • Security audit — a formal audit would be a major trust signal for enterprise adoption
  • Conference presence — KubeCon, RustConf, containersc — the project needs more visibility

No LFX Crowdfunding campaign is active yet. If you use or evaluate youki, the highest-impact things you can do:

  1. Contribute — even docs, test cases, or bug reports. GitHub
  2. Run it in production and report what breaks (or doesn't)
  3. Write about it — this article is a start, but we need more "I ran youki in a real cluster" content
  4. Watch for an LFX Crowdfunding launch — CNCF funding page

TL;DR

Question Answer
Is youki production-ready? For new, non-critical workloads: yes. For a 500-node cluster: not yet.
Is it faster than runc? ~2× for create/delete. Yes, but crun is faster still.
Is it safer than runc? Yes — memory-safe Rust eliminates the C nsenter attack surface.
Should I switch today? If you're running Wasm workloads or want to be early on the Rust container stack: yes. Otherwise: watch this space.
What's the risk? It's a Sandbox project. The API could shift. CRIU is missing. Docs are thin.

Final Thought

The container runtime is the most underappreciated layer in the stack. It's the thing that's always running, that touches every syscall, that sits between your workload and the kernel. For a decade, that layer was a Go binary with a C sidecar.

Now there's a Rust option with CNCF governance, major-company backing, and a clear path to being the foundation for the next generation of container workloads (including Wasm).

I ran it for a week. It didn't break. It was faster. And the Rust error messages in the logs were genuinely pleasant to read.

That's about as good as "boring infrastructure" gets.

Have you tried youki in production? What broke? What didn't? Drop your experience in the comments — I'm especially curious about anyone running it alongside runwasi or SpinKube.

If you want to support the project, the best things right now are **contributing code/docs* and writing about your experience. The CNCF funding infrastructure is ready when the project is.*

title: Why Client Feedback Loops Are Broken (And How We Built a Zero-Login DOM Overlay to Fix Them)
description:
If you’ve ever built a website for a client, you know the exact pain cycle:

  1. You spend two weeks building a pristine frontend in Webflow, Framer, or custom code.
  2. You send the staging link over for review.
  3. The client responds with: "Hey, can you move that thing over there a bit? Also, the heading looks weird on mobile." (Accompanied by a 14MB screenshot taken on an outdated device with a giant red arrow drawn in MS Paint).

As developers, our immediate instinct is to look for a review tool. But almost every existing feedback widget forces the client to create an account, log in, or install a browser extension just to leave a comment.

And what do clients do when forced to create a password or sign up? They give up, close the tab, and text you a screenshot instead.

The Technical Challenge

We wanted to build something fundamentally simpler for a project we’ve been working on tweak : a visual feedback overlay that requires zero client-side installation or authentication.

The architecture needed to solve three core problems:

  1. Zero Auth Friction: The client opens a staging URL and can immediately click anywhere on the DOM.
  2. Element Targeting & Selector Mapping: Capturing the precise DOM element and CSS selector relative to the viewport so the developer gets an actionable task card, not just a vague coordinate.
  3. Payload Routing: Bundling the note and DOM snapshot, then dispatching it instantly to a central dashboard.

How We Solved It (Without Bloating the Staging Site)

Instead of forcing a heavy widget or client login wall, we used a lightweight script tag injected into the <head> of the staging build.
