title: SMS OTP Login API — Resend Cooldowns and Rate Limits for Media Signup
description:
Put the abuse budget in the application, then keep SMS behind a replaceable transport contract. TL;DR: a media signup service should let the provider send and verify codes, while its own server owns resend cooldowns, failed-attempt limits, expiry, and session completion. Delivery reliability is the vendor test. State control is not.

That split matters because swapping the vendor behind the capability should not change signup code. It also gives the team one place to answer a less glamorous question: exactly how much abuse can one phone number, account, IP range, or destination country create before the application says no?

How should a Node.js SMS OTP login API control resends?

Start with a timeline, not an SDK. A reader requests a code, the service admits or rejects that request, a transport sends it, and the reader submits a code. Only then may the signup session advance. Each transition needs one owner.

The browser cannot own the cooldown. Two tabs defeat a countdown, and a script ignores it. The SMS provider cannot own the login session either. A successful code check proves control of the challenged number for that interaction; the application still decides which pending signup it unlocks.

The awkward middle is delivery. An accepted API call is not a received message. For this capability, delivery status and events are pulled rather than pushed, so real-time fallback orchestration is limited. If the product needs delivery insight, poll outside the user's request path with capped backoff. Do not keep an HTTP signup request open while waiting for a carrier state.

Short version: there are three clocks. The resend cooldown controls sends, the challenge expiry controls verification, and the polling budget controls how long delivery observation remains useful. Mixing them into one expiresAt field makes later failures needlessly hard to explain.

Three clocks. Three jobs.

Make the budget executable

I benchmark the admission invariant before comparing dashboards: 10 simultaneous resend attempts for one signup must yield one admitted operation. That number is a test workload, not a universal rate-limit recommendation. The policy thresholds still need evidence from the actual audience and destination mix.

The smallest useful model has explicit terminal states and atomic updates. It also keeps transport details out of the policy. This TypeScript is runnable as an in-process demonstration; replace MemoryStore with a shared store that provides atomic compare-and-update before running more than one application instance.

type Challenge = {
  status: "pending" | "verified" | "locked" | "expired";
  nextSendAt: number;
  expiresAt: number;
  failedAttempts: number;
};

type Decision =
  | { admitted: true; state: Challenge }
  | { admitted: false; reason: string; state?: Challenge };

class MemoryStore {
  private readonly values = new Map<string, Challenge>();

  update(key: string, change: (current?: Challenge) => Decision): Decision {
    const decision = change(this.values.get(key));
    if (decision.admitted) this.values.set(key, decision.state);
    return decision;
  }
}

const cooldownMs = 30_000;
const challengeLifetimeMs = 5 * 60_000;
const maxFailures = 5;

function admitSend(store: MemoryStore, signupId: string, now: number): Decision {
  return store.update(`signup:${signupId}`, (current) => {
    if (current?.status === "verified" || current?.status === "locked") {
      return { admitted: false, reason: `challenge is ${current.status}`, state: current };
    }
    if (current && current.nextSendAt > now) {
      return { admitted: false, reason: "resend cooldown active", state: current };
    }

    return {
      admitted: true,
      state: {
        status: "pending",
        nextSendAt: now + cooldownMs,
        expiresAt: now + challengeLifetimeMs,
        failedAttempts: current?.failedAttempts ?? 0,
      },
    };
  });
}

const store = new MemoryStore();
const now = Date.now();
const decisions = Array.from({ length: 10 }, () => admitSend(store, "reader-42", now));
const admitted = decisions.filter((decision) => decision.admitted).length;

if (admitted !== 1) throw new Error(`expected one admission, received ${admitted}`);
console.log({ admitted, rejected: decisions.length - admitted, maxFailures });

The 30-second cooldown, five-minute lifetime, and five-failure ceiling make the example testable. They are not security guidance. Put them in policy configuration only after deciding who can change them and how that change is reviewed. Config bloat starts when every transport gets its own slightly different copy.

A production store must make admission atomic across processes. It should retain a challenge identifier, terminal status, failed-verification count, next-send time, and expiry server-side. Apply additional budgets by account, normalized phone number, IP range, and destination country. Geographic fencing and country-level spend cutoffs are application responsibilities here.

After admission, call the send operation with an idempotency key tied to that admitted transition. The adapter below is deliberately narrow. INFRAI_OTP_BODY contains JSON already validated against the current public discovery schema; keeping it external avoids inventing request fields that are not part of this article's verified contract. The call uses Bearer authentication, an explicit POST, response-status checks, and bounded exponential retry for HTTP 429 that honors Retry-After. It is runnable on a Node.js release with global fetch.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const apiBaseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_API_BASE_URL;
const rawBody = process.env.INFRAI_OTP_BODY;

if (!apiKey || !apiBaseUrl || !rawBody) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_API_BASE_URL, and INFRAI_OTP_BODY are required");
}

const body: unknown = JSON.parse(rawBody);
const idempotencyKey = `media-signup:${crypto.randomUUID()}`;
const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function sendOtp(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/sms/otp`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      const delayMs = retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)
        ? Number(retryAfter) * 1_000
        : Math.min(500 * 2 ** attempt, 8_000);
      await sleep(delayMs);
      continue;
    }

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`OTP send failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    return response.json();
  }

  throw new Error("OTP send exhausted its retry budget");
}

console.log(JSON.stringify(await sendOtp()));

Verification gets its own explicit POST and must consume a failed-attempt budget atomically. Do not retry a verification blindly: a response can affect the application's attempt counter even when the network result is ambiguous. Generate or validate current request and response fields from discovery rather than copying a payload from an old tutorial. That is a boring boundary. Good. It keeps transport churn from leaking into the signup state machine.

Compare control planes before carrier claims

Vendor selection starts after the state machine passes. The useful comparison is which verification and delivery controls the service manages, because none of these products removes the application's responsibility for its authenticated session.

Option Service boundary Engineering consequence
Twilio Verify Verification-focused send and check workflow Application still owns signup authorization and its broader abuse policy
Vonage Verify Managed verification requests and checks Destination testing and session binding remain application work
AWS End User Messaging SMS SMS delivery within AWS IAM, regional configuration, and quota operations Team builds the complete challenge workflow and verification state
Infrai Stable REST capability contract with public schemas and one credential across backend modules Team owns cooldowns, attempts, geo controls, spend cutoffs, and polling orchestration

Test all four with the same cases: concurrent resend, wrong code, expired challenge, delayed delivery, and rate limiting. Then test physical handsets in the countries the media product serves. There is no honest substitute for that last step, and no supplied runtime measurement supports an uptime or latency winner.

Twilio Verify and Vonage Verify deserve the first look when a managed verification product is the desired boundary. AWS is coherent when IAM, regions, quotas, and operational ownership already sit there. Infrai fits a US/EU application flow when a plain REST contract, low credential sprawl, and a self-describing API matter: its public discovery describes full request and response schemas, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. The broader surface is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which can reduce adapter churn beyond this signup flow.

The limitation is concrete: Infrai is not suitable for a design that requires voice, WhatsApp, RCS, SMTP relay, or webhook-driven fallback. Choose Twilio Verify or Vonage Verify when their managed verification workflow and required channels match the design; choose AWS when AWS-native IAM and regional operations are the stronger constraint. The trade-off is less adapter and credential sprawl versus owning more orchestration in the application. NIST also classifies PSTN out-of-band authentication as restricted. SMS OTP is not phishing-resistant, so do not present it as the final word in account security.

No vendor fixes that.

What changes when signup volume grows

First, move challenge admission and failure consumption into a shared atomic store. Give records explicit retention and deletion rules. A phone identifier used to verify a media account should not quietly become a permanent audience profile.

Second, separate delivery observation from authentication. Poll status or events asynchronously only when the result changes a product decision. Cap attempts, back off, and stop after the observation window. Polling forever is config masquerading as reliability.

Third, make fallback a new state transition. Email fallback is not a managed email OTP feature here; the application must generate, store, expire, and verify that challenge itself. Scheduled email has no cancellation operation. If immediate cross-channel recovery is a hard requirement, pick a provider and architecture with the required push events and managed channels instead of burying this difference in a worker.

This is also where a single global rate limit breaks down. It can reject a legitimate signup spike while distributed abuse stays under each source threshold. Use layered budgets and record which one rejected a request. The exact thresholds belong to production evidence, not tutorial folklore.

The shipping rule

Ship only after one atomic application decision produces at most one idempotent send, and only a current, unexpired, under-budget challenge can complete its bound signup session. Keep that invariant independent of the SMS vendor.

Then choose the provider on delivery results in the real destination mix and on the control plane the team is willing to operate. The contract can stay put while the service behind it moves. The abuse budget stays yours either way.

References

  • NIST SP 800-63B: Authentication and Lifecycle Management
  • Twilio Verify API documentation
  • Vonage Verify API overview
  • AWS End User Messaging SMS documentation
  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance

title: Ten steps at 99% is 90%: retrying multi-step jobs
description:
Part 4 of 10: Reliable background jobs in Node.js, from zero.

By Sandro Dezerio, senior full-stack engineer.

The signup scenario is made up. It is the same one used in Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3. The failure rates come from a simulation with stated assumptions, not from real services.

A job with ten steps, where each step works 99% of the time, finishes about 90% of the time.

Nobody looks at a step that works 99% of the time and calls it unreliable. That is why the problem hides. Each step looks fine on its own, and the job as a whole fails about once in every ten runs.

In Part 3, every job was a single call: send one welcome email. Real jobs are rarely that small. This post looks at a job with several steps, shows what goes wrong when you retry it as one piece, and fixes it with the withRetry wrapper from Part 3, unchanged.

The job grows

Picture the signup job some time later. Sending the welcome email is no longer enough. The job now does ten things, in order:

  1. Save the user
  2. Create the billing customer
  3. Create the workspace
  4. Upload the default avatar
  5. Add the user to the CRM
  6. Subscribe the user to the newsletter
  7. Send the welcome email
  8. Notify the sales channel
  9. Record the analytics event
  10. Schedule the day-3 email

Each step calls something that can fail: a database, a payment provider, an email provider, an internal API. Assume each call fails 1% of the time, independently of the others. For a single call, 99% is a respectable number.

The arithmetic

Reliability multiplies. For the job to succeed, all ten steps must succeed, so the chance is 0.99 multiplied by itself ten times:

0.9910 = 0.904

About 96 jobs in every 1,000 fail somewhere along the way. With twenty steps, it would be about 18 in every 100.

To check this, and to see what each fix does, I wrote a simulation that runs 1,000,000 signup jobs through the queue from Part 2. Without retries, 90.398% of the jobs succeeded. The formula gives 90.438%, so the simulation and the math agree within sampling noise.

The failure rate is only half of the problem. Of the 96,024 jobs that failed, 85,902 failed after at least one step had already done its work. The user exists but has no workspace. The billing customer exists, but nobody got the welcome email. A failed job is often a half-finished job.

The obvious fix: retry the whole job

Part 3 already has a retry wrapper. The quickest fix is to wrap the whole job in withRetry, the same way Part 3 wrapped the email handler. With up to 3 attempts, the success rate jumps from 90.398% to 99.913%. That looks like a win, but the job now has a different problem.

When step 8 fails, the retry starts again from step 1. It saves the user again, creates the billing customer again, and sends the welcome email again. In the simulation, retrying the whole job did 462,891 steps a second time, and 29,564 users received the welcome email more than once. Nobody asked for either.

Some repeats are harmless, such as recording an analytics event twice. Others are not, such as a second billing customer for the same user.

The better fix: retry each step

The fix is to retry the step that failed, not the job. If step 8 fails, try step 8 again. Steps 1 to 7 already worked, so leave them alone.

The code adds one small file, workflow.ts. A job becomes a list of named steps, and the queue from Part 2 and the retry wrapper from Part 3 do not change:

import type { Handler } from "./queue.ts";
import { withRetry, type RetryOptions } from "./retry.ts";

/** One step of a job: a name and the work it does. */
export type Step<T> = { name: string; run: Handler<T> };

/** Run the steps in order. If one throws, the job stops there and the queue records the error. */
export function workflow<T>(steps: Step<T>[]): Handler<T> {
  return async (job) => {
    for (const step of steps) {
      await step.run(job);
    }
  };
}

/** Give each step its own retries, so a failing step never repeats the steps before it. */
export function retryEachStep<T>(steps: Step<T>[], options: RetryOptions): Step<T>[] {
  return steps.map((step) => ({ name: step.name, run: withRetry(step.run, options) }));
}

workflow turns a list of steps into a normal handler, so the queue does not need to know that the job has steps. retryEachStep wraps each step with withRetry from Part 3. The two strategies differ only in where the wrapper goes:

  • Whole job: withRetry(workflow(steps), options)
  • Each step: workflow(retryEachStep(steps, options))

Here is how a job with two steps looks:

import { SimpleQueue, type Job } from "./queue.ts";
import { retryEachStep, workflow, type Step } from "./workflow.ts";

const steps: Step<string>[] = [
  { name: "save the user", run: async (job: Job<string>) => console.log(`saving ${job.data}`) },
  { name: "send the welcome email", run: async (job: Job<string>) => console.log(`emailing ${job.data}`) },
];

const queue = new SimpleQueue<string>(
  workflow(retryEachStep(steps, { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 100, maxDelayMs: 2000, jitter: true })),
);
queue.add("ana@example.com");

The three strategies side by side

These are the results for 1,000,000 simulated signups, with up to 3 attempts in both retry strategies:

Strategy Succeeded Failed jobs Failed after some steps were done Calls per job Steps done again Users with 2+ welcome emails
No retries 90.398% 96,024 85,902 9.56 0 0
Retry the whole job 99.913% 867 865 10.57 462,891 29,564
Retry each step 99.999% 9 8 10.1 0 0

Retrying each step beats retrying the whole job in every column. Only 9 jobs failed out of 1,000,000. No step ran twice. And it made fewer calls than retrying the whole job (10.1 per job compared with 10.57), because a retry repeats one call instead of several.

The success rates also match the formulas. Retrying the whole job needs one attempt in which all ten steps pass, so a job fails only when all three attempts fail: 1 - (1 - 0.9910)3 = 99.913%. Retrying each step needs each step to fail three times in a row, which happens once in a million calls: (1 - 0.013)10 = 99.999%.

Inngest, a tool for running multi-step workflows, uses the same idea: "Each step.run() has its own retry counter, so one failing step does not restart earlier completed steps."

What retrying each step does not fix

A step that worked but did not say so. Sometimes the email provider sends the email, and the reply gets lost on the way back. The step sees a timeout and fails. A retry of that step sends the email again. I ran the simulation again with a lost reply on the email step 0.5% of the time:

Strategy Succeeded Steps done again Users with 2+ welcome emails
Retry each step, reply lost 0.5% of the time 99.999% 4,971 4,939

Retrying each step cannot tell the difference between "it did not happen" and "it happened, but I did not hear back." That is the job of an idempotency key, which Part 5 (coming soon) covers.

The jobs that still fail. Of the 9 failed jobs, 8 stopped halfway through, with some steps done. Per-step retries make this rare, but not impossible, and queue.failed does not say which step failed or which steps already ran. Later parts cover where these jobs go (Part 7) and how to see what happened to each one (Part 8).

Failures that come together. The simulation assumes every call fails independently. Real failures are often correlated: if the email provider is down for five minutes, all three attempts fail. Treat these numbers as a way to build intuition, not as a prediction.

A restart. The queue still lives in memory. If the process dies after step 4, nothing remembers that steps 1 to 4 were done. Part 6 moves the queue to Redis.

Takeaways

  1. Reliability multiplies: ten steps at 99% give a job that succeeds about 90% of the time.
  2. Retry the step that failed, not the whole job, so the steps that worked do not run again.
  3. Per-step retries still repeat a step whose reply was lost, so side effects need idempotency keys.

Try it

This is a teaching version of multi-step jobs. A more complete implementation comes later in the series. Keep queue.ts from Part 2 and retry.ts from Part 3, and save the workflow.ts file from above next to them. Then save this as simulate.ts:

import { SimpleQueue, type Handler } from "./queue.ts";
import { withRetry, type RetryOptions } from "./retry.ts";
import { retryEachStep, workflow, type Step } from "./workflow.ts";

// Illustrative assumptions (not a real system):
const JOBS = 1_000_000; // signups to simulate
const P_FAIL = 0.01;    // every call to a step fails 1% of the time, independently
const LOST_REPLY = 0.005; // table 2 only: the email goes out, but the reply is lost 0.5% of the time
const STEPS = [
  "save the user", "create the billing customer", "create the workspace", "upload the default avatar",
  "add to the CRM", "subscribe to the newsletter", "send the welcome email", "notify the sales channel",
  "record the analytics event", "schedule the day-3 email",
];
const EMAIL = "send the welcome email";
// Up to 3 attempts. The simulation counts outcomes, not time, so it skips the waits.
const retry: RetryOptions = { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 100, maxDelayMs: 2000, jitter: true, sleep: async () => {} };

// A small seeded random generator (mulberry32), so every run prints the same numbers.
function seededRandom(seed: number) {
  let a = seed;
  return () => {
    a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}

// What each signup job carries: how many times each step really did its work.
type Signup = { done: Record<string, number> };

async function simulate(build: (steps: Step<Signup>[]) => Handler<Signup>, lostReply: number) {
  const random = seededRandom(1);
  let calls = 0;
  const steps: Step<Signup>[] = STEPS.map((name) => ({
    name,
    run: async (job) => {
      calls++;
      if (random() < P_FAIL) throw new Error(`${name}: 503 service unavailable`);
      job.data.done[name] = (job.data.done[name] ?? 0) + 1; // the side effect happened
      if (name === EMAIL && random() < lostReply) throw new Error(`${name}: timeout, reply lost`);
    },
  }));
  const queue = new SimpleQueue<Signup>(build(steps));
  let repeatedSteps = 0;
  let twoEmails = 0;
  for (let start = 0; start < JOBS; start += 10_000) {
    const batch: Signup[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
      const signup: Signup = { done: {} };
      batch.push(signup);
      queue.add(signup);
    }
    await queue.onIdle();
    for (const signup of batch) {
      for (const times of Object.values(signup.done)) repeatedSteps += times - 1;
      if ((signup.done[EMAIL] ?? 0) > 1) twoEmails++;
    }
  }
  const failed = queue.failed.length;
  return {
    succeeded: `${((100 * (JOBS - failed)) / JOBS).toFixed(3)}%`,
    failed,
    halfDone: queue.failed.filter(({ job }) => Object.keys(job.data.done).length > 0).length,
    callsPerJob: Math.round((calls / JOBS) * 100) / 100,
    repeatedSteps,
    twoEmails,
  };
}

const pct = (p: number) => `${(100 * p).toFixed(3)}%`;
const oneTry = (1 - P_FAIL) ** STEPS.length;

async function main() {
  console.log(`1. ${JOBS.toLocaleString("en-US")} signups, ${STEPS.length} steps, each call fails ${P_FAIL * 100}% of the time`);
  console.table([
    { strategy: "no retries", formula: pct(oneTry), ...(await simulate((s) => workflow(s), 0)) },
    { strategy: "retry the whole job", formula: pct(1 - (1 - oneTry) ** 3), ...(await simulate((s) => withRetry(workflow(s), retry), 0)) },
    { strategy: "retry each step", formula: pct((1 - P_FAIL ** 3) ** STEPS.length), ...(await simulate((s) => workflow(retryEachStep(s, retry)), 0)) },
  ]);
  console.log(`2. Same, but the email provider loses the reply ${LOST_REPLY * 100}% of the time`);
  console.table([
    { strategy: "retry each step", ...(await simulate((s) => workflow(retryEachStep(s, retry)), LOST_REPLY)) },
  ]);
}
main();

Run it with Node.js 22, the version I tested:

pnpm dlx tsx simulate.ts

It runs 4,000,000 jobs, so it takes 15 to 20 seconds. The random generator is seeded, so you should see exactly these numbers:

1. 1,000,000 signups, 10 steps, each call fails 1% of the time
┌─────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────┬───────────┬────────┬──────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬───────────┐
│ (index) │ strategy              │ formula   │ succeeded │ failed │ halfDone │ callsPerJob │ repeatedSteps │ twoEmails │
├─────────┼───────────────────────┼───────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼───────────┤
│ 0       │ 'no retries'          │ '90.438%' │ '90.398%' │ 96024  │ 85902    │ 9.56        │ 0             │ 0         │
│ 1       │ 'retry the whole job' │ '99.913%' │ '99.913%' │ 867    │ 865      │ 10.57       │ 462891        │ 29564     │
│ 2       │ 'retry each step'     │ '99.999%' │ '99.999%' │ 9      │ 8        │ 10.1        │ 0             │ 0         │
└─────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────┴───────────┴────────┴──────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴───────────┘
2. Same, but the email provider loses the reply 0.5% of the time
┌─────────┬───────────────────┬───────────┬────────┬──────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬───────────┐
│ (index) │ strategy          │ succeeded │ failed │ halfDone │ callsPerJob │ repeatedSteps │ twoEmails │
├─────────┼───────────────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼───────────┤
│ 0       │ 'retry each step' │ '99.999%' │ 11     │ 10       │ 10.11       │ 4971          │ 4939      │
└─────────┴───────────────────┴───────────┴────────┴──────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴───────────┘

Change P_FAIL or add steps to STEPS and see how quickly the "no retries" row drops.

Next: Part 5 (coming soon) looks at jobs that run twice and how idempotency keys stop the duplicates.

title: A dispatch policy should sort candidates, not filter them
description:
Every dispatcher grows an extension point sooner or later. One operation wants the next job to go to the least loaded courier, another to whoever has been on duty longest, and a third wants a rule nobody has written yet. The obvious shape for that extension point is a hook that picks the courier, and that shape is wrong. A hook that can pick can also reject, and a hook that can reject can also accept something the depot's rules never allowed.

We draw the line somewhere else in shift-planner, our library for planning field courier shifts (https://github.com/shipmindlabs/shift-planner). Eligibility is fixed code inside the dispatcher. The plug-in gets exactly one method, and that method returns a sort key over the shifts that already passed.

Two kinds of rule, two kinds of failure

The distinction worth drawing is about cost, not about taxonomy. A preference that is wrong costs you a worse choice: a courier who was slightly more loaded than the one you would have picked takes the job, and the day comes out marginally less balanced. A constraint that gets bypassed costs you a courier sent to the wrong depot, handed a job past the capacity of their shift, or called again ten minutes after they declined one and were put on a cooldown.

Those two failures differ in size, but what matters more is that they differ in when they show up. If you implement a constraint as a strong preference (rank cooling-down couriers last, rank shifts with no capacity left last) the system behaves correctly for as long as somebody better is available. The moment the shortlist is down to a single candidate, the preference has nothing left to prefer and the violation lands. That is lunchtime, or a storm, or exactly the hour the whole plan exists for. A constraint expressed as a preference is a rule that switches itself off precisely when load is highest.

So what you ask of any plug-in point is not "what does it do when it is written correctly" but "what is the worst a wrong one can do". We want that answer to be a bad ordering, and nothing else.

The filter is fixed code

Dispatcher.candidates builds the eligible list itself. A shift survives three checks, and all three are about the job rather than about preference:

def candidates(
    self, job: Job, taken: Mapping[str, int] | None = None
) -> tuple[Candidate, ...]:
    loads = taken or {}
    eligible = [
        Candidate(shift, loads.get(shift.worker, 0))
        for shift in self.roster
        if shift.location == job.location
        and shift.covers(job.at)
        and not self.cooldowns.locked(shift.worker, job.at)
    ]
    return tuple(
        sorted(
            (candidate for candidate in eligible if candidate.spare_capacity > 0),
            key=self.policy.sort_key,
        )
    )

def assign(
    self, job: Job, taken: Mapping[str, int] | None = None
) -> Candidate | None:
    ordered = self.candidates(job, taken)
    return ordered[0] if ordered else None

Three details in that list carry most of the argument.

The location check is an equality, not a distance. A policy cannot quietly widen it into "nearest depot", because a shift that fails the comparison never becomes a Candidate at all.

covers is the shift's half-open interval test, start <= moment < end, applied to the job's moment rather than to the dispatcher's. No moment in this library comes from the wall clock; every check takes the moment as an argument.

The cooldown gets read at job.at too. A courier who declined a job is held back over the half-open interval [since, until) recorded on the CooldownBoard, and that lock lifts by the passing of time rather than by anybody clearing it. Asking the board about the job's own moment is what makes a replay of yesterday's job stream produce yesterday's answers.

Capacity is the fourth check, and it happens after the list is built, because it depends on something the dispatcher does not own: the load. Candidate.taken is read from the caller's mapping, an absent worker counting as zero, and spare_capacity is max(0, self.shift.capacity - self.taken). A candidate with no spare capacity gets dropped before any ordering happens. Only then does sorted run, and assign returns ordered[0] when the tuple is non-empty and None otherwise.

None is the correct answer to "nobody is eligible". It is also the answer no pick-shaped hook can be trusted to give, because a hook asked to pick one will pick one.

The policy is a sort key and nothing else 

class AssignmentPolicy(Protocol):
    """Orders the candidates for a job; the first one gets it."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LeastLoaded:
    """Prefers the courier with the fewest jobs so far, then the earlier shift."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (candidate.taken, candidate.shift.start, candidate.worker)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EarliestStart:
    """Prefers the courier who has been on duty the longest."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (candidate.shift.start, candidate.taken, candidate.worker)

The Protocol is the whole guarantee. A function from a Candidate to a tuple can reorder what survived the filter. It cannot admit a shift the filter rejected, because it is never shown one. It cannot remove a shift the filter passed, because sorting a sequence returns a permutation of it, and the length does not change whatever the key says.

That bound is worth testing against hostile input rather than reasonable input. Here is a policy nobody should ship, sitting next to one that is a legitimate change of emphasis:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MostSpareCapacity:
    """Prefers the courier with the most room left, then the earlier shift."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (-candidate.spare_capacity, candidate.shift.start, candidate.worker)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Perverse:
    """Deliberately bad: hands the job to the busiest eligible courier."""

    def sort_key(self, candidate: Candidate) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        return (-candidate.taken, candidate.worker)

Perverse is about the worst policy anyone can write inside the rules, and the damage it does is this: the busiest eligible courier gets the job. Still at the right location. Still on duty at the job's moment. Still inside their capacity. Still not cooling down.

That is what makes the extension point cheap to review. A reviewer argues about whether a policy expresses a sensible preference, which is an operations judgement, instead of re-deriving whether it is safe, which would be a correctness judgement repeated on every plug-in anyone ever writes.

The key ends in a name

Both built-in policies end their key with candidate.worker, and that last element does more work than you would guess.

Python's sort is stable, so without a final discriminator an exact tie on the leading fields gets settled by the order in which the candidates arrived. In this library that order comes from Roster, which normalises its shifts to a tuple sorted by (start, end, worker). It is deterministic today, and it is still the wrong thing to lean on: it is a detail of how a different class stores its data, and an assignment that quietly depends on it changes behaviour the day that storage changes, with no test anywhere pointed at the thing that moved.

Ending the key with the worker name makes the tie-break a property of the candidates themselves. It also makes the key total, and it is the roster that earns that: two shifts of one worker may never share time. At most one shift per worker can cover job.at, so within a single job's candidate list every worker name appears exactly once. No residual tie is left for arrival order to decide. The same roster, the same taken mapping and the same moment produce the same assignment on every run, in a test, on a laptop, and in production.

This kind of determinism is not an aesthetic preference. It is what lets you argue about a dispatch decision after the fact. When an operations lead asks why this courier and not that one, the answer is a tuple comparison over values that were all passed in as arguments.

What it costs to run

Three things stay your job as the caller, and they are the three that bite.

The load mapping is yours. Nothing in the library ever increments it. Dispatcher.assign reads taken and returns a Candidate; it does not record that the job was handed out, because it does not know whether your transaction committed. In a batch loop you update the mapping yourself, or LeastLoaded will hand every job in the batch to the same courier, each time correctly, each time on the same stale count.

dispatcher = Dispatcher(roster, policy=MostSpareCapacity())
taken: dict[str, int] = {}

for job in jobs:
    chosen = dispatcher.assign(job, taken)
    if chosen is None:
        continue
    taken[chosen.worker] = taken.get(chosen.worker, 0) + 1

Refusals work the same way. The board is immutable, so recording one returns a new dispatcher instead of mutating the one you held:

dispatcher = dispatcher.refuse("anna", job.at)

And candidates walks the whole roster on every call. For a roster drawn over a long horizon that is a linear scan you pay per job, so dispatch against the slice you actually need rather than the full plan.

Close

The rule we apply when a new dispatch rule turns up in review is short. If getting it wrong sends a courier somewhere they must not go, it belongs in the filter, in fixed code, where there is exactly one copy of it. If getting it wrong only costs a worse choice, it belongs in the key. And whatever the key contains, it ends with a name, so that the candidates, and not the order they happened to arrive in, settle the last tie.

title: A post-quantum migration plan should print its arithmetic
description:
A cryptographic inventory lists what you have. A migration plan claims what to do first, and that claim is an opinion wearing a number. If you cannot recompute the score sitting next to a line, you have two moves available: accept the ordering, or ignore the tool. In my experience you ignore the tool.

I hit this building cbomscope (https://github.com/polycratia/cbomscope), which reads Go source and a live TLS handshake and writes a CycloneDX cryptography bill of materials. The inventory part was uncontroversial. A posture says what a quantum computer would do to an algorithm, which is a property of the algorithm, and nobody argues with a list. The plan command was different: it ranks the same assets by the work they imply, and the first version printed a sorted list with a score column and nothing else. It fell over the first time someone disagreed with it. They could not tell me which part they disagreed with, only that an RSA call in a test helper should not be sitting above the signature algorithm on a public endpoint. That is not feedback about the result. It is feedback about a weight, and the output gave them no way to say so.

The constraint

A migration plan gets read by people who have the authority to reorder it and information the tool does not have. This service is being decommissioned next quarter. That endpoint carries data with a ten-year confidentiality requirement. This dependency is pinned because the upgrade breaks an API nobody here controls. None of that is visible to a program that parses syntax trees and completes handshakes.

So the goal is not to be right about the order. It is to be legible enough that you can overrule one factor without throwing away the whole ordering. A hidden score forces an all-or-nothing judgement on the tool's credibility. A printed one shrinks the argument into something much smaller and much more productive: you think exposure should outweigh lifetime here, and now the conversation is about a number instead of about trust.

Small scales, declared

The weights are not literals buried in a scoring function. Each one is a named Factor (a label, a weight, and a reason), and the scoring functions do nothing but choose a row.

// postureFactor reports the weight of a posture, and false where the posture
// implies no migration at all. Anything it does not recognise — including an
// asset that never reached the classifier — is ranked as unjudged rather than
// settled: silence is not a clean bill of health.
func postureFactor(p asset.Posture) (Factor, bool) {
    switch p {
    case asset.QuantumSafe, asset.Hybrid, asset.NotApplicable:
        return Factor{}, false
    case asset.Broken:
        return brokenNow, true
    case asset.QuantumVulnerable:
        return shorFalls, true
    case asset.QuantumReduced:
        return resizable, true
    }
    return unjudged, true
}

func exposureFactor(a asset.Asset) Factor {
    switch {
    case a.Location.Host != "":
        return atEndpoint
    case a.Module != "":
        return inDependency
    default:
        return firstParty
    }
}

func lifetimeFactor(a asset.Asset) Factor {
    switch a.Primitive {
    case asset.KEM, asset.KeyAgree, asset.PKE:
        return keyExchange
    case asset.Signature:
        return signature
    }
    return storedData
}

Three questions, three scales, and the scales are small on purpose. Key exchange weighs 3 and a signature weighs 1, because the two run on different clocks: what is recorded off the wire today can be decrypted years from now, while a signature is forged at the moment it is verified. That is a deadline rather than a leak, and a deadline you can still move. A one-to-three range is a thing you can hold an opinion about. A zero-to-a-hundred range is not. It only looks more precise, and the extra digits are where fabricated confidence hides.

Why posture multiplies and the rest adds

exposure, lifetime := exposureFactor(a), lifetimeFactor(a)
report.Items = append(report.Items, Item{
    Asset:    a,
    Score:    posture.Weight * (exposure.Weight + lifetime.Weight),
    Posture:  posture,
    Exposure: exposure,
    Lifetime: lifetime,
})

The shape of the expression is itself a claim, and it should be one you can defend out loud. Exposure and lifetime add because they are independent reasons to move sooner: being reachable from the internet and protecting long-lived secrets are separate problems, and an asset with one of them is still work. Posture multiplies because it scales both. A classically broken primitive makes every other property worse, and a sound one makes them moot. Addition there would let a pile of mild factors out-rank something already broken, which is the failure mode people notice and do not forgive.

The expression goes next to the line

This is the whole argument in one method:

// Arithmetic is the score written out, so the number in a column can be checked
// against the line that carries it.
func (i Item) Arithmetic() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("%s (%d) × [%s (%d) + %s (%d)]",
        i.Posture.Name, i.Posture.Weight,
        i.Exposure.Name, i.Exposure.Weight,
        i.Lifetime.Name, i.Lifetime.Weight)
}

Every ranked line carries the expression that produced its number, in named terms rather than bare integers. You do not have to find the source, and you do not have to take my word for the ordering: you can see that this line scored where it did because it was found at an endpoint and because it is a key agreement, and you can decide that in your deployment the second term is wrong. The factors also survive the JSON output, along with the formula itself on the report, so a plan that travels into a ticket arrives with its reasoning attached instead of a column of integers somebody has to reverse-engineer later.

The same instinct runs one layer down. The classification table prints on its own, with the published source each verdict was read from, because a reviewer who wants to check a posture should not have to read the source to find out where the verdict came from. And a family missing from that listing is the honest shape of a gap.

Settled, not dropped

The first version filtered out the assets with nothing to do. That is the natural implementation and it is a quiet lie:

// Settled are the assets with no migration work: post-quantum, hybrid, or
// carrying no posture of their own. They are counted rather than dropped,
// because a report that omits what it checked reads exactly like one that
// never looked.
Settled []asset.Asset `json:"settled"`

A plan listing four items and a plan listing four items out of sixty are different documents, and the difference matters most to you when you are deciding whether to believe the first number. Post-quantum algorithms, hybrid key exchange, and protocol versions with no posture of their own all go into Settled with their locations intact. The hybrid line earns its place in particular: on a deployment that has already moved its key exchange, the fact that something was checked and found to need nothing is the single most useful sentence in the report.

The weight I expect to defend

Anything the classifier did not recognise, including an explicit unknown posture, ranks at 2, above the Grover-reduced assets at 1. People read that as a bug. It is the one weight I most want printed, because it is the one most worth arguing with: an asset nobody has judged is not a settled asset, and a ranking that sorts unknowns to the bottom turns a gap in the table into a clean bill of health. The same refusal shows up elsewhere in the tool. A key size of zero means not determined rather than small, the classical security level returns zero rather than invent a number, modulus sizes between the published pairs are left out rather than interpolated, and a citation stays empty on an unknown so that a printed source does not make a gap look checked.

If you decide unjudged should sit below resizable for your codebase, you are now making an informed local decision. That is a better outcome than agreement, I think, and it is only reachable because the number is shown in parts.

What I would do differently

The facts the tool cannot see still have nowhere to go. Today someone who knows a service is being decommissioned has to apply that knowledge in their head, after the sort. I would rather it entered as an exposure override on the input side, so the adjustment shows up inside the printed expression like every other factor. A plan corrected by a human should still be a plan whose arithmetic you can read, not one with a silent post-processing step bolted to the end.

I would also hold the line hard on scale size. Every request to make the ranking smarter arrives as a request for one more factor, and three factors with reasons beat seven with none. The moment the expression stops fitting beside the line it describes, it stops being checkable, and an unchecked score is back to being an opinion.

The product is the expression. The number is just what it evaluates to.
