title: PhotoCraft Review: I Tested the Free, Open-Source Photoshop Alternative With 4 Real Edits
description:
Photoshop costs $22.99 a month. PhotoCraft costs $0, it's open source, and in under three weeks it passed 66,000 stars on GitHub.

So I put it to work on my Mac mini M4 with four real edits, the kind most of us actually do: cutting someone out, a caption meme, fixing a dull photo, and text for a meme video. Here is what worked, step by step, and what it still can't do.

▶ Full video: https://youtu.be/O4necNCA5D4

What is PhotoCraft?

PhotoCraft is a free copy of Photoshop, rebuilt from scratch in the Rust language. It's part of ArtCraft, a family of open-source clones of creative apps.

  • Open source: all the code is public on GitHub, so anyone can read it, fix it or improve it.
  • Runs everywhere: Mac, Windows, Linux, and even in your web browser.
  • Offline: no account, no subscription, no cloud.
  • Opens real PSD files with your layers still editable.

Install and quick tour

  1. Go to getartcraft.com (or the GitHub releases page) and pick the file for your computer.
  2. On a Mac, open the DMG and drag PhotoCraft into Applications.
  3. Open it. If you've used Photoshop, it will feel familiar: 67 tools on the left (move, select, crop, brush, text…) and layers on the right. Every edit sits on its own layer, like sheets of glass.

Edit 1: Cut out anyone (The Rock eyebrow meme)

  1. Open a frame from the meme.
  2. Press Command + F and search for Subject. PhotoCraft finds the person by itself, in about a tenth of a second.
  3. Layer → Layer Mask → Reveal Selection. The background is gone.
  4. Open any background photo, Select All → Copy, and paste it into the meme.
  5. Layer → Arrange → Send to Back, so it sits behind him.
  6. Add a caption with the Type tool, then give it a Stroke from the fx button so it pops on any background.

Result: a brand-new meme, and every layer is still editable.

Edit 2: The classic caption meme (Surprised Pikachu)

  1. Open a frame from the meme video.
  2. Image → Canvas Size. Anchor at the bottom, make it taller, and fill with white. Now there's room on top for the joke.
  3. Type tool, black text, write the caption. Tip: the best captions fit in two lines.
  4. File → Export as a PNG, and post it.

Edit 3: Make a dull photo pop, the pro way

  1. Layer → New Adjustment Layer → Curves. Bend the line into an S shape for more contrast.
  2. Add a Vibrance adjustment layer to bring the colours back.

Adjustment layers never change your original photo: turn them off and it's untouched. The same two layers work on selfies, product photos and thumbnails.

Edit 4: Text for a meme video

  1. File → New, background Transparent.
  2. Write your caption and give it a stroke and a drop shadow.
  3. Export as PNG. The empty parts stay see-through.
  4. Drop that PNG on top of any clip in your video editor.

Bonus: scripts and AI agents can drive it

Every button in PhotoCraft is also a command, over 500 of them. So scripts, and even AI agents, can run the same edits, with the same engine and the same results.

The honest part

  • PhotoCraft is still early alpha. The team says it's not yet a Photoshop replacement for daily professional work.
  • There's no generative AI yet, some tools are missing, and you will hit bugs.
  • But for memes, thumbnails and quick photo fixes, it already does the job, for free.

Price check (October 18, 2026)

  • Adobe Photoshop: US$22.99/month (annual plan, billed monthly, adobe.com)
  • PhotoCraft: free, open source

Links

  • Full video: https://youtu.be/O4necNCA5D4
  • Download PhotoCraft: https://getartcraft.com/apps/photocraft
  • Source code: https://github.com/storytold/photocraft

Would you switch from Photoshop? Tell me in the comments.

title: I Built a Remote to Answer Claude Code From My Phone
description:
Hello there!

If you run Claude Code or Codex for real work, you know the moment. You start a task, it runs for a while, and you go make a coffee. When you come back, the agent has been waiting ten minutes for you to answer one question.

"The fix is in. What should I do with it?"

That question is why I built Farol Remote. It lets you answer your coding agents from your phone, wherever you are, while the work keeps running on your Mac or on your own server.

A bit of context

Farol is a macOS terminal I made for coding agents. Its sidebar shows every session with a small dot: hollow when idle, breathing while the agent works, rippling when it waits for you, filled when it's done.

It tells you when an agent needs you. But only if you're at your Mac.

So the idea was simple. Put that sidebar in my pocket. See the sessions, read the conversation, and answer with a tap.

What the phone does

The iPhone app lists your sessions with their status and opens each one as its agent's conversation, not as a wall of terminal text.

When the agent asks for an approval or a question, the answers show up as buttons. One tap and it carries on. You can also reply with a slash command, send a screenshot for the agent to look at, review what changed file by file, and start a new session in a project.

It notifies you when an agent waits or finishes. And a Live Activity on the lock screen keeps count of the agents that work or wait, even with the app closed.

One phone can know several Macs and servers at once. Your work Mac and a server you run agents on show up in the same list, each session labeled with its host.

The hard part: the middle

A phone and a Mac don't talk to each other directly over the internet. Your Mac sits behind a home router, your phone is on 4G, and neither can reach the other.

So there's a relay in between. Both sides connect out to it, and it passes messages along.

That raises the obvious question. If everything goes through a server, what can that server see? These messages are your code, your prompts, and a phone that can type into your terminal. I didn't want the answer to be "trust me".

The goal became this: the relay passes messages it cannot read, and keeps none of them.

Pairing, once

It all starts with a QR code. On the Mac you turn on Remote in Settings and press Show code. On the phone you scan it.

The code carries three things: the relay's address, the Mac's public key, and a secret made just for that code. It's a link, and everything rides after the #.

func (o offer) link() string {
    text, _ := json.Marshal(o)
    return "https://farol.sh/pair#" + base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(text)
}

The part after the # is never sent to a server. So the secret never reaches the relay, which means the relay can't pair a device of its own.

The phone answers with one sealed message that proves two things at once: it holds the key it claims, and it saw the secret. A code works once and lasts two minutes. After that, the Mac knows the phone's key and the phone knows the Mac's.

Every connection

Each time they connect, both sides say hello in the clear with their public key and a random number made for this connection.

Then each direction becomes its own HPKE stream, sealed to the other side's key and signed with ours. I used CryptoKit's Curve25519_SHA256_ChachaPoly suite. Here's the sending side on the Mac and the phone:

public mutating func connect(to peer: ChannelHello, trusting trusted: [Data]) throws -> Data {
    guard trusted.contains(peer.key) else { throw RemoteError.unknownDevice }
    let sender = try HPKE.Sender(
        recipientKey: Curve25519.KeyAgreement.PublicKey(rawRepresentation: peer.key), ciphersuite: Pairing.suite,
        info: info(from: side, with: peer), authenticatedBy: me.secret)
    self.peer = peer
    self.sender = sender
    return sender.encapsulatedKey
}

The info includes both hello numbers. So a recording of an older connection doesn't open on a new one, and messages only open in the order they were sealed. If one fails to open, the connection ends.

What the relay actually sees

Mostly bytes.

It sees a public key, and a room name that's the hash of the host's key. That's how a Mac and its phones find each other without the relay learning who they are.

func room(public []byte) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256(public)
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

Then it sees encrypted messages and how big they are. It stores none of it, and its log holds totals only.

Notifications without reading anything

This one was fun. I wanted a notification when an agent waits, even with the app closed. That means Apple has to push it, and something has to ask Apple.

The Mac asks the relay to forward a push. The relay sees the phone's notification token and one word: waiting or done. Which session it's about travels sealed, for the phone alone.

The Live Activity works the same way. The host keeps it current through the relay, so the counts on your lock screen move while the app sleeps.

Running Claude Code on a server with tmux

Some people run their agents on a machine that stays on, so they can close the laptop. For them there's farol-host, a small Go CLI.

curl -fsSL https://farol.sh/host.sh | sh
farol-host setup

Setup connects the hooks for Claude Code and Codex, keeps farol-host running with systemd, and shows a QR code to scan. Then every tmux window on that machine is a session on your phone, like a tab in Farol on the Mac.

tmux new -s api -c ~/code/api
claude

One protocol, two languages

The Mac and the iPhone share a Swift package. The server speaks the same protocol, written again in Go.

Two implementations of the same crypto and messages is a great way to have bugs that only show up on a real phone. So they check each other.

The Swift tests write sample messages and a sealed conversation to JSON files. The Go tests open those files and must read them exactly. When a message changes, I regenerate them:

FAROL_WRITE_WIRE=1 swift test

If Go and Swift disagree on a single field, a test fails before any phone sees it.

What's not covered yet

I'd rather say this upfront.

If a host's key were stolen later, traffic recorded from a phone to that host could be read. A host also doesn't prove itself to the relay yet, so someone who learned a room's name could knock the real host off. They couldn't read or send anything, but it's still on my list.

And the pairing and the encryption haven't had an outside review. If that's your thing, I'd love a second pair of eyes. It's all in one small repo, on purpose.

Try it

Farol is free and open source. The iPhone app is free too, in beta on TestFlight. In Farol, open Settings, choose Remote, turn it on, press Show code, and scan it from the app.

The security parts live in farol-remote: the Swift package, the relay, and farol-host. The security page goes deeper than this post.

Hope you find it useful! Feel free to open an issue or contribute. And next time your agent asks you a question while you're out, you can just answer it. ☕

title: I open-sourced Commune: a TypeScript MERN community platform you can fork and build on
description:
I wanted a full-stack project that goes beyond a todo app, something with real
authentication, real data modeling and a structure other developers could learn from.
So I built Commune, an open source community platform on the MERN stack, and I'm
releasing it today.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/Haseeb-MernStack/commune.git

What it is

Commune is a TypeScript monorepo with a React frontend, an Express + MongoDB backend
and a shared package for validation and types.

What's inside

  • Secure auth: short-lived JWT access tokens plus rotating httpOnly refresh cookies. Refresh tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes with a TTL index.
  • Posts, comments and likes: with cursor-based pagination and a database-enforced one-like-per-user rule.
  • Shared Zod schemas: the same validation runs in the browser and on the server, so the two never drift apart.
  • Hardening: Helmet, CORS, rate limiting, body size limits and centralized error handling.
  • Tooling: Docker Compose for MongoDB and the API, plus a GitHub Actions workflow.

Tech stack

React 18 · Vite · TanStack Query · Express · Mongoose · Zod · TypeScript · Docker

Run it locally 

git clone https://github.com/Haseeb-MernStack/commune.git
cd commune
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d mongo
npm install
npm run dev

The API runs on localhost:4000 and the web app on localhost:5173.

Where I'd love your help

  • Follows and a personalized feed
  • Image uploads
  • Real-time notifications
  • Moderation tools
  • More tests, especially database-backed ones

I've labeled a few issues good first issue so it's easy to jump in. If you're
looking for your first open source contribution, this is a friendly place to start.

Feedback welcome

What would you build first? What would you change in the architecture? Tell me in the
comments, and if the project is useful to you, a ⭐ on GitHub means a lot.

title: Design in the material you ship
description:
Designers should understand code the way an architect understands stone: what it can do, not how to cut it. AI now does the cutting.

Early in The Fountainhead, Howard Roark is expelled from architecture school for refusing to design in borrowed styles. The Dean calls him in to explain himself, and Roark gives him a rule instead: “What can be done with one substance must never be done with another. No two materials are alike. No two sites on earth are alike. No two buildings have the same purpose. The purpose, the site, the material determine the shape.”

You don’t have to admire Roark to take the point. He is the architect in the book who spends his time on building sites, among the electricians and steelworkers, learning what the material will and won’t do. His classmates learn to draw facades.

Digital designers have a material too. It is code. For most of the last fifteen years, we have designed in pictures of it. The warning is older than that. John Allsopp asked the web to stop imitating print in 2000, Frank Chimero wrote about working with the web’s grain in 2015, and Jeremy Keith gave its materials a chapter of their own in Resilient Web Design.

The drawing is not the building

A design file is a drawing. It shows one state, at one width, in one language, with the data the designer typed in. The product is every other state.

The name is longer than the box. A short English label can double in length once it is translated. The photo fails to load. The list is empty. The request takes four seconds, or fails. Someone tabs through with a keyboard. The phone is 320 pixels wide. None of those is an edge case to the person it happens to, and none of them exists in the file until someone draws it by hand, which in practice means rarely.

When the file is the source of truth, each of those gaps gets decided by whoever writes the code, after the design is called done, and usually without a conversation. The file and the product drift apart, and the file keeps being presented in reviews as if it were the product.

What changed when the code became the source

When I built 131 variations of one button to study hover feedback, I built them in code. The surprise was what happened to the specification. In a design file, a jelly button is an adjective: tactile. In code, it is a handful of numbers. The pointer starts to count 36 pixels from the edge, the material has a stiffness, and it settles back in under a second. An engineer can build a number. Nobody can build an adjective.

I now work the same way on a product team. The prototype in code is what gets reviewed. The design file still exists, because people like to leave comments on a canvas, but it is regenerated from the code after each pass, never the other way round. Its job is to be a mirror.

Roark’s rule applies almost word for word. A responsive layout, a loading state and a focus ring belong to the browser. Drawing them in a canvas tool is doing with one substance what belongs to another.

You no longer have to write it

This is where the old version of the argument went wrong. For a decade, “designers should code” meant designers should learn to write HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Many tried, many quit, and they were right to resent it. It asked them to become a second, slower engineer. Brad Frost later drew a more useful line, between the front of the front end, which sits close to design, and the application logic behind it.

That argument is over, because AI writes the code. I describe the screen, its states and its numbers, and the model writes it. I correct it by looking at the result and saying what is wrong, the way an architect corrects a site, not by laying the bricks again myself.

Reading code is going the same way. It still helps, and I read diffs most days. But AI review tools read them too, and they are improving quickly. In one benchmark this year, the best reviewer caught 84 of 122 real bugs taken from production codebases such as Sentry and Grafana. The vendor that won ran the test, and two thirds is not all of them. So the claim is not that the machine has replaced the reviewer. It is that the designer no longer needs to be the reviewer.

Engineers reading this will object, and they have a point. In Stack Overflow’s 2025 developer survey, 66 percent named AI answers that are almost right, but not quite, as their top frustration, and 46 percent said they distrust its accuracy. Someone accountable for the system still has to read what goes into it. That person is the engineer who owns it. The designer has a different job.

Understanding is the part you can’t delegate

What Roark took from the building site was not the skill of riveting. It was knowing what steel will do, so that his drawings only asked for things the material could give.

That is the part AI can’t hold for you. It will write whatever you describe, including things the medium handles badly, and it will review the code against the code, not against what the person on the other end needed. Judging that takes someone who knows the material.

You judge the output by running it, not by reading it. Open it at 320 pixels. Paste the longest real name you can find. Set the network to slow. Put the mouse away and use the keyboard. None of those tests needs a line of syntax.

What to learn instead of syntax

  • How layout flows: what wraps, what stretches, what refuses to shrink.
  • Which states exist: empty, loading, partial, failed, offline.
  • The shape of the data, including what a field holds when it holds nothing.
  • What costs a trip to the server and what is free on the device.
  • What a screen reader actually announces on your screen.
  • How to run the product on your own machine, without help.
  • How to ask the AI to explain a change in plain words.

None of these requires writing code. All of them require spending time with it.

The material determines the shape

Roark’s rule ends where this argument does: the purpose, the site and the material determine the shape. Our material hasn’t changed. It is still code, and it still decides what a screen can be. What changed is that we no longer have to hold the chisel to learn what it can cut.

title: A small usability test for personal search tools
description:
A demo search often starts with a query the builder already knows will work. A more useful test starts with a person who remembers the purpose of a resource but not its title.

Here is a small test plan I would use before adding complexity to a personal search tool.

Prepare a realistic collection

Ask a participant to save five to ten resources they genuinely care about. Include a mixture of formats if the product supports them: an article, a screenshot, a link, or a note. Let them add context in their normal words.

Return later rather than testing immediately after saving. The delay is part of the task: the interface should help after the title has faded from memory.

Ask for an outcome, not a query

Instead of “search for onboarding,” ask: “Find the example you wanted to use for your project's welcome screen.” Let the participant choose their own search terms.

Record the first query, any reformulations, which results they inspect, and whether they identify the right resource. Ask them what makes a result look relevant. A result can be retrieved correctly and still be hard to recognize.

Diagnose the failure layer

If the resource never appears, investigate which searchable fields were available. If it appears but is overlooked, examine the title, preview, and saved context. If the user finds it but cannot reuse it, the destination or source may be the problem.

Those are different failures and need different changes. Improving ranking will not repair an unreadable result card.

Repeat after one focused change

Try a change such as exposing the user's note beneath the result title. Use another retrieval task and compare observations. With a small exploratory test, treat the outcome as a design clue rather than a population-wide performance claim.

Némos's “can you find it again?” prompt is useful because it shifts attention from how much we save to what saving lets us do later.
