title: Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial — Complete Guide
description:
Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial — Complete Guide

A practical, in-depth guide to Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial with examples.

INTRO

Modern APIs are expected to be stateless, scalable, and secure out of the box. Yet, every time you spin up a new Spring Boot service, you end up wrestling with session cookies, CSRF tokens, and a maze of configuration classes just to protect a single endpoint. The result is brittle code that either over‑exposes resources or locks down everything, forcing developers to write ad‑hoc filters that are hard to test and maintain.

JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provide a clean solution: a self‑contained, signed token that travels with each request, allowing the server to stay stateless while still enforcing fine‑grained access control. The challenge isn’t the concept—it’s wiring JWT correctly into Spring Security’s filter chain, handling token refresh, and mapping claims to authorities without turning your configuration into a spaghetti mess. This guide cuts through the noise, delivering a production‑ready setup you can drop into any Spring Boot project.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

  • How to generate and sign JWTs with asymmetric keys, keeping private keys out of source control.
  • Configuring Spring Security’s filter chain to validate tokens, reject tampered requests, and populate Authentication objects automatically.
  • Mapping JWT claims to Spring GrantedAuthority objects for role‑based access control.
  • Implementing a refresh‑token endpoint that rotates tokens safely and mitigates replay attacks.
  • Testing the security layer with MockMvc and integration tests to guarantee your endpoints behave as expected.
  • Common pitfalls (e.g., token expiration handling, clock skew, and insecure token storage) and how to avoid them.

A SHORT CODE SNIPPET 

@Component
public class JwtAuthenticationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {

private final JwtProvider jwtProvider;
private final UserDetailsService userDetailsService;

public JwtAuthenticationFilter(JwtProvider jwtProvider,
UserDetailsService userDetailsService) {
this.jwtProvider = jwtProvider;
this.userDetailsService = userDetailsService;
}

@Override
protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
HttpServletResponse response,
FilterChain filterChain) throws ServletException, IOException {
String token = jwtProvider.resolveToken(request);
if (token != null && jwtProvider.validateToken(token)) {
String username = jwtProvider.getUsername(token);
UserDetails userDetails = userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(username);
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken auth =
new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(userDetails, null, userDetails.getAuthorities());
SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth);
}
filterChain.doFilter(request, response);
}
}

The snippet shows the heart of a JWT‑based security filter: extracting the token, validating its signature and expiration, then building a Spring Authentication object that downstream code can rely on.

KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • Stateless security is achievable with Spring Security – By delegating authentication to a JWT filter, you eliminate server‑side sessions and simplify horizontal scaling.
  • Never hard‑code secrets – Use environment variables or a secret manager for signing keys; the guide demonstrates loading RSA keys from a keystore.
  • Claims drive authorization – Store roles or permissions inside the token and translate them to GrantedAuthority objects, keeping your business logic clean.
  • Refresh tokens are a must – Short‑lived access tokens reduce attack windows, while refresh tokens let clients stay logged in without re‑authenticating.

👉 Read the complete guide with step-by-step examples, common mistakes, and production tips:
Spring Security JWT authentication and authorization tutorial — Complete Guide

title: Permissions Hadn't Changed, but QA Said 'I Can't Create' — Answering with a Table Uncovered an Unreachable Branch
description:
The question

QA for our internal business system sent me this:

I can't create a project. Did it change so that only executives can create them now?

Short answer: no, the permission rules hadn't changed at all. But the question turned out to be valuable. While building a permission table to answer it, I cross-checked the code — and found a branch that could never execute. Dead code, alive in production. Here's how it happened.

Background: we had just changed how roles are stored

Shortly before this, we changed how job roles are modeled.

  • Before: one role per user
  • After: one role per affiliation (seat) — to support concurrent posts and secondments, a user can hold multiple affiliations, each with its own role

The project-creation rules themselves were untouched:

Role Can create projects in
Chairman / Secretary Entire group
President / Executive Own company
Department head / Section chief / Team leader Own org and below
Team member Nowhere

The "did the system change?" question almost certainly came because of that recent refactor. When a system is being actively changed, every unrelated symptom starts looking like a side effect of "that change."

Trying to answer with a table, I read the code

I could have just replied "nothing changed," but for permission questions, a table is the most reliable answer. To build the table above, I re-read the actual check:

Scope scopeOf(long userSeq, Role role) {
    if (role == CHAIRMAN || role == SECRETARY) return companyWide();
    if (role == PRESIDENT || role == EXECUTIVE) return ownCompany();
    if (role == TEAM_MEMBER) return denied();  // ← early return

    // Per-affiliation branch (added in the refactor):
    // even if the primary affiliation is "team member",
    // a section chief seat elsewhere can create under that org
    for (Affiliation a : affiliationsOf(userSeq)) {
        if (a.role().isLeaderOrAbove()) {
            return orgScope(a.org());
        }
    }
    return denied();
}

See it? The for loop was added during the per-affiliation refactor, precisely to handle "primary affiliation is team member, but section chief somewhere else." But above it, the pre-refactor early return for TEAM_MEMBER was never removed.

Since the role argument carries the primary affiliation's role, any user whose primary role is team member hits return denied() on line 3 — and the loop below it never runs. The code we wrote for concurrent-post users had never executed, not even once.

The compiler can't warn you about this. Syntactically, both branches are reachable. Code written after a return statement triggers an unreachable-code error, but a branch that's unreachable because of how the conditions combine can only be found by a human reading the code — or by a test.

The fix: drop TEAM_MEMBER from the early return

The fix itself was small: stop short-circuiting on "team member," and read the affiliations before judging.

Scope scopeOf(long userSeq, Role role) {
    if (role == CHAIRMAN || role == SECRETARY) return companyWide();
    if (role == PRESIDENT || role == EXECUTIVE) return ownCompany();

    // If any seat is leader-or-above: that org and below. Otherwise: denied.
    for (Affiliation a : affiliationsOf(userSeq)) {
        if (a.role().isLeaderOrAbove()) {
            return orgScope(a.org());
        }
    }
    return denied();
}

I verified with a user whose primary affiliation is a team member but who holds a section-chief seat at another company:

  • the creation-scope API returns allowed: true with the section-chief org
  • a project-creation POST under that section returns 201
  • creation under the primary org still returns 403

One more thing: deployment timing. If the server restarts while QA is in the middle of testing exactly this permission area, they get confused by unrelated errors. I scheduled the release for 14:00, right after lunch break, so the restart landed between test sessions.

Answering QA

The answer to the original question was simple: "The permission rules haven't changed — here's who can create where," with the table attached. And for the cases where creation still fails, I asked three things:

  • which account, and that account's affiliations and roles
  • whether the create button is missing or clicking it errors out (and if so, the exact message)
  • which organization was selected as the creation target

A bare "it doesn't work" is unreproducible for permission bugs, so having these triage questions templated saves a lot of round trips.

Takeaways

  • When you add a branch below an early return, check that the branch is actually reachable. The compiler won't catch condition-level unreachability; only a human read or a test will. If we'd had a concurrent-post user in the test suite from day one, we'd have caught this at refactor time.
  • Answer permission questions with a table. Building the table forces you to re-read the implementation, and mismatches between the rules and the code — like this dead branch — surface along the way.
  • Schedule permission-related deploys outside QA's testing hours. A single restart at the wrong moment costs you trust.

A naive-sounding "did the system change?" ended up unearthing a latent bug. I'm grateful for the question.

title: Resize Observer and Mutation Observer
description:
The Dynamic Duo of the DOM: Mastering Resize Observer and Mutation Observer

Ever felt like your web page was a shy chameleon, struggling to adapt to its ever-changing environment? Maybe you’ve battled with JavaScript that felt like wrestling an octopus just to know when an element’s size changed, or perhaps you’ve spent hours debugging why your dynamic content wasn’t being picked up by your scripts. If this sounds familiar, then let me introduce you to your new best friends: Resize Observer and Mutation Observer.

These two unsung heroes of the modern web are powerful APIs that allow you to observe changes happening within your Document Object Model (DOM) without the constant need for polling or overly complex event listeners. Think of them as your vigilant guardians, quietly watching for specific events and promptly alerting you when something noteworthy occurs.

In this deep dive, we’ll unravel the magic of these observers, understand when and why you’d reach for them, and arm you with the knowledge and code snippets to wield them like a seasoned web wizard. So, grab a coffee, settle in, and let’s explore the fascinating world of DOM observation!

Introduction: Why Bother with Observers?

Historically, dealing with DOM changes could be a bit of a pain.

  • Resizing elements: If you wanted to know when an element’s dimensions changed (e.g., due to a window resize, a browser zoom, or the user resizing a div), you’d often resort to listening for the resize event on the window object. This is fine, but it’s a blunt instrument. You’d have to manually check the dimensions of every element you cared about within that event handler, which can be inefficient, especially on complex pages.
  • Content changes: When new elements were added, removed, or attributes were modified dynamically, keeping your JavaScript in sync was a challenge. You might have had to re-query the DOM, re-attach event listeners, or implement complex polling mechanisms.

Resize Observer and Mutation Observer were born out of the need for more precise, efficient, and declarative ways to react to these DOM fluctuations. They offer a more performant and less intrusive way to manage dynamic web content.

The Prerequisites: What You Need to Know

Before we dive headfirst into the code, a little foundational knowledge will make things smoother:

  • Basic JavaScript: You should be comfortable with JavaScript fundamentals, including functions, variables, and DOM manipulation (e.g., document.getElementById, appendChild, removeChild).
  • Understanding the DOM: A solid grasp of what the DOM is and how elements are structured within it is crucial.
  • Modern Browser Support: Both Resize Observer and Mutation Observer are well-supported in modern browsers. However, if you need to support older browsers, you might need to consider polyfills, though this is becoming less common.

Section 1: Resize Observer – The Dimension Detective

Imagine you have a flexible layout, a widget that needs to adjust its content based on its available space, or an image gallery that needs to re-render thumbnails when the container size changes. This is where Resize Observer shines.

What is Resize Observer?

Resize Observer is a powerful JavaScript API that allows you to asynchronously observe changes to the dimensions of elements. It fires a callback function whenever the size of one of the observed elements changes. This includes changes to its contentRect, borderBoxSize, and contentBoxSize.

The Magic of the Callback

The core of Resize Observer is its callback function. This function receives an array of ResizeObserverEntry objects, one for each element that has changed. Each ResizeObserverEntry object provides valuable information about the observed element's new dimensions.

Here’s a simplified look at the callback signature:

const resizeObserver = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    // 'entry' is a ResizeObserverEntry object
    console.log('Element size changed:', entry.target);
    console.log('New dimensions:', entry.contentRect); // More accessible in older specs
    // Newer specs provide more granular details:
    console.log('Content Box Size:', entry.contentBoxSize);
    console.log('Border Box Size:', entry.borderBoxSize);
  }
});

How to Use It: A Step-by-Step Guide

  1. Create a Resize Observer instance:

    const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
  // Your logic here to handle size changes
  for (let entry of entries) {
    console.log(`Element ${entry.target.id} has resized!`);
    // You can access various properties of the entry
    console.log('Content Rect:', entry.contentRect);
    // For more precise measurements, use borderBoxSize or contentBoxSize
    if (entry.contentBoxSize) {
      const contentBox = entry.contentBoxSize[0]; // Assuming horizontal-writing mode
      console.log(`New width: ${contentBox.inlineSize}, New height: ${contentBox.blockSize}`);
    }
  }
});

  2. Target the elements you want to observe:
    You can observe one or multiple elements.

    const myElement = document.getElementById('myResizableDiv');
const anotherElement = document.querySelector('.flexible-widget');

observer.observe(myElement);
observer.observe(anotherElement);

  3. Perform actions when dimensions change:
    Inside the callback, you can trigger any JavaScript logic you need. This could be:

    • Adjusting CSS styles.
    • Re-rendering charts or canvases.
    • Fetching new data if the layout dictates.
    • Updating UI elements. 
    const observer = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
  for (let entry of entries) {
    if (entry.target.id === 'myResizableDiv') {
      const newWidth = entry.contentRect.width;
      if (newWidth < 300) {
        entry.target.style.fontSize = '12px';
      } else {
        entry.target.style.fontSize = '16px';
      }
    }
  }
});

const resizableDiv = document.getElementById('myResizableDiv');
observer.observe(resizableDiv);

  4. Stop observing (when you're done):
    It’s good practice to unobserve elements when they are no longer needed to prevent memory leaks.

    observer.unobserve(myElement); // To stop observing a specific element

// To stop observing all elements and disconnect the observer:
observer.disconnect();

When to Use Resize Observer: The Use Cases

  • Responsive Design Helpers: While CSS media queries are king for layout, Resize Observer can be a powerful supplement for JavaScript-driven responsive behaviors within components.
  • Third-Party Widgets: If you’re embedding a widget that needs to adapt to its container size, Resize Observer is the way to go.
  • Drag-and-Drop Interfaces: When users are resizing elements with drag handles, this observer can ensure the content within the resized element updates correctly.
  • Data Visualization: Charts and graphs often need to re-render or adjust their axes and labels when their container changes size.
  • Layout Adjustments: Dynamically calculating positions or dimensions of elements based on their current size.

Advantages of Resize Observer

  • Performance: It’s asynchronous and efficient. It only triggers when actual size changes occur, avoiding the overhead of polling.
  • Granular Control: You get precise information about the element’s dimensions.
  • Declarative: You declare what you want to observe, and the browser handles the rest.
  • Element-Specific: You can observe individual elements, making it very targeted.

Disadvantages of Resize Observer

  • No Window Resize Event: It doesn't directly listen for the window.resize event. You still might need to combine it with window.resize if you need to trigger broader layout adjustments.
  • Browser Support (Minor Concern): While excellent now, always be mindful of your target audience’s browser versions.

Section 2: Mutation Observer – The Content Custodian

Now, let’s shift our attention to another crucial aspect of dynamic web pages: content modification. What if you have a chat application where new messages are constantly being added? Or a dashboard that updates data dynamically? Or perhaps a JavaScript framework that injects or removes DOM elements? This is where Mutation Observer becomes your indispensable ally.

What is Mutation Observer?

Mutation Observer is an API that provides a way to react to changes made to the DOM. It allows you to watch for specific types of mutations (additions, removals, attribute changes) within a target node and its descendants. When a mutation occurs, it triggers a callback function.

The Power of the Callback (Again!)

Similar to Resize Observer, Mutation Observer also relies on a callback function. This callback receives an array of MutationRecord objects, each detailing a specific change that happened.

Here’s a peek at the callback:

const mutationObserver = new MutationObserver((mutationsList, observer) => {
  for (const mutation of mutationsList) {
    if (mutation.type === 'childList') {
      console.log('A child node has been added or removed.');
      // mutation.addedNodes and mutation.removedNodes are useful here
    } else if (mutation.type === 'attributes') {
      console.log(`The ${mutation.attributeName} attribute was modified.`);
      // mutation.oldValue can be useful if observed
    } else if (mutation.type === 'characterData') {
      console.log('Character data (text content) changed.');
    }
  }
});

How to Use It: A Step-by-Step Guide

  1. Create a Mutation Observer instance:
    You need to specify the types of mutations you want to observe.

    const observer = new MutationObserver((mutations, obs) => {
  mutations.forEach(mutation => {
    console.log(`Mutation type: ${mutation.type}`);

    if (mutation.type === 'childList') {
      console.log('Nodes added:', mutation.addedNodes);
      console.log('Nodes removed:', mutation.removedNodes);
      // You can iterate through addedNodes and perform actions
      mutation.addedNodes.forEach(node => {
        if (node.nodeType === Node.ELEMENT_NODE) {
          console.log(`New element added: ${node.tagName}`);
          // Attach event listeners, process content, etc.
        }
      });
    } else if (mutation.type === 'attributes') {
      console.log(`Attribute ${mutation.attributeName} changed from ${mutation.oldValue} to ${mutation.target.getAttribute(mutation.attributeName)}`);
    } else if (mutation.type === 'characterData') {
      console.log(`Text content changed.`);
    }
  });
});

  2. Target the element to observe and configure options:
    You specify the target node and an options object to define what to watch for.

    const targetNode = document.getElementById('contentArea');

const config = {
  attributes: true,        // Observe attribute changes
  childList: true,         // Observe additions/removals of child nodes
  subtree: true,           // Observe all descendants
  characterData: true,     // Observe text content changes
  attributeOldValue: true, // Record the old value of attributes
  characterDataOldValue: true // Record the old value of text content
};

observer.observe(targetNode, config);

  3. Perform actions based on mutations:
    Inside the callback, you can do a variety of things:

    • Process newly added content: If new elements appear, you might need to apply specific styling, attach event listeners, or extract data.
    • Update UI: If attributes change (e.g., a class name that controls visibility), you can react accordingly.
    • Sync external systems: If your web app interacts with other services, mutations might trigger updates.
    • Handle dynamic forms: Adding or removing form fields. 
    const listContainer = document.getElementById('messageList');

const observer = new MutationObserver(mutations => {
  for (const mutation of mutations) {
    if (mutation.type === 'childList') {
      mutation.addedNodes.forEach(node => {
        if (node.classList.contains('new-message')) {
          console.log('New message arrived:', node.textContent);
          // Maybe scroll to the bottom of the list
          listContainer.scrollTop = listContainer.scrollHeight;
        }
      });
    }
  }
});

observer.observe(listContainer, { childList: true, subtree: true });

  4. Stop observing:
    Just like with Resize Observer, disconnect when you're done.

    observer.unobserve(targetNode); // Stop observing a specific node
observer.disconnect();          // Disconnect the observer entirely

When to Use Mutation Observer: The Use Cases

  • Dynamic Content Loading: When content is loaded via AJAX or WebSockets (e.g., chat messages, infinite scroll).
  • Framework Integrations: Many JavaScript frameworks heavily rely on DOM manipulation, and Mutation Observer can be used to react to these changes.
  • Content Management Systems (CMS): When content is updated dynamically within an editor.
  • Live Updates: Any scenario where elements are added, removed, or modified in real-time.
  • Debugging and Analysis: Understanding how other scripts are modifying the DOM.

Advantages of Mutation Observer

  • Real-time Updates: React instantly to changes in the DOM.
  • Efficiency: Avoids the performance hit of constantly polling the DOM.
  • Granular Control: You can specify exactly which types of mutations you care about.
  • Powerful Options: subtree, attributes, childList, characterData give you fine-grained control over what’s observed.

Disadvantages of Mutation Observer

  • Can Be Overwhelming: If you observe too much with subtree: true and broad configurations, you might trigger your callback too often, leading to performance issues. Careful configuration is key.
  • Complexity in Handling Multiple Mutations: When multiple mutations happen in quick succession, your callback might receive several MutationRecord objects. You need to process them efficiently.
  • Doesn’t Handle CSS-Driven Changes: If a change is purely driven by CSS (e.g., a display: none set by a media query), it won’t trigger a mutation unless the class or style attribute itself changes.

Section 3: The Best of Both Worlds – When to Combine Them

Sometimes, the dynamic nature of your web application calls for both Resize and Mutation Observers.

Scenario: Imagine a rich text editor where users can insert various blocks of content. When a new block is inserted (Mutation Observer), you might also want to check its dimensions to ensure it fits within the visible area and potentially adjust its layout (Resize Observer).

// Observe mutations (e.g., new content blocks added)
const mutationObserver = new MutationObserver(mutations => {
  for (const mutation of mutations) {
    mutation.addedNodes.forEach(node => {
      if (node.classList && node.classList.contains('rich-text-block')) {
        console.log('New rich text block added:', node);
        // Now, observe the newly added block for size changes
        resizeObserver.observe(node);
      }
    });
  }
});

// Observe resize changes for elements that might need layout adjustments
const resizeObserver = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
  for (const entry of entries) {
    console.log('Rich text block resized:', entry.target);
    // Logic to adjust layout or content based on new size
    if (entry.contentRect.width < 200) {
      entry.target.style.padding = '5px';
    } else {
      entry.target.style.padding = '10px';
    }
  }
});

const editorContentArea = document.getElementById('editor');
mutationObserver.observe(editorContentArea, { childList: true, subtree: true });

// Initially observe any existing blocks
document.querySelectorAll('.rich-text-block').forEach(block => {
  resizeObserver.observe(block);
});

This synergy allows you to build highly interactive and adaptive user interfaces.

Conclusion: Embrace the Power of Observation!

Resize Observer and Mutation Observer are not just fancy buzzwords; they are fundamental tools for building modern, dynamic, and performant web applications. They empower you to move away from inefficient polling and embrace a more declarative and event-driven approach to managing your DOM.

  • Resize Observer is your go-to for anything related to element dimensions and their impact on your UI.
  • Mutation Observer is your guardian for when content itself changes – elements are added, removed, or their attributes/text are modified.

By understanding their capabilities, mastering their APIs, and knowing when to combine them, you can significantly enhance your web development workflow, create smoother user experiences, and build more robust and responsive applications. So, go forth and observe! Your DOM will thank you for it. Happy coding!

title: Halloween effects on Shopify, WordPress, Wix and Webflow without touching a theme
description:
Most Halloween decoration scripts assume you can edit your <body> tag. On site builders you usually can't, and a script that does document.body.classList.add(...) in the <head> throws, because the body doesn't exist yet.

I ran into this while writing the install guides for halloween.js, a small library that draws spider webs in the corners of the page, blinking eyes, a flying witch, a dropping spider and a tombstone. It is MIT licensed, has no dependencies and weighs about 9 KB gzipped.

The library is switched on by a halloween class on <body>. So the one thing every platform needs is a way to add that class after the page has loaded. This is the snippet I ended up with:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/halloween.js@1.0.3/dist/halloween.iife.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  function apply() {
    document.body.classList.add("halloween", "halloween-screen-left-top", "halloween-screen-right-bottom", "halloween-eyes", "halloween-witches", "halloween-spider-drop", "halloween-tombstones");
  }
  if (document.readyState === "loading") {
    document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", apply);
  } else {
    apply();
  }
})();
</script>

The readyState check is what makes it location-independent. In a head field the script waits for DOMContentLoaded. In a footer field, or when Google Tag Manager injects it after the page has loaded, it runs immediately. It adds classes instead of replacing the class attribute, so the classes your theme already puts on <body> stay.

Where it goes

  • WordPress and WooCommerce: a header/footer code plugin, footer field.
  • Shopify: theme.liquid, just above </body>.
  • Webflow: Site settings, Custom code, Footer code. Custom code only runs on the published site, not in the Designer.
  • Wix: Settings, Advanced, Custom Code, placed in "Body - end".
  • Squarespace: Code Injection, Footer.
  • Tilda: a T123 (Embed HTML Code) block on the page.
  • Ghost: Settings, Advanced, Code injection, Site footer.
  • Blogger: Theme, Edit HTML, above </body>.
  • Google Tag Manager: a Custom HTML tag on All Pages.
  • Framer: Site Settings, Custom Code, end of body (paid site plan).

Each platform has its own page with the exact menu path: halloween.js.org/wordpress/, /shopify/, /wix/ and so on.

The season window

The effects only run between 18 October and 2 November by default. You can leave the snippet on the site all year and it does nothing outside the window. Start and end dates are configurable, and ambient effects stop for visitors with prefers-reduced-motion turned on.

Changing what appears

The playground on the site lets you pick corners, effects, intensity, color and dates, with a live preview. Its "Paste-only" tab produces this whole snippet with your choices.

If something doesn't work on your platform, open an issue on GitHub. Platform menus change often and I can only check what I've seen.

title: I worked like the company was mine. Here is what two and a half years at a Silicon Valley startup taught me.
description:
I was a frontend engineer at Sybill from May 2024 to September 2026.

Founders do not wait for a ticket. For two and a half years, neither did I.

In May 2024 I joined Sybill, a Silicon Valley startup that builds AI for sales teams. I was hired as a frontend engineer. Over the next two and a half years I built a large part of Ask Sybill, our AI chat, from its first version to the day I left. A strong backend team built the AI brain behind it. My job was everything around that brain, so that people enjoyed using it every day.

If something hurt our users or the company, I treated it as my problem, even when nobody had put it on my list. This is the story of what that looked like, day by day.


My GitHub stats from my last two years at Sybill.

It started on day one

On my first day, the browser's developer tools were slow on our app. I wanted to know why. The cause was in our CSS: the same block of style values was copied into the page again and again, once for every file that used it. I removed the copies, the app shipped less CSS, and the tools were fast again. Nobody had asked me to look.

In my first week I moved our build to Vite, a much faster build tool, and a few days later the tests followed. I pushed the team toward TypeScript, which catches mistakes before the code runs, and I started refactoring right away. I did it because I cared about the software we all worked in every day. If the floor creaks, you fix it today.

I gave every screen the same building blocks

Six months in, I noticed that every screen in our app had built its own buttons, modals and menus. Some existed twice. Most of them I would not have approved in a code review. So every new feature started by building the same basic pieces again.

AI could not help much with this yet. When I joined, we used GitHub Copilot in VS Code, and it mostly finished the line you were typing. Then we moved to Cursor with Sonnet 3.5, and its Composer, a chat window that could edit code for you, felt like a huge jump. It could write a function. It could not write good UI that matched the rest of our app.

The old way to go faster was to reuse code. In a product like ours, most screens have to be made for their own job, so you cannot share much of the high-level code. But the small pieces can be shared. A button, a modal and a menu should work the same everywhere.


A Sybill app screen. Buttons, menus and chips like these are the small pieces a shared library gives every screen.

I had wanted a component library for months, so when our CTO mentioned the idea, I was ready. In December 2024 I created syb-ui. I built it with the compound components pattern before I even knew the pattern had a name. It just felt like the natural way to do it. It was also not my first time. I had built component libraries twice before, both in Svelte: once as an open-source side project I never finished, and once at work at Altice.

It paid off. The UI became consistent, we had fewer UI bugs, and new screens were faster to build because we could take an existing screen as a reference. For months I was the only one working on it. Then other engineers started adding to it, and it became a team effort. To me, that was the real sign it worked.

We built an AI chat before the tools for it existed

In January 2025 we started Ask Sybill. Today there are popular frameworks for building an AI chat. Back then they were young and few teams used them, so we built it all ourselves: answers that stream in word by word, a stop button, retries, and a way to manage the huge amount of state an AI chat needs to work.


Sybill's AI agent answering a user query.

For months, almost the whole chat lived in one file. By September 2025 it was about 4,800 lines long. Most people would tell you to split a file like that early. I chose not to. One file kept the total amount of code small, and there were no layers to dig through to understand one click.

It also helped in a way I did not plan. For most of 2025, AI tools did not get much better. Anthropic's models were the best we had. The most expensive models, like Opus and OpenAI's o1 and o3, cost a lot and were not worth it for our daily work. With tools that weak, one big file was a gift: the AI could see everything important in one place. A big file is fine. A big file nobody understands is not.

The right moment to split came when we put Ask Sybill in a sidebar too. The core of the chat moved into one shared piece that both screens used. Each screen kept its own wiring, the code that connects that core to its buttons and lists. About 70% of the two screens behaved the same, but the other 30% had to be different, because the screens did different jobs. With separate wiring, neither screen could break the other. I only connect two parts of the code when the product connects them.

From there, the chat grew up with the rest of the market. At the start, every AI chat was simple: you ask, it answers. Then they learned to run many conversations at once, keep working in the background and use outside tools. Ask Sybill followed the same path. I started with the simplest design that worked and made it more advanced only when the product needed it. The models grew up too. GPT 5 was the first GPT model I really liked, and later Opus 4.5 was another big step.

To keep up, I improved the code all the time. Every time I touched a part of the app, I tried to leave it faster and simpler than I found it. I was known for two things: making the product better, and breaking some of it on the way. During one big refactor of the AI chat, I introduced bugs. I knew it could happen. Refactoring is risky and nobody thanks you for it: when it works, nobody notices, and when it breaks, everybody does. I did it anyway, because I knew what I was doing and better software is worth the risk.

I never let slow or broken things slide

I used our product every day and watched it closely. I watched session recordings of real users and checked our metrics. This was never perfect. We always had more work than time, so these fixes came in small steps, whenever I had a chance. But when something was slow or broken, I did not wait for it to reach the roadmap.

Long chats are a good example. Very few users had them, but for those few, opening a long chat could freeze the app for about 20 seconds. They just stared at the greeting screen, wondering if anything was happening. The code made it clear that this would only get worse as people used the chat more, and I do not like leaving edge cases like that open.

The usual answer is virtualization: draw only the messages you can see on the screen. Virtualization is a fine tool, but it brings its own problems, and I like to understand the root cause first, in code and in life. So I went through the code one function at a time and made each one faster, to raise our baseline. My rule is simple: make the code truly fast first, and add virtualization only when you reach a size where nothing else works.

Then I brainstormed with GPT 6 Astra, and it came up with a clever use of a React feature called startTransition. React uses it to mark an update as not urgent, so the screen stays responsive, for example while you switch tabs. We used it to build a long chat in small pieces: the newest messages show up at once, and the older ones are added quietly in the background. That one idea did about 80% of the job. The freeze went from about 20 seconds to about 1.4 seconds.


Opening a very long chat: newest messages first, older ones in the background.

I thought about the product, not only the code

Fixing what is slow is engineering. Deciding what to build is product. Any product that wants to be good needs both.

Users kept telling us that cutting video clips from their recorded meetings was painful. It took too many steps, it was not clear what to click, and sometimes people lost their work. It was not on the roadmap, and nobody asked me to fix it. So I watched the recordings, read the feedback and designed a new page myself. For ideas, I looked at classic video editors like Sony Vegas, with a real timeline where you can see and shape every clip. Our designer polished the look, and I shipped it. Customers praised it to me directly. That story gets its own article.

We had also wanted, for a long time, to let Ask Sybill build small apps, like dashboards, that run right in the user's browser. That is powerful, but risky: the AI writes code, and that code runs on the user's screen. Our first version was very naive. I started a new project for it, and with a teammate I studied how Claude runs the code it writes. I already had some ideas of my own. In the end we built a sandbox that keeps the code safe and still lets the AI do useful work. For the dashboards we picked shadcn/ui instead of our own library, because Claude already writes it well without any guidance.

I worked on the company, not only in it

We were always running. There was always more to build than time to build it, so I guarded time like money. Every minute lost to bureaucracy or a meeting with no clear point was a minute we paid back at night or on the weekend.

That is why I pushed to keep our processes lean, and sometimes to have almost no process at all. The biggest waste I saw was the distance from our customers. There were too many steps between a customer and an engineer. Feedback got lost on the way, and people forgot how customers really felt. We were fast compared to many companies, but we could be faster. I wanted a key customer to ask for something and get it in one or two days.

So I pushed engineers to talk with customers directly in Slack, to ask the sales team what they were hearing, and to look at the analytics themselves. When one customer asked to sort their data in a new way, we shipped it in a day. That push was mostly mine, and I was still at it when I left.

Saving money was part of the same work. Our end-to-end tests had been broken for six months and still cost about $200 a month to run. We paid about $1,000 a month to store large files in our build pipeline that we did not need. And we sent so much useless noise to Sentry, our error tracking tool, that it cost about another $1,000 a month. Together that is more than $26,000 a year spent on nothing. None of it was my job. If the company were mine, I would want someone to fix it, so I fixed it.

I pushed AI everywhere (when it made sense)

I never treated AI like a religion. Online, the hype was loud long before the tools were good, and I did not let it move me. I watched the tools instead. Each time they got better, I noticed early and put them to work.

In the beginning, AI was only a small help. Still, in September 2024, a few months after I joined, I wrote our first rules file for AI tools: a short guide that tells the AI how we write code. Later I added skills, short guides for specific tasks. With them, anyone could quickly understand a complex component, or take a piece of existing code and turn it into new UI much faster.

Over time, more of the work became agentic, which means AI agents doing whole tasks on their own. We used them for debugging, performance profiling and analytics, and even to click through the app in a real browser to test it.

I pushed AI into places few teams had tried yet. I used it for handoffs and documentation, and I even added an AI step to our hiring process. I said it all the time: documentation is not for people, it is for AI. People rarely read docs. AI reads every word, and then it explains the code to people when they ask.

Then Fable 5 arrived, and my output roughly doubled. For the first time I was not buried in frontend work and tech debt, so I finally had time for the backend too. When a feature needed a backend change, I made it myself instead of waiting. As a team, we moved faster than the roadmap, which left room for the work nobody had planned.

What I would do differently

The first thing is people. There were moments of stress and frustration that could have been fun, with more frank and friendly talk. Today I try to let people be the main character of their own work. I cheer their choices even when I do not agree, and I put being welcoming before being right. It worked with some people and not with others. With some teammates it grew into a strong bond that made both of us happier and more productive, and that is one of the things I am proudest of. What I learned is that it has to start on day one.

The second is tests. I would not have spent time on end-to-end tests, the tests that click through the whole app like a real user. For a long time they did not pay off. They took a long time to write and run, and they kept breaking while the product changed every week. Nobody wanted to take time from features to fix them, so ours sat broken. Fable 5 changed that. It writes a decent test from a short description, so a new test costs almost nothing, and tests that were never worth it suddenly are. Another team brought them back.

The third is cleanup. In August 2026 we spent a week as a team deleting dead code. With Fable 5 we removed a lot of unused code. We tested everything ourselves, and no production issue showed up for a long time after. Still, I think cleanup belongs in every change. A special cleanup week teaches people to wait for the next one.

I left Sybill in September 2026. The lesson I take with me is simple:

Act like the company is yours, even when your title says otherwise.


This is me.

title: I built a GST invoice checker that runs on a laptop, and it caught its own AI's mistake
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

gstsort reads a folder of GST invoices, PDFs or phone photos, and tells you which ones you can claim input tax credit on and which ones you can't yet.

Every Indian business registered for GST claims back the tax it paid on purchases, and the claim only holds if the invoice is right: the supplier's GSTIN is valid, it's billed to your GSTIN, the tax type matches the states involved, and the numbers add up. Freelancers and small agencies collect a pile of these every month and check them by hand, or pay their CA to, and a CA office does the same for dozens of clients. Those are the people who'd pay for this: the freelancer gets a clean sheet in a few minutes instead of an evening, and the CA office gets a first pass over every client's folder before anyone opens a PDF.

Demo

I ran it on ten sample invoices with made-up suppliers. Six of them have a problem planted in them, and it found all six:

All ten took about two minutes on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM, 12 to 16 seconds an invoice, with nothing going over the network.

One catch wasn't planted. On the Inkwell invoice the model read the GSTIN 27ABZPI9054E1Z4 as 27ABZP19054E1Z4, an I turned into a 1. A wrong GSTIN in your purchase register won't reconcile with GSTR-2B, and that's credit you don't get. A GSTIN has a check digit, and the PAN inside it has letters and digits in fixed slots, so gstsort put an I back in the slot that has to be a letter, recomputed the check digit, saw it match, and fixed it. When a fix doesn't make the check digit agree, like the Lensbox invoice where the GSTIN printed on the invoice itself is wrong, it leaves it alone and flags it for a human.

Code

omlahore / gstsort

Check GST invoices for input tax credit problems with a local vision model

gstsort

Point it at a folder of GST invoices (PDFs or phone photos) and it gives you a CSV of everything on them, plus a list of the ones you shouldn't claim input tax credit on yet. A local open-weight vision model reads the invoices, so they never leave your machine.

$ gstsort -gstin 27AKXPS4821M1Z7 samples/
...
06-typo-gstin.pdf (Lensbox Camera Rentals LB-26-0391)
  - supplier GSTIN "27AAKFL4410C1ZQ" fails the checksum, recheck it on the invoice

07-total-mismatch.pdf (INKWELL STATIONERS IW-2207)
  - taxable 1580.00 + tax 284.40 + cess 0.00 doesn't add up to total 1964.40 (off by -100.00)
  ~ read supplier GSTIN as 27ABZP19054E1Z4, fixed to 27ABZPI9054E1Z4 (checksum confirms)
...
10 invoices, 4 clean. Input tax credit ready to claim: ₹3437.82. Held back for review: ₹2406.56
Wrote invoices.csv

What it checks

The model only reads. Everything after that is plain code:

  • GSTIN format and the mod-36 check digit. A misread look-alike (an…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The model is Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, an open-weight vision model, quantized to 4 bits (Q4_K_M GGUF) and served by llama.cpp's llama-server on localhost. The CLI is about 400 lines of Go.

For each invoice:

  1. PDFs get rendered to PNG with pdftoppm, and phone photos get scaled down so the long side is 1400 px. A 4000 px photo blows past the context window of a 7B vision model.
  2. The image goes to llama-server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint with a JSON schema in response_format. llama.cpp turns that schema into a grammar, so the model can only produce valid JSON with the fields I asked for: GSTINs, invoice number, date, taxable value, CGST, SGST, IGST, cess, total and the HSN/SAC codes.
  3. Everything after that is plain Go. The model reads the invoice and never decides whether a credit is claimable.

The checks:

  • GSTIN format and the mod-36 check digit, with the look-alike repair above
  • billed to your GSTIN, and no buyer GSTIN means it's a B2C bill with no credit
  • same state means CGST + SGST, different states means IGST
  • CGST equals SGST, the effective rate is a real GST slab, and taxable + tax + cess equals the total
  • restaurant services (SAC 99633x), which are usually blocked credit under section 17(5)
  • the same supplier and invoice number showing up twice

The output is a CSV with every field, the credit you can claim on each invoice, and the reason for anything held back. Place-of-supply edge cases like a hotel stay in another state still need a human, and the README says so.

I tried letting the model pick an expense category too. It labeled almost everything "travel", including a broadband bill. So that field went, and the food check reads the SAC code instead, which is printed on the invoice and doesn't need guessing.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Invoices are other people's financial data. A CA office holds them for dozens of clients and has every reason not to upload them to someone else's API. With an open-weight model on llama.cpp nothing leaves the machine, it works with the internet off, and there's no per-page API bill, so running a whole year of invoices through it is fine.

Running the inference server myself also means I control the decoding. The JSON schema is enforced as a grammar while the model generates, so I never parse free text and hope. When a better open vision model comes out, I point llama-server at it and nothing else changes.

title: Building Privacy-First Patient Education Interfaces
description:
Healthcare websites increasingly use interactive forms, educational questionnaires, visual explainers, and decision-support interfaces to make complex information more understandable.

But building a medical education interface introduces challenges that ordinary marketing websites rarely encounter.

Developers must balance usability, accessibility, privacy, content accuracy, and the limitations of automated recommendations.

This article explores practical frontend design patterns for creating safer, clearer patient education experiences.

1. Start With Information, Not Recommendations

A common mistake in healthcare interface design is turning educational questionnaires into apparent diagnostic tools.

Consider a person researching fullness beneath the chin.

They may encounter information about localized fat, skin elasticity, facial anatomy, and different treatment categories.

An interactive tool can organize these topics, but it should not determine whether someone needs a medical procedure based on a handful of answers.

A better approach is to build interfaces that explain relevant factors and encourage informed conversations with qualified professionals.

The system should distinguish between three things:

General information: Explanations that apply broadly to a topic.

Personal preferences: Concerns and questions users want to explore.

Clinical assessment: Individual conclusions requiring qualified medical evaluation.

Keeping these categories separate helps prevent educational software from appearing more authoritative than it is.

2. Use Progressive Disclosure

Medical terminology can overwhelm readers, particularly when several unfamiliar concepts appear together.

Progressive disclosure provides additional explanations only when users need them.

For example, HTML provides a simple way to create accessible expandable explanations:

<section aria-labelledby="education-heading">
  <h2 id="education-heading">
    Understanding treatment limitations
  </h2>

  <p>
    Treatment suitability depends on individual
    anatomy and clinical evaluation.
  </p>

  <details>
    <summary>
      Why does skin elasticity matter?
    </summary>

    <p>
      Skin elasticity can influence how tissues
      respond to changes in underlying volume.
      Individual assessment is necessary.
    </p>
  </details>
</section>

The native details and summary elements offer built-in expandable behavior without requiring a JavaScript component library.

Developers should still test keyboard navigation, screen-reader behavior, and mobile readability.

This approach can also be useful for explaining unfamiliar medical terminology, recovery considerations, and procedural limitations.

3. Make Privacy the Default

Health-related questionnaires may involve sensitive personal information.

Not every educational interaction requires user accounts, databases, analytics events, or persistent storage.

For example, a questionnaire that simply organizes questions for a medical consultation may be able to operate entirely within the browser.

Developers should consider whether the interface truly needs to transmit information to a server.

A privacy-conscious design process asks:

Does this feature require personal information?

Can it work without identifying the user?

Is storing individual responses necessary?

Would anonymous, aggregated usage measurements be sufficient?

Data minimization should be considered during product design rather than added after implementation.

Client-side processing alone does not guarantee privacy; third-party scripts, analytics, browser extensions, and other technical factors still matter.

4. Structure Medical Content Around User Questions

Healthcare content is often organized around procedure names, but users frequently begin with questions about their appearance, symptoms, or concerns.

An effective information architecture should support both approaches.

For example, a reader researching a double chin may need to understand the differences between localized fat, skin laxity, and underlying facial structure before exploring individual treatment options.

A Persian-language educational guide about submental liposuction and its limitations illustrates the type of topic-specific resource that can be connected to a broader educational interface.

The important frontend design challenge is ensuring that users can discover relevant context without being pushed toward a predetermined treatment.

This can be supported through descriptive navigation, logically grouped sections, contextual links, and clear explanations of uncertainty.

5. Design for Accessibility and Readability

Medical information should be understandable across different devices, reading abilities, and levels of technical knowledge.

Useful implementation practices include semantic HTML, clear heading hierarchies, properly labeled form controls, readable contrast, descriptive link text, and meaningful feedback messages.

Mobile usability deserves particular attention.

Expandable content should not obscure critical safety information, tables should remain navigable on smaller screens, and interactive controls should have sufficient touch targets.

Accessibility testing should involve more than checking whether a page looks attractive.

Keyboard-only navigation, screen readers, zoomed layouts, and validation behavior should be considered throughout development.

The W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines provide a useful framework for this work.

6. Build Trust Through Transparency

Digital health interfaces should explain their purpose and limitations.

Users should understand whether an interactive feature is providing general education, organizing preferences, or collecting information for a consultation.

Publishing organizations should also identify themselves clearly.

For example, Adina Aesthetic Clinic publishes Persian-language educational information about facial aesthetics and cosmetic procedures.

When clinical organizations publish digital educational resources, transparency about authorship, content limitations, and editorial responsibility helps readers interpret the information appropriately.

From a product-design perspective, transparency should be part of the interface itself, not buried in a long disclaimer.

7. Maintain Content as Carefully as Code

Healthcare information changes over time.

Developers and content teams should therefore treat educational content as something that requires maintenance.

Useful practices include version-controlled content changes, periodic editorial reviews, accessible component patterns, reference checking, and clear responsibility for clinical review.

Automated content-generation tools may assist with organization and readability, but medical statements should undergo appropriate verification.

The quality of a healthcare interface depends on both its technical implementation and the reliability of the information it presents.

Conclusion

Building a useful patient education interface requires more than attractive components and smooth interactions.

Developers must understand the boundaries between information and diagnosis, reduce unnecessary data collection, design accessible experiences, and communicate uncertainty clearly.

Privacy, usability, and medical responsibility should influence architectural decisions from the beginning.

The goal is not to replace professional medical judgment with software.

It is to make complex information easier to understand, explore, and discuss.

title: Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components
description:
title: "Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-14T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [nextjs, react, webdev, frontend]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Static Site Generation (Ssg) With Generatestaticparams: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Parsing Mdx Files: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Syntax Highlighting With Rehype/Remark: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Optimizing Core Web Vitals: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Building a Full-Stack Markdown Blog with Next.js App Router, Tailwind CSS, and Server Components functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Static site generation (SSG) with generateStaticParams, parsing MDX files, syntax highlighting with Rehype/Remark, and optimizing Core Web Vitals."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: React: un inbox de prueba que explica cada espera
description:
Un inbox de prueba en una app React no debería limitarse a mostrar un spinner. Cuando esperamos un correo de verificación, la interfaz necesita explicar que está pasando, que puede hacer la persona y cuando conviene volver a intentar. Este enfoque reduce la incertidumbre y hace que un flujo de pruebas con correo temporal sea mucho más fácil de depurar.

El problema: una espera que parece un fallo

En mis flujos de frontend, el fallo más costoso no siempre está en la API. A veces el endpoint responde bien, pero la pantalla deja al usuario ante un botón desactivado y un indicador que gira sin contexto. Después de unos segundos, la pregunta es inevitable: ¿el email no llegó, la bandeja está vacía o la aplicación se rompió?

Un inbox de prueba tiene varios momentos distintos:

  • todavía no se ha solicitado el mensaje;
  • la solicitud está en curso;
  • la bandeja está esperando un mensaje nuevo;
  • el mensaje llegó y puede abrirse;
  • la espera expiró o devolvió un error.

Me gusta tratar cada momento como un estado de producto, no como un detalle interno de la petición. Así se puede probar un fake email generator, un buzón local o una integración real sin cambiar la expectativa de la interfaz.

Modelar el inbox como estados visibles

Un modelo pequeño evita que los componentes acumulen condiciones contradictorias. Por ejemplo, waiting no significa lo mismo que empty: en el primero hay una consulta activa; en el segundo, la consulta terminó y no encontró nada.

type InboxState =
  | { kind: "idle" }
  | { kind: "waiting"; startedAt: number }
  | { kind: "empty"; checkedAt: number }
  | { kind: "ready"; subject: string; receivedAt: number }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

Con esta separación, el texto de la pantalla puede ser preciso. “Buscando el correo” comunica una acción en progreso; “Aún no hay mensajes” comunica un resultado. Parece una diferencia pequeña, pero ayuda a que el equipo de QA y quien desarrolla hablen del mismo escenario.

Un componente React con feedback útil

El componente no necesita conocer todos los detalles del proveedor de correo. Solo recibe el estado y expone una acción que se pueda repetir de forma segura.

function TestInbox({ state, onRefresh }: Props) {
  const label = {
    idle: "El inbox está listo",
    waiting: "Buscando el correo de prueba",
    empty: "Aún no hay mensajes",
    ready: "Correo recibido",
    error: "No pudimos consultar el inbox"
  }[state.kind];

  return (
    <section aria-labelledby="inbox-title" aria-live="polite">
      <h2 id="inbox-title">Inbox de prueba</h2>
      <p>{label}</p>
      {state.kind === "waiting" && <progress aria-label="Esperando correo" />}
      {state.kind === "ready" && <p>{state.subject}</p>}
      {(state.kind === "empty" || state.kind === "error") && (
        <button type="button" onClick={onRefresh}>Volver a consultar</button>
      )}
    </section>
  );
}

aria-live="polite" anuncia los cambios sin interrumpir una lectura. El botón sigue siendo un botón real, con foco visible y un nombre que explica la acción. Si el chequeo tarda, mantengo el texto “Buscando” cerca del indicador; un spinner por sí solo no ayuda a una persona que navega con lector de pantalla.

También conviene mostrar el tiempo de la última consulta. No hace falta prometer una entrega instantánea: una frase como “Última revisión hace unos segundos” da contexto y evita clics repetidos. En pruebas con tp mail so o con otra fuente, ese dato permite distinguir una demora del proveedor de un problema de renderizado.

Accesibilidad y rendimiento en la misma revisión

La accesibilidad no es una capa para añadir al final. Un estado explícito mejora el rendimiento percibido porque la persona entiende la espera antes de decidir si abandona o pulsa otra vez. En mi revisión de CSS compruebo tres cosas:

  1. El layout no salta cuando aparece el botón o el asunto del mensaje. Reservo espacio para esos elementos y evito cambios bruscos.
  2. El foco no desaparece al actualizar la lista. Si se abre un detalle, lo devuelvo a un encabezado útil o al control que inició la acción.
  3. La animación es opcional. Con prefers-reduced-motion, desactivo el giro y mantengo un indicador textual. 
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .inbox-spinner {
    animation: none;
  }
}

En móvil, reviso que el mensaje de estado y el botón queden juntos, sin obligar a desplazarse para entender el resultado. Es un ajuste simple, pero se nota mucho en una interacion corta de verificación.

Checklist para probar el flujo

Antes de dar por terminado el componente, pruebo estos casos:

  • solicitud lenta: el estado cambia rápido y explica la espera;
  • respuesta vacía: no se presenta como un error del sistema;
  • mensaje recibido: el asunto y la hora son legibles;
  • error de red: existe un camino claro para reintentar;
  • doble clic: no se generan consultas duplicadas sin control;
  • lector de pantalla: cada transición tiene una etiqueta entendible;
  • pantalla estrecha: el contenido no se desborda ni se superpone.

Para investigar mensajes de activación en un producto SaaS, puede servir revisar emails de activación en un SaaS. Y si la validación vive dentro de un formulario, recomiendo validar emails sin fricción visual antes de añadir más lógica al inbox.

Hay un detalle de documentación que suele olvidarse: registrar los nombres usados por el equipo. Un test puede buscar “tepm mail com” o “tempail” por una razón histórica, pero esos terminos no deberian convertirse en etiquetas visibles ni en enlaces. Los dejo como alias de fixture, con una nota breve, para que nadie confunda un typo de prueba con una funcionalidad.

Conclusión

Un inbox de prueba útil no intenta ocultar la espera. La hace legible, medible y recuperable. En React, un modelo de estados pequeño, un mensaje accesible y un layout estable suelen aportar más que otra animación o un botón de reintento colocado sin contexto.

Cuando el frontend explica si está esperando, vacío, listo o bloqueado, el flujo de verificación deja de sentirse misterioso. Y esa claridad sirve tanto para la persona que prueba la app como para quien debe diagnosticarla a las nueve de la mañana, aun con poca paciencia y menos contexto.
