title: 8 Things a Hotel or Villa Website Needs Before Guests Will Book (A Developer's Checklist)
description:
Most guests book their stay from a phone. They often scroll on mobile data, sometimes from an airport gate, and they make up their mind in a few seconds. A hospitality website gets judged by different rules than a portfolio or a company page: it either answers "what will I get, and how do I book it?" right away, or the visitor goes back to a booking platform.

I am a WordPress and Flutter developer in Famagusta, North Cyprus. Many of the small hotels, villas and holiday rentals around me depend on summer visitors from Turkey, the UK, Germany and Russia. Here is the checklist I use when I build or review a hospitality site. If you build sites for clients in tourism, most of it applies wherever you are.

1. Photos that sell the stay, without killing speed

People decide to book by looking. Large, bright photos of the rooms, the pool and the view do more than any paragraph. The technical part is keeping them fast:

  • serve WebP at the size each breakpoint actually needs
  • lazy-load everything below the first screen
  • use a gallery that swipes properly on touch screens
  • put the most convincing photo first, not the reception desk

2. One page per room or villa

Each unit needs its own URL with the essentials visible at a glance: number of guests, beds, bathrooms, distance to the beach, what is included and the price per night or per season. If you can, add an availability calendar. If you can't, a clear "Check availability" button still saves a lot of back-and-forth over email.

3. A direct booking path on every screen

Booking platforms bring visibility, but they take a commission on every booking, and the guest relationship belongs to them. The website's job is to turn returning guests and Google visitors into direct bookings. That means either a booking request form or a connected booking engine, plus one-tap WhatsApp, phone and email buttons. On mobile, a sticky contact bar works well.

4. Every language in its own URL

A Turkish family, a British couple and a German group all trust a booking page more in their own language. For SEO, give each language its own address (/de/, /tr/ and so on), use proper hreflang, and translate menus, forms and confirmation emails as well as the page text. A plugin like WPML handles this in WordPress. Remember that right-to-left languages need their own layout checks.

5. Location and local context

Guests want to know where they'll actually be: how far the beach is, how to get there from the airport, and what's within walking distance. An embedded map, simple directions and a short area guide keep visitors on your site while they plan. They also give Google more local signals to work with.

6. Trust details

Show reviews from past guests and link to your profiles on review platforms. Publish check-in times, cancellation rules and house rules, and show a licence number, a real address and the people behind the business. For a small hotel, this is what makes booking directly feel safe.

7. Speed on mobile data

A heavy theme loses guests before the first photo loads. Page caching, optimised images, fewer third-party scripts and lean CSS let a site look luxurious and still feel fast. On a multilingual WordPress site I helped optimise, the median mobile PageSpeed score went from 51 to 75 on the same page. That shows how much room for improvement most sites have.

8. Local SEO for every season

Write pages for the searches guests actually type, like "villa with private pool in Kyrenia" or "beach hotel near Famagusta". Add Hotel / LodgingBusiness structured data and keep publishing seasonal content, so you show up before travellers settle on a platform.

When an app is worth it

For a larger hotel or a group of villas, a companion app can add digital check-in, room-service requests, local recommendations and return-visit offers. With Flutter, one codebase can share content and APIs with the website, which keeps both in sync.

FAQ

Can the website take bookings directly?

Yes. It can send booking requests to the owner, show live availability or connect to a booking engine. It depends on how many units there are and how many bookings come in.

Do I still need booking platforms?

Usually, yes, because they bring visibility. Your own site works alongside them and turns returning guests into direct bookings.

Can the owner update prices and photos?

With WordPress and Elementor, yes. Seasonal prices, photos and offers can be edited in every language without calling a developer.

Originally published on ehsanabedi.com. Running a hotel or villa in North Cyprus? See my web design services.

title: Build an MCP Server in Java with Spring AI (+ OAuth)
description:
Claude Code can add a task to a team board and show Ana's open tasks as a table. It doesn't have a plugin for that. It talks to a Java server, built with Spring AI, that exposes the board over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This article builds that server step by step: first as a handful of annotated methods, then locked down with OAuth 2, a permission for every tool, and validation on every argument. Getting it to work takes minutes. Making it safe is most of the job.

There's an animated video version of this article too.

TL;DR

  • With Spring AI 2.0, an MCP server is a few annotated methods.
  • Set spring.ai.mcp.server.protocol: STREAMABLE. Without it, Spring AI 2.0.1 serves the older SSE transport and /mcp returns 404.
  • An HTTP MCP server is an OAuth 2 resource server. An anonymous request gets a 401 that points the client at your authorization server.
  • Give every tool its own scope with @PreAuthorize, so a read-only token can't create anything.
  • The model writes every argument, so validate them like input from the internet.

Watch the video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UjGuQt1TsT8

The code is in the spring-ai-mcp-task-board repository, one commit per step: GITHUB-LINK-HERE

What MCP is

MCP is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI applications to tools and data. The AI application is the host: Claude Code, Claude Desktop or your IDE. Inside the host, one client keeps one connection to one server. Our server offers three kinds of things:

  • Tools are actions the model decides to take, such as creating a task. The model is in control.
  • Resources are data the application can read, each with an address such as task://1. The application or the user decides when to put one in front of the model.
  • Prompts are templates the user picks, often from a slash menu. Ours writes a standup update.

Every message is JSON-RPC 2.0. For a remote server, the transport is Streamable HTTP: one endpoint, /mcp. The client POSTs a message, and the server answers with a JSON body or, when it has more to say, a stream. After initialize, the server returns an Mcp-Session-Id header, and the client sends it back with every later request.

Setting up the server

We start from start.spring.io with Spring Web, Model Context Protocol Server and Validation, on Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Java 25. The dependency that matters is the MCP server starter for WebMVC. In the final pom.xml, the relevant part of the dependencies looks like this:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc</artifactId>
</dependency>

The version comes from the Spring AI 2.0.1 BOM.

The configuration gives the server a name, a version and an instruction that clients show the model:

spring:
  ai:
    mcp:
      server:
        name: task-board
        protocol: STREAMABLE
        version: 1.0.0
        instructions: >
          A small team task board. Use the tools to create,
          list and complete tasks.

server:
  port: 8080

The line that's easy to miss is protocol: STREAMABLE. In Spring AI 2.0.1, the WebMVC starter still serves the deprecated SSE transport by default, on /sse, and /mcp returns 404.

Start the application and send the first message every client sends, initialize. The response carries the server's name, version, instructions and capabilities: tools, resources and prompts. The server works, but it can't do anything yet.

The task board

The domain is deliberately small. A task has an id, a title, an assignee, an optional due date and a done flag. A TaskService keeps the tasks in a concurrent map and can create, list, find and complete them.

In a real application, this is the service you already have. MCP sits on top of code you already run.

Tools

TaskTools is a Spring component that gets the service injected. Each tool is a method with an @McpTool annotation. The name and the description are what the model sees, and each parameter gets an @McpToolParam with its own description:

@McpTool(name = "create_task", description = "Create a task on the team board")
public Task createTask(
        @McpToolParam(description = "Short title, e.g. 'Fix login bug'") String title,
        @McpToolParam(description = "Who does it, e.g. 'ana'") String assignee,
        @McpToolParam(description = "Due date as YYYY-MM-DD", required = false) String due) {
    return tasks.create(title, assignee, parseDue(due));
}

Those descriptions aren't comments. They're the only documentation the model ever sees. A vague description means the model guesses, so write each one as if you were explaining the parameter to a new teammate.

The read-only tool, list_tasks, adds a hint:

@McpTool(name = "list_tasks", description = "List tasks, optionally only one person's",
        annotations = @McpTool.McpAnnotations(readOnlyHint = true, destructiveHint = false))

Clients can use hints such as readOnlyHint to ask for less confirmation. They are hints, not security.

Spring AI turns every method into a tool and builds its JSON Schema from the Java types and the descriptions. In tools/list, create_task requires title and assignee, and due is optional.

[UPLOAD IMAGE HERE: mcp-tool-descriptions.png] (alt text: TaskTools.java with the @McpToolParam descriptions highlighted)

Calling create_task with a title, ana and the due date 2026-10-23 returns the new task as text, with id 1. Listing Ana's tasks returns it too.

The interesting case is an error. Completing task 99, which doesn't exist, throws an exception in our service. Spring AI turns it into a normal tool result marked isError: true, with the text No task with id 99 (Spring AI 2.0.1 repeats the message in the text). The model receives the message and can correct itself, instead of the whole call failing.

Resources and prompts

Tools are for actions. For data, MCP has resources. TaskResources has one method, annotated with @McpResource. Its address is a template, task://{id}, and the id from the address is passed straight into the method parameter:

@McpResource(uri = "task://{id}", name = "Task",
        description = "One task with all its details", mimeType = "text/markdown")
public String task(String id) {
    // looks up the task and returns it as a small markdown document
}

On the wire, the client asks for the resource templates, sees task://{id}, and then reads task://1. It gets back a small markdown document:

# Task 1: Fix login bug
- assignee: ana
- due: 2026-10-23
- status: open

The difference from a tool is who is in charge. The model decides to call a tool. The application or the user chooses which resource to put in front of the model.

The third primitive is a prompt. TaskPrompts has one method with @McpPrompt, and its single argument, @McpArg, is whose standup it is. The method loads that person's tasks, turns them into a checklist and wraps them in an instruction.

When a client calls prompts/get for Ana, it receives a ready message with her real tasks already filled in. The user picked the template, and our server supplied the facts.

The problem: anyone can call it

So now we have all three primitives, and they all work. And right now, the server is dangerous.

This client has no credentials at all. It connects, and it completes Ana's task:

Anyone who can reach this port can read every task, create new ones and close the rest. If a model is the client, it will do all of that whenever a document it read tells it to. An MCP server is an API and needs the same protection as one.

OAuth 2

The MCP specification says HTTP servers are OAuth 2.1 resource servers: the client gets an access token from an authorization server and sends it with every request.

For this demo, the authorization server is a small Spring Authorization Server in the same repository, on port 9000, configured entirely in properties. It registers two clients, an agent that may read and write tasks and a dashboard that may only read. Both use client_credentials, the grant for machine-to-machine clients:

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      authorizationserver:
        issuer: http://localhost:9000
        client:
          agent:
            registration:
              client-id: agent
              client-secret: "{noop}agent-secret"   # dev only
              authorization-grant-types: [client_credentials]
              scopes: [tasks.read, tasks.write]
            token:
              access-token-time-to-live: 1h
          dashboard:
            registration:
              client-id: dashboard
              client-secret: "{noop}dashboard-secret"
              authorization-grant-types: [client_credentials]
              scopes: [tasks.read]
          # ...

The {noop} secrets and in-memory clients are for local development only.

Back in the task server, two dependencies turn it into a resource server: the MCP security starter from the Spring AI community, and Spring Boot's OAuth 2 resource server starter.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springaicommunity</groupId>
    <artifactId>mcp-server-security-spring-boot</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.14</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-resource-server</artifactId>
</dependency>

Then one property: the issuer. The task server will only trust tokens signed by that authorization server.

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: http://localhost:9000

Now the anonymous client tries again, and gets a 401:

HTTP/1.1 401
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=http://localhost:8080/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp

The 401 doesn't just say no. The header points to a Protected Resource Metadata document (RFC 9728) that names our authorization server, so the client can discover where to log in without being configured in advance.

The agent asks the authorization server for a token with both scopes, authenticating with its client id and secret:

curl -u agent:agent-secret http://localhost:9000/oauth2/token \
     -d grant_type=client_credentials -d scope='tasks.read tasks.write'

{
  "access_token": "eyJraWQiOiJiOGEyYzJhOS02YjY1…",
  "scope": "tasks.write tasks.read",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3599
}

The access token is a signed JWT. Decoded, its issuer is our authorization server, its subject is the agent, and its scope claim lists both permissions. It expires an hour after it was issued. The task server verifies the signature with keys it downloads from the issuer address.

With that token, initialize works again and returns 200, with a session id of its own.

One scope per tool

A valid token shouldn't mean you can do everything. The dashboard should be able to look, not touch.

We turn on method security with @EnableMethodSecurity in a small SecurityConfig, and then give every tool the scope it needs. Spring Security maps the JWT scope claim to SCOPE_ authorities, so the annotation is a one-liner:

@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_tasks.write')")
@McpTool(name = "create_task", description = "Create a task on the team board")
public Task createTask(/* ... */) { /* ... */ }

Creating and completing tasks need tasks.write. Listing tasks, and reading the task resource, need tasks.read. The @PreAuthorize annotations work on @McpTool methods, because the MCP security starter supports them.

Now the dashboard's token can still list tasks. When it tries to create one, the call comes back as an error:

{
  "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "Access Denied\r\nAccess Denied" }],
  "isError": true
}

The model sees why the call failed, and the board doesn't change. That's least privilege: an agent that only reads gets a token that can only read.

Validate every argument the model sends

The one people forget is validation. Every tool argument was written by a model that may have just read text from a stranger, so treat it like internet input.

The service checks each argument before it touches the board. The title must be between one and 120 characters. The assignee must look like a username: a short, lowercase name without spaces or quotes. The board also caps at 1,000 tasks:

if (title == null || title.isBlank() || title.length() > 120) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("title must be 1 to 120 characters");
}
if (assignee == null || !NAME.matcher(assignee).matches()) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("assignee must be a lowercase username like 'ana'");
}
// ...

The due date gets its own check in the tool. A bad date produces a message that tells the model the exact format to use, instead of a stack trace.

We tried three bad calls. An empty title and an assignee that looks like an SQL injection string are both rejected with a message stating the rule. And next friday as a due date gets this result:

{
  "content": [{ "type": "text", "text": "due must look like 2026-10-23\r\ndue must look like 2026-10-23" }],
  "isError": true
}

The model reads the rule and fixes its own call.

Before production

The demo skips four things that matter in production. First, the audience. Our token's aud is agent, the client, not our server. In production, a token should name the server it's meant for, and that server should reject any token that names someone else. Otherwise a token issued for one service can be replayed against another. The MCP specification requires this check, and the security starter can perform it.

Second, never pass a client's token through to another API. Third, keep tokens short-lived: an hour is fine for a demo, and for agents, minutes are better. Fourth, when a person is behind the client, use the OAuth login with PKCE (RFC 7636), the flow MCP clients use when you sign in from the app. Client credentials are for machines.

The boring parts save you too: rate limits, a log of every tool call, HTTPS, and a real database instead of a map in memory.

Connecting Claude Code

Now let's connect a real agent. We register the server in Claude Code as an HTTP MCP server, with our URL and the agent's token sent as an Authorization header.

Then we ask Claude Code, in plain English, to add a task for Ana to review the MCP security pull request, due Friday, and to show Ana's open tasks. It finds the create-task tool. Because changing the board is a real action, Claude Code asks first and shows the exact arguments, with Friday as a real date. After approval, it lists Ana's tasks and answers with a table, straight from our Java server.

Recap

Spring AI turns annotated methods into tools, resources and prompts and handles the protocol. The real work is making the server safe: OAuth 2 on the endpoint, a scope for every tool, and validation on every argument. The full code is linked above, one commit per step. Build it, break it, then connect your own services.

Further reading

  • Model Context Protocol specification, revision 2025-06-18
  • RFC 9728: OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata
  • MCP authorization (2025-06-18)
  • Spring AI MCP server docs
  • Spring AI community: MCP security
  • RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)

More animated system design and security explainers on the jean code van debug YouTube channel. Java developer? Join the Java devs squad on daily.dev.

title: Building a Cloud-Native School ERP: Architecture, Real-Time Fleet Tracking, and Data Integrity
description:
Educational institutions frequently juggle an unmanageable software stack: a legacy desktop tool for accounting, spreadsheets for grades, fragmented messaging apps for parent communication, and disconnected standalone hardware for attendance.

When administrative tools operate in silos, data bottlenecks arise. Report cards require days of manual exports, fee reconciliation involves cross-referencing physical receipts, and parents are left waiting for fragmented updates.

At AcadHex, we approached this problem as a systems integration and distributed architecture challenge. Below is a look into how we architected a unified, multi-tenant Cloud School ERP designed to automate campus workflows in real time.

1. Core Architectural Pillars

A production-grade School Management System handles wide variations in traffic: minimal load during instructional hours, sudden spikes during morning gate check-ins, and heavy concurrent sessions during report-card releases or fee deadlines.

To balance these patterns, our platform relies on three key design principles:

  • Strict Multi-Tenancy & Data Isolation: Each school network or academy operates with strict logical data isolation. Tenant resolution occurs at the gateway layer via subdomain routing, with database connection pooling ensuring isolated tenant contexts while sharing compute resources efficiently.
  • Event-Driven Communication: Critical campus actions—such as biometric check-ins or fee receipts—emit domain events rather than triggering synchronous write chains.
  • Hardware-Agnostic Ingestion: Campuses deploy diverse hardware setups. Our API abstracts physical hardware (biometric terminals, GPS units) behind standardized webhook and telemetry ingestion pipelines. 
                +---------------------------------------+
                |          API Gateway & Routing        |
                |    (Tenant Resolution via Subdomain)   |
                +-------------------+-------------------+
                                    |
          +-------------------------+-------------------------+
          |                                                   |
+---------v---------+                               +---------v---------+
|  Real-Time Fleet  |                               |   Core Business   |
| Telemetry Service |                               |   Domain APIs     |
+---------+---------+                               +---------+---------+
          | (MQTT/UDP)                                        | (REST/RPC)
+---------v---------+                               +---------v---------+
| Hardware/Vehicles |                               | PostgreSQL / Read |
|   (GPS Devices)   |                               |      Replicas     |
+-------------------+                               +-------------------+

2. Ingesting Live GPS Fleet Telemetry at Scale

Managing student transportation demands reliable, low-latency telemetry. Traditional HTTP polling introduces unnecessary overhead for vehicle tracking updates transmitted every 3 to 5 seconds.

Telemetry Pipeline

  1. Device Packets: Onboard vehicle GPS trackers broadcast lightweight UDP/MQTT packets containing coordinates, speed, ignition status, and vehicle telemetry.
  2. Ingestion Layer: A Node.js worker layer decodes incoming binary/NMEA data payloads and validates device signatures.
  3. Geofencing & Event Triggers: Ingested coordinates pass through an in-memory spatial index. When a vehicle crosses a defined perimeter (e.g., Approaching Stop: Sector 4), the system triggers parent notification events.
  4. Broadcast via WebSockets: Real-time updates are published via Redis Pub/Sub directly to authenticated client dashboard sockets. 
interface VehicleTelemetryPacket {
  deviceId: string;
  tenantId: string;
  latitude: number;
  longitude: number;
  speedKmh: number;
  timestamp: number;
}

// Ingestion validation handler
export async function processTelemetry(packet: VehicleTelemetryPacket): Promise<void> {
  const { deviceId, tenantId, latitude, longitude } = packet;

  // 1. Update latest vehicle state in cache
  await cache.geoadd(`fleet:${tenantId}`, longitude, latitude, deviceId);

  // 2. Publish to authenticated active web/mobile listeners
  await pubsub.publish(`fleet:updates:${tenantId}`, JSON.stringify(packet));

  // 3. Evaluate active route geofences asynchronously
  queue.add('evaluate-geofence', { tenantId, deviceId, latitude, longitude });
}

3. Financial Consistency in Fee Automation

Automated fee collection requires strict consistency. Distributed transactions can fail midway if parent payments, fee concessions, ledger writes, and receipt generation are not handled within transactional boundaries.

We implement atomic transactions with idempotency keys across all collection endpoints:

-- Atomic ledger write pattern for fee processing
BEGIN;

-- 1. Lock invoice record to prevent concurrent double-collection
SELECT id, balance_due 
FROM student_invoices 
WHERE id = 'inv_98234' AND status = 'PENDING'
FOR UPDATE;

-- 2. Register successful transaction entry
INSERT INTO payment_transactions (
    id, invoice_id, amount_paid, gateway_ref, status, created_at
) VALUES (
    'txn_44102', 'inv_98234', 15000.00, 'pay_tok_live_891', 'SUCCESS', NOW()
);

-- 3. Reconcile balance and update invoice status
UPDATE student_invoices 
SET balance_due = balance_due - 15000.00,
    status = CASE WHEN (balance_due - 15000.00) <= 0 THEN 'SETTLED' ELSE 'PARTIAL' END,
    updated_at = NOW()
WHERE id = 'inv_98234';

COMMIT;

Idempotency tokens on payment callbacks prevent duplicate receipts or balance miscalculations if a payment gateway retries a webhook during network fluctuations.

4. Hardware Integration: Biometric Attendance Pipelines

Connecting campus biometric hardware to cloud infrastructure presents practical challenges: school-level devices frequently experience intermittent offline states.

To prevent missing punch records, biometric terminals send batches using local storage replay:

  • Every punch is assigned a monotonically increasing sequence ID per device.
  • Devices buffer attendance records locally during network outages and flush payloads sequentially upon reconnection.
  • The API ingestion service deduplicates punches against a composite key (device_id, student_rfid, timestamp_minute) to guarantee zero duplicate markings while maintaining reliable attendance records.

5. System Design Takeaways

Building software for physical campus environments requires designing for edge-case resilience:

  1. Expect Intermittent Connectivity: Hardware bridges (turnstiles, vehicle tracking) must have built-in queuing and retry guarantees.
  2. Decouple Event Feeds from Query APIs: Separating live tracking feeds and heavy analytics queries prevents dashboard latency during peak morning check-ins.
  3. Prioritize Auditability: Administrative actions—grading adjustments, fee waivers, schedule updates—require immutable audit trails to maintain institutional trust.

By moving schools away from disconnected spreadsheets and legacy systems toward event-driven cloud platforms, administrators gain real-time oversight while parents stay informed.

title: B2B Email Marketing in 2026
description:
In the world of B2B growth, buzzwords come and go. Every quarter, a new social platform or advertising algorithm claims to be the "future of customer acquisition." Yet, when senior revenue leaders examine what actually books meetings, signs enterprise contracts, and closes five-figure deals, the answer remains undisputed: email marketing.

Email is not a rented channel subject to algorithmic mood swings or spiraling cost-per-click (CPC) inflation. It is a direct, private communication highway into the inboxes of business owners, founders, and C-level executives.

However, the game of email marketing has fundamentally shifted in 2026. Stale prospect lists, generic spray-and-pray blasts, and unverified data will not merely fail to produce meetings—they will burn your domain reputation and land your emails in spam purgatory.

Here is the complete, practical guide to mastering B2B email marketing in 2026 and leveraging live data to build a predictable, scalable sales engine.

Why Email Marketing Still Rules B2B Sales

While consumer marketing often leans into TikTok and Instagram, B2B procurement happens in the inbox. Here is why modern business leaders prioritize email marketing above all other outreach mechanisms:

1. Unmatched Return on Investment (ROI)

Across industry studies by Litmus and the DMA, email marketing consistently records an ROI between 3,600% and 4,200%. When compared to paid LinkedIn advertisements (which frequently command $8 to $15 per click with unpredictable conversion), a well-targeted email sequence costs a fraction of the budget while producing measurable pipeline.

2. Full Channel Ownership

When you run campaigns on social networks, you are subject to changing reach algorithms, account suspensions, and bidding wars. With email marketing, you own your list and distribution. A verified prospect database is an enduring corporate asset that you control completely.

3. Hyper-Specific Firmographic Segmentation

In B2B, one size never fits all. Email marketing allows you to slice your target market with surgical precision:

  • By Geography: Target logistics companies specifically in California, or dental clinics across Kuwait and Dubai.
  • By Industry and Niche: Tailor value propositions for SaaS founders differently than manufacturing plant managers.
  • By Digital Footprint: Identify businesses with active websites or high customer ratings.

The 4 Traps Killing Modern Email Marketing Campaigns

If your outbound campaigns are suffering from low open rates or non-existent replies, you are likely falling into one of these four fatal traps:

Trap 1: The 30% Annual Data Decay

Every year, approximately 30% of business contacts change jobs, companies rebrand, email formats shift, or businesses shut down. When you buy a "static database" compiled six months ago, up to a third of those emails are dead on arrival.

Trap 2: Hard Bounces and Blacklisted Domains

title: Pin flights, a real find hotkey, and colored More tiles
description:
Small changes you feel before you name them

Most of the work in a messenger is invisible: delivery state, encryption, reconnects, the thing that happens when the network drops halfway through a photo. Every now and then a batch of much smaller changes lands, and the app simply feels different. This is one of those batches.

Three things changed in GwinG this week. Pinning a chat or a message now has a short flight instead of a snap. The browser-standard find chord works on every search surface. And the three navigation tiles on the More tab picked up an accent color from the active theme.

None of them adds a feature you can point at in a changelog title. All of them remove a tiny moment of doubt.

A pin should move, not teleport

When you pin a chat, the list reorders immediately. That is the correct data behaviour, but it used to be a hard cut: the row you were looking at vanished from one place and appeared in another, and your eye had to find it again.

The new pin flight keeps the row legible. Before the model reorders the list, the UI snapshots the selected row's rectangle. One frame later — after the reordered list has laid out — a ghost tile flies from the old rectangle to the row's new position in 320 ms. The real row is hidden at its destination while the ghost is in the air, so there is never a double image. The ghost's avatar hero is disabled so it cannot collide with the real row's hero.

The details are where the edge cases live:

  • The destination may be off-screen. If the pinned section scrolled out of view, the ghost lands at the list edge — top for a pin, bottom for an unpin — and fades out. The pin still applies.
  • A second pin may arrive mid-flight. The old ghost is cancelled before a new one starts.
  • The optimistic model update may not reach the expected state. In that case the flight is skipped; the list simply reorders as before.
  • The same chat can be mounted in several kept-alive tab pages. The row keys are namespaced per tab, so the flight finds the exact mounted row rather than a lookalike in another tab.

Pinned messages get the same treatment in the other direction. The message bubble measures a compact source rectangle, and the pinned bar is measured one frame after it mounts. A ghost — pin icon plus the same preview text — flies from the bubble to the bar in 340 ms and fades over its last fifth, revealing the real bar underneath. A missing source rectangle or a squeezed bar (the keyboard can do that) skips the flight; the pin still applies. Unpinning deliberately does not animate.

The whole thing is behind a new Settings → Motion → Pin animation toggle. It is on by default and follows the same rule as the other motion work: it only plays at the Full motion level. Reduced or Off means the old instant reorder, which is still perfectly usable.

The entrance bug hiding in the same pass

While adding the flights we fixed a bug that had been making list entrances look wrong. The staggered entrance used a SlideTransition with an offset of 18. SlideTransition treats that number as a fraction of the child's size, not a pixel count. Rows were starting roughly eighteen times their own height below their final position. The fix was to use a Transform.translate in logical pixels, so the rows now move 18 px.

The second half of the fix was about replays. Rows are disposed when they scroll far out of view, so a keyed entrance could replay when they came back. Each row now animates only on its first build for the lifetime of the Friends view. Rows revealed by keyboard navigation still skip the entrance on purpose.

The find chord should mean find

main+F is the browser-standard find chord. On GwinG it is Alt+F by default, or Ctrl+F if you choose the alternative in Settings → Shortcuts. Until now it only worked in some places, which made it feel unreliable: a shortcut that works sometimes is worse than no shortcut, because you stop trusting it.

It now focuses the search field on every search surface:

Surface What happens
Friends chats list Opens the in-place search box and focuses it. Pressing F again re-focuses the field and selects the current query. Escape still closes the box.
In-chat message search Opens the search panel and focuses its field. While the panel is open, its own handler owns F so the query can be re-focused and selected.
Search tab Alias of the existing focus chord, and F additionally selects the current query.
Contacts Focuses the friend filter above the list.
Create Group → Members Focuses the friend picker; inert on the other steps.
Group info → Add members Re-focuses the friend picker in the add-members sheet.

Two implementation details made the difference. On the chats list, the F check runs before the "the search field already has focus" early return, so the chord also works while you are typing. In the chat page, the search panel registers its own keyboard handler while it is mounted, because the chat page's shortcut scope is inactive when the panel is on top.

No new localization keys were needed. The help rows reuse the existing strings for "Search chats", "Search in chat", and "Focus the search box", so the cheat sheet stays consistent without translating the same idea twice.

Color as a signpost

The More tab has three navigation tiles: Settings, My Space, and Switch account. They were all the same default icon color. Now Settings uses the secondary color, My Space uses tertiary, and Switch account uses primary.

The palette is resolved once from the active theme, so the tiles follow light/dark mode and the user's accent preset. There is no behaviour change, no new copy, and no server sync. It is a small piece of wayfinding: three destinations, three visual anchors, one less moment of reading the labels.

FAQ

Does pinning still work if motion is disabled?

Yes. The data change is independent of the animation. With motion off, the row or message simply moves to its new place without the ghost flight.

Does Alt+F work while I am typing in the search box?

Yes. On the chats list the chord is checked before the focus check, and it selects the current query so you can replace it immediately.

Do the More tile colors change with the theme?

Yes. They are resolved from the active theme palette, so they follow the light/dark mode and accent preset rather than being fixed colors.

Why this batch matters

A language-exchange app is a place where people already have to work a little: find the right person, switch languages, read a translation, check a pronunciation. The interface should not add its own small uncertainties on top of that.

A pin that flies is not a feature. A find chord that works everywhere is not a feature. A colored tile is not a feature. But together they make the app feel like it is paying attention — and that is the point of polish work.

If you want the implementation-level companion to this piece, the shared media gallery and photo albums write-ups cover the same "small detail, real feel" territory.

Get GwinG — a language-exchange messenger with live translation.

  • Android: Google Play
  • Windows: .zip or installer
  • Linux: .deb or portable tarball

title: We localise prices for 58 countries from a header, and both our PDF exporters are hard-coded to A4
description:
PubTrivia prints things. Players join by scanning the code on their table, so a venue's first task is to produce a card per table, print it once and reuse it every week. There are two pieces of code that make the printable sheet: one in the dashboard that exports every table's code at once, and a free one on the marketing site that will do it for any web address at all, with no sign-up and no request leaving the browser.

Both of them begin like this:

// A4 dimensions in mm
const A4_WIDTH_MM = 210
const A4_HEIGHT_MM = 297
const PAGE_MARGIN_MM = 15

const doc = new jsPDF({
    orientation: 'portrait',
    unit: 'mm',
    format: 'a4',
})

Elsewhere in the same repository there is a module whose whole job is to notice where the visitor is:

return currencyForCountry(headerList.get('x-vercel-ip-country'))

That map holds 58 countries and 24 currencies, so the pricing page quotes a venue in Mexico in pesos and a venue in Sweden in krona. The same two-letter code, available in the same request, would also answer a question nobody asked it: what size is the paper in that country.

The numbers, because they decide how bad it is

A4 is 210 by 297mm. US Letter, officially ANSI A, is 8.5 by 11 inches, which is 215.9 by 279.4mm, and it is the usual office size in the United States, Canada and the Philippines, with Mexico and Panama mostly using US sizes too. Our country map contains the US, Canada, Mexico, Panama and Puerto Rico.

So an A4 sheet against Letter is 5.9mm narrower and 17.6mm taller. Width is not the problem. Height is: printed at actual size, the bottom 17.6mm falls off the page, and with 15mm margins and a 4-up grid, the thing living in that strip is the label under the bottom row of codes. Printed with "scale to fit", which most drivers default to, everything shrinks to 279.4 / 297, or about 94%, and comes out with an uneven bottom margin.

Neither outcome breaks a quiz night. A QR code at 94% of 82mm still scans from across a table, and the label is the table number, which the person cutting up the sheet already knows. That is exactly why this sat there: the failure is cosmetic, it happens in somebody else's printer dialog, and nobody files a bug that says "my table cards are 6% small".

What the exporter actually does with the space

The dashboard version offers five layouts and derives everything else:

const LAYOUTS: Record<string, LayoutConfig> = {
    '1': { cols: 1, rows: 1, label: '1 per page' },
    '2': { cols: 1, rows: 2, label: '2 per page' },
    '4': { cols: 2, rows: 2, label: '4 per page (recommended)' },
    '6': { cols: 2, rows: 3, label: '6 per page' },
    '9': { cols: 3, rows: 3, label: '9 per page' },
}

const cellWidth = printablWidth / cols
const cellHeight = printableHeight / rows
const cellPadding = 4
const labelHeight = 8 // mm reserved for label text
const qrSize = Math.min(cellWidth, cellHeight - labelHeight) - cellPadding * 2

(Yes, printablWidth. It has been there since the first version and it is spelled that way in both places it is used, which is the only reason it still compiles.)

Because the size is derived rather than fixed, swapping the page format really is a two-constant change. With a 15mm margin, 4-up on A4 gives an 82mm code: width is the binding constraint, so the cell is 90mm wide and the code is that minus two lots of 4mm padding. The same layout on Letter gives about 85mm, because Letter is the wider sheet. The sheet that loses height gains code size, which is a pleasing result and entirely an accident. Everything downstream, including the font size ladder, follows the cell:

doc.setFontSize(perPage === '9' ? 7 : perPage === '6' ? 8 : 10)

Three font sizes, chosen so that nine codes on a page still have a readable number under them. This is the part of the file I would keep unchanged in any rewrite: the layout is a function of the paper, so the paper is the only thing a new size has to change.

The two things I would copy from this exporter

First, jsPDF is imported at the moment the button is pressed, not at the top of the file:

const { jsPDF } = await import('jspdf')

The dashboard page that renders the button is loaded by every host before every quiz. The PDF library is loaded by the subset of them who are printing table cards this week, which is close to all of them once and almost none of them again.

Second, there is no network call in the export, and that is a schema decision rather than a clever bit of client code. Each table row carries its code as a data URL:

doc.addImage(table.qr_code_url, 'PNG', qrX, qrY, qrSize, qrSize)

The images are already in the page's props, so exporting 50 tables is 50 addImage calls and no requests. The free tool on the marketing site reaches the same place from the other direction: it generates the code in the browser with qrcode, so the address you type is never sent anywhere, which is a promise the page makes and the absence of a backend keeps.

The filename is built from what the file contains, too, which costs one line and saves a support thread:

doc.save(`QR_Codes_${activeTables.length}_tables_${perPage}pp_${totalPages}page${totalPages !== 1 ? 's' : ''}.pdf`)

Why the fix is not just adding a dropdown

The obvious change is a page size selector next to the layout selector. I do not think that is the right one, or at least not the first one.

A venue owner printing table cards does not want a choice between ISO 216 and ANSI A. They want the sheet to come out of the printer that is in the room. The country code is already in the request, the paper size follows from it for every country we quote a price in, and the sensible default is the one the request implies, with an override for the minority who are printing for somewhere else. Which is exactly the pattern the pricing page already uses, including the part where the guess is coarse and the override is cheap.

The general shape, and the reason this is worth 1,000 words about paper: we had already decided that locale is something you infer and offer rather than ask about. Then we wrote a feature that produces a physical object and never asked the same question. Internationalisation work tends to stop at currency, language and date format, because those are the three a framework hands you. The list is longer than that, and paper is on it, along with address formats, phone number shapes and which day a week starts on.

Our own audit is now one question per output: for everything this app produces that leaves the screen, which of its properties are facts about the user's country rather than facts about us? The prices got that treatment a month ago. The PDFs are getting it this week.

title: Two dialog components in one app, and the second one exists so it cannot be closed
description:
We have two dialogs. One is the normal one: translucent scrim over the page, close button in the corner, Escape works, clicking outside works. The second one makes the opposite choice on every single point, and it is a separate component rather than a prop on the first.

/**
 * Opaque, full-screen, non-dismissible dialog.
 *
 * Separate from components/ui/dialog.tsx because it makes the opposite choices on
 * purpose:
 *
 *  - The overlay is `bg-background`, not a translucent scrim. These flows ask the
 *    user for one thing, and leaving the dashboard visible behind a see-through
 *    panel invites them to try to interact with it.
 *  - There is no close button, and Escape / outside-click / pointer-down-outside
 *    are all suppressed. The only exits are the actions inside the content.
 */

The implementation is one component and three event handlers:

<DialogPrimitive.Overlay className="bg-background fixed inset-0 z-[100] ..." />
<DialogPrimitive.Content
  // Suppressed rather than merely unhandled: without these, Escape and a
  // click on the backdrop would both close the dialog and skip the question.
  onEscapeKeyDown={(event) => event.preventDefault()}
  onInteractOutside={(event) => event.preventDefault()}
  onPointerDownOutside={(event) => event.preventDefault()}
  className="bg-background fixed inset-0 z-[101] flex flex-col overflow-y-auto ..."
>

Suppressed rather than unhandled

That comment is the one I would keep if I could only keep one.

Radix's dismissal behaviour is not something you opt into. If you render a controlled dialog and simply do not pass onEscapeKeyDown, Escape still closes it, because the primitive fires its own close. "I did not write a handler" and "I prevented the default" look equally quiet in a diff and mean opposite things, which is exactly the sort of difference that gets silently reintroduced by somebody tidying up props they think are unused.

The second half of the comment says what the behaviour costs: Escape and an outside click do not merely dismiss the panel, they skip the question. For a one-time ask, dismissed and answered are the same state, and the user never sees it again.

Non-dismissible does not mean inaccessible

The thing I expected to be a tradeoff here is not one. Radix is still doing all the work that matters for assistive technology: focus trap, focus restore on close, aria-modal, scroll lock on the body. Suppressing three dismissal paths removes none of that.

What it does create is one hard obligation, and it is written into the component's own doc comment:

The content MUST therefore always render a way forward, or the user is stuck.

That is a real failure mode and it is not theoretical. A non-dismissible dialog whose only action is behind a failed network request is an app your user has to reload to escape. Any content that goes in here has to be able to render its exit without a successful fetch.

The place it earns its keep

The one flow that uses it is a one-time ask for a public review, shown to paying customers after enough completed practice to have an opinion, and asked exactly once whether or not it is acted on. It has exactly two outcomes, go and review or skip, and it stores neither an opinion nor a score, only the fact that it was answered.

Which makes the layout rule the interesting part of that component rather than the dialog:

The skip is the same size and full width as the review button, directly below it. Making the way out small is how a one-time ask turns into a resented one: anyone who does not want to review should be able to leave in one obvious click, on the first try, on a phone.

An opaque, un-closable, full-screen modal is about as aggressive as in-app UI gets. The thing that makes it acceptable is that the way out is as big as the way in. Suppressing Escape and then hiding the skip behind a 10 pixel grey link would be a dark pattern, and the component would be the same component.

There is a product decision underneath it that is worth stating plainly. This replaced an in-app star rating, which told us something we could not act on and told the user nothing they could use. The reviews it asks for are public ones, and they are the same reviews quoted on our home page, each card linking to its source so a visitor deciding whether the practice is worth paying for can check that a stranger wrote it. A private rating is a metric. A public review is something the next candidate can read.

When to write the second dialog

The honest test for whether you need two components rather than one with a dismissible prop: list the differences. Ours were the overlay colour, the presence of a close button, three event handlers, two z-index layers and a scroll container, which is most of the component. At that point a prop is not a variant, it is a second implementation wearing the first one's name.

There is now a third dialog in the codebase that is built on neither, a provider picker, and its header comment names both of the others to explain itself: not the default one, whose content hard-codes a centred max-width panel that would have to be undone class by class, and not this one either, because a picker has to be escapable. Three dialogs is more than I would have guessed we needed. Each one knowing why it is not the other two is what keeps that from being a mess.

title: Three things in our app wait for a job to finish, and no two of them poll the same way
description:
CogniPrep has three places where the user is looking at a screen that is not finished yet: a payment that has to be granted, a written exercise whose review is still running, and a recorded interview that is being processed. All three resolve somewhere else, in a webhook or a background job, and all three have to update a page that is already on screen.

They are implemented three different ways. I went looking for the inconsistency to tidy it up and ended up keeping all three, because the differences are each answering a different question: who owns the truth, and what ends the poll.

One: the purchase, which gives up

Every checkout returns the buyer to the thing they bought rather than to a receipt page. That creates a race, because the Stripe redirect is immediate while our webhook may land on a cold function. For a second or two the destination still considers the buyer unentitled, and would otherwise show them the buy panel they have just paid to be rid of.

/** ~30s of polling. Long enough for a cold webhook, short enough to not stall. */
const INTERVAL_MS = 2500;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 12;

useEffect(() => {
  if (granted) return;
  let attempts = 0;
  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    attempts += 1;
    if (attempts > MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
      clearInterval(timer);
      setGaveUp(true);
      return;
    }
    router.refresh();
  }, INTERVAL_MS);
  return () => clearInterval(timer);
}, [granted, router]);

Three things in there matter more than the interval.

granted is a prop, read on the server from the same row every access gate reads. Not from the Stripe redirect, which only says money moved, and not from client state. So router.refresh() is the entire update mechanism: it re-runs the server component, which re-reads the plan, and the parent then renders the real content. There is no second source of truth to keep in step.

The attempt counter exists because this poll has no terminal failure state of its own. If the grant has not landed in half a minute, something is wrong on our side, and an endless spinner is worth less to the buyer than a route to a human:

This is taking longer than usual. Your payment is safe. Reload the page, or contact support and we will activate it for you.

And the one-shot query parameter that brought the buyer here is only dropped once there is nothing left to wait for, because the parent decides whether to render this component from that same parameter. Clear it mid-poll and the next refresh comes back without it.

Two: the exercise review, which has no counter

The written review on a saved exercise attempt uses the same mechanism and deliberately does not count anything:

export function ExerciseReviewRefresher() {
  const router = useRouter();
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => router.refresh(), 5000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, [router]);
  return null;
}

Ten lines, renders nothing. What stops it is not in the component at all, it is in the page that mounts it:

/**
 * The attempts route scores written answers inside its own 60 second budget. A
 * review still marked in progress well after that was cut off and will never
 * finish, so it reads as failed rather than as a spinner that never stops.
 */
const REVIEW_STALE_MS = 2 * 60 * 1000;

function toPanelStatus(status: string, updatedAt: Date): AiPanelStatus {
  if (status === 'complete' || status === 'failed') return status;
  if (status === 'pending' || status === 'processing') {
    return Date.now() - updatedAt.getTime() < REVIEW_STALE_MS ? 'processing' : 'failed';
  }
  return 'not_applicable';
}

The route that produces the review has a 60 second limit, so a row still claiming to be in progress two minutes later is not slow, it is dead: the function was killed and nothing will ever write the terminal status. Deriving that on read means the state machine has a failure state even though nothing wrote one, the page stops mounting the refresher, and the poll ends.

This is the version I would reach for first now. A counter in the component bounds the polling. A staleness rule on the server bounds the status, which bounds the polling for every reader of that row, including one who arrives an hour later on a fresh page load and should see "failed" rather than a spinner.

Three: the interview, which actually calls an API

The odd one out does not use router.refresh():

const POLL_INTERVAL_MS = 30_000;

export function useInterviewStatus(interviewId: string | null): InterviewStatusState {
  // fetch(`/api/interview/sessions/${interviewId}`), set state,
  // and stop the interval as soon as status is 'complete' or 'failed'
}

Two reasons it is different. The processing takes long enough that 30 seconds is the right cadence, and refreshing a whole route tree thirty times would re-run far more server work than reading one status. And the status drives client-side UI that is mid-flow, not a server-rendered panel, so the answer has to land in React state rather than in a re-render of the page.

The honest third reason is that this one is older than the other two. Its own comments still carry the requirement numbers from the spec it was built against, which is a nice archaeological marker for which parts of a codebase were written to a document and which were written to a bug.

What the three have in common

One sentence: every poll has a terminal condition that does not depend on the happy path.

An attempt cap, a staleness rule derived from the producer's own time budget, or a status enum with failure in it. Pick whichever you like, but pick one before you ship the interval, because the failure mode of forgetting is not a crash. It is a spinner that spins forever on a screen you will never see, burning a setInterval and one server render every few seconds in a tab somebody left open.

If you want to see the three surfaces these sit behind: the purchase confirmation is on whatever you bought from the pricing page, the reviewed written answers belong to the assessment centre exercises, and the processing one is the mock interview.

title: My First Post
description:
Hey DEV Community! 👋 I'm Shamil — A Developer Who Loves Building Things

Hello everyone! 👋

I'm Shamil TP, a developer from Kerala, India, and a first-year MCA student at St. Joseph's College (Autonomous), Devagiri.

I enjoy exploring technology, building projects, solving problems, and figuring out how things work behind the scenes. For me, programming isn't just about writing code — it's about turning ideas into something real.

And this is my first post on DEV! 🚀

💻 What I Work With

I'm interested in both frontend and backend development, and I enjoy exploring different technologies rather than limiting myself to one ecosystem.

Some of the technologies I've been working with include:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Next.js
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Django, Node.js, Express
  • Databases: PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis
  • Programming languages: Python, JavaScript, C
  • Tools & technologies: Git, GitHub, Linux, Docker, and CI/CD

I'm also interested in embedded systems and IoT. Experimenting with Arduino, ESP32, and Raspberry Pi boards has made me curious about connecting hardware with websites, APIs, and real-world applications.

🛠️ I Like Building, Not Just Learning

I believe the best way to understand a technology is to build something with it.

Whether it's developing a web application, deploying a backend service on Linux, experimenting with databases, or connecting a microcontroller to a web dashboard, I enjoy learning through practical projects.

I'm especially interested in building applications that are fast, lightweight, useful, and accessible.

I also enjoy exploring SEO and web performance because building a website is only part of the journey — helping people discover it matters too.

🧠 What I'm Exploring Right Now

Technology moves fast, and there's always something new to learn.

Currently, I'm interested in:
