title: A team name is an identity, a recovery code and a display label, and the only thing we validate is the length
description:
Nobody signs in to play a quiz at PubTrivia. Players scan the code on their table, a web page opens, they type a name, and they are in. No account, no app, no email. A hundred strangers in a pub, zero credentials between them.

Which means the name they type is doing three unrelated jobs at once, and I did not notice that until the third one bit.

Job one: validation, and there is almost none 

export function validatePlayerName(
    name: string,
): { valid: true } | { valid: false; error: 'invalid_name' } {
    const trimmed = name.trim()
    if (trimmed.length >= 1 && trimmed.length <= 30) {
        return { valid: true }
    }
    return { valid: false, error: GameError.INVALID_NAME }
}

That is the entire rule. Trim, then between 1 and 30 characters. No character class, no word list, no profanity filter.

The 30 is a layout number, not a safety number. Team names get read out loud and they go on a leaderboard that has to be legible from the other side of a room, and a name that does not fit the row is a worse problem than a name that is too short. There is no minimum beyond "not empty" because a table that wants to be called "7" has earned that.

What is deliberately absent is a filter. A pub quiz team will call itself something rude, that is most of the fun, and the host already has the only enforcement mechanism that works in a room: knowing whose table it is. Shipping a block list would mean maintaining a block list, in every language a tourist might bring in, forever, to solve a problem the person holding the microphone solves in four words.

Just above the validator in the join action there is a second length constant that is doing a genuinely defensive job, and the contrast is the point:

/** Longest answer text accepted. Options are short; this only bounds abuse. */
const MAX_ANSWER_LENGTH = 500

One number is about a leaderboard row. The other is about somebody with curl.

Job two: identity, enforced in application code

Names are unique per quiz, case insensitively, so the leaderboard never shows two of the same thing and nobody can pass themselves off as somebody else. The normalisation happens once, in the action:

const name = playerName.trim().replace(/\s+/g, ' ')
const sameName = (other: string) => other.toLowerCase() === name.toLowerCase()

Leading and trailing whitespace goes, and runs of internal whitespace collapse to one space, so "The Quiz Team" and "The Quiz Team" are the same entry rather than two rows that look identical on screen. That second rule is the one people forget, and a leaderboard is exactly where it shows.

The uniqueness itself is not a database constraint. There is no unique index on (session_id, lower(player_name)). It is one select, inside a transaction, behind an advisory lock:

await tx.execute(sql`SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(${`join:${sessionId}`}, 0))`)

const clashes = await tx
    .select({ ... })
    .from(tableParticipantsTable)
    .where(
        and(
            eq(tableParticipantsTable.session_id, sessionId),
            or(
                eq(tableParticipantsTable.table_id, tableId),
                sql`lower(${tableParticipantsTable.player_name}) = lower(${name})`,
            ),
        ),
    )

One query fetches everybody this join could possibly collide with: the same table, or the same name, in either mode. The lock is there because the check is read-then-write, and two phones at the same table pressing Join in the same second both used to pass it.

It is worth being clear about what this does and does not catch, because "unique, case insensitive" sounds stronger than it is. There is no Unicode normalisation, so a name typed in NFC and the same name in NFD are two rows. There is no confusable folding, so Cyrillic "а" is not Latin "a". Zero-width characters are not stripped, and a name that is one zero-width space is 1 character and therefore valid. None of that matters for the leaderboard, and all of it matters for the next job.

Job three: the recovery code

Phones die. A phone that was holding a team's place in team mode is a real problem, because team mode gives one shared score to the whole table and the table has already joined. So re-typing the team name at the table's own code gives the place back:

if (config.team_mode) {
    const team = clashes.find((p) => p.table_id === tableId)
    if (team) {
        if (sameName(team.player_name)) {
            return { participantId: team.id, playerName: team.player_name, reclaimed: true }
        }
        return GameError.TABLE_ALREADY_JOINED
    }
}

The error message that goes with the second branch spells the rule out, because a player staring at a borrowed phone needs to be told exactly what to type:

This table has already joined. To rejoin on a new phone, enter your team name exactly as before.

So the name is a bearer credential. Knowing it, plus being able to scan the code on that table, hands you that table's participant row and its score.

Written down like that it sounds alarming, and then you remember where the system is. The attacker has to be in the room, at that table, with the card in front of them, typing the name of the team sitting there, while that team watches. The threat model of a pub quiz is not a threat model. The thing that made this design correct is the same thing that makes a paper answer sheet correct: the room is the authentication.

The usual case does not go near any of it. The device remembers:

const storageKey = (tableId: string) => `pub-trivia:player:${tableId}`

A refresh, a crashed tab, or iOS evicting the page while the phone was locked restores { sessionId, participantId, playerName } from localStorage and resumes, keyed per table so one phone can legitimately hold a place at two tables. Every read and write of it is wrapped in try, because private mode throws on access and a player in private mode should get a working game that merely cannot resume. The name-based reclaim only runs when the storage is gone with the phone.

Four refusals, four sentences

The join action can say no in four ways, and each error code maps to one sentence a stranger can act on:

case 'invalid_name':
    return `Please enter a ${teamMode ? 'team name' : 'name'} between 1 and 30 characters.`
case 'name_taken':
    return `That ${teamMode ? 'team name' : 'name'} is already taken in this quiz. Try another.`
case 'late_join_disabled':
    return 'The quiz has started and late joining is disabled. Wait for the next round.'
case 'table_already_joined':
    return 'This table has already joined. To rejoin on a new phone, enter your team name exactly as before.'

The mode-dependent wording is not decoration. In team mode the thing being rejected belongs to four people who chose it together, and "that name is taken" versus "that team name is taken" is the difference between a player retyping and a player assuming the app is broken.

The part I would generalise

The useful question is not "how do I validate a name". It is: how many jobs is this field doing?

Ours does three, and they want opposite things. As a label it wants to be short, loud and rude. As an identity it wants to be unique and normalised. As a recovery code it wants to be unguessable, which is the one property a name chosen to be shouted across a pub can never have.

We resolved that by letting the room carry the security and keeping the field cheerful. That is a correct answer for a quiz night and an obviously wrong one for anything with money in it. The mistake is not picking either, it is not noticing the field had been quietly promoted from label to credential and still being validated like a label.

title: A link that takes two seconds needs its own pending state, and next/link finally reports one
description:
A plain <Link> in the App Router gives the user nothing to look at between the click and the next screen. On a fast route nobody notices. On a route whose layout has to authenticate you and load your account first, the click looks dead for a second or two, and the honest user response to a dead click is to click again.

The usual answer is loading.tsx, and it does not cover this gap. A loading file only renders once the routing boundary it belongs to has been reached, which means after the target segment's layout has resolved. Leaving a practice session for the dashboard means waiting on the dashboard layout's session and user lookup before any loading UI of the destination exists. The window with no feedback is exactly the window loading.tsx cannot reach into.

useLinkStatus reports that window, and it reports it on the element the user is already looking at: the link they clicked.

Three pieces, all of them tiny

The hook only works inside a <Link> descendant, which makes it awkward to use directly and easy to wrap. We have three wrappers.

A spinner that exists only while its link is navigating:

export function LinkSpinner({ size = 16, className }: { size?: number; className?: string }) {
  const { pending } = useLinkStatus();
  if (!pending) return null;
  return <HugeiconsIcon icon={Loading03Icon} size={size} className={cn('animate-spin', className)} aria-hidden />;
}

A swap, for cases where the label itself should change:

export function LinkPending({ children, pending }: { children: React.ReactNode; pending: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { pending: isPending } = useLinkStatus();
  return <>{isPending ? pending : children}</>;
}

And the one that gets used: a button that navigates and reports its own progress, as a drop-in for <Button asChild><Link/></Button>.

<NavButton
  href="/dashboard/games"
  variant="ghost"
  size="sm"
  aria-label="Back to Games"
  icon={<HugeiconsIcon icon={ArrowLeft01Icon} size={16} />}
  pendingLabel="Exiting…"
>
  <span className="hidden sm:inline">Back to Games</span>
</NavButton>

Inside, the pending branch does three things at once: the leading icon becomes a spinner, the label becomes pendingLabel if one was given, and the trailing icon is dropped so the row does not grow while it is busy.

const { pending } = useLinkStatus();

return (
  <>
    {pending ? <HugeiconsIcon icon={Loading03Icon} size={16} className="animate-spin" aria-hidden /> : icon}
    <span aria-live="polite" className="inline-flex items-center gap-2">
      {pending && pendingLabel != null ? pendingLabel : children}
    </span>
    {!pending && trailingIcon}
  </>
);

Two details that were not obvious

The live region. A spinner is a visual-only signal. Swapping "Back to Games" for "Exiting…" inside an aria-live="polite" region means the change is announced rather than merely seen, so a screen reader user gets the same "yes, that worked" the sighted user gets from the spin. The spinner itself is aria-hidden, because announcing a spinner tells you nothing the label change has not already said.

That wrapper is a flex row for a reason. The first version used a plain <span> and any icon passed as a child, rather than through icon or trailingIcon, broke onto its own line. Tailwind's preflight sets svg { display: block }, so an inline SVG inside an inline wrapper stops behaving like text. inline-flex items-center gap-2 puts it back on the baseline. It is a two-class fix for a bug that looks like a React problem and is a CSS reset.

Where it is worth using

These three wrappers are imported by exactly five files, and every one of them sits behind sign-in: the shell around a practice session, the screen a finished session lands on, the shell around an assessment centre exercise, the dashboard, and the empty-state hero a brand new account sees. Eight call sites, three distinct pending labels: five say "Loading…", one says "Loading games…", and the two shells wrapped around work in progress say "Exiting…", because leaving mid-session is the one navigation where the user may be worried about what happens to what they are abandoning.

That is the whole heuristic: pending feedback on an instant link is noise. The prefetched links across our public pages, the provider catalogue or a test format page, resolve fast enough that a spinner on them would only ever flash, and none of them use these components. The buttons that need one are the buttons crossing into a layout that authenticates you first, which is why all five files are inside the signed-in app rather than on the pages describing the mock interview or the assessment centre exercises.

The general version of the rule: find the links that cross a layout doing input or output before it renders, and give exactly those their own pending state. For everything else, loading.tsx was already enough.

title: 1,216 of our stylesheet's 3,133 lines draw two fake phones, and 294 lines serve 420 of our pages
description:
Munchable's marketing site is a Next.js app with 426 URLs and one stylesheet. Not one stylesheet per component: one file, app/globals.css, 3,133 lines, imported once in the root layout.

$ find apps/web -name '*.module.css' | wc -l
0
$ grep -iE 'tailwind|styled|emotion|vanilla-extract' apps/web/package.json
$ ls apps/web | grep -iE 'postcss|tailwind'

Three empty results. The runtime dependencies are Next, React, Supabase, Stripe, Drizzle, Resend, OpenAI and the two workspace packages. There is no CSS tooling in the project at all, because globals.css is plain CSS that the browser could parse as typed: no nesting, no preprocessor, two !important in the whole file.

I did not set out to defend that. I set out to find out whether it had quietly become a problem, which meant counting. The counting is the interesting part.

Where the lines went

The file is divided by section comments, and they make it easy to measure:

Section Lines
Hero demo: the app scanning a real looking product 676
Feature-row phones 540
Support page 190
App store buttons 173
Legal + status pages 146
Editorial pages: conditions, ingredients, answers 148
Pricing 135
Everything else ~1,125

The top two entries are the same thing twice. They draw phones. The landing page shows the app running, five times, and none of those are screenshots: they are divs, spans and inline SVG, animated in CSS. I wrote about the decision to have zero images on that page separately; what I had never done is measure the bill.

1,216 lines, 38.8% of the stylesheet, for decoration on one page. The two prefixes those sections use, .sd- and .pm-, account for 78 of the 221 distinct class names in the file. A third of the stylesheet, and a third of its vocabulary, is scenery.

Now the other direction. 420 of the site's 426 URLs are the condition guides, the answer pages and the recipes. Every one of them renders into the same shell:

$ grep -rl 'legal-inner' apps/web/app --include='*.tsx'
privacy  licenses  answers  [question]  terms  about  recipes  recipes/[slug]  conditions  conditions/[slug]

.legal is a single readable column with type rules on it, 146 lines, and the editorial section that extends it for the guides is another 148. 294 lines carry 420 pages. Four lines of CSS per decorative phone-pixel, and seven-tenths of a line per page of actual content.

I want to be clear that this is not a complaint. Those 1,216 lines are the thing a visitor looks at for the first four seconds, and the 294 are a column of text that is supposed to get out of the way. The ratio is upside down relative to page count and right side up relative to attention. But I did not know the number before I counted it, and "where is my CSS" turned out to be a much better question than "how much CSS do I have".

What makes one global file survivable

The failure mode of a single global stylesheet is not length. It is two people writing .card for different cards. Four things keep that from happening here, and only one of them is a technique.

Prefix per section. .sd- is the scan demo, .pm- is the phone mock, .cond- is the condition guides, .nf- is the 404. The prefix is the module boundary, hand-maintained, visible in the markup. It is what CSS modules would give you automatically, bought with discipline instead of a build step.

Flat selectors. The deepest selector in the file is six parts, and the overwhelming majority are one or two. Nothing is written to out-specify anything else, which is why there are two !important rather than a hundred.

The section comments are the table of contents, and they say why rather than what:

/* ── Editorial pages: conditions, ingredients, food ──────────────────────────
   These share the .legal shell (a single readable column) and add the few
   extras the guides need. */

A token block at the top, 28 custom properties. Colours, three radii, two shadows, the max width, three font stacks. Every rule below pulls from them, so a brand change is a change to the top of one file.

That last one is a deliberate duplicate. The app's palette lives in @munchable/design-tokens, a workspace package the app, the web app and the video renderer all import. This file keeps its own copy, and why the copy is the right call is a decision I stand behind: a CSS custom property and a TypeScript constant are different artefacts, and generating one from the other buys consistency the design does not actually want. The marketing site is allowed to have a warmer section background than any app screen.

The markup side of the ledger 

className attributes across app/ and components/ : 558
.tsx files in those directories                  : 60
inline style objects                             : 2

Nine class attributes per file, and essentially no inline styles. That second number is the one I would watch. Inline styles are where a global stylesheet goes to die: the moment it becomes easier to write style={{ marginTop: 12 }} than to find out whether a utility exists, the file stops being the source of truth and starts being a historical record. Two is a number you can keep at two by looking at it occasionally.

When I would stop doing this

Honestly: when a second person joins, or when the site stops being mostly one page plus three templates.

The entire reason this works is that the site has a small number of page shapes. One landing page with a lot of bespoke art, one editorial shell used by 420 URLs, one form page, one admin area with its own file. A global stylesheet scales with the number of distinct page shapes, not with the number of pages, and those are wildly different numbers here.

What I would not do is adopt a framework to solve a problem I measured and did not find. The counting took ten minutes and answered the question better than any amount of opinion about utility classes would have.

See it working

  • munchable.app is the 1,216 lines. The phones are live DOM: zoom in, select the text on one of them, watch the scan animation run its four phases.
  • munchable.app/conditions/low-fodmap-ibs is the 294 lines, and so is is onion low FODMAP, and so are the other 418.
  • munchable.app/recipes/gentle-rice-congee is the same shell again with a recipe in it.

Reader's exercise, since the numbers above came out of the repository: open DevTools on the landing page and on any answer page and compare what is actually in the cascade for each. The gap is the post.

title: One optional boolean, three states, and the badge next to it only knows about two
description:
Notifio watches rental search pages and emails you when a new listing appears. With the auto-reply upgrade it can also answer the listing on your behalf, by replaying a flow you demonstrated once on that site yourself.

That feature has a setup screen: one row per saved search, each row showing where that site stands. A row needs two things before it can reply. A recording, and a live login on that site, because the reply goes out as the user's own account.

The recording is on disk, so it is known instantly. The login is not. Finding out means asking the main process to open that site's browser profile and look, which is slow enough that you cannot block the list on it.

So the list renders before the answer arrives, and that produces a third state that nothing in the data model has a name for.

Two setStates, one load 

async function load() {
  const [recipeRes, siteRes] = await Promise.all([getRecipes(), getSites()]);
  const recipeList = recipeRes.data?.recipes ?? [];
  if (recipeRes.data?.recipes) {
    setRecipes(recipeList);
    setRecording(recipeRes.data.recording);
    setAvailable(recipeRes.data.available);
  }
  const siteList = Array.isArray(siteRes.data) ? siteRes.data : [];
  setSites(siteList);

  const withLogin = await withLoginState(siteList);
  setSites(withLogin);

  onReadyCountChange?.({
    ready: withLogin.filter(
      (s) => s.loggedIn === true && recipeFor(recipeList, s) !== null
    ).length,
    total: withLogin.length,
    needLogin: withLogin.filter((s) => s.loggedIn !== true).length,
  });
}

setSites twice. The first call puts the rows on screen with names, URLs, reply modes and recordings, all of which are already known. The second call puts the same rows back with one extra field attached.

Collapsing this into a single setSites(withLogin) at the end would be tidier and would be worse. The login probes take as long as they take, and a list that shows nothing until the slowest profile has been opened is a list that looks broken for a second on a cold start. Two renders is the price of showing what you know when you know it.

The counts callback deliberately fires only once, from the second pass. The parent tab uses it for a "4 of 7 ready" summary, and a summary that counts rows nobody has looked up yet would be wrong in a way the user can see.

The type that carries the third state 

/**
 * A search plus whether this tab has confirmed a login for it. Local to the
 * auto-reply tab: it needs one boolean per row and nothing else, and keeping it
 * here means it cannot drift into the monitor's own idea of a session.
 */
interface SetupSite extends Site {
  loggedIn?: boolean;
}

loggedIn?: boolean is three states wearing two states' clothes: true, false, and absent. The component knows this and unpacks it explicitly at the top of the map:

// undefined while the first check is still in flight - not the same as
// signed out, so the row waits rather than accusing them of being out.
const loggedIn = site.loggedIn === true;
const loginChecked = site.loggedIn !== undefined;

One optional boolean in, two booleans out, and every consumer on the row takes both. This is the part of the file I think is right. The alternative, a LoginState union with a "checking" member, would be more honest in the type and would also mean inventing a value that exists purely to describe the absence of a value, in a field that is set exactly once, two lines after it is created. Deriving the pair at the use site keeps the wire format as "the field is there or it is not".

The status line reads both and leads with the unknown case:

function statusLine(recipe, on, loggedIn, loginChecked): string {
  if (!loginChecked) return "Checking your login…";

  // The login comes before everything else it could say, because nothing else on
  // this row can happen without it, not the setup, and not a reply.
  if (!loggedIn) {
    if (!recipe) return "Log in to this site to set it up. Listings are emailed to you meanwhile.";
    ...
  }
  ...
}

And the action button renders nothing at all until the answer is in:

{!loginChecked ? null : !loggedIn ? (
  <button onClick={() => setLoginFor(site)}>Log in</button>
) : !recipe ? (
  ...
)}

Both correct. Three states in, three behaviours out.

The badge forgot 

function SetupBadge({ recipe, loggedIn, loginChecked }) {
  // The badge names the step the row is waiting on, and while signed out that is
  // the login whatever else is or isn't done: no session, no setup and no reply.
  if (loginChecked && !loggedIn) {
    return <span className={...}>Login needed</span>;
  }
  if (!recipe) {
    return <span className={...}>Not set up</span>;
  }
  if (recipe.status === "broken") {
    return <span className={...}>Site changed</span>;
  }
  if (recipe.status === "verified" && loggedIn) {
    return <span className={...}>Ready</span>;
  }
  return <span className={...}>Set up</span>;
}

It takes loginChecked, and it uses it in exactly one place: to avoid claiming "Login needed" before it knows. That guard is correct and it is also the only one. There is no if (!loginChecked) return <Checking /> at the top, so during the in-flight window the function falls through to whatever the recording alone implies.

Which means a row with a verified recording, mid-check, renders like this:

Kamernet, Leiden
Checking your login...                        [ Set up ]

The status line says the answer is not known. The badge, six pixels to its right, is already reporting one. recipe.status === "verified" && loggedIn is false because loggedIn is false because the field is undefined, so it drops to the final return, which is the "recorded but nothing confirmed sent" badge. A real state, shown at a moment when we have no idea whether it is the right one.

Nobody has reported this and I doubt anybody could. The window is one round trip, the two strings do not contradict each other loudly, and the badge settles to the truth a moment later. It is a bug in the sense that the component had the information and did not use it, which is the kind I find most worth writing down, because the cause is not ignorance of the edge case. The parameter is right there in the signature. Somebody threaded loginChecked into this function specifically for the unknown state and then handled one branch of it.

The fix is four lines and an extra grey pill. What I would rather do is stop passing two booleans to three different functions and let the row compute one rowState value once, so that adding a state means updating one switch instead of remembering three call sites. That is the actual lesson: deriving a pair of booleans at the use site is fine when there is one use site, and this row has three.

Two more things in the same function

withLoginState probes once per host, not once per search:

/**
 * Attach each search's login state, one lookup per host.
 *
 * `skipLogin` is about scraping a public results page and buys nothing here,
 * so those searches are reported as signed out rather than exempt.
 */
async function withLoginState(list: Site[]): Promise<SetupSite[]> {
  const hosts = [...new Set(list.map((s) => hostOf(s.url)).filter(Boolean))];
  const results = await Promise.all(
    hosts.map(async (host) => {
      const site = list.find((s) => hostOf(s.url) === host);
      if (!site) return [host, false] as const;
      try {
        const { data } = await getLoginStatus(site.url);
        return [host, data.loggedIn === true] as const;
      } catch {
        return [host, false] as const;
      }
    })
  );
  const byHost = new Map(results);
  return list.map((s) => ({ ...s, loggedIn: byHost.get(hostOf(s.url)) ?? false }));
}

A session belongs to a host, so three searches on one portal are one probe, and the deduplication is what makes the two-render pattern cheap enough to repeat.

And it repeats quite a lot, because while a recording is open the component polls:

// While a recording is open, keep the captured-action count live.
useEffect(() => {
  if (!recording.recording) return;
  const timer = setInterval(() => void load(), 2000);
  return () => clearInterval(timer);
}, [recording.recording]);

Every two seconds, for as long as the user is demonstrating a reply, the whole load() runs: two API calls, then one login probe per distinct host, then two setSites. That interval exists to keep a single number on screen fresh, the count of actions captured so far. It is re-fetching everything to animate one integer.

Also note the ?? false in the last line. A probe that threw and a probe that came back negative produce the same value, so a browser profile that failed to open reads as "signed out" and the row offers a login the user does not need. Three states at the top of the function, two by the bottom of it, which is the same shape as the badge bug one level down.

If you want to see what the thing being set up actually does, there is a guide on writing the first message to a landlord, which is the message the recording ends up replaying.

title: A page-turning book in Remotion is one array of leaves, a rotateY and two faces, and the stacking order is the only hard part
description:
The third video ad we built for Nakodo is a book. It drops onto a desk, the cover opens, twenty pages riffle past under a thumb, and it stops on the first of three spreads. It is React, rendered with Remotion, and there is no 3D library anywhere in it.

The thing I expected to be hard, the page turn, is nine lines of CSS. The thing that actually took the afternoon was deciding which page is on top.

A book in a 9:16 frame

The first decision is not an animation one. A book is landscape and a reel is portrait, so an honest drawing of an open book in a vertical video gives you two tiny pages and a lot of desk.

So the spine sits just inside the left edge:

export const BOOK = { left: 70, top: 250, width: 940, height: 1360 };
export const COVER = { left: BOOK.left - 6, top: BOOK.top - 28, width: BOOK.width + 42, height: BOOK.height + 56 };

The right-hand page fills the frame. The left-hand page exists, and is drawn, at left - width, which is off screen. You never see it, but pages have to turn onto something, and the shadow near the spine only reads as a gutter if there is a page under it.

COVER is the same box plus a margin on three sides, because a hardback's boards overhang its pages, and that overhang is most of what makes a rectangle read as a book.

Every leaf is a row in one array 

type Leaf = {
  start: number;
  turn: number;
  ease: (t: number) => number;
  front: (f: number) => ReactNode;
  back?: ReactNode;
  box?: typeof BOOK;
};

The whole book is one array in that shape: the cover first, then twenty riffle pages, then the three content pages, then the call to action.

const LEAVES: Leaf[] = [
  { start: COVER_OPEN, turn: COVER_TURN, ease: easeInOut, front: () => <Cover />, back: <CoverInside />, box: COVER },
  ...Array.from({ length: RIFFLE_PAGES }, (_, k): Leaf => ({
    start: RIFFLE_STARTS[k],
    turn: riffleTurn(k),
    ease: smooth,
    front: () => <Paper><RifflePage k={k} /></Paper>,
  })),
  ...PAGES.map((Page, i): Leaf => ({ start: TURN_AT[i], turn: TURN, ease: easeInOut, front: (f) => <Paper><Page t={f - PAGE_AT[i]} /></Paper> })),
  { start: 1e9, turn: 1, ease: smooth, front: (f) => /* the end card */ },
];

front is a function of the frame, not a node, because the content of a page animates while the page lies there: a word gets pecked and turns into another word. back is a plain node because the back of a page is blank in every case but one.

start: 1e9 on the last leaf is the laziest possible way to say "this one never turns over". It is the last page; the video ends while it is open. A turnsOver: false flag would have been one more branch in the renderer for one row in the data.

The turn 

export function Turning({ angle, front, back, box = BOOK }) {
  if (angle >= 179.5) return null;
  const { left, top, width, height } = box;
  const lift = Math.sin((Math.min(angle, 90) * Math.PI) / 180);
  return (
    <div style={abs({ left, top, width, height, perspective: 4200, perspectiveOrigin: `0px ${height / 2}px` })}>
      <div style={abs({ inset: 0, transformOrigin: "0 50%", transformStyle: "preserve-3d", transform: `rotateY(${-angle}deg)` })}>
        <div style={abs({ inset: 0, backfaceVisibility: "hidden" })}>
          {front}
          <div style={abs({ inset: 0, background: `rgba(20,30,50,${0.16 * lift})` })} />
        </div>
        <div style={abs({ inset: 0, backfaceVisibility: "hidden", transform: "rotateY(180deg)" })}>{back ?? <Paper />}</div>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

That is the entire mechanism. transformOrigin: "0 50%" puts the hinge on the spine. rotateY(-angle) swings it, 0 lying flat and 180 turned over. Two children both with backfaceVisibility: hidden, the second pre-rotated by 180 degrees, so exactly one of them faces you at any angle and they swap at upright on their own.

perspectiveOrigin at 0px, height/2 puts the vanishing point on the hinge rather than in the middle of the page, which is the difference between a page turning and a page being swung around like a door.

lift darkens the front as it rises, peaking at upright, using sin of the angle clamped to 90. No lighting model, one multiply.

The early return at 179.5 rather than 180 is a practical detail. A page lying flat on the left page is off screen and perfectly flush with whatever is under it, and leaving it mounted means every landed page contributes another composited layer for the rest of the video.

Which page is on top

This is the part that is not obvious, and it is six lines:

const angles = LEAVES.map((l) => angleOf(l, f));
const open = angles.findIndex((a) => a === 0);
const turning = LEAVES.map((l, i) => ({ l, i, a: angles[i] })).filter(({ a }) => a > 0 && a < 180);
const lowest = turning.length ? turning[turning.length - 1].a : 0;

At any frame a leaf is in one of three states, straight out of its angle: not started (0), turning (0 to 180), or done (180). So:

  • the page you can see lying open is the first leaf that has not started to turn, found with a findIndex for a zero;
  • everything turning is drawn after it, in reverse array order, because a leaf later in the book sits under the ones before it, and the ones before it have turned further;
  • lowest is the angle of the last leaf still turning, which is the one closest to the page below, and that is the angle the cast shadow is drawn from. 
{turning.slice().reverse().map(({ l, i, a }) => <Turning key={i} angle={a} front={l.front(f)} back={l.back} box={l.box} />)}

Nothing in the data says what is in front of what. Z-order falls out of array order plus the angles, which means adding a page to the book is adding an object to an array and nothing else. The first version of this had explicit z-index numbers and I got twenty pages into the riffle before I admitted that I was maintaining a second copy of the ordering by hand.

The riffle is two easing curves, not twenty keyframes 

const gapAt = (k: number) => 2 + 2.6 * (1 - Math.sin((Math.PI * k) / (RIFFLE_PAGES - 1)));
export const RIFFLE_STARTS = Array.from({ length: RIFFLE_PAGES }, (_, k) => k)
  .reduce<number[]>((s, k) => [...s, k === 0 ? RIFFLE_FROM : s[k - 1] + gapAt(k)], []);
export const riffleTurn = (k: number) => 6 + 4 * (1 - Math.sin((Math.PI * k) / (RIFFLE_PAGES - 1)));

A thumb released off a stack of pages is slow at the start, fast through the middle and slows to a stop. Both the gap between pages starting and the time each page takes to turn follow the same half-sine: 4.6 frames apart at the ends, 2 frames apart in the middle.

The starts are a cumulative sum, because what you control is the gap and what the renderer needs is the time. Twenty rows of hand-tuned numbers would have been the obvious thing to write and impossible to retime later; this way the whole riffle is two constants and a curve.

The shadow 

const reach = width * Math.cos((angle * Math.PI) / 180);
const k = Math.sin((angle * Math.PI) / 90) * 0.28;

A lifting page casts a shadow onto the page under it, and the shadow is as wide as the page's own projection: width * cos(angle). At 0 it covers the page exactly, at 90 it has gone.

The darkness uses angle * PI / 90, not /180. That doubles the frequency, so the sine peaks at 45 degrees and returns to zero at 90, which is roughly when a real page is darkest against the one below: not flat, not upright, somewhere in between.

The end card is a whole screen stuffed into a page

The last leaf has to show the same call to action as our other two reels, which is a component laid out against the full 1080 by 1920 frame, not against a 940 by 1360 page.

<Paper>
  <div style={abs({ left: -BOOK.left - 4, top: -BOOK.top - 4, width: W, height: H })}>
    <EndCard t={endT(f)} alcy={false} background={C.paper0} headline={<>Find creators<br />who say yes.</>} />
  </div>
</Paper>

Shift it back by the page's own offset and let Paper's overflow: hidden crop it. The alcy={false} prop exists because the shared end card normally flies our bird in to press the button, and in this reel the bird is already on the page and walks to it instead.

Was the book the right idea

The reel argues three things: that the wrong creator will not film your product, that a DM sinks under everybody else's, and that a guessed fee gets no reply. Those are the same arguments as the written guide to vetting a creator and the sponsorship cost calculator, which is the point: the ad is a trailer for pages that already existed.

A field guide was the right container for "three reasons" because turning a page is a free scene transition that an audience already understands. The cost is this file. If you only need one transition, use a crossfade.

The thing I would take to the next project is the leaf array. Any sequence where things overlap in time and stack in space wants to be one list of objects with a start, a duration and a renderer, with the stacking derived rather than stored. The moment the ordering lives in two places, one of them is already wrong.

title: Our relative timestamps round instead of floor, so 91 seconds ago reads as 2m ago
description:
Notifio is a desktop app that checks rental search pages on a loop and emails you when a new listing shows up. Almost every number in its UI is a time: when a search was last checked, how long the check took, when a blocked host gets retried, when a listing turned up.

All of that goes through one 25-line file. I read it properly for the first time last week and found that it rounds, everywhere, and that rounding means two different things depending on which direction the clock is pointing.

The file 

/** Small shared formatters for the status strip and the finds list. */

/** "12s ago", "4m ago", "2h ago". Empty string for a null timestamp. */
export function relativeTime(at: number | null): string {
  if (!at) return "";
  const seconds = Math.max(0, Math.round((Date.now() - at) / 1000));
  if (seconds < 10) return "just now";
  if (seconds < 60) return `${seconds}s ago`;
  const minutes = Math.round(seconds / 60);
  if (minutes < 60) return `${minutes}m ago`;
  const hours = Math.round(minutes / 60);
  if (hours < 24) return `${hours}h ago`;
  return `${Math.round(hours / 24)}d ago`;
}

/** "in 45s", "in 3m". Used for the retry countdown on a blocked search. */
export function countdown(until: number): string {
  const ms = until - Date.now();
  if (ms <= 0) return "any moment";
  if (ms < 60_000) return `in ${Math.max(1, Math.round(ms / 1000))}s`;
  return `in ${Math.round(ms / 60_000)}m`;
}

/** "1.4s". Shown on a row so a slow site is visible rather than guessed at. */
export function seconds(ms: number | null): string {
  if (ms === null) return "";
  return `${(ms / 1000).toFixed(1)}s`;
}

Four Math.round calls in relativeTime, one in countdown. The conventional choice for elapsed time is Math.floor, and I want to argue that the conventional choice is wrong in one of these functions and right in the other.

Rounding an elapsed time can only overstate

relativeTime(Date.now() - 91_000) gives "2m ago". Ninety-one seconds is one minute and thirty-one seconds. Math.floor would say 1m ago, which is true and under-informative. Math.round says 2m ago, which is false and over-informative.

Work out the sign of the error and it stops being a toss-up. A rounded elapsed time is wrong in one direction only: it can claim something is older than it is by up to half a unit, and it can never claim something is newer than it is. Floor does the opposite. It can claim a check that happened 119 seconds ago was "1m ago", which is the direction that matters here, because every one of these timestamps is answering the same underlying question:

Is this thing still working?

A monitor that says last check 1m ago when it was really two minutes is a monitor reassuring you with a number it made up. A monitor that says 2m ago when it was really 91 seconds has rounded against itself. If the app is going to be wrong by up to thirty seconds, I want it wrong in the direction that makes me look at it.

That is not an accident of the implementation, but I cannot claim it was planned either. The comment above the function says "12s ago", "4m ago", "2h ago" and nothing about rounding. I am adopting it after the fact, which is a thing you are allowed to do as long as you write the reason down somewhere, which is partly what this post is.

Rounding a countdown breaks a promise

countdown is a different proposition, because it is not reporting, it is promising. It renders on the retry chip of a search whose host has told us to wait:

{waiting && (
  <button
    onClick={onRetry}
    title="Stop waiting and check this search again now"
    className={`${CHIP} group min-w-[104px] ...`}
  >
    <span className="group-hover:hidden">Retry {countdown(waiting)}</span>
    <span className="hidden group-hover:inline">Retry now</span>
  </button>
)}

With 89 seconds left, Math.round(89_000 / 60_000) is 1, so the chip says Retry in 1m. A minute later nothing has happened, because there are still 29 seconds to go. The chip has by then updated itself to in 29s, so it self-corrects rather than lying permanently, but there is a moment where the app said one minute and meant one and a half.

For a countdown, Math.ceil is the honest function. The error should fall on the same side as it does for elapsed time: never promise sooner than you can deliver. One character.

I have not changed it yet, and the reason is the thing hovering over that chip. Every countdown in this app is skippable. Hover the chip and the text swaps to Retry now, click it and the wait is over. We decided a while back that if the app shows you a countdown it has to let you out of it, and that decision takes most of the weight off the exact number. A countdown you can cancel is a hint. A countdown you cannot cancel is a contract, and a contract should round up.

Note also the Math.max(1, ...) on the seconds branch. Without it, 400ms remaining renders as in 0s, which is the single worst string a countdown can produce: it is both wrong and finished-looking. The floor of 1 means the chip counts in 2s, in 1s, any moment, and any moment is the right register for a number we do not actually control.

The clock that drives all of it

None of these functions are reactive. They read Date.now() when they run, and React does not re-render because time passed. So there is a hook whose entire job is to make a component re-render on a schedule:

export function useNow(intervalMs = 1000, active = true): number {
  const [now, setNow] = useState(() => Date.now());

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!active) return;
    const timer = setInterval(() => setNow(Date.now()), intervalMs);
    return () => clearInterval(timer);
  }, [intervalMs, active]);

  return now;
}

Three components call it, with three different intervals and three different conditions:

// SitesList: one second, but only while something is counting down.
useNow(1000, hasCountdown || app.status === "polling");

// MonitorCard: five seconds, only while the monitor is in an active state.
useNow(5000, isActive);

// RecentFinds: thirty seconds, only if there is anything in the list.
useNow(30_000, app.finds.length > 0);

The intervals are chosen against the formatter, not against the component. SitesList is the only one that renders a countdown, whose output changes every second below a minute, so it ticks every second. RecentFinds renders relativeTime on listings that are minutes to days old, where the string changes at most once a minute, so thirty seconds is already generous and a one-second tick would be 29 wasted renders out of 30.

The active flags matter more than the intervals. This app's whole job is to sit in the background for hours, and a React tree re-rendering once a second while nobody is looking at it is a laptop fan. hasCountdown is computed per render from whether any search has a nextRetryAt:

// Only tick while something is actually counting down.
const hasCountdown = sites.some((s) => {
  const nextRetryAt = app.runtimeFor(s)?.nextRetryAt;
  return nextRetryAt !== null && nextRetryAt !== undefined;
});

So the second-by-second timer exists only while a host is in backoff or a poll is in flight, and the rest of the time the tree is still. The dependency array is [intervalMs, active], so flipping active tears the interval down rather than leaving it running against a stale condition.

There is still a seam in SitesList: above one minute, countdown returns the same string for sixty consecutive ticks. The fix is to compute the next interesting moment and set a timeout for exactly that, and it is not worth it for one chip on an app with at most fifteen searches running.

What I would take from this

Pick the rounding mode from the sign of the error you can live with, not from what reads nicest. "Round to nearest" is the default because it minimises average error, and average error is almost never the thing that matters in a status line. What matters is which way the UI lies when it lies, and whether that direction makes the user check or relax.

Elapsed time: round up, make them look. Countdown: round up, make them wait. Both of those are the same rule, which is a good sign that it is the rule.

The app this came out of is at notifio.app, and there is a page per site it watches under alerts if you want to see what it is timing.

title: How to Convert PDF to JPG Directly in the Browser Using JavaScript and PDF.js
description:
When developing modern web applications or document utility platforms, handling file conversions efficiently on the client side is a game-changer. Processing files directly in the browser reduces server costs, speeds up performance, and ensures complete user privacy.

In this guide, we will explore how to build a robust, pure client-side PDF-to-JPG converter using vanilla JavaScript and the powerful PDF.js library.

Why Choose Client-Side PDF Conversion?

Traditional file conversion relies heavily on backend infrastructure (like Python, Ghostscript, or cloud APIs) to unpack PDF pages and render them as images.

Shifting this process to the browser offers major benefits:

Zero Server Overhead: The client's browser handles all the heavy computation.

Instant Processing: Users do not need to wait for multi-step file uploads and downloads.

Data Security: Sensitive documents never leave the user's local machine.

Step-by-Step Implementation

  1. Include PDF.js via CDN To parse and render PDF files in the browser, Mozilla's PDF.js library is the industry standard. Include the worker and main library scripts in your HTML: 
<script 
src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/pdf.js/3.11.174/pdf.min.js"></script>
<script>
    pdfjsLib.GlobalWorkerOptions.workerSrc = 'https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/pdf.js/3.11.174/pdf.worker.min.js';
</script>

2. Core Conversion JavaScript Logic
Here is an asynchronous function that loads a selected PDF file, extracts the first page, renders it onto an HTML5 Canvas, and converts it into a downloadable JPG image format.

async function convertPdfFirstPageToJpg(pdfFile) {
    if (!pdfFile || pdfFile.type !== "application/pdf") {
        throw new Error("Please upload a valid PDF file.");
    }

    try {
        // 1. Read the PDF file into an ArrayBuffer
        const arrayBuffer = await pdfFile.arrayBuffer();

        // 2. Load the PDF document using PDF.js
        const loadingTask = pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: arrayBuffer });
        const pdfDocument = await loadingTask.promise;

        // 3. Fetch the first page of the PDF
        const page = await pdfDocument.getPage(1);

        // 4. Set up scale and viewport for rendering
        const viewport = page.getViewport({ scale: 1.5 });
        const canvas = document.createElement("canvas");
        const context = canvas.getContext("2d");

        canvas.height = viewport.height;
        canvas.width = viewport.width;

        // 5. Render the PDF page content into the canvas context
        const renderContext = {
            canvasContext: context,
            viewport: viewport
        };
        await page.render(renderContext).promise;

        // 6. Convert canvas content into a JPG Data URL and trigger download
        const jpgDataUrl = canvas.toDataURL("image/jpeg", 0.9);

        const downloadLink = document.createElement("a");
        downloadLink.href = jpgDataUrl;
        downloadLink.download = "converted-page.jpg";
        downloadLink.click();

        console.log("PDF page successfully converted to JPG!");

    } catch (error) {
        console.error("Error during PDF to JPG conversion:", error);
    }
}

Handling Multi-Page PDFs

If your platform needs to handle large multi-page documents and convert every page into an individual JPG image, you can loop through all pages dynamically:

async function convertAllPdfPagesToJpg(pdfFile) {
    const arrayBuffer = await pdfFile.arrayBuffer();
    const pdfDocument = await pdfjsLib.getDocument({ data: arrayBuffer }).promise;

    for (let pageNum = 1; pageNum <= pdfDocument.numPages; pageNum++) {
        const page = await pdfDocument.getPage(pageNum);
        const viewport = page.getViewport({ scale: 1.5 });

        const canvas = document.createElement("canvas");
        const context = canvas.getContext("2d");
        canvas.height = viewport.height;
        canvas.width = viewport.width;

        await page.render({ canvasContext: context, viewport: viewport }).promise;

        const jpgDataUrl = canvas.toDataURL("image/jpeg", 0.85);

        // Save each page iteratively
        const link = document.createElement("a");
        link.href = jpgDataUrl;
        link.download = `page-${pageNum}.jpg`;
        link.click();
    }
}

Best Practices & Error Handling

Memory Management: Rendering high-resolution PDF pages can consume significant browser memory. Adjust the scale parameter (e.g., 1.0 or 1.5) to balance image clarity and performance.

File Validation: Always check the MIME type (application/pdf) and file extensions to prevent unexpected runtime parsing exceptions.

Conclusion
Building a client-side PDF-to-JPG converter gives developers a lightweight, scalable tool without relying on complex backend servers. With PDF.js and HTML5 Canvas, you can render high-quality document previews directly in the browser.

(Note: If you are looking for an instant, ready-to-use production web tool built on these concepts for everyday document management, you can check out pdftojpg.world)

title: Stop Shipping Custom UI That Disappears in `forced-colors` Mode
description:
A QA ticket landed with a screenshot: "Submit button missing on checkout." I opened the page in Chrome. The button was right there — blue, rounded, impossible to miss. I opened it in Firefox. Same button. I assumed a bad screenshot and closed the ticket.

Three days later it came back, same screenshot, same page, from a different tester. This time I asked what they'd changed. "Nothing," they said. "I just use Windows with High Contrast on, because I'm light-sensitive." I flipped that setting on my own machine for the first time in years, reloaded the page, and watched my button disappear into the background like it had never existed.

It wasn't a rendering bug. It wasn't a z-index fight. It was a CSS feature I'd never once had to think about, quietly rewriting my entire color palette out from under me.

The fix that didn't fix anything

My first guess was contrast. The button used background: #2563eb on a white card — readable, passed every automated contrast checker I ran. So I assumed High Contrast Mode was some kind of amplifier: it probably just needed more contrast to work with. I darkened the blue, added a heavier box-shadow for depth, bumped the border a shade, and shipped it.

The next build, the button was still gone.

That's the part that should have told me something was off: I hadn't made the colors fail a contrast check, I'd made them more correct by every metric I knew how to check — and the bug didn't budge. If contrast were the problem, a darker blue should have helped. It changed nothing, because the browser was never reading my blue in the first place.

What forced-colors actually does

Windows High Contrast Mode doesn't ask the browser to render your page with better contrast. It tells the browser to render your page using the operating system's own fixed palette — full stop, author CSS or not. Every modern browser exposes this as a media feature:

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  /* the user has an OS-level forced-colors palette turned on */
}

It only ever matches when the user has flipped an OS-level switch (Windows High Contrast themes are the classic trigger) — you can't turn it on with JavaScript, and prefers-contrast is a different, much gentler feature that just reports a preference for more or less contrast without touching your styles at all. forced-colors is not a hint. When it's active, the browser overrides nearly every color-related property you wrote — color, background-color, border-color, outline-color — and remaps each one onto one of a couple dozen system colors, chosen by what kind of element it's on. Normal text becomes CanvasText on a Canvas background. A button's label becomes ButtonText. None of that is something your stylesheet gets a vote on.

Two more things get treated even more bluntly: box-shadow and text-shadow are forced to none, and any background-image that isn't a url() is forced to none too. There's no sensible way to remap a drop shadow or a gradient onto a small fixed palette, so the browser doesn't try — it just removes them.

Here's the part that explains my exact bug. My button's shape came from background: #2563eb plus a box-shadow for depth, and it had border: none. Under forced colors: the background got remapped to some flat system color, the shadow vanished outright, and because I'd never declared an actual border, there was nothing left for the browser to recolor into a visible edge. The button didn't get uglier — it got structurally invisible, blending straight into the page.

Quick gut check before you keep reading: if a native <button> has the exact same styles — background, box-shadow, border: none — why does it usually survive forced colors when a <div> styled to look like a button doesn't?

Why the real button survived and the fake one didn't

The difference isn't that <button> is magic. It's that most "reset" button styles only remove the parts they're actively replacing, and browsers ship a default border on form controls in their user-agent stylesheet. Unless you've specifically zeroed that out, there's still a border on a native <button> for forced colors to recolor into something visible. A <div> built from scratch as a custom checkbox or button usually never had a border at all — its shape existed only in the properties forced colors throws away.

This is a known enough pattern that there's a standing trick for it: give decorative edges a border: 1px solid transparent instead of border: none in your normal styles. Visually, nothing changes — a transparent border is invisible either way. But forced colors mode remaps border colors, including transparent, onto the system palette. You get a free, correctly colored boundary in forced-colors mode without touching how the component looks the other 99% of the time anyone views it.

The actual fix

The reliable fix isn't fighting the override — it's meeting it, explicitly, with the same palette the browser is already using. System color keywords like ButtonBorder, ButtonFace, Highlight, and CanvasText are valid CSS values any time, and forced colors mode treats them as already correct, so it leaves them alone instead of remapping them to something else:

.custom-checkbox {
  background: #2563eb;
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 2px #93c5fd;
  border: none;
}

@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .custom-checkbox {
    /* box-shadow is gone here no matter what — give it a real border instead */
    border: 1px solid ButtonBorder;
    background: ButtonFace;
  }

  .custom-checkbox[aria-checked="true"] {
    background: Highlight;
    border-color: Highlight;
  }
}

Nothing in the normal-mode styles changes. Inside the media query, the checkbox gets an explicit border using a keyword that already means "the border color controls should have," and its checked state uses Highlight, the same system color the browser uses for selected text and active UI. The result matches how every native control on that user's machine already looks — which is the entire point of the feature.

There's one more lever worth knowing, and it's a trap if you reach for it too fast: forced-color-adjust: none opts an element out of all of this, so your original colors render exactly as written, forced colors mode or not — in browsers that support the property. Unlike forced-colors itself, forced-color-adjust isn't Baseline yet: Chrome and Firefox support it, but Safari doesn't, as of this writing — so don't treat it as a guaranteed universal escape hatch, and still test the element without it. It's tempting to slap it on the whole page the moment you see something break. Don't. The moment you opt out, you own the contrast and visibility guarantees the user just told their OS they need — that's appropriate for a brand logo or a purely decorative illustration, and actively harmful on real text or an interactive control. If you ever use it, use it narrowly, and never on anything the user has to read or click.

Test it before a bug report does

The quickest way to see all of this without touching a single Windows setting: Chromium-based DevTools (Chrome, Edge) can emulate forced colors mode directly — open the Rendering tab and look for the CSS media feature emulation options, flip forced-colors to "active," and reload. Every property swap in this post happens live, on your own page, in your own browser.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

What I actually changed

I didn't rewrite the design system. I added one @media (forced-colors: active) block per component that relied on shadows or background color for its shape, each one just a border and maybe a background swap using system keywords. The checkout button that started this whole thing now has four extra lines of CSS. It's visible to every High Contrast user it was invisible to before, and it looks exactly the same to everyone else.

The lesson that actually stuck with me isn't about this one bug. It's that "I tested it and it looks fine" has a hidden asterisk: fine in whose color scheme. Dark mode earned a place in every component checklist a few years ago. Forced colors deserves the same five-second check before you call something done — because the first time you hear about it, like me, it'll be from someone who can't see your product at all.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Have you checked your own components in forced-colors mode yet? Open DevTools, flip the emulation on, and see what quietly vanishes — I'd genuinely like to know what you find.

title: Go error handling patterns that scale: wrapping, unwrapping, sentinels
description:
Go's error handling gets a lot of criticism from developers coming from exception-based languages. But the real problem isn't if err != nil — it's the patterns that get built on top of it. Most tutorials show you bare error returns and call it a day. In a production codebase, you end up with errors that tell you something failed but not where, why, or what caller context led there.

The Problem with Bare Error Returns

Here's the code you write when you're moving fast:

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return &u, nil
}

This compiles fine. It even works. But when the error reaches your HTTP handler and you log it, you get:

sql: no rows in result set

That's all. No package name, no function name, no request ID, no context about what was being fetched. Multiply this by 50 functions across 15 packages and you have a log that's useless for debugging.

Wrapping Errors with fmt.Errorf and %w

Go 1.13 introduced the %w verb for fmt.Errorf, which wraps an error while preserving the original for later inspection:

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, err)
    }
    return &u, nil
}

Now the error travels up the stack with context attached at each layer:

handler: processRequest: getUser(id=abc123): sql: no rows in result set

The rule I follow: always wrap at the point of origin, never in the middle without adding information. Wrapping fmt.Errorf("getUser: %w", err) inside a loop that calls getUser ten times just adds noise.

One subtle gotcha: %w creates a chain. fmt.Errorf("context: %w", fmt.Errorf("inner: %w", originalErr)) gives you three levels. That's fine — errors.Unwrap navigates the chain, and errors.Is/errors.As traverse it automatically.

Sentinel Errors: When to Use Them

A sentinel error is a package-level variable that callers can compare against:

var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")
var ErrUnauthorized = errors.New("unauthorized")

func getUser(id string) (*User, error) {
    row := db.QueryRow("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
    var u User
    if err := row.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Email); err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, ErrNotFound)
        }
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("getUser(id=%s): %w", id, err)
    }
    return &u, nil
}

The caller can now do:

user, err := getUser(id)
if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) {
    http.Error(w, "user not found", http.StatusNotFound)
    return
}

This works because errors.Is traverses the entire error chain — even though ErrNotFound is wrapped inside fmt.Errorf, errors.Is finds it.

When to use sentinels: when callers need to make branching decisions based on the error type. Not found, permission denied, rate limited — these are meaningful categories that affect control flow.

When not to: for every internal error. Package io has io.EOF because it's a legitimate signal, not just a failure. Your internal database timeout doesn't need to be a sentinel unless callers genuinely need to handle it differently.

Custom Error Types for Structured Data

Sometimes you need to carry structured data in an error — an HTTP status code, a field name that failed validation, a request ID for correlation. That's where custom error types come in:

type ValidationError struct {
    Field   string
    Message string
}

func (e *ValidationError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("validation failed on field %q: %s", e.Field, e.Message)
}

func validateEmail(email string) error {
    if !strings.Contains(email, "@") {
        return &ValidationError{Field: "email", Message: "must contain @"}
    }
    return nil
}

The caller uses errors.As to extract the structured data:

err := validateEmail(input)
var ve *ValidationError
if errors.As(err, &ve) {
    respondWithFieldError(w, ve.Field, ve.Message)
}

errors.As also traverses the chain, so if validateEmail's error gets wrapped by an outer function, errors.As still finds it.

The combination of custom types and wrapping lets you do something powerful: an HTTP handler can catch a *ValidationError and return 400, catch ErrNotFound and return 404, and return 500 for everything else — without knowing the internals of the packages it calls.

Unwrapping: errors.Is, errors.As, and the Chain

Here's the mental model that makes all of this click:

  • errors.Is(err, target) — walks the chain calling == at each step. Use for sentinel comparison.
  • errors.As(err, &target) — walks the chain looking for a type match. Use for custom types.
  • errors.Unwrap(err) — returns the next error in the chain. Rarely call this directly. 
// Chain: wrapErr → ErrNotFound
wrapErr := fmt.Errorf("some context: %w", ErrNotFound)

fmt.Println(errors.Is(wrapErr, ErrNotFound))   // true
fmt.Println(wrapErr == ErrNotFound)             // false — never use == on wrapped errors

This is the most common mistake I see in Go codebases: using == to compare errors after wrapping. It always returns false. Always use errors.Is.

One more thing: if you implement a custom error type that wraps another, implement Unwrap() error to make the chain traversable:

type AppError struct {
    Code    int
    Message string
    Err     error
}

func (e *AppError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("[%d] %s: %v", e.Code, e.Message, e.Err)
}

func (e *AppError) Unwrap() error {
    return e.Err
}

Without Unwrap, errors.Is and errors.As stop at AppError and can't see what's wrapped inside it.

Sanitizing Errors at the API Boundary

For security-hardened applications, consistent error handling isn't just about debuggability — it's about not leaking internal details to API consumers while still giving operators enough context to diagnose issues.

A pattern I've used in production:

type internalError struct {
    Op  string
    Err error
}

func (e *internalError) Error() string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("op=%s: %v", e.Op, e.Err)
}

func (e *internalError) Unwrap() error { return e.Err }

// At the HTTP boundary, sanitize before responding
func sanitizeError(err error) string {
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound):
        return "resource not found"
    case errors.Is(err, ErrUnauthorized):
        return "unauthorized"
    default:
        log.Printf("internal error: %v", err) // full chain logged internally
        return "internal server error"
    }
}

The internal error carries full context for your logs. The API caller gets a safe, generic message. The operator log has everything needed to trace the failure back to its source.

The Takeaway

Go error handling scales when you follow three rules consistently:

  1. Wrap with context using fmt.Errorf("op: %w", err) at every layer that adds meaningful information.
  2. Use sentinels only for errors that callers genuinely need to branch on — not for every internal failure.
  3. Use custom types when you need structured data alongside the error message, and always implement Unwrap() when your type wraps another error.

The errors.Is and errors.As functions handle chain traversal automatically. Once you internalize that model, Go error handling stops being a boilerplate tax and starts being a precise contract between layers.

title: Set the canvas size before configuring the drawing context
description:
If a canvas loses its background on the second render, inspect its size assignments. Look for writes to canvas.width and canvas.height between painting the background and drawing the image.

Assigning either dimension resets the drawing context. The pixels disappear, and settings such as the fill color, transform, and compositing mode return to their defaults. Even assigning the width its existing value causes a reset. MDN documents this behavior in its canvas width reference.

The order that loses the background

Suppose an export should place a transparent image on white. This sequence contains a problem:

const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
ctx.fillStyle = "white";
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
canvas.width = targetWidth;
canvas.height = targetHeight;
ctx.drawImage(image, 0, 0, targetWidth, targetHeight);

The background was painted into the old bitmap. Changing the dimensions clears it before the image is drawn. A preview against a white page may conceal the mistake because the page shows through the transparent canvas.

Set both dimensions first, then establish the drawing state:

canvas.width = targetWidth;
canvas.height = targetHeight;
const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
if (!ctx) throw new Error("A 2D context is required");
ctx.fillStyle = "white";
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, targetWidth, targetHeight);
ctx.drawImage(image, 0, 0, targetWidth, targetHeight);

Here image must already be decoded, and the target dimensions must be positive integers chosen by the application. The example assumes their aspect ratio is intentional. Stretching a photograph into a different ratio would be a separate bug.

Make each render complete

Give the render function the source image and the output settings it needs. After setting the dimensions, apply every setting the drawing operation depends on. That makes the second render follow the same path as the first.

For example, if the application uses a transform for rotation, configure that transform after resizing. If it disables smoothing for pixel art, apply that choice after resizing too. A context object remaining in a variable does not mean its earlier settings survived.

Avoid using canvas.width = canvas.width as an unexplained clearing trick. It also resets state, which can make later edits difficult to reason about. If clearing pixels is the intention, a deliberate clearing operation communicates that intention more clearly, with the current transform and clipping region taken into account.

A small regression case

Use a transparent test image with an opaque colored square in the middle. Render it onto a white background, change the output dimensions, then render it again. Inspect a corner that should contain only the background. The corner should remain white after both renders.

Also exercise the case where the second render requests the same dimensions. A test that only checks changes in size can miss an unconditional width assignment in a shared helper. Keep the test focused on the output pixels and the behavior the user needs, rather than asserting which internal helper ran.

When a preview looks correct but an exported file has an unexpected background, inspect the drawing sequence before adjusting compression. An encoder cannot restore a background that was cleared before encoding began. Put both size assignments near the start of the render function so a later edit does not clear work already drawn.
