title: Best AI UI Design Tools I Wish I Had Found Earlier in My Career
description:
Early in my career, I spent hours on work that had nothing to do with design thinking. I rebuilt the same navbar again and again, recreated card layouts from old projects, and turned rough sketches into clickable screens at the last minute.

AI UI design tools remove much of that setup. They don't replace taste or judgment, but they give you something real to react to in seconds instead of a blank canvas. These are the nine I wish I had found earlier.

TL;DR

  • No single tool wins. Speed comes from chaining tools so you never rebuild work.
  • Stitch, Banani AI, Uizard, and Visily get you to screens fast.
  • Figma Make, v0, Bolt.new, and Lovable AI turn screens into interactive or working products.
  • Framer AI takes polished pages live.
  • Judge every tool by handoff, not by how good the first screen looks.

How I Evaluated These Tools

Almost every tool shows a first screen in seconds, so that isn't the test. I looked at five things:

  • Speed: How fast do you get a draft worth reacting to?
  • **Editability: **Can you make precise changes without re-prompting everything?
  • Handoff: Does it export to Figma or code, or does the work get trapped?
  • Fidelity: Is it a wireframe, a mockup, or a working prototype?
  • Fit: Does it match how you already work?

The Tools at a Glance

Tool Best At Output Handoff
Figma Make Prototypes inside Figma Interactive prototypes Native Figma, publish to web
Google Stitch Fast UI concepts Screens and code Figma, HTML/CSS, Tailwind, JSX
v0 by Vercel UI and React components Code-backed interfaces Code-first, Figma import
Bolt.new Full-stack apps Running apps in browser Deploy, GitHub, Figma import
Lovable AI Chat-built functional sites Hosted working sites Hosting and integrations
Framer AI Polished marketing sites Live, editable pages Publishes from canvas
Uizard Sketch-to-mockup Editable multi-screen designs Figma import, component code
Banani AI Clean multi-screen UI Editable screens Figma, HTML/CSS, MCP
Visily Beginner-friendly wireframes Wireframes and prototypes Built-in prototyping

1. Figma Make

Figma Make is a prompt-to-app capability inside Figma for generating high-fidelity prototypes and refining them in design and code. You can start from a written prompt or from an existing design, so you never begin from zero.

It works best when the design already lives in Figma. You prompt, preview the result, and refine it in the same place, so context doesn't get lost between tools.

Key Features

  • Click an element in the preview, then prompt, style, or swap it directly.
  • Shared AI conversations where teammates prompt, comment, and revise together.
  • Publishing to a dedicated URL.
  • Prototypes that open in a browser without a Figma account.

Best For

Product designers and teams already in Figma who want clickable prototypes without waiting on engineering.

Watch Out For

Prototype quality can be mistaken for product readiness. Review accessibility, responsiveness, and code quality before shipping.

My Takeaway

The fastest way to make an existing Figma design interactive.

2. Google Stitch

Stitch is a Google Labs tool that turns text prompts, sketches, or screenshots into responsive website and mobile app designs. It suits the moment when you have an idea but no layout yet.

Google says it uses Gemini's multimodal abilities to connect design and development more smoothly. The result is a draft you can refine in Figma or hand to developers as code.

Key Features

  • Multiple design variants in one go.
  • Figma export with Auto Layout intact.
  • Clean HTML and CSS download.
  • Tailwind and JSX export for developers.

Best For

Early concepts, MVP screens, and a quick starting layout to finish in Figma.

Watch Out For

Figma export works only in Standard Mode and from text prompts, not images, and the tool is described as experimental and best for rapid prototyping.

My Takeaway

A concept engine: generate options fast, pick one, refine it elsewhere.

3. v0 by Vercel

v0 turns natural-language instructions into interface code. Instead of a flat mockup, you get components like navigation, cards, tables, forms, and dashboards you can build on.

That makes it feel closer to development than design. Its core Figma workflow imports and converts Figma designs into code, rather than sending AI designs back to Figma. One roundup calls it strongest if you're already on Next.js.

Key Features

  • Generates UI components from plain-language prompts.
  • Produces code-backed interfaces for dashboards and apps.
  • Converts Figma designs into code.
  • Works naturally in React and Next.js stacks.

Best For

Developers, design engineers, and teams building dashboards or application interfaces.

Watch Out For

It isn't a no-code canvas. You'll want comfort with code and components.

My Takeaway

Use it when the deliverable is a working interface, not a picture of one.

4. Bolt.new

Bolt.new lets people build websites, prototypes, and full-stack apps through conversation, with Figma and GitHub imports and plain-language changes. You describe the product and get a running app.

The speed comes from where it runs. The filesystem, Node server, package manager, and terminal all run inside your browser through WebContainers. Nothing waits on a remote setup.

Key Features

  • Hosting, custom domains, databases, and authentication through Bolt Cloud.
  • Figma and GitHub imports.
  • One-click export from Google Stitch.
  • Deployment through Bolt Cloud or Netlify, or a push to GitHub.

Best For

Quick MVPs, client prototypes, and internal tools where stakeholders need to click real features.

Watch Out For

It optimizes for generation speed, not production performance, and defaults to standard patterns. If you want a mobile app, say so up front, because web projects don't convert to React Native later.

My Takeaway

The quickest path from an idea to a shareable, working app.

5. Lovable AI

Lovable AI is a chat-first builder. You describe the site or app you want, and it generates a functional version with editable content, forms, SEO controls, and hosting.

It feels closer to talking to an assistant than configuring a tool. One roundup describes it as an opinionated React and Supabase builder with more guardrails and less terminal.

Key Features

  • Chat-based generation and editing.
  • Editable content, forms, and SEO controls.
  • Built-in hosting.
  • Support for integrations.

Best For

Startups, landing pages, and interactive sites built from a clear idea.

Watch Out For

Prompt quality matters. "Make it better" is vague, while "keep the sign-up button in the header and shorten the pricing copy" gets results.

My Takeaway

Design, build, and hosting in one conversation.

6. Framer AI

Framer AI generates pages, sections, copy, and visuals, and the result stays editable on a visual canvas. It sits between AI generation and professional web design.

That makes it a natural finishing tool. You get a fast draft, then adjust spacing, typography, and layout by hand until it looks right.

Key Features

  • AI-generated pages, sections, copy, and visuals.
  • Visual canvas editing.
  • Built-in CMS.
  • SEO, analytics, hosting, and publishing.

Best For

Marketing sites, portfolios, and landing pages where visual control matters.

Watch Out For

It isn't fully automated. Framer rewards people who care about design details.

My Takeaway

The step where a draft becomes a live, polished page.

7. Uizard

Uizard's Autodesigner turns natural-language prompts into complete, editable multi-screen interfaces. It's aimed at founders, product managers, and beginners who want fast early-stage mockups.

Its standout is scanning sketches and screenshots. One review called the sketch scanner one of the stronger, more useful features for the discovery-sprint phase.

Key Features

  • Wireframe Scanner that converts hand-drawn sketches into digital designs.
  • Screenshot Scanner that splits screenshots into selectable layers.
  • A Figma-to-Uizard import plugin.
  • Component-level code handoff.

Best For

Discovery sprints and workshops where sketch-to-mockup speed matters.

Watch Out For

Reviews note that screens are generated independently rather than as a connected flow, and professional designers may miss advanced auto-layout. Test these limits yourself.

My Takeaway

A sketch-to-mockup shortcut for early ideas, not a final design tool.

8. Banani AI

Banani is an AI design tool for mobile and desktop UI. Its own site says it's used by over 100k designers and non-designers. You write a prompt and get clean, multi-screen designs.

Its editing flow is built for small, precise changes rather than full regenerations, which keeps iteration fast.

Key Features

  • Partial editing that changes only a selected part of a design.
  • Image references from screenshots, wireframes, or sketches.
  • Bulk Figma export, pushing multiple screens in one click.
  • MCP connection to AI coding agents.

Best For

PMs, founders, and designers who want clean screens fast, then refinement in Figma.

Watch Out For

Results depend on prompt quality, and brand-specific details still need hand refinement.

My Takeaway

The quickest route from a written idea to Figma-ready screens.

9. Visily

Visily is an AI UI design tool for non-designers who want to go from idea to wireframe without touching Figma. Everything happens on one approachable canvas.

It covers text-to-UI, screenshot-to-design, diagramming, prototyping, and real-time collaboration. That lets whole teams, not just designers, take part in shaping a screen.

Key Features

  • Screenshot-to-design that converts app screenshots into editable components.
  • Sketch-to-design from photos of hand-drawn wireframes.
  • Text-to-UI generation.
  • Prototyping, which cost no AI credits in one hands-on test.

Best For

Fast wireframes and prototypes, especially on teams where not everyone is a designer.

Watch Out For

Advanced features like AI deep design use credits faster than basic screen generation. Check limits before building a workflow around it.

My Takeaway

The friendliest way to get a whole team designing together.

A Workflow That Chains These Tools

The speed comes from chaining tools so nothing gets rebuilt:

  1. Capture the idea: a sketch, a reference screenshot, or a short brief.
  2. Generate options: Stitch, Banani AI, or Visily.
  3. Refine one: export to Figma and fix spacing, branding, and states.
  4. Make it interactive: Figma Make, or v0 for component behavior.
  5. Test it as an app: Bolt.new or Lovable AI.
  6. Publish: Framer AI for marketing pages, or deploy from Bolt.

Every handoff should carry the work forward.

A Prompt Template That Works Across Most Tools

Design a [mobile/desktop] [product type] for [specific user]
who needs to [main job to be done].
Screens: [onboarding, home, detail, settings]
Style: [tone, density, color mood, light/dark]
Components: [nav, cards, table, form]
Constraints: [accessibility, brand colors, must-have features]

Describe the user and the job, name the screens, change one thing per follow-up, and attach references when you can.

Which Tool Should You Pick?

  • You live in Figma: Figma Make, plus Stitch or Banani AI for starting screens.
  • You start from sketches or screenshots: Uizard or Visily.
  • You want a clean multi-screen UI fast: Banani AI or Stitch.
  • You need working code: v0 or Bolt.new.
  • You want a live site from a chat: Lovable AI.
  • You need polished, published pages: Framer AI.

What AI Still Doesn't Do

AI doesn't know your users, which flow confuses them, or whether spacing feels right on a real phone. It also doesn't check accessibility, edge cases, or brand consistency by default. Treat every generated screen and line of code as a strong first draft, and review it before it ships.

Conclusion

The biggest shift isn't one tool. It's the shape of the process. Instead of starting from a blank canvas and building up, you can start with something real and spend your time deciding what to keep, change, and cut.

That's the habit I wish I had built earlier in my career. Don't hunt for one perfect tool. Find the shortest path between the tools you already use, and make sure every step carries your work forward.

What's your current AI design stack? Chaining tools or sticking with one? Tell me in the comments.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best AI tool for UI design?

It depends on your workflow. Figma Make suits teams in Figma; Stitch and Banani AI generate screens quickly; Uizard and Visily handle sketches and wireframes; v0 and Bolt.new focus on code; and Framer AI is strong for published pages.

Can AI replace UI designers?

No. These tools speed up drafting and prototyping, but they don't replace research, user empathy, accessibility work, or design judgment.

Which tools export to Figma?

Google Stitch and Banani AI export designs to Figma, Figma Make works natively inside Figma, and Uizard offers a Figma import plugin. Test the export with your own design before relying on it.

Are AI-generated designs ready for production?

Not by default. Treat them as prototype-grade until reviewed for accessibility, responsive behavior, security, and code quality.

Which tools suit beginners?

Visily, Uizard, and Banani AI work from prompts, screenshots, and sketches, and Lovable AI is easy if you want a working site from a chat.

Do these tools generate real code?

Some do. Stitch exports HTML and CSS; v0 and Bolt.new are code-focused; and Lovable AI generates functional sites. Visily and Uizard lean toward design output.

title: How to Bypass Aggressive JavaScript Anti-Copy Scripts Using Capture-Phase DOM Events
description:
Have you ever tried to copy a snippet of code, an error stack, or reference material from a web page, only to find that right-click is disabled, text selection is blocked, or your clipboard is silently swallowed?

Modern web applications implement anti-copy logic for various reasons (paywalls, content protection, cheating prevention in test portals). However, aggressive implementations frequently break accessibility and degrade basic developer ergonomics.

In this deep dive, let's explore how modern anti-copy scripts work under the hood, why traditional solutions like preventDefault overrides often fail, and how to reliably unblock them at the browser engine level.

1. How Anti-Copy Mechanisms Work Under the Hood

Hostile sites typically attack user interaction across two distinct browser layers:

Layer A: The DOM Event Pipeline

When you highlight text and press Ctrl+C (or right-click to open the context menu), the browser fires a sequence of DOM events:

  • Selection: selectstart, mousedown, mousemove, mouseup
  • Context Menu: contextmenu
  • Clipboard: copy, cut

A typical blocking script hooks into these events:

['copy', 'cut', 'contextmenu', 'selectstart'].forEach(eventType => {
  document.addEventListener(eventType, (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    e.stopPropagation();
    return false;
  });
});

By calling e.preventDefault(), the browser cancels its native default action. By calling e.stopPropagation(), bubbling is halted, preventing parent nodes or plugins from handling the interaction.

Layer B: CSS Selection Suppression

Even if event handlers are neutered, sites will commonly inject aggressive CSS rules to prevent the browser engine from creating text selection ranges:

* {
  -webkit-user-select: auto !important;
  user-select: auto !important;
}

When user-select: none is enforced on the <body> or root nodes, the mouse cursor cannot highlight characters, rendering keyboard shortcuts useless.

2. Why Naive Fixes Break Dynamic Applications

Many quick scripts attempt to solve this by monkey-patching document.oncopy = null or brute-forcing document.querySelectorAll('*').

The fatal flaw: Modern single-page applications (React, Vue, Monaco Editor, Google Docs, etc.) legitimately rely on synthetic event dispatching and custom text measurement. If you blindly strip all event listeners or nuke the DOM prototypes globally without fine-grained scoping, dynamic inputs will glitch, custom dropdowns will fail to close, and form validation will break.

3. The Robust Architectural Solution

To safely restore user control without breaking web application logic, we must intercept the event lifecycle at the Capture Phase:

Step 1: Intercepting at Capture Phase (useCapture: true)

The DOM event dispatch lifecycle has two main phases:

  1. Capture Phase (window -> document -> target)
  2. Bubble Phase (target -> document -> window)

Most blocking scripts listen in the bubbling phase. By registering our handler in the capture phase with high priority, we can intercept the event before the hostile page script even receives it:

const criticalEvents = ['copy', 'cut', 'contextmenu', 'selectstart'];

criticalEvents.forEach(type => {
  window.addEventListener(type, (event) => {
    // Stop other handlers on the current target from being called
    event.stopImmediatePropagation();
  }, { capture: true, passive: false });
});

Step 2: Forcing CSS Selection Overrides

To neutralize CSS suppression, we inject a non-destructive override stylesheet into document.head or document.documentElement:

const style = document.createElement('style');
style.id = '__unblock_selection_override';
style.textContent = `
  *, *::before, *::after {
    -webkit-user-select: auto !important;
    user-select: auto !important;
  }
`;
(document.head || document.documentElement).appendChild(style);

4. Packaging into a Lightweight Offline Extension

If you only encounter blocked pages occasionally, running the snippets above inside your browser's DevTools Console is sufficient.

However, if you deal with documentation portals, learning systems, or technical knowledge bases every day, automating this workflow via a clean, 100% offline browser extension is much more convenient.

I packaged this exact capture-phase bypass, automatic CSS unblocking, and smart whitelist engine into EasyCopy PRO:

  • 100% Offline Execution: Runs locally inside your browser sandbox with zero external network requests or analytics telemetry.
  • Dynamic Site Protection: Isolates unblock rules so dynamic editors (like Google Docs or CodePen) continue functioning normally.
  • Store & Release Access: Currently in review on the official Microsoft Edge Add-ons store, with offline packages and licenses available directly via Gumroad.

Conclusion

The web was fundamentally built as an open, accessible medium for sharing information. While anti-scraping measures have legitimate security use cases, taking away basic user ergonomics like right-click and copy-paste harms normal users far more than automated bots.

Using the capture-phase pattern and CSS normalization above, you can restore full control over your browsing experience safely and reliably.

title: Building MarginCMS, part 3: Tools out of go.mod, a strict linter and a validated edge
description:
Part 2 ended with two next steps: a linter, then auth with mock data. Auth moves to part 4. Adding the linter turned into a dependency hygiene problem first, and fixing that properly took a step of its own.

So this part covers three things: every Go tool in its own module, a strict golangci-lint config and what it caught, and request validation against the OpenAPI spec, so a bad request gets a 422 with field errors before any handler runs and every authenticated endpoint is closed until real auth exists.

Why the tools had to move

In part 2 I pinned oapi-codegen and Air with tool directives in api/go.mod and called it done. The trade-off I accepted there was a longer go.mod. The real cost is bigger than that.

golangci-lint's install docs advise against installing it with go tool or go install, and their reasons apply to every tool:

  • A tool's dependencies can modify the dependencies of another tool or of your project.
  • The binary is built locally with your Go version, not the one the release was tested with.
  • golangci-lint's own replace directives don't apply when it's a dependency of your module.

Their fallback for people who still want go tool is a dedicated module or modfile for the linter.

The mechanism behind the first point is minimal version selection. A tool directive puts the tool's whole dependency graph into the app's module graph, and MVS picks one version per module across that graph, so the tool and the app can move each other's dependencies.

My own api/go.mod already showed the problem without the linter:

  • 42 // indirect lines, almost all of them from the two tools.
  • go mod why -m github.com/gohugoio/hugo traced a path from Air through air/runner to hugo/watcher/filenotify. My API's module graph contained Hugo.
  • make update-deps ran go get -u tool: upgrade every tool and all of their dependencies inside the API's graph. That's exactly the case the docs warn about.

Step 1: Every tool in its own module

Commit: tooling: move each Go tool into its own module

I originally planned to use alternate modfiles next to the API's go.mod, like tools/<name>.mod, selected with -modfile. It took three attempts to land somewhere else.

Attempt 1: alternate modfiles, run from api/

go mod tidy -modfile=tools/air.mod run from api/ still treats api/ as the module root, so it scans the API's packages. The result was chi, cors, envconfig and testify copied into Air's modfile, at freshly resolved versions that differed from the API's own (chi v5.4.0 against the API's v5.3.2). A tools modfile that can't be tidied from where it's used is a dead end.

Attempt 2: one shared nested module for all tools

Next, api/tools/go.mod holding all three tools. My first version reused the API's module path and had only tool lines, no requires. It needs its own module path, and go get -tool to add the requirements and a go.sum.

Once fixed, it worked: the API's go.mod was clean, regenerated code was byte-identical, and every tool ran at its pinned version. But the three tools now shared one graph, which is the same problem one level down. To measure it, I built each tool inside the shared module and on its own, then compared go version -m of the two binaries. That reports what's actually linked; go list -m all also counts test-only modules and overstates the overlap.

Tool Linked deps Built with other versions than its release resolves
oapi-codegen v2.8.0 16 6, including golang.org/x/tools v0.48.0 -> v0.50.0
Air v1.67.4 22 6, including x/sys, x/text
golangci-lint v2.14.0 207 2: spf13/cast v1.5.0 -> v1.10.0, mitchellh/mapstructure v1.5.0 -> a 2023 pseudo-version

go mod graph showed that both golangci-lint bumps came from Air through Hugo. Both libraries sit in the path golangci-lint uses to load its config. A dev reloader was changing how my linter reads .golangci.yml, and golangci-lint --version still said 2.14.0.

oapi-codegen uses x/tools to format the code it generates. The output was identical that day, but a future Air bump could change generated code in a commit that never touched oapi-codegen. That's the kind of diff nobody reviews properly, because nobody expects it.

Attempt 3: one nested module per tool

api/tools/air/, api/tools/oapi-codegen/ and api/tools/golangci-lint/, each with its own module path, go.mod and go.sum:

module github.com/davidporos92/margin-cms/api/tools/air

go 1.27.1

tool github.com/air-verse/air

require (
    dario.cat/mergo v1.0.2 // indirect
    github.com/air-verse/air v1.67.4 // indirect
    // ...
)

Tools run from api/ with the module selected by -modfile, so the working directory stays the API's:

CMD ["go", "tool", "-modfile=tools/air/go.mod", "air"]

go -C tools/air tool air looks shorter, but -C changes the working directory, so Air and the linter would run on the wrong tree. And ./... doesn't descend into nested modules, so tests and lint never see the tool modules.

The result after this step: api/go.mod went from 42 indirect lines to 3, go mod why reports that the main module doesn't need Hugo, make openapi-generate-go produces byte-identical code, and Air starts in the container through the new CMD. golangci-lint's module alone is over 200 lines of go.mod. That's the graph that would otherwise have sat next to the API's.

Option Isolation Cost
tool in the app's go.mod None: tools and app share MVS Nothing extra
One shared tools module From the app, not between tools One module
One module per tool Full A longer command and one module per tool
Release binaries (golangci-lint's recommendation) Full A second install mechanism next to Go's

One mechanism with full isolation won. The cost is a longer command per tool, which lives in Make targets anyway.

make update-tools that finds tools by itself

With go get -u tool gone, the tools need their own update target. I wanted a new tool to be picked up without touching the Makefile.

My first version had cd tools/air on its own line. Make runs each recipe line in a new shell, so every go get -u tool that followed ran in api/. Two more obvious options didn't help: go list tool only warns that the pattern matched no packages in a module with no requires yet, and go get tool@latest is rejected with can't request explicit version of "tool" pattern. What works is reading the tool lines with go mod edit -json and running go get <path>@latest plus go mod tidy in each tools/*/go.mod:

TOOL_DIRS := $(patsubst %/go.mod,%,$(wildcard tools/*/go.mod))

update-tools:
    @for dir in $(TOOL_DIRS); do \
        tools=$$(cd $$dir && go mod edit -json | sed -n '/"Tool"/,/]/s/.*"Path": "\(.*\)".*/\1@latest/p'); \
        echo "Updating $$dir: $$tools"; \
        (cd $$dir && go get $$tools && go mod tidy) || exit 1; \
    done

There's deliberately no -u. Each tool moves to its latest release, and its dependencies stay at what that release requires. That's golangci-lint's rule, applied to every tool, so the linter needs no special case. I checked it: after the update, golangci-lint links spf13/cast v1.5.0 and mapstructure v1.5.0 again, and a second run changes nothing.

Step 2: A strict, curated golangci-lint config

Commits: tooling: add golangci-lint with a strict config, then api: fix lint findings

golangci-lint's tool module stayed out of the step 1 commit and lands here, together with the config.

I haven't used golangci-lint in a while and wanted an up-to-date strict config, so I had Claude generate .golangci.yml. Then I went through it: I checked every key against the v2.14.0 reference config, ran golangci-lint config verify, and ran it on the code.

The shape of the config

The main decision is curated versus exhaustive. default: all with a disable list is the strictest option, but every golangci-lint upgrade can turn on new linters by itself, and a version bump suddenly fails the build for reasons unrelated to the change. So the config is default: standard plus about 40 linters listed by name, each with a one-line reason:

linters:
  # standard: errcheck, govet, ineffassign, staticcheck, unused.
  # Everything else is opt-in, so a golangci-lint upgrade never turns on new linters by itself.
  default: standard
  enable:
    # Bugs the compiler doesn't catch
    - asasalint # []any passed as a single any to a variadic func
    - bidichk # dangerous unicode sequences (trojan source)
    # ...
    # HTTP, context and SQL (the last two matter once Postgres lands)
    - bodyclose # unclosed http.Response bodies, mostly in tests
    # ...
    - rowserrcheck # rows.Err() not checked
    - sqlclosecheck # rows and statements not closed

The groups are bugs, errors, HTTP/context/SQL (sqlclosecheck and rowserrcheck are there for when Postgres lands), security (gosec), logging (sloglint), tests, and style rules that prevent real confusion. Some settings go beyond the defaults:

  • govet runs every analyzer except fieldalignment.
  • errcheck treats an unchecked type assertion as an unchecked error.
  • nolintlint requires a linter name and a reason on every //nolint.
  • revive runs its defaults plus deep-exit.
  • sloglint wants the request's logger and context, not the global logger.

Generated code is excluded with generated: strict, which is the default; the config sets it explicitly because oapi-codegen's header follows the Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT. convention and the exclusion depends on it. Formatting is gofumpt and goimports with the module as the local prefix.

Left out on purpose: wsl, varnamelen, exhaustruct, mnd, lll, the complexity linters, paralleltest and err113. warn-unused flagged an exclusion rule I had for test files as unused, so it's gone until a test needs it.

Every rule that's turned off has its reason in the config:

Rule Why it's off
revive package-comments, exported Internal packages of one binary: a doc comment on every package and exported name would restate the name and add nothing
gocritic hugeParam Passing structs by value is a design choice at this size, not a defect
govet fieldalignment Reordering fields for padding hurts readability for no measurable gain

What it caught

The config and the fixes are two commits on purpose. Lint fails at the first commit, and the second shows exactly what the strict set caught. The first run found 35 issues on a codebase of stubs and one health check; with the doc-comment rules off (see the table above), the lint commit shows 25. The routine ones were 17 unused-parameter findings on the stub handlers, 10 missing doc comments and import grouping. The doc comments went away with the exported decision above, not with new comments. Renaming the stub parameters to _ then surfaced unused-receiver, fixed the same way:

func (server) ListPosts(_ context.Context, _ api.ListPostsRequestObject) (api.ListPostsResponseObject, error) {
    return nil, ErrNotImplemented
}

The interesting ones:

deep-exit: log.Fatal in config.New. A library function that exits the process can't be tested and skips every deferred call on the way out. config.New now returns (*Config, error) and main decides:

func New(ctx context.Context) (*Config, error) {
    var c Config
    if err := envconfig.Process(ctx, &c); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("parse config from environment: %w", err)
    }

    return &c, nil
}

The wrap also clears wrapcheck. Error wrapping has been in the standard library since Go 1.13 (%w, errors.Is, errors.As), with errors.Join and multiple %w since Go 1.20. github.com/pkg/errors, which I used last time, is in maintenance mode. What you lose is stack traces; specific wrap messages read like one.

gocritic exitAfterDefer: log.Fatal in main skips defer stop(). log.Fatal calls os.Exit, which runs no deferred calls. I switched to log.Panic: a panic in main's goroutine unwinds it and runs its deferred calls first. That only holds for the goroutine that panics. The ListenAndServe goroutine panics too, and that crashes the process without running main's defers, which is acceptable for a server that failed to bind.

gosec G706, log injection. The error handler logged r.URL.Path straight into log.Printf. Client-controlled data in a log line can fake entries (%0A in the path decodes to a newline), break log parsers or inject terminal escapes. Checking analyzers/loginjection.go in gosec revealed that the taint sources are *http.Request, *url.URL, os.Getenv and os.Args, and the sinks are every log.Print*, log.Fatal* and log.Panic*, plus the message argument of slog.Info, Warn, Error and Debug.

Quoting both r.Method and r.URL.Path fixed it:

log.Printf("%s %s %s", strconv.Quote(r.Method), strconv.Quote(r.URL.Path), err)

The alternative was log/slog with attributes: the handler escapes attribute values, and G706 doesn't look at them. That's the better long-term answer, and it comes with the move to structured logging, which I'm planning to introduce a bit later in another post.

errchkjson: _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(api.Problem{...}). Problem.Extensions is a map[string]interface{}, so the encoder can't be proven safe, and discarding its error hides a broken response. It's handled now (the full writeProblem is in step 3).

Step 3: Validate every request against the spec

The generated strict server checks types: a string where an integer belongs fails to decode. It doesn't check minLength, format, or required inside nested objects. Writing those checks in each handler duplicates the spec and drifts from it. A validator that reads the spec as data can't drift, so the spec should enforce itself at runtime, not only at compile time.

The embedded spec

Commit: api: generate the embedded spec

The validator needs the spec at runtime, and oapi-codegen can embed it (embedded-spec: true). I decided to generate it to its own file: openapi/oapi-codegen/spec.yaml generates internal/api/spec.go, so the embedded spec shows up as its own diff whenever the spec changes.

package: api

generate:
  embedded-spec: true

output: internal/api/spec.go

kin-openapi becomes a runtime dependency of the API. Step 1 removed it with oapi-codegen; now it comes back for a real reason. I pinned it to v0.142.0, the version oapi-codegen v2.8.0 resolves in its own tool module, so the generated code and the library it calls match. With it and the validator middleware, api/go.mod is back up from 3 indirect lines to 10. Eight of them are linked into the binary; the other two come from test dependencies (testify's YAML support and a test-only dependency of kin-openapi's YAML parser). oapi-codegen v2.8.0 also generates a GetSpec() next to the older GetSwagger(); the server uses GetSpec().

Field errors get named types

Commit: spec: extract FieldError and FieldErrors schemas from Problem

Problem.errors was an inline array of objects, which generated a Go *[]struct{Field, Message string}: awkward to build in the error handler. So I added two new schemas: FieldError (one object) and FieldErrors (an array of $ref: FieldError), both registered in openapi.yaml.

Wiring the validator

Commit: api: validate requests against the spec and deny bearer auth

This commit landed after the second spec change (codes and constraints, described further down). I describe the handler first because the error codes only make sense once the error tree is clear.

The validator is nethttp-middleware v1.2.0, oapi-codegen's net/http wrapper around kin-openapi's openapi3filter. Before writing the error handler, I probed every default against the real embedded spec. Most of them weren't what I'd assumed.

  • Server matching. The spec lists http://localhost:8080/api/v1 under servers. The validator's router matches the Host too, so any other host (Docker's api:8080, production) gets 404 "no matching operation was found" for every request. The fix is DoNotValidateServers: true plus Prefix: "/api/v1". The library logs a warning about this itself, pointing to oapi-codegen issue 882.
  • format: email isn't checked unless a validator for it is registered: globally with openapi3.DefineStringFormatValidator, or per validation through SchemaValidationOptions. I used the global registry, and registered it in the constructor rather than in init(), which the linter forbids anyway.
  • A missing AuthenticationFunc already fails closed: secured operations get 401 "missing AuthenticationFunc". I added an explicit deny-all anyway. It states the intent, keeps an internal message out of responses, and is the seam for part 4.
  • Errors nest. With MultiError: true, a request with several problems arrives as MultiError -> RequestError -> MultiError -> SchemaError, and both a missing email and a missing password come back.
  • Status codes. The validator suggests 400 for bad requests. The contract says 422 (ValidationErrorResponse). With ErrorHandlerWithOpts, which I use, nethttp-middleware reports a wrong method as 404 instead of 405. The API still answers 405, because unroutable requests skip the validator and go to chi.
  • The body is read into memory twice for secured operations: once before the AuthenticationFunc runs, and again for body validation. 
func newServerValidationMiddleware(router chi.Routes) (api.MiddlewareFunc, error) {
    oAPISpec, err := api.GetSpec()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("get spec: %w", err)
    }

    // kin-openapi doesn't check `format: email` unless the format is explicitly registered.
    // The registry is package-global, so this registration applies to every spec in the process.
    openapi3.DefineStringFormatValidator("email", openapi3.NewRegexpFormatValidator(openapi3.FormatOfStringForEmail))

    return nethttpmiddleware.OapiRequestValidatorWithOptions(oAPISpec, &nethttpmiddleware.Options{
        DoNotValidateServers: true,
        Prefix:               "/api/v1",
        Options: openapi3filter.Options{
            MultiError:         true,
            AuthenticationFunc: authFunc,
        },
        ErrorHandlerWithOpts: errHandler,
        // Let chi answer requests which we cannot route
        // This will automatically set Allow for 405
        Skipper: func(r *http.Request) bool {
            return !router.Match(chi.NewRouteContext(), r.Method, r.URL.Path)
        },
    }), nil
}

func authFunc(context.Context, *openapi3filter.AuthenticationInput) error {
    return ErrUnauthenticated
}

Closed by default is the point of authFunc. Leaving the bearer endpoints open until part 4 would mean every new endpoint is public until someone remembers to protect it. With deny-all, part 4 opens endpoints one at a time by verifying a token, and forgetting something fails safe.

Where it's mounted

There were three candidate places for the validator:

Where Problem
Strict middlewares They run after the body is decoded into typed request objects, too late
chi's Middlewares option Generated code runs these per operation, after routing and parameter parsing, so ?limit=abc gets the generated plain-text 400 and unknown routes get chi's plain-text 404/405
Around the whole router Sees every request first

So it wraps the whole router: cors(maxBytes(validator(chi))). CORS stays outermost so preflight OPTIONS requests, which aren't in the spec, still work. The body limit sits outside the validator so the validator's own read is capped too. All of this wiring moved from main.go into server.New, which the tests can now call:

func New(cfg *Config) (*http.Server, error) {
    router := chi.NewRouter()
    router.NotFound(func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) {
        writeProblem(w, api.Problem{Status: http.StatusNotFound})
    })
    serverInterface := api.NewStrictHandlerWithOptions(server{}, newServerMiddlewares(), newServerOptions())
    handler := api.HandlerWithOptions(serverInterface, api.ChiServerOptions{
        BaseURL:    "/api/v1",
        BaseRouter: router,
    })

    serverValidationMiddleware, err := newServerValidationMiddleware(router)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to initialize server validation middleware: %w", err)
    }

    handler = maxBytesReaderMiddleware(cfg)(serverValidationMiddleware(handler))
    handler = cors.Handler(cors.Options{
        // ...
    })(handler)
    // ...
}

The error handler

There are three kinds of failure. No matched route is a 404 or 405. A security failure anywhere in the tree is a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. Schema problems are a 422 with one field error each. Anything unrecognised is logged and answered with a 500, and err.Error() never reaches the client.

var result validationResult
result.collect(err)

switch {
case result.unauthenticated:
    // Check unauthenticated first:
    // Unauthenticated caller doesn't get to learn what's wrong in a request.
    w.Header().Set("WWW-Authenticate", "Bearer")
    writeProblem(w, api.Problem{Status: http.StatusUnauthorized})
case result.tooLarge:
    writeProblem(w, api.Problem{Status: http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge})
case result.unknown != nil:
    log.Printf("validate %s %s: %v", strconv.Quote(r.Method), strconv.Quote(r.URL.Path), result.unknown)
    writeProblem(w, api.Problem{Status: http.StatusInternalServerError})
default:
    writeProblem(w, api.Problem{
        Status: http.StatusUnprocessableEntity,
        Errors: &result.fields,
    })
}

Auth is checked first, so an anonymous GET /posts?limit=abc is a 401, not a 422: a caller without a token doesn't learn what else is wrong with the request.

The tree walk uses a type switch, not errors.As, and that's deliberate:

// collect walks kin-openapi's error tree. With MultiError on, a request with
// several problems arrives as MultiError -> RequestError -> MultiError -> SchemaError.
//
// It switches on concrete types on purpose: MultiError implements As, so
// errors.As on it returns only the first match and drops the rest.
func (v *validationResult) collect(err error) {
    //nolint:errorlint // see above, errors.As would flatten MultiError
    switch e := err.(type) {
    case openapi3.MultiError:
        for _, inner := range e {
            v.collect(inner)
        }
    case *openapi3filter.SecurityRequirementsError:
        v.unauthenticated = true
    case *openapi3filter.RequestError:
        v.collectRequestError(e)
    default:
        v.unknown = errors.Join(v.unknown, err)
    }
}

kin-openapi's MultiError implements As, so errors.As returns the first match and drops the rest. Worse, errors.As(requestErr, &multi) unwraps past the RequestError and loses the parameter name with it. I hit exactly this while iterating: I replaced the switch with errors.As to satisfy errorlint, and every schema error became a 500, because the bare SchemaErrors matched nothing and fell through to unknown. Build, vet and lint all passed. The strict linter had pushed a deliberate type switch into a bug, so the switch is back, with //nolint:errorlint and a reason, which is exactly the case nolintlint's required reason is for.

writeProblem takes the whole api.Problem. Type defaults to about:blank and Title to Go's status text. With about:blank, RFC 9457 wants the title to be the status code's recommended phrase, not a custom one. Go's http.StatusText still uses the older names for two codes this server sends: "Request Entity Too Large" and "Unprocessable Entity", where RFC 9110 now says "Content Too Large" and "Unprocessable Content".

func writeProblem(w http.ResponseWriter, problem api.Problem) {
    if problem.Type == "" {
        problem.Type = "about:blank"
    }
    if problem.Title == "" {
        problem.Title = http.StatusText(problem.Status)
    }

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/problem+json")
    w.WriteHeader(problem.Status)

    err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(problem)
    if err != nil {
        log.Printf("write problem: %v", err)
    }
}

Localizable errors: codes, not prose

Commit: spec: replace FieldError message with a code and constraint

The frontend translates its messages, so the server should return required, not property "email" is missing. kin-openapi already records the failed keyword in SchemaError.SchemaField (required, format, type, minLength and so on), separately from the English Reason. I verified that on real requests before building on it.

The contract is a code enum on FieldError listing only the keywords my schemas use, plus an invalid catch-all. Unknown keywords map to invalid, so none of kin-openapi's strings become API without being in the spec first. Adding a keyword is a deliberate one-line spec change, and the TypeScript types list every code.

Messages like "at least 8 characters" also need the limit. My first version had a typed FieldErrorParams (min, max, format, allowed) filled by a switch per keyword. It worked, but a number with minimum came back without params: every new keyword needed new Go code. Before writing the next case, I checked whether this already existed somewhere:

Option Gives Why not
nethttp-middleware One error No field-level output; the default handler writes err.Error() as text
kin-openapi's message customizer A rewritten message string Still a string, and the tree walk is still needed
santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema v6 (already in the graph) Typed error kinds per keyword, localization through x/text kin-openapi only uses it for OpenAPI 3.1 and flattens it to SchemaError{Reason: string}; my spec is 3.0.3
RFC 9457 The envelope, and an example errors extension The example is illustrative, not a standard field, and has no machine-readable code

So the tree walk is unavoidable, but it's written once and doesn't grow with the spec. The per-keyword switch isn't unavoidable. The generic version reads the failed keyword's value straight from the failing schema, which kin-openapi attaches to the error as SchemaError.Schema:

func fieldErrorConstraint(schemaErr *openapi3.SchemaError) any {
    if schemaErr.SchemaField == "required" || schemaErr.Schema == nil {
        return nil
    }

    raw, err := json.Marshal(schemaErr.Schema)
    if err != nil {
        return nil
    }

    var keywords map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &keywords); err != nil {
        return nil
    }

    return keywords[schemaErr.SchemaField]
}

minimum, maxLength, enum and format all work with no per-keyword code. The exception is required, whose value is the parent's whole list, so it has no constraint. The trade-off is on the client: TypeScript gets unknown and has to check the type against code. In return, the contract describes one rule instead of a growing set of keys:

  code:
    type: string
    description: Machine-readable reason. Clients can use this to localize the error messages.
    enum:
    - required
    - type
    - format
    # ...
    - invalid
  constraint:
    description: |
      Value of the schema keyword named by `code`, for example 3 for maxLength
      or ["draft", "published"] for enum. Absent for required.

I did consider dropping constraint altogether. The admin's forms validate client-side from the same rules, so server field errors are a safety net rather than the main path. I kept it: the frontend translates code and reads constraint for messages like "at least 8 characters", so even the safety net shows the limit in the user's language.

$ curl -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"foo","password":"bar"}'
{"errors":[{"code":"format","constraint":"email","field":"email"}],"status":422,"title":"Unprocessable Entity","type":"about:blank"}

Two gotchas

The Allow header. A 405 must carry Allow. No library I found sets it together with a problem+json body. But chi's default 405 handler already sets Allow from its routing tree, with an empty body. The validator was answering unmatched routes before chi ever saw them. The fix is nethttp-middleware's Skipper: skip anything chi can't route (router.Match) and let chi answer. chi gets its own router through BaseRouter, with a problem+json NotFound. A custom MethodNotAllowed would lose Allow, since it has no access to the allowed methods, so 405 keeps chi's default: an empty body, where the status and Allow say everything. That's no routing code and no method list of my own.

413 in the spec. Bodies are capped at 10 MiB by default (SERVER_MAX_BYTES_TO_READ) through http.MaxBytesReader. OpenAPI 3.0 has no global responses: components.responses still needs a $ref per operation, which is exactly the thing that gets forgotten. The spec doesn't require it either, since the Responses Object "is not necessarily expected to cover all possible HTTP response codes". So the limit and its 413 are documented once, in info.description.

Tests through the whole handler

The tests are in the same commit. They're table tests through the real server.New handler, in a black-box server_test package, so every case goes through CORS, the body limit, the validator, chi and the strict server. Unit tests of the error walk alone would have missed the errors.As bug above, because the walk only breaks on the error tree kin-openapi builds for a real request.

"GET /posts?limit=abc - without token, auth wins over the param error": {
    method:      http.MethodGet,
    route:       "/posts?limit=abc",
    wantStatus:  http.StatusUnauthorized,
    wantBody:    errUnauthorized,
    wantHeaders: map[string][]string{"WWW-Authenticate": {"Bearer"}, "Content-Type": {"application/problem+json"}},
},

The 13 cases cover:

  • 200 for the health check
  • 422 for a missing Content-Type, an empty body, a bad email and broken JSON
  • 501 for a valid login (for now)
  • 413 for an oversized body
  • two 401s, including auth winning over a bad ?limit=
  • 404 for an unknown route
  • 405 with Allow on a templated path
  • a CORS preflight, and a bare OPTIONS that gets a 405

The setup builds an explicit server.Config instead of calling config.New, which would read my real SERVER_* environment. It also lets the 413 case use a 1 KiB limit instead of a 10 MiB test body. Expected responses are fixture files under testdata/response/, embedded with //go:embed. For one-line bodies that's more ceremony than needed, but the fixtures will earn their place once the responses are full Post payloads.

httptest's default host is example.com, so every case already runs against a non-localhost host. The server-matching problem from earlier is covered without a case of its own. I also checked that the suite catches the errors.As bug: with it reintroduced in a scratch copy, the empty-body and email cases fail.

What writing the tests turned up:

  • The login test got invalid on body instead of two required errors. The case sent {} without a Content-Type. kin-openapi picks the body decoder by media type, and the spec only defines application/json, so it never validated against Credentials. It returned a plain "header Content-Type has unexpected value" error, not a SchemaError, and my handler mapped that to invalid on body. That was the correct answer for the wrong request, so every body case now sends the header. It raised a real design question: a missing or wrong Content-Type is a 415. kin-openapi has no error type for it, only a message, so detecting it would mean string matching. I kept 422 and pinned it with its own test case, so it's a decision, not an accident.
  • 413 on login regardless of body content or Content-Type. kin-openapi reads the whole body before the media-type check, so an oversized body hits MaxBytesReader first. A body of exactly the limit still passes and gets the 501.
  • OPTIONS /posts returned 405, not the CORS answer. A bare OPTIONS isn't a preflight: go-chi/cors only treats it as one when both Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method are present. Without them it passes the request through, the Skipper sees chi can't route OPTIONS, and chi answers 405 with Allow. I kept both cases. A real preflight gets 200 with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and a bare OPTIONS gets 405. Together they document that CORS only answers preflights.
  • A flaky Allow assertion. The test expected [DELETE GET PATCH] and once got [GET PATCH DELETE]. chi collects the allowed methods by ranging over a map in tree.go, so the order is random per run. Allow is a set, so the assertion has to ignore order. All header expectations now use ElementsMatch; single-value headers lose nothing. Afterwards I ran the suite with -count=20 -race -shuffle=on to make sure nothing else depends on order.

Step 4: One entry point for the API's make targets

Commit: tooling: add root make targets for the API

Every API target can now run from the repo root: api-lint, api-lint-fix, api-fmt, api-test, api-build, api-update-deps and api-update-tools in the root Makefile. They all go through $(MAKE) -C api <target> rather than cd api && make, so the same make binary runs and flags like -n, -j and -k reach the sub-make.

What changes in production

  • Auth is deny by default. Part 4 opens endpoints by verifying tokens; nothing is open because someone forgot it.
  • Validation is the first line against malformed input. It doesn't replace the body size limit, which is a separate middleware and runs before the validator reads anything.
  • The cost per request is unmeasured. It's a route lookup against the spec plus a schema check, and the body is buffered in memory, twice for secured operations. With a 10 MiB cap that's bounded. I haven't load-tested it yet.
  • Responses aren't validated. Checking responses against the spec belongs in integration tests, once there are real responses to check.

What I'd tell myself before starting

  • A tool directive is a dependency like any other: it shares minimal version selection with your app. And when you judge dependency drift, measure what's linked into the binary (go version -m), not the module list.
  • Probe a validation library's defaults against your real spec before writing the handler. Server matching, unchecked formats and fail-closed auth were all different from what I'd assumed.
  • Don't errors.As through a library's multi-error type without reading its As method: it can silently return only the first error.
  • When a mapping grows one case per spec keyword, look for the data the library already carries (here, the failed schema) before writing the next case.
  • Test HTTP behaviour through the whole handler, not the pieces.
  • A strict linter will push correct code into a bug if you let it. Before "fixing" a finding in deliberate code, check that the finding applies, and if it doesn't, write the reason next to the //nolint.

Next steps

  1. Auth with in-memory stores. Login, refresh, logout and GET /me with Argon2id and JWTs, behind store interfaces that Postgres will implement later. The deny-all AuthenticationFunc becomes real token verification.
  2. Postgres, Ent and Atlas. The database, the schema and migrations.

Originally published on my blog, where the comments live. The code for this post is on GitHub.

title: React: estados accesibles para email de prueba
description:
Una pantalla de email de prueba parece sencilla: un botón envía el mensaje, un inbox muestra el resultado y una alerta confirma lo ocurrido. En la practica, esa pequeña interfaz mezcla asincronía, estados visuales, lectores de pantalla y cambios de layout que pueden hacer sentir lenta la aplicación.

La solución no es agregar más spinners. Es modelar con claridad qué sabe la interfaz en cada momento. Un usuario debería distinguir entre “todavía estamos esperando”, “llegó un mensaje”, “la búsqueda expiró” y “algo falló”. Si todos esos casos usan el mismo texto, el flujo se vuelve confuso aunque el backend funcione bien.

El problema no es solo esperar un email

Un inbox temporal o de prueba suele tener este recorrido:

  1. El usuario solicita un email.
  2. React muestra que la solicitud está en progreso.
  3. El servidor acepta el evento, pero el mensaje todavía no es visible.
  4. El mensaje aparece y puede abrirse o copiarse.
  5. La espera termina por timeout o por un error recuperable.

Cada paso necesita una señal distinta. “Cargando” no explica si el mensaje fue enviado, si el inbox está consultando o si la conexión se perdió. En pruebas de frontend, también conviene separar el estado del request del estado del mensaje: una respuesta HTTP correcta no garantiza que el email ya pueda leerse.

Este enfoque se parece a diseñar alertas de trial que sí orientan: el copy debe decir qué pasó y cuál es el siguiente paso, no solo mostrar un color verde.

Modela los estados antes de escribir JSX

Un union type pequeño evita que el componente dependa de varios booleanos que pueden entrar en combinaciones imposibles:

type InboxState =
  | { kind: 'idle' }
  | { kind: 'waiting'; startedAt: number }
  | { kind: 'received'; subject: string; receivedAt: string }
  | { kind: 'expired'; retryable: boolean }
  | { kind: 'error'; message: string };

Con isLoading, hasMessage, hasError y isExpired es facil terminar con una alerta de éxito y error al mismo tiempo. Un estado discriminado obliga a que la vista elija una sola lectura principal. También hace más simple probar las transiciones: idle → waiting → received, o waiting → expired.

El texto debe ser concreto. “Esperando confirmación” ayuda más que “Procesando”. Para un timeout, “No vimos el email en 60 segundos; puedes volver a intentar” ofrece contexto y una acción. Si el usuario usa un lector de pantalla, esa diferencia es todavía más importante.

Un componente React con layout estable

El feedback no debería empujar el botón ni mover el inbox cuando cambia. Reserva una región con altura mínima y usa aria-live solo para cambios relevantes:

function InboxStatus({ state }: { state: InboxState }) {
  const text = {
    idle: 'Listo para comprobar el inbox.',
    waiting: 'Esperando el email de prueba.',
    received: 'El email ya está disponible.',
    expired: 'La espera terminó; puedes reintentar.',
    error: 'No pudimos consultar el inbox.'
  }[state.kind];

  return (
    <p className="status" role="status" aria-live="polite">
      {text}
    </p>
  );
}

.status {
  min-block-size: 1.5rem;
  margin-block: 0.75rem;
  color: var(--text-muted);
}

.status:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid var(--focus-ring);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

role="status" anuncia el cambio sin interrumpir cada acción del usuario. No conviene poner un contador que se actualiza cada segundo en esa misma región: un lector de pantalla podria repetirlo demasiado. Muestra el tiempo restante en otra parte, con una etiqueta visible y un ritmo de actualización razonable.

Un botón deshabilitado durante la espera debe conservar una explicación. El texto “Comprobando…” es mejor que dejar solo un icono. Para conexiones lentas, evita reemplazar todo el contenido; conserva el contexto del inbox y actualiza la parte que cambió.

Accesibilidad y rendimiento en la misma revisión

La accesibilidad no es un paso posterior al rendimiento. Un árbol pequeño, mensajes estables y menos renders suelen beneficiar a ambos. Calcula el copy del estado en el componente y evita recrear listas grandes del inbox cuando solo cambió la etiqueta.

También reviso estos puntos:

  • El contraste del estado secundario sigue siendo legible en modo oscuro.
  • El foco no desaparece cuando llega el mensaje.
  • El título del email y el timestamp tienen nombres accesibles.
  • La respuesta de error no depende solo de rojo o verde.
  • El polling se cancela al desmontar el componente.
  • prefers-reduced-motion evita animaciones innecesarias.

Para un flujo de CI, los límites de confianza para emails de CI también sirven como recordatorio de que cada ejecución debe tener un contexto claro. En la UI, eso significa mostrar el inbox o identificador de la ejecución, sin exponer datos que no corresponden al usuario.

Checklist para una interfaz de email de prueba

Antes de dar por terminado el componente, comprueba:

  1. ¿Existe un estado explícito para espera, éxito, expiración y error?
  2. ¿El layout mantiene su espacio cuando aparece el feedback?
  3. ¿El mensaje importante se anuncia una sola vez?
  4. ¿El foco y el teclado siguen funcionando después de un reintento?
  5. ¿El polling termina cuando el componente se desmonta?
  6. ¿El inbox se identifica con un nombre entendible, y no como “dummy e mail”?

Si el flujo necesita un buzón aislado para una comprobación manual, un temp mail puede ser parte del entorno de prueba. El enlace no arregla la UX por sí solo: la interfaz aún debe explicar quién está esperando, qué llegó y qué puede hacer la persona después.

Cierre

Una buena interfaz de email de prueba convierte la asincronía en información útil. En React, un modelo de estados claro, una región de feedback estable y una revisión conjunta de accesibilidad y rendimiento suelen ser suficientes para evitar gran parte de la fricción.

No hace falta llenar la pantalla de indicadores. Hace falta elegir palabras precisas, respetar el foco y mantener el contexto cuando el servidor tarda. Ese detalle pequeño se nota mucho cuando el flujo se usa en una prueba real, con una conexión lenta o con tecnologías de asistencia.

title: "An invalid form control is not focusable": Hidden Steps
description:
The short version

A three-step application form was built as a single <form>, with each step shown or hidden using the hidden attribute (equivalent to display:none). The required fields live on step 1; the submit button lives on step 2. Step 1's "Continue to confirmation" button is type="button" and validates nothing, so a user can reach step 2 with required fields still empty. Pressing the step 2 submit button (type="submit") then triggers the browser's native validation, which finds the empty required fields — but by then step 1's section is hidden and unfocusable, so the browser has no way to surface an error and silently aborts the submit. The fix: add noValidate to the form to disable native validation, and run an explicit check inside "Continue to confirmation" that renders an error message on the spot instead.

Symptom

The /apply form for signing up for the school-advertising support program has three steps — choose a school (step 0), enter listing details and contact info (step 1), and confirm and submit (step 2) — driven by a step value in useState. All three steps' inputs live inside a single <form action={formAction}>, and which step is visible is decided purely by wrapping each step in a <section> with the hidden attribute.

<form action={formAction}>
  {/* STEP 0: choose school + period */}
  <section hidden={step !== 0}>...</section>

  {/* STEP 1: listing content (required contact fields live here) */}
  <section hidden={step !== 1}>
    ...
    <input id="sf_name" name="name" required maxLength={200} ... />
    <input id="sf_email" name="email" type="email" required maxLength={200} ... />
    ...
    <button type="button" onClick={() => setStep(2)}>Continue to confirmation</button>
  </section>

  {/* STEP 2: confirm and submit (the only submit button is here) */}
  <section hidden={step !== 2}>
    ...
    <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>Submit</button>
  </section>
</form>

During a live production walkthrough by the author and Claude, we advanced to the step 2 confirmation screen without ever filling in the contact name or email, and pressing "Submit" produced no change on screen whatsoever — no error message, no loading state, not even a visible reaction to the click. The only trace was a single warning in the browser devtools console:

An invalid form control with name='name' is not focusable.

Cause

Moving between steps is implemented with a type="button" that only mutates React state.

<button type="button" onClick={() => setStep(2)}>
  Continue to confirmation
</button>

Clicking a type="button" is not a form submission, so native browser input validation never runs here at all. The required name and email fields can be empty and the user still advances straight to the step 2 confirmation screen without any friction.

The only type="submit" button anywhere in the form is "Submit," on step 2.

<button type="submit" disabled={pending}>
  {pending ? "Submitting…" : "Submit"}
</button>

The moment a user presses it, the browser runs native HTML5 validation against the entire <form>. name and email are required, so an empty value is correctly flagged as invalid — but at this point step is 2, and the step 1 section containing those fields has hidden={step !== 1} evaluate to true, making it display:none. An element with display:none cannot receive focus. The browser tries to focus the offending field to show the validation error to the user, fails, logs a warning to the console, and silently cancels the submission. No visible error, no scroll, nothing.

In other words, what looked like "the user can just fill in the required field later" was actually a structure where the only way to reach that required field was already gone from the screen by the time submission was attempted.

Fix

noValidate was added to the form element, disabling native browser validation entirely.

{/* noValidate: the input gate is goConfirm (which shows errors) plus server-side
    validation. Native validation silently blocks when a required field sits in a
    hidden section, which looks like a hang, so it's disabled. */}
<form action={formAction} noValidate>

In its place, step 1's "Continue to confirmation" button now calls goConfirm, which runs an explicit check.

const goConfirm = () => {
  const missing: string[] = [];
  if (creativeMode === "omakase") {
    if (!omBiz.trim()) missing.push("business type");
    if (!omMessage.trim()) missing.push("key message");
  }
  if (!company.trim()) missing.push("business/company name");
  if (!contactName.trim()) missing.push("contact name");
  if (!email.trim()) missing.push("email address");
  else if (!EMAIL_RE.test(email.trim()))
    missing.push("email address (check the format)");
  if (missing.length > 0) {
    setStepError(`Missing fields: ${missing.join(", ")}`);
    return;
  }
  setStepError(null);
  setStep(2);
};

If anything is missing, a role="alert" message renders right there — on step 1, which is still visible — and the user is not advanced to step 2.

{stepError && (
  <p role="alert" className="mt-4 rounded-lg border border-red-200 bg-red-50 px-3 py-2 text-sm text-red-700">
    {stepError}
  </p>
)}

This check can also cover fields the HTML5 required attribute never saw, like the business type and key message that only apply when omakase mode is selected. Native validation only looks at fields marked required; goConfirm can express business rules (these two fields are mandatory only in omakase mode) directly in code. Final validation is still left to the server-side Server Action, unchanged.

Prevention

Packing multiple steps of input into a single <form> and toggling visibility with hidden is fundamentally at odds with native HTML5 validation. Browser input validation looks at the whole form and hunts for "the first invalid field that can receive focus" — it has no concept of which step is currently displayed. The moment required fields and the submit button end up on different steps, it becomes possible for the field validation needs to reach right when submission is attempted to have already vanished from the screen.

To stay safe with this pattern, pick one of two approaches up front: (1) treat any multi-step form as noValidate by default and write an explicit check on every step transition, or (2) split each step into its own separate <form> so native validation stays self-contained within a single step. A form that "looks like it works but silently can't submit" is hard to catch with automated tests — this one only surfaced through a live, hands-on walkthrough in production.

title: A Resolved Task Is Not a Resolved Case: Building ReturnTrail with FalkorDB
description:
Two records. One failed pickup. Two different explanations.

“Pickup cancelled by customer.”

“Pickup failed because the courier was unavailable.”

This is a fictional example from ReturnTrail, the project we built for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks.

Finding different words is the easy part. The useful questions come next: do these records describe the same pickup attempt? What did an earlier reply actually explain? If another document arrives, does that old explanation still cover the evidence?

Those questions shaped our graph model, our investigation tools and the way we handle “resolved” tasks.

Try ReturnTrail · Source code and setup

Product capture using fictional records and a local FalkorDB instance. Case API responses were not mocked for this capture.

The job we chose

ReturnTrail helps a shopper prepare an evidence-linked support conversation about a disputed return pickup.

The output is a reviewable brief: original claims, their source connections, follow-up questions and the history of manual explanations. We keep those explanations separate from the records they describe.

Our current prototype uses four seeded fictional cases and bounded fictional text additions. We have not validated customer demand or measured real-world dispute outcomes. The hackathon gave us a focused implementation to put in front of users.

Why the pickup attempt belongs in the graph

An order can have more than one pickup attempt. Different failure reasons on different attempts need not contradict each other.

Our graph connects:

  • A case to its order, item and return request.
  • Each pickup attempt to its return request.
  • Each statement to the pickup it describes and the document that recorded it.
  • Each follow-up action to its reviewed documents.
  • Each manual clarification to its follow-up action.

Here is the evidence query documented in the repository:

MATCH (c:Case {id:$caseId})-[:HAS_ORDER]->(o:Order)-[:CONTAINS]->(i:Item)
MATCH (c)-[:HAS_RETURN]->(r:ReturnRequest)-[:RETURNS]->(i)
MATCH (p:PickupAttempt)-[:ATTEMPTS]->(r)
MATCH (s:SupportStatement)-[:ABOUT]->(p)
MATCH (s)-[:RECORDED_IN]->(d:EvidenceDocument)
RETURN DISTINCT c.id AS caseId, o.id AS orderId, i.id AS itemId,
r.id AS returnId, p.id AS pickupId, s.id AS statementId,
s.claimedStatus AS claimedStatus, s.text AS statement,
d.id AS evidenceId, d.sourceType AS sourceType
ORDER BY evidenceId, statementId;

The backend chooses the authorized workspace graph and binds the case ID. Both ownership paths through the order/item and return/item must match. The API exposes source connections derived from the executed query results.

CASE-002 is our negative example: records describe separate pickup attempts, so the supported rule does not flag them as a same-attempt disagreement.

FalkorDB supplies the evidence traversal and stored workflow context. Java applies explicit rules to the returned records.

What an earlier explanation actually covers

Our most useful design decision was connecting a saved action to the documents it reviewed:

Case → Action → REFERENCES → EvidenceDocument

A manual reply is linked through:

Action → HAS_CLARIFICATION → ClarificationRecord

This lets us ask a more precise question than “Was this task resolved?”

Does the reviewed source set, including its evidence revision, match the current source set?

In our implementation, coverage requires a nonempty current source set, matching evidence IDs and a matching revision. The ContextCoverage implementation exposes reviewed sources, newly added sources, task state and saved-note context.

A later document can therefore require fresh review while the earlier task remains resolved in history. We preserve what happened instead of rewriting the old task as if it had reviewed information that did not exist yet.

A matching source set still does not verify a manual explanation. It establishes its context boundary.

Context lab: preview the missing connection

Context lab lets a user temporarily set aside one source and inspect the result.

For CASE-001, setting aside DOC-001 leaves only the courier-unavailable claim. Our bounded disagreement rule no longer has two conflicting reasons to compare.

The application runs a parameterized, read-only graph query with a source exclusion. It returns the remaining evidence connections and evaluates that result. Original records and saved tasks stay unchanged.

This is a diagnostic preview. It does not establish that the excluded document is false or that the remaining claim is true. It shows how the available evidence changes the supported next question.

CASE-004 extends the demonstration: add a reviewed fictional source to a case with an earlier manual reply, then inspect the changed coverage.

The agent's job is bounded

Our Spring Boot backend exposes four investigation tools:

  1. get_case_evidence
  2. get_case_clarifications
  3. get_case_findings
  4. prepare_followup_action, when a finding is pending

The AI workflow must retrieve the current evidence and saved context before proceeding to findings and a local follow-up action. The backend enforces the sequence and renders the final report from tool results.

These are application tool calls. We did not build an MCP server, and the model does not generate arbitrary Cypher or decide who caused the failed pickup.

A separate Review rules & prepare question action performs the deterministic workflow without a model request. Users can then record an explicit manual outcome and export a fresh brief. The application does not send that draft to a courier or issue a refund.

What we tested—and what those tests establish

We tested the distinctions that could otherwise produce a misleading answer: same versus different attempts, unknown reasons, changed source context, stale writes and workspace isolation.

Recorded check Scope
93 backend tests successful; 2 skipped Hosted default suite at commit 275fb37; zero failures or errors
14 frontend tests passed Domain, draft and public-video input boundaries
Five public API workflow groups passed Actual hosted application and external FalkorDB; synthetic writes, history, retries, version protection and guest isolation
One real hosted AI investigation passed Four model requests, all four required tools in order and one OPEN local follow-up

The validation record distinguishes mocked contracts, actual graph checks and the hosted model request. The twenty labelled synthetic rule fixtures are a regression set, not an accuracy benchmark.

A deployment lesson: readiness has a limited meaning

When we enabled OAuth providers, the graph readiness endpoint stayed UP while the homepage returned HTTP 500.

The authorization resolver was treating an ordinary page path as a possible provider path. At the root URL, that produced an empty registration ID. We reproduced the exception, restricted lookup to OAuth authorization routes and added three regression tests.

That failure changed our release check: we verify the homepage, sign-in shell, provider redirects and a fresh guest workflow alongside database readiness.

The backend and frontend run together on Render; the graph runs on FalkorDB Cloud. The current free preview can lose sessions and graph data. Its database tier has no TLS, persistence or backups, so it is an evaluation environment for fictional data, with no durable-account promise. See hosting boundaries before using or reproducing it.

Try the part that changes the next action

Open the demo as a guest and start with CASE-001:

  1. Compare the original claims in Evidence.
  2. Inspect their paths in Connections.
  3. Set aside one source in Context lab and compare the assessment.
  4. Prepare the question, record a fictional manual outcome and export Case brief.

Then try CASE-002 and CASE-004. The interesting outcome is whether the graph context supports another question, and which sources make that question necessary.

Next, we want to observe nontechnical users completing this brief workflow and speak with support operators about the information they need. We need those observations before claiming that the product saves time or fits an operational process.

The lesson we are taking forward is specific: a saved answer needs a record of the evidence it covered. When that evidence changes, the application should make the boundary visible.

Built by Om Singh Jadon and Ajeet Gadekar for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks, under Agents That Act on Connected Data.

ChatGPT assisted with planning, implementation.

title: Quy Uớc Đặt Tên (Naming Conventions) Trong Java
description:
Quy ước đặt tên là một tập hợp các quy tắc thống nhất về cách đặt tên cho các thành phần ngôn ngữ như class, biến, phương thức, v.v. trong Java. Việc tuân theo quy ước đặt tên giúp code dễ đọc, dễ hiểu và dễ bảo trì. Dưới đây là một số quy ước đặt tên phổ biến trong Java:

Quy ước đặt tên trong Java

Ⅰ. Quy ước CamelCase

        CamelCase là quy ước đặt tên thường được sử dụng để đặt tên cho biến, phương thức và class. Trong CamelCase, chữ cái đầu tiên của mỗi từ được viết hoa, ngoại trừ chữ cái đầu tiên của từ đầu tiên.

Quy ước CamelCase 
myVariableName

calculateAverage()

CustomerAccount

Ⅱ. Quy ước PascalCase

    PascalCase là quy ước đặt tên thường được sử dụng để đặt tên cho class và interface. Trong PascalCase, tất cả các chữ cái đầu tiên của mỗi từ được viết hoa.

Quy ước PascalCase

MyVariableName

CalculateAverage

CustomerAccount

Ⅲ. Quy ước chung

    ↳ Tránh sử dụng các ký tự đặc biệt như &, $, #, v.v. để đặt tên.

    ↳ Tránh sử dụng các từ khóa trong Java để đặt tên.

    ↳ Tên nên có ý nghĩa và mô tả rõ ràng chức năng của thành phần ngôn ngữ.

    ↳ Nên sử dụng tên ngắn gọn, dễ nhớ.

    ↳ Nên sử dụng tên nhất quán trong toàn bộ chương trình.

Sử dụng các công cụ hỗ trợ:

    Nhiều IDE (Integrated Development Environment) như Eclipse, IntelliJ IDEA có các tính năng hỗ trợ đặt tên theo quy ước. Ví dụ, khi bạn nhập tên cho một biến, IDE sẽ tự động gợi ý tên theo CamelCase.
