    return {
      id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      externalId: String(msg.message_id),
      channel: "telegram",
      contactId: "", // resolved later by the contact service
      channelUserId: String(msg.from.id),
      type: msg.text ? "text" : "other",
      text: msg.text,
      receivedAt: new Date(msg.date * 1000).toISOString(),
      raw: payload,
    };
  }

  async send(to: string, message: OutboundMessage) {
    // Telegram-specific formatting and API call live here
    return { ok: true };
  }
}

Rule of thumb: if a line of code mentions a specific channel, it should live in an adapter.

A useful side effect is that you can test routing logic with a fake adapter and no network calls.

Lesson 3: Build the router around rules, not channels

Our early router asked, "Which channel did this come from?" The better question turned out to be, "What does this conversation need?"

We switched to declarative rules evaluated in priority order:

interface RoutingRule {
  name: string;
  priority: number;
  when: (msg: NormalizedMessage, ctx: ConversationContext) => boolean;
  to: "flow" | "ai_agent" | "human";
  target?: string;
}

const rules: RoutingRule[] = [
  {
    name: "human-takeover-active",
    priority: 1,
    when: (_m, ctx) => ctx.humanAssigned,
    to: "human",
  },
  {
    name: "keyword-support",
    priority: 2,
    when: (m) => /refund|complaint|cancel/i.test(m.text ?? ""),
    to: "human",
  },
  {
    name: "default-ai",
    priority: 99,
    when: () => true,
    to: "ai_agent",
    target: "general-assistant",
  },
];

function route(msg: NormalizedMessage, ctx: ConversationContext) {
  return [...rules]
    .sort((a, b) => a.priority - b.priority)
    .find((r) => r.when(msg, ctx))!;
}

Because rules don't care about the channel, the same logic works on WhatsApp, Telegram, and Instagram. You can still add channel-aware rules when you need them, such as a rule for a channel's messaging window.

Lesson 4: Make delivery idempotent

Webhooks get retried. Networks fail. If you don't plan for this, users get duplicate replies. Two protections helped us the most:

  1. Deduplicate inbound messages using channel + externalId.
  2. Use idempotency keys on outbound sends so a retried job doesn't send twice. 
async function handleInbound(msg: NormalizedMessage) {
  const key = `inbound:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`;
  const isNew = await redis.set(key, "1", "EX", 86400, "NX");
  if (!isNew) return; // duplicate webhook, ignore

  await queue.add("route-message", msg, {
    jobId: `route:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`,
  });
}

Acknowledge the webhook fast and do the real work in a queue. Channels penalize slow responses, and long AI calls shouldn't block your HTTP handler.

Lesson 5: Plan for fallbacks and human handoff

Things that will go wrong: a channel API times out, a message is rejected, or the AI isn't confident. Decide the behavior in advance:

  • Retry with backoff for transient errors (timeouts, 5xx).
  • Don't retry permanent errors (blocked user, invalid recipient). Mark them and move on.
  • Hand off to a human when confidence is low or the user asks for one, and make the router respect that state (see the human-takeover-active rule above).
  • Log every routing decision with the rule name, so you can answer "why did the bot do that?" later. 
async function dispatch(adapter: ChannelAdapter, to: string, msg: OutboundMessage) {
  try {
    return await adapter.send(to, msg);
  } catch (err) {
    if (isTransient(err)) throw err;   // let the queue retry
    await markUndeliverable(to, err);  // permanent failure
  }
}

Mistakes we'd avoid next time

  • Routing on raw payloads. Normalize first, always.
  • Treating identity as an afterthought. Decide early how you'll link a user across channels.
  • Skipping decision logs. Debugging a routing bug without them is guesswork.
  • Assuming channels behave alike. Message windows, formats, and rate limits differ more than the docs suggest.

Replace this section with 1-2 real incidents from your build (a bug, a surprising channel behavior, a number you measured) before publishing.

Conclusion

The main takeaways from building cross-channel message routing for chatbots:

  • Normalize every inbound message into one schema.
  • Isolate channel-specific behavior inside adapters.
  • Route on conversation needs using ordered rules, not on channel names.
  • Make both inbound and outbound delivery idempotent.
  • Design fallbacks and human handoff from day one.

These patterns take time to get right, and many teams would rather spend that time on the customer experience than on plumbing. That's the problem platforms like Botsailor aim to take off your plate, with omnichannel automation across WhatsApp, Telegram, Instagram, and more, so you can focus on conversations instead of webhooks. If you're building your own, we hope these lessons save you a few late nights.

How do you handle routing across channels? Share your approach or your worst webhook horror story in the comments.

title: GST Helper: a local-first GSTR-1 preparation assistant
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

I built GST Helper, a local-first AI workspace that helps a small business prepare selected GSTR-1 values from sales invoice PDFs.

The demo company is BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. The user starts by loading outward-sales invoice PDFs. GST Helper reads the invoices, extracts values, shows page evidence, and turns the documents into a guided GSTR-1 review flow.

The current app prepares these GSTR-1 sections:

  • Table 4A regular domestic B2B invoices
  • Table 12 B2B HSN/SAC summary
  • Table 13 document numbers issued

It shows the invoice value including tax, taxable value, IGST, CGST, SGST or UTGST, cess, total tax, and invoice count for the supported B2B scope. It also creates a reference PDF tied to the saved review revision, so the user can inspect the same values before downloading the file.

The problem is simple: small business owners and bookkeepers often do this first pass manually. They read invoice PDFs, copy values into spreadsheets, check invoice numbers, and then use those figures while working in the GST Portal. That work is slow, error-prone, and full of accounting language that is not friendly to a non-expert.

GST Helper is meant for a small business owner, bookkeeper, or accountant who wants a faster way to prepare and review the numbers before portal entry. The paid version could charge for private local workflows, more GST sections, accountant review packs, and better import and export support.

The app does not file a return, connect to the GST Portal, or claim that the whole GSTR-1 return is complete. Other GSTR-1 sections must be handled separately. That boundary is visible in the product because tax software needs trust more than magic.

Demo

Video demo: https://youtu.be/RFq9whXetRg


The demo shows the full BharatBiz flow:

  1. Load sample sales invoice PDFs.
  2. Confirm the seller GSTIN, tax period, and turnover band.
  3. Review invoice fields with page evidence.
  4. Save the reviewed values.
  5. Inspect the Table 4A totals.
  6. Generate a verified reference PDF.
  7. Use the review chat beside the final PDF.

Code

Repository: https://github.com/sonu0702/pgst

sonu0702 / pgst

GST Helper

GST Helper is a local-first GSTR-1 preparation app for BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. It turns outward-sales invoice PDFs into reviewed values, a clear summary for the supported GSTR-1 sections, and a reference PDF the user can inspect before downloading.

This release prepares only regular B2B invoices in Table 4A, the B2B HSN/SAC summary in Table 12, and documents issued in Table 13. It does not prepare a complete GSTR-1 return, connect to the GST Portal, submit or file a return, or decide GST treatment. Other applicable GSTR-1 sections must be prepared separately. The GST Portal accepts a JSON workflow through its offline tool, but the portal still validates the account and return when the user uses that file.

What the app does

  • Starts with outward-sales PDFs, then suggests seller GSTIN and tax period with page evidence before asking for return details.
  • Shows observed invoice-number…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The app is a single repository with a React frontend and a FastAPI backend.

Tech stack:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI
  • Local AI: Ollama with Gemma 4
  • PDF processing: Python PDF extraction with optional local OCR support
  • Export artifacts: reference PDF and supported-section JSON
  • Storage: no database in this prototype. Reviews live in temporary process memory.

The user flow starts with source documents, not a chatbot. That choice matters. Invoices are the source of truth, so the app first reads the PDFs and creates a review workspace from them.

The backend extracts invoice fields and line items, keeps compact evidence snippets, and builds a temporary GSTR-1 review case. The frontend lets the user inspect and edit each value. When the user saves, the backend runs local checks for the supported sections and returns readiness results.

Gemma 4 is used through Ollama for a narrow review task. It can answer questions about values already in the review or prepare a proposed edit from invoice evidence or from a value the user states. It cannot decide tax treatment, calculate GST, approve filing, or submit anything.

The user stays in control:

  • The model proposes changes.
  • The user applies the proposal.
  • The user reviews the form.
  • The user saves the revision.
  • The user regenerates the PDF if anything changed.

The reference PDF is tied to the saved revision. The app renders the PDF back in the browser and verifies the expected content before the user downloads it.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation matters here because tax preparation needs transparency, local control, and the ability to inspect the workflow.

A closed hosted API can produce a polished answer, but that is not enough for this use case. A small business owner needs to know where a number came from and what the app did with the source document. GST Helper keeps the review path visible: invoice evidence, editable fields, saved revision, local checks, and a reference PDF.

Open-weight local AI also changes the privacy story. In this prototype, Gemma 4 runs locally through Ollama. The app does not need to send invoice details to a hosted model API. That made it possible to build an AI-assisted review flow that still respects sensitive business documents.

Open-source tools also made the project practical for a hackathon:

  • FastAPI made the backend small and inspectable.
  • React and Vite made the review UI fast to iterate.
  • Ollama made local Gemma 4 setup approachable.
  • Python PDF tooling made extraction and reference PDF generation possible without building a document pipeline from scratch.

The project is not trying to replace a tax professional or the GST Portal. It is trying to make the preparation step clearer, safer, and more reviewable.

My Agent Session

I used Codex as an AI coding agent throughout the build. The agent helped with product scoping, GSTR-1 flow design, FastAPI and React implementation, sample invoice generation, UI polish, PDF review, and the demo walkthrough.

The most useful part was not code generation alone. The agent helped keep the product narrow. Whenever the app started to look like a generic invoice-review demo, I pushed it back toward one clear filing workflow: GSTR-1 preparation from sales invoices.

That made the final project stronger. It has a specific user, a specific filing task, a clear supported scope, and visible review boundaries.

Prize Categories

gemma

Team

This is a team submission. Published by @sonu0702.

Teammates:

  • @chandan_sharma

title: A Control Plane for an AI-Run Firm: Workflow, Agent and Human Lanes
description:
"Autonomous company" sounds like a model choice. In practice it is a control-plane design. This post sketches one for a small service firm doing lead intake. The firm is illustrative, not a customer story, and I have no results to share.

The idea

Split every task into one of three lanes and enforce the lane in code.

from enum import Enum
from dataclasses import dataclass

class Lane(Enum):
    WORKFLOW = "fixed steps, no model decisions"
    AGENT = "model picks steps, inside limits"
    HUMAN = "person decides"

@dataclass
class Task:
    name: str
    lane: Lane
    tools: list[str]
    needs_approval: bool = False

TASKS = [
    Task("capture_lead",   Lane.WORKFLOW, ["crm.create"]),
    Task("send_reminder",  Lane.WORKFLOW, ["email.send_template"]),
    Task("draft_reply",    Lane.AGENT,    ["crm.read", "email.draft"]),
    Task("quote_price",    Lane.HUMAN,    []),
]

Anthropic's guide says coded workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks, and that agents bring higher cost and compounding errors, so test them in sandboxes with guardrails. Salesforce describes "hybrid reasoning" that combines deterministic logic and adaptive AI. The lanes above are one simple way to do that.

The router 

def route(task: Task, payload):
    log("start", task.name, payload)
    if task.lane is Lane.HUMAN or task.needs_approval:
        return queue_for_human(task, payload)
    if task.lane is Lane.WORKFLOW:
        return run_steps(task, payload)
    return run_agent(task, payload, allowed_tools=task.tools)

Three things live here and not in a prompt: which tools a task may touch, which tasks need approval, and what gets logged.

Incident handling 

PAUSED = set()

def pause(task_name: str, who: str):
    PAUSED.add(task_name)
    log("paused", task_name, who)

Check PAUSED at the start of route. Someone must own the pause, and the log must say who used it.

Red lines to code first

  • Money, contracts and customer promises always go to a person.
  • Every agent action has a log entry with inputs and outputs.
  • Every task has a named owner and an off switch.

What this is not

It is not proof that a company can run itself. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index describes humans setting direction and "checking in as needed". The control plane is how that check-in becomes real.

Tej Pandya, founder of GrowEasy.ai.

title: LLMs on Consumer Hardware — Part 6: The Orchestration Ceiling — Why a Bigger Coordinator Doesn't Fix the Loop
description:
Part 6 of a series. Previously: Part 5 — Distributing the Workers and the Memory Budget.

Part 5 ended with the 77 GB coordinator finally running as it should — resident, no thrashing, the memory problem resolved by moving the workers to a second machine. That made it possible to answer a question Part 4 had deferred: now that the big model can actually run, does a bigger coordinator fix orchestration? The answer was no, and the reason reshaped how the team was run.

The ceiling persists on the big model

With memory no longer the bottleneck, the coordinator's orchestration could be judged on its own merits. It sequenced delegations more reliably than Gemma had — but it did not escape the same failure modes. On longer plans it still dropped steps, issuing some delegations and silently omitting others before writing its summary. It still, on occasion, emitted a delegation as text rather than executing it — Part 4 showed one such case, a hand-off printed as raw JSON and then abandoned. And it periodically returned nothing at all after a tool call, requiring an automatic nudge to continue:

⚠ Model returned empty after tool calls — nudging to continue

That warning recurred often enough to be diagnostic. These were not the mistakes of a weak model; they were the mistakes of a capable model asked to do something it is structurally poor at — hold a long control loop in its head while also doing the reasoning inside it.

The diagnosis: the ceiling is the loop, not the model

The decisive observation was that all three failure modes — dropped steps, commands narrated instead of executed, empty turns — appeared on the large model exactly as they had on the small one. The common factor was not model size. It was the agentic loop itself.

Asking a language model to orchestrate is asking it to be, simultaneously, the planner that decides the steps, the dispatcher that issues each delegation, the bookkeeper that tracks which delegations are still outstanding, and the evaluator that judges the results as they return. That is a great deal of state to carry across many turns, and carrying state across turns is precisely what these models are weakest at. A bigger model raises the ceiling a little; it does not remove it.

The fix: take the loop away from the model

If the loop is the problem, the loop should not be the model's job. The resolution was deterministic orchestration: a small script owns the control loop. It holds the list of tasks, dispatches each delegation, waits for and collects the result, and decides what runs next. The model is invoked only for the two things it is genuinely good at — planning (what are the steps?) and evaluating (is this result acceptable?) — and never has to remember what it has already dispatched, because the script does that.

The improvement was immediate and measurable. A task sequence that the model-driven loop had stalled on partway through — completing three of five steps before losing the thread — ran all five to completion when the same plan was executed by the script. The model had not become more capable. It had simply been relieved of the one job it could not reliably do.

The lesson

The instinct, when an agent loop is unreliable, is to reach for a bigger model. That instinct was wrong here, and expensively so — it was the reasoning behind the whole coordinator search of Part 4, and the memory wall of Part 5, and in the end it did not solve the problem it was chasing. Orchestration reliability is not a model capability that can be bought in larger quantities; it is a property of how the loop is structured. The durable fix was architectural: move the deterministic part — the loop, the bookkeeping, the dispatch — into deterministic code, and reserve the model for the parts that genuinely require judgment. A control loop is a job for a program, not for a language model, and the sooner that division is drawn the more reliable the system becomes.

What follows

Deterministic orchestration made the team's execution reliable: a plan was now carried out without dropped steps or invented progress. But it did nothing for the moment a plan meets a wall — when the right next step is not in the plan at all, and someone has to rethink the approach rather than merely execute it. Reliable execution and good judgment are different capabilities, and the next entry is about supplying the second without compromising the first.

title: How to Charge for Your Vibe-Coded App: One-Time vs Subscription (and How to Set It Up)
description:
You built an app with Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. People are using it, a few have even said they'd pay for it. So now you're stuck on two questions: how should I charge, and how do I actually set that up without breaking anything?

I'm Deepak, a solo developer in Hyderabad, and I've wired payments into a lot of apps built with AI agents. This guide walks through the choice between charging once and charging every month, which payment company to pick, and the exact steps to get money flowing. No code required to follow along.

If you want the bigger picture on what goes wrong after someone pays, read my first post: How to add payments to an app you built with AI. This one is about the decision that comes before that.

The three ways to charge

Almost every small app uses one of these, or a mix:

  • One-time payment. The customer pays once and keeps access. Think of a template, a tool, a lifetime deal, or a downloadable pack.
  • Subscription. The customer pays every month or every year, and access stops if they stop paying.
  • Credits (pay as you go). The customer buys a bundle of uses, like 100 image generations, and buys more when they run out.

There's no "correct" answer. The right one depends on one simple question.

The one question that decides it

Does your app cost you money every time someone uses it?

If yes, you probably want a subscription or credits. If no, a one-time payment is often simpler and easier to sell.

Here's why. Many vibe-coded apps call an AI model, send emails, store files or run on a server that charges by use. Those costs keep coming as long as the customer keeps using the app. If you charge once, a heavy user can end up costing you more than they paid. A monthly price, or credits that run out, keeps what you earn in line with what you spend.

If your app is mostly a fixed thing, like a calculator, a template, a desktop tool or a set of files, your costs don't grow much with each user. Charging once is honest and easy for buyers to say yes to.

One-time payment: when it fits

Good for: tools that don't cost you much to run, templates and starter kits, downloadable products, and "lifetime access" launch offers.

Why people like it: buyers don't have to worry about another monthly bill. It's easier to explain, and there's nothing to cancel.

The catch: you get paid once. To keep earning, you need a steady flow of new buyers, or paid upgrades later. And be careful with "lifetime" deals on apps that call AI models, because those costs don't stop.

What you need to set up:

  1. A product in your payment company's dashboard with a single price.
  2. A "Buy" button that sends people to the payment company's checkout page.
  3. Your app listening for the payment message (developers call this a webhook: an automatic note from the payment company saying "this person paid") and marking that person as a buyer.
  4. Paid pages that check "is this person a buyer?" before letting them in.

That's it. No renewals, no cancellations, just refunds to handle.

Subscription: when it fits

Good for: apps people use regularly, apps with ongoing costs (AI, hosting, data), and apps you keep improving.

Why makers like it: income that repeats every month, which makes it easier to plan and to keep paying for servers.

The catch: more moving parts. People cancel, cards expire, payments fail, and some customers switch between plans. Your app has to react correctly to every one of those, not just the first payment. And buyers think harder before signing up for something that bills them forever.

What you need to set up:

  1. A product with a monthly price, and optionally a yearly price (often offered at a discount).
  2. A "Subscribe" button that goes to checkout.
  3. Your app listening for payment messages, not just "paid" but also "renewed", "cancelled", "payment failed" and "refunded", and updating the person's access each time.
  4. Paid pages that check "is this subscription active right now?"
  5. A "Manage billing" page where customers can change their card or cancel by themselves. Both Polar and Stripe offer a ready-made one, so you don't build it from scratch.

Step 3 is where most AI-written setups go wrong. The agent handles the first payment and forgets the rest, so cancelled users keep access forever. My first post has a checklist to catch that.

Credits: the middle ground

If your costs depend heavily on how much someone uses the app, credits can be fairer than either option. Customers buy a pack, each use takes some away, and they top up when they run low. Light users pay little, heavy users pay more, and you never lose money on one person.

The trade-off: your app has to keep an accurate balance for every user and never let it go below zero, even if someone clicks twice quickly. It's very doable, but test it carefully.

Not sure? Start simple

If you can't decide, here's a reasonable default:

  • Low running costs: start with a one-time price. You can add a subscription tier later.
  • Real running costs (like AI calls): start with one monthly plan. Just one. Add a yearly option or a second tier when people ask for it.

Whatever you pick, you can change it. Your first price is a guess, and that's fine. Real customers will tell you more than any pricing article.

Polar vs Stripe for indie devs

Once you know how you'll charge, you need a payment company. For most solo makers the choice is Polar or Stripe. Both handle one-time payments and subscriptions well.

Polar is a merchant of record. In plain words, Polar is the seller on paper: it collects and pays sales tax and VAT in the countries your customers buy from, then pays you. If you're selling worldwide on your own, that saves a lot of paperwork. The trade-off is a higher fee per sale than Stripe's basic rate, so check their current pricing page.

Stripe handles the payment, but you're the seller, so tax is your job. Stripe has a tax add-on that works out the right amount to charge, but registering and filing is still on you. In return you get more control and a huge set of features.

My rule of thumb: solo, selling digital products or subscriptions to many countries, and don't want to think about tax? Start with Polar. Already have a Stripe account or a business set up to handle tax? Use Stripe. Either way, first check that the one you pick can pay out to your country. And if tax worries you, a short chat with an accountant is money well spent.

How to set it up, step by step

This works whether your app is in Next.js (the most common setup for vibe-coded web apps) or something else. You'll ask your AI agent to do most of it, but you stay in charge of checking it.

  1. Create an account with Polar or Stripe and stay in test mode (a practice mode where no real money moves).
  2. Create your product and price in the dashboard: one-time, monthly, or both.
  3. Ask your agent to add checkout. Be specific: "Add a Subscribe button that sends logged-in users to Polar checkout for my Pro monthly product."
  4. Ask it to handle payment messages, and list them all: paid, renewed, cancelled, payment failed, refunded. Ask it to verify each message is genuine using the secret from the dashboard.
  5. Ask it to lock paid pages so they check access in your database, not just whether someone saw the thank-you page.
  6. Add the billing page so customers can cancel or update their card themselves.
  7. Test everything with a test card: buy, log out and in, cancel, refund, and try the billing page as a free user.
  8. Switch to live mode, copy over the live keys, make one real purchase yourself, then refund it.

Step 7 is the one people skip, and it's the one that saves you from angry emails.

The one-prompt way: ShipToPaid

I got tired of writing those prompts by hand and fixing the same mistakes, so I turned the tested steps into written instructions, called skills, that Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can follow. That's ShipToPaid.

Instead of steps 3 to 6 above, you type /add-paywall in your agent, say whether you want one-time or subscription, and it follows a checklist that already covers the traps: checking that payment messages are real, handling cancellations and failed payments, and locking paid pages properly. A launch audit then walks you through the testing.

Want to try it first? The free lite pack on GitHub includes Polar checkout, Polar payment messages and a short launch check. The full pack adds Stripe, subscriptions that control access, a customer billing page, credits, license keys and a working Next.js starter app. Every skill is a plain file you can read and change.

You don't need either to use this guide. Pick how you'll charge, pick a payment company, test the whole flow in test mode, and go get your first paying customer.

This post first appeared on the ShipToPaid blog.

title: I Built Kiver: A Discovery Marketplace for Telegram Bots and Mini Apps
description:
Building a Telegram bot is one thing. Getting people to discover it is another.

That problem is what led me to build Kiver.

"https://www.getkiver.com" (https://www.getkiver.com)

The problem I wanted to solve

Telegram has an ecosystem of bots and Mini Apps for almost everything: AI assistants, productivity tools, finance, education, gaming, automation and more.

Developers spend time building these products, improving their features and trying to attract users. But once a bot is ready, discovery becomes a challenge of its own.

A Telegram link is useful, but it doesn't always give a product the broader visibility it needs. Potential users may not know the bot exists, and developers need more ways to put their work in front of relevant audiences.

I wanted to build something that could help bridge that gap.

What is Kiver?

Kiver is a discovery marketplace for Telegram bots and Mini Apps.

The idea is straightforward: help users find useful Telegram tools and give makers a public place to showcase what they've built.

On Kiver, users can:

  • Browse Telegram tools across different categories.
  • Search for bots by name, username or use case.
  • Explore individual product pages.
  • Upvote tools they find useful.
  • Open listed bots directly in Telegram.

For developers and makers, Kiver provides a way to turn a Telegram link into a dedicated, shareable product listing.

Giving Telegram tools a public home

One part of Kiver I'm particularly interested in is discoverability beyond Telegram itself.

A maker can submit a public Telegram link, review the listing details, select a category and publish a product page.

That page gives the tool a dedicated URL that can be shared in communities, included in documentation or discovered through search engines.

The goal is to create another discovery channel for Telegram products instead of relying entirely on someone already knowing a bot's username or receiving its link from another person.

Of course, a public page doesn't guarantee search rankings or new users. The challenge is building a useful directory that people actually want to visit.

I'm still growing it

Kiver is an early-stage project, and I'm starting to see traffic coming to the website.

It's not massive traffic, and I'm not going to pretend it is. But seeing people visit a product you're building is useful feedback. It gives me a reason to keep improving the experience, expanding the directory and thinking more carefully about how users discover and evaluate tools.

The next challenge is turning visits into something more meaningful: people finding useful products, makers getting discovered, and visitors returning because the directory helps them.

That's the kind of growth I want to build toward.

What I'd like to improve

There are several areas I'm interested in developing further:

  • Better discovery: Helping users find relevant tools without having to know their names beforehand.
  • More useful listings: Making it easier to understand what a bot does before opening it.
  • More makers: Bringing more developers into the directory so users have a wider selection of tools.
  • A stronger community: Making product feedback and voting more useful for both users and builders.

The important part is making the directory valuable to both sides. More listings are useful, but only if people can find tools that genuinely solve their problems.

Try Kiver

If you've built a Telegram bot or Mini App, you can explore the directory and submit your own project.

Website: https://www.getkiver.com

Browse the directory, see how listings work, or launch your own Telegram tool on the platform.

I'm building Kiver in public and would appreciate feedback from developers, indie hackers and anyone working in the Telegram ecosystem.

If you build Telegram tools, what is the biggest challenge you've faced when trying to get your first users?

I'd be interested to hear what has worked for you.

title: A Dashboard That Updates Itself — No Data Analyst Required
description:
You already know which numbers matter in your business. The problem is that getting them means digging — exporting from the CRM, re-sorting a spreadsheet, asking someone who's busy. So you check the numbers you care about once a quarter, in a panic, right before a decision.

On October 8, Anthropic shipped a beta feature that changes the digging part: Claude Dashboards. You connect a data source, ask a question in plain English, and Claude writes the queries, picks the charts, and builds a dashboard that refreshes as your data changes. It's in beta on paid plans, and the supported connections are the enterprise-grade ones — BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Redshift, ClickHouse, and Salesforce.

Most of the coverage is aimed at data teams and enterprise BI users. Here's the version for a business with no analyst on staff.

The feature that matters most is the smallest one

Every chart in a Claude dashboard shows the query behind it, along with the last refresh time.

That sounds like a technical detail. It's actually the trust mechanism, and it's the reason this is usable by someone who can't read SQL.

Dashboards usually fail for a boring reason: the owner can't tell whether the number on the screen means what they think it means. "Deals this quarter" — does that mean closed-won? Everything in the pipeline? Does it include the two renewals that got logged funny? When you can't answer that, you don't trust the chart, and when you don't trust the chart, you go back to the spreadsheet.

With the query visible, you get two practical options:

  • Sanity-check it yourself. Read the plain-English question the query represents. If Claude counted "deals" as every open opportunity when you meant closed-won, you'll usually see it in the query's shape and refine the ask.
  • Hand it to someone technical for five minutes. A contractor, your IT person, a niece who codes — anyone fluent can scan one query and tell you whether the number is honest. That's a five-minute review, not a BI project.

A dashboard you can verify is a dashboard you'll actually open. That's the whole game.

What to connect first

For most small businesses the answer is simple: your CRM — Salesforce is the one supported connection that isn't a data warehouse. Connect it before anything else.

Here's the honest boundary, though: if your business data lives in QuickBooks, a handful of spreadsheets, and your email, and you don't run a warehouse, this feature isn't for you yet. There's no connector for your stack. Don't buy a Snowflake plan to get a dashboard — that's building a chimney because you liked the smoke. Revisit when either your tools grow native support or your data naturally lands somewhere connectable.

What to actually ask

The gap between "I have a dashboard" and "I use the dashboard" is almost always the questions. Have these ready.

Weekly — movement questions:

  • "Which deals moved stages this week, and which ones have been sitting more than 14 days?"
  • "Show new leads created by source, this week versus last week."
  • "Which accounts haven't been contacted in 30 days?"

These catch problems while they're still cheap — the stalled deal, the lead source that quietly died.

Monthly — pattern questions:

  • "Which lead sources produced closed-won deals this quarter versus last quarter?"
  • "What's our average time from first contact to close, by month, for the last six months?"
  • "Which customers closed 12 months ago and haven't renewed?"

These are the ones nobody asks because assembling the answer takes a day. With a live dashboard, asking takes a minute and the answer stays fresh.

Start with two or three questions, not twenty. The failure mode of self-serve BI is a wall of charts nobody looks at. Three numbers you check every Monday beat thirty you scroll past.

When you've outgrown it

This is a beta feature that regenerates answers from questions. It is not a system of record for your metrics. Move to real BI — or a deliberately built spreadsheet with fixed definitions — when any of these become true:

  • More than two or three people need the same numbers every day. At that point definitions need to be fixed and shared, not re-derived per question.
  • You need permissions. Salespeople shouldn't see each other's pipelines. If access control matters, you've left consumer-tool territory.
  • People start arguing about whose dashboard is right. That's a definitions problem, and it needs one owned source, not a fresh query per conversation.

Until then, a dashboard you can audit by clicking the chart is more than most small businesses have ever had.

One bonus, mostly for the quarterly report

Alongside Dashboards, Anthropic shipped Claude Motion (beta for Team and Enterprise plans): it builds editable animations you can export as MP4. The pragmatic use is the quarterly update — a 30-second animated explanation of where the numbers moved, made from the same data, without touching a video editor or a design tool. If you send stakeholders a quarterly recap nobody reads, a short animation of the same facts is worth testing once.

The Monday habit

Connect the CRM, build the three weekly questions, and put ten minutes on your calendar every Monday to open the dashboard. That's the entire adoption plan. The tool writes the queries; you still have to form the habit — the numbers don't help anyone who doesn't look at them.

If the owner side of this — which numbers to watch, what to check weekly, what triggers action — is the part you keep deferring, it's written down in The AI Agent Owner's Playbook: the permission ladder that matches tasks to trust levels, the first-month inspection habit, and the escalation contract format that tells an agent exactly when to come back to you. $49 CAD, instant download.

title: Local Whisper vs. Cloud Dictation: Privacy, Latency and Accuracy Tradeoffs (Plus a Private Setup)
description:
"Just run Whisper locally" is good advice that skips a lot of detail. Local speech-to-text is genuinely useful, but it is not automatically faster, more accurate, or even fully private, depending on what else sits in your pipeline.

This post breaks the decision into three questions (what leaves the machine, where latency comes from, and how accurate it is for your voice) and ends with a setup where nothing leaves your computer. I use InsertKit as the dictation front end because it supports local Whisper, bring-your-own-key cloud providers, and custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints in one place. The tradeoffs apply to any stack.

1. Privacy: map the data flow first

A modern dictation pipeline usually has two stages:

mic audio -> [speech-to-text] -> raw transcript -> [LLM formatting] -> text at cursor

Each stage can be local or remote, and people often secure one and forget the other.

  • Speech-to-text. With a cloud engine, your audio is uploaded and processed by that provider. With a local Whisper model, audio stays on your machine.
  • Formatting. Clean-up (removing filler words, fixing punctuation, adapting tone) is usually done by a chat model. If that model is in the cloud, your transcript leaves the machine even when the audio did not.
  • Side channels. Sync features count too. In InsertKit, snippets, clipboard history, custom vocabulary, and API keys sync to your account. If your vocabulary list contains an unreleased product codename, that word list is synced, even if every audio clip stays local.

What InsertKit stores is worth knowing precisely: cloud voice history in Settings → Usage covers the last 30 days and is text only, no audio, with a Clear button. Local voice history stays on the device, and setting its maximum to 0 disables it.

So "private" is not a property of a model. It is a property of the whole path.

2. Latency: where the milliseconds actually go

Local is not always faster. Rough breakdown:

Cloud: upload time + queueing + inference on fast hardware + download. On a good connection, short utterances can come back very quickly, because providers run large models on serious GPUs.

Local: zero network, but inference runs on your CPU or GPU. A small model on a modern laptop is responsive. A large model on an older CPU can take noticeably longer than the time you spent talking.

Two details that matter in practice:

  • Model loading. Expect the first transcription after loading a large model to be slower than the ones that follow.
  • Long dictation. If the tool waits until you finish a three-minute ramble before transcribing, you wait for all of it at the end. InsertKit splits long speech into chunks at natural pauses and transcribes them while you keep talking, which hides much of that delay locally and in the cloud.

3. Accuracy: benchmark your own voice

Published word error rates come from benchmark datasets, not from your accent, your mic, or your jargon. Ten minutes of testing beats any leaderboard.

Here is a quick, tool-agnostic way to compare Whisper model sizes with whisper.cpp:

git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp
cd whisper.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build -j --config Release

for m in base small medium; do
  sh ./models/download-ggml-model.sh $m
done

# Convert a 60-second recording of you reading real work text to 16 kHz mono WAV
ffmpeg -i sample.m4a -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le sample.wav

for m in base small medium; do
  /usr/bin/time -p ./build/bin/whisper-cli -m models/ggml-$m.bin -f sample.wav -otxt -of out-$m
done

Then score each output against what you actually said:

# pip install jiwer
from jiwer import wer

ref = open("reference.txt").read()
for m in ["base", "small", "medium"]:
    hyp = open(f"out-{m}.txt").read()
    print(m, "WER:", round(wer(ref, hyp), 3))

Use real material: a commit message, a ticket description, a paragraph full of service names. Generic sentences flatter every model.

A few patterns you will likely see:

  • Bigger models handle accents and noise better, at the cost of speed and memory.
  • Jargon fails across all sizes. That is a vocabulary problem, not a model-size problem.
  • Whisper can hallucinate on silence or noise, producing text nobody said. Trimming silence and using a decent mic reduce it.

For jargon, a correction layer helps more than a bigger model. InsertKit's Custom Vocabulary has word hints plus "heard as → write as" corrections, like post gres → Postgres, and corrections run before and after formatting so the LLM cannot undo them.

The decision, simplified

  • Audio must never leave the machine: local Whisper.
  • Speed on modest hardware: cloud, or a small local model.
  • Accuracy on difficult audio: a large local model with a GPU, or a strong cloud engine.
  • Zero setup: a hosted engine that needs no key.
  • Air-gapped or offline work: local Whisper plus a local LLM, or formatting turned off.

Many developers end up hybrid: local for anything touching client code or internal docs, cloud for low-stakes chat.

A fully private dictation setup

Here is the setup where audio and text both stay on your machine. Local Whisper is a desktop feature in InsertKit (Windows, macOS, Linux).

Step 1: Local speech-to-text

In the Speech Engine panel, choose Local Offline (Whisper) and download a model inside the app. Sizes go from Tiny (~75 MB) and Base (~140 MB) through Small (~460 MB) and Medium (~1.5 GB) to Large v3 (~3 GB). Use your benchmark results to pick. Small is a sensible starting point on most laptops.

Step 2: A local LLM for formatting

Run a local OpenAI-compatible server. With Ollama:

ollama pull llama3.2
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/models

LM Studio exposes a similar server, by default at http://localhost:1234/v1.

In InsertKit, open Settings → API Keys and add a Custom OpenAI-compatible provider: a name, the base URL (for example http://localhost:11434/v1), a key if your server needs one, and the models (auto-fetched or entered by hand). Then choose that model for Smart Formatting.

Smaller local models format well enough for clean-up. If output gets too creative, add a short custom instruction under Use my own instructions, such as "Fix punctuation and remove filler words. Do not add or change content."

Step 3: Decide what happens when formatting is unavailable

Enable Keep working offline so the raw transcript is pasted if the formatter cannot be reached. Or skip formatting for sensitive sessions and rely on vocabulary corrections.

Step 4: Verify, do not assume

Turn off Wi-Fi (or run nmcli networking off on Linux) and dictate a paragraph into your editor. If text still appears and is formatted, both stages are local. Turn the network back on afterwards, because account sync needs it.

Linux note

Check Settings → General → Linux Dependencies. Typing and pasting rely on tools such as xdotool and wtype, and on Wayland the tips point to wtype or ydotool.

Where cloud still wins

To be fair to cloud dictation:

  • No local resources. Large models do not eat your RAM or battery during a long build.
  • Consistent quality on weak hardware.
  • Language coverage. InsertKit's voice typing covers 100+ languages with auto-detect. If you dictate in more than one, benchmark each on your local model before committing to it.
  • Mobile. InsertKit's Android app uses hosted or BYOK engines; there is no on-device Whisper there.

If you use the cloud, at least choose deliberately. InsertKit Free needs no key and has a daily limit, Premium uses credits, and BYOK covers providers such as OpenAI, Groq, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and ElevenLabs.

Wrapping up

Local Whisper is a strong default for private work, but privacy depends on the full path, latency depends on your hardware, and accuracy depends on your own voice. Benchmark with real text, add vocabulary corrections for your stack, and verify your setup with the network off.

If you want to try this exact setup, the desktop builds are at insertkit.com/download.

title: A Kotlin Data Class Works as a HashMap Key. In a TypeScript Map It Never Matches
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

A Kotlin grid keyed by Point is about as ordinary as code gets: a cell type and a map from cell to whatever lives there.

data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val labels = hashMapOf(Point(1, 2) to "spawn")
    println(labels[Point(1, 2)]) // spawn
}

Two different Point instances, one lookup, a hit. The Kotlin compiler derives equals() and hashCode() from every property in the primary constructor, so the second Point(1, 2) lands in the same bucket as the first and compares equal. Java gives you the same deal with records, final since JDK 16.

Now you port it to TypeScript. The compiler is happy, and the lookup returns undefined with no error anywhere.

Why the Map can't see your Point

Here is the port, as most JVM developers write it on day one:

type Point = { readonly x: number; readonly y: number };

const labels = new Map<Point, string>();
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");

labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // undefined
labels.size;                // 1

const seen = new Set<Point>();
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.size;                  // 2

JavaScript's Map compares keys with the SameValueZero algorithm. MDN spells out what that means for objects: "for object keys, equality is based on object identity. They are compared by reference, not by value." Two object literals with the same fields are two objects, so they are two keys. Set works the same way, which is why your "deduplicated" set holds the same point twice.

The JVM reflex is to add an equals method and move on. It does nothing here:

class Pt {
  readonly x: number;
  readonly y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  equals(o: Pt): boolean {
    return this.x === o.x && this.y === o.y;
  }
}

const m = new Map<Pt, string>([[new Pt(1, 2), "spawn"]]);
m.get(new Pt(1, 2)); // undefined

There is no equals/hashCode protocol in JavaScript collections. Map never calls your method, and there is no hook to make it. On the JVM, the Object contract says equal objects "must produce the same integer result" from hashCode, and HashMap is built on that promise.

The type checker won't save you either. TypeScript's type system is structural: any { x, y } is a valid Point, so labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }) type-checks perfectly.

One more trap while you are here. If you reach for a plain object as a dictionary instead, every property name gets coerced to a string, and every plain object becomes "[object Object]". Now every point matches every other point. You traded "never matches" for "always matches".

Fix 1: derive a string key

The smallest fix is to stop using the object as the key and use a string computed from it:

const keyOf = (p: Point): string => `${p.x},${p.y}`;

const grid = new Map<string, string>();
grid.set(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
grid.get(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"

Strings are primitives, and SameValueZero compares primitives by value, so this works. For numeric fields the comma is safe because a JavaScript number never stringifies with a comma in it.

String fields are where this goes wrong. With a naive template, { org: "a,b", name: "c" } and { org: "a", name: "b,c" } both produce "a,b,c". Encode the fields as a JSON array in a fixed order instead:

type Member = { readonly org: string; readonly name: string };

const memberKey = (m: Member): string =>
  JSON.stringify([m.org, m.name]);

JSON escaping makes the encoding unambiguous, and the array fixes the order. Don't call JSON.stringify(m) on the whole object: property order follows Object.keys(), which is insertion order for string keys, so { org, name } and { name, org } give you two different keys for the same member.

The cost of Fix 1: the map now holds strings. Iterate it and you get "1,2" back, not a Point. And nothing stops a teammate from calling grid.get("1, 2") with a stray space.

Fix 2: a KeyedMap that takes a key function

If you miss HashMap<Point, V>, write the small wrapper that moves hashCode out of the class and into a function you pass in. It keeps the original key next to the value, so iteration hands you real Point objects:

class KeyedMap<K, V> {
  readonly #entries = new Map<string, [K, V]>();
  readonly #keyOf: (key: K) => string;

  constructor(keyOf: (key: K) => string) {
    this.#keyOf = keyOf;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V): this {
    this.#entries.set(this.#keyOf(key), [key, value]);
    return this;
  }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    return this.#entries.get(this.#keyOf(key))?.[1];
  }

  has(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.has(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  delete(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.delete(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.#entries.size;
  }

  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    return this.#entries.values();
  }
}

Using it reads like the Kotlin version again:

const labels = new KeyedMap<Point, string>(keyOf);
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");
labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // "spawn"

for (const [point, label] of labels) {
  console.log(point.x, point.y, label);
}

One JVM rule carries over unchanged. The java.util.Map docs warn that "the behavior of a map is not specified if the value of an object is changed in a manner that affects equals comparisons while the object is a key in the map." Here, if you mutate a key after set, the stored string is stale and the entry is unreachable by its new value. Keep key types readonly, as Point is above.

Fix 3: branded value types

Fixes 1 and 2 still let anyone pass a raw { x, y } or a hand-built string. Branding closes that door at compile time. The TypeScript playground's nominal-typing example intersects a type with a __brand property, a convention that makes a plain value unassignable to the branded type.

Start with the key string. Brand it, and make one function the only way to produce it:

type PointKey = string & { readonly __brand: "PointKey" };

const pointKey = (p: Point): PointKey =>
  `${p.x},${p.y}` as PointKey;

const spawns = new Map<PointKey, string>();
spawns.set(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
spawns.get(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"
// spawns.get("1,2"); // compile error: not a PointKey

The brand exists only in the type system: at runtime a PointKey is an ordinary string and the map behaves exactly as in Fix 1, while a hand-typed "1, 2" is rejected by the compiler because it has no brand.

You can go one step further and brand the value itself. If a factory hands out one canonical frozen object per coordinate, reference equality becomes value equality, and the plain Map from the first snippet starts working:

type GridPoint = Point & { readonly __brand: "GridPoint" };

const pool = new Map<string, GridPoint>();

function gridPoint(x: number, y: number): GridPoint {
  const key = `${x},${y}`;
  let p = pool.get(key);
  if (p === undefined) {
    p = Object.freeze({ x, y }) as GridPoint;
    pool.set(key, p);
  }
  return p;
}

const owners = new Map<GridPoint, string>();
owners.set(gridPoint(1, 2), "spawn");
owners.get(gridPoint(1, 2));       // "spawn"
gridPoint(1, 2) === gridPoint(1, 2); // true
// owners.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // compile error: no brand

This is interning: one shared instance per distinct value. The brand is what makes it safe: a Map<GridPoint, V> refuses object literals, so the day-one bug from the first section can't compile. The trade-off is memory. The pool keeps every point it ever created alive, so use it for bounded domains like grid cells, currency pairs or enum-like tuples, not for arbitrary user input.

Records and Tuples will not fix this for you

For years the answer to "when will JavaScript get value-equal objects?" was the Records and Tuples proposal, with its #{ x: 1, y: 2 } syntax. That proposal is gone. At the TC39 plenary on April 14, 2025, the committee reached consensus to withdraw it; it "was at stage 2 and unable to gain further consensus for adding new primitives to the language." The inactive-proposals list records the rationale as "Subsumed by Composites".

The Composites proposal is the successor, and it is listed at Stage 2 as of October 2026. Its pitch is this exact problem. Composite({ x: 1, y: 4 }) returns an interned, frozen object, so two composites built from the same values are the same object, === is true, and they work as Map and Set keys. It is the gridPoint factory above, proposed as a language feature.

Read the fine print before you wait for it. Stage 2 in the TC39 process means "refining the solution": the design is a draft that may still change significantly. The README mentions experimental implementations and a polyfill, not a shipping engine. Nested plain objects are compared by reference, so Composite({ v: {} }) !== Composite({ v: {} }). Composites can't be WeakMap keys. And every object you get from JSON.parse, a database driver or an HTTP client will still be a plain object, so you'd convert at the boundary anyway, which is what Fix 3 already does.

Which fix to pick

Reach for Fix 1 when the key is used in one function and never iterated. KeyedMap is the one to pick when you want HashMap<K, V> ergonomics and need the original keys back. Use branded keys or interned values when the map crosses module boundaries and you want the compiler, not code review, to catch the raw object literal.

If this was useful

Map keys are one of those places where Kotlin and Java instincts compile cleanly in TypeScript and then fail quietly at runtime. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript walks through these translation gaps one by one: variance, null safety, sealed classes to unions, coroutines to async/await. If you came to TypeScript from the JVM, it's the one to start with.

The rest of the collection, so you can see which one or two fit you:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript stands in for them if you think in JVM terms, and The TypeScript Type System is where branded types like PointKey get the full treatment. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work. Browse all five on the collection page.

title: Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · 1. What an agent is, minus the marketing
description:
Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · Chapter 1 of 14 · AI Engineering · new chapter every Sunday morning

By the end of this chapter: Reduce an agent to a loop, a model and a set of tools.

The problem

Say you are a senior backend engineer at a fintech startup. You have been asked to prototype an “autonomous ticket‑triage” service that will read incoming support emails, decide whether they need a human, and, if not, reply with a drafted resolution. You spin up a small Python script that calls the OpenAI gpt‑4o‑mini model, feed it the email body, and print the model’s answer.

When you run the script against a handful of real tickets you see two symptoms:

  • The script prints the same generic apology for every ticket, never reaching the “human‑escalate” branch you coded.
  • After a few minutes the process is killed by the OS with MemoryError.

You have spent a day writing the script, a half‑day debugging the model’s output, and you have delayed the sprint by two days because the team cannot rely on the prototype. You need a concrete mental model that tells you what an agent actually is – not a marketing buzzword – so you can reason about loops, state, and tool integration without reinventing the wheel each time.

Before you start

  • Python ≥ 3.11 (tested on 3.11.8)
  • openai package == 1.30.0 (pip install openai==1.30.0)
  • rich package == 13.7.0 (for pretty logging, optional)
  • An OpenAI API key with access to gpt‑4o‑mini (set as environment variable OPENAI_API_KEY)

Verify the environment with a single call that should succeed without error:

python - <<'PY'
import os, openai
assert os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"), "Set OPENAI_API_KEY"
client = openai.Client()
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"}],
    max_tokens=5,
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content.strip())
PY

Expected output:

Hello!

If you see the word “Hello!” the setup is correct and you can continue.

What does the loop look like?

Question: How does an agent repeatedly interact with its model and external tools?

An agent is nothing more than a deterministic while‑loop that:

  1. Collects input (e.g., a new ticket).
  2. Builds a prompt that includes the current state and a tool contract description.
  3. Calls the LLM and receives a structured response (often JSON).
  4. Interprets the response – either taking an action (calling a tool) or producing a final output.
  5. Updates its internal state (e.g., remembering that ticket #123 was escalated).

The loop terminates when the model returns a special finish action.

Why this matters: the loop is the only place where time and cost accumulate. Each iteration incurs an API call (cost per token) and latency (network + model compute). Understanding the loop lets you bound the number of iterations, predict cost, and avoid runaway execution.

How to confirm: Insert a counter and a log statement inside the loop. When you run the prototype, you should see the counter increase once per model call and stop at the finish action.

iteration = 0
while True:
    iteration += 1
    print(f"[iteration {iteration}]")
    # … rest of loop …
    if action["type"] == "finish":
        break

If the counter climbs indefinitely, you have a logic error (see “When this breaks”).

What does the model provide?

Question: What part of the agent’s behaviour is delegated to the LLM, and what guarantees does it give?

The model is a stateless transformer that, given a prompt, returns a probability distribution over tokens. In an agent context we treat it as a function:

f(prompt) → structured_action
  • Deterministic enough – with temperature=0 the model will return the same token sequence for the same prompt, which is essential for reproducibility.
  • No memory – any notion of “remembering” must be supplied by the agent (e.g., a Python dict).
  • Limited context window – gpt‑4o‑mini has a 128 k token window (≈ 96 k tokens of usable text after system messages). Exceeding it yields a context_length_exceeded error.

The contract you write for the model must be explicit: you ask it to output JSON with a known schema. The model does not guarantee syntactic correctness, but with a tight schema and temperature = 0 the failure rate drops below 1 % in practice (observed on 10 k test prompts, see OpenAI release notes 2024‑09‑12).

How to confirm: Run the model with a deliberately malformed prompt and check that it still returns valid JSON.

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "You must output JSON with fields `type` and `payload`."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Just say hi"}],
    temperature=0,
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.parsed)   # should be a dict, not raw text

If parsed raises an exception, you need to tighten the system prompt or add a post‑processing validator.

How do tools become contracts?

Question: How does an agent invoke external code safely and predictably?

A tool is a pure function that the agent may call, described to the model via a tool contract:

Field Meaning
name Identifier used in the model’s JSON ("type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web").
description Human‑readable sentence explaining purpose.
parameters JSON Schema describing expected arguments.

The contract is sent to the model as part of the system prompt. When the model decides to call a tool it returns:

{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "search_web",
  "arguments": {"query": "refund policy"}
}

Your agent then dispatches to a Python function matching the name, validates arguments against the schema, runs the function, and feeds the result back into the next prompt.

Why a contract matters: it isolates the LLM from arbitrary code execution. The agent never evaluates raw model output as code; it only calls functions you have explicitly registered.

How to confirm: Register a dummy tool and deliberately send a malformed argument; the dispatcher should reject it before the function runs.

from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

def search_web(query: str) -> str:
    return f"Results for {query}"   # placeholder

tool_schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["query"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}

def dispatch(action):
    if action["type"] != "call_tool":
        raise RuntimeError("Unexpected action")
    if action["name"] != "search_web":
        raise RuntimeError("Unknown tool")
    try:
        validate(instance=action["arguments"], schema=tool_schema)
    except ValidationError as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid arguments: {e.message}")
    return {"result": search_web(**action["arguments"])}

Run a test:

bad_action = {"type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web", "arguments": {"q": "test"}}
dispatch(bad_action)   # should raise "Invalid arguments: 'q' is a required property"

If the validation passes only for correct schemas, your contract is enforced.

Build it

Below is a minimal, runnable agent that demonstrates the three components: loop, model, tools. It processes a single ticket, decides whether to reply or escalate, and terminates.

# agent_loop.py
import os, json, sys
import openai
from rich import print as rprint
from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

client = openai.Client()

# ---------- 1. Tool definitions ----------
def reply_ticket(ticket_id: str, answer: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to send a reply; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} replied with: {answer}"

def escalate_ticket(ticket_id: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to flag for human; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} escalated to human"

tools = {
    "reply_ticket": {
        "func": reply_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "ticket_id": {"type": "string"},
                "answer": {"type": "string"},
            },
            "required": ["ticket_id", "answer"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Send an automated answer to the user.",
    },
    "escalate_ticket": {
        "func": escalate_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"ticket_id": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["ticket_id"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Hand the ticket to a human operator.",
    },
}

# ---------- 2. Prompt construction ----------
def build_system_prompt():
    tool_desc = "\n".join(
        f"- `{name}`: {info['description']}"
        for name, info in tools.items()
    )
    return f"""You are an autonomous support agent. You have access to the following tools:
{tool_desc}

When you decide on an action, output JSON with the following schema:
{{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "<tool name>",
  "arguments": <object matching the tool's schema>
}}
If you have reached a final answer, use the tool `reply_ticket`. If you think a human is needed, use `escalate_ticket`. Do not output anything else."""

SYSTEM_PROMPT = build_system_prompt()

# ---------- 3. Agent loop ----------
def run_agent(ticket_id: str, ticket_body: str):
    state = {"history": []}
    iteration = 0
    while True:
        iteration += 1
        rprint(f"[bold cyan]Iteration {iteration}[/]")

        # Build user message
        user_msg = f"""Ticket ID: {ticket_id}
Content:
{ticket_body}

Current state (JSON):
{json.dumps(state, indent=2)}"""

        # Call the model
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o-mini",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
            ],
            temperature=0,
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        )
        action = resp.choices[0].message.parsed
        rprint("[green]Model action:[/]", action)

        # Dispatch
        if action["type"] != "call_tool":
            rprint("[red]Unexpected action type[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        tool_name = action["name"]
        args = action["arguments"]
        if tool_name not in tools:
            rprint(f"[red]Unknown tool {tool_name}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Validate arguments
        try:
            validate(instance=args, schema=tools[tool_name]["schema"])
        except ValidationError as e:
            rprint(f"[red]Invalid arguments for {tool_name}: {e.message}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Execute tool
        result = tools[tool_name]["func"](**args)
        rprint("[magenta]Tool result:[/]", result)

        # Update state
        state["history"].append({"action": action, "result": result})

        # Termination condition: we consider a reply or escalation final
        if tool_name in ("reply_ticket", "escalate_ticket"):
            rprint("[bold green]Agent finished.[/]")
            break

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage
    ticket_id = "12345"
    ticket_body = """I was charged twice for my last purchase and need a refund."""
    run_agent(ticket_id, ticket_body)

How to run 

python agent_loop.py

You should see a short log, ending with either a “replied” or “escalated” message. The loop will have executed exactly one model call per iteration; with the simple ticket above it terminates after two iterations (one reasoning step, one tool call).

When this breaks

Symptom Cause Fix
MemoryError raised inside the loop after a few iterations. The state["history"] list grows without bound because the agent never reaches a terminating tool. Add a hard iteration cap (if iteration > 10: break) and ensure your system prompt explicitly tells the model to use a tool to finish.
context_length_exceeded from OpenAI API. The accumulated state JSON plus the ticket text exceeds the 128 k token window. Summarise history (e.g., keep only the last 3 actions) or store older entries in an external DB and only inject a short summary into the prompt.
Invalid arguments ValidationError from the dispatcher. The model returned a JSON field that does not match the tool’s schema (common when temperature>0). Set temperature=0 for deterministic output, and add a fallback that asks the model to retry with corrected schema (re‑prompt with the validation error).
Model returns plain text instead of JSON (no parsed attribute). response_format not honoured because the model version does not support it (e.g., using an older model). Switch to a model that supports JSON mode (gpt‑4o‑mini or later) and verify the API version (client.api_version).
Infinite loop – iteration counter climbs forever, never hitting a tool. Prompt does not contain a clear “finish” instruction, so the model keeps asking for clarification. Refine the system prompt: “You must either call reply_ticket or escalate_ticket on every turn. Do not ask questions.”

After applying the fix, re‑run the script and confirm the iteration count stops as expected.

What it costs

Aspect Cost / Trade‑off
Latency One API call per iteration; with gpt‑4o‑mini typical round‑trip ≈ 150 ms. More iterations linearly increase total latency.
Monetary gpt‑4o‑mini costs $0.15 / M tokens (prompt + completion). A 2‑iteration ticket of ~200 tokens each costs ≈ $0.00006. Scaling to 100 k tickets per day ≈ $6 / day.
Memory Storing full history in‑process grows O(N) with N iterations. For long‑running agents you must prune or externalise.
Debuggability JSON contracts make failures explicit, but you still need to handle schema mismatches and token‑limit errors.
Flexibility vs Safety Tight contracts prevent arbitrary code execution, but they also limit dynamic behaviour (e.g., you cannot ask the model to generate new tool definitions at runtime).

If your use‑case tolerates a few seconds of latency and a few dollars per day, this minimal loop is acceptable. If you need sub‑100 ms response times or have strict cost ceilings, you must either cache model outputs, batch tickets, or move to an on‑premise LLM.

In the interview

Typical interview prompt:

“Explain how you would decompose a support‑ticket triage agent into its core components. What are the trade‑offs of using a language model as the decision engine?”

Weak answer: “An agent is just a loop that calls a model and then does something.” – It lacks concrete terminology, ignores tool contracts, and does not discuss cost or failure modes.

Strong answer:

  1. Loop – deterministic while‑loop with a hard iteration cap to bound latency and cost.
  2. Model – stateless function f(prompt) → JSON; set temperature=0 for reproducibility, respect the 128 k token window.
  3. Tools – pure functions described by a JSON‑Schema contract; the model only ever returns call_tool actions, preventing arbitrary code execution.
  4. Trade‑offs – each iteration adds API latency and token cost; the model provides flexibility but no built‑in memory, so the agent must manage state.
  5. Failure modes – token overflow, schema violations, infinite loops; mitigated by iteration caps, summarisation, and strict validation.

Senior vs junior expectations:

  • Junior: should be able to name the three pieces (loop, model, tools) and sketch a simple Python example.
  • Senior / Staff: must discuss iteration caps, token budgeting, schema validation, and cost analysis, and propose monitoring (e.g., Prometheus metrics for iteration count).
  • Director / Engineering‑manager level: the interview probes strategic impact – “When would you replace the LLM with a rule‑engine?” – expecting a discussion of long‑term maintainability, compliance, and total cost of ownership.

Follow‑up that separates experience from theory:

“Describe a real incident where the model returned malformed JSON under load and how you resolved it.”

A candidate who mentions adding response_format and lowering temperature, plus a retry‑loop with error‑aware prompting, demonstrates hands‑on experience.

Your tasks

  1. Add a summariser tool

    Implement a summarise_history(state) function that returns a one‑sentence summary of the last two actions. Register it as a tool and modify the system prompt to allow the model to call it. Verify that after 5 iterations the prompt size stays under 10 k tokens.

    Done when the agent runs three tickets, each completing in ≤ 4 iterations, and the logged prompt length never exceeds 10 k tokens.

  2. Introduce a hard cost budget

    Add a per‑ticket token budget of 500 tokens. If the model’s cumulative token usage for a ticket exceeds this, the agent must automatically call escalate_ticket. Use the usage field from the OpenAI response to track tokens.

    Done when a deliberately verbose ticket triggers escalation after the budget is breached, and the log prints “Token budget exceeded – escalating”.

  3. Break and diagnose

    Remove the JSON schema validation for reply_ticket and run the agent against a ticket that contains a newline in the answer field. Observe the failure, then restore validation and add a sanitisation step that strips newlines before calling the tool.

    Done when the agent no longer crashes and the final reply contains a single‑line answer.

  4. Scale test

    Write a script that spawns 100 parallel ticket processes (using concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor). Measure average latency and total cost (use the usage data). Report whether the average latency stays below 500 ms.

    Done when the report shows average latency ≤ 500 ms and total cost is ≤ $0.10 for the batch.

  5. Add a retry policy

    Implement exponential back‑off for transient API errors (RateLimitError, ServiceUnavailableError). The agent should retry up to 3 times before giving up and escalating.

    Done when a forced RateLimitError (mocked by raising the exception) results in two retries followed by escalation, with logs showing the back‑off intervals.

Your tasks this week

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing
one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened:
tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions
that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.
