title: Building a WhatsApp Interactive Button & List Message Handler in TypeScript
description:
Interactive messaging is one of the most effective ways to increase user engagement and eliminate typing friction on WhatsApp. Rather than forcing users to type out responses like "1", "YES", or "MENU", the official Meta WhatsApp Cloud API supports interactive buttons (quick replies, call-to-action buttons) and scrollable list menus (up to 10 options).

In this tutorial, we will build a production-ready, type-safe interactive message handler in TypeScript that parses incoming interactive payloads and routes them into conversational flows.

Understanding WhatsApp Interactive Payloads

When a recipient taps an interactive button or list item, Meta delivers an inbound webhook payload where the message type is set to "interactive".

Inside the interactive object, you will receive either:

  1. button_reply: Contains the id and title of the clicked quick-reply button.
  2. list_reply: Contains the id, title, and optional description of the chosen list row.

Step 1: Defining TypeScript Interfaces

Let's define the strict typings for incoming interactive webhook events:

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveListReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  description?: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveMessage {
  from: string;
  id: string;
  timestamp: string;
  type: 'interactive';
  interactive: {
    type: 'button_reply' | 'list_reply';
    button_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply;
    list_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveListReply;
  };
}

Step 2: Sending Interactive Quick-Reply Buttons

Here is how to construct and send an interactive button message using Axios and TypeScript:

import axios from 'axios';

interface ButtonPayload {
  to: string;
  bodyText: string;
  buttons: Array<{ id: string; title: string }>;
}

export async function sendInteractiveButtons({ to, bodyText, buttons }: ButtonPayload) {
  const url = `https://graph.facebook.com/v21.0/${process.env.WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID}/messages`;

  const payload = {
    messaging_product: 'whatsapp',
    recipient_type: 'individual',
    to,
    type: 'interactive',
    interactive: {
      type: 'button',
      body: { text: bodyText },
      action: {
        buttons: buttons.map(btn => ({
          type: 'reply',
          reply: { id: btn.id, title: btn.title }
        }))
      }
    }
  };

  const response = await axios.post(url, payload, {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.WHATSAPP_CLOUD_API_TOKEN}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json'
    }
  });

  return response.data;
}

Step 3: Dispatching to Conversational CRM and AI Handlers

Once the interactive webhook arrives at your server, you should route it based on the action ID:

export async function handleInteractiveReply(msg: WhatsAppInteractiveMessage) {
  const customerPhone = msg.from;
  const replyType = msg.interactive.type;
  const actionId = replyType === 'button_reply' 
    ? msg.interactive.button_reply?.id 
    : msg.interactive.list_reply?.id;

  console.log(`Received action ${actionId} from ${customerPhone}`);

  switch (actionId) {
    case 'ACTION_BOOK_DEMO':
      // Move customer into 'Demo Scheduled' stage in CRM
      break;
    case 'ACTION_TALK_HUMAN':
      // Trigger human agent assignment
      break;
    case 'ACTION_FAQ':
      // Pass inquiry to AI Knowledge Base
      break;
    default:
      console.warn('Unhandled interactive ID:', actionId);
  }
}

Enterprise Production Considerations

Managing raw button schemas, translation dictionaries, and state machines across hundreds of concurrent chats can quickly become complex.

Platforms like AI Soul provide a visual drag-and-drop conversational designer where interactive buttons, list menus, and AI fallbacks can be configured with zero boilerplate code. Incoming selections are automatically reflected inside the Conversational CRM and can trigger automated WhatsApp Drip Campaigns or AI Chatbot Solutions.

Conclusion

Interactive WhatsApp messages drastically improve completion rates compared to plain text replies. By modeling strict TypeScript contracts and decoupling interactive events from business logic, your integration remains reliable and maintainable.

title: Why I Want My AI Coding Assistant to Ask Before It Acts
description:
Most AI coding tools are built around one promise: speed. Type a prompt, get code, move on.

But after a while I noticed the speed was costing me something. The AI would edit files I didn't expect, delete things I still needed, or run a command I hadn't read. I'd spend the next hour undoing work I never approved.

The problem with "just do it" AI

When an AI agent has full permission to write, delete, and execute, every action is a small act of trust you didn't explicitly give. For a throwaway script that's fine. For a real codebase it's not.

The failure mode isn't dramatic. It's quiet:

  • A helper function gets "cleaned up" and something subtle breaks
  • A config file gets rewritten with slightly different values
  • A dependency gets bumped and nothing works the next morning

What I actually want

I want an assistant that treats my codebase like it belongs to someone else. That means:

  1. Ask before writing. Show me the change, let me approve it.
  2. Show diffs, not summaries. "I updated the auth logic" tells me nothing. A diff tells me everything.
  3. Checkpoint every step. If step 4 was wrong, I want to rewind to step 3 — not start over.
  4. Ask before running commands. A shell command is the most powerful thing an agent can do. It should be the most gated.

The trade-off is worth it

Yes, this is slower per action. But it's dramatically faster per outcome, because I'm not spending my afternoon fixing things I never agreed to.

If you're on Windows and want an AI editor that works this way, that's the idea behind Arcwright — it's free to start. But the principle applies to whatever tool you use: the AI should earn your trust one approved change at a time.

title: Why parsing real estate contracts with LLMs is ten times harder than tutorials claim
description:
When we started building the data pipeline for NovAsia (a property catalog and market tool for Southeast Asia), the plan looked embarrassingly simple on paper:

Grab property PDFs and developer contracts (SPAs).

Run them through a modern vision LLM.

Dump structured JSON into PostgreSQL.

Call it a day.

Two weeks in, the pipeline was completely broken. Here is why standard tutorial advice fell apart in production, and what we had to change to get reliable data out of scanned documents.

The stuff tutorials don't warn you about
Most LLM document parsing demos use crisp, born-digital PDFs with clean typography. In emerging markets like Cambodia and Thailand, reality looks very different:

Phone scans: Half the documents are multi-generation scans or photos taken with a phone camera under uneven lighting.

Dual-language layout: Khmer or Thai text mixed with English, often in adjacent table columns where line baselines don't match.

Physical stamps: Red rubber stamps, signatures, and notary seals placed directly over critical numbers (payment milestone dates, sinking fund fees, transfer taxes).

The 40-page prompt trap: If you shove a 35-page PDF into a long-context model and ask for "all fees and payment dates", it will extract 80% correctly and quietly hallucinate the rest with total confidence.

Three practical changes that fixed it
Instead of trying to find one magic model that does everything, we broke the pipeline down into smaller, boring steps:

  1. Aggressive image cleanup before text extraction

Before any model sees the page, we run basic OpenCV passes: deskewing, binarization, and contrast normalization. Removing phone-scan shadows did more for extraction accuracy than upgrading to a larger model tier.

  1. Section-level chunking with rigid schema validation

We stopped asking the model to parse whole documents at once. We chunk by specific section (e.g., "Schedule of Payments", "Maintenance Obligations") and enforce strict Pydantic schemas. If a field fails validation or falls outside expected bounds, the pipeline flags it for manual check rather than guessing.

  1. Treating tables and narrative text as separate problems

Vision models are great at answering qualitative questions ("under what conditions is the deposit refundable?"), but notoriously sloppy with columns in financial tables. We split table extraction into dedicated passes with explicit row-by-row checks.

The takeaway
If you're building with LLMs on messy, physical-world paperwork, raw context window size won't save you. Most of the reliability comes from image hygiene and strict schema boundaries.

Happy to trade notes if anyone else here is wrestling with noisy scans and table extraction.

title: Stop Squinting at Messy LESS: How to Beautify Your Stylesheets in Seconds
description:
We've all been there. You inherit a project, open styles.less, and it looks like someone typed the whole thing in a single breath. Nested rules collapsed onto one line, mixins with no spacing, variables jammed against their values.

You can still read it. But every minute you spend decoding formatting is a minute you're not fixing the actual bug.

In this post I'll walk through what LESS is (quickly), why formatting matters more than people admit, and how a LESS beautifier can clean up a file in seconds. I'll also show you real before and after examples so you can judge for yourself.

Quick refresher: what is LESS?

LESS is a CSS preprocessor. It extends plain CSS with features like variables, nesting, mixins, functions and operations, then compiles down to regular CSS that browsers understand. The official LESS documentation is the best place to go deep on the language itself.

A tiny taste:

@primary: #3b82f6;

.button {
  background: @primary;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }
}

That nesting and the darken() function are what make LESS pleasant to write. But they're also what make badly formatted LESS painful to read, because the structure is the logic.

Why formatting matters more in LESS than in plain CSS

In plain CSS, a messy file is annoying. In LESS, a messy file can actually hide bugs. Here's why:

  • Nesting depth is meaning. A rule nested one level too deep (or too shallow) changes the compiled selector. If indentation doesn't match nesting, you can't see the mistake.
  • Mixins and guards are easy to miss. A mixin call buried in a long line is easy to overlook when you're debugging why a style is applied.
  • Missing braces are brutal. One unclosed } in a deeply nested block can break compilation, and the error message often points somewhere unhelpful.
  • Code review gets noisy. If every developer formats differently, pull requests fill up with whitespace changes that hide the real ones.

Consistent formatting isn't about being picky. It's about making the structure of your styles visible at a glance.

What does a LESS beautifier actually do?

A beautifier takes your LESS code and rewrites its whitespace and layout without changing what it means. Typically that includes:

  • Consistent indentation for nested blocks
  • One declaration per line
  • Sensible spacing around colons, braces and operators
  • Line breaks between rules so blocks are easy to scan

Crucially, it should not change your logic. Variables, mixins, operations and nesting stay exactly as you wrote them. Only the presentation changes.

A real before and after

Here's the kind of LESS you might get from a quick copy-paste, a minified export, or a teammate in a hurry:

@primary:#3b82f6;@radius:6px;
.mixin-card(@pad:16px){padding:@pad;border:1px solid #eee}
.btn{color:#fff;background:@primary;border-radius:@radius;&:hover{background:darken(@primary,10%)}.icon{margin-right:4px}}
.card{.mixin-card(24px);h2{font-size:1.25rem;a{color:@primary}}}

Technically valid. Practically unreadable. Now the same code after running it through a beautifier:

@primary: #3b82f6;
@radius: 6px;

.mixin-card(@pad: 16px) {
  padding: @pad;
  border: 1px solid #eee;
}

.btn {
  color: #fff;
  background: @primary;
  border-radius: @radius;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }

  .icon {
    margin-right: 4px;
  }
}

.card {
  .mixin-card(24px);

  h2 {
    font-size: 1.25rem;

    a {
      color: @primary;
    }
  }
}

Same code, same output once compiled, but now you can see that .icon lives inside .btn, that .card calls the mixin, and that the link color sits three levels deep. That last one is a good reminder to watch your nesting depth, which you'd never notice in the single-line version.

How to use an online LESS beautifier

When I just need to clean up a snippet or a single file, I don't want to configure a toolchain. An online tool is the fastest path. I put together the LESS Beautifier on 99tools for exactly this situation. The workflow is simple:

  1. Paste your messy LESS into the input box.
  2. Run the beautifier.
  3. Copy the cleaned-up result back into your editor.

No install, no config file, no setup. It's handy when you're:

  • Reviewing LESS from a client or a legacy project
  • Cleaning a snippet before sharing it in a bug report or Stack Overflow question
  • Reading code that was minified or exported from another tool
  • Teaching or learning LESS and wanting readable examples

A quick tip: as with any online tool, don't paste proprietary code or anything containing secrets if your company policy says otherwise. For sensitive projects, use a local formatter instead (more on that below).

Beautifier vs. linter vs. compiler

These three get confused a lot, so here's the short version:

Tool What it does Changes your code?
Beautifier / formatter Fixes indentation, spacing and layout Whitespace only
Linter Flags problems and style violations Usually no (some auto-fix)
Compiler (lessc) Turns LESS into CSS Produces new output

A beautifier won't catch a typo in a variable name, and it won't tell you your nesting is too deep. Use it alongside a linter like Stylelint and your normal compile step, not instead of them.

Best practices for clean LESS

Formatting is the baseline. Here are a few habits that keep LESS maintainable once it's tidy:

  • Keep nesting to 3 levels or fewer. Deep nesting creates overly specific selectors that are painful to override.
  • Group variables at the top or in a dedicated file so theme changes happen in one place.
  • Name mixins clearly and keep them small and single-purpose.
  • Agree on one style as a team (2 spaces vs 4, blank lines between rules) and automate it so nobody argues in code review.
  • Run a formatter before committing, so diffs show real changes only.

When an online tool isn't the right fit

I want to be upfront: an online beautifier is great for quick jobs, but it isn't the answer to everything.

If your team formats code on every commit, you'll be better served by an automated local setup, such as Prettier, which supports LESS, wired into your editor or a pre-commit hook. And if you're starting a brand new project, it's also worth knowing that native CSS now supports nesting, which covers some of what people originally reached for preprocessors to do. The MDN guide to CSS nesting is a good overview if you're weighing your options.

That said, LESS is still used in plenty of real projects, and a lot of us are maintaining it for years to come. For those moments, having a quick way to make messy code readable is genuinely useful.

Wrapping up

Readable code isn't a luxury. It's how you spot bugs sooner, review faster, and onboard people without a lecture. A LESS beautifier takes about ten seconds and removes one whole category of friction.

If you have a messy .less file sitting around, try the LESS Beautifier on it and see how the structure changes. And if you've got your own tips for keeping LESS clean, or a horror story from a legacy stylesheet, drop it in the comments. I'd love to hear it.

Happy styling! 🎨

title: React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked
description:
I compiled a Next.js 16.4 app with no compiler, the Babel React Compiler and the experimental Rust one, then counted re-renders in Chrome. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes your components and hooks, so you no longer write most useMemo, useCallback and memo calls by hand. In Next.js it is one config flag, reactCompiler: true, stable since Next.js 16.0. Next.js 16.4 adds an experimental native Rust version.

I built a Next.js 16.4.2 test app and compiled it three ways: compiler off, the Babel compiler, and the Rust compiler. Then I counted re-renders in a real browser. With the compiler on, 20 clicks on a counter caused 0 list-row re-renders instead of 20,000, and scripting time fell from about 60 ms to about 7 ms. The Babel version more than doubled compile time. The Rust version cost about a quarter of a second and produced byte-identical output.

TL;DR: should I turn on the React Compiler in Next.js?

Yes, for most App Router projects. Turn it on with reactCompiler: true, run the compiler lint rules first, and try experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler if you build with Turbopack. In my test the compiler removed almost all wasted re-renders for free. It does not replace memo on list items whose parent re-renders, and it skips code that breaks the Rules of React.

Compiler off Babel compiler Rust compiler (experimental)
Config default reactCompiler: true + experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true
Extra install none babel-plugin-react-compiler none
Compile step (median, my app) 2.25 s 5.65 s 2.5 s
Full next build (median) 7.7 s 11.1 s 8.2 s
Client JS, gzip 178,305 B 181,295 B 181,295 B (identical to Babel)
Row re-renders, 20 counter clicks 20,000 0 0
Works with webpack yes yes no (Turbopack only)

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool that rewrites your components so they cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders, and recompute them only when their inputs change. The React Compiler v1.0 announcement calls it "a build-time tool that optimizes your React app through automatic memoization." Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025.

It works with React 17 and later, and on React Native. The introduction docs say that in most cases its memoization "will be as precise, or moreso, than what you may have written." Meta reports that in the Meta Quest Store, "initial loads and cross-page navigations improve by up to 12%, while certain interactions are more than 2.5× faster."

You keep writing plain components. The compiler does the bookkeeping at build time.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js 16?

Install the Babel plugin and set the top-level reactCompiler option in next.config.ts. It moved out of experimental in Next.js 16.0. Next.js does not run Babel on every file: per the reactCompiler docs, "Next.js uses a custom SWC optimization that only applies the React Compiler to relevant files—like those with JSX or React Hooks."

npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler@1.0.0

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

That is the whole setup. New projects can also pick the compiler in the create-next-app prompts.

Can I enable it only for some components?

Yes. Set compilationMode: "annotation" and add the "use memo" directive to the components or hooks you want compiled. This is a good way to start on a large codebase. Add "use no memo" to a component to opt it out in the default mode while you fix it.

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: { compilationMode: "annotation" },
};

export default function Dashboard() {
  "use memo";
  // ...
}

What is the Rust React Compiler in Next.js?

It is a native Rust port of the React Compiler that runs inside Turbopack instead of through Babel in Node.js. It was merged into the React repo in June 2026 (PR #36173) and added to Next.js 16.3 as an experimental option. The Next.js 16.4 release added a fast check that skips files that don't need compiling.

Next.js 16.4 says the Turbopack team's memory changes "reduced the React Compiler's memory usage by 30% and compile time by 15%." To turn it on:

// next.config.ts
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
  experimental: {
    turbopackRustReactCompiler: true,
  },
};

From the turbopackRustReactCompiler docs:

  • It "requires reactCompiler to be enabled". It picks the implementation but doesn't switch the compiler on.
  • It works only with Turbopack. "Using it with webpack will throw an error."
  • You do not need babel-plugin-react-compiler installed.

How I tested it

I wanted numbers from a real Next.js app, not a toy counter, so I measured both build cost and runtime behaviour.

  1. App: Next.js 16.4.2, React 19.3.1, Turbopack, Node 24, on an 8-vCPU Linux box. The client dashboard has 1,000 product rows, a filter input, a counter, a stats panel and one deliberately "bad" component. Nothing uses useMemo or useCallback.
  2. Build load: 300 more generated client components on a /gen route, so compile time is measurable.
  3. Three builds: one next.config.ts read an RC_MODE variable (off, babel, rust). I deleted .next before every build, so the Turbopack disk cache never helped, and ran 5 rounds. The tables use the median of rounds 2-5. Round 1 was a cold start: 3.3 s, 12.6 s and 2.9 s of compile time.
  4. Re-renders: each component calls a tiny useRenderCount(name) hook that increments a counter in an effect. Puppeteer drove headless Chrome against next start, and Chrome's ScriptDuration metric measured JavaScript time. I ran each scenario 3 times, and the render counts were identical every run. 
// lib/useRenderCount.ts
"use client";
import { useEffect } from "react";

export function useRenderCount(name: string) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const r = (window.__renders ??= {});
    r[name] = (r[name] ?? 0) + 1;
  });
}

The counter lives in an effect on purpose. Writing to a global during render breaks the Rules of React, and the compiler would skip that component.

Does the React Compiler reduce re-renders?

Yes, dramatically for state that doesn't touch a component's props. Clicking the counter 20 times re-rendered every component on the page with the compiler off: 20,000 row renders. With either compiler, only the two components that actually use the count re-rendered. Rows, stats, the list and even the uncompilable component were all skipped.

Scenario (renders counted) Off Compiler Compiler + memo(Row)
20 counter clicks: Row renders 20,000 0 0
20 counter clicks: JS time 55-62 ms 6-7 ms 6-7 ms
Type "99" in filter: Row renders 290 290 0
Select 10 rows: Row renders 10,000 10,000 19
Select 10 rows: JS time 26-31 ms 14 ms 8 ms

The Babel and Rust builds produced exactly the same render counts, which you would expect from identical output.

The click case is the common one in real apps. Some unrelated state changes high in the tree, and with the compiler off everything below it re-renders.

Why do list rows still re-render with the compiler?

Because the compiler memoizes inside components. It does not turn every component into React.memo. When ProductList must re-render, for example because selectedId changed, its .map() creates new <Row> elements and each row runs. The compiled Row is cheaper to run, since its internals are cached, so JS time still halved from about 28 ms to 14 ms. But all 1,000 rows rendered on each click.

Wrapping the row in memo() fixed it. Selecting 10 rows then rendered 19 rows (1 + 9×2: the newly selected row and the previously selected one).

import { memo } from "react";

function Row({ item, selected, onSelect }: RowProps) {
  return (
    <li style={{ fontWeight: selected ? 700 : 400 }} onClick={() => onSelect(item.id)}>
      {item.name}
    </li>
  );
}

const MemoRow = memo(Row); // still worth it for big lists

Without the compiler, the same memo(Row) did nothing: still 10,000 renders. The parent passes onSelect={(id) => setSelectedId(id)} as a new function every render, which breaks memo's prop comparison. The compiler caches that callback automatically. That pairing is what makes memo reliable: compiler for stable props, memo for big lists.

What does the compiled code look like?

The compiler adds a small cache array per component (_c(n) from react/compiler-runtime) and wraps each computation in an "inputs changed?" check. This is what the Babel plugin produced for my Stats component, which totals prices on every render in the source:

function Stats(t0) {
  const $ = _c(10);
  const { items } = t0;
  let onSale, t1, t2, t3;
  if ($[0] !== items) {
    const total = items.reduce(_temp, 0);
    onSale = items.filter(_temp2).length;
    // ...store results in $[1..4]
  } else {
    onSale = $[1]; // reuse cached values
    // ...
  }
  // the returned <p> is cached the same way
}

The expensive reduce and filter run only when items changes. This is the same thing you would do by hand with useMemo, applied to every value in every component.

Does the React Compiler slow down next build?

The Babel version does, the Rust version barely does. In my 300-component app the compile step went from 2.25 s with the compiler off to 5.65 s with Babel, about 2.5 times longer. The Rust compiler took 2.5 s, only 0.25 s more than no compiler at all. Full next build wall time was 7.7 s, 11.1 s and 8.2 s.

Both compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript: the same chunk hashes and the same sizes. Compiled code is larger, because every component now carries cache checks. Raw client JS grew by 213,496 bytes (+28.9%), but after gzip the difference was only 2,990 bytes (+1.7%). The cache checks are repetitive and compress well.

These are numbers from one small app on one machine. Your ratio will differ with codebase size, but the direction should hold: Babel adds noticeable compile time and Rust mostly removes it.

Which code does the React Compiler skip?

Components that break the Rules of React. The compiler checks your code, and if it can't prove a component is safe to memoize it leaves that component uncompiled instead of guessing. The build does not fail. My Bailout component reads and writes ref.current during render, and the Babel plugin's logger reported CompileError: Cannot access refs during render.

export function Bailout({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const renders = useRef(0);
  renders.current += 1; // breaks the rules: ref mutation during render
  return <aside>{label} (render #{renders.current})</aside>;
}

Notice from the render table that Bailout was still skipped on counter clicks. The compiled parent cached the <Bailout label="legacy widget" /> element, so React never re-rendered it. Code the compiler skips simply misses its own internal optimizations. It doesn't break.

How do I find code the compiler can't optimize?

Use the latest eslint-plugin-react-hooks (7.x today). Since React Compiler 1.0, the compiler-powered lint rules ship in the plugin's recommended preset: refs, purity, immutability, set-state-in-effect, set-state-in-render, globals, static-components, incompatible-library and more. You don't need the separate eslint-plugin-react-compiler package any more.

// eslint.config.mjs
import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";

export default [
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
];

On my test app, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 flagged the Bailout ref access three times. It also caught a real bug pattern in my generator: 300 components called setState inside useEffect. The rule message says this "can trigger cascading renders". I fixed the generator before benchmarking.

Run the linter before turning on the compiler, fix what it reports, and treat the warnings as a list of components that won't be optimized.

Step by step: adopt the React Compiler in an existing Next.js app

  1. Upgrade. Use Next.js 16.x and React 19.x. The compiler also supports React 17 and 18 through react-compiler-runtime.
  2. Lint first. Add reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended, run eslint . and fix or note the errors.
  3. Install and enable. Run npm i -D babel-plugin-react-compiler, then set reactCompiler: true. On a large app, start with compilationMode: "annotation" and add "use memo" to hot paths.
  4. Try Rust on Turbopack. Add experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true and compare next build times.
  5. Test behaviour. Run your end-to-end tests. Watch effects that depend on memoized values.
  6. Keep memo on big lists. The compiler stabilizes props. memo still decides whether a list item renders.
  7. Remove manual memoization slowly. The React team advises keeping existing useMemo and useCallback or testing carefully before removing them, because removal can change compilation output.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback?

Not in a hurry. For new code, write plain components and let the compiler memoize. In existing code, leave useMemo and useCallback alone until you have tests. The React docs say the hooks "can continue to be used with React Compiler as an escape hatch", for example to keep an effect dependency stable. Removing them can change what the compiler outputs.

Common React Compiler mistakes in Next.js

  • Expecting it to fix big lists alone. It doesn't add React.memo to children. Keep memo() on heavy list items.
  • Mutating during render. Ref writes, global writes or prop mutation make the compiler skip the component, with no build error.
  • Using the Rust flag with webpack. turbopackRustReactCompiler throws with webpack. Remove it or switch to Turbopack.
  • Enabling it without the lint rules. You won't know which components were skipped.
  • Benchmarking with a warm cache. Turbopack's build disk cache hides compile cost. Delete .next between comparison builds.
  • Expecting Server Component wins. The compiler targets components that re-render on the client. Server Components render once per request.

If you are on Next.js 16.4, pair this with the other new client-side features in my guides to React View Transitions in Next.js and the use cache directive.

Related: the React Compiler lint rules from eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7 don't all survive a linter switch. Oxlint ported 12 of 14, Biome none; see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint.

Related: wondering whether to leave Next.js entirely? In TanStack Start vs Next.js I built the same app in both: TanStack Start shipped 111 KB of gzipped JS to Next.js 16.4's 139 KB and built in 1.26 s vs 4.86 s.

Key takeaways

  • React Compiler 1.0 automatically memoizes components and hooks at build time; in Next.js 16 enable it with reactCompiler: true.
  • In my Next.js 16.4.2 test, 20 counter clicks caused 0 row re-renders with the compiler versus 20,000 without, and JS time fell from about 60 ms to 7 ms.
  • The compiler does not make children React.memo; list rows still re-rendered until I wrapped them in memo(), which then cut 10,000 renders to 19.
  • The Babel compiler made the compile step 2.5x longer (2.25 s to 5.65 s); the experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 s.
  • Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript; gzipped size grew only 1.7%.
  • experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler needs reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack, and needs no Babel plugin.
  • Run eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules first; components that break the Rules of React are silently skipped.

FAQ

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes components and hooks. It rewrites your code to cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders and recompute them only when inputs change, replacing most manual useMemo, useCallback and memo calls. Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025, and it supports React 17 and later.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js?

Install babel-plugin-react-compiler as a dev dependency and set reactCompiler: true at the top level of next.config.ts. The option became stable in Next.js 16.0, moving out of experimental. Next.js applies the compiler only to files with JSX or hooks, using an SWC pre-check, to keep build cost down. Use compilationMode: 'annotation' to opt in per component.

What is turbopackRustReactCompiler?

It is an experimental Next.js option, added in 16.3, that runs the native Rust port of the React Compiler inside Turbopack instead of the Babel plugin. It requires reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack and throws with webpack, and needs no babel-plugin-react-compiler install. In my test it compiled in 2.5 seconds versus 5.65 seconds for Babel.

Does the React Compiler make next build slower?

With the Babel plugin, noticeably. In my 300-component Next.js 16.4.2 app the compile step went from 2.25 seconds to 5.65 seconds, and full next build from 7.7 to 11.1 seconds. The experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 seconds to compile and 8.2 seconds in total, so most of the cost disappeared.

Does the React Compiler replace React.memo?

Not for list items. The compiler memoizes inside each component and caches child elements, but when a parent re-renders and maps over data, every child still runs. In my test, selecting a row re-rendered all 1,000 rows with the compiler alone. Wrapping the row in memo() cut 10,000 renders to 19, because the compiler kept its props stable.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback when using the React Compiler?

Not right away. Write new code without them, but keep existing calls until you have tests, because the React team notes that removing them can change compilation output. The hooks still work as an escape hatch, for example to keep an effect dependency stable so the effect doesn't fire repeatedly when its inputs haven't meaningfully changed.

What happens if my code breaks the Rules of React?

The compiler skips that component and leaves it unoptimized; the build does not fail. In my test, a component that mutated ref.current during render produced a 'Cannot access refs during render' compile error in the logger and was left as written. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules report the same problems in your editor.

Does the React Compiler increase bundle size?

Slightly. Compiled components carry cache checks, so in my test raw client JavaScript grew 28.9 percent, by 213,496 bytes, but gzipped size grew only 1.7 percent, by 2,990 bytes, because the generated code compresses well. The Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical bundles in Next.js 16.4.2.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: RingBreaker: An AI Agent That Breaks UPI Mule Rings on FalkorDB
description:
RingBreaker is an AI agent that investigates UPI mule rings inside a FalkorDB graph, freezes the ring only after a human approves, and then proves with one more graph query that no money path is left.

  • Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com
  • Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker
  • Built for: Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (FalkorDB), Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data. Solo, built Oct 15 to 18, 2026.
  • The loop in one line: investigate → verdict → human approval → freeze → verify ("13 open routes, then 0").

The problem

A scam victim pays a "KYC update" fee over UPI. Within hours the money has hopped through four accounts and is gone.

  • Each hop looks harmless. A Rs 8,000 transfer between two accounts is normal on its own.
  • The pattern lives in the connections. Brand-new accounts, minimal KYC, shared phones and devices, money fanning in and out within minutes.
  • Tables hide it. Following money four hops deep in SQL means four self-joins, and the query has to know the shape in advance.
  • Most fraud demos stop at "flagged". Nobody acts on the alert, and nobody checks that the action worked.

In simple words

Think of a bucket brigade passing stolen water down a line of people. You could question each person on their own, and each one would only say "I passed a bucket."

  • RingBreaker looks at the whole line at once: who passed to whom, who stands on the same spot (a shared phone or device), and where the water ends up.
  • It then asks a person: "Remove these five from the line?"
  • After they say yes, it checks again that no bucket can still reach the end. That last check is the point of the project.

The stack

  • FalkorDB: the only datastore. Accounts, transactions, devices, alerts, verdicts and the audit trail all live in one graph. Docker locally, FalkorDB Cloud in production.
  • Node.js + Express: the API, the agent loop and the tools, using the official falkordb client.
  • Groq (groq-sdk) with function calling: openai/gpt-oss-120b as the main model, qwen/qwen3.8-27b as a fallback when the daily quota runs out.
  • React + Vite + react-force-graph-2d: the three-pane dashboard and the live graph canvas.
  • Server-Sent Events: each tool call streams to the browser as it happens.
  • Render: one Docker image serves the API and the built UI on a single URL.

The agent reaches FalkorDB only through read-only tools; the single write path runs from the API after a person approves.

How it actually works, step by step

  1. You click an alert, for example a victim complaint: "paid ~25,000 for a fake KYC update; money moved on within hours."
  2. The API starts the agent and streams every step over SSE. The agent picks graph tools (get_alert, money_trail, fan_stats, shared_identity, expand_ring and others). Each one runs a parameterized Cypher query.
  3. The canvas lights up the exact nodes and edges each query touched. A "Show Cypher" toggle reveals the query behind every step.
  4. The agent submits a structured JSON verdict: ring_confirmed, suspicious or benign, ring members with roles (victim, layer, collector, cashout), evidence citing graph facts, and recommended freezes.
  5. The server validates the verdict and saves it as a Case node in the graph.
  6. You review the evidence, untick anything you disagree with, type your name and press Approve freeze.
  7. The server freezes the approved accounts, writes an audit edge for each, re-runs the verify query and shows the result, for example 13 open routes → 0. The alert then moves to Closed.

The agent proposes; a person decides; the graph proves it.

The dashboard: alert queue with live status on the left, the graph canvas in the middle, the agent trace on the right, and the four-stage tracker in the header.

Mid-investigation on ALT002 (Ring B, the device farm). Every account, device and phone the agent touched is on the canvas, with its latest step glowing. The trace shows each tool call, its arguments and timing, and the switch to the fallback model when the daily quota ran out.

The graph and the agent's tools

One FalkorDB graph, ring, with 7,847 nodes and 25,962 edges, all synthetic and generated from a seeded random generator so every demo is reproducible.

  • Nodes: Account (1,911), VPA, Device, Phone, Alert (7), plus Case nodes written at run time.
  • Edges: SENT (20,007, one per transaction, with amount and ts), USES_DEVICE, LINKED_PHONE, HAS_VPA, ABOUT, and the audit edges INCLUDES {role} and ACTION {type, ts, approved_by}.
  • Transactions are edges, not nodes. A trail of N transfers is an N-hop path, so -[:SENT*1..4]-> answers "where did the money go?" in one query.
  • Planted scenarios:
    • Ring A, a layering chain: 4 victims → 3 first-layer mules → 2 second-layer mules → 1 collector → 1 cash-out, with amounts split into chunks minutes apart.
    • Ring B, a device farm: 6 accounts on 2 devices and 1 phone, each collecting small payments from many senders, then sweeping to one account.
    • Ring C, a decoy: 3 accounts on a shared device but with no money link. The right answer is "suspicious, monitor", not a freeze.
    • Benign look-alikes: a busy merchant with high fan-in, and a family sharing one phone. Neither may be flagged.
  • Tools the model can call (read-only):
Tool What it asks the graph
money_trail Follow money forward or backward up to N hops, with all(r IN relationships(p) WHERE r.ts >= $since) on every edge
shared_identity Who else uses this device or phone: `(a)-[:USES_DEVICE\
{% raw %}fan_stats In/out degree, totals and pass-through ratio
expand_ring Grow a candidate ring along money and identity links at once (UNION ALL)
account_profile Age, KYC level, and how many accounts share each device or phone
get_alert The alert and its target account
run_readonly_cypher A guarded free-form fallback for anything else
  • Every tool starts from an indexed lookup (Account.id, Device.id, Phone.number, VPA.handle, Alert.id, Case.id). Queries take 5 to 30 ms locally and 230 to 470 ms from Render to FalkorDB Cloud.
  • Every tool call emits a trace event: tool, arguments, the exact Cypher, a one-line summary, and the node and edge IDs it touched. The canvas highlights from those IDs.

Act, then prove it

Flagging is half the job. RingBreaker acts on the verdict and then checks its own work.

  • The model cannot freeze anything. Action tools (create_case, freeze_account, verify_cutoff, close_case, generate_report) are never offered to the LLM. Only the approval API calls them.
  • The approval gate is one Cypher statement. It freezes an account only if the case proposed it and it is still active, and writes the audit edge in the same query: 
MATCH (c:Case {id: $case_id}), (a:Account {id: $account_id})
WHERE $account_id IN c.proposed_freezes AND a.status = 'active'
SET a.status = 'frozen'
CREATE (c)-[:ACTION {type: 'freeze', ts: $now, approved_by: $approved_by, reason: $reason}]->(a)
  • Verify counts open money routes into the ring's end account that avoid every frozen account: 
MATCH p = (src:Account)-[:SENT]->(m:Account)-[:SENT*0..5]->(t:Account)
WHERE m.id IN $ring AND t.id IN $terminals AND NOT src.id IN $ring
  AND none(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n.status = 'frozen')
RETURN count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id]) AS routes
  • It counts distinct routes, not raw paths. Each transaction is its own edge, so split payments multiply paths: Ring A has 1,488 raw paths but 13 distinct routes. After the freeze: 0.
  • A leak check stops the proof from fooling itself. It counts ring money that already reached an active account the case never named. The cut-off counts as verified only when routes and leaks are both 0.
  • Alerts close themselves from graph state. Each alert shows Open, Awaiting approval, Closed, Needs review, Monitoring or Dismissed, derived from its latest case.
  • A report is generated from graph data only: accounts and roles, the agent's evidence, every approved action with approver and time, and the live verify result.

Safety: an agent that writes Cypher on untrusted data

The agent reads text it cannot trust and writes queries, so safety lives in code, not in the prompt.

  • Reads physically cannot write. Every read tool runs as GRAPH.RO_QUERY, so FalkorDB itself refuses any write. A test bypasses our own guard and confirms the database still blocks it.
  • Free-form Cypher passes a guard (guard.js): it rejects CREATE, MERGE, DELETE, SET, REMOVE, DROP, CALL, LOAD, FOREACH and multiple statements, enforces a LIMIT of at most 100, and runs with a server-side timeout.
  • Every query is parameterized. Values arrive as $parameters, never spliced into query text, including the seed script.
  • Verdicts are grounded. The validator rejects ring members no tool returned, freezes on victims or non-members, and any freeze on a verdict weaker than ring_confirmed. An invalid verdict gets one retry.
  • Graph text is data. Holder names, UPI handles and alert text are marked untrusted in the system prompt. Even a successful prompt injection could not freeze anything: the model has no action tools.
  • Hard limits per run: 10 model steps, a 10-minute timeout, a 120K-token cap, and one investigation at a time.
  • Public demo hygiene: investigations and approvals need a demo passcode, resetting the graph needs an admin secret, both compared in constant time. No secrets in the repo.

Built to run on a free tier

The whole project runs on Groq's free tier: about 8K tokens per minute and 200K tokens per day, per model. The agent loop is designed around that.

  • Compact tool results. Tools return summaries and distinct transactions, not hundreds of near-duplicate paths.
  • Context trimming. Once the prompt passes about 5.5K tokens, older tool results shrink to their one-line summaries.
  • Model fallback mid-run. When the main model's daily quota runs out, the loop switches to the fallback model and continues from the same step. The trace shows the switch.
  • Self-adjusting requests. If a model rejects a request as too large (Qwen allows 7K input and 1K output tokens per minute), the loop trims the context or lowers the output cap and redoes the step.
  • Malformed tool calls are retried with a hint to send shorter arguments, so a truncated verdict does not fail the same way twice.
  • The report is a template, not LLM prose. It costs zero tokens and can only contain facts that are in the graph.
  • Cost of one investigation: roughly 18K to 35K tokens and 1 to 5 minutes, almost all of it waiting on rate limits. The graph queries are a rounding error.

What fought back

  • The proof could fool itself. In the final test the agent stopped at the collector and missed the cash-out account, which still held Rs 65,202. Verify still said "11 routes → 0". The route count only looks at paths through the case's own members, so freezing everything proposed always gives 0. The fix: a leak check that asks whether ring money already sits in an active account the case never named. That run now reads "Routes cut, but money leaked" instead of a false pass.
  • One transaction, one edge, hundreds of paths. Split payments multiply paths fast: 1,488 raw paths for 13 real routes. Counting distinct sequences of account IDs (count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id])) made the number something a reviewer can read.
  • Some things cannot be Cypher parameters. Edge direction, variable-length bounds and labels cannot be $params. money_trail pre-builds one query per (direction, hops) pair from constants, so user input never becomes query text.
  • Epoch milliseconds vs date strings. The agent compared ts to '2026-10-07' in free-form Cypher and got empty results. The tool description now says times are epoch ms.
  • Free-tier walls. A daily quota that runs out mid-investigation, a fallback model with 1K output tokens per minute, and verdicts cut off mid-word (tool_use_failed). Each became a handled case in the loop, with a test that replays the real error.
  • Prompting is not free. Telling the agent to also trace forward from the collector raised Ring A recall from 0.57 to 0.71. A stricter "run both trails" rule made it loop until the step cap, so it was dropped. Every prompt change was measured, not assumed.

What it does now

npm run eval runs the agent on all 7 alerts and scores it against a ground-truth file. 7 of 7 verdicts correct, 0 unsafe freezes: no victim, merchant or family account was ever recommended for freezing.

Alert Scenario Expected Got Freeze precision / recall
ALT001 Ring A complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 0.71
ALT002 Ring B complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT003 Ring B fan-in ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT004 Ring C decoy suspicious suspicious, no freeze
ALT005 Merchant benign benign
ALT006 Family benign benign
ALT007 Noise benign benign
  • Live run on the deployed site: Ring A's complaint named all 8 accounts (the victim plus all 7 mules, including the cash-out); after approval, verify went from 13 open routes to 0 with no leak, and the alert closed.
  • 53 automated tests: the Cypher guard, the read-only backstop, the approval gate, verify and the leak check, the passcode, verdict validation, and every free-tier failure mode, replayed with a fake LLM client so they cost no tokens.
  • The dashboard: an alert queue with live status, the graph canvas with role-colored rings and a step-by-step HUD, the agent trace with each step's Cypher, the verdict card with a confidence meter and run stats, and a before/after proof card.

The live demo after approval: Ring A frozen (red) with roles on the canvas, each proposed freeze and its reason, and the proof card: 13 open routes before the freeze, 0 after, no leak.

Who this is for

Fraud and risk teams at banks, payment apps and UPI providers who already get alerts but spend hours tracing each one by hand. It is also a pattern for anyone building agents that act on data: let the model read and recommend, keep writes behind a human and a single audited query, and end every action with a query that proves it worked.

What I learned

  • Graphs make the question short. "Where did this money go, four hops out, after Tuesday?" is one Cypher pattern, not four joins.
  • Put safety in the database, not the prompt. GRAPH.RO_QUERY is a stronger guarantee than any instruction to "only read".
  • Verify the verifier. A proof that only checks the agent's own case can pass while money sits in an account the agent missed.
  • Give the model less, not more. Compact tool results, one-line summaries and a short required checklist beat long instructions on a small token budget.
  • Measure every prompt change. A rule that sounded better made the agent worse; only the eval showed it.

What's next

  • Upstream leak detection: flag a missed mule that feeds money into the ring, not only one that receives from it.
  • Streaming ingestion: real-time transaction feeds into FalkorDB, so investigations start the moment a pattern appears.
  • Real integrations: bank and UPI freeze APIs behind the same approval gate.

Try it

Needs Node.js 22.9+, Docker and a free Groq API key.

git clone https://github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker && cd ringbreaker
cp .env.example .env               # add GROQ_API_KEY
docker compose up -d               # FalkorDB on :6379, Browser on http://localhost:3000
(cd server && npm install) && (cd web && npm install)
npm run generate && npm run seed   # seeded synthetic graph into FalkorDB
(cd server && npm start)           # API on http://localhost:8080
(cd web && npm run dev)            # UI on http://localhost:5173

Open the UI, click ALT001, approve the freeze, and watch the open routes drop to 0.

Disclosures: all data is synthetic; no real people, accounts or UPI handles. Built with help from an AI coding assistant; I reviewed the code and can explain every part of the architecture and its safety model.

Built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents by FalkorDB, Track 01. Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com · Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker

title: Portfolio v2.0: three themes, one headline, and every number checked against the repo
description:
My portfolio just hit v2.0. It's a Django 5.2 + DRF API with a React 19 build embedded and served by Django, PostgreSQL on Neon, deployed on PythonAnywhere.

The visible change is a theme switcher in the top-right corner with three palettes: Cian (the default, a midnight background with a cyan-to-violet aurora), Violeta (light) and Ámbar (warm and sober). The less visible change taught me more: making sure my portfolio, my CV and my LinkedIn tell the same story with the same numbers.

👉 Live: nicolasandrescl.pythonanywhere.com · backend · frontend

Part 1 — A theme system that never re-renders React

Themes as plain data

Every component was already styled with Stitches tokens ($accent, $surface, $syntaxFunction…). So I didn't need a ThemeProvider. A theme is just a set of token values, written as plain data with no Stitches import:

// src/themes/palettes.js (trimmed)
export const THEMES = [
  {
    key: 'cian',
    label: 'Cian',
    dark: true,
    colors: { background: '#070b14', accent: '#22d3ee', onAccent: '#04111a', /* … */ },
    fonts: { heading: "'Space Grotesk', 'Segoe UI', sans-serif", /* … */ },
  },
  // violeta, ambar …
];

Keeping it free of Stitches means I can test it without a styling runtime. This test catches the most common theming bug, a theme that quietly inherits a color from another one because it forgot to define a token:

it('every theme defines the same tokens', () => {
  const base = getTheme(DEFAULT_THEME);
  const colorKeys = Object.keys(base.colors).sort();
  THEMES.forEach((t) => {
    expect(Object.keys(t.colors).sort()).toEqual(colorKeys);
  });
});

One class on <html>

Each palette becomes a Stitches createTheme class, and switching themes just swaps a class on <html>:

export const themes = Object.fromEntries(
  THEMES.map((t) => [t.key, createTheme(themeClass(t.key), { colors: t.colors, fonts: t.fonts })]),
);
Object.values(themes).forEach((t) => t.className); // ← more on this line below

export function applyTheme(key, root = document.documentElement) {
  const theme = getTheme(key);
  THEMES.forEach((t) => root.classList.remove(themeClass(t.key)));
  root.classList.add(themeClass(theme.key));
  root.dataset.theme = theme.key;
  root.style.colorScheme = theme.dark ? 'dark' : 'light';
  // …and updates <meta name="theme-color"> for the mobile browser bar
}

Why <html> and not a wrapper <div>? Radix renders dropdowns in a Portal attached to <body>. If the theme lived on a div inside the app, every menu would open with the wrong colors.

The switcher itself is a Radix DropdownMenu with a RadioGroup. That gives menuitemradio roles, keyboard navigation, Escape to close and focus management for free. The choice is stored in localStorage, wrapped in try/catch: private mode or blocked storage falls back to Cian instead of breaking the site.

No flash on reload

If you apply the saved theme in a useEffect, every reload paints the default theme first and then switches. The fix is a tiny inline script that runs before React loads:

<style>
  html { background: #070b14; color-scheme: dark; }
  html[data-theme="violeta"] { background: #fbf8ff; color-scheme: light; }
  html[data-theme="ambar"] { background: #130d0a; }
</style>
<script>
  (function () {
    var keys = ['cian', 'violeta', 'ambar'];
    var key = 'cian';
    try { key = localStorage.getItem('portafolio-theme') || key; } catch (e) {}
    if (keys.indexOf(key) === -1) key = 'cian';
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = key;
    document.documentElement.classList.add('theme-' + key);
  })();
</script>

I verified it with Playwright: save Ámbar, reload, screenshot immediately. Even the loading spinner was already amber.

Four traps I stepped on

1. Stitches injects themes lazily. A createTheme rule only reaches the stylesheet when something reads theme.className. My inline script added theme-ambar to <html> before any component had touched that theme, so the class existed but styled nothing. That's the reason for the "useless-looking" line above: reading .className for every theme when the module loads forces the injection.

2. Django wasn't serving Vite's index.html. The production page comes from Django's templates/index.html, which resolves the hashed assets from Vite's manifest. Anything I added to Vite's <head> (the anti-flash script, Google Fonts) would never reach production. It now lives in both files, and the keys have to match.

3. A light theme exposes every hard-coded color. Going from dark to light turned up three problems:

  • color: 'white' on buttons became unreadable on the bright cyan accent. That gave me a new onAccent token.
  • Section wrappers with backgroundColor: '$background' hid the aurora painted on <body>. They're transparent now.
  • The Radix <Theme> paints its own background by default. It now uses hasBackground={false}.

4. docker compose restart served the old bundle. The built dist/ is copied into the image, so after npm run build you need up -d --build. I noticed because the index-*.js hash in the HTML hadn't changed.

Part 2 — One headline, verified numbers

While shipping the themes, I noticed something a recruiter would notice first. My portfolio said "Backend Python Developer | Automation & Reliability", my CV said "Backend Python Developer · DevOps & Reliability", and LinkedIn said something else. Three versions of the same person don't build trust.

So LinkedIn became the source of truth: Backend Engineer → SRE | Python · Django · Kubernetes · Terraform · CI/CD. The portfolio, the CV (versioned HTML → PDF via headless Edge) and my GitHub profile now say exactly that.

Then I went further and re-measured every number I publish against the actual repositories (pytest --collect-only, git shortlog, counting the Postman collection). Several were stale. The test count of my main automation project was off by thousands, a Postman collection had grown from 79 to 82 requests, and one coverage claim described a target instead of the 80% floor the CI actually enforces. I also caught my own mistake: I counted 18 releases when there were 19, because two versions only appear in the project's README, not in commit messages.

The lesson: a number on your CV is a claim someone can check. Measure it from the source, write down where it came from, and prefer wording like "2,800+ tests" when the exact count changes every week.

How it ships

  • 35 frontend tests (Vitest + Testing Library) and 49 backend tests (~91% coverage) with mypy.
  • A scripts/verificar.sh in each repo replays the CI on a clean clone of HEAD, with the same Node and Python versions as GitHub Actions. If Python 3.12 isn't installed locally, it runs inside a python:3.12-slim container. The runner only sees what's committed, so that's what gets tested.
  • End-to-end check in Docker (Django + Postgres + the embedded build) with Playwright: all three themes, desktop and 375 px mobile, no horizontal scroll.
  • CD with Jenkins: test gate → image build → deploy → healthcheck → smoke test, with a stage that guarantees the deploy can never point at the production database.

The two themes besides Cian were ported from an internal tool I built earlier (CmdVault), where they were NiceGUI palettes. Same idea, different stack. That's the part of side projects I enjoy most: the ideas move from one project to the next.

If you try the site, tell me which theme you'd keep. And if you have your own trick for flash-free theming, I'd love to hear it. 👇

title: These are ALL you NEED to get started with Python PANDAS
description:
Pandas is a Python library used for data manipulation, analysis, and cleaning. It provides fast and flexible data structures designed to work with tabular data (similar to an Excel spreadsheet or a SQL table)

Dataframes and Series

  • DataFrame: A 2-dimensional labeled data structure with rows and columns (a complete table)
  • Series: A 1-dimensional labeled array capable of holding any data type (like a single column in a spreadsheet).

Before getting started with pandas we need to install it first.

pip install pandas

import pandas as pd

# 1. Create a simple DataFrame
data = {
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'Age': [25, 30, 35],
    'City': ['New York', 'London', 'Paris']
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# 2. Load data from an external file
# df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

# 3. View the first 5 rows
print(df.head())

Reading files in pandas

CSV Files (.csv): Use pd.read_csv() to import comma-separated values.

df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

Excel Spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls): Use pd.read_excel() to load spreadsheets. You can specify a sheet using the sheet_name parameter.

df = pd.read_excel('budget.xlsx', sheet_name='Q1_Report')

JSON Data (.json): Use pd.read_json() to convert JSON strings or files into tabular format.

df = pd.read_json('users.json')

Parquet Files (.parquet): Use pd.read_parquet() for highly optimized, columnar storage files common in big data workflows.

df = pd.read_parquet('large_dataset.parquet')

SQL Database Tables: Use pd.read_sql() to pull data directly into Pandas via a database connection (e.g., utilizing an engine from the SQLAlchemy project)

import sqlalchemy
engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine('sqlite:///my_database.db')
df = pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM employees', con=engine)

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) using Pandas is the foundational step in any data science workflow. It allows you to understand the structure, distributions, relationships, and anomalies within a dataset before moving to modeling

.head()

  • first n rows of a DataFrame or Series. It is primarily used to quickly inspect and verify the structure, column names, and data types of a dataset after loading it.
  • Inside the brackets you can put the number of rows you want to inspect. 
df.head()
df.head(10)

.tail

  • The df.tail() method in pandas returns the last n rows of a DataFrame or Series. 
df.tail()

.shape

  • df.shape is an attribute that returns a tuple representing the dimensions of a DataFrame or Series. It provides a quick way to see how many rows and columns your dataset contains. 
df1.shape

Output:

(5632, 27)

Structural & Descriptive Summaries

  • Before analyzing trends, verify how data types are registered and look at basic statistical summaries. 
# Check data types, memory usage, and non-null counts
df.info()

Output:

# Summary statistics for numerical columns (mean, min, max, quartiles)
df.describe()

Output

# Summary statistics for ALL columns (including categorical frequencies)
df.describe(include="all")

Output

Exploring Single Variables

  • Examine individual variables to understand their distribution, frequency, and pull out any categorical unique counts 
# For Categorical Data: Count frequencies of unique values
df["category_column"].value_counts()
df["category_column"].unique()  # List unique entries
df["category_column"].nunique()  # Total number of unique entries

# For Numerical Data: Quick pandas native plotting
df["numeric_column"].hist(bins=20)  # Check skewness and distribution
df["numeric_column"].plot(kind="box")  # Identify outliers

Data Cleaning

  • Before cleaning is done, a quick EDA must be done to know the areas to clean and what to clean. Below is a sample code to have a sneek- peek of what to actually clean. 
# Find duplicate rows and drop them
print(df.duplicated().sum())
df.drop_duplicates(inplace=True)

# Find missing values
print(df.isnull().sum())

Deal with missing values

  • Missing values in a dataset can either be dropped or imputed depending on the size of the data, importance and number of missing values.
  • Here are some of the ways to deal with missing values: 
df.dropna(subset=["critical_column"], inplace=True)  # Drop missing rows

df["numeric_column"] = df["numeric_column"].fillna(
    df["numeric_column"].median()
)  # Impute with median

Dealing with DataTypes

  • Values may be recorded in a datatype which may not be fit for them. In anycase this occurs, they can be changed to the correct datatypes.

  • Using pd.to_numeric() Best for converting text or mixed-type columns into numbers. Use errors='coerce' to turn unconvertible entries (like random text or symbols) into NaN.

df['price'] = pd.to_numeric(df['price'], errors='coerce')
  • Using pd.to_datetime() Converts date and time strings into proper datetime64 objects 
df['sale_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['sale_date'], errors='coerce')
  • Dealing with mixed date formats e.g dd/mm/yyyy, mm/dd/yyyy, yyyy/mm/dd 
df1['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(
    df1['order_date'],
    format='mixed',
    errors='coerce'
)

df1['payment_method'] = df1['payment_method'].str.strip().str.capitalize()
  • replace(), used when you want to change items inside a column to ensure consistency in values recorded and reliability. 
df1['payment_method'] = df1['payment_method'].replace({
    'Mpesa' : 'M-pesa',
    'Visa': 'Card'
})
  • If the column has mixed characters and values for example here in unit_price, you can also use replace function to standardize the column and maybe change the datatype if need be. 
df1['unit_price_kes'] = df1['unit_price_kes'].str.strip().str.replace(r'[^0-9]','', regex = True).astype(float)

Creating new columns

  • You can also be required to create a new column maybe from from a condition as below or from a calculation. In such a scenario, here's how to deal with it. 
df1['phone_validity'] = np.where(df1['customer_phone'].astype(str).str.len() == 10, 'valid', 'invalid')

# Calculate total cost (multiplication)
df['total_cost'] = df['price'] * df['quantity']
  • The code above will create a new column called total_cost.

Deleting columns

  • You can delete columns from a DataFrame using .drop() 
# deleting a single column
df = df.drop(columns=['B'])

#  deleting multiple columns
df = df.drop(columns=['C', 'D'])

Aggregation in pandas

  • Aggregations in Pandas reduce a collection of numerical or categorical values into a single summary value (such as a sum, mean, or count). You can perform these operations on an entire Pandas DataFrame, specific columns, or groups of data using the groupby() 
# Clean, flat DataFrame output with custom column names
clean_summary = df.groupby('Department').agg(
    total_salary=('Salary', 'sum'),
    average_bonus=('Bonus', 'mean'),
    employee_count=('Employee', 'count')
).reset_index()

Concatenation and Merging in Pandas

Concatenation (pd.concat)

  • Use pd.concat() when your datasets have the same structure and you want to glue them together along an axis. • axis=0 (Default): Stacks DataFrames vertically (appends rows). • axis=1: Stacks DataFrames horizontally (appends columns) aligned by their index. 
import pandas as pd

df1 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [5, 6], 'B': [7, 8]})

# Stack vertically (Row-wise)
vertical_stack = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)

# Stack horizontally (Column-wise)
horizontal_stack = pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1)

Merging (pd.merge)

  • Use pd.merge() when you have different datasets that share a common identifier column (like an ID or SKU) and you want to align them side-by-side. 
left = pd.DataFrame({'User_ID': [1, 2, 3], 'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']})
right = pd.DataFrame({'User_ID': [1, 2, 4], 'Salary': [50000, 60000, 70000]})

# Merge on a matching column
merged_df = pd.merge(left, right, on='User_ID', how='inner')

Saving the final dataframe

  • You can save a Pandas DataFrame to different file formats in Python using specific df.to_*() export methods 
import pandas as pd

# Assume 'df' is your existing DataFrame
# 1. Save as CSV (excluding the default index)
df.to_csv("data.csv", index=False)

# 2. Save as Excel
df.to_excel("data.xlsx", index=False)

# 3. Save as JSON
df.to_json("data.json", orient="records")

# 4. Save as Parquet (requires pyarrow or fastparquet)
df.to_parquet("data.parquet")

# 5. Save as Pickle
df.to_pickle("data.pkl")

Conclusion

Python pandas is the foundational, industry-standard tool for modern data manipulation, cleaning, and analysis. Built around its core DataFrame and Series structures, it transforms raw, messy data into structured, tabular insights by providing powerful, intuitive functions for merging datasets, handling missing values, and performing complex aggregations like groupby. While it integrates seamlessly with the broader Python ecosystem—including NumPy, Matplotlib, and scikit-learn—pandas does suffer from high memory usage and reduced performance when processing massive, multi-gigabyte datasets. Despite these scaling limitations, it remains an indispensable cornerstone of data science workflows, unmatched for exploratory data analysis and rapid prototyping.

title: Agent Mail: Tencent Just Gave AI Agents Their Own Mailbox
description:
Agent Mail: Tencent Gives AI Agents Their Own Mailbox (@agent.qq.com), Open Source & Free in Beta | Lieke AI

  • @agent.qq.comDedicated agent mailbox Apache-2.0Open source 50/dayBeta send quota 6+ platformsMajor agents supported

In one line: why AI agents need their own mailbox

Two old paths for letting agents handle email — grant access to your personal inbox (privacy risk) or run your own SMTP (ops cost). Tencent QQ Mail's answer: give the agent a digital identity independent from humans: an isolated xxx@agent.qq.com address that can never touch your personal QQ/WeChat mail.
Internal beta opened June 23, 2026. Source code is Apache-2.0 on GitHub (Tencent/AgentlyMail); official site: agent.qq.com.

3-step setup, tested in ~5 minutes

Let the agent install it: ask your agent to read https://agent.qq.com/doc/cli-setup.md and follow the steps to install & configure Agent Mail CLI.

  • It runs automatically:npm install -g @tencent-qqmail/agently-clinpx skills add Tencent/AgentlyMail -g -yagently-cli auth loginOpen the printed authorization link in a browser.

  • Scan to authorize: after OAuth, run agently-cli +me — it returns xxx@agent.qq.com when configured.

Works with WorkBuddy, Claude Code, Cursor, Kimi Work, Doubao, Codex, Hermes and other mainstream agents. Read, send, search, attachments and live watch — all via one CLI.

Security: three layers built for agent workloads

Layer What it does
Physical isolation Agent gets a fresh data space; even a compromised agent cannot reach personal mail
Two-stage confirmation Send/reply/forward/delete requires the agent to generate a summary + confirmation token, then the user approves
Prompt-injection defense Malicious instructions inside inbound mail are treated as plain text, never as system commands

Six practical use cases (hands-on)

  • Invoice auto-expense: agent extracts amount/tax ID and files reimbursement reports

  • Newsletter digest: forward newsletters, get a daily AI summary

  • Order reconciliation: agent pulls order numbers into your sheets

  • A2A business email: procurement agent ↔ supplier agent, fully auditable

  • Verification-code relay: use Agent Mail for signups, agent auto-fills codes

  • AI job applications: dedicated address for resumes and interview scheduling

Competitive landscape: the agent-mail race

Agently Mail (Tencent) AgentMail (YC) Mail4Agent
Integration WeChat scan + CLI API + SDK API-first
Pricing Free in beta 3 mailboxes free, $20-200/mo paid Not public
Security Two-stage confirm + injection defense (unique) DIY DIY
China access No VPN needed VPN needed Fair
Ecosystem CLI + Skill path Python/TS SDK, MCP Server, Webhook Multi-framework

Bottom line: Agently Mail is the lowest-friction option for CN developers; AgentMail suits large overseas API/SDK deployments.

Beta limitations (stated honestly): 50 sends/day, 1GB per address — not production-ready until quotas open up; official Skill has Windows HTML-email layout issues (community fixes exist); A2A cross-domain protocol not yet documented; mailbox prefix can be changed only once.

Before your agent can run 24/7, you need reliable cloud compute

Agently Mail is just the first piece of agent infrastructure. The real backbone is elastic cloud servers that keep agents online around the clock. Lieke AI helps you get official promotional pricing.

Check Alibaba Cloud ECS deals →

FAQ

Does authorization leak my QQ password? No. It uses the standard OAuth device-code flow; the CLI never stores your QQ password.
Install fails or is slow? Make sure npm can reach the public registry; if the auth link won't open, check access to agent.qq.com.
How does this differ from AgentMail / Mail4Agent? Same category, different positioning: Agently Mail focuses on China accessibility + CLI/Skill + unique security; AgentMail targets overseas API/SDK scale.
Production-ready? Beta quotas are tight (50/day, 1GB). Start with daily reports and newsletter digests; wait for quota release for production scale.
