title: Sports Score Feeds: Realtime API Boundaries Under Serverless Connection Limits
description:
Short answer: use a realtime API surface that fits serverless connection limits, and make reconnect, expiry, authorization, and duplicate delivery explicit parts of the sports score feed rather than accidental behavior.

The feed is a small distributed system, even when the payload is only a score change. A browser or mobile client holds a connection for as long as it can; a serverless function, by contrast, is designed to start, do bounded work, and disappear. Treating those two lifetimes as interchangeable is how a match-winning goal turns into a stale screen.

What is the bill and the boundary in a live score feed?

The visible spend is rarely the whole cost. A useful workload model has four terms: connection lifetime, fan-out publishes, recovery traffic, and the engineering needed to reconcile state. Connection lifetime is the first boundary to measure because a serverless runtime may not be the right place to keep thousands of sockets open. The publish path should therefore be short-lived and stateless, while a dedicated realtime service owns connection management.

For a sports feed, the dominant business event is not “the client received bytes.” It is “the client can prove which score revision it has.” Attach a stable event identifier and a monotonic feed revision to each event in your domain model. On reconnect, the client sends the last revision it has acknowledged; the recovery path can then replay or refresh state without guessing whether a duplicate is new.

That choice changes downstream spend. You may retain fewer transient delivery records because the durable ledger is the score snapshot plus an audit trail of revisions, not an infinite socket transcript. The catch is that deleting delivery history removes a convenient forensic trail: when a broadcaster disputes a late update, you need the audit record and request identifier to explain what was published and when.

Infrai is one candidate for this short-lived boundary. Infrai has one key and one bill through a plain REST API, letting any runtime call the realtime publish operations without installing or versioning an SDK while leaving the connection fleet with a service designed to own it.

Keep these signals separate. Authentication answers who may connect, subscription state answers which channel they joined, and business events answer what happened in the game. Mixing them makes a token expiry look like a score correction and makes incident review unnecessarily expensive.

How should serverless connection limits shape API boundaries?

The boundary should be a command interface for short work: publish one event or publish a bounded batch, then return. In the verified realtime surface, those operations are POST /v1/realtime/publish and POST /v1/realtime/publish/batch. A serverless handler can validate the event, attach its stable identifier, call the publish operation, and exit; it does not need to poll or own a long-lived client socket.

This is where a plain REST API can be a practical fit. Infrai exposes backend capabilities through HTTP, so a Go service can use the standard library and keep its existing deployment model; there is no SDK lifecycle to coordinate with a short-lived function. The same request boundary also lets an operations team observe request IDs, latency, vendor metadata, and cost alongside the application trace, which is useful when a feed is busiest and the reconciliation queue is growing.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the stateless publish boundary when your team values one HTTP integration and wants authentication, delivery telemetry, and business-event accounting kept in the same operational vocabulary. It is not a reason to move connection ownership into a function, and it does not remove the need for a client-side recovery protocol.

Here is a deliberately schema-neutral Go caller. The payload is supplied by the application, so the example does not pretend to know fields that belong to your score domain.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := os.Getenv("INFRAI_PAYLOAD")
    if key == "" || payload == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_PAYLOAD are required")
    }
    // Equivalent probe shape for discovery tooling: curl -X POST https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish -d '{}'

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "score-feed-"+os.Getenv("FEED_EVENT_ID"))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: %s", body)) }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("publish rate limit did not clear after retries")
}

Measure first.

Which realtime option fits a sports score feed?

There is no universal winner. The right choice depends on who owns the socket, how much recovery state you retain, and whether your existing platform already supplies identity and fan-out.

Option Where it fits Trade-off to verify
Infrai realtime API Stateless HTTP publish from serverless handlers; one key and one REST surface can simplify a mixed backend You still design connection lifecycle, replay, and client trust; validate the exact limits for your regions
Ably A managed pub/sub product for teams that want connection and presence concerns in a specialist service Adds another platform boundary and its own channel, identity, and retention model
Pusher Channels A focused hosted channel service with familiar client integrations The application must map its authorization and recovery semantics onto the provider's channel model
AWS AppSync Useful when the feed already lives in an AWS GraphQL and identity stack GraphQL schema and resolver operations become part of the operational surface, which may be more machinery than a small publish command

Those descriptions are starting points, not benchmarks. Your mileage may vary with regional latency, burst size, and the number of subscribers per match; I am not sure which provider will produce the lowest effective bill without your event rate and retention policy. Compare the complete operating bill, including connection capacity, replay storage, observability, and the staff time spent maintaining adapters.

What does recovery look like when delivery is duplicated?

Assume reconnects, expiry, and partial failures are normal states. A client can receive an event, lose its acknowledgement, and receive the same event again. The consumer must treat the stable event identifier as an idempotency key, persist the highest verified revision, and make applying an older revision a no-op.

Authorization deserves the same precision. Issue a token scoped to the competition, match, or channel the client is allowed to read; do not infer trust from the fact that a socket was once authenticated. On expiry, refresh credentials and resubscribe deliberately. If authorization changes during a match, the client should stop rendering private updates before it attempts recovery.

Testing should exercise realistic latency, duplicate delivery, and rejected authorization, not only the happy path. A useful test records the sequence of revisions seen by the client, injects a reconnect between two publishes, and verifies that the final score and audit trail are identical whether the second event arrives once or twice. Test partial batch acceptance as a first-class result if your publish contract allows it; a caller that assumes an all-or-nothing outcome can silently drop one game in a multi-match update.

The short version is boring by design: stable identifiers, observable boundaries, and an explicit replay decision. Boring systems reconcile cleanly.

No polling.

Where should you choose a specialist instead?

Choose Ably or Pusher when the main problem is operating a large connection fleet and you prefer a specialist's client, presence, and channel tooling. Choose AppSync when GraphQL authorization, schema evolution, and AWS-native operations are already non-negotiable. Stick with a direct provider integration when your compliance team requires a narrowly scoped data path or when an existing contract gives you the recovery semantics you need.

Infrai is a poor fit when your organization cannot accept a general REST integration boundary, needs a provider-specific feature outside the published realtime surface, or requires connection behavior that your serverless platform cannot observe. Cost is one dimension of the decision, not the decision itself; model the retained score snapshots, recovery reads, and on-call effort before comparing invoices.

For any option, document the invariant that matters most: after a reconnect, a client can reconcile to the authoritative score without trusting delivery order. That invariant is more durable than a vendor label or a per-call price.

If this boundary fits your system, verify the request contract in the realtime publish documentation before wiring it into a serverless handler.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/realtime
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://ably.com/docs
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appsync/

Further reading

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/realtime
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: UUIDv7 in PostgreSQL 18: uuidv7() vs UUIDv4 vs bigint Primary Keys, Benchmarked
description:
I loaded 10 million rows into PostgreSQL 18 tables keyed by bigint, UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 and compared load time, WAL, index size and insert throughput. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

UUIDv7 is a UUID that starts with a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds, so new IDs sort in creation order. PostgreSQL 18 generates it natively with uuidv7(). As a primary key it keeps the B-tree index compact like a bigint sequence does, while staying globally unique like a random UUIDv4.

I loaded 10 million rows into three otherwise identical PostgreSQL 18.6 tables, keyed by bigint, uuidv4() and uuidv7(). UUIDv7 matched bigint on load time (37.3 s each), while UUIDv4 took 84.2 s and wrote 2.2x more WAL. I also found one trap: filtering with uuidv7(interval ...) directly in a WHERE clause skips the index.

TL;DR: should I use UUIDv7 primary keys in Postgres?

Yes, if you want UUID primary keys and the IDs do not need to hide when a row was created. On PostgreSQL 18, use id uuid primary key default uuidv7(). On PostgreSQL 17 or older, generate UUIDv7 in your app. Keep UUIDv4 for tokens and IDs whose creation time must stay private, and keep bigint if you never need IDs outside one database.

bigint identity UUIDv4 UUIDv7
Size 8 bytes 16 bytes 16 bytes
Generated by One sequence in the database Anyone, anywhere Anyone, anywhere
Sort order Insert order Random Creation time (ms)
Reveals Row count, insert order Nothing Creation timestamp
10M-row load (my test) 37.3 s 84.2 s 37.3 s
PK index after load 214 MB 385 MB 301 MB
Postgres built-in Always gen_random_uuid() / uuidv4() uuidv7() since 18

What is UUIDv7?

UUIDv7 is the time-ordered UUID version defined in RFC 9562, published in May 2024. The first 48 bits hold the Unix timestamp in milliseconds, then 4 version bits, then random or counter bits. Because the timestamp comes first, sorting UUIDv7 values as bytes sorts them by creation time, which B-tree indexes handle well.

The RFC describes it as featuring "a time-ordered value field derived from the widely implemented and well-known Unix Epoch timestamp source," and says "implementations SHOULD utilize UUIDv7 instead of UUIDv1 and UUIDv6 if possible."

A UUIDv7 from my test database, read left to right:

01a14a80-6c02-7160-b932-6c5ecd65f3c7
└──────┬─────┘ │
  timestamp    version 7   (rest: sub-millisecond precision + random)

Does PostgreSQL support UUIDv7?

Yes, since PostgreSQL 18, released on September 25, 2025. It added uuidv7(), an alias uuidv4() for gen_random_uuid(), and uuid_extract_timestamp(), which reads the timestamp back out. The PostgreSQL 18 docs say the timestamp uses "millisecond precision + sub-millisecond timestamp + random." PostgreSQL 17 and older have no uuidv7().

```sql title="PostgreSQL 18.6"
SELECT uuidv7(), uuidv4();
-- 01a14a74-450a-7a7e-a2f5-713a6b1da251 | 8c13f904-b813-4570-92de-5622dbb59443

SELECT uuid_extract_version(uuidv7()), uuid_extract_timestamp(uuidv7());
-- 7 | 2026-10-17 20:21:36.266+05

SELECT uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'); -- a UUIDv7 with a timestamp shifted one hour back




On PostgreSQL 17 the same call fails with `ERROR: function uuidv7() does not exist`. There, generate UUIDv7 in your application (Prisma's `uuid(7)` or the npm `uuid` package's `v7()`), or upgrade.

The [PostgreSQL 18 release announcement](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-18-released-3142/) calls it "the database-friendly uuidv7() function that provides better indexing and read performance for UUIDs." Here is what that looked like in my test.

## Is UUIDv7 faster than UUIDv4?

For inserts, yes. Loading 10 million rows took 37.3 s with UUIDv7 and 84.2 s with UUIDv4, and UUIDv4 wrote 4.6 GB of WAL against 2.1 GB. With 8 clients each inserting one row per transaction, UUIDv4 managed about 15% fewer inserts per second. UUIDv7 was within 2% of a `bigint` sequence on every insert test.

![UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 B-tree inserts: random UUIDv4 keys land on any leaf page and split pages across the index, while time-ordered UUIDv7 keys append to the rightmost leaf like a bigint sequence](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792251441/fabwaseem/blog/uuidv7-postgres/diagram-btree.jpg)

### Benchmark setup

- PostgreSQL 18.6 with default settings (`shared_buffers` 128 MB), on an 8 vCPU Xeon with 15 GB RAM.
- Three tables: `id` (the key under test), `created_at timestamptz default now()` and a 64-character `payload`.
- Bulk load: one `INSERT ... SELECT` of 10,000,000 rows per table after a `CHECKPOINT`. WAL is measured with `pg_current_wal_lsn()` and index density with [pgstattuple](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgstattuple.html)'s `pgstatindex()`.
- Concurrent inserts: `pgbench`, 8 clients, 60 seconds of single-row `INSERT`s into the preloaded tables, 2 rounds. The table shows the average of the two rounds.



```sql title="The three tables"
CREATE TABLE t_bigint (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE t_uuidv4 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv4(),                created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE t_uuidv7 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),                created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);

Results

Metric bigint UUIDv4 UUIDv7
10M-row bulk load 37.3 s 84.2 s 37.3 s
WAL written by the load 1,964 MB 4,598 MB 2,098 MB
Table (heap) size 1,116 MB 1,202 MB 1,202 MB
Primary key index size 214 MB 385 MB 301 MB
Index leaf density 90.0% 70.3% 90.0%
Index leaf fragmentation 0.0% 49.8% 0.0%
Single-row inserts, 8 clients 49,528/s 41,331/s 48,690/s

UUIDv7's index is 41% larger than bigint's, because each key is 16 bytes instead of 8, but it is packed just as tightly (90% leaf density). UUIDv4's index is 28% larger again than UUIDv7's, because random inserts split pages all over the tree and leave them about 70% full.

Why are random UUIDv4 primary keys slow?

Each new UUIDv4 lands at a random position in the B-tree, so inserts touch pages spread across the whole index. Once the index is larger than memory, every insert can mean reading a cold page, dirtying it, and logging a full-page image to WAL after each checkpoint. UUIDv7 keys always go to the rightmost leaf, the same hot page a sequence uses.

That explains each number in the table. The 2.2x WAL comes from full-page writes for thousands of different leaf pages. The 70% leaf density comes from 50/50 page splits in the middle of the tree. In my test the UUIDv4 index (385 MB) was three times shared_buffers (128 MB), so the gap in single-row inserts (15%) was smaller than in bulk loading (2.3x). It will grow as the table and index outgrow memory.

How do I use UUIDv7 as a primary key in PostgreSQL 18?

Declare the column as uuid with DEFAULT uuidv7(). Keep the native uuid type, not text: it stores 16 bytes instead of 36 characters plus overhead. Existing UUIDv4 rows can stay. Both versions share one uuid column, and new UUIDv7 keys simply sort after the old random ones.

```sql title="New table"
CREATE TABLE orders (
id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
total_cents integer NOT NULL,
created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);






```sql title="Existing table: new rows get UUIDv7"
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN id SET DEFAULT uuidv7();

Changing the default does not rewrite old rows or rebuild the index. It only changes how future keys are generated, so the right edge of the index starts behaving like a sequence from then on.

How do I use UUIDv7 with Prisma and Drizzle?

In Prisma, use @default(uuid(7)) to generate the ID in Prisma Client, or @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) to let PostgreSQL 18 generate it. In Drizzle, use uuid().primaryKey().default(sql\uuidv7()). I tested all three on PostgreSQL 18.6. Every ID came out as version 7, and 1,000 sequential creates sorted exactly in creation order.

```prisma title="prisma/schema.prisma (Prisma 7.10.1)"
// UUIDv7 generated by Prisma Client in Node.js
model Order {
id String @id @default(uuid(7)) @db.Uuid
total Int
createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}

// UUIDv7 generated by PostgreSQL 18
model Invoice {
id String @id @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) @db.Uuid
total Int
createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}




The two Prisma options are not equivalent. `prisma migrate dev` created `"id" UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7()` for `Invoice` but no default at all for `Order`. So a raw SQL insert into `Order` failed with `null value in column "id" ... violates not-null constraint` (code 23502), while the same insert into `Invoice` worked. If anything other than Prisma Client writes to the table (SQL scripts, another service, a queue worker), use `dbgenerated("uuidv7()")`. The [Prisma schema reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/prisma-schema-reference) documents both.



```ts title="schema.ts (Drizzle 0.45.4)"
import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { integer, pgTable, timestamp, uuid } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const invoices = pgTable("invoices", {
  id: uuid().primaryKey().default(sql`uuidv7()`),
  total: integer().notNull(),
  createdAt: timestamp({ withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
});

drizzle-kit generate turned that into "id" uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7() NOT NULL. Drizzle's .defaultRandom() still means gen_random_uuid(), which is UUIDv4. For which ORM to pick in the first place, see my Drizzle vs Prisma benchmark.

Can I query by time using a UUIDv7 key?

Yes, because UUIDv7 order is time order: ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 returns the newest rows from the primary key alone. For a time range, compare against uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'), but wrap it in a subquery. Used directly, the volatile function forced a full parallel scan of 15.8 million rows in my test.

```sql title="Rows from the last 30 seconds"
-- Slow: uuidv7() is VOLATILE, so it cannot be an index condition
SELECT count(*) FROM t_uuidv7 WHERE id >= uuidv7(interval '-30 seconds');
-- Parallel Seq Scan, Rows Removed by Filter: 5,280,621 per worker, 3,430 ms

-- Fast: a scalar subquery is evaluated once (InitPlan) and used as the index bound
SELECT count(*) FROM t_uuidv7 WHERE id >= (SELECT uuidv7(interval '-30 seconds'));
-- Parallel Index Only Scan using t_uuidv7_pkey, Index Cond: (id >= (InitPlan 1).col1), ~42 ms




Both queries returned the correct count. The fix only changes the plan. The boundary is approximate within a millisecond, because the bound has random bits after the timestamp, so keep a real `created_at` column for exact cut-offs and reports. `ORDER BY id DESC` on a UUIDv4 table also runs fast, but its "latest" rows are random ones.

## Is UUIDv7 safe to expose in URLs?

Only if creation time is not sensitive. Anyone can decode the timestamp from a UUIDv7: `uuid_extract_timestamp()` returned `2026-10-17 20:32:57.748+05` for a row whose `created_at` was 10 ms earlier. RFC 9562 says "if UUIDs are required for use with any security operation within an application context in any shape or form, then UUIDv4 SHOULD be utilized."

Practical rules:

- **Fine as UUIDv7:** orders, posts, messages, events, internal IDs, anything you would happily sort by date.
- **Use UUIDv4 or a random token:** password reset tokens, invite links, API keys, session IDs, and records where signup time is private (for example, user IDs in a service where account age matters).
- **Never rely on any UUID for authorization.** Unguessable is not the same as access control.

## UUIDv7 vs bigint vs ULID: which should I use?

Use `bigint` identity when IDs are created only by one database and never leave it: smallest index, fastest joins. Use UUIDv7 when clients, services or offline devices create IDs, or when you merge data across databases. ULID gives similar time-ordered properties, but it needs a text column or a conversion, while UUIDv7 fits the native 16-byte `uuid` type.

![Decision chart: bigint identity for single-database internal IDs, UUIDv7 for distributed or client-generated IDs, UUIDv4 for secrets and tokens, ULID only when you need its text format](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792251442/fabwaseem/blog/uuidv7-postgres/diagram-decision.jpg)

| Need | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| Internal IDs, one database, maximum speed | `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` |
| IDs generated in the app, mobile or other services | UUIDv7 |
| Merging rows from several databases or regions | UUIDv7 |
| IDs that must not reveal creation time | UUIDv4 |
| Secrets: tokens, reset links, API keys | Random token (UUIDv4 or longer) |
| Existing ULID system | Keep ULID, or store it as `uuid` (both are 128 bits) |

Before relying on `uuidv7()`, run `SELECT version();` on every environment, including CI and local Docker containers, since a server still on 17 will reject it. If you self-host Postgres next to your app as in my [Coolify self-hosting guide](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/self-host-nextjs-with-coolify), the major version is set by the database image you choose.

## Common UUIDv7 mistakes

- **Storing UUIDs as `text` or `varchar(36)`.** Use the `uuid` type: 16 bytes, faster comparisons.
- **Calling `uuidv7(interval ...)` directly in `WHERE`.** Wrap it in `(SELECT ...)` or compute the bound in the app, or the index is skipped.
- **Using Prisma `uuid(7)` when other writers exist.** It sets no database default. Use `dbgenerated("uuidv7()")`.
- **Expecting `uuidv7()` on PostgreSQL 17.** It does not exist there. Generate in the app or upgrade to 18.
- **Exposing UUIDv7 where timing is private.** Its first 48 bits are the creation time.
- **Dropping `created_at`.** The UUID timestamp is approximate and set by whoever generated the ID. Keep a real column for reporting.

## Key takeaways

- UUIDv7 starts with a 48-bit millisecond Unix timestamp, so IDs sort by creation time; PostgreSQL 18 generates it with uuidv7().
- In my 10M-row test, UUIDv7 loaded as fast as bigint (37.3 s) while UUIDv4 took 84.2 s and wrote 2.2x more WAL.
- UUIDv4's primary key index ended 28% larger than UUIDv7's, with 70% leaf density and 50% fragmentation.
- With 8 concurrent clients, UUIDv4 inserted about 15% fewer rows per second than UUIDv7.
- Wrap uuidv7(interval ...) in a scalar subquery for time-range filters; called directly, it forced a full table scan.
- Prisma's uuid(7) generates IDs in the client with no database default; dbgenerated("uuidv7()") puts the default in Postgres.
- UUIDv7 reveals creation time, so keep UUIDv4 or random tokens for secrets and private timestamps.

## FAQ

### What is UUIDv7?

UUIDv7 is the time-ordered UUID version from RFC 9562, published in May 2024. Its first 48 bits are a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, followed by version bits and random or counter bits. Because the timestamp comes first, UUIDv7 values sort by creation time, which keeps B-tree indexes compact when they are used as primary keys.

### Does PostgreSQL support UUIDv7?

Yes, since PostgreSQL 18, released on September 25, 2025. It added the uuidv7() function, an optional interval argument that shifts the timestamp, uuidv4() as an alias for gen_random_uuid(), and uuid_extract_timestamp() to read the time back. PostgreSQL 17 and older return an error that uuidv7() does not exist.

### Is UUIDv7 faster than UUIDv4 in Postgres?

For inserts, yes. In my PostgreSQL 18.6 test, a 10-million-row load took 37.3 seconds with UUIDv7 and 84.2 seconds with UUIDv4, and UUIDv4 wrote 2.2 times more WAL. With 8 clients inserting single rows, UUIDv4 managed about 15 percent fewer inserts per second. UUIDv7 stayed within 2 percent of bigint.

### Should I use UUIDv7 or bigint as a primary key?

Use bigint identity when one database creates every ID and the IDs never leave your system, because its index is smallest and joins are fastest. Use UUIDv7 when the app, mobile clients or other services create IDs, or when you merge data across databases. In my test UUIDv7's index was 41 percent larger than bigint's.

### How do I use UUIDv7 with Prisma?

Use @default(uuid(7)) to generate the ID in Prisma Client, or @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) on PostgreSQL 18 to generate it in the database. Add @db.Uuid for the native type. The uuid(7) option sets no database default, so raw SQL inserts fail with a not-null error; dbgenerated works for every writer.

### How do I use UUIDv7 on PostgreSQL 17?

PostgreSQL 17 has no uuidv7() function, so generate UUIDv7 in your application and store it in a uuid column. Prisma's uuid(7) default and the npm uuid package's v7() both produce RFC 9562 version 7 values. When you upgrade to PostgreSQL 18, switch the column default to uuidv7() without rewriting old rows.

### Is it safe to expose UUIDv7 in URLs?

Only when creation time is not sensitive. Anyone can decode the first 48 bits, and uuid_extract_timestamp() returns the time in PostgreSQL. RFC 9562 says UUIDv4 should be used if UUIDs are involved in any security operation. Keep UUIDv4 or random tokens for reset links, invites, API keys and private user records.

### Can I query a time range using UUIDv7 ids?

Yes. Compare the key against uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'), but wrap the call in a scalar subquery such as id >= (SELECT uuidv7(interval '-1 hour')). Because uuidv7() is volatile, calling it directly in WHERE forced a full parallel scan of 15.8 million rows in my test, about 3.4 seconds instead of about 42 milliseconds.


---

title: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant: Benchmarked for RAG in 2026
description:
I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings into pgvector and Qdrant and measured recall, latency, index build and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its docs only, since I didn't run it. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that stores embeddings in a vector column and searches them with HNSW or IVFFlat indexes, next to your normal tables. Qdrant is an open-source vector database you run yourself or use as a managed cloud. Pinecone is a fully managed, serverless vector database you only reach through an API.

For a RAG app, the real question is whether you need a separate vector database at all. I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings (1,536 dimensions) into pgvector 0.8.7 on PostgreSQL 18.6 and into Qdrant 1.19.2 on one machine. Then I measured recall, latency, build time and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its official docs and limits only, because I didn't run it and I won't invent numbers for it.

TL;DR: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant, which should I use?

Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres and have up to a few million vectors. One database, SQL joins, transactions and backups you already have. Choose Qdrant when vector search is the core workload and you need the best recall per millisecond or heavy filtering. Choose Pinecone when you want zero infrastructure and accept a managed service with usage pricing.

pgvector Qdrant Pinecone
What it is Postgres extension Vector database (open source) Managed vector database (closed)
Hosting Anywhere Postgres runs Self-host or Qdrant Cloud Pinecone's cloud only
Index HNSW, IVFFlat HNSW per segment Managed (serverless, object storage)
Max indexed dims 2,000 vector, 4,000 halfvec 1,536 tested here 20,000 dense
Filtering SQL WHERE (post-filter, iterative scans) Payload indexes + filter-aware HNSW Metadata filters (40 KB per record)
Consistency Transactional (ACID) Upserts readable after wait=true Eventually consistent
Recall@10 at ~2.6 ms, my test 0.978 (ef_search 100) 0.985 (hnsw_ef 40) not tested
Cost to start Your Postgres Free binary / free cloud tier Free Starter; Standard $50/month minimum

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Usually not at first. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, pgvector adds vector search without a second system to deploy, secure, back up and keep in sync. In my test it answered top-10 queries over 100,000 OpenAI embeddings in 1.5-4 ms, with 95-99% recall. A dedicated database starts to pay off at very large scale, under heavy filtering, or when search load needs to scale separately.

The hidden cost of a separate vector store is synchronisation. Every document insert, update and delete has to reach two systems, and a failed write leaves them disagreeing. With pgvector the embedding sits in the same row and the same transaction as the document it describes.

What is pgvector?

pgvector is an open-source PostgreSQL extension that adds vector, halfvec, bit and sparsevec types, distance operators like <=> (cosine) and <-> (L2), and approximate HNSW and IVFFlat indexes. Per the pgvector README, it "performs exact nearest neighbor search, which provides perfect recall" by default. An index trades a little recall for speed.

CREATE EXTENSION vector;

CREATE TABLE documents (
  id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id int NOT NULL,
  content   text NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(1536) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- top 5 chunks for a question, inside one tenant
SELECT id, content
FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 5;

Index limits matter for model choice. HNSW can index a vector of "up to 2,000 dimensions" and a halfvec of "up to 4,000 dimensions". A 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large needs a halfvec index or a shorter output size.

What are Qdrant and Pinecone?

Qdrant is an open-source vector search engine written in Rust. It stores points (vectors plus a JSON payload), builds an HNSW index per segment, and adds payload indexes so filters run inside the graph search. You can run a single binary, Docker or Qdrant Cloud.

Pinecone is a managed, serverless vector database. Per its architecture docs, "all your vector data is stored in highly efficient, distributed object storage." Pinecone "separates write and read operations into different paths, with each scaling independently based on demand." There is no self-hosted version.

How I benchmarked pgvector and Qdrant

  1. Data. The first 100,000 rows of the public DBpedia OpenAI embeddings dataset: 1,536-dimension text-embedding-ada-002 vectors of Wikipedia entities, a typical RAG shape. 1,000 held-out rows from the same dataset served as queries.
  2. Ground truth. Exact cosine top-10 for every query, computed with NumPy. Recall@10 is the share of those 10 that each engine returned.
  3. Machine. One 8-vCPU, 15 GB Linux box, everything on localhost, no Docker.
  4. pgvector. PostgreSQL 18.6 with pgvector 0.8.7, shared_buffers = 2GB, maintenance_work_mem = 2GB. HNSW with defaults (m = 16, ef_construction = 64), loaded with binary COPY through psycopg 3.
  5. Qdrant. The Qdrant 1.19.2 release binary, cosine distance, m = 16 and ef_construct = 64 to match pgvector, default optimizer settings (it made 4 segments). Loaded with the official Python client over gRPC from a single process.
  6. Queries. One client, sequential, 50 warm-up queries, then 1,000 timed queries. Latency includes the Python client round trip on both sides.
  7. Filters. Every vector got a random category from 0 to 9, about 10% of rows each. Filtered queries asked for the top 10 inside one category.

Is pgvector fast enough? Recall and latency results

Yes, at this scale both engines are fast. pgvector reached 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms median with default settings, and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with hnsw.ef_search = 200. Qdrant reached 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms median and 0.999 at 5.4 ms. At roughly equal recall (about 98.5-98.8%), Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster: 2.6 ms against 4.0 ms.

Engine and setting Recall@10 p50 latency p95 latency Queries/s (1 client)
pgvector, ef_search = 40 (default) 0.948 1.45 ms 2.16 ms 683
pgvector, ef_search = 100 0.978 2.60 ms 3.70 ms 389
pgvector, ef_search = 200 0.988 4.02 ms 5.82 ms 249
pgvector halfvec index, ef_search = 100 0.973 2.33 ms 3.30 ms 433
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 40 0.985 2.63 ms 3.56 ms 368
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 100 0.997 3.73 ms 4.66 ms 255
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 200 0.999 5.37 ms 6.99 ms 176
pgvector exact (no index) 1.000 380 ms 445 ms 3
Qdrant exact (no index) 1.000 24.7 ms 32.6 ms 39

Why does Qdrant get higher recall at the same ef? It splits the collection into segments (4 here) and searches each one with that ef, so it explores more candidates in total. Compare the engines at equal recall, not equal settings.

How fast do they load and index?

Qdrant indexed faster: 30.8 seconds from the first upload to a fully indexed collection, with the upload itself taking 20.2 s from one Python process. pgvector loaded the rows with COPY in 3.9 s, then needed 69.1 s to build the HNSW index with the default 2 parallel workers.

pgvector Qdrant
Load 100k vectors 3.9 s (COPY) 20.2 s (Python client, gRPC)
Build HNSW index 69.1 s included, indexed at 30.8 s
Table / data size 798 MB —
HNSW index size 781 MB (vector), 391 MB (halfvec) —
Server memory after test Postgres buffers + OS cache 1,293 MB RSS

Use the halfvec trick in pgvector: indexing embedding::halfvec(1536) halved the index from 781 MB to 391 MB and cost about half a point of recall (0.973 against 0.978 at ef_search = 100). Query the index with the same cast:

CREATE INDEX ON documents
  USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(1536)) halfvec_cosine_ops);

SELECT id FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding::halfvec(1536) <=> $1::halfvec(1536)
LIMIT 10;

How does filtered vector search compare?

Qdrant handled filters best. With a payload index on category, filtered top-10 queries returned 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms median. pgvector gave three very different results depending on the plan Postgres picked, so you need to know how its filtering works.

Filtered query (10% of rows match) Rows returned (of 10) Recall@10 p50
pgvector, planner's choice (B-tree on category, exact sort) 10 1.000 44.2 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = off 3.92 0.389 1.77 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = strict_order 10 0.915 3.62 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = relaxed_order 10 0.953 3.37 ms
Qdrant, payload index 10 0.993 2.11 ms

Why does pgvector return fewer rows with a filter?

Because HNSW filters after the index scan. The README explains: "If a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average." I measured 3.92. Since pgvector 0.8.0, iterative index scans keep walking the graph until enough rows match.

-- once per session or per transaction (SET LOCAL)
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;

SELECT id, content FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 10;

Postgres often picks the exact plan by itself for a selective filter. In my test it used the category B-tree and sorted about 10,000 rows exactly: perfect recall, but 44 ms instead of about 3 ms. That is fine for one tenant with a few thousand chunks. For large tenants, check EXPLAIN and turn on iterative scans. If one filter dominates, consider a partial index or partitioning by tenant.

What does Pinecone offer that pgvector and Qdrant don't?

Fully managed, serverless scaling with nothing to run. Reads and writes scale separately, storage lives in object storage, and you never tune ef or m. The trade-offs are documented:

  • Eventual consistency. The known limitations page says "Pinecone is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records are available to query."
  • Operation limits. Per the operation limits: dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions, 40 KB of filterable metadata per record, 1,000 records or 2 MB per upsert batch, and top_k up to 10,000.
  • Plans. The object limits give the free Starter plan 2 GB of serverless storage and 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Pinecone pricing lists the Standard plan at a $50/month minimum.
  • Network hop. Every query leaves your VPC. Expect your cloud region's round-trip time on top of search time. My localhost latencies are not comparable to Pinecone and I did not measure it.

When should I choose each one?

Decide by what you already run and what dominates your workload. The pgvector default is strong for product teams. Move when you measure a reason, not before.

  1. Choose pgvector when your data lives in Postgres, you need joins, row-level security or transactions with your embeddings, and you have up to a few million vectors per index. Add pgvectorscale (StreamingDiskANN) if the index outgrows RAM.
  2. Choose Qdrant when search is the product: tens of millions of vectors, many filters, multi-vector or hybrid search, or quantization to cut memory. Its quantization guide says scalar quantization achieves "4x compression with minimal accuracy loss."
  3. Choose Pinecone when nobody on the team should run a database, traffic is spiky, and a usage bill plus eventual consistency are acceptable.

How do I move from pgvector to Qdrant later?

Keep embeddings and IDs portable from day one. Use the same primary key in both systems, store the embedding model name and dimensions with each row, and write a re-sync job that streams rows by ID. Qdrant accepts integer or UUID point IDs, so a UUIDv7 primary key maps across directly.

Then run both side by side, compare recall on a fixed set of real queries, and switch reads before you stop writing to Postgres.

Common mistakes with vector search in production

  • Indexing 3,072-dimension vectors as vector. HNSW on vector stops at 2,000 dimensions. Use halfvec or a smaller output dimension.
  • Forgetting iterative scans. Filtered HNSW queries in pgvector can silently return fewer than LIMIT rows.
  • Comparing engines at equal settings. ef means different work in different engines. Compare at equal recall.
  • Measuring recall on random vectors. Use real embeddings from your model. Random data hides graph quality.
  • Creating Qdrant payload indexes after loading. The indexing docs say payload indexes should be created before ingesting data, so filter-aware HNSW edges get built.
  • Ignoring re-embedding cost. Switching embedding models means re-embedding everything, whichever store you use.

If you want a working starting point, my open-source Next.js AI starter kit, Forgekit, ships RAG on pgvector. For self-hosting Postgres or Qdrant next to your app, see self-hosting Next.js with Coolify.

Key takeaways

  • With 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector 0.8.7 hit 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms with defaults and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with ef_search 200.
  • Qdrant 1.19.2 hit 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms, about 1.5x faster than pgvector at roughly equal recall.
  • pgvector's HNSW filters after scanning: a 10% filter returned only 3.92 of 10 rows until iterative scans were enabled.
  • Qdrant's payload index gave the best filtered search in my test: 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms.
  • A halfvec HNSW index halved pgvector's index size (781 MB to 391 MB) for about half a point of recall.
  • Pinecone is serverless and eventually consistent, supports 20,000-dimension vectors, and its Standard plan has a $50/month minimum.
  • Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres; move to Qdrant or Pinecone when measurements show a need.

FAQ

Is pgvector as good as Pinecone or Qdrant?

For most RAG apps up to a few million vectors, yes. In my test of 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector reached 0.988 recall@10 at 4.0 ms median, and Qdrant reached 0.985 at 2.6 ms. Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster at equal recall and better at filtered search, but pgvector keeps embeddings in the same transactional database as your data.

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Not usually at the start. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, the pgvector extension adds vector columns and HNSW indexes without a second system to deploy, back up and keep in sync. Consider a dedicated vector database when you reach tens of millions of vectors, need heavy filtering at low latency, or need to scale search separately.

Why does pgvector return fewer results than my LIMIT?

Because pgvector's HNSW index applies WHERE filters after scanning the index. With a filter matching 10 percent of rows and the default ef_search of 40, about 4 rows match on average; I measured 3.92. Set hnsw.iterative_scan to relaxed_order or strict_order, available since pgvector 0.8.0, so the scan continues until enough rows match.

How many dimensions can pgvector index?

pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat indexes support the vector type up to 2,000 dimensions, halfvec up to 4,000 and bit up to 64,000. For a 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large, index the column as halfvec or request a smaller output dimension. Pinecone supports dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions.

Is Qdrant faster than pgvector?

In my single-machine test, yes, at equal recall. Qdrant 1.19.2 returned 0.985 recall@10 at 2.6 ms median against pgvector's 0.988 at 4.0 ms, and indexed 100,000 vectors in about 31 seconds against pgvector's 69-second HNSW build. With default settings, pgvector was faster per query but at lower recall, 0.948 at 1.45 ms.

How much does Pinecone cost?

Pinecone has a free Starter plan with 2 GB of serverless storage and up to 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Its Standard plan for production has a $50 per month minimum, after which you pay as you go for usage, according to Pinecone's pricing page. Qdrant's open-source build and pgvector are free to self-host.

What is halfvec in pgvector?

halfvec is pgvector's half-precision vector type, storing each dimension in 2 bytes instead of 4. Indexing an expression like embedding::halfvec(1536) halves the HNSW index size; in my test it shrank from 781 MB to 391 MB with recall dropping from 0.978 to 0.973. It also raises the indexable limit to 4,000 dimensions.

Is Pinecone eventually consistent?

Yes. Pinecone's documentation states that it is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records can be queried, and suggests checking index stats to confirm counts. pgvector writes are transactional and visible on commit, and Qdrant upserts sent with wait=true are applied before the call returns.
