title: Participant Lists in Live Calls — 4 Rules to Clean Empty Rooms
description:
Keep room membership as a server-owned lease, not as a side effect of an open socket. For a live-shopping video call, four invariants are enough to guide the design: one logical participant can own only one current session generation; stale disconnects cannot remove a newer generation; a room disappears only after its last lease expires; and every participant snapshot carries a revision. This produces accurate lists through reconnects without promising that a transient transport is perfectly reliable.

Short answer: expose a snapshot-plus-revision read path, issue a new generation on every successful reconnect, renew membership with bounded leases, and delay empty-room deletion until the final lease is unquestionably expired. Typing indicators may be lossy. Read receipts and membership transitions need identity, ordering, and idempotency.

That distinction matters in commerce. A missed "typing" event is cosmetic; an agent who vanishes from a buyer's call roster, or a receipt attributed to an earlier session, changes what people believe happened. Treating all three signals alike makes the most important path no safer and makes the least important path needlessly expensive.

How should Node.js list participants and clean empty rooms?

WebRTC defines peer connections and the media negotiation surface, but the application still owns signaling and participant presence. A connected peer connection is therefore evidence about media transport, not the canonical room roster. Browsers suspend, networks change, tabs duplicate, and reconnect attempts can overlap. The roster needs its own model. Use stable application identities for people and opaque identifiers for connection attempts. A useful membership record contains room_id, participant_id, generation, lease_deadline, and a small amount of display data. Keep authorization outside that display data: being listed in a room must never grant permission to join it. This model does add periodic writes and a sweeper, so it is not suitable for a disposable demo whose entire state may vanish with one process. That is a deliberate trade-off: production recovery is worth the machinery; a local prototype may reasonably skip it.

The generation is the sharp edge. Suppose generation 7 loses its network path, then generation 8 authenticates and joins. The delayed close callback for generation 7 may arrive afterward. If cleanup means "delete this participant," the valid generation 8 membership disappears. Cleanup must mean "delete this participant only if the stored generation is still 7."

One stale callback is enough.

The room also owns a monotonically increasing revision. Increment it for visible membership changes, not for every heartbeat. A list response can then return a coherent snapshot with revision 42, while a subscription continues from changes after 42. If the consumer sees a revision gap, it discards local assumptions and fetches another snapshot.

Name the failure boundaries before choosing storage

The delivery guarantee is bounded by the state transition, not by the fan-out mechanism. Once a join or leave is committed, notifications may be duplicated, delayed, or missed during a disconnect. Consumers must be able to recover from the durable snapshot. Exactly-once delivery across a database, a process, and a browser is not the invariant here; idempotent application and a repair path are.

State or signal Required behavior Recovery rule Retention
Participant membership Durable within its lease; ordered by room revision Fetch a snapshot after a gap Until explicit leave or lease expiry
Read receipt Idempotent and monotonic per message and reader Re-send the highest acknowledged position Product and compliance policy
Typing indicator Best effort and short lived Let it expire; do not replay it Seconds, in memory
Empty-room marker Conditional on no live membership Recheck after a grace interval Until cleanup completes

This table prevents a common overcorrection: persisting every keystroke-like signal because membership needs durability. A typing indicator should carry an expiry time and disappear without a compensating event. Replaying "agent is typing" after a reconnect is worse than dropping it.

Read receipts sit on the other side of the line. Model them as progress, such as the highest message sequence a participant has read, so retries are naturally idempotent. Do not model them as a growing bag of socket events. Compliance also enters here: receipt retention, access, and deletion should follow the message policy rather than the lifetime of an in-memory room.

The critical path is a compare-and-delete state machine

The following Python models the storage contract behind an HTTP framework and a realtime transport. It deliberately leaves database syntax out: the important operations are conditional writes that a transaction, compare-and-swap primitive, or server-side script can enforce atomically.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic
from uuid import uuid4


@dataclass
class Member:
    participant_id: str
    generation: str
    lease_deadline: float


@dataclass
class Room:
    revision: int = 0
    members: dict[str, Member] = field(default_factory=dict)
    empty_since: float | None = None


class PresenceStore:
    def __init__(self, lease_seconds: float = 30.0, empty_grace: float = 15.0):
        self.rooms: dict[str, Room] = {}
        self.lease_seconds = lease_seconds
        self.empty_grace = empty_grace

    def join(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
        now = monotonic()
        room = self.rooms.setdefault(room_id, Room())
        generation = uuid4().hex
        room.members[participant_id] = Member(
            participant_id=participant_id,
            generation=generation,
            lease_deadline=now + self.lease_seconds,
        )
        room.empty_since = None
        room.revision += 1
        return generation, room.revision

    def renew(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        member.lease_deadline = monotonic() + self.lease_seconds
        return True

    def leave(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        del room.members[participant_id]
        room.revision += 1
        if not room.members:
            room.empty_since = monotonic()
        return True

    def snapshot(self, room_id: str) -> dict:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id, Room())
        return {
            "revision": room.revision,
            "participants": sorted(room.members),
        }

    def sweep(self) -> list[str]:
        now = monotonic()
        deleted = []
        for room_id, room in list(self.rooms.items()):
            expired = [
                participant_id
                for participant_id, member in room.members.items()
                if member.lease_deadline <= now
            ]
            for participant_id in expired:
                del room.members[participant_id]
                room.revision += 1
            if not room.members and room.empty_since is None:
                room.empty_since = now
            if (
                not room.members
                and room.empty_since is not None
                and now - room.empty_since >= self.empty_grace
            ):
                del self.rooms[room_id]
                deleted.append(room_id)
        return deleted

The sample is single-process so the contract stays visible. In production, join, renew, leave, revision allocation, and the final empty check must use storage operations with equivalent atomicity. A process-local dictionary is correct only when one process owns every event for a room and restart loss is acceptable.

An Express application can expose the same contract through authenticated join, renew, leave, and snapshot handlers, while its socket layer publishes revisioned changes. The exact framework callback is secondary. Authenticate the participant before accepting participant_id; derive room access from server-side policy; and never trust a client-supplied generation until it has been matched to that participant's current stored record.

Fan-out follows commit. Publish a compact event containing the room, revision, operation, and participant identity after the state change succeeds. Duplicate events are harmless when clients ignore revisions they have already applied. A gap is actionable: fetch the list again. If publication can fail independently after commit, use an outbox record in the same transaction as the membership mutation, then let a worker retry publication.

How should reconnect races be tested?

Start with reordered operations, because happy-path integration tests rarely expose presence errors. Join generation A, join generation B for the same participant, then deliver A's close callback. B must remain. Next, expire A immediately before its renewal is processed; the renewal must either win atomically or receive a rejection that forces a fresh join. An ambiguous half-renewed state is unacceptable.

Test two participants leaving on different workers. Only the worker observing the atomic transition to zero may schedule cleanup, and the cleanup job must recheck emptiness before deletion. Then join a new participant during the grace interval. The room and its new revision must survive. There are more mundane cases too: duplicated leave messages, a heartbeat received after explicit leave, two browser tabs sharing one user identity, and a consumer reconnecting with an old revision. Put those permutations in a deterministic state-machine test. Reserve browser tests for signaling and UI behavior; they are slower and worse at exploring reorderings. Operationally, graph lease expirations separately from explicit leaves. A rising expiration ratio often points to transport trouble, suspended clients, or overloaded event loops. Track snapshot repairs caused by revision gaps, cleanup lag, current members per room, and rejected stale generations. Avoid participant identifiers in high-cardinality metric labels. Structured logs can carry a pseudonymous identifier under an access and retention policy. During a rolling restart, old processes may emit late disconnect callbacks after new processes have accepted reconnects, which is precisely why generation checks belong in shared state. A sweeper should be safe to run concurrently, and its work should be partitioned or claimed so a large room set does not create a synchronized scan spike.

Measure the boundary.

Rejected option: delete on the last socket close

Deleting a room as soon as the last locally known socket closes is attractive because it is short, cheap, and easy to explain. It is also the wrong default for horizontally scaled video-call presence. The closing process may not know about a connection accepted elsewhere, and a reconnect can race the deletion.

The option remains valid for an ephemeral, single-process prototype where rooms contain no durable state, all connections are owned by that process, and restart loss is explicitly acceptable. State those boundaries in the decision record. Once recordings, receipts, moderation state, or multiple workers enter the design, socket lifetime and room lifetime have separated.

The practical rule is compact: a disconnect is a hint; an expired, generation-matched lease is evidence. Make snapshots authoritative, make fan-out repairable, and make deletion conditional. Those choices keep participant lists believable during the exact moment a buyer or support agent is already dealing with a shaky call.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: EIA's January "forecast" of this year's solar additions was the developers' plan, 2020-2024
description:
Every January EIA publishes two numbers for how much utility-scale solar will be added that year. Today in Energy reports what developers plan, from the EIA-860M inventory. The Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), the same month, says what EIA forecasts. Last week I compared the two for 2025 and called it one year, not a track record. So I pulled the archived STEO PDFs for 2020-2025, wrote four predictions down before reading the 2020-2022 editions, and scored both numbers against what EIA's own Form EIA-860 finally recorded.

For solar in 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024 the two numbers were the same number. The STEO's own capacity table implies same-year solar additions of 13.5, 15.4, 21.4 and 36.4 GW. The developers' plans were 13.5, 15.4, 21.5 and 36.4 GW. Wind agreed within 0.3 GW in 2020-2023. The STEO carried the EIA-860M schedule into its forecast rather than discounting it.

What the scoring shows:

  • Neither was better. Over 12 solar and wind cases, 2020-2025, the STEO was closer to the final in 5, the plan in 6, with one tie. Mean solar error: STEO 6.0 GW, plan 5.7 GW.
  • Both overshot solar almost every year. The plan was above the final in all six years, the STEO in five. In 2022 both were about 10 GW too high (21 GW expected, 11.1 GW built).
  • EIA departed from the schedule three times. 2024 wind: STEO 7.0 GW against 8.2 planned, 5.2 built, so the discount helped. 2025 solar: 25.7 against 32.5, 29.5 built, so it over-corrected and 2025 is the only year the STEO was under the final. 2023 solar: the STEO was above the plan (31.7 against 29.1; 18.9 built).
  • All four pre-registered predictions held, and the result is stronger than I predicted: I expected the STEO to sit within 3 GW of the plan, not to match it to 0.1 GW.
  • Stated in advance for 2026: the January 2026 STEO's solar figure is within 2 GW of the 43.4 GW plan, and the 2026 final comes in below both. Scored when the data arrive.

EIA does not hide this. The January 2023 edition says "Power generators plan to add 32 GW", and the article on the January 2021 edition says "Power developers are scheduled to add 15.4 GW". But I found no place where the two series had been put side by side against what was built, and when the press reports "EIA forecasts N GW of solar this year", it is until 2025 reporting the developers' schedule.

Every figure was read twice (the narrative sentence and the capacity table), the sentence extractor, the CSV, the pre-registration and the limits (net change versus gross additions, sector, rounding) are in the repository: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip/blob/main/docs/steo-vs-plan.md

I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code, data compilation and this post were made with AI agents working in my name.

title: Pricing Flag Incident Reconstruction — Node.js Uptime Failure Alerts from Health Endpoint Metrics API
description:
For a Node.js pricing rollout, use regional health polling for reachability, a metrics poll for bad outcomes, and a heartbeat for missing work; page only when the evidence agrees, but retain every signal under one rollout identifier for reconstruction. The deciding constraint isn't how quickly one probe can turn red. It's whether an engineer can later answer which flag variant, region, and pricing-rule revision produced a wrong checkout result.

Short answer: a simple uptime alert should combine an outside-in health endpoint, outcome metrics, and a scheduled heartbeat, because each observes a different failure boundary and none can reconstruct a flagged pricing incident alone.

This is an experiment note, not a vendor ranking. The tempting first pass is one poll against /health and one alert on any failure. That approach is easy to demo, yet it confuses transport trouble with pricing correctness and creates almost no evidence for an evaluation harness. The better experiment treats the rollout as the unit of analysis: every observation carries a synthetic checkout case, flag variant, rule revision, region, and timestamp. Then the alert links to the observations that justified it.

No magic here.

The incident record we need to reconstruct

A process-level health endpoint can prove that a caller reached the service and received the expected response shape. It cannot, by itself, prove that a flagged pricing rule selected the intended price. A metrics API can show the count or ratio of evaluated outcomes, but aggregation can hide one region or variant. A heartbeat can show that a scheduled synthetic checkout ran, while saying nothing about whether its assertion was correct unless the payload records that assertion.

The useful question is therefore not “is the app up?” It is “what claim does each signal support?” For this rollout, the external poll supports reachability, the outcome poll supports behavioral change, and the heartbeat supports evaluator liveness. An alert becomes actionable when it names the failed claim and preserves the dimensions needed to replay it.

I first reach for the smallest possible signal set because every label and event has storage and review cost. But prompt-cost awareness offers a useful analogy: dropping context makes an evaluation cheaper until the result can no longer be explained. Observability has the same cliff. Removing rule_revision or flag_variant may reduce cardinality, but it also makes two different pricing behaviors look identical during an incident.

Use a compact event contract before choosing a monitor:

Signal Claim it supports Required reconstruction context Misleading green state
Regional health poll The public path answered as expected region, observed status, latency bucket, rollout ID Pricing output is wrong but the route responds
Outcome metrics poll Evaluated results remain within the rollout's tested bounds variant, rule revision, region, evaluation window Aggregation masks a narrow failure
Evaluator heartbeat The scheduled check completed run ID, expected cadence, last completion, rollout ID The check ran but asserted the wrong thing

That table is also an alert review checklist. If a page cannot identify its supported claim, it probably belongs in a dashboard or deployment record instead.

How should a Node.js health endpoint poll metrics API and heartbeat monitor work?

Run the synthetic evaluator from at least the two deployment geographies named in the rollout plan, EU and US in this example. Each run calls the public Node.js health endpoint, evaluates one fixed cart against the active pricing flag, reads the corresponding aggregate outcome window, and emits a completion heartbeat. The evaluation input must be stable enough to replay: currency, item identifiers, quantities, expected variant, and rule revision belong in the test fixture, while secrets and customer data do not belong in logs.

The collector below is Python because notebook-to-prod work benefits from keeping the evaluation record explicit. It uses only the standard library, accepts observations from generic adapters, and returns an alert decision plus the evidence that produced it. Network calls are intentionally outside the function; the hard part is the decision contract, not an SDK.

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Iterable


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Observation:
    region: str
    rollout_id: str
    flag_variant: str
    rule_revision: str
    health_ok: bool
    pricing_assertion_ok: bool
    completed_at: datetime


def evaluate_rollout(
    observations: Iterable[Observation],
    expected_regions: set[str],
    now: datetime,
    heartbeat_window: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=5),
) -> dict:
    recent = [
        item
        for item in observations
        if now - item.completed_at <= heartbeat_window
    ]
    seen_regions = {item.region for item in recent}
    missing_regions = sorted(expected_regions - seen_regions)
    failed = [
        item
        for item in recent
        if not item.health_ok or not item.pricing_assertion_ok
    ]

    return {
        "alert": bool(missing_regions or failed),
        "missing_heartbeats": missing_regions,
        "failed_observations": [asdict(item) for item in failed],
    }


decision = evaluate_rollout(
    observations=[
        Observation(
            region="eu",
            rollout_id="pricing-rule-42",
            flag_variant="candidate",
            rule_revision="r7",
            health_ok=True,
            pricing_assertion_ok=True,
            completed_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        ),
        Observation(
            region="us",
            rollout_id="pricing-rule-42",
            flag_variant="candidate",
            rule_revision="r7",
            health_ok=True,
            pricing_assertion_ok=False,
            completed_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        ),
    ],
    expected_regions={"eu", "us"},
    now=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
)

The focused failure is deliberately boring: EU completes and passes; US completes but fails the pricing assertion. The heartbeat is healthy, so labeling this “monitor down” would destroy information. The health check is also healthy, so labeling it “uptime failure” alone would send the responder toward networking rather than the flagged rule. The decision keeps all three facts and points at candidate, r7, and pricing-rule-42. That is enough to compare the exact fixture against the control variant and the deployment record without guessing which aggregate moved first.

This example doesn't prescribe the pricing threshold. That number must come from the rollout's eval cases and business invariant, and I'm not sure a global percentage can represent mixed currencies, promotions, and tax paths without more domain evidence. Your mileage may vary. Resolve that uncertainty before deployment by defining expected outputs for representative carts, then make the online assertion use the same versioned fixtures.

A pricing flag failure, replayed backward

A single failed poll should become an observation, not automatically a page. Require a policy that accounts for repeated failure, regional agreement, or a pricing assertion failure tied to the candidate flag. The exact threshold is an operational choice; inventing a universal retry count would hide differences in poll interval, traffic, and recovery objectives.

This matters during a flag rollout because causality is easy to overstate. A health probe might fail near the same moment that a pricing metric changes, yet timestamps alone do not prove the rule caused the probe failure. Preserve the raw observations, clock basis, rollout ID, and deployment event. Then let the incident timeline show what happened rather than embedding a causal claim in the alert title.

Keep the page compact — region, failed claim, first and latest observation, variant, revision, and a link to the retained evidence are enough. Keep the evidence richer. OWASP's logging guidance warns that logs may contain sensitive information and calls for attention to data handling, so synthetic identifiers are safer than customer details for this check. Cart fixtures should be designed for evaluation, not copied from production requests.

There is a second privacy surface in the monitoring toolchain itself. Command-line telemetry should respect the DO_NOT_TRACK convention when supported, especially in local eval and CI workflows where an engineer may reasonably disable ancillary usage reporting. This doesn't replace a data inventory. It makes the intent machine-readable at one boundary.

Privacy and operational boundaries

The simplest architecture is a scheduler, two regional runners, an append-only observation store, and a small decision worker. A free or cheap SaaS may host one or more of those pieces, but price should not choose the evidence model. Free tiers, retention, regional execution, and alert routing can change; verify current terms directly before adopting any service.

The catch is that an external hosted monitor is not suitable when policy forbids sending endpoint metadata or evaluation dimensions to a third party. Use a self-hosted runner and store in that case. Conversely, stick with a hosted check when the team cannot operate an independent scheduler reliably; putting the monitor on the same failure boundary as the application creates a blind spot. For strict data residency, confirm where checks execute and where event data is stored rather than treating an “EU region” label as proof of the whole data path.

Do not force all signals into one retention class. High-volume outcome observations may need short detailed retention plus longer aggregates, while alert decisions and rollout metadata are small and valuable for later review. Also budget label cardinality before exposing metrics: rollout_id and bounded variants are useful, but cart or request identifiers can explode the series count. Detailed per-run context fits an event record better than a metric label.

This architecture is intentionally replaceable. The scheduler, probe adapter, metric reader, and notifier meet at plain records, so a team can move between self-hosted and SaaS components without rewriting the evaluation rule. That's more important than finding one service that claims to cover every box.

The pre-rollout scorecard

Before making this pattern the default, measure detection delay by failure class, the fraction of pages with enough context to identify a variant and revision, duplicate pages per incident, evaluator completion rate, and storage volume by dimension. Also replay known-good and deliberately failing fixtures through the decision function in CI. An alert pipeline without an eval harness is still untested application logic.

Track cost as an engineering constraint, not a victory metric. Poll frequency multiplies requests, regional runners multiply them again, and high-cardinality evidence changes storage. Start from the maximum acceptable detection delay and the incident reconstruction window, then calculate the required cadence and retention. Don't choose a one-minute poll merely because a UI defaults to it.

Finally, run a paper reconstruction after the first staged rollout. Give another engineer only the page and retained evidence, and ask them to identify the affected region, flag variant, rule revision, missing or failed signal, and replay fixture. If they must search chat history or infer a revision from wall-clock time, the experiment failed even if every notification arrived.

Ship the signal contract first.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://consoledonottrack.com/

title: Go Retrieval Architecture for Multi-Tenant SaaS Help Center Pagination (10k Tenants)
description:
Short answer: paginate a tenant-scoped, immutable retrieval snapshot, then rerank a bounded candidate set once and carry citation lineage through every page. That decision keeps page boundaries stable while the help-center index changes, which is the condition needed for grounded answers.

The unit of work is a retrieval run, not an HTTP page. Normalize the question, bind it to the authenticated tenant and access policy, retrieve candidates, rerank them, and assign a deterministic order before returning page one. A later request slices that same order. Re-running retrieval for every page feels fresh, but it creates gaps, duplicates, and citations that point at a different revision. This also gives the platform team one place to account for work: candidate retrieval, reranking, snapshot storage, and generation can each have a budget, and the run can be rejected before it consumes the rest of the latency SLO when the candidate cap or tenant quota is already exhausted. That is a capacity decision, not a pagination trick.

I treat a cursor like a distributed job handoff. It is state, not authority. A client can decode ordinary base64, so the token must be signed and its tenant, query fingerprint, policy version, snapshot ID, boundary, page size, and expiry must be checked server-side.

How should pagination shape retrieval architecture for a multi-tenant SaaS help center?

Use two orders. The snapshot order controls continuity; the answer order controls how citations are displayed. Never use a displayed citation number as a pagination key. Every item should retain document ID, document revision, chunk ID, and the exact source span supplied to generation. The Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper describes generation conditioned on retrieved passages; preserving that passage identity across pages is what makes the citation claim auditable.

Choose a stable tie-breaker such as chunk ID after the relevance score. If a reranker has any nondeterminism, persist the resulting ordered IDs for the cursor lifetime rather than calculating page two again. A 50-item page is a practical example, not a universal target; capacity planning should set the candidate cap from labeled relevance tests, memory headroom, and the latency budget for the retrieval SLO.

Small boundary, big blast radius.

Measure it.

The snapshot gives consistency, not unlimited freshness. A newly published article may wait until the next query, while current authorization still has to be applied on each continuation. The catch is that this design is not suitable when revoked content must disappear from an already-running answer immediately; in that case, recheck policy per page and accept that a page can shrink.

What signal exposes citation drift before users report it?

The useful alert names an invariant violation, not a vague “pagination failed.” Track overlap between pages, citations outside the authorized result set, revision mismatches, scope-rejected cursors, expired snapshots, and normal exhaustion as separate outcomes. An exhausted result set is healthy; combining it with errors makes an SLO dashboard lie.

Consider a trace for tenant acme-17. Page one ends at chunk billing:rev-8:0042, and page two starts with the same ID. The trace should show the query hash, policy version, snapshot revision, candidate count, page size, cursor age, returned-ID digest, and cited-ID digest. It does not need the customer's full question or document text in routine metrics. Put replayable detail in access-controlled traces with a retention policy that matches the data classification.

The first check is the cursor invariant: the next ID must be strictly after the stored boundary in snapshot order. If that holds, compare the cited revision with the retrieved revision. If both hold, inspect the answer assembly. This ordering keeps an indexing or authorization defect from being misdiagnosed as a model-quality problem.

A signed Go cursor keeps the boundary explicit

The token below is opaque to callers but explicit to the service. HMAC-SHA256 protects integrity; a key ID allows rotation. The decoder validates structural limits before the caller resolves a snapshot.

package cursor

import (
    "crypto/hmac"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/base64"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Payload struct {
    Version      int    `json:"v"`
    KeyID        string `json:"kid"`
    TenantID     string `json:"tenant"`
    QueryHash    string `json:"query_hash"`
    Policy       string `json:"policy"`
    SnapshotID   string `json:"snapshot"`
    NextOffset   int    `json:"next_offset"`
    PageSize     int    `json:"page_size"`
    ExpiresAtUnix int64  `json:"expires_at"`
}

var (
    ErrMalformed = errors.New("malformed cursor")
    ErrSignature = errors.New("invalid cursor signature")
    ErrExpired   = errors.New("expired cursor")
)

func Encode(p Payload, key []byte) (string, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(p)
    if err != nil { return "", err }
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, key)
    _, _ = mac.Write(body)
    enc := base64.RawURLEncoding
    return enc.EncodeToString(body) + "." + enc.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)), nil
}

func Decode(token string, key []byte, now time.Time) (Payload, error) {
    var p Payload
    parts := strings.Split(token, ".")
    if len(parts) != 2 { return p, ErrMalformed }
    enc := base64.RawURLEncoding
    body, err := enc.DecodeString(parts[0])
    if err != nil { return p, ErrMalformed }
    sig, err := enc.DecodeString(parts[1])
    if err != nil { return p, ErrMalformed }
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, key)
    _, _ = mac.Write(body)
    if !hmac.Equal(sig, mac.Sum(nil)) { return p, ErrSignature }
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &p); err != nil { return p, ErrMalformed }
    if p.Version != 1 || p.PageSize < 1 || p.PageSize > 50 || p.NextOffset < 0 {
        return p, ErrMalformed
    }
    if now.Unix() >= p.ExpiresAtUnix { return p, ErrExpired }
    return p, nil
}

After decoding, compare TenantID, QueryHash, and Policy with values derived from the current request. Resolve SnapshotID, take the slice at NextOffset, filter it through current authorization, and sign the advanced offset. Because the snapshot is immutable, this offset is not an offset into a changing search index.

Continuation must be idempotent. A network retry can submit the same cursor twice, and both responses should describe the same slice while the snapshot is available. Do not consume a single-use token before the response is durable unless the protocol also has a request idempotency key and replay store.

Verification, rollout, and rollback are part of the design

Test malformed signatures, unknown versions, exact-boundary expiry, tenant and query mismatches, and page sizes 0, 1, 50, and 51. Property tests can generate unique ordered IDs, paginate with random legal sizes, and assert that concatenating pages reproduces the snapshot exactly once. An integration test should update the live index after page one and verify that page two still reads the original snapshot while applying current authorization.

Relevance tests belong beside cursor tests. Use a labeled set from the real help-center intents, evaluate retrieval and reranking before generation, and verify that each answer claim is supported by one cited span. Pagination is correct only when changing the boundary does not change that evidence contract.

Roll out with shadow traces, then a small tenant cohort, then broader traffic. Watch duplicate-result rate, cursor rejection by reason, empty continuation pages, snapshot lookup latency, and citation validity. A rollback should stop issuing the new cursor version while retaining its verification key until outstanding tokens expire.

Set alert thresholds against an actionable SLO. One cross-tenant result is an immediate containment event; one expired cursor usually is not. I'm not sure a single citation-coverage threshold transfers from account recovery to configuration help, because acceptable evidence differs by intent class. Per-intent labels and review are what would resolve that uncertainty.

The operational rule is simple: freeze the evidence order for a traversal, recheck authorization, and make every boundary observable. Stick with fresh per-page retrieval only when freshness is more important than continuity and citation reproducibility.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Go crypto/hmac package documentation: https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/hmac
  • Go encoding/base64 package documentation: https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/base64

title: Build a Hiring-Signal Feed from Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and SmartRecruiters (with Python)
description:
"They just opened 6 SDR roles" is one of the strongest timing signals in outbound. If a company is hiring for the team that would use your product, you have a reason to reach out now. Most teams get that signal from LinkedIn scrapes or expensive data vendors. But most tech companies already publish their entire job board as clean JSON through their applicant tracking system (ATS). This tutorial shows how to turn that into a company-level hiring-signal feed you can refresh every week.

The data source: public ATS job-board APIs

Career pages are usually powered by one of a handful of ATSs, and each exposes a public, unauthenticated endpoint meant for embedding job lists:

ATS Public endpoint pattern
Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs?content=true
Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json (EU: api.eu.lever.co)
Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{slug}?includeCompensation=true
SmartRecruiters https://api.smartrecruiters.com/v1/companies/{id}/postings

These are the employer's system of record. Roles show up here first and disappear when they're filled, so the data is fresher and cleaner than most aggregators.

A 20-line DIY version (Greenhouse only) 

import httpx, collections

def greenhouse_signal(slug):
    jobs = httpx.get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs",
                     params={"content": "true"}, timeout=30).json()["jobs"]
    by_dept = collections.Counter(
        (j.get("departments") or [{"name": "Other"}])[0]["name"] for j in jobs)
    sales = [j for j in jobs if any(k in j["title"].lower()
             for k in ("sdr", "bdr", "account executive", "sales"))]
    return {"company": slug, "open_roles": len(jobs),
            "sales_roles": len(sales), "top_departments": by_dept.most_common(5)}

print(greenhouse_signal("stripe"))

That works, but a real feed also needs:

  • detection of which ATS a company uses,
  • Lever's EU cluster and SmartRecruiters' paging,
  • seniority classification,
  • salary parsing,
  • memory between runs, so you can say "+11 roles since last week".

That last part is what makes it a signal rather than just a list.

The hosted version: Hiring Signal Feed

Hiring Signal Feed is an Apify Actor that does all of the above. It returns one row per company, with:

  • open_roles, roles_by_department, roles_by_seniority, remote_roles
  • new_roles_7d and new_roles_30d
  • open_roles_change, roles_added_since_last_run and roles_closed_since_last_run, from a snapshot it keeps for you
  • salary_bands and the ats the company uses

Optionally, it also returns normalized job rows. Pricing is $0.01 per company row (or $0.0015 per job row), plus $0.02 per run.

pip install apify-client pandas

import os, pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
accounts = ["greenhouse:stripe", "greenhouse:discord", "ashby:ramp",
            "https://jobs.lever.co/spotify", "notion"]   # bare names are auto-detected

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/hiring-signal-feed").call(run_input={
    "companies": accounts,
    "outputMode": "companies",
    "titleKeywords": ["sales", "sdr", "bdr", "account executive"],
    "snapshotStoreName": "my-sales-hiring-watch",
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
df = df[df.row_type == "company"]
print(df[["company", "ats", "open_roles", "new_roles_30d", "roles_added_since_last_run"]]
      .sort_values("new_roles_30d", ascending=False))

Because titleKeywords is set, every count is computed only on sales roles. So new_roles_30d = 9 means nine new sales jobs this month.

Score and route accounts 

df["score"] = (df.new_roles_30d.fillna(0) * 2
               + df.roles_added_since_last_run.fillna(0) * 3
               + df.open_roles.fillna(0) * 0.2)
hot = df[df.score >= 10].sort_values("score", ascending=False)
hot.to_csv("hot_accounts.csv", index=False)

Get the actual postings for personalization

Run again with outputMode: "jobs" for just the hot accounts. Each job row includes title, department, location, posted_at, salary and the posting url. That's ideal for a first line like "Saw you're hiring a Founding AE in Austin…".

Make it weekly

  1. Save the input as an Apify Task and attach a Schedule (for example, Mondays at 07:00).
  2. Keep snapshotStoreName the same, so each run diffs against the last one.
  3. Pipe results to your CRM:
    • In Clay, use an HTTP API column that calls run-sync-get-dataset-items.
    • In n8n, Make or Zapier, use the Apify app (Run Actor, then Get dataset items, then upsert into HubSpot or Sheets).

cURL for the HTTP column:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/eligible_fame~hiring-signal-feed/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"companies":["{{domain_or_slug}}"],"outputMode":"companies"}'

Signals beyond sales hiring

The same feed answers other questions. A few common ones:

  • Selling data tools: filter for data engineer and analytics.
  • Selling security: watch for security and GRC roles.
  • Investors: track open_roles_change_pct across a portfolio for early momentum or slowdowns.
  • Recruiters: look for companies whose new_roles_7d jumps in your niche.

A sudden spike in manager and lead/principal seniority often means a new team is being built. That's usually a better trigger than one-off backfills.

Limitations to know

  • It only covers companies that use these four ATSs. That's most venture-backed tech, plus many enterprises on SmartRecruiters, but not every employer. If a company isn't found, you get a free error row.
  • posted_at semantics differ between ATSs. Some companies repost roles, so the snapshot diff (roles_added_since_last_run) is the most reliable "new" signal.
  • Salary only appears where the employer publishes it.

Wrap-up

Hiring data is the cheapest high-intent signal there is, because companies publish it themselves. Whether you write the 20-line script or use Hiring Signal Feed, the key is tracking change over time at the company level, not just collecting rows.

title: How to Get Google Trends Data in Python Without 429 Errors (a pytrends Alternative for 2026)
description:
If you've ever written pytrends.build_payload(...) and seen TooManyRequestsError: The request failed: Google returned a response with code 429, you're not alone. pytrends was archived, Google's official Trends API is still invite-only alpha, and Trends now rate-limits automated traffic aggressively. This tutorial shows a dependable way to pull interest over time, interest by region and related queries for hundreds of keywords from Python, and explains why the usual fixes stop working.

Why pytrends gets 429s

The Google Trends front end calls a handful of internal endpoints:

  1. /trends/api/explore returns a list of "widgets", each with a short-lived token.
  2. /trends/api/widgetdata/multiline returns the timeline.
  3. /trends/api/widgetdata/comparedgeo returns regions.
  4. /trends/api/widgetdata/relatedsearches returns related queries and topics.

Every response starts with an anti-JSON-hijacking prefix ()]}'), and every call needs a valid NID cookie. When you send many requests from one IP, Google returns 429 or redirects you to /sorry/. The common advice of time.sleep(60) plus retries=3 works for ten keywords. It doesn't work for a thousand, and it doesn't work from cloud IPs at all, because those are often blocked from the very first request.

What actually works is:

  • a fresh session (cookie plus new tokens) after each block,
  • rotating egress IPs,
  • per-widget retries, so one failed section doesn't throw away the whole query,
  • honest status reporting, so you know which rows are complete.

You can build that yourself, or use a hosted Actor that already does it.

Option A: a hosted API (about 5 minutes)

Reliable Google Trends API on Apify handles the warmup, proxy rotation, retries and residential fallback. It charges $0.002 per successful query, and failed queries are free. In our 34-query gate runs on Apify, it returned 34 of 34 results in every proxy mode we tested.

Install the client:

pip install apify-client pandas

Run a comparison:

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/reliable-google-trends").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": [
        "chatgpt, claude, gemini",     # one query comparing 3 terms
        "air fryer",                   # a second query
    ],
    "geo": "US",
    "timeframe": "today 12-m",
    "interestOverTime": True,
    "interestByRegion": True,
    "relatedQueries": True,
})

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
for r in rows:
    print(r["keywords"], r["status"], r["errors"])

Turn the timeline into a DataFrame 

def timeline_df(row):
    recs = [{"date": p["time"], **p["values"]} for p in row["interest_over_time"]]
    return pd.DataFrame(recs).set_index("date")

df = timeline_df(rows[0])
print(df.tail())
df.plot(title="ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini, US, 12 months")

Rising queries (breakouts) 

for kw, rq in rows[1]["related_queries"].items():
    for q in rq["rising"][:10]:
        print(kw, "->", q["query"], q["formatted_value"])

Bulk keyword lists

Each searchTerms entry is its own query, so you can pass 500 entries in one run. To set different options for each query, use customQueries:

run_input = {"customQueries": [
    {"keywords": "bitcoin, ethereum", "geo": "GB", "timeframe": "today 5-y", "property": "news"},
    {"keywords": "lofi music", "property": "youtube"},
]}

Every run also writes a RUN_SUMMARY record to the key-value store with the success rate and block counts:

summary = client.key_value_store(run["defaultKeyValueStoreId"]).get_record("RUN_SUMMARY")["value"]
print(summary)

Option B: roll your own (what you need to handle)

If you'd rather run it yourself, here's the minimum:

import httpx, json, time, random

def warm(client):
    # A headers-only request is enough to obtain an NID cookie
    with client.stream("GET", "https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?geo=US") as r:
        pass

def explore(client, kw, geo="US", tf="today 12-m"):
    req = {"comparisonItem": [{"keyword": kw, "geo": geo, "time": tf}],
           "category": 0, "property": ""}
    r = client.get("https://trends.google.com/trends/api/explore",
                   params={"hl": "en-US", "tz": 0, "req": json.dumps(req)})
    if r.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("blocked")
    return json.loads(r.text[r.text.index("{"):])["widgets"]

From here you still need to: call each widget endpoint with its token; rotate the session and the IP whenever you get a 429 or /sorry/; back off with jitter; and treat related topics as optional (Google often withholds them from sessions it labels USER_TYPE_SCRAPER). In practice the proxy bill and the maintenance cost far more than the code.

Gotchas that apply either way

  • Values are relative (0–100), not search volume. Only compare keywords that were in the same query.
  • More than 5 keywords? Use a shared anchor term in every batch (for example "weather") and rescale each batch against it.
  • Timeframe strings follow the Trends URL format: now 7-d, today 3-m, today 5-y, all, 2024-01-01 2024-06-30.
  • Last data point is often is_partial: true. Drop it before you fit a forecast.

Schedule it

In the Apify console, open the Actor, save your input as a Task, and add a Schedule (for example, daily at 06:00). Then use a webhook or the n8n/Make/Zapier Apify app to push new rows into Google Sheets or your warehouse.

Wrap-up

pytrends taught a generation of analysts to love Trends data, but the 429 wall is real. If you need a few queries a week, a careful DIY script with backoff can be enough. If you need hundreds of keywords on a schedule, without babysitting proxies, try Reliable Google Trends API. It's pay-per-result, and failed queries are free.

title: What I Learned Building the Cloud Resume Challenge on Azure
description:
What I Learned Building the Cloud Resume Challenge on Azure

I'm working toward a cloud and systems administration career, and I wanted a project that proved I can do more than pass certification exams. So I took on the Cloud Resume Challenge (Azure): built a resume website, add a live visitor counter, and do it the way a real team would, with infrastructure as code, automated pipelines, and good security habits.

Live site: https://stresumelvoc8r.z1.web.core.windows.net/
Code: frontend · backend

Below is what I built, what broke along the way, and how each lesson connects to the jobs I'm applying for.

What I built

  • Frontend: an HTML/CSS resume hosted as a static website on Azure Storage.
  • Visitor counter: a small JavaScript file calls an API every time the page loads.
  • API: a Python Azure Function on the Flex Consumption plan (serverless, scales to zero).
  • Database: Cosmos DB (NoSQL, serverless) stores one record: the visitor count.
  • Infrastructure as code: everything in Azure is defined in Terraform.
  • CI/CD: GitHub Actions pipelines test, plan, and deploy every change, and production changes wait for my approval.

The rule I set for myself: no passwords, keys, or secrets stored anywhere. Not in the code, not in GitHub, not in the database connection.

Lesson 1: Infrastructure as code beats clicking around the portal

I've built plenty of things by clicking through the Azure portal. Terraform changed how I think about it. My entire environment (storage, database, function, monitoring, permissions) lives in text files I can read, review, and rebuild.

The concept that clicked for me was Terraform state. Terraform keeps a record of what it has built. I stored that state remotely in an Azure Storage account with versioning and soft delete turned on, so a mistake can be rolled back.

On the job: any team managing more than a handful of resources needs repeatable builds. Being able to say "I can define and rebuild an environment from code" is the difference between an admin who maintains things and one who can scale them.

Lesson 2: Pipelines without stored secrets (OIDC)

The old way to let GitHub deploy to Azure is to create a service principal, copy its secret, and paste it into GitHub. That secret can leak, and it expires at the worst possible time.

Instead I used OIDC (workload identity federation). GitHub proves to Azure who it is with a short-lived token, and Azure trusts that token only if it comes from my repo, in a pull request or the production environment. No secret exists to steal.

What broke: my first deploy failed with AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record. The error showed that GitHub's token now includes the numeric IDs of my account and repo, not just their names. That stops someone from deleting a repo and recreating one with the same name to hijack the trust. My Azure configuration only trusted the old name-only format. Once I added credentials matching the new format, it worked.

On the job: reading an authentication error carefully and comparing "what was sent" with "what was expected" is everyday identity troubleshooting, the same skill I use for Entra ID sign-in issues.

Lesson 3: Least privilege, for real

It's easy to give a pipeline Owner and move on. I didn't. The pipeline's identity is:

  • Contributor on one resource group, not the whole subscription.
  • Allowed to grant permissions only from a short approved list of data roles, enforced with an Azure ABAC condition. Without that limit, an identity that can assign roles could make itself Owner.

On the job: "who has access to what, and why" comes up in every audit and security review. I can now explain role scope, privilege escalation risk, and how to prevent it, not just in theory.

Lesson 4: Managed identities mean no database keys

The Function App connects to Cosmos DB with a managed identity: Azure gives the app its own identity, and I granted it a database role. Cosmos DB has key-based access disabled entirely, so even if someone found my code, there's no key in it to use.

On the job: removing stored credentials from apps is one of the most effective security improvements an admin can make, and managed identities are how you do it in Azure.

Lesson 5: MFA isn't just for the portal anymore

Partway through, every Azure CLI command started failing with AADSTS50076, an MFA requirement, and it never actually prompted me for MFA. The cause: on Windows, the CLI was quietly reusing a cached sign-in through the Windows account broker, and that cached sign-in had no MFA. Clearing the cached tokens and signing in with az login --use-device-code forced a proper MFA sign-in.

On the job: Microsoft now requires MFA for Azure management from the CLI and other tools, not just the portal. When scripts or users suddenly fail to authenticate, knowing about cached tokens and broker sign-ins saves hours.

Lesson 6: The small stuff breaks things

Some of my most useful lessons were the least glamorous:

  • Line endings: Windows saves files with different line endings than Linux. A bash script saved the Windows way fails with confusing errors. A .gitattributes file fixed it for good.
  • Git Bash path conversion: Git Bash on Windows quietly rewrites anything starting with /, which broke Azure resource IDs until I turned that behavior off.
  • Ignored files don't reach the pipeline: my Terraform variables file worked on my PC but not in GitHub Actions, because my .gitignore (correctly) excluded it. I passed the value as a GitHub variable instead.

On the job: most real outages aren't exotic. They're a setting, a path, or an assumption about which machine a file lives on. Patience and methodical checking matter more than knowing everything.

Lesson 7: Pull requests and approval gates

Every change goes through the same path:

  1. Open a pull request, and the pipeline runs a Terraform plan that shows exactly what would change.
  2. Merge, and the deploy pauses for my approval.
  3. Approve, and it deploys.

I also learned to wait for green checks before merging. I merged a failing change once, and the deploy failed in exactly the way the check had warned me it would.

On the job: this is change management. Reviewing a change before it runs, and having an approval step for production, is the same idea as a change advisory process, just automated.

Lesson 8: Writing code I can test

The counter logic is small, but I wrote it carefully:

  • It uses a Cosmos DB atomic increment, so two visitors arriving at the same moment can't overwrite each other's count.
  • The logic is separate from the web layer, so I could write pytest tests that use fake (mocked) database objects. The tests run on every pull request without touching Azure.
  • Errors return a generic message to the browser, and the details go to Application Insights for me to investigate.

On the job: even as an admin, I write scripts that other people depend on. Testing them before they run in production, and logging errors somewhere useful, is a habit that prevents incidents.

How this applies to the jobs I'm applying for

What I did in this project Where it shows up at work
Defined infrastructure in Terraform Building and rebuilding environments consistently; documenting what exists
OIDC and managed identities Removing stored passwords and keys; securing automation accounts
Scoped roles and ABAC conditions Access reviews, audits, least-privilege design in Entra ID and Azure
Troubleshot MFA and token errors Sign-in and Conditional Access issues for users and service accounts
Pull requests and approval gates Change management and peer review
CI/CD pipelines Automating repetitive admin tasks safely
Monitoring with Application Insights Finding the cause of failures quickly
Serverless and pay-per-use services Keeping cloud costs low and predictable

What's next

  • Custom domain with HTTPS through Cloudflare.
  • An end-to-end test that checks the live site and API after every deploy.
  • A containerized app on Kubernetes, to build on what I learned here.

If you're working through the Cloud Resume Challenge yourself, my advice is: read the error message twice before searching it. Almost every problem I hit was explained right there in the error, once I slowed down enough to compare what was sent with what was expected.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn.

title: TanStack Start vs Next.js in 2026: Same App, Real Benchmarks
description:
I built the same small store in TanStack Start 1.0 and Next.js 16.4 and benchmarked both on one machine. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

TanStack Start vs Next.js got a lot more interesting on October 13, 2026, when TanStack Start 1.0 went stable. I built the same small store in both frameworks, with the same routes, data, components and Tailwind styles, and measured them on one machine. TanStack Start served 2.9× more server-rendered list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more JSON API calls per second than Next.js 16.4. It also shipped 20% less JavaScript and built 3.9× faster. Next.js still won where it was designed to win: a prerendered page, and a far bigger set of built-in tools.

Here are the numbers, how I got them, and how I'd choose between the two in 2026.

TL;DR: is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes, by a wide margin in my tests. Every route that rendered per request was 2.9× to 8.6× faster on TanStack Start, with much lower tail latency. On the client the gap is smaller: 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript against 135 KB, and an interactive button 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU. Next.js led only on its prerendered home page, because it serves static HTML while Start rendered that page on every request.

Same app, Node 24.22, 2 cores Next.js 16.4.2 TanStack Start 1.169.3 Difference
Home page, req/s 3,220 (static) 2,920 (SSR) Next +10%
Product list, 100 items, SSR, req/s 220 637 Start 2.9×
Product page, SSR, req/s 512 2,341 Start 4.6×
JSON API route, req/s 2,165 18,515 Start 8.6×
p99 latency, product list 754 ms 194 ms Start 3.9× lower
Server memory at idle 94 MB 60 MB Start −36%
Client JS on /products, gzip 135 KB, 7 files 109 KB, 3 files Start −20%
Interactive button, 4× CPU throttle 324 ms 289 ms Start −35 ms
Production build 4.86 s 1.26 s Start 3.9×
Dev server, first page 2.96 s 1.52 s Start 1.9×
Deploy output 38 MB 1.4 MB Start 27× smaller

If you mostly ship content that can be cached, these server numbers matter less. If you run a dashboard, an API-heavy app or anything that renders per user, they matter a lot.

What is TanStack Start?

TanStack Start is a full-stack React framework built on TanStack Router. It adds server-side rendering, streaming, typed server functions, server routes for raw HTTP and middleware, and it builds with Vite (or Rsbuild). The 1.0 announcement calls it ready for production after a long release-candidate phase, and the first stable package was @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0.

The big design difference from Next.js is the component model. In Next.js App Router, pages and layouts are React Server Components by default and you opt into client code with "use client". In Start, components are ordinary React components that render on the server and hydrate on the client. You put work on the server explicitly with createServerFn() or a route loader. Server Components in Start exist, but they are experimental and off by default, so treat them as a preview, not a reason to pick it.

How I benchmarked TanStack Start and Next.js

I wanted a fair app, not a hello world. Both apps have:

  • Home page: a heading and a link. Next.js prerenders it as static HTML; Start has no static prerender by default, so it renders it per request.
  • Product list: 100 products rendered on the server on every request, with a timestamp so neither framework can cache it. In Next.js that's an async Server Component with await connection(). In Start it's a route loader calling a GET server function.
  • Product page: one product plus a client-side "Add to cart" counter, so both frameworks must hydrate interactive code.
  • JSON API: a route returning 20 products. A Next.js route handler with dynamic = "force-dynamic", and a Start server route.

Versions: Next.js 16.4.2 with Turbopack and React 19.3.0, TanStack Start 1.169.3 with Vite 8.3.4, Nitro and React 19.3.1, Tailwind 4 in both. Both ran on Node 24.22 in production mode: Next.js as its standalone server.js, Start as its Nitro Node output. A quick check with next start gave the same results (2,377 req/s on the API, 534 on the product page).

The server was pinned to 2 CPU cores with taskset, and the load generator oha ran on 6 other cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM. Each run used 64 connections for 10 seconds after a 4 second warm-up, and every number is the median of 3 runs on a fresh server process. All runs returned 100% HTTP 200. Client metrics came from Playwright and Chromium: script bytes on each page (gzip level 6), and the time from navigation to a working button click with a 4× CPU slowdown, median of 6 runs.

This is a small synthetic store, not your app. Your database, auth and caching will usually dominate. Treat these as the cost of the framework layer itself.

Server performance: how many requests can each handle?

Server-rendered pages. The product list is where per-request rendering cost shows. Start served 637 pages per second with a p99 of 194 ms; Next.js served 220 with a p99 of 754 ms. On the lighter product page, Start served 2,341 per second versus 512. My reading is that Next.js does more work per request: it renders the Server Component tree to the RSC payload and then renders HTML from it, and it embeds that payload in the page. You can see that in the HTML: the 100-item list was 92 KB raw in Next.js and 60 KB in Start (8.5 KB versus 6.4 KB gzipped).

API routes. This was the biggest gap. A Start server route answered 18,515 requests per second; a Next.js route handler answered 2,165. That's 8.6×. Start's server routes are close to a plain handler on Nitro, while every Next.js request goes through the full Next server and router. For context, Hono on raw Node served 73,000 JSON requests per second on the same 2 cores in my Hono vs Express benchmark, so neither framework is the right place for a hot, high-volume API.

Static pages. Next.js led here: 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second. Next serves the prerendered HTML file, while Start rendered the home page with React each time and still came within 10%. This is the important caveat for Next.js: anything you can make static or cache, with "use cache" or prerendering, skips most of the per-request cost. I covered how to do that in Next.js "use cache".

Memory. Next.js idled at 94 MB and peaked at about 504 MB under the SSR list load. Start idled at 60 MB and peaked at 363 MB. Both are fine for a small VPS, but on a 1 GB box running several apps, Start leaves more room.

Bundle size, hydration and client navigation

On /products, Next.js loaded 7 script files totalling 135 KB gzipped (453 KB raw). Start loaded 3 files totalling 109 KB gzipped (337 KB raw). Most of both is React and React DOM, so the difference is framework runtime: about 26 KB gzipped.

With Chromium's CPU throttled 4×, the "Add to cart" button on a fresh product page became interactive in 289 ms on Start and 324 ms on Next.js. Client-side navigation from the list to a product took 160 ms on Start versus 182 ms on Next.js. Start made 2 requests per navigation (the route chunk and the server function), while Next.js made about 10.

So on the client, Start is faster, but not dramatically. On a real app with a large component library, your own code will outweigh this 26 KB.

Build time, dev server and deployment

Production build: Next.js took 4.86 s (5 clean runs, including its TypeScript check) and Start took 1.26 s with Vite. Running tsc --noEmit separately on the Start app took another 1.54 s, so even with a type check added, Start's build was about 1.7× faster.

Dev server: from launching the dev command to the first fully rendered /products page, Next.js took 2.96 s cold and 2.91 s warm. Start with Vite took 1.52 s cold and 1.45 s warm.

Deploy output: Next.js standalone output was 38 MB because it traces and copies the parts of node_modules it needs, including Next itself. Start's Nitro output was 1.4 MB, fully bundled. In a Docker image that difference is real, but small next to a Node base image. My Next.js Dockerfile guide shows how to keep the Next.js side lean. Installed node_modules were 354 MB for the Next.js app and 152 MB for Start.

Developer experience: what's different day to day?

Numbers aside, the daily work feels different:

  • Data loading. Next.js fetches data inside async Server Components. Start uses route loaders and server functions, usually with TanStack Query for client caching. If you already use TanStack Query, Start will feel natural.
  • Server code. Next.js has Server Actions and route handlers; I compared them in Server Actions vs Route Handlers. Start has createServerFn() with validators, GET or POST, and middleware that runs on both client and server.
  • Type safety. Start's router generates types for every path, param and search param, so a broken link is a type error. Next.js has opt-in typedRoutes, which covers links but not validated search params.
  • Caching. Next.js has a framework cache (Cache Components, "use cache", cacheLife). Start has no server data cache: you use HTTP headers, a CDN, or your own store. That's simpler to reason about and more work for content sites.
  • Built-ins. Next.js ships next/image, next/font, metadata APIs and a huge ecosystem of examples. In Start you bring your own image and font handling.
  • Hosting. Next.js runs best on Vercel and works anywhere with Node or Docker, as I do with Coolify. Start deploys through Nitro or plugins to Node, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

One gotcha I hit in Next.js: my generated project wired Tailwind 4 through a turbopack.rules entry for *.css in next.config.ts (the @tailwindcss/turbopack loader). When I overwrote the config to add output: "standalone", the CSS came out empty and the Tailwind compiler ended up in the client bundle: 280 KB of gzipped JavaScript instead of 135 KB. If you edit that file, keep the rules block, and check your bundle after config changes.

Should I switch from Next.js to TanStack Start?

Pick TanStack Start if:

  • your app renders per user or per request (dashboards, SaaS, internal tools), so server cost matters
  • you want typed routes and search params, explicit server functions and no framework-level cache
  • you like Vite, or want to deploy to Cloudflare Workers or a small VPS without Vercel
  • you already use TanStack Query, Router or Table

Stay with or pick Next.js if:

  • your site is mostly content that can be prerendered or cached, where Next served static pages fastest
  • you rely on React Server Components today, or on next/image, next/font and the metadata API
  • hiring, templates and third-party SDK examples matter more than raw speed
  • you host on Vercel and want its integration

For an existing, healthy Next.js app, I wouldn't rewrite just for these numbers. Cache what you can first. For a new interactive app, Start 1.0 is now a serious default. The official TanStack Start vs Next.js page has a fair feature-by-feature comparison too.

How do I migrate from Next.js to TanStack Start?

The rough steps I'd follow, based on building the same app in both:

  1. Move app/ routes to src/routes/ files using createFileRoute. Dynamic segments change from [id] to $id.
  2. Replace data fetching in async Server Components with a route loader that calls a createServerFn().
  3. Remove "use client" directives. Every component in Start is a normal component.
  4. Turn route handlers into server routes with server: { handlers: { GET } }.
  5. Replace Server Actions with POST server functions, and add an input validator.
  6. Replace next/link with TanStack Router's Link (to plus typed params), and next/image and next/font with your own components or plain tags.
  7. Add Nitro (or a hosting plugin) to vite.config.ts for your deploy target.

Migrate one representative route end to end first, including auth and a mutation, before committing the whole app.

Common mistakes when comparing Next.js and TanStack Start

  • Comparing a static Next.js page to an SSR Start page and calling Next faster. Make the rendering mode the same on both sides, or report it, as I did for the home page.
  • Forgetting to copy .next/static into the standalone folder. Next's standalone server doesn't serve client assets without it, so hydration silently never happens. My first client test showed a 30 second timeout for exactly this reason.
  • Benchmarking dev mode. Always build and run with NODE_ENV=production.
  • Running the load generator on the same cores as the server. Pin them apart or your numbers mostly measure contention.
  • Leaving devtools in production. Check that router and query devtools aren't in your client bundle.

Key takeaways

  • TanStack Start 1.0 went stable on October 13, 2026, and its Server Components support is still experimental.
  • On the same app and 2 cores, Start served 2.9× more SSR list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more API calls than Next.js 16.4.
  • Next.js won on its prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 req/s, so caching closes the gap for content you can cache.
  • Start's p99 on the 100-item SSR page was 194 ms versus 754 ms, and it idled at 60 MB versus 94 MB.
  • Start shipped 20% less client JavaScript (109 KB vs 135 KB gzipped) and became interactive 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU.
  • Start built in 1.26 s versus 4.86 s and its dev server answered in 1.5 s versus 3.0 s.
  • Choose Start for per-request, interactive apps and typed routing; choose Next.js for cacheable content, RSC and its built-ins.

Related: if you're weighing other parts of your toolchain too, see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint and React Compiler in Next.js.

FAQ

Is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes in my tests. With the same app on 2 CPU cores, TanStack Start 1.169.3 served 637 server-rendered list pages per second versus 220 for Next.js 16.4.2, 2,341 product pages versus 512, and 18,515 API requests versus 2,165. Next.js was faster only on a prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second.

Is TanStack Start stable and production ready?

Yes. TanStack Start 1.0 was announced as stable on October 13, 2026, with @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0 as the first stable release. Its React Server Components support is still experimental and off by default.

Does TanStack Start ship less JavaScript than Next.js?

Somewhat. On the same product list page, TanStack Start loaded 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript in 3 files and Next.js loaded 135 KB in 7 files. Most of both is React itself, so the framework difference was about 26 KB gzipped.

Does TanStack Start support React Server Components?

Yes, but experimentally. You opt in with @vitejs/plugin-rsc and rsc: { enabled: true } in the tanstackStart plugin, and the docs say the feature will stay experimental into early v1. Start's normal SSR, loaders and server functions don't need Server Components.

Should I migrate my Next.js app to TanStack Start?

Not just for speed if the app is healthy. Cache or prerender what you can in Next.js first, since static pages were Next's fastest case. Consider Start for new interactive apps, apps that render per user, or teams that want typed routes and search params, Vite and simple hosting.

How much faster does TanStack Start build than Next.js?

In my test app, vite build for TanStack Start took 1.26 s and next build took 4.86 s, averaged over 5 clean runs. next build includes a TypeScript check; adding tsc --noEmit (1.54 s) to the Start build still left it about 1.7× faster.

Can TanStack Start be self-hosted?

Yes. It builds through Nitro to a self-contained Node server, which was 1.4 MB in my test versus 38 MB for the Next.js standalone output. It also deploys to Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

What is the difference between Next.js Server Actions and TanStack Start server functions?

Next.js Server Actions are tied to forms and React's pending and error states. TanStack Start server functions are typed RPC calls created with createServerFn, can use GET or POST, accept an input validator and compose middleware that runs on both client and server. Both need runtime validation and server-side authorization.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Integrating OpenAI Function Calling with Meta WhatsApp Cloud API
description:
Traditional chatbot flows rely on static decision trees (Press 1 for Sales, Press 2 for Support). While predictable, they create severe user friction when a prospect wants a personalized answer or needs to check order status, book an appointment, or check flight updates.

By integrating OpenAI's Function Calling (Tools API) directly into your WhatsApp Cloud API webhook, your AI agent can converse naturally while executing backend API calls deterministically.

In this architecture guide, we demonstrate how to connect an LLM tool loop with WhatsApp interactive messaging.

The Function Calling Execution Loop

When a user messages on WhatsApp:

  1. Ingest Inbound Message: Webhook receives the message payload from Meta.
  2. Query Model with Tool Declarations: Pass the user's message along with defined tool schemas (e.g., check_order_status, book_demo_slot).
  3. Model Tool Decision: If the user intends to perform an action, the LLM emits a tool_calls payload instead of raw text.
  4. Execute Internal Business Logic: Run the database lookup or CRM update with the LLM's structured arguments.
  5. Synthesize Final Natural Response: Pass the tool output back to the LLM to format a friendly WhatsApp response.
  6. Dispatch WhatsApp Message: Send the formatted text or interactive button back via WhatsApp Cloud API.

Step 1: Defining the Tool Schema

Declare your functions using JSON schema:

const tools = [
  {
    type: "function",
    function: {
      name: "check_order_status",
      description: "Lookup the real-time shipping status and tracking code for an order",
      parameters: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
          order_id: {
            type: "string",
            description: "The 6 to 8 character order tracking ID, e.g. ORD-1092"
          }
        },
        required: ["order_id"]
      }
    }
  }
];

Step 2: The Agentic Execution Function 

import OpenAI from "openai";
const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY });

async function handleWhatsAppAgentQuery(customerPhone, userMessage) {
  const messages = [
    { role: "system", content: "You are the helpful customer service assistant for our store on WhatsApp. Keep responses concise, warm, and mobile-friendly." },
    { role: "user", content: userMessage }
  ];

  const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({
    model: "gpt-4o-mini",
    messages: messages,
    tools: tools,
    tool_choice: "auto"
  });

  const responseMessage = response.choices[0].message;

  // Check if model decided to call a function
  if (responseMessage.tool_calls) {
    for (const toolCall of responseMessage.tool_calls) {
      if (toolCall.function.name === "check_order_status") {
        const args = JSON.parse(toolCall.function.arguments);

        // Execute real DB query
        const orderData = await queryOrderDatabase(args.order_id);

        messages.push(responseMessage);
        messages.push({
          role: "tool",
          tool_call_id: toolCall.id,
          content: JSON.stringify(orderData)
        });

        // Get final answer from LLM
        const secondResponse = await openai.chat.completions.create({
          model: "gpt-4o-mini",
          messages: messages
        });

        return secondResponse.choices[0].message.content;
      }
    }
  }

  return responseMessage.content;
}

Step 3: Guardrails and Human Agent Handoff

Even the best LLMs can misunderstand complex edge cases. In production:

  • Set strict confidence thresholds: If the user expresses frustration or asks to "talk to human", trigger an immediate handoff flag.
  • Lock session context: Store the conversation history in Redis or PostgreSQL keyed by the user's phone number with a 24-hour expiration window.

Turnkey AI Agents with AI Soul

Rather than maintaining custom OpenAI token budgets, rate limit queues, vector embeddings, and WebSocket handoffs yourself, platforms like AI Soul offer an enterprise-ready solution.

With AI Soul's WhatsApp AI Chatbot, you can train autonomous LLM agents directly on your website URL, product catalogs, and PDFs with zero code. Furthermore, AI Soul's built-in Conversational CRM provides visual Kanban deal pipelines and multi-agent shared team inboxes so your human team can intervene whenever needed.

Summary

OpenAI Function Calling transforms WhatsApp bots from simple FAQ repeaters into autonomous digital employees capable of booking appointments, qualifying B2B prospects, and recovering lost sales.
