title: Model Pest Control So Activity Has a Location and an Owner: Device, DeviceCheck, Sighting and CorrectiveAction
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In most factory systems, pest control does not exist as data. It is a PDF the contractor emails once a month, filed in a shared folder that nobody queries. Finance sees a supplier invoice. Quality sees a binder. Nobody can answer a simple question like "which bait station has shown activity three visits in a row, and what did we do about it?"

That is a modelling problem before it is a hygiene problem.

The standards are explicit about what the records should prove. The Codex General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969), section 11.2, says that even when monitoring is outsourced, the food business should review monitoring reports and make sure corrective action is taken; that the cause of an infestation should be identified; and that records should be kept of infestation, monitoring and eradication. In Kenya, the Food, Drugs and Chemical Substances (Food Hygiene) Regulations, 1978 require effective measures to exclude pests from food areas and pesticide use that does not contaminate food or packaging (regulation 12).

"Review", "cause", "corrective action" and "records" are all things a schema can enforce. Here is how I would model it for a food or agro ERP.

The entities 

Site ─┬─ Zone (EXTERNAL | INTERNAL_NON_FOOD | INTERNAL_FOOD)
      │     └─ Device (bait station, trap, insect light trap) — numbered, on a map
      │           └─ DeviceCheck (who, when, finding)
      ├─ Sighting (staff report between visits)
      ├─ PestFinding (opened from a check or sighting)
      │     ├─ RootCause (ENTRY_POINT | FOOD_SOURCE | HARBOURAGE | INCOMING_MATERIAL)
      │     ├─ CorrectiveAction (owner, due date, closed_at, verified_by)
      │     ├─ Treatment (product, registration ref, quantity, applicator)
      │     └─ LotExposure → Lot (hold / release)
      └─ MonthlyReview (trend sign-off)

Zone and Device 

CREATE TABLE zone (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  site_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES site(id),
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  zone_type   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (zone_type IN ('EXTERNAL','INTERNAL_NON_FOOD','INTERNAL_FOOD'))
);

CREATE TABLE device (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  zone_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  code        TEXT NOT NULL,           -- the number painted on the device
  device_type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (device_type IN ('TOXIC_BAIT','NON_TOXIC_MONITOR','SNAP_TRAP','GLUE_BOARD','INSECT_LIGHT_TRAP')),
  map_x       NUMERIC, map_y NUMERIC,
  active      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  UNIQUE (zone_id, code)
);

The zone type matters because Codex says traps and detectors should be designed and located so they cannot contaminate raw materials, products or facilities. Make the policy a constraint, not a memo: for example, reject TOXIC_BAIT in an INTERNAL_FOOD zone with a trigger or an application-level rule your site agrees with its qualified provider.

DeviceCheck: append-only 

CREATE TABLE device_check (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  device_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES device(id),
  checked_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  checked_by  TEXT NOT NULL,           -- staff or contractor technician
  source      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (source IN ('INTERNAL','CONTRACTOR')),
  finding     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (finding IN ('NO_ACTIVITY','BAIT_TAKEN','DROPPINGS','CATCH','DAMAGED','MISSING')),
  catch_count INT,
  notes       TEXT
);

Two design choices carry most of the value:

  1. One row per device per check. If the contractor's report is a PDF, import it into rows. A PDF cannot tell you a station's history; rows can.
  2. No updates. A check is evidence. Corrections are new rows with a reference to the one they correct.

Sightings close the gap between visits 

CREATE TABLE sighting (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  zone_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  seen_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  reported_by TEXT NOT NULL,
  pest_type   TEXT NOT NULL,           -- rodent, cockroach, stored-product insect, bird, fly...
  description TEXT
);

This is the cheapest table in the schema and the one that changes behaviour most: a phone form on the floor that anyone can submit.

Findings must end in a cause and a verified action 

CREATE TABLE pest_finding (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  opened_from   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (opened_from IN ('DEVICE_CHECK','SIGHTING','INTAKE','AUDIT')),
  source_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  opened_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  root_cause    TEXT CHECK (root_cause IN ('ENTRY_POINT','FOOD_SOURCE','HARBOURAGE','INCOMING_MATERIAL','UNKNOWN')),
  status        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN' CHECK (status IN ('OPEN','ACTION_PENDING','VERIFIED','CLOSED'))
);

CREATE TABLE corrective_action (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  finding_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  action      TEXT NOT NULL,           -- "fit door brush, side door B"
  owner       TEXT NOT NULL,
  due_date    DATE NOT NULL,
  closed_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  verified_by TEXT,
  verified_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);

The business rule: a finding cannot move to CLOSED while root_cause is null or any action is unverified. That single rule encodes the Codex expectation that the cause is identified and corrective action taken, and it stops the classic failure where the same station shows activity every month and the only action is "bait replaced".

Treatments carry the chemical audit trail 

CREATE TABLE treatment (
  id               BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  finding_id       BIGINT REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  applied_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  product_name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  registration_ref TEXT NOT NULL,      -- registration details as recorded from the regulator's list
  quantity         NUMERIC NOT NULL,
  unit             TEXT NOT NULL,
  zone_id          BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  applicator       TEXT NOT NULL,
  applicator_cert  TEXT                -- evidence of the provider's qualification/certificate
);

In Kenya, the Pest Control Products (Inspection and Certification) Regulations, 2024 set qualifications for the person in charge of a pest control service (regulation 12(6)) and require a Board certificate for fumigation with Restricted Class 1 products (regulation 14). Storing the evidence next to each treatment is far easier than reconstructing it during an audit.

LotExposure links hygiene to traceability 

CREATE TABLE lot_exposure (
  finding_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  lot_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES lot(id),
  decision    TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (decision IN ('HOLD','RELEASED','REWORK','WRITE_OFF')),
  decided_by  TEXT NOT NULL,
  decided_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (finding_id, lot_id)
);

When a finding is in or next to an INTERNAL_FOOD zone, query which lots were in that zone during the exposure window and propose holds. A WRITE_OFF decision should post a stock adjustment with a pest-damage reason code, so it does not show up later as an unexplained variance.

Queries that answer real questions

Stations with activity on three or more consecutive checks:

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT device_id, checked_at,
         finding <> 'NO_ACTIVITY' AS active,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY checked_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM device_check
)
SELECT device_id
FROM ordered
WHERE rn <= 3
GROUP BY device_id
HAVING bool_and(active);

Findings older than 14 days still waiting on an action:

SELECT f.id, f.opened_at, a.action, a.owner, a.due_date
FROM pest_finding f
JOIN corrective_action a ON a.finding_id = f.id
WHERE a.verified_at IS NULL
  AND f.opened_at < now() - interval '14 days';

The monthly review becomes a report on those two queries plus trend charts by zone, signed off as a monthly_review row.

Where IoT fits, and where it does not

Connected traps and insect light traps with catch counters can write device_check rows automatically. Treat them as another source, not a replacement for people walking the building. A sensor will not notice the torn mesh or the pallet stacked against the wall; the weekly entry-point walk still produces corrective_action rows.

Records

Design these tables for retention and audit, not edits. The goal is that, on any given day, you can show an inspector or auditor the map, the checks, the findings, the causes, the actions and who verified them.

The full operations checklist for factory teams, with an FAQ, is here: Pest Control Checklist.

title: ChaosProxy: Bulletproof Your Microservices with Automated Fault Injection and Network Chaos Testing
description:
Modern distributed architectures are inherently fragile. Microservices, multi-region database clusters, third-party payment gateways, and external SaaS dependencies fail continuously, unpredictably, and silently.

Most engineering teams rely on unit tests, integration tests, and staging environments to validate reliability. Yet, traditional testing paradigms suffer from a fatal assumption: the network is reliable. The first of the eight fallacies of distributed computing continues to trigger multimillion-dollar outages across the tech sector.

When a downstream payment processor suddenly introduces a 4,500ms tail latency spike, does your service timeout gracefully, or does it saturate connection pools, trigger cascading thread starvation, and bring down your entire ingress tier?

Enter ChaosProxy—the lightweight, programmable, high-performance fault-injection reverse/forward proxy engineered to simulate real-world network turbulence before it hits your production revenue.

The Chaos Engineering Imperative: Why Unit Tests Lie

In modern cloud computing, standard synthetic tests run under pristine local network conditions. In production, your microservices face:

  • Jitter and bufferbloat across cross-zone cloud boundaries.
  • Intermittent HTTP 502/503/504 errors during rolling deployments.
  • Malformed payloads and truncated responses caused by abrupt connection resets.
  • TCP half-open connections that bypass simplistic health-check implementations.

Without real-world validation, your resilience mechanisms—circuit breakers (e.g., Resilience4j, Envoy retries), dead-letter queues, and fallbacks—are merely untested theoretical constructs.

ChaosProxy bridges the gap between static testing and chaotic production realities.

What is ChaosProxy?

ChaosProxy is an ultra-low-latency, zero-dependency proxy built for engineers and platform teams who need deterministic failure testing. Positioned inline between your service and upstream/downstream dependencies, ChaosProxy dynamically manipulates network traffic based on declarative rules or dynamic API calls.

+------------------+         +------------------+         +----------------------+
|  Your Service    | ------> |    ChaosProxy    | ------> |  Target Dependency   |
| (API/Worker/K8s) |         | (Fault Injection)|         | (DB/Gateway/REST/gRPC|
+------------------+         +------------------+         +----------------------+
                                      ^
                                      | Dynamic Rules via REST / CLI
                             +------------------+
                             | Chaos Controller |
                             +------------------+

Whether deployed as a local Docker container in continuous integration pipelines, a Kubernetes sidecar, or an edge interceptor, ChaosProxy allows developers to inject chaos deterministically with microsecond accuracy.

Core Capabilities of ChaosProxy

1. Deterministic Latency Injection & Tail-Jitter

Simulate real-world network delays using granular mathematical models:

  • Fixed Latency: Force exact delays (e.g., 350ms) to verify timeout configurations.
  • Normal & Pareto Distributions: Simulate tail latency (p95, p99, p99.9) to detect thread exhaustion and queuing vulnerabilities.
  • Jitter: Add variance buffers to uncover synchronization and race condition bugs.

2. Protocol-Level Fault Simulation (HTTP, gRPC, TCP)

  • Status Code Forcing: Intercept outgoing calls and return arbitrary status codes (500 Internal Server Error, 429 Too Many Requests, 503 Service Unavailable).
  • Connection Resets & Drops: Sever the TCP stream mid-transmission (RST packets) to verify how clients handle dropped sockets.
  • Truncated Responses: Deliver partial HTTP response bodies to test parser resiliency and deserialization error handling.

3. Bandwidth Throttling & Packet Manipulation

  • Emulate constrained cellular or satellite environments (e.g., 2G/3G/4G bandwidth caps).
  • Corrupt arbitrary byte sequences across network payloads to validate cryptographic checks and defensive schema validation.

4. Headless Dynamic Control via REST API

Manage chaos on the fly without restarting pods or containers. Integrate directly into CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) to fail PRs that violate recovery SLAs.

Technical Deep Dive: Implementing ChaosProxy

Quickstart Deployment via Docker

Run ChaosProxy alongside your local service stack with zero overhead:

version: '3.8'

services:
  web-api:
    image: my-company/web-api:latest
    environment:
      - PAYMENT_GATEWAY_URL=http://chaos-proxy:8080
    depends_on:
      - chaos-proxy

  chaos-proxy:
    image: ghcr.io/chaosproxy/engine:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:8080" # Proxy Port
      - "9090:9090" # Control API Port
    environment:
      - TARGET_UPSTREAM=https://api.stripe.com
      - PROXY_PORT=8080
      - CONTROL_PORT=9090

Injecting Faults Dynamically via API

Once running, programmatically trigger network anomalies using a simple REST request:

Example: Injecting a 2.5-second p99 Latency Spike with 30% Probability 

curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "fault": "latency",
    "target_path": "/v1/charges",
    "params": {
      "delay_ms": 2500,
      "jitter_ms": 500,
      "probability": 0.30
    }
  }'

Example: Simulating Upstream Gateway Collapse (HTTP 503) 

curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "fault": "http_error",
    "target_path": "/v1/charges",
    "params": {
      "status_code": 503,
      "body": "{\"error\": \"Service Temporarily Unavailable\"}",
      "probability": 1.0
    }
  }'

Automated CI/CD Integration (GitHub Actions)

Add continuous resilience testing directly to your pull requests:

- name: Run Chaos Proxy Resilience Suite
  run: |
    # 1. Start test environment
    docker compose up -d

    # 2. Inject 5000ms latency on downstream dependencies
    curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
      -d '{"fault": "latency", "params": {"delay_ms": 5000, "probability": 1.0}}'

    # 3. Execute End-to-End Test (Must gracefully fallback within 500ms)
    npm run test:resilience

Architectural Comparison: Why ChaosProxy?

Feature Standard Mocks Linux tc / netem Chaos Mesh / Gremlin ChaosProxy
Layer Application OS / Kernel Kubernetes Cluster Application / L7 Proxy
Privileges Unprivileged Root Required Root / Cluster Admin Unprivileged / App Level
Granularity Static endpoints Network interface Pod/Container level HTTP Route / Payload / Header
CI/CD Fit Easy (but blind) Complex Too Heavy Instant / Native
Dynamic API No No Complex CRDs Simple JSON REST API

Unlike low-level kernel tools like iptables or tc netem, ChaosProxy requires zero elevated root permissions, making it completely secure for shared enterprise CI/CD runners and restricted cloud deployments. Unlike heavyweight cluster tools, ChaosProxy starts in under 15 milliseconds with less than 20MB of memory overhead.

The Economic ROI of Chaos Engineering

Downtime is not an abstract engineering metric—it is a direct financial loss.

  • The average cost of enterprise downtime ranges between $5,600 to $9,000 per minute (Gartner).
  • 70% of enterprise microservice failures are caused by unhandled cascade effects rather than root-cause logic bugs.

By identifying fragile downstream calls, misconfigured timeouts, and missing fallbacks during development, ChaosProxy:

  1. Reduces MTTR (Mean Time to Resolution) by 60% through deterministic bug reproduction.
  2. Eliminates cascading outages before code reaches production environments.
  3. Validates SLAs with concrete empirical data before signing upstream vendor agreements.

Supercharge Your Resilience Engineering Today

Do not wait for a midnight PagerDuty incident to discover that your circuit breakers don't trip properly. Build systems that embrace entropy, absorb downstream failures, and guarantee 99.99% availability under adverse network conditions.

Get immediate, production-grade access to the enterprise-ready ChaosProxy suite:

👉 Access ChaosProxy Enterprise & Tooling Now

Arm your engineering organization with the infrastructure required to build fault-tolerant, antifragile cloud architectures today.

title: The trust account invariant: one bank balance, many owners, and the check that catches commingling
description:
A property manager's trust account obeys one invariant: bank balance = every owner's balance + every security deposit held, at every moment. A second rule catches quieter commingling: no single owner's balance may go below zero, because if it does, another owner's money paid that owner's bill. Check both after every posting, not only at month end.

I work on ZeraBooks, and this is the cleanest data model I know for trust money. Below is a Python sketch. All figures are fictional and match the worked month on our property management page.

How do you model a trust account in code? 

from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal as D

class Trust:
    def __init__(self):
        self.bank = D("0")
        self.owner = defaultdict(lambda: D("0"))     # owed to each owner
        self.deposits = defaultdict(lambda: D("0"))  # held for each owner's tenants

    def post(self, owner: str, amount: D, kind: str):
        """amount is signed from the bank's view: + in, - out."""
        self.bank += amount
        if kind == "deposit":
            self.deposits[owner] += amount
        else:
            self.owner[owner] += amount
        self.check(owner)

    def check(self, owner: str):
        held = sum(self.owner.values()) + sum(self.deposits.values())
        assert self.bank == held, f"bank {self.bank} vs held {held}: does not reconcile"
        assert self.owner[owner] >= 0, f"{owner} is negative: another owner's money was used"

The first assertion is the reconciliation. The second is the one most spreadsheets don't have.

What does a clean month in the trust account look like?

Twelve units, three owners, an 8% fee on rent collected. The trust opens May with $9,600 of deposits.

t = Trust()
for owner, amt in [("Maple", "4800"), ("Elm", "3200"), ("Cedar", "1600")]:
    t.post(owner, D(amt), "deposit")                 # opening deposits, 9,600

t.post("Maple", D("8700.00"), "rent")
t.post("Elm",   D("6400.00"), "rent")
t.post("Elm",   D("75.00"),   "late fee")            # owner's under this agreement
t.post("Cedar", D("4200.00"), "rent")
t.post("Cedar", D("2100.00"), "deposit")             # new tenant

for owner, fee in [("Maple", "696.00"), ("Elm", "512.00"), ("Cedar", "336.00")]:
    t.post(owner, -D(fee), "fee to operating")

t.post("Maple", D("-640.00"), "repair")
t.post("Elm",   D("-380.00"), "repair")

for owner, paid in [("Maple", "7364.00"), ("Elm", "5583.00"), ("Cedar", "3864.00")]:
    t.post(owner, -D(paid), "owner payout")

print(t.bank, dict(t.owner), sum(t.deposits.values()))
# 11700.00, every owner balance 0.00, deposits 11700.00
Trust account, May Maple Court Elm Street Cedar Lane Total
Rent collected 8,700.00 6,400.00 4,200.00 19,300.00
Late fee 0.00 75.00 0.00 75.00
Management fee at 8% (696.00) (512.00) (336.00) (1,544.00)
Repairs paid (640.00) (380.00) 0.00 (1,020.00)
Paid out to owner (7,364.00) (5,583.00) (3,864.00) (16,811.00)
Owner balance, May 31 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00

Every post passes both assertions. On May 31 the bank shows $11,700.00, exactly the deposits held.


The bank side of the same idea in ZeraBooks: deposits, withdrawals and net must agree with the statement before a month is signed off.

How does commingling show up in the data?

Run the same month in a different order. Pay the Elm Street plumber on May 2, before Elm's rent has come in:

t = Trust()
# ...opening deposits as above...
t.post("Elm", D("-380.00"), "repair")
# AssertionError: Elm is negative: another owner's money was used

The bank balance is still positive, and the first assertion still holds, because the bank doesn't know whose money is whose. The $380 came out of money that belongs to Maple's owner or Cedar's tenants. In many states, that is what trust account rules prohibit, even if Elm's rent arrives the next day.

A month-end reconciliation can pass even when an owner went negative for two weeks in the middle. Check after every posting.

No code fixes this after the fact. The practice does: pay a repair from trust only when that owner's balance covers it, or have the owner fund a reserve first.

Which design choices keep the model honest?

  1. Keep deposits separate from owner balances. Both are liabilities, but deposits belong to tenants. An owner payout should never reach into the deposit total.
  2. Move fees out of trust as a transfer. The 8% fee is the manager's income only once it has moved to the operating account. In the trust model it is money leaving that owner's balance.
  3. Check after every post. Month-end checks miss mid-month negatives.
  4. Use Decimal for money. The invariant is an equality to the cent, and float sums drift.

Key takeaways

  • Invariant: trust bank balance = owner balances + deposits held, always.
  • Second rule: no owner below zero, or another owner's money paid their bill.
  • In the worked May, $1,544.00 of fees moved to operating and the trust closed at $11,700.00, all deposits.
  • Assert after every posting; month-end reconciliation alone can hide commingling.

FAQ

Why can the bank balance be fine while trust rules are broken?

Because the bank balance is a total. It can't tell whose money paid a bill. Only per-owner balances show that.

Is a security deposit an owner's money?

No. It is a liability to the tenant until the lease ends, so it is tracked apart from what is owed to the owner.

Does ZeraBooks keep tenant ledgers?

No. ZeraBooks is a general ledger, not property management software. It has no tenant ledgers, rent collection or portals; managers send reports from their property software.

The full month, with the owner statement mapped to Schedule E lines, is in the guide to bookkeeping for property management. Disclosure: I'm on the ZeraBooks team. ZeraBooks bookkeeping services reconcile trust and operating accounts monthly from uploaded statements, from $150 a month in U.S. dollars.

title: SQuAD's answer normalizer can mark a wrong answer correct: three verified hazards
description:
The exact-match and F1 scores in most question-answering and many open-ended LLM evals run every answer through one tiny, famous function first: SQuAD's normalize_answer. It lowercases, strips punctuation, drops the articles a/an/the, and collapses whitespace. It's pure standard library, so you can reproduce and check it exactly.

I built squad-normalize-hazards: a dependency-free, labeled, execution-verified corpus of three places where that normalization makes the score disagree with the obviously-intended outcome. Everything is pinned to HuggingFace evaluate commit 86baf12 and recomputed by stdlib tests.

1. Empty-collapse false positives (the squad metric)

A gold answer that is a bare article (a, an, the) or punctuation-only (...) normalizes to the empty string. The v1.1 scorer builds its gold list without filtering and compares by equality, so any prediction that also normalizes to empty — an article, punctuation, whitespace, even an empty refusal — scores exact-match 1.0.

Gold "the", prediction "a" → EM 1.0.

This is the same root cause that mosaicml/llm-foundry#1897 reported for a startswith-based matcher. The new part: it also bites the canonical, equality-based HF squad metric, not just prefix matchers. (I credited #1897 and did not open a PR — the reporter offered to.)

2. squad vs squad_v2 disagree on the same data

squad_v2 does filter golds that normalize to empty. So with a real co-alias — gold ["the", "red car"], prediction "a" — squad scores 1.0 (the wrong answer matches "the") while squad_v2 scores 0. Re-scoring a dataset from one to the other silently drops these spurious hits.

3. Punctuation glues articles in place

remove_punc runs before remove_articles and deletes punctuation without inserting a space. So a missing space keeps the article attached:

input normalized
end. the end
end.the endthe
the car car
the-car thecar

A model that writes end.the or the-car scores 0 against a gold the normalizer would otherwise have made equal — a false negative that depends only on spacing.

Reproduce 

python -m unittest -v test_squad_normalize_hazards.py

Standard library only. Code Apache-2.0, corpus CC BY 4.0.

Repo: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/squad-normalize-hazards

These are edge cases of a deliberate design choice, not a claim that the metric is broken in general — but they're exactly the inputs LLM graders produce, so they're worth knowing.

This research and write-up were made with AI, by MV2 of Munim, Inc.

title: Supabase SECURITY DEFINER RPC Callable by anon: Revoke It
description:
The short version

PostgreSQL grants EXECUTE to the PUBLIC role by default the moment CREATE FUNCTION runs. SECURITY DEFINER is the modifier that makes a function run with the privileges of the role that owns it rather than the role that called it. Create a write function with that modifier and leave it without an explicit REVOKE, and it becomes directly callable from the anon (unauthenticated) or authenticated role through Supabase's PostgREST layer.

  • Even with no GRANT written anywhere, EXECUTE for PUBLIC is there from the start
  • RLS policies on the table are irrelevant, because a SECURITY DEFINER function runs as the owner
  • Closing it means writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC explicitly and re-GRANTing only to the roles that need it

What it looks like

We created a function to push records for asynchronous delivery into a table called sync_outbox. Its definition pins search_path. search_path is the schema search path deciding which schema an unqualified object name resolves from inside a function, and pinning it to public is standard practice to stop a caller rewriting it so that a fake same-named object outside public resolves first.

create table if not exists public.sync_outbox (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  kind          text not null,
  ref_id        uuid,
  payload       jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,
  status        text not null default 'pending'
                check (status in ('pending','sent','failed','dead')),
  attempts      int  not null default 0,
  -- (omitted)
);

alter table public.sync_outbox enable row level security;
create policy sync_outbox_staff_read on public.sync_outbox
  for select using (public.is_staff());

create or replace function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(p_kind text, p_ref_id uuid, p_payload jsonb)
returns uuid language sql security definer set search_path = public as $$
  insert into public.sync_outbox (kind, ref_id, payload)
  values (p_kind, p_ref_id, coalesce(p_payload, '{}'::jsonb))
  returning id;
$$;

The table's RLS says only "allow SELECT for the staff role". There is no policy anywhere permitting INSERT for anon. The function was written on the premise that only the app's backend (a cron worker) calls it. Pinning search_path was handled, but that guards a different kind of attack and does nothing for the problem here.

But this function is SECURITY DEFINER, and EXECUTE for PUBLIC is granted by default the instant CREATE FUNCTION runs. Supabase's PostgREST automatically exposes functions in the public schema at /rest/v1/rpc/<name>. It connects as anon or authenticated depending on the JWT the caller sends, and both roles inherit PUBLIC's privileges, so any function not explicitly revoked can be called directly by anyone.

That is what the review flagged. The table's RLS correctly narrowed reads to staff, and the function's execute privilege had never been narrowed at all.

Why

Three facts stack up.

① SECURITY DEFINER runs with the function owner's privileges

Not the calling role's privileges but those of the role that owns the function. That much is as specified.

② CREATE FUNCTION grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC by default

Even with no GRANT ever written, the function is callable by anyone the moment it is created. This is the opposite of tables, whose GRANT is closed by default (nobody can touch them without explicit permission): functions are open by default.

③ PostgREST automatically exposes public schema functions as RPCs

anon / authenticated are the connection roles Supabase provides, and they inherit PUBLIC's privileges as they are. With not a single GRANT on the table, one forgotten REVOKE on a SECURITY DEFINER function leaves a write path open that bypasses RLS entirely.

table GRANT        → closed by default → nobody touches it without explicit permission
function EXECUTE   → open by default   → anyone calls it unless explicitly revoked

This asymmetry is the cause of the oversight. Look only at the table and conclude "RLS protects this", and the hole on the function side goes unseen.

Fixing it

Strip the default PUBLIC privilege and re-allow only the roles that need it.

-- Close the SECURITY DEFINER write function to direct calls from anon/authenticated
-- (via PostgREST). Strip the default PUBLIC EXECUTE, allow only the backend (service_role).
revoke all on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) from public;
grant execute on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) to service_role;

REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC cuts off every inheritance source including anon / authenticated, and GRANT EXECUTE returns it to service_role alone, which actually needs to call it. The function definition itself is unchanged. All that happened is an open door was closed, with no effect on the intended calling path from the backend.

Checking it

Joining pg_proc and pg_roles gives you a function's owner and its execute privileges.

select p.proname, r.rolname as owner, p.proacl
from pg_proc p
join pg_roles r on r.oid = p.proowner
where p.proname = 'enqueue_sync_outbox';

Look for EXECUTE for PUBLIC remaining in proacl (notation like =X/<owner>). Unless this check is run on every new SECURITY DEFINER write function, the same path opens once per function whose revoke was forgotten.

Making it not recur

This fix went in as an addition of revoke / grant to the existing migration file rather than recreating the function. Unless writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC paired with every SECURITY DEFINER function becomes the rule, the next write function added opens the same path.

  • Write REVOKE / GRANT directly beneath the creation SQL for any SECURITY DEFINER write function, so that adding only one of them is structurally impossible
  • Include the function's EXECUTE privilege in the same review item as the table's RLS review (on the premise of the asymmetry: tables closed by default, functions open by default)
  • Verify whether something is anonymously writable by actually querying pg_proc.proacl, not by reading the wording of a policy

However carefully the RLS policies are written, it means nothing if another door — the function's execute privilege — stands open. Another case shaped as an overlooked SECURITY DEFINER is in The function owner and the migration role. That one is about an intended bypass ceasing to work; this one about an unintended bypass working. Both start from the same property: SECURITY DEFINER behaviour is decided by who created the function, not by who called it.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

title: Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?
description:
Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?

For months, the artificial intelligence trade seemed unstoppable. Giant chipmakers, cloud providers, and data-center builders lifted Wall Street to one record after another. This week, the music stopped — at least temporarily — as a brutal sell-off swept through the technology sector and forced investors to confront a question they had been happy to ignore: what happens if the most expensive technology bet in history stops paying off?

A Week of Red Numbers

The damage was fast and broad. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite posted its first weekly loss in five weeks, and the S&P 500 logged its worst week since June. Chip stocks — the engine of the AI boom — took the hardest hits. Micron Technology fell more than five percent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped over five percent, Broadcom slid more than four percent, and Intel lost close to six percent on Friday alone. AI data-center infrastructure company CoreWeave, a major Nvidia customer, plunged more than seven percent after a double-digit decline earlier in the week.

The rout was global. Seoul's tech-rich Kospi briefly triggered a trading halt after diving more than eight percent, with Samsung sinking over nine percent and SK hynix down more than eleven percent. Tokyo shed close to five percent, dragged down by chip-linked names like Advantest and Kioxia as well as investment giant SoftBank.

Why Now? Inflation and the Cost of Money

The immediate trigger was economic, not technological. US inflation data came in hotter than expected, with the consumer price index jumping to 3.7 percent in September and wholesale inflation surging 6.3 percent year-on-year — its biggest jump since 2022. Those numbers stoked fears that the Federal Reserve, which raised rates in September for the first time in three years, may have to tighten further, with futures markets now pricing in a high probability of another hike by December.

Higher rates matter more to AI companies than to almost anyone else. Tech giants have financed an unprecedented infrastructure spree — data centers, GPU clusters, and power-hungry compute farms — largely through debt markets. With bond yields climbing to their highest levels in years, the cost of financing that buildout is rising exactly as patience with unprofitable AI ventures is wearing thin. A week before the crash, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had called AI "the most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime. Investors this week appeared to decide that consequence cuts both ways.

The IMF's Warning Shot

The market turmoil coincided with an uncomfortable warning from the International Monetary Fund. At the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the fund released a report projecting that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 percent by 2028, and cautioned that "weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction."

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva did not mince words: if confidence evaporates and "money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks" that "would be felt across the world." Yet the same meetings underscored how central AI already is to the global economy. The fund noted that global trade grew 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025 — a figure that would have been closer to 4.6 percent without AI-related products. Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem put it bluntly: "It is here, and it's just the beginning."

Bubble or Growing Pains?

Not everyone reading the sell-off sees a bubble bursting. The Dow Jones actually rose on Friday, suggesting investors are rotating out of tech rather than abandoning equities altogether. Earnings expectations for the quarter remain strong, and companies at the heart of the AI supply chain — from TSMC to memory makers — have continued to report robust demand. Nvidia shares, though down more than five percent for the week, remain up dramatically over the longer arc of the AI era.

The bear case, though, is no longer fringe. Critics point to debt-financed capital expenditure, stretched valuations, and monetization that still lags the hype. Analysts this week cited "worries about the AI buildout, bubbly valuations, lower-than-expected earnings growth at leading US frontier labs, and Chinese competition" as compounding pressures. Moody's Analytics economists added that a prolonged Middle East conflict, by pushing up energy prices and interest rates, could "puncture" the AI boom by straining the economics behind AI investment.

What to Watch

Three signposts will matter in the coming weeks. First, the Fed's October 28 policy decision, landing a week before the US midterm elections — a hawkish surprise could renew the pressure on rate-sensitive tech names. Second, the ongoing earnings season, where markets will demand evidence that AI revenue is catching up to AI spending. Third, and hardest to measure: confidence. As Georgieva noted in Bangkok, "if there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities."

Whether this week proves to be a healthy correction in a long structural boom or the first crack in a bubble, one thing is clear: the era of unquestioned AI enthusiasm on Wall Street is over. From now on, the market will want receipts.

title: The Domain Was Just the Beginning: Building GraphGuard AI with FalkorDB
description:
The Domain Was Just the Beginning: Building GraphGuard AI with FalkorDB

One suspicious domain. A web of relationships. A different way to investigate.

By Team SynapGraph | Graph Hacks 2026 | Track 1 — Agents That Act on Connected Data

Every Threat Leaves a Trail. Can You Connect It?

Imagine an analyst investigating a suspicious domain.

At first, there is only a name on a screen.

But that name might point to an IP address. It might be associated with a digital certificate. It might appear in a threat-intelligence report. Each connection offers another clue, and every clue raises a new question.

Is this connection meaningful? Where did the information come from? What should the analyst investigate next?

The challenge is not simply collecting more security data. It is discovering how the pieces connect without confusing a clue with proof.

That question became the starting point for GraphGuard AI.

We are Team SynapGraph, and for Graph Hacks 2026, we set out to explore how graph databases and AI-assisted investigation workflows could make cybersecurity evidence easier to follow, understand, and investigate.

Our chosen track was Track 1: Agents That Act on Connected Data.

Our central idea was simple:

Don't just show the indicator. Show the relationships that give it context.

Meet GraphGuard AI: An Investigation That Follows the Connections

GraphGuard AI is a graph-powered cybersecurity investigation prototype designed to explore relationships between domains, IP addresses, certificates, and reports.

Instead of treating every indicator as an isolated record, the application uses a connected graph to retrieve related information and present it through an investigation workflow.

The technology stack brings together three key components:

  • FalkorDB — the relationship engine. Stores and queries the connected cybersecurity entities that underpin the investigation.
  • FastAPI — the investigation interface. Connects the backend workflow to API endpoints.
  • Streamlit — the analyst's workspace. Provides a dashboard for submitting indicators and reviewing results.

Docker supports the local development and demonstration environment.

Together, these components form a practical experiment in making connected security evidence easier to explore.

Why We Chose a Graph Instead of Another List

Traditional lists are useful when you need to know what you have.

Graphs become especially useful when you need to understand how things are connected.

Consider a simplified investigation:




Suspicious Domain
demo.example



RESOLVES_TO



IP Address
192.0.2.10 · documentation-only example IP



MENTIONED_IN



Intelligence Report
REPORT-001 · synthetic demonstration data

Illustrative graph path based on the project's synthetic demonstration data, not a real threat finding.

In FalkorDB, these connections can be represented as relationships between nodes and retrieved using graph queries.

GraphGuard AI's model includes paths such as:

  • Domain → RESOLVES_TO → IPAddress
  • Domain → PRESENTED_CERTIFICATE → Certificate
  • IPAddress → MENTIONED_IN → Report

This structure lets an investigation move beyond a single indicator and inspect the related entities that the graph contains.

The difference is important: the graph does not automatically establish guilt. It gives the analyst more context to evaluate.

Under the Hood: Turning Connections into Context

The investigation begins when a user submits a domain through the dashboard.

The backend receives the request and queries FalkorDB for matching graph entities and their relationships. The returned information can include associated IP addresses, certificate records, and intelligence-report references when those records exist in the graph.

The application then presents the available findings to the user.

The process follows a clear path:

Indicator → Graph Query → Connected Evidence → Analyst Review

FalkorDB is central to this workflow because the investigation depends on retrieving connected entities, not merely storing unrelated records.

The project also explores the wider possibility of passive intelligence enrichment, including DNS, registration information, certificate transparency, and public threat-intelligence sources. Any live enrichment must be distinguished from existing graph records so that users can tell where each observation originated.

The Most Important Feature Is What We Don't Claim

In cybersecurity, an incorrect conclusion can be more dangerous than an incomplete result.

Two domains sharing an IP address does not automatically make them malicious. A certificate connection does not prove an attack. A mention in a report must be interpreted in context.

That is why GraphGuard AI is designed around an evidence-first principle:

A connection is a lead. Evidence supports a hypothesis. Verification builds confidence.

The prototype's synthetic dataset demonstrates the investigation workflow; it is not proof of real-world detection accuracy. Likewise, any confidence value shown by the application should not be mistaken for a statistically validated probability of maliciousness.

Our aim is to help users follow the evidence, understand the relationships, and decide what deserves further investigation—not to replace human judgment with an unexplained verdict.

Building Under Hackathon Pressure

Graph Hacks 2026 gave us an opportunity to turn a concept into a working prototype within a short development window.

As Team SynapGraph, we focused on connecting the database, backend API, and dashboard into one locally runnable application.

The process involved more than writing code. We needed to think about the graph data model, how relationships should be queried, how findings should be presented, and how someone else could run the project.

We used AI-assisted development tools to accelerate parts of the workflow while keeping the project's actual implementation and limitations in view.

One lesson stood out: a project becomes much easier to explain when the architecture follows a clear idea. For GraphGuard AI, that idea is the relationship between an indicator and the evidence surrounding it.

What Comes Next: From Connected Data to Better Investigations

GraphGuard AI is a starting point, not a finished security platform.

Future work could explore:

  • More passive intelligence providers and clearly attributed observations.
  • Stronger provenance, freshness, and source-quality indicators.
  • Additional graph traversal and relationship analysis.
  • More comprehensive tests using carefully labelled datasets.
  • Better ways to explain why a particular connection is relevant.
  • Evaluation against known examples to measure where the approach succeeds and fails.

The long-term goal is not simply to produce a larger graph. It is to make the graph more useful to the person investigating it.

See the Project in Action

Explore the source code:

https://github.com/sudhir734/GraphGuard-Ai

Watch the demo:

https://youtu.be/gMyqtCTPSv8

GraphGuard AI is a hackathon prototype intended for demonstration and experimentation. Its findings should be independently verified before use in operational security decisions.

One Final Thought

A suspicious domain is a starting point, not a conclusion.

The real investigation begins when we ask what connects to it, what those connections actually mean, and which pieces of evidence deserve our attention.

With GraphGuard AI, we are exploring a simple but powerful idea: cybersecurity is not only about finding signals. It is about understanding the relationships between them.

Follow the connections. Question the evidence. Investigate with context.

Team SynapGraph | Graph Hacks 2026

title: AI Is Redrawing the US Data Center Map
description:
Power access is shaping where new campuses rise, when they come online, and the networks connecting them.

October 18, 2026

In June 2024, construction began on the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas. Within a year, its first two buildings had been energized. By September 2025, Crusoe said the site was running early training and inference workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The planned campus would eventually contain eight buildings. Crusoe’s account captures both the speed of the AI infrastructure boom and its defining complication: large campuses become useful in stages.

That progression is changing the geography of computing. Developers need sites where land, electricity and equipment can come together on a workable schedule. As established markets fill up, new locations become attractive, and connecting distant facilities becomes an engineering problem of its own.

The spending curve shows how quickly this has become a national construction story. In November 2022, private US data center construction was running at an annualized pace of $13.9 billion. By August 2026, that rate had reached $85.0 billion, roughly six times as much. These Census Bureau figures cover data centers broadly and measure construction work, including fixed electrical and mechanical systems. They exclude racks and servers, whose costs sit on top of the building investment.

Figure 1. Monthly construction spending expressed as a seasonally adjusted annual rate, in current dollars. The August figure is a spending pace, rather than money already spent during 2026. Source: US Census Bureau.

Construction spending was already increasing before ChatGPT’s launch. Because the figures are in current dollars, the curve combines changes in construction prices with changes in the amount being built. It establishes the growing scale of spending without measuring computing capacity.

The next question is where that work can happen. In its August report, JLL placed 77% of North American data center capacity under construction in frontier markets, highlighting West Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and the Carolinas. Its market analysis describes a buildout extending well beyond the industry’s established hubs.

Texas illustrates the shift. JLL reported 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity across the state, compared with 13 GW in Virginia. Northern Virginia remained the largest individual market, with nearly 7 GW of inventory. The state totals show the direction of investment while including projects that still have to become operating facilities.

Figure 2. State totals combine existing capacity and capacity under construction, including hyperscalers’ own facilities. They do not measure electricity currently being consumed. Source: JLL, Midyear 2026.

A large pipeline creates a planning problem for utilities. They must decide how much infrastructure to build before they know which projects will arrive, when their servers will be installed, or how quickly customer workloads will fill them. A speculative request can therefore influence planning long before it becomes a substantial electricity load.

AEP Ohio’s experience shows how that pipeline changes as commitments become binding. Its new tariff required developers to advance through paid studies and financial commitments. About one-fifth of the initial requested capacity reached signed contracts. AEP attributed the narrowing to the filtering of speculative or uncertain projects. The utility still had 17.9 GW of total contracted data center projects, including earlier contracts, scheduled to come online progressively through 2035. AEP’s February update distinguishes those future obligations from operating demand.

Figure 3. Successive stages of one AEP Ohio intake cohort, as reported in February 2026. The final bar excludes contracts signed before the tariff. Source: AEP Ohio.

Texas faces its own version of the credibility problem. ERCOT’s September board update documented a pause in energization approvals for relevant new data center and cryptocurrency facilities of at least 75 MW while verification and community-impact reviews proceeded. Projects received provisional classifications; those classifications did not constitute final permission to connect. The operator expected to publish its community-impact report by December 10.

For developers, that makes the location of available power consequential to computing design. Microsoft offers a concrete example. Its Fairwater facilities in Wisconsin and the Atlanta area are linked through a dedicated network intended to let sites cooperate on large AI workloads. Microsoft explicitly identifies land and power availability as reasons to spread work across locations. Its description of the architecture connects the choice of geography to the need for new networking infrastructure.

Distance introduces costs of its own. Large training jobs require frequent communication among processors; slow exchanges can leave expensive hardware waiting. Microsoft describes dedicated fiber and changes to network protocols designed to reduce bottlenecks between sites. Finding land and power therefore creates another task: making the resulting facilities operate efficiently together.

There are also ways to change the terms on which a facility receives electricity. In a report published October 14, the International Energy Agency examines connection agreements that allow consumption to be curtailed, phased in or adjusted to grid conditions. Such arrangements can help projects connect sooner by changing the reliability or timing of their access.

The tradeoff is practical. Interrupting expensive AI hardware can be costly, and a facility operator may have limited control over customers’ workloads. The IEA’s analysis identifies coordination among computing customers, facility operators and electricity networks as a condition for greater flexibility. Onsite generation also brings equipment lead times and engineering requirements of its own.

The buildout is consequently creating an architecture that extends beyond each campus. Transmission studies, substations, fiber routes and electricity agreements increasingly influence where AI work can run. Abilene’s first buildings became useful when several of those pieces came together. Repeating that achievement across a much larger pipeline will determine how quickly the new map translates into computing capacity.

Data: Figures use the research snapshot checked October 18, 2026. Each chart retains its source’s geography, period and definition. Charts are original graphics based on the cited figures.

title: PolicyPath
description:
PolicyPath: Turning Organizational Policies into Connected Intelligence with FalkorDB

Introduction

What if an organization could do more than store its policies? What if it could understand how each policy connects to risks, controls, and responsible people?

That question inspired me to build PolicyPath, a graph-powered policy intelligence platform, for FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 under the Company Brain track.

The Problem

Organizations often maintain policies, compliance requirements, risk records, and control documentation separately. Understanding how these pieces relate can take time, especially when someone needs to identify which controls enforce a policy, which risks are associated with it, or who is responsible for approval.

Simply storing documents does not make these relationships easy to explore. I wanted to build a tool that makes organizational knowledge more connected and understandable.

My Solution: PolicyPath

PolicyPath transforms policy information into a connected graph that users can explore through an interactive application.

The project models policies, controls, risks, and owners as graph nodes, with relationships connecting them. This structure helps users investigate policy information and understand how different parts of an organization's knowledge fit together.

The application includes:

  • Policy Explorer: Browse and inspect policy information.
  • Graph Explorer: Explore connections between policies, controls, risks, and owners.
  • Risk Heatmap: Review risk information visually.
  • Ask PolicyPath: Ask policy-related questions through a simple assistant.
  • Decision Brief: Generate and download structured decision summaries in JSON format.

My goal was to make policy analysis easier to navigate and more useful for decision-making.

Why I Chose FalkorDB

FalkorDB is central to PolicyPath because the project depends on relationships, not just individual records.

I used FalkorDB as the graph database and Cypher queries to retrieve connected information. For example, a policy can be linked to the control that enforces it, a risk it relates to, and the person responsible for approval.

Representing these connections as a graph makes relationship-based exploration a natural part of the application. Instead of treating every policy as an isolated entry, PolicyPath helps users examine the wider context around it.

How I Built It

I developed the application using Python and Streamlit, with FalkorDB handling the graph data. I also used Pandas and Plotly as part of the data and visualization stack.

The process involved designing the graph model, connecting the application to the database, building the exploration interface, and adding risk and decision-support features.

I also deployed the application online and prepared a public GitHub repository and demo video so others could explore the project.

Project links

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/Monika-2108/PolicyPath
  • Live application: https://policypath-dnr7owzmvjhxfoib9bcmls.streamlit.app/
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/4WEKiY_XiL8

Challenges and Learnings

One of my biggest learnings was that choosing a graph database is not enough by itself. The graph model and relationships must reflect the actual questions users need to answer.

I learned to think about data as connected entities rather than isolated tables or documents, and to use Cypher queries to retrieve information through those relationships.

I also learned how important it is to connect the backend to a usable interface, deploy an application, document the setup, and communicate a technical idea through a working demonstration.

Building PolicyPath also reminded me that prototypes have limitations. Visualizations, question-answering behavior, and deployment configuration all require testing and refinement. Being aware of those limitations is part of building reliable software.

What's Next?

I would like to extend PolicyPath with richer natural-language querying, more advanced graph analytics, improved visualizations, and more comprehensive policy and risk relationships.

These improvements could help organizations move toward more connected, explainable, and accessible policy intelligence.

Final Thoughts

Building PolicyPath gave me practical experience with graph databases and showed me how connected data can support real organizational workflows.

For me, FalkorDB is more than a place to store records in this project. It provides the relationship layer that makes policy exploration possible.

I hope PolicyPath demonstrates how graph technology can help turn disconnected organizational information into knowledge that people can explore and use to make better-informed decisions.

Built for FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 — Company Brain track.

title: Anatomy of a Paid AI Video Job: What Happens Between Upload and MP4
description:
A walkthrough of the lifecycle behind a two-photo trend video generator: validation, quotes, credit holds, async rendering and data expiry.

Consumer AI video looks like a single button: upload photos, get a clip. Behind that button sits a long-running, paid, failure-prone job, and most of the product work goes into making that job predictable for someone who just wants a funny video of their friends.

This post follows one job through AIHotelLobby.win, a single-purpose tool that recasts the Hotel Lobby trend video with two uploaded portraits. It makes a good example because its public guides, help page, terms and privacy policy spell out every stage, from upload checks to how long each file lives. Everything below is based on those pages; the snippets are simplified sketches of the behavior they describe.

Stage 1: Reject bad input before anything expensive happens

A GPU minute costs far more than a file check, so the cheapest quality control is at the upload box. Each photo has to be a JPG, PNG or WebP, at least 512 × 512 pixels and no larger than 10 MB, showing one clearly visible adult.

const ACCEPTED = ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'];
const MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024;

function checkPhoto(type: string, bytes: number, w: number, h: number): string | null {
  if (!ACCEPTED.includes(type)) return 'Use a JPG, PNG or WebP image';
  if (bytes > MAX_BYTES) return 'Keep the file under 10 MB';
  if (w < 512 || h < 512) return 'Use an image at least 512 × 512 pixels';
  return null;
}

Two details worth noting. Metadata is stripped when the images are prepared, which removes location data people forget their phones attach. And the docs are explicit that these checks only cover the file: they do not verify identity, age or consent. Being honest about what validation can't do is part of the design.

Stage 2: Keep the draft alive through the login wall

Users can pick both photos, assign left and right, and choose length and sound before creating an account. The draft is kept on the device while they sign in, so the login wall doesn't throw away their work. Signing out clears it.

This is a conversion detail as much as a technical one. The moment someone is asked to sign in is the moment they are most likely to leave, and making them redo the upload afterwards doubles that risk.

Stage 3: Quote first, then hold the credits

After sign-in, the photos upload privately and the server returns a quote: length, format and credit cost. Prices are fixed per length (5 seconds is 30 credits, 10 is 50 and 15 is 70), and the quote is pinned to the task.

type Quote = {
  durationSeconds: 5 | 10 | 15;
  aspect: '16:9';
  audio: 'original' | 'silent';
  credits: 30 | 50 | 70;
  configRevision: string; // the model, template and price recorded for this task
};

The terms make the pinning explicit: prices and models can change for new requests, but an existing task keeps the provider, settings and price recorded in its quote. Confirming the quote reserves the credits. They are captured only after a valid video has been stored, and released if the task definitively fails. Buying credits is a separate flow and never starts a job by itself.

Stage 4: Hand off to the model, then let the user leave

The configured model is Kling 3.0 Omni, accessed through KIE as the API provider. (A second model, Seedance 2.0 Mini, is integrated but not enabled for customers.) The provider receives the two photos, the reference video and the instructions for that task.

From here everything is asynchronous. The published examples list render times from about three to seven and a half minutes, which is far too long to hold a browser tab hostage. The user can close the page; the task keeps running and shows up in My videos on any device signed in to the same account.

The hard case is a timeout during submission: the provider may or may not have accepted the job. Releasing the credits risks giving away a video that will finish anyway; capturing them risks charging for nothing. The answer here is a holding state:

type Job =
  | { state: 'reserved' }
  | { state: 'running' }
  | { state: 'needs_review' } // submission outcome unknown; credits stay held
  | { state: 'completed'; videoKey: string } // credits captured
  | { state: 'failed' }; // confirmed failure; credits released

The page on credits and task recovery tells users what this means for them: losing the connection does not stop generation, an uncertain task keeps its credits reserved while it is checked, and they should follow that same task rather than start a duplicate. Credit returns and cash refunds are also kept separate, which saves a lot of support confusion.

Stage 5: Deliver briefly, then delete

Personal photos are a liability the moment you no longer need them, and the retention schedule reflects that:

Data How long it stays
Validated photos never submitted for a task 24 hours
Photos needed by an active or uncertain task Up to 48 hours
Task inputs after the task reaches a final state Scheduled to expire within 24 hours
Finished videos 7 days
A download link 5 minutes

Downloads use short-lived signed links. Deleting a file stops new links from being issued, though a link already handed out can work until it expires, and the privacy policy says so plainly. It also notes that provider copies and backups follow their own schedules, which is the kind of caveat most products leave out.

What's worth copying

  • Validate cheaply, and say what validation can't check.
  • Let the draft survive authentication.
  • Pin the quote to the task, so a price or model change never rewrites a job already in flight.
  • Model the unknown state explicitly instead of guessing between refund and charge.
  • Publish retention times as numbers, not "as long as necessary".

None of this is specific to trend videos. Any product that runs a slow, paid job on someone's personal media faces the same five stages, and users notice when one of them is handled carelessly.

AIHotelLobby.win is an independent service. It is not an official Kling, Seedance or KIE product and is not affiliated with the artists behind "Hotel Lobby". Details come from its public pages as of October 18, 2026.

title: Retrieval Platform vs Specialist Candidate Search: 4 Failure-Recovery Rules (My Choice)
description:
Short answer: for a game studio's recruiting search, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback. A general retrieval platform is a good fit for the web-context stage; a specialist search service is the better choice when regional residency, deletion SLAs, or contractual processor boundaries are the deciding requirement.

The bill is usually not the first thing to model. The dominant term is the work you repeat: fetching the same public page, embedding unchanged candidate material, and reranking a wide result set after a timeout. Keep raw pages and embeddings only as long as your recruiting policy permits, then delete them deliberately. The trade-off is real: a deleted snapshot cannot help explain a decision made six months ago.

That loss is deliberate.

Start with a retrieval contract, not a vendor

For a game hiring team, “find a gameplay engineer with console networking experience” is an answer contract, not an implementation. Define the fields the UI can show, the maximum number of candidates, and the evidence each hit must carry. The contract should require tenant ID, access-control labels, source URL or document ID, fetch time, and a deletion deadline on every indexed item.

Use two collections: one for public web context and one for first-party candidate records. They have different owners and retention rules. A web result may be refreshed; a candidate resume may need immediate deletion when a person withdraws consent. Mixing them makes an innocent rerank request cross a trust boundary.

Infrai fits the public-context leg because it exposes web and vector capabilities through plain REST, without making the recruiting system install and track a client SDK. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and needs no key, so an integration check can read the request schema, response schema, and runnable examples before a protected request crosses the boundary. Infrai uses a single API key and one bill across the platform's capabilities; for this workflow, that means one credential policy across the fetch and index stages instead of separate key rotation and invoice reconciliation. Those are two concrete maintenance advantages when several services participate in recovery.

The recovery path is intentionally boring. Search a bounded slice, record which stage answered, and return citations with the context. If web search reaches its timeout, the first-party collection can still produce a useful answer that clearly identifies the stages used. This is preferable to silently blending stale pages into a confident shortlist, especially when the user is an internal recruiter who will act on the ordering rather than inspect every source. Preserve the source URL or document identifier in each result so a reviewer can trace what contributed to the result without assuming the indexed copy is still authoritative.

How should retrieval architecture handle candidate search failure recovery?

Use a short, explicit state machine: fetch, normalize, index, retrieve, rerank, and cite. Each transition gets a timeout and a retry budget. A retry must not create a second vector record, so the upsert key is derived from the source document ID and content version. Standard queues are at-least-once; consumers therefore need the same idempotency rule.

Before wiring protected requests, this runnable check confirms that discovery advertises the web-search entry route. It sends an explicit method, handles rate limits, checks status, and makes no assumptions about undeclared request fields.

import os
import time
import requests

url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

for attempt in range(3):
    response = requests.request(
        method="GET",
        url=url,
        headers=headers,
        timeout=8,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        delay = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
        time.sleep(delay * (2**attempt))
        continue
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
    advertised = {item["path"] for item in response.json()["capabilities"]}
    required = {"/v1/web/search"}
    missing = required - advertised
    if missing:
        raise RuntimeError(f"routes unavailable: {sorted(missing)}")
    print("retrieval routes available")
    break
else:
    raise TimeoutError("discovery retry budget exhausted")

The important invariant is that tenant and access-control metadata never disappear during normalization. Treat a retry as a scheduling decision rather than a reason to widen the query: honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, back off exponentially, and keep the total attempt count bounded. For writes, derive an idempotency key from the source document ID and content version. Then a repeated upsert represents the same fact instead of duplicating context. If a source cannot supply the required tenant and access labels, stop at fetch; don't guess.

Small budgets win here.

Retention is part of relevance quality

Deletion changes recall. Set a retention clock per collection, delete expired source text and vectors together, and retain only the minimum audit record allowed by policy: document ID, tenant, decision timestamp, and the source pointer needed for review. The exact record depends on the recruiting policy and processor contract. Do not retain a public page forever just because it was easy to crawl.

One key can cover the web and vector calls while the specialist provider remains the system of record for candidate data. This reduces credential rotation and reconciliation work across the two retrieval stages. It does not collapse their retention policies into one, and it is not a promise that a routing layer supplies residency or contractual deletion guarantees.

The catch is important. If your legal team requires a named processor in a specific region, an auditable deletion SLA, or private networking into the applicant-tracking system, choose the specialist service that can sign those terms. A unified API does not replace that contract.

Four options under the same failure budget

The comparison below is about operating boundaries, not a popularity contest. Measure retrieval quality and tail latency with your own candidate queries before committing.

Option Retrieval and recovery shape Trust-boundary fit Choose it when
Elasticsearch Mature filters, analyzers, and shard-level controls; you own retry and replay logic. Strong control in your deployment, with more operational surface. You need deep boolean filtering beside vector search.
OpenSearch Familiar Lucene lineage and self-managed deployment choices. Useful for teams that require infrastructure ownership. You already operate AWS-compatible search clusters.
Pinecone Managed vector index with simple scaling model. Verify region, deletion behavior, and processor terms for your data. You want a vector specialist and can keep sensitive records elsewhere.
Infrai web + vector routes Staged web and vector calls over one REST surface; bounded requests and your own collection policy. Good for public or low-sensitivity context; residency and contractual guarantees remain with the specialist provider. You want HTTP-only integration for the context leg and a separate system of record for candidate data.

Do not compare these on a single top-20 score. A retrieval miss caused by a deleted document is a policy outcome, while a miss caused by a low-quality embedding is a relevance problem. Log them separately. I’m not sure any off-the-shelf benchmark captures that distinction for your hiring corpus; your mileage may vary with language mix, stale profiles, and access rules.

A practical decision rule

Run a two-week replay of anonymized queries. Cap web fetches, cap vector candidates, and inject timeouts into each stage. Track answer coverage, citation coverage, p95 latency, and the number of records removed by tenant or ACL filters. Then ask one uncomfortable question: can an auditor reconstruct why this candidate appeared without restoring deleted personal data?

Try Infrai for the public web-context portion if the answer is yes and your team values a plain HTTP integration across languages. Keep a specialist search backend for restricted candidate records when region, retention, or processor language is non-negotiable. That split preserves failure recovery without pretending every backend has the same trust boundary.

Further reading

References: Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper, Elasticsearch reference, OpenSearch documentation, and Pinecone documentation. If this public-context boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's reranking guide.

title: Paid Apps and In-App Purchases in a Google Play Closed Test: What Testers Pay
description:
Disclosure: 12Testers14Day publishes this article and sells Google Play closed-testing help.

If your app costs money, or sells one-time products or subscriptions, a closed test raises a practical question: will your testers be charged? Google's answer depends on the testing track and on whether each tester is a license tester. Getting this wrong can mean testers paying real money, or a 14-day test where nobody ever touches your purchase flow.

The short answer

Based on Google's Play Console Help and Android Developers documentation:

Situation Paid app install In-app purchases and subscriptions
Internal test Free for testers Charged, unless the tester is a license tester
Closed or open test Testers must buy the app Charged, unless the tester is a license tester
License tester on a test track See the note below Test payment methods, no real charge

Google's test setup article says: "Testers must purchase paid apps when participating in open or closed tests. For internal tests, testers can install paid apps for free." It also says internal testers pay for in-app purchases unless you add them to a license testers list.

Google's billing testing guide adds that users "incur actual charges for their test track purchases unless the user is a license tester."

Note on paid apps and license testers: Google's license testing article says your own publishing account can buy your app as a test purchase, and that license testers can buy one-time products and subscriptions without being charged. Before you promise testers a free install of a paid app in a closed test, try it with one license-tester account and check the price shown on the Play Store page.

Why this matters for the 12-tester requirement

If your personal developer account was created after November 13, 2023, Google's testing requirements article says you need a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days before you can apply for production access. (See our 12-testers requirement explainer for details.)

That has two consequences for monetized apps:

  • A paid price is a barrier to opting in. Every closed tester has to buy the app. Fewer people will agree, and anyone who doesn't install can't give you much feedback.
  • An untested purchase flow is a launch risk. If testers avoid your paywall because they don't want to spend money, your billing code ships with almost no real-device use.

Option 1: Keep in-app purchases testable with license testers

For a free app with in-app products or subscriptions, add your closed testers as license testers as well.

  1. In Play Console, go to Settings > License testing.
  2. Choose testers with an email list (up to 2,000 addresses per list) or a Google Group (no user limit, according to Google).
  3. Save your changes.
  4. Make sure the same people can receive your release. Being a license tester doesn't put someone on your closed track. They still need to be in the track's tester list and opt in through the opt-in link. Our guide to inviting testers and fixing access problems covers the common opt-in issues.
  5. Make sure your one-time products and subscriptions are published. Google says they must be published before they can be tested.

Once that's done, license testers see test payment methods at checkout. Google's billing guide lists several, including:

  • Test instrument, always approves, for a successful purchase.
  • Test instrument, always declines, for a failed payment.
  • Slow test card, approves after a few minutes and Slow test card, declines after a few minutes, for pending purchases.
  • A test instrument that simulates a user-initiated chargeback.

Things that behave differently for license testers

Tell testers about these so their reports make sense:

  • Subscriptions renew fast. A monthly or weekly test subscription renews about every 5 minutes, and a yearly one about every 30 minutes. Test subscriptions renew at most six times, not counting free trials and introductory periods.
  • Unacknowledged purchases are refunded. Google says a license-tester purchase is refunded after 3 minutes if your app doesn't acknowledge it. If testers report that "the purchase disappeared", check your acknowledgement code first.
  • Resubscribe and pause are always on. Google says these features are always enabled for license testers even if you've disabled them in Play Console.

Google also recommends testing with some non-license-tester accounts, either occasionally or after large changes, so your app doesn't depend on test-only behavior.

Option 2: Decide what to do about a paid app price

If your app has an up-front price, you have a few choices. Each has trade-offs.

  • Ask closed testers to buy it. This matches Google's rules, but expect fewer people to agree, and be clear with them about the cost before they opt in.
  • Use internal testing for early paid-app checks. Internal testers install paid apps free, but an internal test doesn't count toward the 12-tester closed-testing requirement. Google also says people who opt in to internal testing aren't eligible for your closed test, even if they're on its tester list. Our internal vs closed testing guide compares the two.
  • Think hard before making a paid app free. Google's pricing article says you can change an app from paid to free, but "once your app has been offered for free, the app can't be changed to paid." To charge again you would need a new app with a new package name. Moving to a free app with an in-app purchase or subscription is a separate product decision, not a testing shortcut.

A pre-test checklist for monetized apps

  • [ ] Decide whether testers should make purchases, and write it in your tester instructions.
  • [ ] Add every closed tester to License testing if you want purchases tested without real charges.
  • [ ] Publish the one-time products and subscriptions you want tested.
  • [ ] Confirm each tester is on the closed track's tester list and has opted in.
  • [ ] Check that your app acknowledges purchases, so test purchases aren't refunded after 3 minutes.
  • [ ] Give testers specific purchase journeys, such as "buy the monthly plan, cancel, then restore purchases".
  • [ ] Run at least one check with a non-license-tester account before production.

Our free closed-testing checklist covers the rest of the setup.

FAQ

Do closed testers pay for in-app purchases?
Yes, unless they're license testers. Google says users are charged for test-track purchases unless they're license testers.

Do license testers count toward the 12 testers?
License testing and the closed-test tester list are separate settings. Google's requirement counts testers who are opted in to your closed test. A license tester who isn't on the track and opted in doesn't count.

Can testers use promo codes instead?
This article doesn't cover promo codes. Check Play Console Help for the current rules before relying on them.

Does a paid-app closed test affect production access?
Google decides production access based on your testing, your app and your answers. The price alone isn't something this article can predict. What helps is a test where testers actually use the app, including the paid features. See what tester activity looks like.

If you'd rather not recruit testers yourself

12Testers14Day provides Google Play closed-testing help: about 14 testers for about 16 days, as a buffer around Google's 12-tester, 14-day requirement. Packages are one-time ($15 Basic for one app, $29 Premium for two, per the pricing page on October 18, 2026). If your app is paid or you want testers to make test purchases, contact the team before you buy so they can confirm what's possible. You can also read how a testing run works.
