Official references: Set up an open, closed, or internal test · Test in-app billing with application licensing · Test your Google Play Billing Library integration · Set up your app's prices · App testing requirements for new personal developer accounts

title: Distributed Cron Jobs
description:
Regular cron runs on one server. What happens when you have 10 servers? Each runs the job 10 times. That's a problem.

The Problem 

Single server cron: ✅ Job runs once at 2am
10-server fleet:    ❌ Job runs 10 times at 2am — duplicate emails, double charges!

Solutions

1. Dedicated Scheduler Node

  • One designated machine runs all cron jobs
  • ✅ Simple
  • ❌ Single point of failure — if this node dies, no cron jobs run

2. Leader Election + Cron

  • Cluster elects a leader (using etcd/ZooKeeper)
  • Only the leader runs cron jobs
  • If leader dies → new leader elected → cron resumes
  • ✅ No SPOF | ❌ Leader election complexity

3. Distributed Lock Before Job Execution 

def run_job():
    lock = redis.set("cron:daily-email", "locked", nx=True, ex=300)  # 5min TTL
    if not lock:
        return  # another node is running it
    try:
        send_daily_emails()
    finally:
        redis.delete("cron:daily-email")
  • ✅ Simple, works with existing Redis
  • ❌ Lock expiry must be > job duration, or use heartbeat extension

4. Dedicated Scheduling Services

  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler — cron without servers
  • Temporal.io — workflow orchestration with scheduling
  • Airflow — DAG-based job scheduling
  • Sidekiq-Cron (Ruby), Bull (Node.js)

Exactly-Once Execution

For critical jobs (billing, emails):

  1. Use idempotency keys in the job itself
  2. Record execution in DB before running: INSERT INTO job_runs (job_id, run_date) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING → if 0 rows inserted, skip
  3. Use a distributed lock with heartbeat

Observability for Cron

  • Alert if a job DIDN'T run (missed heartbeat)
  • Track job duration — sudden increase = something is wrong
  • Log job result (success/failure, records processed)
  • Tool: Healthchecks.io — cron monitoring via ping

title: Hono vs Express vs Fastify (and NestJS) in 2026: Real Benchmarks on Node 24, Node 26 and Bun
description:
I ran these benchmarks myself, and every number below comes from those runs. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Hono vs Express in 2026 is a closer race than the benchmark charts you've seen suggest. On Node.js 24, Hono served 1.44× as many JSON requests per second as Express 5 in my tests, and Fastify was right next to it. But Fastify beat Hono on route parameters and POST bodies, and NestJS added 21 to 23% overhead on top of whichever engine it ran on. The biggest jump didn't come from the framework at all: moving Hono from Node to Bun gave another 1.6×.

I benchmarked seven setups (raw node:http, Hono, Express, Fastify with and without response schemas, and NestJS 12 on both its Express and Fastify adapters) across three workloads, two Node versions and Bun. Here's every number, how I got it, and which framework I'd pick for which job.

TL;DR: Hono vs Express vs Fastify, which is fastest?

On Node, Hono and Fastify are tied for first, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express. Hono won the plain JSON test, Fastify won route parameters and POST bodies. Express 5 is the slowest of the three but still served 50,000 requests per second on two CPU cores, which is more than most APIs will ever see. On Bun, Hono pulls clearly ahead at 118,000 requests per second.

Node 24.22, 2 cores, requests/s (median) JSON Route param POST JSON body Startup to first response Install size
node:http (no framework) 78,870 73,049 41,917 76 ms none
Hono 4.13.13 73,067 70,128 36,553 94 ms 3.9 MB, 2 packages
Fastify 5.12.7 71,786 76,746 38,936 153 ms 14.4 MB, 48 packages
Express 5.3.0 50,744 48,335 28,569 116 ms 4.3 MB, 65 packages
NestJS 12.1.3 + Fastify 56,434 59,499 33,418 425 ms n/a
NestJS 12.1.3 + Express 38,893 35,829 23,011 320 ms 22.4 MB, 98 packages

My pick: Hono for new APIs, especially anything that might run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or another edge runtime. Fastify for Node-only services where you want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express when the team and middleware already exist, because it's fast enough. NestJS when the codebase is big enough that structure matters more than 20% of throughput, and then put it on the Fastify adapter.

What are Hono, Express and Fastify?

All three are HTTP frameworks for JavaScript and TypeScript, and they come from different eras.

  • Express is the 2010 original and still the default. Express 5 finally shipped native promise support in route handlers and dropped a lot of legacy API. It has the largest middleware ecosystem by far: 145 million npm downloads in the week of October 6 to 12, 2026.
  • Fastify was built for speed on Node. It compiles JSON schemas into fast serializers and validators, has a strict plugin system with encapsulation, and logs with Pino by default. 15.4 million downloads that week.
  • Hono is built on web standards: handlers take a Request-like context and return a Response. The same app runs on Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda and Vercel. It's tiny and has zero dependencies. 74 million downloads that week, partly because other tools bundle it.
  • NestJS isn't a fourth HTTP engine. It's an application framework with modules, dependency injection and decorators that runs on top of Express (the default) or Fastify. I covered the latest release in my NestJS 12 upgrade guide.

The code looks similar for a simple route. Here are the three handlers I benchmarked:

// Hono
app.get('/users/:id', c => c.json({ id: c.req.param('id'), fields: c.req.query('fields') ?? null }))

// Express 5
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

// Fastify 5
app.get('/users/:id', async req => ({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

How I benchmarked them

Benchmarks of web frameworks are easy to get wrong, so here's exactly what I ran.

  1. Machine. An 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB of RAM. Each server was pinned to 2 cores with taskset. The load generator, oha 1.16.0, ran on the other 6 cores with 64 connections.
  2. Runtimes. Node.js 24.22.0, Node.js 26.12.0 and Bun 1.4.3.
  3. Versions. Hono 4.13.13 with @hono/node-server 2.1.5, Express 5.3.0, Fastify 5.12.7, and NestJS 12.1.3 with @nestjs/platform-express and @nestjs/platform-fastify. These were the latest npm releases on October 17, 2026.
  4. Workloads. GET /json returns {"message":"Hello, World!"}. GET /users/42?fields=name reads a route parameter and a query string. POST /echo parses a 907-byte JSON body and returns a count.
  5. Fair settings. No logging. ETags off in Express and in NestJS on Express, and x-powered-by off in Express. Fastify ran twice, once without schemas and once with response schemas. Every app returns the same JSON.
  6. Method. Each run started a fresh server, warmed it up for 4 seconds, then measured for 10 seconds. I ran 3 rounds per setup and report the median. Four setups had one noisy round, so I re-ran those with 5 rounds. That's 32 setups and more than 65 million measured requests, with a 100% success rate.

Absolute numbers depend on hardware. The ratios between frameworks are what transfer to your servers.

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. On Node 24, Hono handled 1.44× Express's throughput on plain JSON (73,067 vs 50,744 requests per second), 1.45× on route parameters and 1.28× on POST bodies. Latency followed: p99 on the JSON test was 1.50 ms for Hono against 2.12 ms for Express.

Two details matter more than the headline:

  • Hono came within 8% of raw node:http on the JSON test. There's very little left to optimize in the framework itself.
  • Hono's lead shrinks on POST. On Node, Hono goes through @hono/node-server, which turns Node's request into a web-standard Request before your handler sees it. Parsing a body through that layer costs more than Fastify's native parser. On Bun, where Request is native, the same Hono app did 80,749 POST requests per second, 2.2× its Node result.

Express 5 pays for its flexible middleware pipeline and the extra properties it adds to every request and response. It's still not slow. Fifty thousand requests per second on two cores is about 4 billion requests a day. Your database will give out long before Express does.

Hono vs Fastify: which is faster?

It depends on the route. On Node 24:

Requests/s, Node 24 Hono Fastify Fastify + response schema Winner
JSON 73,067 71,786 74,567 tie (within 4%)
Route param + query 70,128 76,746 75,526 Fastify, +9%
POST JSON body 36,553 38,936 39,045 Fastify, +7%

Fastify's router is a radix tree (find-my-way), and it beat even my hand-written node:http router on the route parameter test (76,746 vs 73,049), because my raw version builds a URL object per request. Adding response schemas, which Fastify compiles into a serializer with fast-json-stringify, was worth only about 4% on these small responses. The bigger value of schemas is validation and documentation, not speed.

So on Node, call it a draw. Pick between them on design: web standards and portability (Hono), or schemas, plugins and Node depth (Fastify).

Fastify vs Express: is it worth switching in 2026?

On raw speed, Fastify was 1.41× faster on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST. Its p99 latency was 25 to 40% lower too.

Whether that justifies a rewrite depends on where your time goes. If a typical request spends 20 ms in Postgres and 0.3 ms in the framework, cutting the framework's share in half changes nothing a user can feel. Switch when profiling shows the framework near the top, when you want schema validation built in, or when you're starting fresh anyway. Don't switch because of a chart, including this one.

How much overhead does NestJS add?

NestJS adds a layer of decorators, guards, pipes and interceptors on top of the engine. In my tests that cost 23% of Express's throughput (38,893 vs 50,744 on JSON) and 21% of Fastify's (56,434 vs 71,786). It also used more memory: about 100 MB idle versus 65 MB for plain Express.

The fix is easy and well documented in the NestJS performance guide: NestJS on Fastify was 1.45× faster than NestJS on Express on JSON and POST, and 1.66× faster on route parameters. It was also faster than plain Express on every test. If you use NestJS and none of your middleware is Express-specific, the Fastify adapter is the cheapest performance win available.

Do Node 26 and Bun change the ranking?

Node 26 made every framework faster without code changes. On the JSON test, Express and Fastify gained about 12%, NestJS 10%, Hono 6% and raw node:http 7%.

JSON requests/s Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Hono 73,067 77,454 118,432
Fastify 71,786 80,220 86,269
Express 50,744 56,627 72,479
NestJS + Express 38,893 42,923 not tested

On Bun, the ranking changes. Hono uses Bun's native server directly, so it ran 1.62× faster than on Node 24 and opened a 37% lead over Fastify. Express and Fastify also got faster on Bun (1.43× and 1.20×) but they run through Bun's node:http compatibility layer instead of calling Bun.serve directly. If you plan to run on Bun, Hono is the obvious choice. I compared the runtimes themselves in Bun vs Node.js in 2026.

Memory, startup time and install size

Throughput isn't the only cost. Startup matters for serverless and autoscaling, and install size matters for container images and cold deploys.

Node 24 Startup to first 200 Peak RSS at startup RSS idle Peak RSS under JSON load
node:http 76 ms 62 MB 58 MB 97 MB
Hono 94 ms 67 MB 63 MB 104 MB
Express 116 ms 75 MB 65 MB 97 MB
Fastify 153 ms 78 MB 72 MB 105 MB
NestJS + Express 320 ms 100 MB 98 MB 143 MB
NestJS + Fastify 425 ms 109 MB 106 MB 138 MB
Hono on Bun 14 ms 24 MB 20 MB 43 MB

Startup is the time from launching the process to the first successful response, measured with hyperfine over 20 runs. Hono on Bun was ready in 14 ms, which is why it's popular for serverless functions. NestJS needed about 2.8 times as long as the plain framework underneath it, because it scans modules and builds its dependency graph at boot.

Install size, measured in a fresh folder with npm: Hono plus its Node adapter is 2 packages and 3.9 MB. Express 5 is 65 packages but only 4.3 MB. Fastify is 48 packages and 14.4 MB. A minimal NestJS app on Express (core, common, platform-express, reflect-metadata, rxjs) is 98 packages and 22.4 MB. If you ship Docker images, my Next.js Dockerfile guide has the same multi-stage tricks that keep a Node API image small.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

If you need... Pick Why
A new API with the fewest moving parts Hono Within 8% of raw Node, zero dependencies, web-standard code
To run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda Hono Same app everywhere; 118k req/s on Bun
The best Node throughput on real routes Fastify Won route params and POST; schemas and plugins built in
An existing team and Express middleware Express 5 50k req/s is plenty; huge ecosystem; easy hiring
Structure for a large team (modules, DI) NestJS on Fastify 1.45 to 1.66× faster than NestJS on Express
End-to-end typed clients Hono (RPC) or Fastify with TypeBox Types flow from routes to clients

Two more points rarely show up in benchmark posts:

  • Ecosystem. Express still has the most middleware, tutorials and Stack Overflow answers. Fastify's plugin ecosystem covers most production needs. Hono's middleware set is smaller but growing, and anything built on web standards tends to just work.
  • Typed clients. Hono's RPC mode lets a frontend import the API's types directly. If your frontend is Next.js, also check whether you need a separate API at all; I covered that in Server Actions vs Route Handlers.

How do I migrate from Express to Hono or Fastify?

You don't need a big-bang rewrite. Both frameworks can sit next to Express while you move routes.

// Fastify: run existing Express middleware during a migration
import Fastify from 'fastify'
import expressPlugin from '@fastify/express'
const app = Fastify()
await app.register(expressPlugin)
app.use(legacyExpressMiddleware)

// Hono: same handler shape on every runtime
import { Hono } from 'hono'
const app = new Hono()
app.get('/health', c => c.json({ ok: true }))
export default app // Bun, Workers, Deno; use @hono/node-server on Node

A safe order: move health checks and read-only routes first, measure them in production, then move the routes that write data. Keep the request and response shapes identical so clients never notice. Watch for Express habits that don't carry over: mutating req from middleware, res.locals, and error handlers with four arguments.

Common mistakes when benchmarking web frameworks

  • Running the load generator on the server's cores. Pin them apart, or you measure contention.
  • Benchmarking only /hello. Hono won plain JSON, Fastify won routes with parameters and bodies. One endpoint gives you one answer.
  • Leaving logging on. Fastify with a logger and Express with morgan are both much slower. Compare like with like.
  • Trusting a single run. Four of my 32 setups had one round 10 to 20% below the others. Take the median of several runs.
  • Comparing frameworks on different runtimes. "Hono is 2× faster than Express" is often Hono on Bun versus Express on Node.
  • Ignoring where time actually goes. Profile one real request. The framework is rarely the bottleneck.

Related: if your API is meant for AI agents, read MCP vs API before choosing a framework, because the protocol choice changes more than the framework does.

Key takeaways

  • On Node 24, Hono (73,067 req/s) and Fastify (71,786) are tied on JSON, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express 5 (50,744).
  • Fastify won route parameters (+9% over Hono) and POST bodies (+7%). Hono won plain JSON and came within 8% of raw node:http.
  • NestJS costs about 21 to 23% throughput and about 2.8× the startup time. On the Fastify adapter it's 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express.
  • Node 26 sped every framework up by 6 to 12% with no code changes.
  • On Bun, Hono jumped to 118,432 req/s, 1.62× its Node result, with 14 ms startup and 43 MB under load.
  • Hono installs as 2 packages (3.9 MB). Express is 65 packages (4.3 MB), Fastify 48 (14.4 MB), and NestJS 98 (22.4 MB).
  • Even Express handled 50,000 requests per second on 2 cores. Pick on design and ecosystem first; the framework is rarely your bottleneck.

FAQ

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. In my October 2026 benchmark on Node 24, Hono 4.13.13 served 73,067 JSON requests per second against 50,744 for Express 5.3.0, which is 1.44× faster. It was 1.45× faster on route parameters and 1.28× faster on POST bodies, with lower p99 latency.

Is Hono faster than Fastify?

On Node they're tied. Hono won plain JSON by 2%, but Fastify won route parameters by 9% and POST bodies by 7%. On Bun, Hono pulls ahead: 118,432 requests per second versus 86,269 for Fastify, because Hono uses Bun's native server directly.

Is Fastify faster than Express in 2026?

Yes. Fastify 5.12.7 was 1.41× faster than Express 5.3.0 on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST bodies, with 25 to 40% lower p99 latency. Express still handled about 50,000 requests per second on two cores, which is enough for most APIs.

How much slower is NestJS than Express or Fastify?

NestJS 12.1.3 cost about 23% of Express's throughput and 21% of Fastify's on the JSON test, used about 100 MB of memory at idle, and took about 2.8× as long to start. Using the Fastify adapter made NestJS 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express, and faster than plain Express on every test.

Should I switch from Express to Hono or Fastify?

Only if you have a reason beyond a benchmark. Switch when profiling shows the framework is a real cost, when you want built-in schema validation (Fastify), or when you need to run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or other runtimes (Hono). If most request time is spent in the database, a faster framework won't be noticeable.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

Hono for new APIs and anything that may run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda. Fastify for Node-only services that want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express 5 for teams with existing middleware and experience. NestJS on the Fastify adapter for large codebases that need modules and dependency injection.

Does Node 26 make Express, Fastify and Hono faster?

Yes. With no code changes, Node 26.12 improved JSON throughput over Node 24.22 by about 12% for Express and Fastify, 10% for NestJS, 7% for raw node:http and 6% for Hono.

How did you benchmark Hono, Express and Fastify?

Each server ran on 2 pinned CPU cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM, with oha 1.16.0 on the other cores at 64 connections. Every run started a fresh server, warmed up for 4 seconds and measured for 10 seconds. I report the median of 3 rounds, or 5 rounds for setups with a noisy round, across 32 setups on Node 24.22, Node 26.12 and Bun 1.4.3.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Bun vs Node.js in 2026: Bun 1.4 vs Node 24 and 26, Benchmarked
description:
I ran these benchmarks myself on one machine, and every number below comes from those runs. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Bun vs Node in 2026 comes down to this: Bun is a JavaScript runtime, package manager, bundler and test runner in one binary, built on JavaScriptCore and now written in Rust. Node.js is the V8-based runtime almost every server, library and hosting platform targets. Bun 1.4 reports Node.js 26 compatibility, so for many apps switching is now a runtime swap rather than a rewrite.

I benchmarked Bun 1.4.3 against Node.js 24.22 (the current LTS) and Node.js 26.12 (LTS from October 28) on one machine. I measured HTTP throughput with Hono, Express and plain node:http, a real Postgres-backed API, a large in-memory heap, startup, TypeScript execution, npm install vs bun install, next build, and native addons like sharp and bcrypt. Every number below comes from those runs.

TL;DR: should I switch from Node to Bun?

Use Bun as your package manager and script runner today: bun install was 13 to 29 times faster than npm in my tests and changes nothing at runtime. Consider Bun as your production runtime for new or dependency-light APIs, CLIs and serverless functions, where it was 1.4 to 1.8 times faster and used 25-70% less memory under load. Stay on Node.js for large existing services that depend on Node-specific APM, long-running stability or exotic native addons, and move to Node 26, which was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on most of my HTTP tests.

Node.js 24.22 Node.js 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Engine V8 V8 JavaScriptCore
Status (Oct 2026) LTS, maintenance from Oct 20 Current, LTS from Oct 28 Stable, 1.x
Hono JSON API, req/s 53,408 60,431 98,145
Express 5 JSON, req/s 35,764 38,530 55,382
Hono + Postgres, req/s 21,749 21,008 32,254 (pg), 33,694 (Bun.sql)
RSS under load, Hono JSON 105 MB 105 MB 36 MB
Startup (-e 0) 28.5 ms 26.3 ms 3.3 ms
Run a .ts file 62.6 ms 59.1 ms 3.8 ms
Install a Next.js app (cold) 15.4 s (npm) 1.15 s (bun)
Native addons tested All work All work All work (sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2)

What is Bun, and how is it different from Node.js?

Bun is an all-in-one toolkit: a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, an npm-compatible package manager, a bundler and a Jest-style test runner in one executable. Node.js is just the runtime and leans on npm, tsc or a loader, a bundler and a test framework from the ecosystem. Bun runs on Apple's JavaScriptCore engine; Node runs on Google's V8.

Bun aims to be a drop-in replacement. It implements Node's built-in modules (node:http, node:fs, node:crypto and the rest), reads package.json and node_modules the same way, and runs N-API native addons. It also adds its own faster APIs such as Bun.serve, Bun.sql and bun:sqlite.

What's new in Bun 1.4?

Bun 1.4 shipped on August 20, 2026, and it is the first Bun written in Rust instead of Zig. Per the Bun 1.4 release post, it adds "+1,517 tests from the Node.js test suite", fixes "over 2,900 issues", cuts idle CPU by 5x and memory by up to 35%, and "starts 50% faster on Linux." Bun now reports itself as Node.js 26 (process.versions.modules is 147).

It also absorbs common dependencies into the runtime: Bun.Image (image processing), Bun.WebView (headless browser), Bun.markdown, Bun.cron(), Bun.Terminal, plus bun run --parallel and bun test --parallel. Upgrading from 1.3 isn't free: the breaking changes list includes stricter TLS verification, YAML 1.2 parsing and no .env auto-loading when Bun is invoked as node. Vercel made 1.4 an explicit opt-in on its platform for the same reason.

How I benchmarked Bun vs Node.js

  1. Machine. An 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB RAM. Each server was pinned to 2 cores with taskset. The load generator, oha 1.16.0, ran on the other 6 cores with 64 connections.
  2. Runtimes. Node.js 24.22.0, Node.js 26.12.0 and Bun 1.4.3, all official Linux x64 builds.
  3. Apps. The same files ran on every runtime: a node:http hello server, a Bun.serve hello server (Bun only), a Hono 4.13 app, an Express 5.3 app, and a Hono route that reads one row from PostgreSQL 18 through pg 8.23 (or Bun.sql on Bun) with a 10-connection pool, across 10,000 users at random IDs.
  4. Method. For every configuration: start the server, warm up for 4 seconds, measure for 10 seconds, read RSS from /proc. Each configuration ran 3 times and I report the median. Every request returned 200.
  5. CLI timings used hyperfine 2.0.0 (40 runs for startup, 3 to 5 for installs and builds).

Postgres ran on the same machine without pinning, so the database test also measures a shared CPU. That's closer to a small VPS than to a tuned cluster.

Is Bun faster than Node.js?

For HTTP servers, yes, clearly. On the Hono JSON route Bun served 98,145 requests per second against 53,408 on Node 24 and 60,431 on Node 26: 1.84 times Node 24 and 1.62 times Node 26. Bun's advantage held on Express (1.55x Node 24) and on the plain node:http module (1.42x), and Bun.serve reached 128,461 requests per second.

Server (median of 3 x 10 s, 64 connections) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3 Bun vs Node 24
node:http hello 74,200 req/s 83,301 req/s 105,434 req/s 1.42x
Bun.serve hello 128,461 req/s 1.73x
Hono, 10-item JSON 53,408 req/s 60,431 req/s 98,145 req/s 1.84x
Express 5, same JSON 35,764 req/s 38,530 req/s 55,382 req/s 1.55x
Hono + Postgres (pg) 21,749 req/s 21,008 req/s 32,254 req/s 1.48x
Hono + Postgres (Bun.sql) 33,694 req/s 1.55x
600k-entry in-memory cache 53,314 req/s 61,908 req/s 68,134 req/s 1.28x

Latency followed throughput. On the Hono JSON route p99 was 2.10 ms on Node 24, 1.95 ms on Node 26 and 1.17 ms on Bun. On the Postgres route p99 was 4.75 ms, 6.95 ms and 3.98 ms, and 3.50 ms with Bun.sql.

Two results surprised me. First, Bun stayed about 1.5 times faster even with a real database query in every request, which is where many "it's all the database anyway" arguments end. My database was local and fast, though. Over a real network, round trips will shrink that gap. Second, Node 26 alone was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of the five HTTP tests (the Postgres route was a tie), so upgrading Node is the cheapest speedup available.

Does Bun use less memory than Node.js?

Yes. Idle, a node:http server used 58 MB RSS on Node 24 and 23 MB on Bun, while Bun.serve used 16 MB. Under load the Hono app held 105 MB on both Node versions and 36 MB on Bun. On the Postgres route Node 24 grew to 206 MB against 61 MB for Bun with pg and 56 MB with Bun.sql.

RSS (MB): idle / after 10 s load / peak Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
node:http hello 58 / 95 / 95 60 / 97 / 97 23 / 55 / 74
Hono JSON 70 / 105 / 105 66 / 105 / 105 28 / 36 / 45
Express JSON 65 / 97 / 97 66 / 96 / 96 40 / 72 / 81
Hono + Postgres 70 / 206 / 206 66 / 151 / 151 28 / 61 / 69
600k-entry cache 411 / 455 / 455 370 / 410 / 410 261 / 300 / 491

The cache test is the exception worth reading. Bun started with less memory but briefly peaked higher (491 MB) than Node (455 MB). Bun's garbage collector is a known weak spot under large, long-lived heaps. A Bun pull request from this year described a GC "storm" that made allocation-heavy handlers run "at roughly half of Node.js" with a 150 MB live set. That PR #35431 was closed without merging. In my 1.4.3 run with a bigger heap Bun was still 28% faster than Node 24, but test your own workload, not a hello world.

How fast does Bun start compared to Node.js?

Bun starts about 8 times faster. An empty script took a median 3.3 ms on Bun against 28.5 ms on Node 24 and 26.3 ms on Node 26. Running a TypeScript file took 3.8 ms on Bun against 62.6 ms on Node 24. Node's built-in type stripping uses a WebAssembly-based parser, and here it added about 34 ms over an empty script. bun run launched a package.json script in 3.1 ms against 95.1 ms for npm run.

Command (hyperfine median) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Empty script (-e 0) 28.5 ms 26.3 ms 3.3 ms
hello.ts (type annotations) 62.6 ms 59.1 ms 3.8 ms
import('express') 94.1 ms 65.3 ms
Run a no-op package.json script 95.1 ms (npm run) 3.1 ms (bun run)

Startup matters for CLIs, cron jobs, serverless cold starts and test watchers. It barely matters for a long-running API server. Both runtimes run TypeScript directly now: Node's type stripping has been stable since v24.12.0 but only removes erasable syntax and ignores tsconfig.json, while Bun transpiles full TypeScript, including enums.

Is bun install faster than npm?

Much faster. On a Next.js 16.4.2 app with Tailwind, ESLint and TypeScript (458 packages), a cold install with empty caches and no lockfile took 15.4 seconds with npm and 1.15 seconds with Bun, 13 times faster. A CI-style install from a lockfile with a warm cache took 4.6 seconds with npm ci and 0.16 seconds with bun install --frozen-lockfile, 29 times faster.

Install, Next.js 16.4.2 app (458 packages) npm 11.19 bun 1.4.3 Speedup
Cold: no cache, no lockfile (median of 3) 15.4 s 1.15 s 13x
Warm cache + lockfile (median of 5) 4.6 s 0.16 s 29x
Peak memory, warm install 758 MB 13.5 MB

This is the safest win in the whole comparison. bun install writes a normal node_modules, so you can keep running the app on Node. The cold number includes downloads over my server's network, so yours will vary.

# use Bun only as the package manager and script runner
bun install            # writes bun.lock and a normal node_modules
bun run build          # runs your package.json script with Node, as before
node server.js         # production stays on Node.js

Does Next.js work with Bun?

Yes. A Next.js 16.4.2 production build ran fine with bun --bun next build, in a median 3.03 seconds against 3.22 seconds on Node 24, about 6% faster. Turbopack does the heavy lifting in Rust either way, so the runtime matters less for builds than for serving requests. Without --bun, bun run build launches the Next.js CLI with Node because of its shebang.

bun install
bun --bun next build   # build with the Bun runtime
bun --bun next start   # serve with the Bun runtime

If you deploy with Docker, the base image changes from node:24-slim to oven/bun, and the rest of a production Next.js Dockerfile stays the same.

Do native modules work in Bun?

The common ones do. On Bun 1.4.3, sharp (image resize), better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2 and pg all installed from npm and passed the same smoke test as on Node 24. Bun runs N-API addons, which covers most popular native packages. Packages that pick a prebuilt binary by NODE_MODULE_VERSION need a build for 147, the ABI Bun 1.4 reports.

What still bites people is less about compatibility tables and more about operations: APM agents that patch Node internals, rare Node APIs, and memory behavior under months of traffic. The Bun Node.js compatibility page lists module-by-module status.

Is Bun faster at raw JavaScript?

Sometimes. CPU-bound micro-benchmarks were mixed, so don't expect a blanket speedup. Bun was about 3 times faster at parsing small JSON and 1.4 times faster than Node 26 on a 67 KB document, but JSON.stringify tied Node 26. Node 26 made a big jump over Node 24 on JSON, 1.8 times faster on stringify.

Single core, ops/s (mean of 2 runs) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
JSON.parse, 110 B 1,711,027 1,881,418 5,226,338
JSON.parse, 67 KB 3,854 5,224 7,118
JSON.stringify, 67 KB 6,539 11,634 11,644
SHA-256 of 1 KB (node:crypto) 751,142 751,912 853,054
Sort 100,000 numbers 55 60 90
Map set + get, 100,000 keys 102 134 168

I dropped one test: a regex replace on a constant string ran at 196 million operations per second on Bun, which means JavaScriptCore optimized the work away. That's the trouble with micro-benchmarks. Trust the HTTP and real-app numbers more than these.

Should I use Bun in production in 2026?

For new services, it's a reasonable default now. Bun 1.4 is fast, frugal and broadly compatible, and platforms such as Vercel Functions run it. For existing Node services, migrate only when you can measure the benefit and you have tested memory over days, not minutes. Trigger.dev reported a 5x throughput gain moving a service to Bun and also hit a Bun-only memory leak on the way.

Situation My pick
New API, CLI or worker with mainstream dependencies Bun (runtime + package manager)
Serverless or cron jobs where cold start dominates Bun
Existing large Node service with APM and on-call Node 26 + bun install in CI
Heavy use of exotic native addons or Node internals Node.js
NestJS or Next.js app Node in production for now, Bun for installs and scripts; test Bun in staging

How do I migrate a Node.js app to Bun?

Move in three steps and keep a way back at each one. First swap the package manager, then run your tests on Bun, then switch the production runtime behind a canary.

# 1. package manager only (zero runtime risk)
bun install                 # creates bun.lock next to package-lock.json

# 2. run tests and scripts on Bun
bun run test                # your existing test script
bun --bun run test          # force the Bun runtime even for "node" shebangs

# 3. run the server on Bun, keep the code portable
bun src/server.ts

// portable entry point: Bun.serve on Bun, @hono/node-server on Node
import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()
app.get('/health', (c) => c.json({ ok: true }))

if (typeof Bun !== 'undefined') {
  Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch: app.fetch })
} else {
  const { serve } = await import('@hono/node-server')
  serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 })
}

Frameworks built on Web standards, like Hono, make this painless because the same fetch handler runs on both. For database access, pg worked unchanged on Bun in my test, and Bun.sql is the built-in Postgres client that was 4% faster than pg on Bun in my test. If you're choosing an ORM, see Drizzle vs Prisma. If you self-host, Coolify runs a Bun Dockerfile like any other.

Common mistakes when comparing Bun and Node.js

  • Benchmarking hello world only. Bun.serve vs node:http showed a 1.73x gap; Express showed 1.55x and a large-heap handler 1.28x.
  • Comparing against an old Node. Node 26 was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of five HTTP tests. Compare against the Node you would actually run.
  • Ignoring memory over time. A 10-second run says nothing about a slow leak. Watch RSS for days in staging.
  • Running the load generator on the same cores. Pin the server and the load generator to separate CPUs, or the numbers mostly measure contention.
  • Forgetting --bun. bun run executes scripts whose CLI has a #!/usr/bin/env node shebang with Node unless you pass --bun.
  • Switching runtime and dependencies at once. Swap the package manager first; it gives most of the day-to-day win with none of the runtime risk.

Related: I also ran a NestJS 12 app on Bun 1.4.3: it served 1.49 times Node 24's requests per second on a hello route and started in 264 ms vs 361 ms. See the NestJS 12 migration guide.

Related: framework choice matters on Bun too. In Hono vs Express vs Fastify, Hono served 118,432 JSON requests per second on Bun 1.4.3, 1.62× its Node 24 result, while Express and Fastify gained less.

Key takeaways

  • Bun 1.4.3 served 1.84 times Node 24's requests per second on a Hono JSON API, and 1.48 times with a Postgres query in every request.
  • Bun used 25-70% less memory under load, for example 36 MB vs 105 MB RSS for the Hono app.
  • Bun started in 3.3 ms versus 26-29 ms for Node and ran a TypeScript file in 3.8 ms versus about 60 ms.
  • bun install was 13 times faster than npm cold and 29 times faster with a warm cache and lockfile.
  • Node 26 alone was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of five HTTP tests, a free upgrade when it becomes LTS on October 28.
  • sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2, pg and a Next.js 16.4 build all worked on Bun 1.4.3.
  • Adopt Bun as package manager first, then as runtime for new services; keep large existing Node services on Node 26 until you've tested memory over days.

FAQ

Is Bun faster than Node.js?

For HTTP servers, yes. In my tests Bun 1.4.3 served 98,145 requests per second on a Hono JSON API against 53,408 on Node.js 24 and 60,431 on Node.js 26. With a Postgres query in every request Bun was 1.48 times faster than Node 24. CPU-bound micro-benchmarks were mixed, so the gap depends on the workload.

Does Bun use less memory than Node.js?

Usually. Under load my Hono app used 36 MB RSS on Bun versus 105 MB on Node 24 and 26, and the Postgres route used 61 MB versus 206 MB on Node 24. With a large in-memory cache Bun idled lower but briefly peaked higher, at 491 MB against 455 MB, so test memory with your own data.

Is Bun production ready in 2026?

For many services, yes. Bun 1.4 passes 1,517 more Node.js test-suite tests than 1.3, runs common native addons, and is offered on platforms such as Vercel Functions. Teams still report Bun-specific memory issues under long-running load, so canary it and watch memory for days before moving a large existing service.

Is bun install faster than npm?

Yes. On a Next.js 16.4.2 app with 458 packages, a cold install took 15.4 seconds with npm and 1.15 seconds with Bun. A lockfile install with a warm cache took 4.6 seconds with npm ci and 0.16 seconds with bun install --frozen-lockfile. It writes a normal node_modules, so the app can still run on Node.

Does Next.js work with Bun?

Yes. A Next.js 16.4.2 production build succeeded with bun --bun next build in 3.03 seconds against 3.22 seconds on Node 24. Use the --bun flag, because bun run otherwise launches the Next.js CLI with Node due to its node shebang. Turbopack compiles in Rust either way, so builds gain little.

Do native modules like sharp and bcrypt work in Bun?

The popular ones do. On Bun 1.4.3, sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2 and pg installed from npm and passed the same smoke test as on Node 24. Bun runs N-API addons and reports NODE_MODULE_VERSION 147, so packages that select a prebuilt binary by ABI need a build for 147.

Should I upgrade to Node 26 or switch to Bun?

If you have a large existing service, upgrade to Node 26 first: it was 8 to 16 percent faster than Node 24 on most of my HTTP tests and becomes LTS on October 28, 2026. Switch the runtime to Bun when you start a new service or can measure a clear gain in staging.

What changed in Bun 1.4?

Bun 1.4, released August 20, 2026, is the first Bun written in Rust instead of Zig. It reports Node.js 26 compatibility, adds 1,517 Node.js test-suite tests, fixes over 2,900 issues, starts 50 percent faster on Linux, and adds built-ins such as Bun.Image, Bun.WebView, Bun.markdown and Bun.cron. It also has breaking changes worth reviewing.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Graph on one server: a 4-hop query 19 to 388 times faster than the incumbents
description:
Originally published on the Semurg blog: https://one.semurg.io/blog/graph-on-one-server. Every figure below is a row on https://one.semurg.io/benchmark#graph with the release it was measured on.

Graph databases are judged on traversals: start from one node, follow relationships out several hops, and return what you reach. We
ran that question on a public social graph against six graph databases, on one bare-metal server, with every engine's answer checked
against two independent reference implementations before anything was timed. This post has the results, the one place where it is
close, a mistake in our own benchmark kit, and the one command that reruns the whole thing on your own machine.

What we ran

  • The data: SNAP's com-Orkut social graph: 3.07 million people and 117.2 million relationships, loaded as published.
  • The machine: one Vultr bare-metal server, AMD EPYC 4345P (8 cores, 16 threads), 64 GB of memory, two NVMe disks, no GPU.
  • The engines: Semurg, Neo4j, ArangoDB, FalkorDB, FalkorDBLite, ArcadeDB and SurrealDB, each in Docker on that server, one after another, each with every thread, both data disks and no memory cap, its own recommended settings, and its fastest query form.
  • Two shapes of use: inside your application (Semurg linked into the client; the other engine's embedded mode where it has one, otherwise its fastest connection) and as a server (each engine through its own fastest connection).
  • Three cycles: cold, warm, warm again; the figure is the median of the warm cycles.

One query, 4 hops

Starting from one person, every distinct person within 4 hops (455,604 of them). As a server, Semurg answered in 3.83 ms; ArcadeDB
took 73.14 ms, FalkorDBLite 164.14 ms, FalkorDB 205.89 ms, Neo4j 281.40 ms and SurrealDB 1,484.92 ms. Across those
five server rows that is between 19 and 388 times faster. Inside the application the picture is the same: 3.84 ms for
Semurg against 93.08 ms for ArcadeDB's embedded mode and 1,360.65 ms for SurrealDB's.

Many queries at once

The same 4-hop question from 16 clients at once, each side driven by the same number of clients. As a server, Semurg answered 240.2
queries per second, ArcadeDB 28.0, FalkorDB 8.5 and Neo4j 2.6.

Walks to 131,072 hops

The ladder walks from the same person to every depth from 2 to 131,072 hops, checking each step against the reference. On this graph
everything reachable is reached within a few dozen hops, so past that point every engine is timing one full walk of the reachable
graph. As a server, Semurg's full walk took 95.22 ms; ArcadeDB's took 113.71 ms, FalkorDB's 412.67 ms and Neo4j's
14,033.83 ms. Inside the application Semurg's took 96.88 ms and ArcadeDB's embedded mode 459.74 ms.

The server comparison with ArcadeDB is the close one, and we care about it most. ArcadeDB answers its traversals from what it calls a
Graph Analytical View: an index of the whole graph it builds in memory when the database opens (the build is counted in its load
time). Semurg needs no such build when it opens. The next release carries two speed-ups to the graph walk; in our own test build they took the full walk from 96.4 ms to 81.1 ms on 8 threads (a test build, not a published release), and the published number follows the release.

What did not run, and why

A result we could not judge is shown as held, never dropped. In this run:

  • ArangoDB answered the 4-hop question correctly, but it was stopped by the out-of-memory killer during the many-at-once test, and the walk that followed found it already stopped. Our benchmark kit read that as a failure of the walk itself and set aside all of ArangoDB's results, its correct ones included. That was our kit's mistake, not ArangoDB's: the kit now checks that an engine is running before a walk starts, and ArangoDB is re-run on the next release. Until then its cells on the benchmark page read results pending.
  • FalkorDBLite's many-at-once run had failed requests and SurrealDB's had a zero median, so neither has a throughput figure; load times are held for every engine until each load has its run-to-run band.

Bigger than memory

Every domain we publish runs four classes: in the application and as a server, each on a dataset that fits in memory and one that
does not. This graph fits. The bigger-than-memory run uses SNAP's com-Friendster, a far larger social graph, with each engine held to a
fixed memory budget; its reference answers are still being computed, and the results go on the benchmark page when they finish.

Run it yourself

The kit that produced every number above is published. On a Linux machine with Docker, one command runs the graph benchmark for every
engine: curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/bench | sudo bash -s -- --graph. On a machine like ours it needs about 22 GB of free disk,
about 48 GB of memory for the largest engine, and about eight and a half hours (test tree, not a published release). Every figure,
every held row and the reason for each is on the benchmark page.

title: Node.js Error Alerting by Polling Metrics APIs (with 429 Retry Backoff)
description:
For a nightly Node.js pipeline, use a small cron worker to poll error search or metrics, retry HTTP 429 responses with bounded exponential backoff, and suppress duplicate notifications inside an incident window. Choose a specialist alerting stack instead when you need managed threshold evaluation, notification routing, or traces.

TL;DR: polling is a sound alerting shape only if three invariants hold: the same failed run cannot page twice, rate limiting delays an evaluation rather than dropping it, and a separate heartbeat detects the run that never emitted an error. Infrai fits the query side of this design because it exposes observability through a plain REST API, so the worker needs no vendor SDK. Infrai uses a single API key across 295 routes in 20 modules, reducing credential sprawl if this pipeline later calls another backend capability. It does not provide native alert delivery or threshold routing; the worker owns that control loop.

This distinction matters during incident reconstruction. “The job failed” is an alert. “Which tenant, import stage, attempt, and pipeline run failed together?” is a logging question. Preserve those fields as structured data and make pipeline_run_id the deduplication anchor. Otherwise the first page becomes an invitation to search loose strings at 03:00.

How should a Node.js cron worker poll an error or metrics API?

There are two viable architectures.

The first is a polling control loop: the Node.js job writes structured errors and metrics, then a separate cron worker queries them. That worker classifies the result, acquires a dedupe key such as nightly-import:2026-10-09:failed, and calls the team's notification system. Infrai is a deliberate option for the query service in this shape. Its API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; each documented capability includes request and response schemas plus runnable examples. That is useful here because the filters for logs search and metrics query are not fully declared in discovery parameters: start with a simple query, inspect the documented schema and returned envelope, and promote a filter to production only after that probe succeeds.

The invariants are operational, not cosmetic:

  • Evaluation has a stable time window with a small overlap, so a delayed event is not lost at the boundary.
  • Dedupe state outlives all retries and is keyed by the pipeline run, not by the poll attempt.
  • A 429 advances the retry schedule; it never becomes “no failures found.”
  • Alert delivery is recorded separately from query success.
  • A heartbeat deadline covers silent non-execution.

The second architecture sends metrics to Prometheus, evaluates rules there, and routes alerts through Grafana Alerting or another alert manager; Sentry can own application error grouping and richer error investigation, while Healthchecks watches the cron deadline. This has more components, but notification policy, grouping, and escalation live in systems designed for them. Its invariant is different: instrumentation labels must remain bounded, and alert state must survive individual application processes. Prometheus explicitly warns against high-cardinality labels. A tenant ID or run ID belongs in logs, not in a metric label that grows without limit.

My decision rule: use the polling architecture when the team already has a notification destination and needs a narrow failure detector over searchable structured events. Use the specialist architecture when paging policy itself is production infrastructure.

Build the poller as a control loop

Do not place the poll inside the nightly job. A process cannot report that it was never scheduled, and a crash can interrupt its own last notification. Run the poller independently, a few minutes after the expected completion time, with its own timeout and durable dedupe storage.

I would try Infrai for the error-search or metrics-query leg when a team wants one plain HTTP integration across backend capabilities and does not want another client library lifecycle in the cron worker. It uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, which lets this worker reuse the same credential and interface conventions if the pipeline later needs another backend capability. The supporting advantage is discovery: every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, so the worker can validate the capability schema before rollout instead of pinning an SDK merely to issue a query. The limitation is firm. It does not own threshold rules, phone, SMS, webhook routing, uptime checks, distributed trace trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. If managed paging policy or specialist error investigation is the requirement, Infrai is not a fit; use Grafana Alerting or Sentry for that responsibility.

The following Go program is intentionally limited to transport behavior. It calls the verified error search route and lets a separate classifier consume the successful JSON body. That separation prevents an undeclared filter shape or response assumption from getting buried in retry code.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    queryURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/search"
    if apiKey == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := queryWithBackoff(ctx, http.DefaultClient, queryURL, apiKey, 5)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func queryWithBackoff(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, queryURL, apiKey string, maxAttempts int) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, queryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query transport: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("read response: %w", readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if attempt == maxAttempts-1 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after %d attempts: %s", maxAttempts, body)
        }

        delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    return base + time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(base/2)+1))
}

Five attempts produce base delays of 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds before the final request, with jitter unless the server supplies Retry-After. Those numbers are an example policy, not a service guarantee. Bound the entire operation with a deadline, as the sample does. A retry loop without a wall-clock budget can make a late alert indistinguishable from a missing one.

Keep dedupe outside this process. A unique row in Postgres or an atomic insert in the team's existing durable store is enough: key it by rule, pipeline run, and alert state; record the delivery result; expire it only after the incident window. In-memory maps reset during deploys. Bad choice.

Compare the ownership boundaries

Tool choice follows the failure you need to explain. These products overlap, but they do not erase one another's boundaries.

Option Strong fit in this pipeline Boundary to accept
REST query service Error or metrics queries from a small cron worker; public discovery helps verify schemas The team implements evaluation, dedupe, delivery, and heartbeat monitoring
Prometheus Numeric time-series collection and rule evaluation High-cardinality run or tenant identifiers should stay out of labels; logs remain necessary for reconstruction
Grafana Alerting Central alert rules, grouping, and contact-point workflows over supported data sources Adds an alerting control plane that must be configured and operated
Sentry Application error grouping and investigation It is a specialist error workflow, not proof that a scheduled job ran at all
Healthchecks Dead-man-switch monitoring for a cron job that missed its expected ping It detects absence; structured logs still explain the failed stage and affected data

Sentry is the better choice when developers need specialist error investigation beyond a query result. Prometheus plus Grafana Alerting is the better choice when metric rules, pending durations, and managed routing are central requirements. Healthchecks belongs beside either architecture for missed runs. For JVM services that feed the same B2B pipeline, a Logback appender is another ingestion boundary, not an alert manager; keep that distinction visible when a mixed-language estate shares an incident process.

There is also a privacy and retention boundary to assess before standardizing. The REST option described here does not expose per-user log deletion, bulk export, or subscription interfaces, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed. A system with strict deletion or archival workflows needs another log store or an upstream data-minimization design. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a distributed trace query or span tree.

Verify, page, and roll back

Ship the detector in shadow mode first. For three scheduled executions, store its decision without sending a notification. Seed one known failed run, one successful run, and one run that emits nothing. The failed run should yield one incident key even when the polling window overlaps; the successful run should stay quiet; the absent run should be caught by the heartbeat system rather than the log query.

Then force the transport cases. Return a 429 with Retry-After in a staging proxy and confirm the next request waits. Return a non-429 4xx and confirm the response body reaches the operator rather than being treated as an empty result. Stop the worker mid-retry and restart it. Durable dedupe should prevent a second delivery.

Page on evidence, not on parser accidents.

The rollback is uncomplicated: disable notification delivery while leaving decision records enabled, then revert the rule version or query shape. Do not delete dedupe rows during rollback; doing so can replay the same incident when the old rule returns. If a production query begins returning an unexpected shape, fail the evaluation visibly and keep the previous known-good rule active. “Zero matching failures” is a business result. “Could not evaluate” is an operational failure, and those states must never share a code path.

Finally, put four links in the runbook: the query discovery page used to validate the request, the poller's last-success record, the dedupe record, and the heartbeat status. An incident commander should be able to answer, in order, whether the job ran, whether it failed, whether the detector evaluated, and whether a notification was delivered.

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's public discovery documentation and validate the chosen query schema before enabling delivery.

References

  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Sentry Alerts documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Logback appenders manual
  • Infrai discovery: errors.capture
  • Infrai documentation

title: TIL: What the User Count Option Really Affects in GBase Database
description:
During a typical installation of GBase Database (GBase 8s), the installer asks you to select an expected user count:

1 - 1–100
2 - 101–500
3 - 501–1000
4 - 1000+

It's tempting to accept the default 1–100 and move on. For a quick test, that may be perfectly reasonable. But this option is worth understanding before you initialize an instance for a larger workload.

What Does the User Count Option Affect?

The expected user count helps the installer choose initial instance configuration parameters appropriate for the anticipated workload.

Depending on the installation script and configuration template, these settings may include resource limits related to concurrent connections and other instance resources.

In other words, you're giving the installer a rough indication of how many users the database is expected to serve. It is a sizing input, not a guarantee that the instance will support exactly that number of concurrent connections.

Important: The selected range should not be treated as a direct connection limit. Actual connection capacity depends on the resulting configuration, available system resources, workload, and other relevant limits.

Which User Count Should You Choose?

A simple rule of thumb can help:

  • Feature validation: The default 1–100 range is generally a reasonable starting point.
  • Development and functional testing: Choose a range that reflects the expected test environment.
  • Concurrency testing: Select a range based on the planned workload, then verify the resulting connection and resource settings.
  • Larger deployments: Review the generated configuration and size the instance according to actual workload requirements rather than relying on the installer choice alone.

For example, if you're only validating SQL syntax or checking whether an application can connect, a small user-count range may be sufficient.

If you're preparing a concurrency test with hundreds of simulated users, accepting the default without checking the resulting configuration could leave the instance poorly suited to the test.

Don't Stop at the Installation Wizard

After the typical installation finishes, inspect the generated instance configuration to understand which values were selected.

Check the relevant resource and connection parameters, and confirm that they match your testing or deployment requirements. The exact parameters to review depend on the configuration produced by your GBase Database installation.

For production environments, also consider memory, CPU, storage performance, connection behavior, and workload characteristics. The user-count selection is only one part of database sizing.

Final Takeaway

The user-count option in the GBase Database (GBase 8s) typical installer is more than a cosmetic question. It helps guide the initial instance configuration based on the expected scale of use.

For quick feature validation, the default may be enough. For concurrency testing or larger deployments, choose the range deliberately and verify the resulting settings.

A useful installation habit: don't just ask what value the wizard wants. Ask what configuration that choice will produce.

Have you ever discovered that an installation default affected your database testing or deployment? Share your experience in the comments.

title: TIL: How to Find the Default Port of a GBase Database Instance
description:
After installing GBase Database (GBase 8s) using the typical installation option, you may notice that the instance is ready to use, but you're not sure which port it listens on.

In this setup, the port may be assigned automatically. For the instance discussed here, the default port is 30490. But rather than relying on memory, you can verify the actual configuration in two ways.

Method 1: Check the Instance Script and /etc/services

First, find the instance name in the generated instance script:

grep GBASEDBTSERVER /opt/GBASE/gbase/ol_gbasedbt1210.ksh

Then look up the corresponding service entry:

grep ol_gbasedbt1210 /etc/services

If the service is registered there, the output should show its configured port and protocol. The exact entry depends on your installation.

Note: /etc/services maps service names to port numbers and protocols. It does not, by itself, prove that the database is running or listening on that port.

Method 2: Check the sqlhosts File

The instance-specific sqlhosts file is another useful place to check connection settings:

cat /opt/GBASE/gbase/etc/sqlhosts.ol_gbasedbt1210

A typical entry might look like this:

ol_gbasedbt1210  onsoctcp  hostname  30490

The fields identify the server name, connection protocol, host, and port. In this example, onsoctcp indicates a TCP/IP connection, and 30490 is the configured port.

Replace hostname with the actual host value shown in your configuration.

For connection troubleshooting, make sure the client uses the correct server name and that the host and port match the instance's actual configuration.

Which Method Should You Use?

Both methods are useful, but the sqlhosts file is a good starting point when you're investigating client connection settings. The instance script and /etc/services provide additional context about the configured server name and service mapping.

If a connection still fails, verify that the instance is running and confirm that the expected port is listening. A configured port alone does not guarantee a successful connection.

Final Takeaway

With GBase Database (GBase 8s), installation scripts may configure values automatically, but you can still inspect them afterward.

Once you've confirmed the instance name and port, document both in your environment notes. This small habit makes connection setup, application configuration, and future troubleshooting much easier.

Have you ever spent time troubleshooting a GBase Database connection only to discover that you were using the wrong port?

title: TIL: GBase Database Default Character Set Can Cause Chinese Text Issues
description:
I recently ran into a character encoding issue while testing GBase Database (GBase 8s). The installation completed successfully, and the database was running normally. However, when I inserted Chinese text, the characters did not display as expected.

The problem wasn't necessarily the SQL statement or the application. It could be related to the database locale and character encoding configuration.

Why Does This Happen?

A typical GBase Database installation is designed to help users get an instance running quickly. However, its default locale settings may not be suitable for every language requirement.

For example, an environment using en_US.8859-1 may not be appropriate for an application that needs to store and process Chinese text.

Character encoding issues can occur when the database locale, client locale, and application encoding are incompatible. Depending on the configuration, symptoms may include garbled Chinese characters, conversion errors, or unexpected text output.

The important lesson is that a successful installation does not guarantee that the default character set meets your application's requirements.

Step 1: Check the Locale Configuration

Before changing anything, check the relevant environment variables:

echo "$DB_LOCALE"
echo "$CLIENT_LOCALE"

These commands show the values currently set in your shell. Keep in mind that they do not independently confirm the actual locale of an existing database.

You should also verify the database's locale configuration and check which locale values are supported by your GBase Database installation.

Step 2: Set the Locale Before Creating a Database

If you're setting up a new database, one approach is to configure the appropriate environment variables before creating it.

For example:

export DB_LOCALE=<supported_chinese_locale>
export CLIENT_LOCALE=<compatible_client_locale>

Replace the placeholders with locale values supported by your installation and compatible with your application. A value such as zh_CN.utf8 may be worth evaluating, but do not assume it is available or appropriate for every environment.

After setting the variables, create the database using the intended locale configuration.

Then test the complete workflow:

  • Insert Chinese text.
  • Query the stored text.
  • Confirm that the results display correctly in your client.
  • Verify that your application uses compatible encoding settings.

This approach is particularly useful when preparing a new development or test environment because you can establish the required locale before creating the database.

Step 3: Recreate the Database if Its Locale Is Unsuitable

What if the database has already been created with an unsuitable locale?

In some situations, recreating the database with the correct configuration is a practical solution, especially for a test instance that contains no important data.

The general process is:

  1. Back up any data that needs to be retained.
  2. Confirm the supported locale values and required configuration.
  3. Set the relevant environment variables.
  4. Create a new database with the intended locale.
  5. Restore or migrate the required data.
  6. Test Chinese text insertion, retrieval, and application compatibility.

Important: Changing environment variables alone does not automatically change the locale or character set of an existing database. If the database contains production data, plan the migration carefully and verify whether data conversion is required.

Step 4: Verify the Entire Encoding Path

Even after creating the database with the intended locale, don't stop at checking a single environment variable.

Confirm that the following components work together:

  • Database locale: Determines the database's locale and character-handling behavior.
  • Client locale: Affects how the client handles character data exchanged with the database.
  • Application encoding: Must be compatible with the data being sent and received.
  • Terminal or display settings: Can affect how text appears when viewed through command-line tools.

Testing both insertion and retrieval is important. Text that looks correct in one tool may still display incorrectly in another if their encoding configurations differ.

Final Takeaway

GBase Database (GBase 8s) makes it convenient to get an instance running, but default installation settings aren't necessarily suitable for every application.

If your application needs Chinese text, check the locale configuration early. For a new database, setting the appropriate environment variables before creation may be sufficient. If an existing database uses an unsuitable locale, recreating it and migrating the data may be necessary.

A few minutes spent validating the locale can save hours of troubleshooting later.

Have you encountered Chinese character encoding issues in GBase Database? Did you solve them by adjusting environment variables, recreating the database, or changing your client configuration? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Trust Is a Feature: Verification Lessons From Building the Calendrz Mobile Backend
description:
Trust was everywhere in my LinkedIn feed last week. LinkedIn is testing a feature that lets verified members confirm their connections’ work and school history, with enough confirmations earning a profile badge. Its engineering team also explained how it detects low-quality AI content. And in Europe, the AI Act’s transparency rules had their first real effect: OpenAI said it will add invisible watermarks to text generated in the EU.

Each of those is a different problem, but the theme is the same. “Trust me” isn’t good enough any more. Platforms are being asked to prove things: that a person really worked where they say, that a piece of text really came from where it claims, that an account is really who it says it is.

I’ve spent the last couple of weeks on a less glamorous version of the same problem: preparing the Calendrz backend for native iOS and Android apps. Most of that work wasn’t about features. It was about making sure that the thing calling our API really is who it claims to be, and that the trust stops when it should.

Why mobile apps make trust harder

A web app has an easy setup: a session cookie, on a domain you control, in a browser that enforces a lot of rules for you. A mobile app is a public client. It runs on a device you don’t control, it can’t keep a secret (anything shipped in an app binary can be extracted), and it stays signed in for weeks. If a token leaks, you need to know, and you need to be able to shut it down.

Calendrz holds access to people’s work and personal calendars. That’s sensitive data: who you meet, when, and often why. So the bar here isn’t “good enough for a to-do app”.

What we built: verification at every hop

Here’s a quick tour of the trust-related pieces that landed in the Calendrz backend over the past couple of weeks.

1. Proof of who’s calling: PKCE public clients

The iOS and Android apps are registered as first-party OAuth clients with no secret, because a secret in an app isn’t really secret. They sign in with PKCE instead, which proves that the app finishing the login is the same app that started it. A malicious app that intercepts the redirect can’t do anything with the code it grabbed.

2. Proof that the link is really ours: Universal Links and App Links

When a login finishes, the browser has to hand control back to the app. Custom URL schemes can be claimed by any app, so we serve the Apple and Android “well-known” verification files from our own domain. That’s how the operating system knows a link to calendrz.com really belongs to the Calendrz app. If an environment isn’t configured, the files return a 404, so a misconfigured server can never claim links it shouldn’t.

3. Detecting stolen tokens: refresh-token reuse detection

This is the one I’m proudest of. The mobile apps get short-lived access tokens (60 minutes) and a refresh token that rotates: every time it’s used, it’s replaced. The catch is that a plain rotation setup only knows about the current token. If an attacker copied an older one, the server just sees an unknown token and rejects it, but never notices that something is wrong.

So we now keep a record (a SHA-256 hash, never the token itself) of every refresh token that has been rotated out. If one of those shows up again, that’s the signature of a stolen token chain, as described in the OAuth security best-practice RFC (RFC 9700). Calendrz then revokes the whole authorization, so both the attacker and the legitimate app have to sign in again, while the user’s other sessions are left alone. Refreshes for a given authorization are serialized at the database level, so two refreshes racing each other can’t be mistaken for an attack, and can’t undo a revocation.

4. Trust that ends when it should: revoke on account deletion

When you close your Calendrz account, or unlink one of your connected calendar accounts, every OAuth authorization tied to that identity is now removed. That covers the mobile apps and any AI assistants you’ve connected over MCP. Their refresh tokens die with the account. The revocation runs only after the deletion has committed, so a failure can’t leave you half-deleted.

5. Failing honestly instead of failing quietly

A smaller one, but it’s the same idea. When the new mobile event endpoints can’t load your calendar from Google or Microsoft, they now return an explicit “service unavailable” error instead of an empty list. An empty calendar is a claim (“you’re free all day”), and an app or agent would act on it. If we can’t verify the answer, we say so.

Trust is a feature, even if nobody sees it

LinkedIn’s colleague vouching will show up as a badge on a profile. Most of the work I’ve described won’t show up anywhere. Nobody opens an app and thinks “great refresh-token rotation”. But it follows the same principle: don’t take identity on faith; verify it, and be able to revoke it.

There’s also a lot of AI in this story. Much of this backend work was planned, written and code-reviewed with AI agents, and several of the review rounds caught real issues: a race between two concurrent refreshes, a revocation that could have been rolled back, a log line that leaked more than it should have. As more code gets written this way, having automated checks verify the work before it ships is the engineering version of the trust problem LinkedIn and the EU are trying to solve for content.

The Calendrz mobile apps are still in progress, but most of the trust layer underneath them is already in place. That felt like the right order: build the part people need to rely on before the part they’ll see.

Calendrz keeps your work and personal calendars in sync, privately and securely. Find out more at calendrz.com.
