title: Building GoRoute: An Ultra-Lightweight (<15MB RAM) LLM Gateway in Go
description:
Most developers using terminal coding agents like Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, or Cursor end up running an LLM router in the background to handle rate limits, multiple accounts, and model failovers.

Popular tools like OmniRoute and LiteLLM work, but running a full Node.js or Python runtime 24/7 just to proxy HTTP requests consumes 150MB to 300MB of RAM and introduces cold-start latency.

I wanted something that idles at < 6MB RAM, starts instantly, and never panics. So I built GoRoute.

What is GoRoute?

GoRoute is a zero-dependency, compiled LLM gateway and multi-agent router written in Go.

It acts as a local reverse proxy (http://127.0.0.1:8128) sitting between your developer agents and AI providers.

+-------------+       +-------------------+       +-----------------------+
| Claude Code | ----> |                   | ----> | Google Antigravity    |
| OpenCode    | ----> | GoRoute (Go Proxy)| ----> | OpenAI / Anthropic    |
| Codex/Cursor| ----> |   (<15MB RAM)     | ----> | Custom Endpoints      |
+-------------+       +-------------------+       +-----------------------+

Key Capabilities

  1. Sub-15MB Memory Footprint: Compiles to a single 16MB binary with zero external dependencies. Idles under 6MB RAM.
  2. Automatic 429 Failover & Round-Robin: Automatically rotates accounts and instantly fails over across keys if rate limits are hit.
  3. Dual Protocol Translation: Speak OpenAI (/v1/chat/completions) or Anthropic Messages API (/v1/messages) seamlessly.
  4. 1-Click Agent Setup: Automatically configures Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, Cursor, Aider, and Cline with a single command: 
   goroute setup all
  1. Seamless OmniRoute Migration: If you already have OmniRoute configured, import your existing credentials and routes in 1 second: 
   goroute import-omniroute

Installation & Quick Start

You can install GoRoute directly via curl:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ziuus/goroute/main/install.sh | bash

Or run via npm:

npx goroute setup all

Once installed, check status:

goroute status

Check out the GitHub repo here: https://github.com/ziuus/goroute

I'd love to hear your feedback, feature requests, or questions!

title: I Built a Pixiv Alternative in Go (and Taught It SEO)
description:
Pixiv is wonderful. It's also, architecturally, a black box you can't learn from. So I built my own illustration community platform — Lumiina — live at https://www.lumiina.art, open source at Nyanns/lumiina.

The stack: Go (Gin + GORM) on the backend with strict Clean Architecture, PostgreSQL + Redis, and a React 19 + Vite SPA frontend. The interesting part wasn't the CRUD — it was everything around it: auth hardening, an image pipeline that doesn't melt your bandwidth bill, and making a JavaScript SPA actually rank on Google.

Here's what I learned.

1. SPAs are invisible to Google unless you fight for it

A client-rendered gallery is a ghost town for crawlers. I implemented bot pre-rendering: when the user-agent smells like Googlebot, the server returns fully rendered HTML with real <title>, meta/OG tags, and JSON-LD structured data per artwork — instead of an empty <div id="root">.

On top of that, every artwork publish fires an IndexNow ping, so Bing/Yandex learn about new content in minutes instead of weeks. Combined with a proper sitemap.xml and robots.txt, the site went from "exists" to "indexed" without waiting on Google's mercy.

Lesson: if your SPA needs SEO, server-side rendering isn't the only answer. Targeted bot pre-rendering is cheaper and keeps your SPA architecture intact.

2. Uploads are an attack surface — treat them like one

Anyone who's run a public upload endpoint knows the dread. My pipeline:

  • Magic-byte validation — never trust the extension or the Content-Type header.
  • Decompression bomb guard — decode config first, reject absurd dimensions before allocating a single pixel.
  • Client-side downsampling — a Canvas GPU pipeline shrinks 10–20 MB master illustrations to ~800 KB WebP before network transit. The server never sees the giant file, and neither does my Cloudinary bill.

Lesson: push expensive work to the client when you can. The cheapest byte to process is the one that never reaches your server.

3. Auth: boring, paranoid, and proud of it

  • bcrypt with constant-time dummy-hash execution so username enumeration via timing attacks doesn't work.
  • JWT (strict HS256) with Redis-backed revocation and a password-change epoch — changing your password kills every session, everywhere.
  • Rate limiting in layers, account lockout, and generic error messages that never reveal whether the username or the password was wrong.

None of this is novel. That's the point — auth should be boring. The novel bugs are the ones that end up on Have I Been Pwned.

4. IDs people can share

Artwork URLs use Sqids hash IDs (/artwork/v06sDC) instead of sequential integers. Short, non-guessable, and they don't leak "we have exactly 47 artworks" to competitors. Trivial to implement, surprisingly nice UX.

5. What I'd do differently

  • httpOnly cookies instead of localStorage JWT. It's the stronger default; the current setup works but cookies win on XSS resilience.
  • Start the content flywheel earlier. I over-invested in infrastructure before having content. A gallery with no art is a very fast empty room. Now there's a daily publishing rhythm — one new original artwork every day — and that's what actually moves the SEO needle. Tech gets you indexed; content gets you ranked.

The code

Everything is MIT-licensed: github.com/Nyanns/lumiina. The live site is lumiina.art.

If you're building a content platform in Go — or fighting SPA SEO — happy to answer questions in the comments. What would you have done differently?

title: The wappalyzer npm package is deprecated: options for detecting tech stacks in code
description:
For years, npm install wappalyzer was how developers detected a website's technologies in code. The package's last release, 7.0.3 from August 2023, is now marked deprecated on npm ("Package no longer supported"), and the open-source GitHub repository is no longer public. Wappalyzer continues as a commercial product. If you need tech detection in your own code, here are the options.

Option 1: Wappalyzer's paid service

The browser extension is still the quickest way to check a single site by hand, and Wappalyzer sells API access. That's a good fit if you want a managed service and the pricing works for your volume.

Option 2: the open-source fingerprints plus your own engine

The community fork webappanalyzer (GPL-3.0) keeps the technology fingerprints up to date and is actively maintained. It's data only, so you write the engine:

  1. Fetch the page.
  2. Match each technology's patterns against the HTML, script URLs, headers, cookies and meta tags.
  3. Apply the implies, requires and excludes rules.
  4. Pull versions out of the regex groups, and add up confidence.

A basic matcher is a weekend project. Getting versions, implied technologies and false positives right takes longer.

Option 3: a hosted API built on those fingerprints

We maintain a Tech Stack Detector on Apify that runs that engine for you, against a list of any size. It also reads public DNS, which a browser extension can't see. MX and SPF records show the email provider and sending services, and TXT verification records reveal connected SaaS tools such as Atlassian, DocuSign or Zoom.

From Node.js (npm install apify-client):

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN });
const run = await client.actor('rimulabs/tech-stack-detector').call({
    domains: ['basecamp.com', 'allbirds.com'],
    includeDns: true,
});
const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const site of items) console.log(site.domain, '->', site.techStack);

Real output from 18 October 2026:

basecamp.com -> Atlassian Cloud, Bootstrap, Cloudflare, Cloudflare DNS, Google Search Console, MailChimp, Microsoft 365, Open Graph, Priority Hints, Stimulus, Zoom
allbirds.com -> Apple Pay, Cloudflare, Cursor, DocuSign, Google Search Console, Google Tag Manager, HSTS, HTTP/3, Microsoft 365, Miro, Open Graph, PayPal, Priority Hints, Shopify, Swiper

Each site also has a technologies array shaped much like the old package's output, plus foundIn, the evidence behind each detection:

[
  { "name": "Shopify", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Ecommerce"], "foundIn": ["meta", "scripts"] },
  { "name": "PayPal", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Payment processors"], "foundIn": ["html"] },
  { "name": "Microsoft 365", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Webmail", "Email"], "foundIn": ["dns:mx", "dns:txt"] },
  { "name": "DocuSign", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Miscellaneous"], "foundIn": ["dns:txt"] }
]

It also has ready-made columns such as cms, ecommerce, analytics, email, hosting and cdn for spreadsheets. A filter returns only sites using the technologies you name, and a monitor mode reports what was added or removed since the last run.

Differences from the old npm package

  • No headless browser. The old package could drive Chrome and see tools that load only after JavaScript runs. The Actor reads the page as served, which is faster and cheaper, but some tag-manager-loaded pixels can be missed. DNS checks make up for part of that.
  • Polite by design. It fetches each home page once, respects robots.txt, and reports sites behind a bot check as blocked rather than trying to get around it.
  • Nothing to host. There are no Chrome binaries or fingerprint updates to manage. Results come back as JSON, CSV or Excel.

Cost: $3.00 per 1,000 sites checked. Sites that are unreachable, blocked or closed to crawlers are free. A weekly check of 50 competitors costs about $0.60 a month.

The full guide, kept up to date, is at rimulabs.com/guides/wappalyzer-alternative.

Disclosure: Rimu Labs builds and maintains the Actor in this post. It was written by the AI assistant for Rimu Labs and checked against real runs on 18 October 2026. Questions or corrections: support@rimulabs.com.

title: Go 1.27 Finds Leaked Goroutines With the Garbage Collector. Here's What It Misses
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

When researchers pointed a prototype detector at one of Uber's production Go services, it found hundreds of previously hidden partial deadlocks: goroutines parked on a channel or a lock that nothing would ever release. Each one kept its stack and everything that stack pointed to. None of them raised an error.

That detector now lives in the Go runtime. Go 1.26 shipped it as an experimental profile behind GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile. Go 1.27, released on 19 August 2026, made the goroutineleak profile generally available and deleted the experiment flag. You read it from runtime/pprof or from the /debug/pprof/goroutineleak endpoint.

The interesting part is how it decides that a goroutine is leaked. There are no timers and no "blocked for more than ten minutes" heuristics. The runtime asks the garbage collector a reachability question. Once you see the question, you can predict which leaks it will report and which ones it will never notice.

What "leaked" means to the runtime

The release notes define it precisely: a leaked goroutine is one "blocked on some concurrency primitive (channels, sync.Mutex, sync.Cond, etc) that cannot possibly become unblocked."

Think about what it takes to wake a goroutine stuck on ch <- v. Some other goroutine has to run <-ch. To do that, it needs a reference to ch. If no goroutine that could ever run again holds a pointer to that channel, the send can never complete. And "who holds a pointer to what" is exactly what the garbage collector computes on every cycle.

The Go blog post on leak profiles states the rule inductively. A goroutine is live if it is not blocked, or if at least one primitive blocking it is referenced by another live goroutine. Everything else is leaked.

The primitives covered are channel sends and receives (nil channels included), blocking select (empty select {} included), sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, sync.WaitGroup and sync.Cond, per the same post. A goroutine blocked on file or network IO, a raw system call, or a hand-rolled primitive that is not built on those is never reported.

How the mark phase answers "can anything wake this up?"

In a normal GC cycle, every goroutine's stack is a root. A leak-detection cycle changes that. The design document by Georgian-Vlad Saioc and Milind Chabbi lays out the loop:

  1. Treat only runnable goroutines as goroutine roots.
  2. Mark everything reachable from the roots.
  3. Check each unmarked, blocked goroutine. If the primitive it waits on was marked, some live goroutine can reach it, so this goroutine is "eventually runnable." Add it as a root.
  4. Resume marking from step 2. Stop when no new goroutine gets promoted.
  5. Every blocked goroutine that never became a root is leaked. Mark from those too, so the heap ends up marked the same way a regular cycle would mark it, then sweep as usual.

That final step matters for what you expect in production. The profile reports leaks; it does not reclaim them. The blog says the last round lets the GC "mark all the memory it would have marked during a regular run."

There is one wiring problem the loop has to solve. A blocked goroutine is attached to its channel through a sudog, the runtime's record for "a g in a wait list." In runtime2.go, the sudog's channel field is a maybeTraceableChan and its data field is a maybeTraceablePtr. Sudogs are reachable from the global goroutine list and the semaphore table, according to the design doc. If the GC traced those fields normally, every channel with a waiter would be marked through the waiter itself, and nothing would ever look leaked.

So the pointer is stored twice: once as a uintptr (vu, the "source of truth") and once as an unsafe.Pointer (vp, "for liveness only"). When a leak-detection cycle starts, the runtime makes the vp half of every sudog untraceable, so the GC cannot follow the pointer while the address stays recorded. When the cycle ends, it makes them traceable again. The waiter still knows which channel it is parked on, and that knowledge no longer counts as a reason to keep the channel alive.

The blocked goroutine's own stack gets the same treatment by construction. It is not a root until it gets promoted, so the ch variable sitting in its closure does not mark the channel either. A goroutine that survives the whole loop ends up in a new status, _Gleaked, which runtime2.go documents as "a leaked goroutine caught by the GC."

A leak it catches

Here is the classic timeout leak. The worker sends on an unbuffered channel, the caller gives up first, and the send blocks forever.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "runtime/pprof"
    "time"
)

func fetch(ctx context.Context) error {
    ch := make(chan error) // unbuffered: the bug
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        ch <- nil // nobody receives after a timeout
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-ch:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

func main() {
    for range 3 {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
            context.Background(), 10*time.Millisecond)
        _ = fetch(ctx)
        cancel()
    }
    time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond) // senders block

    p := pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak")
    if p == nil {
        fmt.Println("needs Go 1.27, or 1.26 with " +
            "GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile")
        return
    }
    p.WriteTo(os.Stdout, 1)
}

On Go 1.27, go run . is enough. On Go 1.26, build with GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile go run .. Writing the profile triggers a leak-detecting GC cycle and waits for it, as the design doc describes, and debug=1 gives you the text format with function names and line numbers.

Walk through it with the loop above. After each fetch returns, main's frame no longer holds ch. The only remaining references live in the sender's closure and in its sudog. The sender is blocked, so its stack is not a root. The sudog's channel pointer is hidden for the cycle. Nothing marks the channel, so none of the three senders gets promoted, and all three should land in the profile with stacks pointing at the ch <- nil line. I haven't run this exact snippet, so treat that as what the mechanism predicts, not pasted output.

The fix is the one the Go blog gives for its own timeout example: give the channel a buffer of size 1. Then make(chan error, 1) lets the late sender drop its value and exit.

A leak it cannot see

Now move the channel to package level.

var results = make(chan error) // package-level

func fetchGlobal(ctx context.Context) error {
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        results <- nil // same leak as before
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-results:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

The leak is the same: every timed-out call can strand a sender. Sharing the channel also adds a second bug, because a later call can now receive an earlier call's stale result. The profile stays quiet.

Package-level variables are always roots. In step 2 the GC marks results straight from the global, the blocked senders look "eventually runnable" in step 3, and they never reach the leaked set. The Go 1.26 release notes spell this out: "the runtime may fail to identify leaks caused by blocking on concurrency primitives reachable through global variables or the local variables of runnable goroutines."

The second half of that sentence catches more real code than the first. A long-lived worker goroutine that keeps a map of per-request channels in a local variable, and never reads some of them, keeps every one of those channels marked. So does a struct of channels hanging off a server object that a running goroutine still references. The design doc puts it plainly: the detector's "effectiveness is reduced the more heap resources are over-exposed in memory."

That gives you a design rule the detector rewards. Create channels as close to their use as you can, scope them to one request or one call, and do not park them in registries that outlive the work. The narrower the reachability, the more the GC can prove.

Running it in production and in tests

If a service already imports net/http/pprof, Go 1.27 adds the endpoint with no code change. The blog's workflow, with the address left as a placeholder:

# ADDR: wherever net/http/pprof listens in your service
curl "$ADDR/debug/pprof/goroutineleak" > leak.prof
go tool pprof leak.prof

Inside pprof, list fetch (or whatever function spawned the goroutine) shows the blocked line in context.

On cost, the Go 1.26 notes say the feature is designed "to not incur any additional run-time overhead unless it is actively in-use." When you do request it, there is a worst case. The blog describes a leak-free "daisy chain" where runnable G0 references the primitive blocking G1, G1 references the one blocking G2, and so on. Each link only proves live after the previous one, which serializes marking and gives O(n²) steps for one GC cycle, with n the number of goroutines. The blog's answer is to profile periodically, every 4 hours in its example, since a leak that can be observed once stays observable.

The design doc calls the approach "theoretically sound, i.e., there are no false positives," and the blog describes it as "precise" with "little-to-no false positives," so treat a goroutine in the report as a strong signal that it is stuck. The detector also only sees leaks that have already happened. The blog recommends pairing it with goleak in test suites, which flags goroutines still running when a test ends, and with testing/synctest, whose fake clock lets a timeout path run deterministically.

When the profile comes back empty and memory still climbs, check your package-level channels first.

If this was useful

The leak profile makes sense once you know what the runtime does underneath your code: how goroutines park on channels and what the garbage collector treats as a root. The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers the runtime and its concurrency primitives with that picture in mind, including the channel and context patterns that keep a goroutine from getting stranded in the first place.

title: Introducing @zervonex/baileys - A Tailored Fork of the Baileys WhatsApp Web API
description:
As developers working heavily with automation, we often rely on the incredible WhiskeySockets/Baileys library to interact directly with the WhatsApp Web API.

However, maintaining long-term stability, implementing niche patches, and ensuring rapid upstream syncs for specific organizational workloads can sometimes require custom overrides.

To solve this for our production pipelines, we have officially published and open-sourced our custom-tailored ecosystem variant: @zervonex/baileys.

🚀 Why Use @zervonex/baileys

The @zervonex/baileys package is a dedicated, scoped fork built to ensure predictability, seamless integration, and stable session management in Node.js environments. By utilizing a scoped npm package under @zervonex, we ensure that updates are controlled, thoroughly tested, and safe from unexpected upstream breaking changes.

Key Highlights:

  • Fully Scoped & Managed: Eliminates package naming collisions and guarantees clean dependency trees.
  • Production Ready: Built out of a necessity for reliable, automated multi-device connectivity.
  • Seamless Transition: Maintains structural compatibility with the core Baileys API so you don't have to rewrite your codebase.

🛠️ Quick Start & Installation

You can integrate our fork into your Node.js or TypeScript application instantly using your preferred package manager.

# Using npm
npm install @zervonex/baileys

# Using yarn
yarn add @zervonex/baileys

# Using pnpm
pnpm add @zervonex/baileys

Basic Initialization Example 

async function connectToWhatsApp() {
    // Dynamically importing the modules using await import
    const { default: makeWASocket, useMultiFileAuthState } = await import("@zervonex/baileys");

    const { state, saveCreds } = await useMultiFileAuthState('auth_info_zervonex');

    const sock = makeWASocket({
        auth: state,
        printQRInTerminal: true
    });

    sock.ev.on('creds.update', saveCreds);

    sock.ev.on('connection.update', (update) => {
        const { connection, lastDisconnect } = update;
        if(connection === 'close') {
            console.log('Connection closed, reconnecting...');
            connectToWhatsApp();
        } else if(connection === 'open') {
            console.log('Opened connection successfully via @zervonex/baileys!');
        }
    });
}

connectToWhatsApp();

📦 View on Registry

Take a look at the live release, version history, and dependencies directly over on the npm registry:
👉 View @zervonex/baileys on npm

We are actively looking forward to refining this fork. Feel free to leave a comment below if you have any feature suggestions or compatibility questions!

title: Next.js ~Prefetching~
description:
In this section, I gann talk about story about App Router that is enabled to use Cache Components + Partial Prefetching (cacheComponents: true and partialPrefetching: true are set in next.config.ts). New app that is created by create-next-app is enabled to use them by default.

Default action

  • Router prefetches each routes of App Shell automatically.
  • App Shaell includes static contents and session data from cookies() and headers().
  • App Shell is a static shell (HTML + RSC payload) in which the URL-dependent portions have been replaced with a fallback.

In case of <Link prefetch={true}>

  • If URL to navigation (searchparamsor dinamic parms)is comfirmed, the root of component tree is re-renderd.
  • And then, three prefetches followed are included.
    • A fallback of <Suspense>: Parts that are not cached remains as a fallback, and are streamed when requesting.
    • use cache: private:Runs in server, and is cached in browser.
    • use cache that is passed as a param of runtime value.

Example

If prefetch a link to /search?q=shoes, searchParams is resolved from link of URL, cached result of search() is prepared before click. Browser re-uses it untill stale time has passed or searchParams has been changed.

Additional Information

  • The cached data that is prefetched is treated as fresh data during term of stale.
  • Refferencies: Adopting Partial Prefetching / Optimizing prefetching / prefetch refference

description: "A practical engineering guide to Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [nodejs, redis, backend, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Producers And Consumers: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Delayed And Recurring Jobs: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Concurrency Control: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Exponential Backoff Retries: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Producers and consumers, delayed and recurring jobs, concurrency control, exponential backoff retries, and monitoring queue health with Arena."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Course Tutors: Relevance Tuning Without Lock-In
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an online course tutor aggregating listings from several sources, the durable design is a contract around relevance, latency, and access metadata, not a permanent commitment to one vector database.

Start with the bill and the retention decision

The largest operational term is usually retained and re-embedded course material, not the handful of query calls a learner makes. Keep raw listings only as long as the product needs them, and keep a compact source record (source URL, tenant, ACL, version, and chunk hash) beside each vector. A changed chunk gets a new version; an unchanged hash does not get embedded again. That one rule moves the bill more than shaving a few milliseconds from a query.

Retention has a cost beyond storage. If an instructor deletes a lesson, stale chunks can produce a confident but wrong answer until the index is updated. I would retain deletion tombstones for the same audit window as answer traces, then remove vector payloads after that window. You deliberately stop keeping old text; the trade-off is that a later support investigation may have only the hash and citation metadata, not the original chunk. Compliance and course-owner requests should win over a sentimental archive.

Measure twice.

What should a retrieval contract contain for a course tutor?

Write the contract before choosing an engine. It should state the input (learner query, tenant, locale, and access claims), a bounded candidate count, filters that must be enforced before ranking, and the output fields required for citation. The answer service should never receive an anonymous blob of text. It receives source IDs, titles, URLs, versions, and the retrieval scores that led to the context.

Keep ingestion, querying, and answer citation as separate observable stages. Measure recall against a small set of representative documents and deliberate failures: near-duplicate lessons, outdated syllabi, cross-tenant IDs, and a query whose best answer is lexical rather than semantic. Precision matters too. A top-20 full of vaguely related courses makes a tutor sound fluent while missing the exact prerequisite.

For this particular boundary, Infrai is worth a controlled trial early in the adapter. Its discovery endpoint is public and self-describing, with request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so an engineer can inspect a capability before wiring it into the tutor. That shortens the experiment without making the provider the application contract.

I keep the query budget explicit: retrieve a modest semantic candidate set, optionally blend a lexical set, then rerank only that bounded union. The latency budget belongs in the contract, so a slow reranker cannot quietly become the user experience. Your mileage may vary by corpus shape; I am not sure a single top-k works for both short course cards and long transcripts, which is why the evaluation set needs both.

A small, replaceable vector boundary

The application owns a narrow adapter. Below, the payload is intentionally ordinary JSON and the paths are the documented vector operations. The adapter can be swapped for a specialist service without changing tutor logic.

import os
import time
import uuid
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}


def post(path, payload):
    urls = {
        "/vector/collection/create": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/create",
        "/vector/upsert": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/upsert",
        "/vector/query": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query",
    }
    for attempt in range(4):
        url = urls[path]
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query" if path == "/vector/query" else url,
            headers=HEADERS,
            json=payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("vector request remained rate-limited")


collection = post("/vector/collection/create", {
    "name": "course-listings-v1",
    "metadata": {"tenant_scope": "support-course"},
})

item_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
post("/vector/upsert", {
    "collection": "course-listings-v1",
    "items": [{
        "id": item_id,
        "text": "Lesson: HTTP caching and validators",
        "metadata": {
            "tenant_id": "tenant-42",
            "access": "enrolled",
            "source_url": "https://courses.example/lesson/http-cache",
            "version": 3,
        },
    }],
})

result = post("/vector/query", {
    "collection": "course-listings-v1",
    "query": "How do validators reduce stale course content?",
    "top_k": 8,
    "filter": {"tenant_id": "tenant-42", "access": "enrolled"},
})
print(result)

There are two practical Infrai reasons to test this boundary. Its public discovery surface describes each capability and provides runnable examples, so wiring a new backend operation starts with reading a schema instead of learning another SDK. The same platform also exposes a plain REST surface across many backend capabilities, which can reduce the number of authentication and client conventions your adapter has to carry. That is useful during migration; it is not a promise that every corpus or ranking policy fits one service.

How do specialist and general platforms change migration work?

The adapter keeps the comparison honest. Each option is good at a different boundary, and none removes the need for relevance tests.

Option Useful fit Migration consideration
Pinecone Managed vector search with a focused operational surface You still own metadata contracts and export/import procedures
Weaviate Vector plus schema-oriented search and hybrid patterns Its object and module model becomes part of your adapter unless normalized
OpenSearch Teams already operating search clusters and lexical analysis More cluster policy and tuning can mean a larger operations footprint
Infrai A self-describing REST boundary when several backend capabilities share one integration Validate ranking controls and regional requirements against your evaluation set

Stick with Pinecone when a managed vector specialist and its surrounding tooling are the priority. Choose Weaviate when its schema and hybrid model are central to your product. OpenSearch is sensible when existing cluster ownership and BM25-style analysis matter more than a small integration surface. Try Infrai for the course-listing retrieval adapter when self-describing discovery and one consistent REST contract reduce the migration work across your other backend calls.

The catch is portability still depends on what you normalize. Store your own chunk IDs, source metadata, embedding version, and evaluation fixtures. Export a golden query set before switching providers, replay it after the switch, and compare recall, precision, citation completeness, and p95 latency under the same candidate bound. A provider can satisfy the HTTP contract while changing the ordering that your tutor relies on.

Every indexed item carries tenant and access-control metadata. Enforce those filters in retrieval, then re-check authorization before rendering a citation. Log the request ID, collection version, candidate IDs, and final cited IDs; redact lesson text from logs unless policy explicitly permits it. A citation that points to a private source is a security bug in the application layer even when the vector query was technically successful.

The final quality gate is a failure matrix, not a demo. Include empty results, conflicting editions, deleted lessons, multilingual titles, and a query that should abstain. Review false positives with instructors and false negatives with support agents. Relevance tuning becomes a controlled migration when those cases are versioned alongside code.

One more operational detail pays off during a cutover: run the old and new adapters in shadow mode for a sample of sanitized queries, persist only ranked IDs and scores, and compare disagreements by failure class. That lets you change collection versions or ranking weights without exposing an unreviewed answer to learners. When the distributions settle, switch the read path behind a flag and keep the old writer available until deletion and citation checks have completed. It is slower than a one-line provider swap, but it leaves a clear rollback point.

For example, a support team might discover that “course 101 refund policy” retrieves a marketing page above the enrollment policy. Keep that miss in the fixture set, label the expected source, and test the same query after every chunking or reranking change. If a migration improves semantic recall but drops the exact policy below the citation threshold, it has failed the product contract even if a generic relevance score rises. This is the kind of edge case that rate-limit dashboards will never reveal.

Keep the boundary boring.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the vector capability schema and reproducing the evaluation cases above.

References

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Pinecone documentation: https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • Weaviate documentation: https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • OpenSearch documentation: https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/

title: What a Clinic Website Actually Has to Do in the UAE
description:
Most clinic websites are built like brochures: a hero, a list of services, a contact page. Patients do not use them like brochures. A patient arrives with one job — book the right doctor, fast, on a phone — and every screen that does not serve that job is friction.

We shipped a healthcare solutions page today and had to make these decisions for real, so here is the checklist that survived contact with an actual build:

1. Booking is the product, not a feature

The appointment action has to be reachable from every key screen, not parked on a contact page. On mobile that means the booking/contact action stays in reach while the visitor reads — the same pattern we use for enquiries generally: a lead is a WhatsApp message, a call, or a form submit, and the path to one of those three should never be more than a tap away.

2. Doctor profiles are decision pages

Patients choose people, not departments. A doctor profile needs the things a patient actually compares: specialty, languages spoken, location, and a direct booking route from that profile. A grid of names with no detail forces the patient to call and ask — and many simply book elsewhere instead.

3. Arabic is not a translation toggle

In the UAE, an Arabic version that is a shallow copy of the English page reads as an afterthought to the exact audience it is meant to serve. Proper RTL layout and genuinely reviewed Arabic copy are part of the build, not a plugin. We treat bilingual work as its own scope for this reason.

4. Trust content belongs before the ask

Insurance partners accepted, accreditations, and what happens at the first visit — placed before the booking prompt, not after it. Patients hand over health details and payment information on these sites; the proof has to arrive before the form does.

5. Speed and security are patient-experience issues

A slow mobile page loses the booking. A neglected site — outdated software, no maintenance routine — risks the one incident a clinic cannot afford. Security patching and backups are not IT chores on a healthcare site; they are part of patient trust.

The full breakdown of how we structure this — patient journey, booking flow, doctor profiles, bilingual build, and the maintenance side — is here: clinic and healthcare website solutions in Dubai.

If you run a clinic site, audit it against the patient's job, not the brochure: can a new patient, on a phone, in Arabic or English, reach the right doctor's booking in under a minute? Everything else is decoration.

title: Privacy Budgets for Test Email in Web Apps
description:
Email is often treated as harmless test plumbing. In a web application, it is closer to a small data store: messages can contain personal-looking addresses, sign-in links, verification codes, and enough context to explain what a user did. When a test fails, that data may then be copied into CI logs, screenshots, artifacts, or a developer's laptop.

A useful pattern is to give test email a privacy budget. The budget is not a single number. It is a set of limits for who owns a fixture, how long it lives, what evidence may be retained, and which parts of a message can be exposed to a test. This makes Privacy a design property of Web Development, rather than a cleanup task at the end.

Why test email deserves a privacy budget

Browser and API tests need realistic signals. A signup flow may need to prove that a message is delivered, that the correct link changes account state, and that a second click is rejected. But a test does not need to preserve the entire email forever to prove those things.

Without explicit limits, a shared inbox can let one parallel run read another's message, a failed assertion can print a verification URL into a long-lived log, and a retry can reuse an address or token. A cleanup job can also remove the message before a developer understands the failure.

The first question are not “which temporary inbox is cheapest?” It is “what is the smallest piece of email evidence that proves this behavior?” Search phrases such as tempmailso and temp mail mail may appear in product or test discussions, but the engineering decision should be based on isolation, retention, and access control.

Define the budget before choosing an inbox

Start with the assertion. If the test only checks that a verification message arrived, a receipt may be enough:

{
  "run_id": "ci-1842-attempt-2",
  "fixture_id": "signup-7f31",
  "message_id": "msg-9081",
  "received_at": "2026-10-18T02:20:00Z",
  "subject": "Verify your account",
  "result": "matched"
}

If the test must follow a link, grant the browser step temporary access to the link while keeping it out of ordinary logs. The test helper can return a short-lived value in memory, then replace it with a token identifier once the assertion finishes.

This separation matters because message metadata and authentication material have different sensitivity. A subject and timestamp are useful for diagnosing delivery. A complete URL with a bearer token may be enough to sign in as the test account. It also make the failure record much safer to share with a teammate.

The budget should answer four questions: who owns the fixture, how long the raw message lives, what the test can read, and what survives cleanup. The answers should favor one run attempt per address, bounded retention, narrow access, and a redacted receipt instead of the whole message.

Keep ownership and retention explicit

Give every fixture a run id and attempt number. A retry should get its own address, message correlation value, and token. It is tempting to retry a failed fetch against the same inbox, but that makes old and new messages indistinguishable. A retry should get it's own evidence trail.

The provider adapter should own fixture creation, message lookup, short-lived link claims, and release receipts. The application test should own expected behavior. This division makes it possible to change from a hosted temporary inbox to a local mail capture service without rewriting every test. The runner requests release in a finally-style cleanup step; a janitor removes expired fixtures, and repeated cleanup returns an ordinary “already released” result.

For old fixtures, even a query string like temp gamil com can reveal how legacy test data was generated. A phrase such as temp org mail may also be present in search or compatibility cases. Keep these typo keywords as plain test data only; do not use them as selectors, links, or supported domain examples.

Collect evidence without collecting secrets

Good CI evidence is specific enough to explain a failure and small enough to be safe. A layered receipt works well:

  1. Correlation: run id, attempt, fixture id, and environment.
  2. Delivery: message id, received time, and a normalized subject hash if needed.
  3. Consumption: token id, response status, and whether the token was accepted, expired, or already used.
  4. Cleanup: expiry time, release status, and janitor outcome.

Avoid printing the complete HTML body, query strings, authorization headers, or screenshots of the inbox. Redact before logging, not in a dashboard query after the value has already been copied to several systems. A small allowlist of fields is easier to review than a large blocklist of secret-looking fields.

There is a related lesson in turning API tests into useful CI receipts: the result should describe what happened, not preserve every input. For signup flows, idempotent signup email handling provides another useful boundary. A receipt can say that an event was handled once without retaining the triggering message.

A small implementation contract

Teams do not need a large platform to start. They need a few invariants that are tested alongside the application:

  • A fixture belongs to one run attempt and one environment.
  • A message is accepted only when its recipient and correlation value match.
  • A verification token is single-use, purpose-bound, and short-lived.
  • A retry creates new fixture and token identifiers.
  • Logs contain identifiers and outcomes, never raw links or message bodies.
  • Cleanup is repeatable and a janitor handles crashes.
  • Access to message content is narrower than access to test receipts.

These rules reduce flakiness as well as exposure. The boundary stay understandable when a provider changes or a browser test runs in parallel. It is a modest contract, but it turns email from hidden shared state into an owned test resource.

Review checklist

Before adding an email-dependent test, ask: can two runs claim the same message; does a failure expose a clickable URL; does every retry have a new fixture and token; is raw data deleted after a crash; can a developer diagnose delivery from a redacted receipt; and are screenshots covered by the same retention policy?

If the answers are explicit, the test is checking both product behavior and the safety of its own evidence. That prevent a common failure mode: a green test suite that quietly creates a growing archive of sensitive email.

Questions teams usually ask

Should every test use a hosted temporary inbox?

No. A local mail capture service is often best for application semantics; use a provider-like fixture when delivery integration itself is under test. Keep the same ownership and retention contract in both cases.

title: Cold Starts, Lost Files, and Green Dots: Five Myths About Using a Free Server as Staging
description:
My demo broke at 9:58 PM. The same URL answered at 9:40. My code did not change in between.

That gap is the whole lesson. A free server is a shared, sleeping, replaceable machine. It is not a staging environment.

Below are five myths I kept repeating out loud. Then comes a 90-second probe that turns each one into a measurement.

Myth 1: "It returned 200, so it's up"

A 200 tells you one request finished. It says nothing about the next request.

Cold containers queue, boot, then answer. The status code hides all of that work.

So what did you actually measure? The status, or the latency budget?

Correct mental model: split the question into three.

  1. Liveness — the process exists.
  2. Readiness — it can serve a real request.
  3. Warmth — it can do that without a boot penalty.

Record connect time, time to first byte, and full body time separately. One number is not a diagnosis.

Myth 2: "My files will be there tomorrow"

Free tiers often rebuild the container between requests. Sometimes hourly. Sometimes weekly. You rarely get told which.

So don't assume persistence. Test it.

A canary is the cheapest test you have. Write a value, wait, read it back.

stamp=$(date +%s)
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/canary" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"v\":\"$stamp\"}"
sleep 120
curl -s "$BASE/canary?v=$stamp"

If the read-back is empty, your "temporary" upload directory is a story you tell your demo.

Correction: treat the filesystem as a cache. Keep state in an external store, or ship a seed script that rebuilds it on every boot.

Myth 3: "Free means I can retry CI forever"

Retries are cheap for you. They are not cheap for the host.

Many free tiers count requests, not successes. Worse, retry storms hit a cold service and trigger more boots.

Your pipeline gets slower. Your logs get noisier. Nothing gets fixed.

Correction: exponential backoff with jitter, a hard attempt cap, and one pre-warm request before the real one.

for i in 1 2 3; do
  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --max-time 20 "$BASE/healthz")
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && break
  sleep $(( (2 ** i) + RANDOM % 3 ))
done

Myth 4: "Green locally means green remotely"

At least six things differ between your laptop and a free container:

  • Timezone — logs land on the wrong day.
  • Clock — token expiry and signed URLs drift.
  • Env vars — one missing key kills a code path you never exercised.
  • Filesystem — sometimes read-only, sometimes wiped.
  • Memory ceiling — your build is fine until it isn't.
  • Outbound network — allowlists and DNS behave differently.

None of these appear in a unit test. All of them appear in a demo.

Myth 5: "The health check proves demo readiness"

Most health endpoints are shallow. They return 200 while the connection pool is still warming.

A green dot means the route exists. It does not mean the first real user succeeds.

Correction: add one endpoint that touches a real dependency. Hit it twice before you present.

The probe: one script, one receipt

Here is the template I use now. It needs only bash, curl, and the Python standard library.

You supply two routes: /healthz and /canary. The second one stores and returns a small value.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# probe.py <base_url> [sleep_seconds] — stdlib only, writes receipt.json
import datetime, json, sys, time, urllib.request

BASE = sys.argv[1].rstrip("/")
WAIT = float(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 0.0

def timed(path, payload=None, timeout=25):
    req = urllib.request.Request(BASE + path, method="POST" if payload else "GET")
    if payload:
        req.add_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, data=payload, timeout=timeout) as r:
            body = r.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
            return {"path": path, "status": r.status,
                    "ms": round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1),
                    "body": body[:200]}
    except Exception as e:
        return {"path": path, "status": None,
                "ms": round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1),
                "error": str(e)[:200]}

stamp = str(int(time.time()))
checks = [
    timed("/healthz"),                                   # possibly cold
    timed("/healthz"),                                   # hopefully warm
    timed("/canary", payload=json.dumps({"v": stamp}).encode()),
]
time.sleep(WAIT)
checks.append(timed("/canary?v=" + stamp))               # canary read-back

receipt = {
    "base": BASE,
    "at": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    "wait_seconds": WAIT,
    "checks": checks,
}
json.dump(receipt, open("receipt.json", "w"), indent=2)
print(json.dumps(receipt, indent=2))

Run it twice. Once cold, once after a short pause.

python3 probe.py https://your-app.example 0 > cold.json
python3 probe.py https://your-app.example 120 > warm.json

Reading the receipt

Do not eyeball the whole file. Check four fields.

Field Healthy sign What a bad value means
healthz[0].ms vs healthz[1].ms Second call much faster Cold-start tax is real; pre-warm before demos
canary status 200 with the stored value Your endpoint is broken, not the host
read-back body Contains your stamp State did not survive; treat FS as cache
any error Empty Timeout or TLS issue; fix before blaming the app

Two runs prove very little about a month. Two runs prove a lot about tonight's demo.

Where a free model fits (and where it does not)

I use a model to summarize the receipt into three sentences for a shared channel. That is it.

A summary is not a gate. Never let a generated paragraph decide whether you ship.

For that write-up step I have used MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option, so the probe and the summary live in one place. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Run the probe yourself regardless of host. The numbers are yours, not mine.

Decision table: is a free server enough?

Situation Free server OK? What to do instead
Internal demo, one audience, you can redeploy Yes Pre-warm, keep a seed script ready
Overnight CI on every commit Risky Cache artifacts, cap retries at 3
Data you cannot rebuild No External database with backups
Latency-sensitive user tests No Paid tier or local container
Load or soak testing No Isolated environment you control
Teaching a workflow, first pass Yes Keep the probe in the repo

Limitations and who should not use this

The probe measures only what you instrument. It cannot see the host's scheduler, quotas, or eviction policy.

It also cannot promise anything about next month. Free tiers change shape without notice.

Skip this approach entirely if you need an SLA, handle regulated data, or run stateful services. Skip it if a mid-demo redeploy would cost you the deal.

Also skip it if you cannot write the canary endpoint. Without it, you are guessing.

What I changed

I stopped calling the free box "staging". I call it a demo target with a timer.

The receipt file now lives in the repo. Every demo starts with two runs and one glance at the table.

What would your 9:58 PM failure look like, if you measured it at 9:40?

title: Properties Without Witnesses Are Decorations: A Falsifiability Gate for Agent Patches
description:
A property that passes on the patched tree and on the pre-patch tree carries no information. That is the first thing to measure, before you trust any property an agent wrote for you.

Most agent-written property tests fail this way. The agent reads the diff, writes an invariant that the new code obviously satisfies, and the suite goes green in both trees. The test is not wrong. It is simply unable to distinguish the two states, which makes it a decoration, not a check.

This post describes a gate with three rules and one artifact. Properties need a committed witness and a measured detection rate on the baseline. Fixtures must be isolated per sample, verified by transcript hashing. Flaky-frozen tests are forbidden from acting as oracles. The gate is small enough to run on every agent patch.

The three roles, and what each one can lie about

Role What it claims How it lies Gate check
Property "This invariant holds for the domain" Domain is one hand-picked example Fail-rate on pre-patch tree ≥ floor
Fixture "Setup is deterministic" Sample N sees state left by sample N-1 Set of per-sample transcript hashes has size 1
Freeze "This test is temporarily excused" Frozen test becomes the only oracle Freeze list ∩ oracle set = ∅

Each row fails independently. A property with a real domain can still be useless if the fixture leaks state between samples; a clean fixture cannot save an invariant that holds by construction.

Step 1: Commit a witness next to every property

A witness is the concrete input that proves the property can fail. It is not a test case the agent is allowed to invent during the run — it lives in the repository, reviewable, in its own file.

{
  "id": "inv_total_never_negative",
  "seed": 20261018,
  "input": {"lines": [{"qty": 1, "unit_cents": -5}], "discount_cents": 0},
  "expected_on_baseline": "fail",
  "expected_on_patched": "pass"
}

The two expected_* fields are the whole point. On the merge-base tree the witness must reproduce the bug. On the patched tree it must pass. If the witness passes on both, the patch fixed nothing the witness can see, and the review should stop there.

# gate/witness.py — runnable sketch; plugin points are stubbed
import json, subprocess

def replay(tree_dir, prop_id):
    w = json.load(open(f"witnesses/{prop_id}.json"))
    return subprocess.run(
        ["python", "-m", "props.run", prop_id, json.dumps(w["input"])],
        cwd=tree_dir, capture_output=True, text=True,
    ).returncode == 0

Step 2: Measure detection power on the baseline, not on the patch

Passing the witness is necessary and cheap. The expensive question is whether the property generalizes past that one input. Sample the declared domain under a seeded generator on the pre-patch worktree, and count how often the invariant fails.

# gate/power.py
import random

def detection_power(prop, baseline_tree, gen, run_invariant, fixture_hash):
    rng = random.Random(prop.seed)
    fails, transcripts = 0, set()
    for _ in range(prop.samples):
        example, transcript = gen.sample(prop.domain, rng)
        transcripts.add(fixture_hash(transcript))       # rule 2, below
        if not run_invariant(baseline_tree, prop.invariant, example):
            fails += 1
    return fails / prop.samples, transcripts

Set power_floor from your own baseline run, not from this post. A property whose fail-rate on the buggy tree is near zero is a description of the current code, not a check on it. A fail-rate near one usually means the generator produces out-of-domain inputs and the property is failing for the wrong reason.

Rates in between need a human eye. There is no universal threshold; the number is a policy knob your repo owns and reviews.

Step 3: Isolate fixtures per sample and prove it with hashes

Property sampling multiplies whatever your fixture does. If setup writes rows, mutates a module-level cache, or advances a clock, sample 12 is running against sample 11's leftovers — and your fail-rate is measuring ordering, not behavior.

Give each sample a reset hook and hash the setup transcript (touched tables, env keys, temp paths, fake clock value). Across a run, the set of hashes must have exactly one member.

power, transcripts = detection_power(prop, baseline_tree, gen, run_invariant, fixture_hash)
if len(transcripts) != 1:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: fixture state varies across samples → {sorted(transcripts)[:3]}")
if power < prop.power_floor:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: detection power {power:.2f} < floor {prop.power_floor:.2f}")

A set of size greater than one is a deterministic, reproducible red — the kind of failure you can hand back to the agent without a discussion.

Step 4: Freeze the flaky tests, and keep them out of the oracle set

Freezing a flaky test so the suite stays green is a reasonable maintenance move. Letting that frozen test quietly become the only thing validating an agent patch is not.

Pass the freeze list into the property runner explicitly. Any intersection between the frozen set and the tests the property run actually executed is a hard failure, not a warning.

frozen = {l.strip() for l in open("tests/frozen.txt") if l.strip()}
ran    = run_property_suite(patched_tree, prop.id)      # returns test node ids
leaked = frozen & ran
if leaked:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: frozen tests used as oracle → {sorted(leaked)}")

The same list should carry an expiry date per entry. A freeze without an end date silently becomes a permanent hole in coverage.

Step 5: Wire it as one gate with three exit codes

Run the three steps in a fixed order and stop at the first failure. Exit code 0 means the property is falsifiable, its fixture is deterministic, and its oracle is un-frozen. Anything else is a reviewable artifact, not a vibe.

git worktree add ../baseline "$(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)"
python -m gate.run --prop inv_total_never_negative \
  --baseline ../baseline --patched . --samples 200 --power-floor 0.10
# 0 = accepted, 1 = property rejected, 2 = harness error
git worktree remove ../baseline

Per-property cost is samples × setup_time. Two hundred samples across a ten-property patch is a few minutes of wall clock on a modest machine — acceptable per pull request, not acceptable on every keystroke.

The proposal side of this loop does not need a frontier model; scanning a diff and drafting invariants is well inside what free model access handles, and running the sampler on the free server option keeps the 200-sample loop off a laptop that is already running the app under test. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Availability of free tiers is not a guarantee — check the current terms on your own account before wiring it into CI, and do not send proprietary code or credentials to a shared runner.

Limitations and who should skip this

  • Property sampling only works on domains you can generate. Stateful protocols and payment flows usually need a hand-built model first.
  • The power floor is a heuristic. It catches decorative properties; it does not prove the invariant is the right one.
  • Suites with heavy fixtures (containers, seeded production snapshots) will spend the whole budget on setup resets.
  • Teams with data-residency constraints should run the harness entirely in-house; the remote runner is a cost convenience, not a requirement.

Start with the witness registry. It is the cheapest file to commit and the fastest way to discover that half of your agent's properties pass on both trees. When the power floor turns out to be the number you have to lower, that lower number is the finding worth writing down.
