title: Why I built an open source alternative to Terra for wearable data
description:
Every wearable speaks its own dialect. Apple Health sends one JSON line per HealthKit sample, with heart rate in count/min and oxygen saturation as a fraction. Withings sends a daily activity object keyed by date and intraday series keyed by Unix epoch. Oura, WHOOP and Fitbit each have their own idea of what a day, a device and a duplicate are.

So every health app I worked on ended up writing the same layer: a parser per provider, a table per provider, a cron job per provider. It works until the second provider, the first re-sent upload, the first mapper bug that needs a backfill, or the first person who asks you to delete everything you hold about them.

The obvious answer is a hosted API

There is a whole category of products that solve this for you. Terra is the best known: one API, one widget for your users to connect their devices, and data pushed to your webhook or database. It advertises more than 500 integrations, Garmin included, and states SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and GDPR compliance. If you need Garmin today, or a long tail of devices under one contract, and you don't want to run a server, it is a very reasonable choice.

It did not fit what I was building, for four reasons.

Price per connected user. Terra's public pricing starts at $399 a month billed annually ($499 monthly) with 100,000 credits, and each source a user connects costs 200 credits a month. By my arithmetic that covers about 500 connections. A product with 2,000 users who each connect one source would pay around $2,000 a month at the listed starting prices, before any volume discount. That is fair for a funded product. It is a lot for a free tier, a research study or a side project.

The data passes through someone else. With a hosted API, your users' health data lands in the vendor's cloud before it reaches you. Terra's end-user privacy policy says it is usually kept there for two days and at most six months. That is a short window, but for some projects any third party in the path is one too many.

Raw payloads. I wanted every payload kept verbatim, on my side, forever. Mappers have bugs. When I fix one, I want to re-process a user's whole history from the original files, not from a normalized copy that already lost the detail.

Standards. I wanted FHIR R4 that passes the official HL7 validator and Open mHealth data points, so the data can go to a clinical system or an analysis tool without another conversion.

What I built instead

Open Health Sync is an open source, self-hosted health data aggregator. It is one Go binary plus Postgres with TimescaleDB, and it does the boring parts once:

  • 13 sources: Apple Health and Health Connect (uploaded by a phone app, or imported from the Health app export), plus Withings, Oura, WHOOP, Fitbit, Polar, Strava, Suunto, Ultrahuman, intervals.icu, Dexcom and OMRON over OAuth, with provider webhooks triggering pulls of just what changed.
  • Raw first: every payload is stored verbatim on disk or S3 before anything else happens, and re-sent uploads are de-duplicated by content hash.
  • One model, one unit per quantity: UCUM units, LOINC codes, and "today" means the local calendar day of the record's time zone, not UTC.
  • One answer per question: when a ring and a watch both record the same night, reads return one merged view, with priorities per user and metric, and the raw rows stay available.
  • Many ways out: a REST API (OpenAPI 3.1), FHIR R4 Observations, Open mHealth, CSV and Parquet exports, signed webhooks, and a read-only MCP server so an AI agent can read one person's data with a token that cannot write.
  • Erasable: DELETE /v1/users/{id} removes the rows and the raw files.

It idles at about 22 MB of memory and runs on a Raspberry Pi 5.

Try it in a few minutes

You need Docker with Compose, plus curl, jq and openssl:

git clone https://github.com/soma-intelligence/open-health-sync.git && cd open-health-sync
cp .env.example .env
sed -i.bak "s|^OHS_ENCRYPTION_KEY=.*|OHS_ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)|" .env
docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait
docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm ohs doctor

No wearable at hand? This loads 90 days of synthetic data from six overlapping sources and prints an API key with calls to try:

docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml exec ohs /ohs seed --demo

It prints the demo user's id and an API key once. Export them, then read one merged day, or the same heart rate data as FHIR:

export OHS_URL=http://localhost:8080 OHS_API_KEY=ohs_sk_... USER_ID=...   # values printed above
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OHS_API_KEY" "$OHS_URL/v1/users/$USER_ID/daily"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OHS_API_KEY" \
  "$OHS_URL/v1/users/$USER_ID/fhir/Observation?code=http://loinc.org%7C8867-4&limit=5"

Your own Apple Health history loads from the export the Health app writes on your iPhone (Health app, your picture, Export All Health Data), with the ohs binary from the releases page and a user token (the README shows how to create one):

OHS_TOKEN=$TOKEN ohs import apple-health export.zip --url $OHS_URL

It reads the zip as a stream, so memory stays flat whatever the size of the export, and running it twice uploads nothing twice.

What you give up

Self-hosting is not free of trade-offs, and I would rather say them up front:

  • You register your own developer app with Oura, WHOOP, Withings and the others. A hosted API does that part for you. Each connector guide lists the steps.
  • 13 sources, not 500. Garmin is not available.
  • No certification. There are building blocks for a compliant setup (consent per source and data category, an append-only audit log, hard deletes, a per-user archive), but compliance depends on how and where you run it.
  • AGPL-3.0. Using it unmodified, or calling it from closed source apps over HTTP, is fine. If you run a modified version as a service, you share your changes.
  • Early days. It is v0.1.0, and the API may change in any 0.x release.

It is not the only open source option

Open Wearables solves the same problem and came first. It has the larger community, a web dashboard, Garmin, and an MIT license, which matters if AGPL is a problem for you. I benchmarked both on the same machine with the same Apple Health data: Open Health Sync stored the records 2 to 3 times faster end to end and used about 22 MB of memory idle against about 494 MB, while Open Wearables used 3.4 times less disk. Those are numbers for one user, one machine and synthetic data, and the scripts are in the repository for anyone to run again.

I wrote two comparison pages that try to be fair, including when the other option is the better pick:

  • Open Health Sync and Terra
  • Open Health Sync and Open Wearables

Feedback welcome

The code is at github.com/soma-intelligence/open-health-sync. I would love to hear which source you need next, what you think of the data model, and what you would build if your users' health data were one SQL query away. Issues, discussions and pull requests are all open.

title: 12 developers are not 12 testers per app. The small mistake that breaks a Google Play testing group.
description:
You find 12 Android developers. Everyone agrees to test everyone else's app.

Problem solved?

Each app has 11 other people available to test it. The owner isn't an extra tester.

I got this wrong in an earlier Dozena post. A reader pushed me to explain the dropout math more clearly. Here's the model I'm building now — including where it can fail.

The group size is not the tester count

Assume each developer brings one app and tests every other app:

Developers in the group Other developers per app Margin above 12
12 11 Below the minimum
13 12 None
15 14 Two

The formula is simply testers per app = participating developers − 1.

These are potential testers, not confirmed opt-ins. The table only holds if everyone actually joins each relevant test. Fifteen names in a group chat aren't fourteen testers in Play Console.

The calendar matters as much as the headcount

For personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023, Google's current requirement includes at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before applying for production access. Meeting that threshold doesn't guarantee approval.

Google's official testing requirements

Consider an app starting with exactly 12 eligible testers:

  • Day 1: all 12 opt in.
  • Day 9: one opts out.
  • Day 9: a new person joins.
  • Day 14: the newcomer has not accumulated 14 consecutive days.

The replacement hasn't inherited the departing person's history.

That doesn't mean the remaining testers lose their own history. It means this app no longer has the required twelve people with the necessary continuous opt-in history at that point.

Starting with 14 confirmed testers can absorb two opt-outs if the remaining twelve stay continuously opted in. That's a buffer, not a promise that people won't leave.

Attendance still isn't useful feedback

A counter can't tell you whether onboarding makes sense.

One reader suggested asking for the screen name and what the tester expected to happen. That's much more actionable than collecting “looks good” until a text box reaches its character minimum.

For a testing round, I'd want to know:

  • Which flow did you try?
  • Where did the result differ from what you expected?
  • What changed after the developer fixed it?

The aim is to improve the apps, not just exchange names on a list.

Why I'm building Dozena

Dozena is my attempt to organize this into synchronized rounds of 13–16 developers, targeting 15: a shared setup period, the same testing window, check-ins and private feedback.

It's still in development. The public site explains the format and accepts waitlist signups. I haven't completed a real pilot yet. The MVP will be free and open source.

It won't sell testers, ask for public Play Store ratings or promise Google approval.

If your Android app is approaching closed testing, and you're willing to test other developers' apps too, join the Dozena waitlist.

I'm the developer behind it. The math above is useful whether you use Dozena or organize your own group.

title: Codex Swapped Its Default Model and Retired GPT-5.5 in 15 Days. Did Your Evals Notice?
description:
• Book: Observability for LLM Applications
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On September 29, a pull request merged into Codex gave GPT-6.1 Sol "the highest catalog priority" (#49318). That line made it the model the bundled catalog hands a Codex session when you don't ask for one.

Nine days later, Codex CLI 0.162.0 changed where a fresh terminal thread gets its default model from. Six days after that, GPT-5.5 left Codex for everyone signed in with ChatGPT.

Three changes in 15 days, and none of them showed up in your repo's diff. If your agent runs on whatever the default is, the thing your evals measure may have moved while your code stood still.

My take: a model you didn't choose is a dependency you didn't pin. Pin it per task, and write it down next to every result.

What changed between September 29 and October 14

Here is the sequence, from OpenAI's own release notes and docs:

Date Change Who it hits
Sep 29 Codex CLI 0.159.1: GPT-6.1 Sol becomes the default in the bundled catalog CLI users who never set a model
Oct 7 0.161.0 lists it again: default in the bundled and Amazon Bedrock catalogs The same, plus Bedrock users
Oct 8 0.162.0: new TUI threads respect the server's model defaults TUI users who launch without a model override
Oct 14 GPT-5.5 retires from Codex for ChatGPT sign-ins, at noon PDT (19:00 UTC) Anyone who picked gpt-5.5 and signs in with ChatGPT

The October 8 change is the quiet one. The release note says Codex will "respect server model and reasoning-summary defaults for new TUI threads while retaining explicit launch overrides." The pull request behind it (#50013) puts it more plainly: "Fresh TUI threads should use the app server's model settings unless the launch explicitly overrides them." The server here is the Codex app server the TUI talks to, a local daemon or a remote one (#50913). The same release stopped appending "(default)" to entries in the TUI model picker (#51235).

The October 14 change hits the opposite group: people who did pin a model. OpenAI's models page says the retirement covers ChatGPT sign-ins only and API-key sessions are not affected. It points Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users to GPT-6.1 Sol, and Free and Go users to GPT-6 Luna in the desktop app, both "when available."

To be fair to OpenAI, none of this was hidden. Every change is in a release note or the changelog, the retirement came with an exact time and a named replacement, and 0.162.0 also moved the model and reasoning effort near the top of task details (#50727). GPT-6.1 Sol may well be the better model for you. OpenAI says it nearly matches GPT-6 Astra at about a fifth of Astra's token price (Unite.AI, The Batch), though those are OpenAI's own numbers. An upgrade still moves your numbers, and your evals should say so.

Who picked the default? A catalog file

Look at what "default" meant in #49318. Nobody on your team chose GPT-6.1 Sol. It got the highest priority in a catalog file that ships inside the CLI, so it won.

Codex isn't unusual here. Claude Code's model docs say the aliases opus, sonnet and haiku "point to the recommended version for your provider and update over time." Same doc: "To pin to a specific version, use the full model name, for example claude-opus-5-5." So claude --model opus is a moving target by design, and claude --model claude-opus-5-5 is a pin.

Moving targets are fine for a chat. You want the newest model when you ask a question at 11pm. They are a problem for anything you measure, compare or promise to a teammate.


A default model can change between two eval runs without a single line of your repo changing.

Your evals measure the model, so they need its name

An agent eval can be a formal suite. More often it is a sentence in a team chat: "Codex is worse at migrations than Claude Code." "That AGENTS.md rewrite made the agent better." "This task took 40 minutes last week and 12 this week."

Each of those is a claim about a model. If the model was a default, you don't know which one it was. Did your prompt get better, or did the catalog move? Did Codex get worse at migrations, or did a fresh thread pick up a different server default than the one you tested last month?

The model is not the only hidden variable either. Reasoning effort changes results, and #50013 treats it like the model: if the launch doesn't set it, a fresh TUI thread takes the server's default. The account matters too: the GPT-5.5 retirement hit ChatGPT sign-ins and left API-key sessions alone, so the same gpt-5.5 setting meant two different things depending on how you logged in.

So the minimum record for any agent result is four fields: the model, the effort, the account type and the commit it ran against. Without them, a before-and-after comparison is two numbers with no explanation attached.

Pin it per task, then write it down

For daily work in Codex, a profile is the cleanest pin. Per the advanced config docs, a profile is a file in ~/.codex/ with top-level keys:

# ~/.codex/pinned.config.toml
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_reasoning_effort = "medium"

Start it with codex --profile pinned. PR #50013 keeps explicit profile launches on the resolved configuration, so the profile's model holds even for fresh TUI threads.

For anything you compare, put the pin and the record in the same script. codex exec takes -m for the model (models page), and -c sets any config key (the config docs say a value that isn't valid TOML is treated as a string):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run-task.sh "<task>" : one pinned run, one logged row
set -u
task="$1"
model="gpt-6.1-sol"
effort="medium"
account="chatgpt"   # or "apikey": how this run signs in

codex exec -m "$model" \
  --sandbox workspace-write \
  -c model_reasoning_effort="$effort" \
  "$task" > last-run.log
agent=$?
npm test > test.log 2>&1
tests=$?

printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
  "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
  "$model" "$effort" "$account" "$agent" "$tests" >> runs.tsv

By default codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox (non-interactive mode docs), so --sandbox workspace-write is what lets the agent edit the checkout before the tests run. The agent column keeps Codex's own exit status, so a failed agent step shows up in the row instead of hiding behind a test result on untouched code.

Swap npm test for your own check, and set account to match how the machine signs in. Every row in runs.tsv now carries all four fields: which model, effort and account produced which test result on which commit.

Pinning has a cost, and October 14 showed it. Anyone pinned to gpt-5.5 with a ChatGPT sign-in had to edit their config. OpenAI's list of what to update covers "workspace defaults, saved model settings, managed configurations, custom agents, scheduled tasks, and scripts that still select gpt-5.5" (changelog).

That is the good kind of break. You change one line in a diff, rerun your tasks, and compare the new rows against the old ones.

Where Hermes IDE fits

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent's own CLI in a real terminal, Codex and Claude Code included, each task on its own branch and worktree.

The part that matters here: when you start a task with ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux), you pick the agent, model, effort and account for that task, and you can save combinations you use often as presets (README). Several accounts per agent are supported, so the sign-in a task runs under is something you choose when you start it.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: agent, project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, the model and effort chips, and a preview of the command Hermes will run.

After launch, every session shows its own spend: the cost the agent reports, or an estimate from its transcript marked as estimated, with token totals. Since 2.3.4, a Claude Code or Codex session keeps showing its own model and cost even when the conversation mentions another company's model. The bar above each session puts Model in the same place for every agent.


Codex and Claude Code side by side in Hermes 2.3.4, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with status, context use, cost and branch per session in the sidebar.

What it doesn't do: Hermes doesn't write your runs.tsv, and it can't stop a vendor from retiring a model you picked. It makes the choice explicit per task and keeps it visible per session. The record is still yours. Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with OpenAI, Anthropic or any other agent vendor.

So, which model ran your last eval?

Open the last result you shared with your team, a benchmark, a "this agent is better at X" message, a before-and-after on a prompt change. Can you name the model and effort that produced it?

If not, you were testing a catalog entry. Tell me in the comments whether you pin your agent's model, or whether you'd rather ride the default and take the upgrades as they come.

If this was useful

Writing the model next to every result is the smallest piece of LLM observability. Observability for LLM Applications covers the rest of it: tracing each call, running evals that catch quality regressions when a model changes, and tracking cost per feature in production. If you run several agents, Hermes IDE is free and lets you set the model per task (GitHub).

title: avoiding race conditions in async cascade deletes for event‑sourced services
description:
you've got an event‑sourced aggregate that emits a UserDeleted event, and several downstream services react by cleaning up related rows in their own stores. the cleanup runs in background workers, so a second request that references the same user can slip through the cracks and hit a foreign‑key violation.

the race condition

in a typical setup each service subscribes to the UserDeleted topic and issues a cascade delete against its own tables. because the subscription processing is asynchronous, a request that arrives after the UserDeleted event is published but before the worker finishes will see stale data. the DB then throws an error, and the client gets a 500 instead of a graceful "not found".

a deterministic approach

the trick is to make the delete operation idempotent and observable before the request reaches the service. one pattern is to store a tombstone flag in a shared cache (e.g. Redis) as part of the same transaction that publishes the event. workers check the flag before proceeding, and request handlers read it to short‑circuit.

// publish + tombstone atomically
await redis.multi()
  .set(`tombstone:user:${userId}`, '1', 'EX', 300) // 5 min TTL
  .publish('user.deleted', JSON.stringify({ userId }))
  .exec();

workers then do:

const flag = await redis.get(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);
if (!flag) return; // nothing to clean up
await db.transaction(async trx => {
  await trx('orders').where({ userId }).delete();
  await trx('profiles').where({ userId }).delete();
});
await redis.del(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);

trade‑offs

  • latency vs consistency – adding the cache lookup adds a few milliseconds to every request, but it eliminates sporadic DB errors.
  • cache eviction – the TTL must be long enough to cover the slowest worker, otherwise a stale request could still hit the DB.
  • failure handling – if the worker crashes after deleting rows but before clearing the tombstone, subsequent requests will be rejected even though the data is gone. a periodic reconciler that scans for orphaned tombstones can mitigate this.
  • testing – simulate the race by issuing a delete and a read in parallel within integration tests; assert that the read returns a 404 rather than a DB exception.

when to apply

if your service experiences occasional 500 spikes after bulk deletions, or if you already use a message broker for domain events, the tombstone pattern is a low‑overhead way to enforce eventual consistency without locking the DB.

anyone using a similar approach with different stores (e.g. DynamoDB streams) or who prefers optimistic concurrency controls instead? how do you keep the delete path safe without sacrificing throughput?

title: We changed one word in a prompt and broke a feature nobody was watching
description:
The change was one word in a system prompt. "Concise" became "brief." The diff was a single line. What broke: a summarization feature that our team judged by vibes — read the output, seems fine, ship it — had started omitting a detail that mattered, and three weeks passed before anyone noticed. Nobody was to blame individually. There was just no mechanism in place that could catch it, because we treated prompts like config when they behave like code.

30-second takeaway

  • 3-week bug discovery window collapsed to 60 seconds with prompt regression guards
  • "Concise" vs "brief" — one-word diff → feature silently broke for 8% of users (my own users)
  • Prompts are code: same regression-test arguments apply, and almost nobody I know actually gates them in CI (my own observation, not a measured rate)
  • CI-native: eval gates run where ships already get gated, no manual checklists

(Confession: I changed one word in a system prompt — "concise" to "brief" — and a summarization feature silently degraded for 8% of users (my own users). Nobody noticed for three weeks. Three weeks! I treated prompts like config when they behave like code. Same arrogance, different medium.)

(Caveat: your eval set is only as good as the cases you pick. Ship broken tests = ship broken prompt. And eval sets drift too — revisit them quarterly.)

Prompts are code without a test suite

Every argument for regression testing applies to prompts: changes have non-local effects, behavior varies across inputs you didn't test, and "it seems fine on the two examples I tried" is exactly the confidence level that produces three-week-late bug reports. But most teams' prompt testing process is a human squinting at a handful of outputs — slow, inconsistent, and not something that runs before every ship.

Eval checklists instead of vibes

TestPilot turns prompt testing into a repeatable gate: paste your prompt and the expected behavior, get an eval checklist and a version regression guard — so "brief" vs "concise" gets compared across a real set of cases before it ships, not discovered by users after. It's aimed at dev and QA teams shipping LLM-powered features, with CI integration so the check runs where ships already get gated, and version compare so you can see what actually changed when you touched the prompt.

The version-compare framing matters. The unit of change in an LLM app is the prompt+model+params combination, and "what did this change affect" is only answerable if you can diff behavior across versions, not just diff the text.

The realistic version of this practice

Full honesty about costs: building an eval set is real work, the checklist you define is only as good as your understanding of what the feature should do, and LLM outputs are probabilistic — expect some eval noise, and design thresholds with that in mind rather than demanding perfect determinism. Start embarrassingly small: ten cases that capture what "correct" means for your feature, including the inputs that broke it before. Ten good cases beat a hundred mediocre ones, and the set grows every time reality surprises you.

What it is not

It doesn't score abstract "quality" — it checks the behaviors you specify, which means the hard part (deciding what correct looks like) stays with you. It won't catch biases or failure modes absent from your case set. And CI integration gates what you run it against; a feature with no eval cases has no guard, just the vibes you started with.

The one-feature start

Pick the single LLM feature whose silent failure would embarrass you most. Write down what it must always do and must never do. Turn that into ten test cases, and run the next prompt change against them in TestPilot before it ships. Free to try — and if the first regression it catches pays for the hour you spent, that's the moment prompt testing stops being an idea and becomes a habit.

Every argument for regression testing applies to prompts: changes have non-local effects, behavior varies across inputs you didn't test, and "it seems fine on the two examples I tried" is exactly the confidence level that…

Is TestPilot free to try?

Free to try — and if the first regression it catches pays for the hour you spent, that's the moment prompt testing stops being an idea and becomes a habit.

References

  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications — Nondeterministic model behavior is why prompt changes need regression coverage.

title: Node.js Feature Flag Rollouts: Reversible Releases for US and EU Tenants
description:
A percentage rollout is useful only if a bad release can be stopped before noisy telemetry hides the real failure. For a Node.js backend that searches structured logs from a nightly gaming data pipeline, use a flag as a release-control boundary: start off, admit internal traffic, then raise exposure in deliberate steps across US and EU tenants.

TL;DR: keep flag evaluation behind a small application interface, assign tenants deterministically, and record every control-plane change in your own admin log. Infrai is a practical fit when simple percentage rollout is enough and one key and one bill across backend services reduces operational sprawl. It is not a substitute for an experiment platform, an audit system, or a missed-job monitor.

How should a SaaS staged rollout use a percentage feature flag?

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. In a nightly pipeline, those two outcomes make percentage releases more dangerous than they first appear: a rollout may change which tenants can search fresh logs, while the underlying job can fail silently or deliver the same batch twice. A flag answers "who receives this code path?" It does not answer "did tonight's job run exactly once?"

That distinction is the invariant. Release control, workload correctness, and observability are separate controls even when one incident touches all three.

Three controls. Three owners.

For this gaming system, I would keep the initial flag off. Internal accounts go first. A small, stable tenant slice follows, then larger percentages only after comparing useful search results, empty-result rates, errors, and latency by region. Signal quality is the decision axis: more events are not automatically more evidence. A flood of successful searches can conceal the handful of EU tenants whose nightly index is stale.

The rollout should also be boring to reverse. Store a stable tenant identifier, flag key, evaluated variant, region, and release identifier with each search event. Do not log raw query text unless its data classification permits that. When the dashboard turns red, the operator needs to correlate exposure with the pipeline run without reconstructing state from memory.

A contract that survives the next provider

The application should not import vendor-specific flag types throughout route handlers. Give the Node.js service one narrow contract: evaluate a Boolean flag for a stable subject, fail closed for this risky search path, and return enough context to annotate telemetry. The provider adapter owns polling, authentication, and response translation.

This is where one combined backend API can earn a place in the design. The verified flag surface includes POST /v1/flags/rollout/{key} and reads for flag state, while the public, unauthenticated discovery surface exposes request and response schemas. That concrete REST boundary matters during migration: an adapter can target plain HTTP, without installing an SDK or spreading its objects through business logic. Infrai also groups 295 routes across 20 backend modules under one credential and one bill, which removes key rotation and invoice reconciliation work when the same team operates several services.

Teams running a straightforward US/EU tenant rollout should try Infrai for the release-control layer when a discoverable REST contract and fewer service credentials matter more than experimentation analytics.

Keep the boundary honest. These flags have no built-in change audit trail, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, or recycle bin for deletion, and clients poll. If release governance matters, write actor, old value, new value, reason, and release ID to your own append-only admin log. If you need conversion analysis, exposure-event analysis, or complex dependencies, choose a specialist.

The same separation applies to observability. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id, but this surface has no distributed trace query or span tree. There are no alert or notification routes, synthetic checks, or heartbeat monitoring. Use a Healthchecks-style monitor for "the nightly job never started," and connect alerting to the metrics system that owns your service-level signals. Do not ask log search to prove absence.

Deterministic rollout without sticky surprises

Percentage assignment must be stable. Random evaluation on every request makes one tenant bounce between old and new behavior, contaminates comparisons, and turns rollback analysis into guesswork. A Node.js service should obtain remote state through its narrow adapters, then keep provider response types out of route handlers. This runnable Go probe exercises the adjacent log-search HTTP boundary during a migration rehearsal, where operators inspect rollout evidence. It uses a verified read route, never embeds a key, handles rate limiting, and treats every non-success response as evidence rather than silently assuming 200. No filters are appended because the discovery parameters for log search are not declared; guessing them would produce a persuasive-looking sample with an unsupported contract.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(header string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func searchLogs(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string) (map[string]any, error) {
    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search"
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        var result map[string]any
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &result); err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        return result, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("log search remained rate limited")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    result, err := searchLogs(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}, key)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    encoded, _ := json.MarshalIndent(result, "", "  ")
    fmt.Println(string(encoded))
}

The probe deliberately prints the response instead of asserting fields that are not in its application contract. A production adapter should decode only fields declared by the live discovery schema and reject malformed responses. The flag adapter needs the same discipline. During a provider migration, run both flag adapters against a fixed corpus of internal, US, and EU tenant contexts; compare decisions without serving the shadow result. If two providers use different native bucketing, preserve assignment in the adapter or accept the reshuffle as an explicit release event. Never discover that difference on live traffic.

Coarse targeting deserves separate keys when the operational decision differs. A US rollout and an EU rollout may advance independently because data residency, pipeline completion time, and on-call coverage differ. A beta cohort or tenant tier can also have its own key. Resist encoding every combination into one clever rule tree; it becomes hard to inspect under pressure.

One trap remains. The sample computes assignments locally, while a hosted provider may evaluate them remotely or publish configuration for polling. Pick one authority. Two evaluators with superficially similar percentages can disagree at the tenant boundary, so migration tests should use a fixed corpus of tenant IDs and compare decisions before traffic moves.

How the real alternatives differ

LaunchDarkly, Unleash, and ConfigCat are credible flag alternatives, not fallback names on a checklist. Datadog, Grafana, and Better Stack belong in the adjacent log-search decision. Evaluate them with the same failure modes and governance requirements. The useful comparison is architectural, not a price grid that will age badly: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or ConfigCat can own feature evaluation while Datadog, Grafana, or Better Stack owns richer investigation and alerting. That split adds credentials and operating surfaces, but a specialist is the right trade when its deeper control plane or query workflow is required.

Option Best fit in this decision Boundary to verify before committing
Combined REST backend Simple percentage release through a discoverable REST surface, especially when one backend credential already covers other services Supply your own audit log and evaluation analytics; clients poll
LaunchDarkly Teams shopping for a dedicated feature-management product and willing to adopt its evaluation model Test exportability of flag definitions and tenant assignments in a migration rehearsal
Unleash Teams that want a specialist feature-flag system and value deployment control over the flag service Budget for operating ownership and verify strategy parity with the current rollout
ConfigCat Teams that prefer a focused hosted flag service with client-facing integration choices Confirm polling behavior, cache staleness, and deterministic targeting across regions

Those boundaries should be proved with a thin adapter and contract tests, not inferred from a feature matrix. Create the same flag, run a fixed set of tenant contexts, record decisions, disable the provider, and observe the fallback. Then export or recreate the configuration with a second provider. A reversible choice is one you have rehearsed.

Rehearse it quarterly.

For this particular workload, the combined API is the smaller control-plane choice when basic rollout is the whole requirement. A specialist is better when the release team needs native evaluation analytics, governed change history, sophisticated targeting, or experimentation workflows. Direct ownership may also be rational for a tiny number of flags, but then the team owns storage consistency, polling, access control, audit history, and every edge case around concurrent changes.

The rollout runbook

Start at 0%. Enable internal tenants and verify that their structured searches return the expected pipeline run, not merely HTTP success. Move to a small regional cohort only after the nightly completion signal is green.

At each step, compare old and new paths using a release identifier. Watch result usefulness, empty results, error rate, and latency separately for US and EU tenants. Pause on a signal-quality regression even if aggregate availability looks healthy. If evidence is ambiguous, hold the percentage. Fast movement is not the objective.

Silence is not success.

Every change gets an operator, timestamp, previous percentage, new percentage, reason, and ticket or release ID in the admin log. Use optimistic concurrency when the provider contract exposes it so two operators cannot silently overwrite each other. Deletion should require an explicit retirement procedure because there is no recycle bin.

Rollback is one control-plane change, but recovery may require more. Turning the flag off stops new exposure; it does not repair a stale index, retract duplicate pipeline output, or notify anyone that a scheduled job did not run. Keep an idempotency key at the batch boundary, make consumers safe for repeat delivery, and let the heartbeat monitor page on absence.

Small steps. Clear evidence.

When this pattern is the wrong tool

Do not use a percentage flag to answer a causal product question. Without built-in evaluation analytics, exposure data and outcome analysis belong elsewhere, and an experiment platform is the clearer choice. Do not use it as a regional compliance boundary either; percentage assignment is release control, not proof of residency or authorization.

It is also the wrong primary control for an emergency that demands instant propagation if clients only poll. Measure the configured polling interval and worst-case staleness, then put that delay in the runbook. For destructive changes, database migrations, or incompatible event schemas, use an expand-and-contract migration so both code paths remain valid during the rollout.

The practical standard is simple: a flag limits who sees a change, telemetry tells you what happened, and independent scheduling checks tell you whether the work happened at all. Keep those jobs separate and vendor replacement stays a planned exercise instead of an incident project.

If this boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's public discovery contract and generate the adapter from the live schema rather than guessing request fields.

Sources

  • Infrai flag discovery: request and response schema
  • OpenTelemetry metrics signal concepts
  • LaunchDarkly documentation
  • Unleash documentation
  • ConfigCat documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
