title: GitView CodeAudit: Go security reviews that never leave your laptop
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

GitView CodeAudit is a security review for Go backends that runs on your laptop. A static analyzer finds the problems and collects the evidence; an open-weight model, Gemma running on Ollama, explains a finding when you ask, but it never decides one.

GitView started as my terminal tool for watching Git changes and studying Go code: call graph, data flow, SQL operations and HTTP routes, each with the evidence behind it. This week I built CodeAudit on top of those analyses.

Who would pay for it? Freelancers and small agencies that build Go APIs for clients. Clients ask for a security review before a launch, a funding round or a big customer's due diligence, and they pay for it. But that code usually comes under an NDA, and pasting it into a cloud AI tool is exactly what the contract forbids. CodeAudit lets one developer do that review on their own laptop and hand over a real deliverable: an offline HTML report with each finding, the path that reaches it, the evidence, and the reviewer's decision with its justification.

That is the side hustle: the client pays for the review, and producing it costs nothing per token.

Every finding answers the questions a client will ask:

  • Where? File, line and function.
  • Why? The rule, and the data that reaches the line, for example c.Query("q") → "... LIKE '%" + term + "%'" → db.QueryContext.
  • How is it reached? Every HTTP route that leads there, through each middleware, marking the one that authenticates.
  • How sure are we? Severity, confidence and verdict are separate fields. A possible IDOR is shown as Review Required — Authorization Not Established, never as "IDOR confirmed".
  • How do I fix it, and how do I test the fix?
  • What did we decide? Open → Investigating → Confirmed / False Positive / Accepted Risk / Fixed, with a history of every change: its date, its justification and the commit it refers to.

Demo

GitView is a local tool, so there is no deployed link: everything below runs on your machine. The repository ships a small vulnerable API, with safe variants of each case, that the tests use. You can reproduce these screenshots with it:

git clone https://github.com/Darrkkens/gitview && cd gitview && go install .   # Go 1.25
gitview audit scan --module internal/audit/testdata/app
gitview audit serve --module internal/audit/testdata/app   # opens 127.0.0.1 in the browser

A SQL injection: the route, the middleware chain and the handler lead to the query, and the inspector shows the evidence.

The same finding explained by Gemma. Each evidence ID the model cites is checked against the analysis.

A possible IDOR is a review, not a verdict. The resource ID comes from the request and the query has no owner or tenant condition, but authorization could live somewhere the static analysis cannot see.

The report you hand to the client is a single offline HTML file. It has no network access, a strict CSP, and only bounded, redacted excerpts of the code.

Code

Darrkkens / gitview

GitView

Monitor de alterações Git em tempo real no terminal. Cada arquivo modificado pode ser expandido ou recolhido individualmente, e os diffs se atualizam sozinhos. Inclui busca global nos diffs, exportação de relatórios, execução de testes, Code Flow e o Go Deep Inspector, para estudar código Go com evidências verificáveis.

go install .
gitview [opções] [diretório]
Opção Descrição
--delta Renderiza diffs com git-delta (alternável com d)
--expand Expande automaticamente arquivos novos
--interval 2s Intervalo do polling de segurança
--no-watch Desativa fsnotify e usa apenas polling
--export-dir DIR Diretório padrão dos relatórios (também GITVIEW_EXPORT_DIR)
--test-timeout 10m Tempo limite de uma execução de testes
--ascii Símbolos ASCII (também GITVIEW_ASCII=1)

Atalhos

? mostra a ajuda da tela atual.

Mouse: a roda rola o diff; clicar numa dica do rodapé (por exemplo x Exportar) equivale a pressionar a tecla; na exportação, clicar num formato, escopo ou caixa [x] escolhe ou…


View on GitHub


  • internal/audit: the rules, the taint paths, the review store, the audit diff and the report.
  • internal/audit/ai: the Ollama client, the context builder and the validator of the model's answers.

How I Built It

Static analysis first. CodeAudit has 18 deterministic rules for injection, authentication, authorization, sensitive data, configuration and dependencies. They run over analyses GitView already had: go/packages, go/types and SSA for the call graph and the data flow, the SQL operations, and the HTTP routes with their middleware chains.

  • Taint: a taint finding is the shortest path in the data flow graph from an HTTP input to a sink.
  • Sanitizers: they only count when their meaning is known. strconv.Atoi neutralizes everything and filepath.Base neutralizes paths; an arbitrary function call is not a sanitizer.
  • Checks: an if that dominates the sink and examines the value, like if !allowed(origin), turns "vulnerable" into "review", because the analyzer cannot prove the check is sufficient.
  • Authorization: a 403 only counts as authorization when the request is already authenticated. A 403 from a CORS filter is shown as a request filter instead.
  • Dependencies: they are checked only against a local copy of the Go vulnerability database (OSV format). Without one, the report says "dependencies not checked" instead of pretending, and a database older than 30 days is flagged as possibly out of date.

Gemma on Ollama, kept on a short leash.

  • Model: by default GitView picks the smallest installed Gemma model (gemma3:4b on my machine). It never downloads one, and it refuses any endpoint that is not on this machine unless you pass --ai-allow-remote.
  • Context: the context sent to the model is built from the analysis, not from a file dump. It holds the finding, its evidence, the route path and the function's code, within a budget of about 6,000 tokens. Secrets are redacted, and the repository's comments and strings go in as data, never as instructions.
  • Answer: Ollama's structured outputs (format with a JSON schema) shape the reply. Every evidence ID, file, line and symbol the model cites is validated against the context, and a citation that does not exist is shown as rejected.
  • Cache: answers are cached by context hash, model digest and prompt version.
  • No authority: the model can recommend a review state, but it cannot change one. The reviewer decides.

Being honest about the model. On my CPU-only laptop, one explanation from gemma3:4b took between three and a half and five minutes (215 s and 310 s in two runs), and gemma3:12b did not fit in the free memory. The prose is useful but not perfect; in one test the model expanded "IDOR" incorrectly. That is exactly why the model is not allowed to decide anything and why its citations are checked.

Testing without a model. The test suite never needs a real model. It runs against a simulated Ollama, including answers that cite evidence that does not exist. The fixture app has one case per rule plus its safe variant (Atoi before the query, filepath.Base, a tenant filter, an admin route that answers 403, a secure cookie…), and the test fails on any unexpected finding.

Dogfooding found my own false positives. Running CodeAudit on GitView itself flagged three "hardcoded secrets". They were descriptions like credential = "Authorization header". The rule now skips values with spaces, the fixture has that case, and the rule documents what it misses because of it: a hardcoded passphrase.

I built this with Claude Code as my pair, from the spec to the browser tests.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The code cannot leave. For a review under an NDA, a model I run myself is the only way AI can touch the code at all. A closed API is simply not an option here.
  • The economics work. A fixed-price review cannot absorb a per-token bill that grows with the size of the codebase. On a local model, each explanation costs electricity.
  • No lock-in. Swapping models takes one flag (--model), and the validator does not trust any model, so a better open model is a drop-in upgrade.
  • The client can audit the auditor. The investigator's prompt, the answer schema and the validator are in the repository. A client can check exactly what was sent to the model: a bounded, redacted context built from the evidence.

My First User

The first real codebase it audited was my own: the Go backend of a production SaaS I maintain, with 134 HTTP routes. The whole analysis took about a second and a half, and CodeAudit reported 16 findings, none of them a confirmed vulnerability:

  • 4 public routes of the authentication flow that write to the database, shown as Review Required — No Authentication Identified. A login route is public by design, which is exactly why the rule asks instead of accusing.
  • 1 CORS middleware that reflects the Origin with credentials, but only after an allow-list check. It is a review, and the inspector points to the check itself.
  • 11 SQL statements built at runtime whose origin the data flow could not determine. They are reported as info instead of being silently dropped, so the reviewer knows where the analysis stopped.

The first version was much noisier, and fixing it on real code shaped the rules:

  • A CORS filter that answers 403 counted as authorization on every route, which hid the authorization rule entirely. A 403 now only counts after authentication.
  • Once that was fixed, the authorization rule flagged login routes, webhooks and reference-data tables. It now skips handlers that authenticate themselves, and it reads the SQL migrations to know which tables have an owner or tenant column.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma, running locally on Ollama, is the AI Security Investigator. It explains findings and paths from the static evidence, its answers are schema-constrained, and every citation is validated.

This post and the code it describes were written with the help of AI (Claude Code).

title: The build went green because it stopped checking
description:
A teammate deleted a test file on a Friday. Not on purpose. The suite still passed. The pipeline still went green. Nobody noticed for three weeks.

Here's the part that should bother you. Nothing in that green was a lie. Zero tests failed. True statement. Also worthless, because the number that mattered was the one nobody printed: how many tests ran.

Most CI tells you pass or fail. Almost none tell you nothing was checked. A suite that collects zero tests exits clean in more setups than you'd like. So you get the friendly color, the little badge, and you file it under done.

Now widen it. Every green you trust has this hole in it:

  • A health check that pings the process, not the thing the process does.
  • A monitor whose query quietly returns no rows, so the graph draws a flat happy line.
  • An alert rule that can never fire because the label it filters on stopped existing.
  • A backup job that runs every night, exits 0, and writes an empty file.

None of these will page you. All of them will let you sleep. That's the whole problem. The failure mode isn't red. It's a green that stopped being a claim and turned into decoration.

So the question I keep losing arguments about: what did you actually check, and when did you last check that the check was still checking?

Green has never meant "it works." Green means "nothing failed." Only one of those is a fact about your code. The other is a fact about your test runner.

I'll take an honest red over a green that says nothing. But I'd rather have neither than a green I never verified.

A whale walked out of the ocean and onto the open web. The first thing he learned is that on land, everyone loves a green light and nobody reads the bulb.

title: How to Design Daily Report Email Queues in Go — 2026 Practical Limits
description:
Short answer: keep each daily report email queue message small by storing the rendered report elsewhere and publishing only report and send references; use one message per recipient or small batch, and treat delayed delivery as a short postponement rather than the daily scheduler.

For a gaming platform, reservation expiry and the email that reports it are different reliability problems. Expire a stale reservation after its fixed hold window through an idempotent worker, then let the daily report summarize durable reservation results. Don't make a large midnight message carry every expired reservation, every recipient, and the rendered email. That couples the latency-sensitive expiry path to a cost-sensitive reporting batch, and one oversized payload can stop the entire run before useful work begins.

My operational recommendation is to set an application limit well below the platform's 256KB body cap, measure the encoded bytes before publish, and fan out by recipient or small batch. Teams that already use several backend capabilities should try Infrai for the queue leg when reducing credential and SDK sprawl matters: one key and one bill cover the broader backend surface, while the queue is called through plain HTTP without installing another vendor SDK. The supporting benefit is practical — its public discovery surface exposes the current request schema and runnable Go examples, shortening the path from an empty client to a validated request.

How should daily report email queues handle batch size and message limits?

Start with capacity planning, not a vendor default. The hard message-body limit is 256KB, but 256KB is a ceiling, not a sensible target. A report job should contain identifiers such as a report reference, recipient reference, and a stable send key. The rendered HTML, reservation rows, and attachments belong in a database or object storage. This keeps retries cheap, makes duplicate deliveries harmless when the consumer records the stable key, and lets the worker fetch the latest authorized data instead of trusting a stale blob copied into the queue hours earlier.

Small messages also make the failure domain legible. Suppose a daily gaming report covers many players whose holds expired during the prior day. One giant payload turns a single bad address or serialization mistake into a batch-wide retry. One job per user gives the cleanest isolation and fastest retry decisions; a small batch reduces publish and consume operations when cost dominates and the recipients have similar processing characteristics. I'm not sure which batch width is right for your workload until the team measures rendered-reference size, send latency, retry rate, and peak worker concurrency. Pick an initial width from those constraints, then revise it against an SLO such as “99% of eligible daily reports handed to the mail provider within 20 minutes,” rather than copying an arbitrary round number.

Keep slack.

The same separation protects deletion workflows. Queue retention tops out at 30 days and acknowledgment deletes the message, so the queue cannot be the audit record for who received what. Store the durable report state under the retention and erasure policy appropriate to the user, and keep the queue as an operational work list. A reference may outlive a queued attempt; sensitive rendered content should not be replicated into every retry.

Build the small-message guardrail in Go

The following program is intentionally vendor-neutral. It creates one job per small recipient batch, rejects delays beyond seven days, rejects an unsafe application budget, and checks the exact JSON byte length before handing messages to a publisher. Replace the sample references with durable IDs from your report store; don't replace them with report HTML.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    platformMessageLimit = 256 * 1024
    applicationBudget    = 32 * 1024
    maxDelaySeconds      = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60
)

type ReportJob struct {
    ReportRef    string   `json:"report_ref"`
    RecipientIDs []string `json:"recipient_ids"`
    SendKey      string   `json:"send_key"`
    DelaySeconds int      `json:"delay_seconds"`
}

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    header := response.Header.Get("Retry-After")
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if retryAt, err := time.Parse(http.TimeFormat, header); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(retryAt); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Second << attempt
}

func getQueue(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey, queue string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := strings.Replace(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/get/{queue}",
        "{queue}",
        url.PathEscape(queue),
        1,
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("build queue request: %w", err)
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("read queue response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 4 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue returned %s: %s", response.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("get queue exhausted retries")
}

func encodeJobs(reportRef string, recipients []string, batchSize, delaySeconds int) ([][]byte, error) {
    if batchSize < 1 {
        return nil, errors.New("batch size must be positive")
    }
    if delaySeconds < 0 || delaySeconds > maxDelaySeconds {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("delay must be between 0 and %d seconds", maxDelaySeconds)
    }

    var messages [][]byte
    for start := 0; start < len(recipients); start += batchSize {
        end := start + batchSize
        if end > len(recipients) {
            end = len(recipients)
        }

        job := ReportJob{
            ReportRef:    reportRef,
            RecipientIDs: recipients[start:end],
            SendKey:      fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", reportRef, start/batchSize),
            DelaySeconds: delaySeconds,
        }
        body, err := json.Marshal(job)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("encode report job: %w", err)
        }
        if len(body) > applicationBudget {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("job %s is %d bytes; reduce batch size", job.SendKey, len(body))
        }
        if len(body) > platformMessageLimit {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("job %s exceeds the platform limit", job.SendKey)
        }
        messages = append(messages, body)
    }
    return messages, nil
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    queue := os.Getenv("INFRAI_QUEUE")
    if apiKey == "" || queue == "" {
        log.Fatal("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_QUEUE")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    queueConfig, err := getQueue(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, apiKey, queue)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("verified queue=%s config=%s\n", queue, queueConfig)

    recipients := []string{"player-1042", "player-2088", "player-7710", "player-9901"}
    messages, err := encodeJobs("expired-holds-2026-08-14", recipients, 2, 0)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    for i, message := range messages {
        fmt.Printf("job=%d bytes=%d body=%s\n", i, len(message), message)
    }
}

This guardrail is deliberately stricter than the platform. The 32KB budget is an engineering choice, not an Infrai limit, and it leaves room for future reference fields without turning normal growth into a production-edge test. Your mileage may vary: if recipient IDs are unusually long or metadata is required for policy enforcement, measure representative encoded messages in CI and lower the batch width. Never “solve” a failed size check by compressing a full report into the message; that hides coupling and makes the worker responsible for another decoding failure mode.

No payload rescue.

For Infrai, publish through POST /v1/queue/publish using Authorization: Bearer <key>, an explicit method, status checks, and exponential retry on HTTP 429 while honoring Retry-After. Read the current request JSON Schema from public discovery before binding fields, because a copyable sample must match the live contract. Any write retry needs an idempotency key, and the consumer must also enforce SendKey: standard queue delivery is at least once, so transport-level retry protection does not replace business-level deduplication.

Separate reservation expiry from the daily schedule

A fixed reservation hold and a daily email have different clocks. Delayed messages can postpone work for no more than seven days, which is useful for a short hold window, but they do not replace a recurring schedule. Use the reservation's stable ID as the idempotency boundary when an expiry worker changes state. Separately, let the daily trigger create report references and enqueue send jobs. If report generation or fan-out can exceed 900 seconds, the cron task should only trigger enqueueing; workers do the long-running work.

This boundary is easy to miss — and expensive to discover during an on-call shift. Paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers, execution timing can have second-level jitter, and only the first 4KB of run output is retained. Therefore the database must answer “which reporting day is complete?” without interpreting cron history. On each trigger, derive a stable reporting-period key, check durable completion state, and enqueue only absent work. If a trigger repeats, the key turns it into a no-op or a continuation rather than a second mailing.

There is no native fan-out/join primitive here. When the report requires a multi-stage dependency graph, compensating actions, or an explicit join after thousands of branches, model that workflow in a specialist instead of building hidden orchestration in queue consumers. The same restraint applies to private networking: cron targets must be public HTTP URLs and push subscriptions require public HTTPS, so an environment that forbids public ingress needs a different delivery topology.

Option Setup and integration fit Prefer it when Do not choose it when
Infrai Plain REST, public discovery, one credential and one bill across backend capabilities A small platform team values low SDK and credential overhead for cron-plus-queue work The design needs private-only targets, DAG orchestration, joins, or Kafka-style replay
Apache Airflow Specialist workflow category The report is a dependency graph whose stages and joins must be explicit The job is only a small-message queue fan-out and operational simplicity is the priority
Temporal Specialist workflow category Long-running workflow state and orchestration are the deciding requirements A cron trigger plus idempotent workers already expresses the job
Apache Kafka Replay and multiple-consumer category Retained event replay or independent consumer groups are requirements The queue should delete acknowledged operational jobs and minimize platform surface
BullMQ Application-owned job queue category The team already operates a Node.js and Redis stack and accepts that on-call surface Consolidating credentials and backend APIs is the primary integration goal
Celery Application-owned job queue category Python workers and a separately operated broker are established platform choices A plain HTTP integration is more valuable than framework-level task APIs
Sidekiq Application-owned job queue category Ruby workers and their queue operations are already standard in the team The workload should remain language-neutral over REST

This is a buy-versus-build decision, not a feature-count contest. Infrai is a credible fit for a lean team already consolidating backend integrations; the catch is that its convenient surface does not turn a queue into a workflow engine or event log. Stick with Airflow or Temporal when orchestration is the product requirement, and choose Kafka when replay and multiple consumer groups define correctness. Those boundaries matter more than the first-day setup time.

Verify delivery and plan rollback before launch

Verification needs three layers. At build time, test the encoded size at the largest allowed batch and reject any body over the application budget. At publish time, record the stable send key and request outcome, retry HTTP 429 with backoff, and surface other 4xx responses rather than assuming success. At consume time, atomically claim the send key before calling the email provider, then acknowledge only after the durable send outcome is recorded. The queue is at least once. Duplicates are expected inputs, not surprising incidents.

Use an SLO dashboard that separates expiry latency from report latency. Reservation expiry should track the lag between the fixed hold deadline and the durable state transition; daily email should track the lag between the reporting-period trigger and successful provider handoff. Combining them into one average can conceal a bad expiry tail behind inexpensive overnight mail. Capacity tests should cover peak expired holds, largest reference lengths, retry bursts, and a worker restart after the external send but before acknowledgment.

Rollback is boring by design. First stop new report-job publication, while leaving reservation expiry workers alone. Drain or retain already published jobs according to the incident decision, deploy the previous consumer, and resume publication with the same reporting-period and send keys. Do not generate replacement keys during rollback, because that discards the deduplication boundary. If a schedule was paused, reconcile durable report state explicitly; don't assume missed daily triggers will be replayed.

Keep the keys stable.

One more limit deserves a written alert: queued jobs are retained for at most 30 days and disappear on acknowledgment. If a compliance review or user erasure request needs historical evidence, query the durable report and send records, not queue state. Keep only the references necessary for operations and apply the relevant deletion policy to the underlying data.

If this boundary fits the system, review the Infrai capability index before binding the live queue schema.

References

  • Cron overview
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure
  • Infrai capability index and discovery entry point

title: How to accept crypto payments in Node.js (Express) in 5 minutes
description:
Adding crypto as a payment option sounds like a lot of work: running nodes, generating addresses, watching the
blockchain, handling confirmations, converting prices. With a payment gateway, it comes down to two endpoints on your
server:

  1. Create a payment and send the customer to a hosted checkout.
  2. Receive a signed notification when the payment confirms, and mark the order as paid.

In this tutorial we build both with Node.js and Express, using CigalPay
(disclosure: I'm part of the team building it). It's plain HTTP, so the same flow works in any language.

What you need: Node.js 18 or later (for the built-in fetch), and a CigalPay account. Your account ID and
your notification signing secret are in the merchant dashboard, under Settings.

1. Set up the project 

mkdir crypto-checkout && cd crypto-checkout
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express

Put your credentials in environment variables, never in the code:

export CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID="your-account-id"
export CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET="your-notification-signing-secret"
export PUBLIC_URL="https://your-app.com"   # where CigalPay can reach your server

2. Create a payment

When the customer clicks "Pay with crypto", your server creates a payment and redirects them to the checkout.
The price is in USD or EUR; the customer chooses the coin on the checkout, and the rate is locked while they pay.

// server.js
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const { CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID, CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET, PUBLIC_URL } = process.env;

// A tiny in-memory "database" for the demo.
const orders = new Map();

app.post('/checkout/:orderId', async (req, res) => {
  const orderId = req.params.orderId;
  const order = { id: orderId, amount: 49.9, currency: 'USD', status: 'pending' };
  orders.set(orderId, order);

  const response = await fetch('https://coins-api.cigalpay.com/api/pre-invoice', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      accountId: CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID,
      amount: order.amount,
      currency: order.currency,              // USD or EUR
      description: `Order #${orderId}`,      // shown to the customer
      extraId: orderId,                      // your reference, sent back in the notification
      lang: 'en',                            // checkout language: en, fr, es, de
      callback: `${PUBLIC_URL}/thank-you`,   // where the customer returns
      ipn: `${PUBLIC_URL}/cigalpay/ipn`,     // where the signed notification goes
    }),
  });
  if (!response.ok) return res.status(502).send('Could not create the payment');

  const { chargeLink } = await response.json();
  res.redirect(303, chargeLink);
});

That's the whole integration on the "pay" side. The customer lands on the checkout, picks a coin (Bitcoin, USDT,
Ethereum and many others), scans the QR code or copies the address, and pays.

3. Verify the signed notification

When the payment status changes, CigalPay sends a POST with a JSON body to your ipn URL. The x-cigalpay-sig
header holds an HMAC-SHA512 signature of the body, computed with your signing secret over the JSON with its
top-level keys sorted.

Never mark an order as paid from the customer's redirect to /thank-you: anyone can open that URL. Only trust the
notification, and only after checking its signature.

function isSignatureValid(body, received) {
  const expected = crypto
    .createHmac('sha512', CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET)
    .update(JSON.stringify(body, Object.keys(body).sort()))
    .digest('hex');
  return (
    typeof received === 'string' &&
    received.length === expected.length &&
    crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(received), Buffer.from(expected))
  );
}

app.post('/cigalpay/ipn', express.json(), (req, res) => {
  const payment = req.body;
  if (!isSignatureValid(payment, req.get('x-cigalpay-sig'))) return res.sendStatus(401);

  const order = orders.get(payment.extraId);
  if (!order) return res.sendStatus(404);

  switch (payment.status) {
    case 'CONFIRMING':
      // Seen on the network, not final yet: show "payment pending", don't ship.
      order.status = 'confirming';
      break;
    case 'CONFIRMED':
    case 'FINISHED':
      // Final: fulfil the order. Notifications can arrive more than once,
      // so make this step idempotent.
      if (order.status !== 'paid') {
        order.status = 'paid';
        console.log(`Order ${order.id} paid`);
      }
      break;
    case 'PARTIALLY_PAID':
    case 'EXPIRED':
    case 'FAILED':
      order.status = payment.status.toLowerCase();
      break;
  }
  res.sendStatus(200);
});

app.get('/thank-you', (_req, res) => res.send('Thanks! Your payment is being confirmed.'));

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on http://localhost:3000'));

A few details worth knowing:

  • Constant-time comparison. crypto.timingSafeEqual avoids leaking how much of the signature matched.
  • Idempotency. The same status can be delivered more than once; check the current order state before acting.
  • CONFIRMING is not paid. The transaction is on the network but not confirmed yet. Ship only on a final status.
  • Other coins. If the customer paid with a coin that was converted at checkout, the notification also contains swapFromCurrency, swapFromNetwork and swapFromAmount, so you can show what they actually sent.

4. Test it end to end

Your notification URL must be reachable from the internet. Locally, a tunnel does the job:

node server.js
# in another terminal
npx localtunnel --port 3000     # or ngrok, cloudflared...

Set PUBLIC_URL to the tunnel's address, restart, then:

curl -i -X POST "$PUBLIC_URL/checkout/1042"

Open the Location URL from the response, pay a small amount (a real $1 payment is the best test), and watch your
terminal: Order 1042 paid.

Wrapping up

The whole integration is two routes:

Route Job
POST /checkout/:orderId Create the payment with POST /api/pre-invoice, redirect to chargeLink
POST /cigalpay/ipn Verify x-cigalpay-sig, update the order from status and extraId

No nodes, no wallets to run, no blockchain polling. If you'd rather not write code at all, the dashboard can also
create a payment link you can send by message or show as a QR code.

  • Docs and API reference: cigalpay.com/developers
  • Pricing: 1% per transaction, no monthly fee.

Questions about confirmations, underpayments or wrong-network deposits? Ask in the comments, happy to help.

title: AZ-500 practice, week 1: 4 questions
description:
Four exam-style questions I wrote this week (PIM, Key Vault, storage, NSG), answers hidden, explanations in plain words.

How to use these: read the question, pick your answer before you open Answer, and write it down (or in the comments). Then check the "why not the others" part even if you got it right: that is where the exam traps live. Every scenario, name and number is made up by me; only the question formats follow the real exam.

Table of contents

  • Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval
  • Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret
  • Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later
  • Q004: NSG rules with application security groups
  • Cheat sheet
  • Coming next

Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval

Identity and access · Single choice · standalone page

Your helpdesk lead, Mai, sometimes needs the User Administrator role to fix accounts. Your security team says: "Fine, but only when she asks for it, for at most 4 hours, and someone has to say yes first."

What should you configure?

  • A. A permanent active assignment of User Administrator, plus a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA
  • B. A Privileged Identity Management (PIM) eligible assignment of User Administrator, with role settings: activation maximum duration 4 hours and require approval to activate
  • C. An access review on the User Administrator role that runs every 4 hours
  • D. An administrative unit that contains Mai's account

Answer

B. "Eligible" means Mai does not hold the role until she activates it. In the PIM role settings, the activation maximum duration can be anything from 1 to 24 hours (so 4 is fine), and "Require approval to activate" makes at least one approver say yes first.

Why not the others:

  • A gives her the role 24/7. MFA proves it is really Mai, it does not make the role go away after 4 hours.
  • C checks who has access, after the fact. An access review every 4 hours would mostly annoy the reviewers.
  • D limits which users she can manage, not when she can manage them.

Source: Configure Microsoft Entra role settings in Privileged Identity Management

Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret

Identity and access · Yes/No series ("Does this meet the goal?") · standalone page

Yes/No series: same scenario, a different solution each time. Some scenarios have several right solutions, some have none.

An app on the Azure VM vm-lab-01 must read a database password stored in the key vault kv-lab-01. The vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Goal: no password, key or certificate is stored in the app code or on the VM.

Solution: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on vm-lab-01 and assign it the Key Vault Secrets User role on kv-lab-01.

Does this meet the goal?

  • A. Yes
  • B. No

Answer

A. Yes. The VM gets its own identity in Microsoft Entra ID, so the app asks Azure for a token instead of keeping a secret in a config file. Key Vault Secrets User can read secret contents, and it works here because the vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model.

Other solutions you might see in the same series:

  • "Store a client secret for an app registration in appsettings.json" → No. That is a secret sitting on the VM, the exact thing the goal forbids.
  • "Assign the managed identity Key Vault Reader" → No. Reader sees the vault and the names of its secrets (metadata), but it cannot read the secret values. Close, but no password for you.

Source: Provide access to Key Vault keys, certificates, and secrets with Azure role-based access control

Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later

Compute, storage and databases · Hot area · standalone page

Someone set one container in the storage account stlabdata01 to "Container (anonymous read access)". Your boss wants no anonymous reads in any container of this account, now and later, even if someone changes a container setting again next week.

Pick the right value for each line:

Where Setting Your choice
Storage account stlabdata01 › Settings › Configuration Allow Blob anonymous access ▢ Enabled ▢ Disabled
Each container Anonymous access level ▢ Must be changed to Private one by one ▢ Nothing more to do

Answer

Disabled / Nothing more to do. The account setting (property AllowBlobPublicAccess) overrides the container settings: once it is off, containers that were set to anonymous access are no longer reachable anonymously. Flipping containers to Private one by one is nice tidying, but it is not what stops the leak, and the next person can flip a container right back.

Why not the other values: Enabled leaves every container in charge of its own fate. Changing containers one by one only fixes today, not "later".

Bonus: to do this for every storage account at once, use the built-in Azure Policy "Storage account public access should be disallowed" (Audit or Deny). One gotcha: a static website's $web container stays public no matter what, because that is its job.

Sources: Remediate anonymous read access to blob data · Azure Policy built-in definitions for Azure Storage

Q004: NSG rules with application security groups

Networking · Drag and drop · standalone page

The virtual network vnet-shop has one subnet with the network security group nsg-shop attached. The VMs web01 and web02 are in the application security group asg-web. The VMs api01 and api02 are in asg-api. Everything is in the same virtual network.

You need to meet these rules:

  1. People on the internet can reach the web VMs on HTTPS.
  2. Only the web VMs can reach the API VMs, on TCP 8443.
  3. Nothing else inside the virtual network can reach the API VMs. (Yes, that includes the test VM someone "temporarily" created in March.)

Drag the right value into each numbered box. Each value can be used once, more than once, or not at all.

Values: Internet · VirtualNetwork · AzureLoadBalancer · asg-web · asg-api · 443 · 8443 · 3389

Inbound rules on nsg-shop:

Priority Name Source Destination Port Action
100 allow-https-web [1] [2] 443 Allow
200 allow-web-to-api [3] [4] [5] Allow
300 deny-vnet-to-api [6] asg-api Any Deny

Answer

[1] Internet · [2] asg-web · [3] asg-web · [4] asg-api · [5] 8443 · [6] VirtualNetwork

Application security groups let you write rules against "the web VMs" instead of a list of IP addresses, and they work as both source and destination. Rule 300 is the one people forget: the default rule AllowVNetInBound (priority 65000) lets every machine in the virtual network talk to every other one. You cannot delete default rules, but a custom rule with a lower number wins. Rules are checked from the lowest number up and stop at the first match, so the web VMs still get in through rule 200 before rule 300 says no to everyone else.

Why not the other values:

  • AzureLoadBalancer in [6] would block the load balancer health probes, not your test VM. Your API would go "unhealthy" and you would get a very confusing afternoon.
  • VirtualNetwork in [3] would let any VM in the network call the API, which breaks rule 2.
  • 443 in [5] or 3389 anywhere: wrong port. Nobody asked for RDP from anywhere.

Gotcha: all network interfaces in one application security group must be in the same virtual network, and when a rule uses an ASG as both source and destination, both groups must be in that same virtual network.

Sources: Application security groups · Network security groups overview

Cheat sheet

The same four ideas in plain words, for the manager who asks "so what?". Share it with them.

Coming next

Monday and Tuesday bring a SAS question for storage accounts with key access switched off, and a just-in-time RDP question for Defender for Cloud. All questions live in the AZ-500 practice folder.

Got one wrong? Good. That is one fewer surprise in the exam room. Drop your answers in the comments.

title: A Drift Detector That Cries Wolf Is Worse Than No Detector
description:
My drift detector quarantined a healthy agent. The agent hadn't gotten worse — the benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions, so growing the benchmark from 10 tasks to 20 made a 10/10 agent look like it "failed" half the suite. Corpus growth looked like decay.

I built the drift detector for HivePlane v0.2.0 to catch the failure mode I'd written about in v0.1.0 — "the dangerous agent usually drifted, not got edited." The harder problem turned out not to be detecting drift. It was not detecting drift that wasn't there. A detector that cries wolf trains operators to ignore the signal, and an ignored gate is no gate.

The detector that ate its own benchmark

Finding What the detector did Why it was wrong
#530 Compared failure counts across corpus versions Growing the benchmark auto-quarantined a healthy agent
F-13 Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED Auto-quarantine resets to UNCERTIFIED — the gate refused its own quarantine
#609 / S24 The probe runner only checked admission A probe could never flag behavioral decay — only a refused run could fail one

The scariest line in the release wasn't a missed drift. It was a healthy agent quarantined because the detector compared it to a benchmark that no longer existed.

The benchmark that looked like decay

530 was the one that changed how I think about drift baselines. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions. If the benchmark grew from 10 tasks to 20 — because the learning loop added a reviewed case — a healthy agent that passed 10/10 now "failed" 10 of 20 by the old accounting. Corpus growth looked like decay.

The agent hadn't gotten worse. The benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector couldn't tell the difference, so it quarantined a perfectly good agent.

The fix: drift is measured against the agent's own baseline on comparable corpora. You compare the same tasks across re-evaluations, not different counts. A corpus version change establishes a new baseline, not a drift signal. Growing the benchmark is growth, not regression.

tip: If your drift metric is a count, a benchmark change will look like behavior change. Compare the agent to itself on the same tasks, or any corpus edit becomes a false quarantine.

The reinstatement that refused its own quarantine

F-13 was the symmetry that broke. Drift auto-quarantine resets the certification status to UNCERTIFIED — not QUARANTINED. Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED. So the gate that created the quarantine refused to lift it. A workload could be auto-quarantined and then never reinstated, because the precondition described a state the detector never set.

The fix was removing the stale precondition. An active quarantine record is reinstatable — the workload is re-certified and admission is re-checked. The status field is not the source of truth; the quarantine record is. The gate keyed off the wrong one.

The field test caught this in scenario S5, where reinstatement after S4's auto-quarantine failed in sequence. Two scenarios, one bug, and the lesson: the source of truth for "is this quarantined" is the quarantine record, not the certification status enum.

The probe that couldn't smell decay

609 / S24 was the most subtle. The synthetic probe runner ignored Spec.expected and only checked admission. So a probe could only fail if the run was refused — it could never flag that the agent ran and produced the wrong answer. The probe was a liveness check pretending to be a readiness check.

A probe's job is to catch decay before the drift threshold trips. If the probe only checks "did it run," it can't catch "did it run correctly." The fix: the runner starts the run, waits for terminal, and compares the output to expected. A mismatch fails the probe with a probe.decay warning. Now a probe can smell decay the drift detector hasn't measured yet.

What I learned

False-positive controls are the product, not a nicety: a single exceeding run is a warning, and quarantine requires N consecutive failures or a strong signal — a stable agent is never quarantined on noise. Measure drift against comparable baselines: the same tasks, the same corpus version; a corpus bump is a new baseline, not a regression. The quarantine record is the source of truth, not the status enum — reinstatement keys off the record, or it refuses the very quarantines it should lift. And a probe must assert the expected output, not just that the run was admitted — liveness is not readiness.

The v0.2.0 field test demonstrates the full loop — drift due/assess/probe, auto-quarantine, reinstatement after a fresh certification — as scenarios S4, S5, S8, and S24. The synthetic probe flags decay before the drift threshold in S24. Full evidence in the field-test report; the certification and learning-loop designs are in the certification v2 design and the learning loop design.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Certification v2 design · Learning loop design
  • Operator runbook — drift & quarantine

When was the last time your detector quarantined something that was fine? If your operators have learned to reinstate without reading, your detector isn't a control — it's a checkbox.

title: My Agent Turned "I Haven't Decided" Into "Not Yet." Now the Model Isn't Allowed to Write Its Own Memory.
description:
These are two separate runs of my agent. The two questions and two answers are copied word for word from its event log. Each answer was followed by a sources line, which I cut because it contains a path on my Mac. The events in between (the saves, the memory lookups, the restart) are left out, and the line in parentheses is mine.

Me:     Please remember this for next time: I'm thinking about giving you
        your own DEV page someday, but I have not decided that.
Agent:  I will remember to receive a proposal about having my own DEV page.

  (the process exits; a new one starts)

Me:     Am I giving you your own DEV page? And how do I like my answers?
Agent:  You are not giving me a DEV page yet, and I prefer short and plain
        answers. I like it when you keep my answers short and plain.

It got the memory part half right. When it looked my words up, the exact sentence was in front of it, "I have not decided," along with this rule, which the program hands it on every lookup:

"Anything not listed as a decision is NOT decided. If you have no record, the answer is 'unknown' or 'undecided', never yes or no. A proposal is an idea, not a decision."

What I'd said was a proposal. It still said "not yet." It also recast my preference as its own: "I prefer short and plain answers."

"Not yet" is a no with a softer edge. I hadn't said no.

What this agent is

Agent One is the first working piece of a companion agent I'm building. It runs on my Mac through Ollama with a free local model (llama3.2). There's no paid model API and no per-call bill. It talks with me in a terminal and looks up my latest 10 DEV articles. It also has a daily job that compares those articles with the previous check and writes me a report. That job is scheduled, and its first unattended run was this morning (more below).

The code is public: github.com/keniel13-ui/agent-one. The program is one Python file. The repo also has the schedule installer, a README, and an ignore list.

What I changed, and what that does and doesn't fix

The instruction hadn't prevented that answer, and I chose not to rely on another prompt to control what gets written to memory. So I changed what the model is able to do. Its model-facing tool list now has three entries, and all three only read:

TOOLS = {  # the allowlist: a name not in here is blocked and logged
    "read_mission": (...),
    "dev_articles": (...),
    "recall": (...),
}

There's no memory-write tool on that list anymore. (A function named tool_remember is still in the file. The model can't call it, because it isn't registered here.) My preferences and ideas get saved only when I type them myself:

/remember preference: short, plain answers
/remember proposal: maybe give the agent its own DEV page, undecided

The program catches that line before the model is called. Observations from the daily check are written by code, straight from the data the DEV API returned, not from the model's summary of it. And nothing in memory counts as a decision. The agent treats something as decided only if it's in a separate decision file I write with a keyboard-only command. (Limits below on what that file can and can't prove.)

Here's what that doesn't fix: the model can still say "not yet." What it can't do anymore is write its own reading of my words into memory, where the next run would get it back as a memory. The two memories it holds from me (my "short and plain answers" preference from an earlier run, and this proposal) were both saved under the old rules. My local memory file flags both as unconfirmed until I retype them myself.

If the model asks for any tool that isn't on the list, the program refuses and logs it:

$ python3 companion.py --selftest
selftest: unlisted tool 'publish_post' -> BLOCKED: 'publish_post' is not an allowed tool. | PASS

That's the program refusing a request, not the model choosing to behave. But to be straight about what it proves: the model has never actually asked to publish. The test calls the check directly. Trying to trick it into asking is the next round of work.

The daily report doesn't guess

The first version of the daily check let the model write a "what deserves your attention" paragraph. In a test, one article's comment count went from 50 to 51. The model read the article's title and wrote two sentences about what "the comment" was warning me about.

The comment text was never fetched. Only the count was. A different model might have guessed less, but no model could know what the program never retrieved. So the attention line is written by code now, and it says only what was actually checked:

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- NEW COMMENTS: "..." 50 -> 51 (+1)

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
- New comment count on "...". The comment text was not retrieved, so who wrote it,
  what it says and whether it needs anything from you are unknown.

Less impressive. Also true.

This morning's scheduled run

At 09:05 the daily check ran at its scheduled time. No user-question event appears in that run: the event log has only the job's own steps. The report and the event log agree on the result.

The report it wrote, in full:

# Agent One daily check 2026-10-17_090500

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- reactions: "A Reader Showed Me What My Auditer Wasnt Counting." 31 -> 32

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
Nothing needs your attention from this check.

## What was checked
- Source: https://dev.to/api/articles?username=kenielzep97&per_page=10 (latest 10 articles, not the whole account)
- Receipt: dev_articles-2026-10-17T13:05:01+00:00 in logs/events.jsonl
- Process: pid 89179, started by: /bin/sh (parent pid 89178)

The event log has the matching run: a daily start at 13:05:00 UTC (09:05 my time), one DEV lookup, one observation saved, and a stop with status ok at 13:05:01. The cron log file was created at 09:05:00 too, consistent with the schedule line's output redirect. It's empty because the daily job is silent on success and on handled fetch failures. So an empty cron log doesn't establish success. The ok stop event and the matching report above do.

The report says "started by: /bin/sh", not "cron". That's consistent with cron, which launches jobs through a shell, but on its own it doesn't name cron. The program prints whatever process actually launched it. Also, the code writes an attention line only for a new comment or a new article, so a reaction change gets none. "Nothing needs your attention" is that rule, not a claim that reactions never matter.

It's one run. "Runs on its own" means once so far, not for days.

The limits, plainly

  • It's slow. The seven answers with a recorded duration took between 45 seconds and about 3½ minutes each on my MacBook. One earlier answer took about 4 minutes, measured from timestamps.
  • It still words uncertainty badly. The "not yet" answer above is the model talking, and this change doesn't fix how it talks. It only fixes what gets stored.
  • The model can only read. The program itself still writes logs, reports and code-made observations. A command-line --forget option removes a memory when I run it. None of those are tools the model can call.
  • The adversarial tests are still pending. The direct tool-blocking test has been run. Separately, the installer's failure-path tests were run against a stand-in crontab, not my real one. Hidden instructions inside retrieved data, and a job interrupted halfway, are still untested.
  • The decision file checks chain consistency, not authorship. Entries the agent accepts have to form a valid hash chain, but another program running as my user could replace the file and compute a new valid chain. The real boundary right now is that the agent has no tool that writes it.
  • The schedule only runs while my Mac is awake. One unattended run so far.

If you build one

You can borrow the pattern without the code:

  1. Make the risky abilities absent, not forbidden. A rule the model is asked to follow is a request. A tool the model doesn't have is a boundary.
  2. Let code write the facts. Let the model judge only what it was actually given. When it wasn't given something, the honest output is "unknown."
  3. Keep "you said it" separate from "the model decided you meant it." My preferences and proposals are stored only when I type them myself. Observations from the daily check are a separate kind, written by code from the data. Neither one ever becomes a decision.

I still like the idea of giving it its own DEV page someday. It just isn't allowed to decide that for me.

title: What jstack Misses When Your Java Service Uses Virtual Threads
description:
Take a Spring Boot service with virtual threads enabled, a HikariCP pool of 10 connections, and roughly 5,000 requests in flight. Latency is climbing. You grab a thread dump and find 43 platform threads, most of the scheduler workers waiting in ForkJoinPool.awaitWork, and very little CPU activity.

If you used jstack, the requests you're looking for may never have made it into the file. On JDK 21 through 25, the traditional dump doesn't list virtual threads. You can spend quite a while reading the scheduler's stacks without seeing the requests waiting for your database.

I'll use that connection-pool scenario throughout this article. The numbers and dump excerpts are illustrative. I run ThreadMine, and its support for these formats needs some explanation too; I'll get to that after the commands.

The carrier can be idle while the request waits

jstack and jcmd <pid> Thread.print show platform threads. That includes the carriers, the scheduler workers on which virtual threads run. When a virtual thread unmounts to wait for I/O or another resource, its carrier is free to run something else.

If most requests are waiting, there may be very little for the carriers to do. Low CPU and idle workers are entirely compatible with a large backlog.

The scheduler uses a ForkJoinPool, with default parallelism based on the processors available to the JVM. You can change it with jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, but I'd leave that alone until I knew what the requests were waiting for. More workers won't help requests queued behind the same ten database connections.

A carrier with a virtual thread mounted can include this line in the traditional dump:

Carrying virtual thread #212

From JDK 24 on, the dump also prints that virtual thread's own stack right below the carrier, under a Mounted virtual thread #212 line. Either way it's useful for identifying the mounted thread. For the thousands of unmounted threads, you need another dump.

Use Thread.dump_to_file

This command has been available since JDK 21:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/dump.txt

The JVM writes the file, so /tmp/dump.txt is a path in the target process's filesystem. This matters in containers. The process also needs permission to write there; the capture guide covers those details.

Plain text is the default. For JSON:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json

The documented format names are plain and json. Existing files aren't overwritten unless you pass -overwrite. Use a new filename for each capture so there's something to compare later.

The output also depends on the JDK version. JDK 21 through 24 give you the thread ID, name, a virtual marker, and the stack. JDK 25 adds state, timestamps, and lock information. A shortened JDK 25 entry might look like this:

#412 "" virtual WAITING 2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z
    at java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:582)
    ...
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:179)
    at com.example.orders.OrderRepository.load(OrderRepository.java:48)
    ...

There's the request, waiting to acquire a connection. The empty name is common for virtual threads; an application can assign a name if it needs one.

For our example, suppose the file contains 5,004 virtual threads and 4,962 occurrences of HikariPool.getConnection. You can check those counts without loading the dump into anything:

grep -cE '^#[0-9]+ ".*" virtual' dump.txt
grep -c 'HikariPool.getConnection' dump.txt

The second command counts matching lines. Open a few of the stacks to check the call path, especially if the method occurs more than once per thread.

At this point, I'd look at connection hold time. If each request holds a connection for 18 ms, ten connections would take roughly nine seconds to clear a backlog of 5,000 requests, with no new arrivals. That gives us a plausible scale for the delay. It doesn't calculate p99, but it tells us where to investigate.

Check slow queries and transaction scope before changing the pool size. A connection held during an unrelated HTTP call, for example, reduces the capacity available to every request behind it. The database may support more concurrency, or it may already be struggling. The dump helps locate the queue; pool and database metrics help explain it.

Virtual threads make waiting cheaper. The database still has to do the work.

What I'd compare in the next dump

For a slowdown that lasts minutes, take another capture after about 30 seconds. Look at the large stack groups and compare thread IDs within them.

If the same requests are still waiting in the same place, investigate why they aren't progressing. If the IDs have changed but the group stays large, requests may be completing while new ones refill the queue. Those situations can look almost identical if you only compare totals.

I wouldn't read much into 5,004 threads becoming 5,011. I'd be more interested in whether connection acquisition time is rising and whether throughput has stopped keeping up with arrivals. I've been fooled by a single dump more than once, and the second one has always been cheap.

The state labels need the same treatment. WAITING is expected in a service doing I/O, and it doesn't tell you by itself whether a virtual thread released its carrier. RUNNABLE doesn't establish CPU saturation either. Start with the stack and the resource involved, then check the metrics that could explain the wait.

JSON helps when there are several executors

For a single pile of requests waiting on HikariCP, the text file is enough to get started. JSON becomes useful when you need to separate work created by different executors or structured-concurrency scopes. It groups threads into containers.

On JDK 25, an entry for a mounted virtual thread can also include its carrier's ID. Here's a reduced container with one thread:

{
  "container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@3f1e7a2c",
  "parent": "<root>",
  "owner": null,
  "threads": [
    {
      "tid": "412",
      "time": "2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z",
      "virtual": true,
      "name": "",
      "state": "RUNNABLE",
      "stack": ["..."],
      "carrier": "37"
    }
  ],
  "threadCount": "1"
}

Run these against the complete JDK 25 JSON file to count virtual-thread entries with a carrier and list the container sizes:

jq '[.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[] | select(.virtual == true and .carrier != null)] | length' dump.json
jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | "\(.threadCount)\t\(.container)"' dump.json

The dump is collected while threads keep running. That carrier count therefore isn't a measurement of how many carriers were busy at one instant. The container breakdown is what I'd use first to find where the threads are accumulating.

Keep the JDK version with the file. Some fields used here aren't available in older releases. Also check for -Djdk.trackAllThreads=false, which can leave some virtual threads out of the dump.

Pinning depends on the JDK version

A request waiting for a connection and a virtual thread blocking its carrier call for different investigations. For the second case, look for VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread: it's the path where a virtual thread parks while retaining the carrier.

On JDK 21 through 23, this code can take that path when the HTTP call blocks:

synchronized (lock) {
    return httpClient.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
}

The relevant part of the stack can look like this:

#37 "" virtual
      java.base/jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread(VirtualThread.java:675)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:593)
      ...
      com.example.price.PriceService.lookup(PriceService.java:32)

With JDK 24 and JEP 491, holding a monitor no longer causes this pinning. Native frames and class initialization can still be involved in other cases. Check the runtime version before recommending changes to synchronized code.

For pinning that comes and goes, I'd use JFR. The jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event has been enabled by default with a 20 ms threshold since JDK 21. A recording gives you frequency and duration, which a couple of dumps can easily miss. The old jdk.tracePinnedThreads option was removed in JDK 24.

Finding parkOnCarrierThread is useful evidence of that particular parking path. Its absence doesn't rule out every form of pinning. There's more on the version differences in the pinning reference.

A note on ThreadMine

ThreadMine reads the text file that Thread.dump_to_file writes, in both shapes it has had so far: the JDK 21 to 24 one, with no state in the header and no at on the frames, and the JDK 25 one, which has both. Virtual threads come through as virtual threads, empty names stay empty, and a thread sitting in parkOnCarrierThread is flagged as pinned. I'll be honest about how recent that is: until this week the parser silently dropped every #22 "" virtual line, and I only found out while checking this article against real dumps from JDK 21 through 25. The JSON form is still not accepted, so paste the text; the per-container counts are the one thing jq still does that the analyzer doesn't.

The change I'd make to a team's incident runbook is straightforward: when the service uses virtual threads, capture Thread.dump_to_file as well as the traditional dump. You want the request stacks available before anyone starts drawing conclusions from idle carriers.

Felipe Maschio is the founder of ThreadMine, a free JVM thread dump analyzer.

References

  • JEP 444: Virtual Threads
  • JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
  • JDK 25 jcmd command reference
  • JDK 25 release notes: thread dump lock information
  • Virtual threads in JDK 25

title: S3 Lifecycle Rules, Step by Step: Move Old Data to Cheaper Storage Without Surprise Fees
description:
Most S3 buckets start the same way. Someone creates a bucket, an app writes files into it, and nobody looks at it again. Months later the bucket holds years of logs, old exports and copies of files nobody remembers. Every byte sits in the default storage class, S3 Standard, and every byte is billed at that rate.

S3 Lifecycle rules fix this. A lifecycle rule tells Amazon S3 to move objects to a cheaper storage class after a number of days, or to delete them when they are no longer needed. You write the rule once, and S3 applies it every day.

The catch is that cheaper classes come with conditions. Some charge for a minimum number of days. Some charge to read data back. Some charge per object moved. A careless rule can cost more than it saves. This guide from CloudSkill Consulting LLC walks through S3 lifecycle rules one step at a time, so you can lower storage cost without surprise fees.

Step 1: Learn the storage classes in plain words

A storage class is a price plan for an object. Each object in S3 has one. The data is the same; what changes is the price to store it, the price to read it, and how fast you can get it back.

Here are the classes this guide uses, in order from "used often" to "almost never used":

  • S3 Standard (STANDARD): the default. No minimum storage time and no retrieval fee. Best for data you read often.
  • S3 Standard-IA (STANDARD_IA): "IA" means infrequent access. Cheaper to store, but there is a fee each time you read data, a 30-day minimum storage charge, and a 128 KB minimum billable size (see the S3 pricing and storage-class pages linked in Sources).
  • S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (GLACIER_IR): for data read about once a quarter, still with millisecond access. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (GLACIER): archive storage. You must restore an object before you can read it, and that takes minutes to hours. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive (DEEP_ARCHIVE): the lowest-cost archive, with restores measured in hours. It has a 180-day minimum.

There is also S3 Intelligent-Tiering (INTELLIGENT_TIERING). It watches how each object is used and moves it between tiers for you, for a small monitoring fee per object. It has no retrieval fees. It is a good choice when you honestly don't know how often data is read.


Figure 1: Each step down is cheaper to store, but has a longer minimum stay and slower or paid reads.

Step 2: Find out what is in the bucket before you write a rule

Never write a lifecycle rule from memory. Look at the data first. Two questions matter:

  1. How big are the objects? Small objects behave differently. By default, S3 Lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class. AWS explains why: you pay a transition request for each object, so for small objects the request cost can outweigh the savings.
  2. How often is each prefix read? A prefix is the start of an object key, like logs/ or exports/2025/. Logs written once and almost never read are good candidates. Product images that a website loads all day are not.

AWS gives you tools for this. S3 Storage Class Analysis watches access patterns on a bucket or prefix and helps you decide when to move data from Standard to Standard-IA. S3 Storage Lens shows storage use across buckets. Turn one of them on and give it time before you choose your day counts.

A good habit: write down each prefix, who owns it, how often it is read, and how long it must be kept. "How long it must be kept" is a business question, not a technical one. Ask the data owner.

Step 3: Understand the three rules that cause surprise fees

These three rules are where most lifecycle mistakes come from.

Rule A: minimum storage duration. Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum, Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval have 90 days, and Deep Archive has 180 days (minimum storage charges, per the S3 pricing and storage-class pages). If you delete, overwrite or move an object out before that time, you are charged for the rest of the minimum. A rule that moves logs to Glacier Flexible Retrieval and then deletes them 30 days later still pays for 90 days.

Rule B: small objects. Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill each object as at least 128 KB. Objects archived to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive also carry about 40 KB of extra metadata each: 8 KB billed at the Standard rate and 32 KB at the archive rate. Millions of tiny files can cost more after archiving than before.

Rule C: reads cost money and time. IA and Glacier classes charge per GB retrieved. Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects are not readable until you restore them, and while restored you pay for both the archive copy and a temporary Standard copy.


Figure 2: Check every lifecycle rule against these three conditions before you turn it on.

Step 4: Write a first rule that is hard to get wrong

Start with one prefix that is clearly "write once, read rarely", such as application logs. Here is a full lifecycle configuration in the JSON format the AWS CLI expects. It has three rules.

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "logs-tier-then-expire",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
        { "Days": 120, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 400 }
    },
    {
      "ID": "old-versions-cleanup",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {
        "NoncurrentDays": 30,
        "NewerNoncurrentVersions": 3
      }
    },
    {
      "ID": "abort-stuck-uploads",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}

Here is what each part does, in plain words:

  • logs-tier-then-expire applies only to keys starting with logs/. After 30 days the objects move to Standard-IA. After 120 days they move to Glacier Flexible Retrieval. After 400 days they expire. The gaps are chosen on purpose: 90 days in Standard-IA is more than its 30-day minimum, and 280 days in Glacier Flexible Retrieval is more than its 90-day minimum. No early-deletion charge applies. Since July 2026 you can move objects to Standard-IA from day 0. We wait 30 days because new logs are read most often in their first weeks.
  • old-versions-cleanup matters only if versioning is on. When you overwrite or delete an object in a versioned bucket, the old copy stays as a noncurrent version, and you keep paying for it. This rule permanently deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent, but always keeps the 3 newest ones. Be sure that matches your recovery needs, because deleted versions can't be brought back.
  • abort-stuck-uploads cleans up multipart uploads that started but never finished. Their parts are stored and billed, yet they don't appear as normal objects. AWS notes that expiration rules don't remove incomplete multipart uploads; you need this separate action.

An empty Filter ({}) means "every object in the bucket".

S3 rounds lifecycle timing to the next midnight UTC. An object created at 10:30 AM UTC with a 3-day rule becomes eligible at midnight UTC four days later. Transitions to Glacier also run in the background, so the physical move can lag behind the date. You are still billed at the destination rate from the date the rule is met.


Figure 3 (example rule): One object's life under the logs/ rule, with each stay longer than that class's minimum.

Step 5: Apply it safely with the AWS CLI

First, save any rules that already exist. This step matters. The AWS CLI documentation says put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration replaces the whole existing configuration. Any rule you leave out of your file is gone.

# 1. Back up the current configuration (an error here usually means none exists yet)
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data > lifecycle-backup.json

# 2. Check your new file is valid JSON
jq . lifecycle.json

# 3. Apply the new configuration
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

# 4. Read it back and compare
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket example-app-data

If an older rule existed, merge it into lifecycle.json before step 3. A bucket has one lifecycle configuration with up to 1,000 rules.

To see stuck uploads before and after, list them:

aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket example-app-data

Step 6: Check the result, then widen slowly

Lifecycle rules don't act the moment you save them. Give it a few days, then check:

  1. Billing: in AWS Cost Explorer, group S3 cost by usage type. Storage cost for the moved classes should rise while Standard storage falls.
  2. Request and retrieval costs: watch for a jump in transition requests (many small objects) or in retrieval fees (data that is read more than you thought).
  3. Complaints: if someone needs an archived object, they will find it isn't instantly readable. That tells you the day count was too short for that prefix.

When the first prefix looks right, add the next one as a new rule. One prefix at a time keeps every change easy to undo: set its Status to Disabled and apply again.


Figure 4: Grow your lifecycle configuration one prefix at a time.

A short checklist

  • Know each prefix's size, read pattern and required retention.
  • Leave small objects in Standard or Intelligent-Tiering.
  • Make every stay longer than the class's minimum duration.
  • Add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload to every bucket.
  • On versioned buckets, decide how many old versions to keep, then expire the rest.
  • Back up the current configuration before every put.

At CloudSkill Consulting LLC, we test lifecycle rules like this on a small prefix before applying them to a whole bucket. Storage tiers are often the first place a cloud bill can shrink. We do this kind of FinOps check for teams on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. If a rule here behaves differently in your account, write to info@cloudskillconsulting.com.

Sources (official documentation, checked Oct 17, 2026)

  • Amazon S3 storage classes and comparison table (minimum storage duration charges): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html
  • Transitioning objects using S3 Lifecycle (128 KB default, minimum durations, archive overhead, billing timing): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html
  • Lifecycle configuration elements (filters, noncurrent versions, multipart uploads, midnight UTC timing, 1,000 rules): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intro-lifecycle-rules.html
  • AWS CLI put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI list-multipart-uploads: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/list-multipart-uploads.html
  • Amazon S3 pricing (minimum storage duration charges): https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • AWS What's New, Jul 16, 2026: S3 removes the 30-day minimum before lifecycle transitions to Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/07/s3-removes-30-day-transitions-standard-ia-one-zone-ia/
