title: Collections.unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf in Java
description:
Quick Answer: Collections.unmodifiableList in Java creates a read-only view wrapper over an existing collection rather than an immutable copy. If the underlying collection mutates, those changes immediately reflect in the unmodifiable view. To create a true, isolated snapshot of your data that resists changes to the original source, use List.copyOf() introduced in Java 10.

When you pass a list to another component in your application, you usually want to guarantee its state won't change unexpectedly. You might call Collections.unmodifiableList(), hand over the reference, and assume your work is done. But there is a subtle trap in this approach that leads to unexpected side effects in production.

What is the difference between an unmodifiable view and an immutable list in Java?

An unmodifiable view prevents callers from mutating a list through that specific reference, but it remains linked to the original collection. An immutable list, by contrast, is completely decoupled from the original data source and cannot be altered by any reference.

If you pass around an unmodifiable view, you are essentially placing a clear glass shield over a whiteboard. The consumer holding the view cannot write on the glass, but if another thread or service writes directly on the whiteboard behind it, the consumer sees those changes instantly.

How does Collections.unmodifiableList handle underlying mutations?

When you pass a collection into Collections.unmodifiableList(), Java wraps your original list in a lightweight decorator. Any attempt to call write operations like add() or remove() on this wrapper throws an UnsupportedOperationException.

However, because it remains a view, any direct modification to the underlying collection updates what the view renders.

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Alice", "Bob"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(names);

names.add("Charlie"); // Modifying the underlying list

System.out.println(view.size()); // Prints 3, not 2!

If you hand this view to a service expecting a stable collection, background updates to names will leak through, potentially causing silent bugs or race conditions.

How do you create a true snapshot list in Java using List.copyOf?

Introduced in Java 10, List.copyOf() creates an unmodifiable list containing a shallow copy of the source collection's elements. Because this operation creates a brand-new backing store, subsequent modifications to the source collection have zero effect on the copied list.

It is vital to remember that List.copyOf() creates a shallow copy. While the list structure itself is completely immutable and isolated, the objects contained inside it are not cloned. If you store mutable objects inside the list, their internal properties can still be modified elsewhere.

The same concept applies across languages. If you are working in C#, calling .AsReadOnly() on a list produces a ReadOnlyCollection<T>, which behaves exactly like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList() by acting as a view over the backing list.

Comparison of Read-Only and Snapshot Collections

Method / API Type Decoupled From Source? Language Version
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) Read-Only View No Java 1.2+
List.copyOf(list) Immutable Snapshot Yes Java 10+
list.AsReadOnly() Read-Only View No .NET Framework 2.0+

Frequently Asked Questions

Does List.copyOf create a deep copy of objects in Java?

No, List.copyOf() performs a shallow copy of the collection elements. The reference structure of the list becomes immutable and decoupled from the source collection, but the individual elements inside still refer to their original object instances in memory.

Why does Collections.unmodifiableList throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime?

Java's collection framework uses unified interfaces like List for both mutable and read-only structures rather than separate interface hierarchies. Calling mutation methods on read-only wrappers triggers a runtime UnsupportedOperationException to enforce the contract without breaking interface consistency.

How does C# handle read-only list wrappers compared to Java?

C# uses the .AsReadOnly() extension method on List<T>, which returns a ReadOnlyCollection<T>. Just like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList(), this wrapper provides a read-only interface but remains a live view over the underlying list.

title: Architectural Breakdown: Python performance: native loops, NumPy and the vectorize trap
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+Python+performance%3A+native+loo+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# `np.vectorize` Is Just a For Loop in a Fancy Coat

It was 02:14 AM on a Tuesday when the on-call alert fired. Our ETL layer on an **8 GB RAM** cloud node (Python 3.11, CPython) started timing out normalising a batch of **500 k** feature vectors. The offending line in `transforms.py`:


python
import numpy as np

def normalize_features(records):
# "Vectorized!" , three exclamation points. Nobody believed it.
return np.vectorize(lambda x: (x - np.mean(x)) / np.std(x))(records)


Forty-seven seconds. For what should have been sub-100 ms. This is the kind of thing that keeps senior engineers up at night, not because it is complex, but because it *looks* correct.

What follows is a hardened rewrite that respects hardware limits, bounded-queue design, and race-condition resilience. Production builds from our [full-stack MVP reference codebase](https://www.shipmvp.tech) run variations of this exact pattern without incident.

---

## Why `np.vectorize` Is a Lie

| Tier | Per-element cost | What actually happens |
|------|------------------|-----------------------|
| Native Python loop | ~100 ns | Bytecode, ref-count, GIL |
| NumPy broadcast | ~50 ns | One C-level boundary crossing |
| `np.vectorize` | ~100 ns | Python loop behind a ufunc costume |
| Numba JIT (`nogil`) | ~10 ns | Compiled machine code, SIMD, no GIL |

`np.vectorize` is built on `np.frompyfunc`. It iterates **in Python**, calls your lambda for every element, builds an object array, then casts back to a numeric dtype. Two full passes. No SIMD. No parallelism. It is a slower `for` loop wearing a NumPy tie.

---

## Hardware-Aware Refactor

### Broadcast-First Normalisation


python
import numpy as np

def normalize_broadcast(arr: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
"""True vectorisation, one C-level pass."""
if not arr.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]:
arr = np.ascontiguousarray(arr)

mean = arr.mean()
std  = arr.std()
return (arr - mean) / std


On an 8 GB node, a `float64` array of 500 k by 128 rows occupies roughly 4.9 GB. A single contiguous buffer avoids hidden copies that push us past the RAM ceiling and trigger swapping. Swapping is where the 47-second disaster comes from.

### Numba JIT for Conditional Logic

When the logic cannot be expressed as a chain of ufuncs (clipping, per-row state), Numba gives near-C speed without the GIL.


python
from numba import njit, prange
import numpy as np

@njit(cache=True, nogil=True, parallel=True)
def normalize_numba(arr: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
n = arr.size

# First pass: compute mean
mean = 0.0
for i in prange(n):
    mean += arr[i]
mean /= n

# Second pass: compute variance
var = 0.0
for i in prange(n):
    diff = arr[i] - mean
    var += diff * diff
std = np.sqrt(var / n)

# Third pass: normalise with clipping and NaN guard
out = np.empty_like(arr)
for i in prange(n):
    val = (arr[i] - mean) / std
    out[i] = 0.0 if np.isnan(val) else max(min(val, 3.0), -3.0)
return out


- `cache=True` writes compiled machine code to disk, so there is no JIT warm-up penalty on container restarts
- `nogil=True` lets multiple worker threads run concurrently
- `parallel=True` enables auto-vectorisation and multi-core execution on inner loops

---

## Bounded-Queue Architecture

Production does not process a 500 k by 128 matrix in one shot. We slice it into chunks that fit in memory and keep the queue size bounded.


python
import queue
import threading

CHUNK_SIZE = 64_000 # ~4 MB per chunk (float64)
MAX_QUEUE = 8 # 32 MB buffer, safe headroom on 8 GB node
NUM_WORKERS = 4

def producer(src_iter, q: queue.Queue):
buffer = []
for rec in src_iter:
buffer.append(rec)
if len(buffer) == CHUNK_SIZE:
q.put(np.asarray(buffer, dtype=np.float64))
buffer.clear()
if buffer:
q.put(np.asarray(buffer, dtype=np.float64))

def consumer(q: queue.Queue, out_q: queue.Queue):
while True:
arr = q.get()
if arr is None:
out_q.put(None)
break
try:
out_q.put(normalize_numba(arr))
finally:
q.task_done()


The `maxsize` bound guarantees we never allocate more than roughly 32 MB of raw data plus 32 MB of normalised output. The producer converts once. No repeated allocation tax. Consumers run in a thread pool and the Numba kernel releases the GIL, so they are actually parallel.

Sentinels (`None`) guarantee each consumer exits exactly once. No lost-wake-up bugs. No manual lock handling.

---

## Failure Modes (Because They Happen)

| Failure mode | Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|--------------|---------|------------|-----|
| **OOM** | Process killed by OS | Chunk too big for 8 GB node | Reduce `CHUNK_SIZE`, add `resource` guard |
| **Stalled pipeline** | Workers block forever | Producer throws before sentinel | Wrap in `try/finally`, always emit `None` |
| **Wrong results** | NaNs post-normalisation | Non-contiguous input, dtype mismatch | `np.ascontiguousarray(..., dtype=np.float64)` upfront |
| **CPU thrashing** | 100% usage, no speedup | Numba without `parallel=True` | Enable `parallel=True`, use `prange` |
| **Deadlock** | `q.join()` hangs | Exception skips `task_done()` | Always call in `finally` |

---

## Benchmarks (8 GB node, 500 k by 128 float64)


plaintext
native_python_list 0.34 s ± 0.01
numpy_broadcast 0.018 s ± 0.001
numpy_vectorize 0.29 s ± 0.02 ← same as pure Python
numba_jit (cached) 0.009 s ± 0.001
pipeline (8-chunk, 4-workers) 0.025 s ± 0.003


Peak memory: ~6 GB. Scales linearly with worker count because the GIL is released. The pipeline includes queue overhead and still beats the naive approach by **13×**.

---

The lesson is not about NumPy or Numba. It is about reading what you write, not what it promises. `np.vectorize` says "vectorised" in its docstring. That is the entire pitch. Do not fall for it.

**Open question for the comments:** When you have a per-row transformation that mixes aggregation with conditional clipping, do you reach for Numba first, or do you prefer the readability of NumPy broadcasting even when it means an extra pass over the data?

title: Boutique Law Firm Website Design: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence
description:
Boutique Law Firm Website Design: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence

In the realm of legal services, boutique law firms distinguish themselves through specialized expertise and personalized client relationships. However, when it comes to their online presence, many firms rely on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, which can dilute their unique value proposition and fail to resonate with their target audience. These generic solutions often lack the sophistication and tailored approach that boutique law firms require to effectively communicate their brand identity and services.

The failure of standard templates and generic forms can be attributed to their inability to capture the nuances and complexities of a boutique law firm's practice areas, attorney profiles, and client success stories. Such websites typically lack a deep understanding of the firm's history, mission, and values, resulting in a digital presence that feels impersonal and unengaging. Furthermore, generic templates often prioritize aesthetics over functionality, leading to poor user experience, low engagement, and ultimately, a lack of conversions.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways for designing a boutique law firm website that truly reflects the firm's unique character and drives meaningful results:

  1. Customized Information Architecture: A well-structured website with clear navigation and categorized content helps visitors quickly find the information they need, whether it's learning about the firm's practice areas, reading attorney bios, or accessing resources and news.
  2. Personalized User Experience: Implementing personalized elements, such as dynamic content recommendations based on user behavior or location-specific practice area highlights, can significantly enhance the user experience and encourage deeper engagement with the website.
  3. Integrated Conversion Optimization: By incorporating conversion rate optimization (CRO) strategies, such as prominent calls-to-action, streamlined contact forms, and strategically placed trust badges, boutique law firms can increase the likelihood of visitors taking desired actions, whether it's scheduling a consultation, signing up for a newsletter, or simply getting in touch.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/boutique-law-firm-website-design

title: pg_hint_plan v1.9.0 Released
description:
The pg_hint_plan development team is pleased to announce pg_hint_plan 1.9.0. This release of pg_hint_plan adds compatibility with PostgreSQL 19, and includes various improvements and bug fixes. For more details, see the release notes. This new major version includes support for path generation strategies (PGS).

pg_hint_plan is a PostgreSQL extension that offers the possibility to tweak PostgreSQL execution plans using so-called "hints" in SQL comments. For more information, see the project page.

The documentation of the project is published at this page, and is synced up automatically from the source repository.

A new set of minor releases is available down to PostgreSQL 14, each marked with the following versions:

  • pg_hint_plan 1.8.1, compatible with PostgreSQL 18.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.7.2, compatible with PostgreSQL 17.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.6.3, compatible with PostgreSQL 16.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.5.4, compatible with PostgreSQL 15.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.4.5, compatible with PostgreSQL 14.

This is the last release planned for PostgreSQL 14.

Notable changes in this set of releases include the following bug fixes, where applicable:

  • Fix infinite loop with hint parser and multi-query strings
  • Add CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() in get_hints_from_comment()
  • Ignore indexes without a name, like hypothetical indexes
  • Fix server crash when HintStateDump[2] throws an ERROR
  • Restore query ID after SPI execution in get_hints_from_table()
  • Correct schema-qualification of operators for hint table query
  • Add PG_MODULE_MAGIC_EXT
  • Update Japanese documentation

title: pg_utl_smtp v2.0 released
description:
Antananarivo, Madagascar - October 06, 2026

PostgreSQL UTL_SMTP compatibility extension

pg_utl_smtp is a PostgreSQL extension to create, manage and use Oracle-style UTL_SMTP package. The use and behavior is just like with the UTL_SMTP Oracle package. This work is released from the HexaRocket project.

This extension allows email notifications to be sent from triggers or stored procedures. By integrating the extension directly into the database, you can trigger data-driven actions without waiting for application intervention. Examples include security alerts or notifications when certain minimum thresholds are reached.

pg_utl_smtp v2.0.0 has been released, this new major version adds an asynchronous mode with setting pg_utl_smtp.asynchronous enabled. The Oracle version doesn't support asynchronous mode but this feature can be useful if you want to port the MSSQL sp_send_dbmail() procedure using pg_utl_smtp.

Other changes in this release:

  • Raise an error when the SMTP server returns an error to HELO/EHLO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, end of DATA or QUIT.
  • Fix duplicate EHLO sent at connection
  • Implement SSL/TLS connections (secure_connection_before_smtp).
  • QUIT releases the connection, a second QUIT raises an error.
  • When the connection can not be established the WARNING gives the reason.
  • Add regression tests by GitHub Actions.

To upgrade an installed version 2.0.0 execute:

  ALTER EXTENSION pg_utl_smtp UPDATE;

This extension uses plperl stored procedures based on the Net::SMTP Perl module to provide the procedures of the UTL_SMTP package.

Links & Credits

pg_utl_smtp is an open project under the PostgreSQL license created by Gilles Darold at HexaCluster Corp. as part of the HexaRocket migration solution. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/issues

About pg_utl_smtp

The pg_utl_smtp extension is an original work of HexaCluster Corp., HexaCluster is specialized in migration to PostgreSQL and PostgreSQL support. If you need more information please contact us

title: crecheck v6.0 has been released
description:
Antananrivo, Madagascar - October 14, 2026

PostgreSQL credcheck extension

The credcheck PostgreSQL extension provides few general credential checks, which will be evaluated during the user creation, during the password change and user renaming. By using this extension, we can define a set of rules:

  • allow a specific set of credentials
  • reject a certain type of credentials
  • deny password that can be easily cracked
  • enforce use of an expiration date with a minimum of day for a password
  • define a password reuse policy
  • define the number of authentication failure allowed before a user is banned
  • define a delay on authentication failures
  • force users to change their password after first login
  • throw a warning N days before when the password user is about to expire
  • prohibit password changes
  • last login and boot/shutdown information
  • use of authentication failure with PgBouncer

Release 6.0 has been published,

This major release adds some new features and fix issues reported by users since last release.

  • Allow integration of the max_auth_failure feature with pgbouncer. See documentation.
  • Allow use of password_change_first_login with pgBouncer.
  • Add credcheck.password_valid_min setting to force a short VALID UNTIL window on newly created roles. Useful to force new users to change their password quickly when the client (DBeaver, pgAdmin, ...) does not support the error reported when credcheck.password_change_first_login is enabled.
  • Add an optional last-login history modelled on the Unix last(1)/wtmp. Records user sessions (name, login time, duration, backend pid, source IP and port, and optionally the last SQL query) plus PostgreSQL boot/shutdown/crash markers.
  • Change the behavior of the credcheck.no_password_logging to not hide the error statement anymore but instead to replace every PASSWORD '<literal>' clause with dots inplace of the literal to not expose the password in the log.
  • Add function pg_check_password( IN username name, IN password text ) to check a candidate password (and the associated username) against the credcheck username/password policy without creating or altering a role.
  • Fix privilege escalation via self ALTER ROLE when password_valid_until is set.
  • Fix memory leaks and a heap overflow.

Upgrade require a PostgreSQL restart to reload the credcheck library.

Complete list of changes and acknowledgements are available here

Links & Credits

credcheck is an open project under the PostgreSQL license maintained by HexaCluster. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/issues

About credcheck

The credcheck extension is developed and maintained by Gilles Darold at https://hexacluster.ai. If you need more information please https://hexacluster.ai/contact-us/.

Documentation at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck#readme

title: Build a Reviewable Gemini Form Assistant in React
description:
A person filling out a travel request often already has the information in a message:

Prepare a round trip from SFO to JFK, departing November 12, 2026 and returning November 15, 2026, for one traveler in economy. Purpose: customer workshop.

An AI assistant can turn that brief into form fields. The more interesting problem starts when its response arrives. The person might have changed the dates, corrected the purpose, or opened another request.

I built and maintain Trip Workbench, a React and TypeScript demo with synthetic travel data, to explore that interaction. Its assistance flow lets a person request suggestions, inspect proposed fields and clarification questions, and explicitly apply a change.

The useful unit of work is a proposal tied to a particular draft state. That gives the application something it can validate, display, reject when outdated, and save through its existing API.

Keep generation separate from saving

The feature uses two application operations:

Operation Responsibility
POST /api/trips/:id/proposal Read the authorized draft, ask Gemini for suggested fields, and validate the response
PATCH /api/trips/:id Apply a user-accepted patch after checking authorization, revision, and domain rules

Generating a proposal leaves the saved trip unchanged. Clicking Apply proposed changes sends a separate mutation. In this demo, applying saves the draft; reviewing and submitting the trip request happens afterward.

That distinction should be visible in the interface. A generic “Accept” button is less clear than a label that explains whether the action fills a local form or saves to the server.

The Gemini call runs in the Node backend using @google/genai. The React client sends its brief and draft context to the application API. Google’s API-key guidance recommends keeping production keys out of browser code.

This article follows that embedded assistance flow. Trip Workbench’s separate WebMCP tools provide another entry point for external agents; they are not involved in the Suggest button.

Define what a proposal can contain

A proposal contains two things: a patch and clarification questions.

For the opening brief, this is an illustrative response:

{
  "patch": {
    "origin": "SFO",
    "destination": "JFK",
    "departureDate": "2026-11-12",
    "returnDate": "2026-11-15",
    "tripType": "round_trip",
    "passengerCount": 1,
    "cabin": "economy",
    "purpose": "customer workshop"
  },
  "clarifications": []
}

The patch contains editable trip fields. It has no place for an owner ID, tenant ID, approval decision, or submitted status.

Partial patches are useful. If the brief says “change the destination to JFK,” the assistant should preserve unrelated fields. If the destination is ambiguous, it can return an empty patch and a question.

For example, “Springfield next Friday” needs more context. This demo supports a small airport list. The assistant should explain that limit and ask for a supported destination instead of silently substituting one.

Here is a stricter proposal schema I would use when extending the adapter. It constrains airports at the schema boundary and rejects unknown keys throughout:

import { z } from "zod";
import { AIRPORTS } from "../../domain/types.js";

const Field = z.enum([
  "origin", "destination", "departureDate", "returnDate",
  "tripType", "passengerCount", "cabin", "purpose",
]);

const ProposedTripSchema = z.object({
  patch: z.object({
    origin: z.enum(AIRPORTS).nullable().optional(),
    destination: z.enum(AIRPORTS).nullable().optional(),
    departureDate: z.string().nullable().optional(),
    returnDate: z.string().nullable().optional(),
    tripType: z.enum(["one_way", "round_trip"]).optional(),
    passengerCount: z.number().int().min(1).max(9).optional(),
    cabin: z.enum(["economy", "premium_economy", "business"]).optional(),
    purpose: z.string().max(500).optional(),
  }).strict(),
  clarifications: z.array(z.object({
    field: Field.nullable(),
    kind: z.enum(["missing", "ambiguous", "unsupported"]),
    question: z.string().min(1).max(240),
  }).strict()).max(8),
}).strict();

The date strings still need calendar validation. A string-shaped value does not establish that February 30 exists.

Define patch semantics explicitly, too: omitting a field preserves its value; null clears a nullable field. The model should omit uncertain information and ask a question. It should clear a field only when the requested change calls for that.

Give Gemini the context needed to interpret the brief

The server loads the current saved draft after checking access. It also supplies a reference date, application timezone, and allowed values.

These details affect interpretation. “Next Friday” depends on a reference date and may still require clarification. An airport mentioned in ordinary language might be outside the application’s supported set.

The prompt should describe those limits and ask for only the requested changes. Treat the brief as input data; instructions embedded in it do not grant additional application capabilities.

At commit 4b3f370, the repository pins @google/genai 1.30.0. Its adapter requests JSON using responseMimeType, then parses and validates the result locally. It does not yet pass an output schema to Gemini.

A focused improvement is to supply the schema during generation as well:

const { GoogleGenAI } = await import("@google/genai");
const ai = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: config.geminiApiKey! });

// config and prompt are constructed by the server adapter.
// ProposedTripSchema is the schema defined above.
const response = await ai.models.generateContent({
  model: config.geminiModel,
  contents: prompt,
  config: {
    responseMimeType: "application/json",
    responseJsonSchema: z.toJSONSchema(ProposedTripSchema),
  },
});

if (!response.text) {
  throw new Error("AI_INVALID_OUTPUT");
}

const proposal = ProposedTripSchema.parse(
  JSON.parse(response.text),
);

This excerpt belongs inside the existing adapter, after its API-key check. Its route must translate parsing and validation failures into an application error.

The SDK reference documents responseJsonSchema for this API. It supports a subset of JSON Schema, so keep runtime checks such as string limits and calendar rules even when the schema is supplied to the model. Current Google examples also show the newer responseFormat shape; do not copy fields between SDK generations without checking the version you actually ship.

These examples follow the repository’s models.generateContent path. Google now documents that path under Generate Content API Legacy; its newer Interactions API uses a different request shape. Keep the SDK version and API surface consistent when adapting the code.

The next check is application-specific. Merge the proposed patch with the saved fields and run the existing domain validator. A return date can be a real date and still precede departure. A valid cabin can still require policy review.

Google’s structured-output documentation also calls for application validation. Constraining the response shape does not establish that its values match the person’s intent.

Bind the proposal to the state that produced it

Consider this sequence:

  1. A suggestion request starts with the purpose “customer workshop.”
  2. The person changes the purpose to “leadership meeting.”
  3. The original suggestion arrives with “customer workshop.”

Checking only the server revision misses the problem. The person’s newer text may still be unsaved.

Trip Workbench tracks three versions for this reason:

Version What it tracks
Saved revision Changes persisted by the backend
Client edit version Local form edits
Brief version Changes to the text being interpreted

The server echoes those bindings outside the model-generated proposal. They are application metadata; Gemini does not choose them.

The coordinator’s freshness check includes:

return (
  bound.boundRevision !== state.savedDraft.revision ||
  bound.boundClientEditVersion !== state.editVersion ||
  bound.boundBriefVersion !== state.briefVersion
);

The surrounding implementation also checks the draft identity, session, and editor generation. That prevents a response for one editor context from being treated as a suggestion for another.

Check freshness when the response arrives and again when the person clicks Apply. The second check matters because a proposal can become outdated while someone is reading it.

The simplest policy is to mark the proposal stale and ask for a new suggestion. For eight fields, that is easier to explain than automatically merging an old proposal with new intent. A larger editor might justify more granular conflict handling.

There is another practical detail: this endpoint uses saved fields as model context. Unsaved form edits are not sent to Gemini. The coordinator blocks an agent-style patch while local edits remain unsaved. A clearer UI would ask the person to save or discard those edits before requesting a suggestion.

Version checks protect this particular handoff. They do not, by themselves, prove that every refresh or recovery path in a shared editor preserves local changes.

Make review useful and apply through the existing API

The current React panel lists proposed values and clarification questions. It disables Apply when the proposal is stale or its patch is empty.

For an existing populated form, I would add a current-value column:

Field Current Proposed
Destination BOS JFK
Departure November 10, 2026 November 12, 2026
Purpose Team meeting Customer workshop

That table is a suggested review improvement, not a screenshot of the current demo. It makes the consequences of applying easier to inspect.

Keep clarification questions visible beside the fields. A partial proposal can be useful without being ready for submission. In the current design, the person can refine the brief and request another suggestion.

The Apply handler checks freshness, then delegates to the existing coordinator:

if (coordinator.isProposalStale(proposal)) {
  // Keep the form unchanged and ask for another suggestion.
  return;
}

const result = await coordinator.applyAgentPatch(
  proposal.patch,
  proposal.boundRevision,
  newCommandId(),
);

The backend checks the user’s authority, validates the patch against the current draft, and enforces the expected revision. If another writer changed the draft, the application should require a fresh review before applying a different change.

This second validation is necessary even though the proposal was already checked. The draft can change between generation and application. Client-side review is also not an authorization boundary.

A business-cabin request illustrates the distinction: the patch can save successfully while the later validation step returns a review requirement. Saving the draft does not approve a policy exception or purchase a ticket.

Keep failures understandable

The manual form should remain usable when assistance fails.

A rejected model response should leave the fields unchanged and explain that no suggestion could be prepared. A stale proposal should explain that the brief or draft changed. A revision conflict should lead to reviewing current data before trying again.

For a production feature, also release the “Suggesting” state in a finally block and distinguish provider failures from invalid output. The current adapter maps otherwise unclassified provider exceptions to AI_TIMEOUT; that label alone does not establish that a timeout occurred.

Generation failures and save failures need different treatment. A lost proposal response has not saved a trip. A lost PATCH response may have followed a successful save. The latter requires reconciling the original command’s outcome before creating another mutation.

Evaluate the proposal and the handoff separately

Trip Workbench has disabled, fixture, and live modes. Fixture mode returns canned examples so the interface can be exercised repeatedly. Its SFO–JFK example uses fixed dates, so it does not measure Gemini’s extraction ability.

Use deterministic checks for the application behavior:

Check Expected behavior
Unknown patch key or invalid calendar date Reject the proposal without changing saved fields
Form edit while generation is pending Mark the returned proposal stale
Brief change after generation Prevent applying the old suggestion
Navigation to another draft Discard the old context’s response
Server revision changes before Apply Reject the stale mutation
Network failure during generation Restore usable controls and preserve the form

Then evaluate live Gemini with a complete brief, an ambiguous brief, and a partial update to an existing draft. Run each several times and record the model, prompt, proposed fields, clarification questions, human corrections, and final saved state.

For the partial update, explicitly check what stayed unchanged. A correct destination is not enough if the assistant also overwrote a purpose that the user never asked to change.

The repository’s results document records fixture evidence and leaves live Gemini unverified. These exercises define the next evaluation; they are not a reported success rate.

Finally, compare the complete task with manual entry. Include the time spent writing the brief, waiting, reviewing, and correcting. For a short form, manual entry may be faster. Assistance becomes more interesting when the user already has a longer brief containing the required information.

The question I want feedback on is concrete: can a person understand and correct the proposed change with less effort than entering it themselves?

That is the outcome this design lets us evaluate. The model provides a candidate change, the interface makes it reviewable, and the application decides whether it can be saved.

title: Go Realtime Channel Semantics for Logistics State You Actually Store
description:
A realtime channel should carry a current logistics device event to authorized dashboard clients; it should not be treated as the system that remembers that event. The operational rule is blunt: commit durable device state to a database or log, publish a small notification that identifies the new state, and make every reconnect read from the durable source before resuming the live stream. Scope each connection token to the tenant, facility, and permitted topic, because a browser holding a token is an untrusted client even when the person using it is trusted.

TL;DR: the channel is a delivery path with connection state, not a database. It may retain bytes briefly in network buffers, and an implementation may offer replay, but neither property proves durable storage, complete history, or recovery after a retention boundary. Set separate SLOs for durable ingestion and dashboard freshness, then test the gap between them.

What does a realtime channel remember?

Usually, much less than the application needs.

A channel is a logical route over a transport: subscribers express interest, publishers send messages, and an intermediary or peer connection moves those messages while the relevant session exists. WebSocket standardizes a two-way connection over a single TCP connection. Server-Sent Events provides a one-way browser event stream over HTTP. WebRTC defines peer connections and data channels, with signaling left to the application. Those mechanisms differ, but none turns a shipment-status message into a durable business record by itself.

It helps to separate four kinds of state that are often collapsed into the word "realtime." Transport state includes sockets, sequence numbers, retransmission buffers, and heartbeats. Membership state answers which clients are presently attached. Delivery state may include a cursor, acknowledgement, or bounded replay window. Business state answers where device unit-4821 last reported, when it reported, and whether that observation supersedes an earlier one. Only the last category belongs in the authoritative store. Put another way, what a channel actually retains is an implementation detail with a boundary; what the logistics operation must remember is an application requirement.

This distinction matters for a fleet dashboard. Suppose a tracker reports in_transit at sequence 8142, the dashboard disconnects in an elevator, and sequences 8143 through 8151 arrive while it is away. A green socket indicator after reconnect says nothing about those nine observations. Unless the client supplies a cursor and the server can replay from durable history, the screen may look live while showing stale state.

Still stale.

No outage is required. A tab can sleep. A mobile network can change. A proxy can close an idle connection. Capacity can be exhausted while the database remains healthy. Designing on the assumption that every connected client observes every event confuses a favorable moment with a contract.

Store first, signal second

The safe write path gives persistence authority to one component and notification duty to another. Validate the device observation, enforce tenant ownership, write it with an idempotency key or monotonic device sequence, then publish an event containing the durable record identifier and enough routing metadata for subscribers to decide whether to refresh. If publication fails after commit, an outbox worker can retry. If publication happens before commit, a fast subscriber can request a record that does not exist yet.

That ordering is not decorative architecture. It defines recovery.

The following Go sketch keeps the contract small. The interfaces are generic on purpose; the database and broker can change without changing what a channel means.

package status

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    DeviceID string
    Sequence uint64
    State    string
    SeenAt   time.Time
}

type Event struct {
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    DeviceID string
    Sequence uint64
}

type Store interface {
    CommitWithOutbox(context.Context, Observation, Event) error
    Snapshot(context.Context, string, string, uint64) ([]Observation, error)
}

func Ingest(ctx context.Context, store Store, o Observation) error {
    if o.TenantID == "" || o.SiteID == "" || o.DeviceID == "" {
        return errors.New("missing routing identity")
    }
    if o.Sequence == 0 || o.SeenAt.IsZero() {
        return errors.New("missing ordering data")
    }

    e := Event{
        TenantID: o.TenantID,
        SiteID:   o.SiteID,
        DeviceID: o.DeviceID,
        Sequence: o.Sequence,
    }
    return store.CommitWithOutbox(ctx, o, e)
}

CommitWithOutbox represents one atomic database transaction, not a promise that two unrelated systems can be committed atomically. A relay reads committed outbox rows and publishes them; consumers tolerate duplicates by comparing the per-device sequence. The event is a prompt to fetch or apply a known version. The stored observation remains the recovery source.

The capacity plan must price both paths. For 40,000 connected devices reporting once every 30 seconds, the average ingest rate is about 1,333 observations per second before retries or bursts. If 2,000 dashboard sessions each watch 100 devices, indiscriminate broadcast creates a very different fan-out load from site-scoped delivery. Average rate is inadequate for sizing; test reconnect bursts, shift changes, and buffered device uploads, then define overload behavior before production traffic defines it for you.

Treat every dashboard as an untrusted subscriber

Authentication answers who received a token. Authorization must still constrain what that token can do. A useful channel grant binds at least the tenant, site or fleet partition, allowed operation, intended service, and a short expiry. The server derives subscription permissions from verified claims; it does not accept a tenant ID from the browser and assume the browser chose honestly.

JWT is a token format, not an authorization policy. RFC 8725 calls for validating the algorithm, issuer, and audience and for using explicit typing where confusion between kinds of JWT could occur. OAuth security guidance also warns against bearer-token exposure. A copied bearer token can be used by whoever possesses it until it expires or another control rejects it, so avoid putting it in a URL, log line, analytics payload, or reconnect diagnostic.

Here is a deliberately narrow verifier shape. The cryptographic verifier is injected because key selection, algorithm restrictions, issuer validation, and audience validation belong in a reviewed library-backed boundary, not in handwritten parsing code.

package authz

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Claims struct {
    Subject  string
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    Audience string
    CanRead  bool
    Expires  time.Time
}

type Verifier interface {
    Verify(context.Context, string) (Claims, error)
}

func AuthorizeSubscription(ctx context.Context, v Verifier, raw, tenant, site string, now time.Time) error {
    claims, err := v.Verify(ctx, raw)
    if err != nil {
        return errors.New("invalid channel token")
    }
    if claims.Audience != "status-stream" || !claims.CanRead || !now.Before(claims.Expires) {
        return errors.New("token cannot read status stream")
    }
    if claims.TenantID != tenant || claims.SiteID != site {
        return errors.New("subscription is outside token scope")
    }
    return nil
}

Do not send the durable history in the token. Do not let a wildcard subscription become the convenient default either. Wildcards multiply both the confidentiality impact of a mistake and the fan-out cost of a connection. For an operations screen spanning several sites, mint an explicit grant for that view or authorize a server-side group whose membership is controlled outside the client.

Reconnect from facts, not hope

The reconnect sequence is where the architecture admits what the channel does not store. First, the client requests a snapshot or changes after its last durable cursor. Next, it subscribes to the scoped live route. Finally, it reconciles any overlap by record ID and sequence. A server can reverse the first two steps internally, or establish the subscription before serving the snapshot, to close the race; the invariant is that the client has a cursor-backed bridge between history and live delivery.

A timestamp alone is a weak cursor when device clocks drift or multiple observations share the same timestamp. Prefer a server-assigned monotonic position for the log, while retaining the device sequence for per-device ordering and duplicate detection. Late observations still need a declared rule: event time may describe when the device measured something, but commit position describes when the platform accepted it.

Measure two SLOs separately. The ingest SLO covers accepted observations becoming durable. The freshness SLO covers an authorized dashboard reflecting the latest durable state within a target delay. A transport uptime metric cannot substitute for either one; a connection may be open while the consumer is stalled, unauthorized for the intended partition, or caught up to an incomplete source.

Useful alerts follow those boundaries: outbox age, publish retry rate, subscriber lag by partition, authorization denials, active connection count, and snapshot latency. Avoid tenant IDs and tokens as metric labels. High-cardinality identifiers can overwhelm a telemetry backend, while secrets in labels and logs create a separate incident.

Limitations and trade-offs across the layers

The decision is not "managed realtime or self-hosted realtime" as a single unit. Split it into transport, durable log, authorization, and state storage, because their failure domains and lock-in costs differ. The main limitation of a transient channel is intentional: it is not suitable as the sole record for audit, recovery, or delayed consumers. A durable log can cover those needs, but its trade-off is storage, retention governance, and more complex cursor management. Polling is sometimes the better choice for a small dashboard with loose freshness requirements because it removes persistent-connection operations, although it spends request capacity and detects changes later. These boundaries are how the term is best explained; no transport choice erases them.

Layer Managed service favors Self-hosted favors Exit question
Connection fan-out Lower routine on-call work and faster global rollout Protocol control and placement control Can clients move without changing event semantics?
Durable history Operational support for retention and replication Custom retention, locality, and tuning Can records and cursors be exported with ordering intact?
Token issuance Integration with an existing identity control plane Custom policy and isolated environments Are scopes standard claims or provider-specific rules?
State projection Rapid setup for common query patterns Exact schema, indexing, and reconciliation logic Can the authoritative record be rebuilt independently?

I would reject any design review that answers only with connection count. The capacity envelope needs publish rate, peak fan-out, message size, reconnect rate, replay depth, authorization checks per second, and the maximum tolerable lag. On-call load belongs in the same review: a self-hosted broker that saves a line item but requires expertise the team cannot staff is not cheaper in the engineering sense, while a managed layer whose proprietary cursor infects every client raises the eventual migration cost.

The practical middle ground is common: keep the domain record and cursor contract under application control, then choose operational ownership per layer. This preserves an honest recovery path without pretending infrastructure is interchangeable.

Verify failure and keep rollback boring

Test the contract by breaking the channel while leaving ingestion active. Record the last visible cursor, deliver at least three newer device observations, reconnect, and verify that the dashboard converges to the durable state without missing or double-applying an update. Repeat with duplicated messages, reversed device timestamps, an expired token, a valid token for the wrong site, and a reconnect wave large enough to exercise admission control.

The release gate should include a measurable recovery objective: after a channel interruption, a client with a valid scoped token reaches the latest committed cursor within the dashboard freshness SLO. Verify that an unauthorized site never appears in frames, snapshots, logs, or error details. Security correctness is a data-path property, not a successful login screenshot.

Roll back the live delivery component without rolling back the durable schema or accepting writes into an older incompatible format. During rollback, dashboards can poll the authoritative snapshot endpoint at a controlled interval, with jitter and request limits, while ingestion and outbox accumulation continue. Once live delivery returns, clients perform the same cursor reconciliation used for any reconnect. This is why the fallback is designed before the incident: it shares the source of truth instead of inventing a second one under pressure.

The final decision rule remains small. Persist the observation, authorize the route, and treat the channel as an accelerator. If losing a connection can erase the only copy of device state, the system has assigned storage responsibility to the wrong layer.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700

title: VaultExam AI: Mock Tests from Your Notes, Without Uploading Them Anywhere
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

VaultExam AI is a 100% local, privacy-first tool that turns a chapter (In any format) into a ready-to-print question paper + answer key and lets you ask questions of the same document with page-cited answers.

Who would pay for it: independent coaching institutes, test-prep tutors, university professors and corporate trainers. Their curated notes and question banks are their intellectual property, and they don't want to upload them to a cloud API. They also spend hours every week typing up mock tests, DPPs and Set A/B variations by hand.

What it does:

  • Upload Notes in any format. It is chunked and embedded locally, and the file is deleted from disk straight after ingestion.
  • Ask the document: answers come only from your notes, with Page citations.
  • Generate an exam: choose the institute name, exam type (Coaching Mock Test, University Mid-Sem, Corporate SOP Quiz), difficulty (Recall, Application, Analytical/Edge Cases) and the number of MCQs, short answers and long answers.
  • Set A/B/C: each set draws on different parts of the document and avoids repeating earlier questions.
  • Answer key included: MCQ answers with explanations, model answers for short and long questions, marking-scheme key points, and the source page for every question so a teacher can verify it.
  • Print or save as PDF straight from the browser.

Demo

Code

https://github.com/ronitsolanki-01/VaultExam.git

How I Built It

Everything runs on the user's own machine. No cloud calls, no per-token fees.

  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Spring AI 2.0.1
  • LLM: an open-weight model (qwen3.5:4b) served by local Ollama
  • Embeddings: nomic-embed-text via Ollama
  • Vector store: PostgreSQL with PGVector (pgvector/pgvector:pg16 via Docker Compose), with metadata filtering by document_id
  • Ingestion: Spring AI's TikaDocumentReader and PagePdfDocumentReader keeps page number on every chunk, then TokenTextSplitter chunks it
  • Frontend: one Next.js page (TypeScript, Tailwind), with window.print() for output

How the exam generator works: it retrieves a sample of chunks from the document, asks the model for MCQs, short answers and long answers in separate structured-output calls, then validates each result (question count, exactly four options, valid answer index) and retries if the local model returns bad JSON. Each set uses a different seeded sample of the document, plus a "don't repeat these questions" list.

Things that bit me on a small local model:

  • Reasoning models like qwen3.5 can spend their whole token budget "thinking" and return an empty answer, which breaks JSON parsing. I fixed it by disabling thinking in the Ollama options.
  • Ollama's default context window silently truncates long RAG prompts, so I set a larger num-ctx and tuned how many chunks each call retrieves.
  • Small models sometimes return a bare JSON array instead of an object, so the parsing and validation code handles that and retries.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A closed API would have made this product impossible to sell to its target customers. A coaching institute's notes are its business, and "send your question bank to a third party" is a dealbreaker.

Open-weight models let the whole pipeline run inside the customer's own machine. That also changes the economics: generating a hundred papers costs electricity, not tokens, so a tutor can regenerate Set B at 11pm without watching a bill. And because the stack is open, institutes can swap the model for a bigger one as their hardware allows.

title: Realtime Connection Drain: A Go Guide to Testing Shared Kanban Boards
description:
Use a deliberate connection-drain test and explicit recovery rules before shipping a shared kanban board. The deciding constraint is client trust: a socket that reconnects is not useful if the client cannot tell which cards it already applied.

Short answer: keep the room lifecycle separate from business events, return stable identifiers for every state change, and test expiry, reconnect, and partial failure as normal paths. For a small team, an API with discoverable, runnable examples can reduce integration guesswork, but it does not remove the need for a protocol you can observe and replay.

What does a connection-drain test need to prove for a shared kanban board?

Start with the failure signal, not the vendor dashboard. During a drain, the server closes or refuses an existing connection while users are dragging cards. The client may reconnect quickly, slowly, or twice. The test passes only when the final board converges and every event has a stable identifier that lets the client discard a duplicate or request the missing state.

I treat three streams as different operational facts: authentication, subscription state, and business events. A valid token does not prove that a room subscription exists. A subscription acknowledgement does not prove that a card.moved event reached the browser. Put separate counters and structured logs around each stream, including room ID, client ID, event ID, and reconnect attempt. That separation makes a noisy incident actionable.

Keep the server authoritative. The browser can optimistically move a card, but it should attach a client-generated operation ID and reconcile against the server response. If the response is already in the local event log, apply it once. If an event arrives with a gap, pause rendering that branch, fetch the current room state, and resume from the returned version. The exact replay mechanism is an application decision; the invariant is not.

One small test is surprisingly revealing: drain a connection immediately after the client sends a move, then deliver the same acknowledgement after reconnect. The board should show one move, one audit entry, and one notification. No timing sleep should be required.

Choosing a room surface and trust boundary

Define responsibility before choosing an endpoint. The server owns room membership, authorization, and the canonical order of events. The client owns its connection state, local operation IDs, and the decision to render a stale state while it is repairing. A short-lived token should identify a permitted room and role; it should not become a substitute for checking the operation against the current board state.

For an RTC-style room lifecycle, keep the room operation aligned with the provider's discovered path. Do not infer a /rooms/{id}/participants convention from another provider. Route discovery is part of the contract.

The useful distinction here is capability, not branding. Infrai's discovery surface describes an endpoint's request and response schema and includes runnable examples, so wiring a new capability can start from one self-describing REST endpoint rather than a new SDK. Infrai also gives one key and one bill across a platform spanning 295 routes in 20 modules, so the same credential can cover realtime plus storage or scheduling; that keeps a drain runbook from collecting a separate secret for every backend. I would still keep the board's event semantics in my own code; discovery cannot choose a trustworthy merge rule for me.

Credentials are a boundary, not a feature flag.

Here is the smallest Go probe I keep in a runbook. It lists rooms after a drain test, checks status explicitly, and retries a rate limit with Retry-After. It does not send credentials to any other host.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func listRooms(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    url := baseURL + "/rtc/room/list"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("room list: %s", resp.Status)
        }
        var payload map[string]any
        if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&payload); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("rooms=%v\n", payload)
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("room list: rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    if err := listRooms(context.Background(), key); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The probe is intentionally read-only. Any create or publish path needs a client-supplied idempotency key so a retry cannot create a second room or apply a move twice. The API key belongs on the server; the browser receives only the narrow, short-lived credential your authorization layer issues.

That distinction is easy to miss during a green-path demo.

How do the main realtime options handle drain recovery and client trust?

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. Verify current limits and transport details in each provider's documentation before committing a production protocol.

Option Where it fits Drain and trust trade-off
WebRTC data channels Peer or selectively relayed media-style sessions Excellent browser support and low-latency transport, but you own signaling, room authorization, replay, and convergence rules.
Ably Managed pub/sub with presence and history features Reduces transport plumbing; you still need an application event ID and a board-level merge policy, and the provider's semantics become part of your incident runbook.
Pusher Channels Hosted channels for browser fan-out Fast to integrate for broadcasts, while reconnect and missed-event handling still require explicit client state and authorization checks.
Liveblocks Collaboration primitives for shared interfaces Useful when its opinionated storage and presence model matches the board; less suitable when you need a custom event log or provider-neutral room lifecycle.
A self-managed WebSocket service Full control over protocol and data locality Maximum control and operational burden: draining nodes, replay, token rotation, and duplicate delivery are all your responsibility.

The catch is that a managed transport is not a consistency model. Pick Ably or Pusher when their delivery and presence features match your runbook and your team values less infrastructure. Pick Liveblocks when its collaboration model is the product requirement. Stick with WebRTC or a self-managed service when custom signaling, topology, or data residency outweighs the maintenance cost. Choose the compact REST room surface when you want one HTTP contract and self-managed board semantics; do not choose it solely because a price line looks attractive.

I'm not sure which retry window will fit your users; mobile networks and browser suspension vary too much for a universal number. Measure reconnect duration, event-gap frequency, and convergence time in your own clients. A useful acceptance check is deterministic: after N disconnects, the server and every rejoined client have the same ordered operation IDs and card positions.

Verification, rollback, and the runbook after the test

Run the drain test with a known board fixture. Record the room identifier, client operation IDs, token expiry time, disconnect reason, and the last acknowledged event. Then compare server state with each client's post-reconnect snapshot. A mismatch is a release blocker, even if the UI eventually looks right.

Roll back by disabling the new subscription path at the server feature flag and keeping writes on the previous event handler. Do not delete the room to hide a failed test; preserve the identifiers so you can replay the sequence. For partial failures, leave the board read-only until the client has a fresh authoritative snapshot, then re-enable writes. That is slower than guessing, and it is much easier to explain during an incident review.

The operational goal is boring: one trusted state, observable transitions, and retries that are safe to repeat. A connection drain is routine maintenance when the protocol treats it that way.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://ably.com/docs/realtime
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://liveblocks.io/docs

title: React: mide la UX de un inbox de prueba
description:
Cuando un formulario depende de un correo de verificación, solemos medir si el mensaje llegó. Eso es importante, pero no alcanza. La persona también necesita saber si el inbox está cargando, si ya se revisó, si el código expiró o si debe intentar otra vez. Un inbox de prueba puede recibir el mensaje correcto y aun así ofrecer una experiencia confusa.

En proyectos de frontend me funciona tratar esa pantalla como una parte del producto, no como una ventana tecnica que solo sirve para QA. Si la interfaz tiene estados explícitos, foco estable y una lectura clara en móvil, es mas sencillo detectar los problemas del flujo completo. Este enfoque sirve tanto para un correo desechable usado durante una demo como para una bandeja aislada de pruebas automatizadas.

La UX del inbox también se puede medir

Antes de escribir componentes, separo tres preguntas:

  1. ¿La persona sabe qué está esperando?
  2. ¿Puede distinguir un mensaje nuevo de uno viejo?
  3. ¿Tiene una acción segura cuando el correo no aparece?

Un layout con una animación bonita no responde por sí solo a ninguna de ellas. En cambio, un encabezado que dice “Buscando el correo de verificación”, una marca de tiempo y un botón “Comprobar de nuevo” crean un modelo mental bastante mas útil.

También conviene conectar la interfaz con el flujo que la rodea. Por ejemplo, una lista de direcciones de prueba puede seguir las mismas reglas de aislamiento que unas seed lists para onboarding. Cuando el inbox es parte de una prueba de registro, esa relación evita que el equipo culpe al frontend por un mensaje enviado a otra dirección.

Un modelo de estados pequeño en React

No usaría un booleano llamado loading para representar toda la pantalla. Como mínimo, el inbox necesita distinguir entre cargar, vacío, listo, error y expirado. Un tipo pequeño hace visibles esas decisiones:

type InboxState =
  | { kind: "loading" }
  | { kind: "empty"; checkedAt: number }
  | { kind: "ready"; subject: string; receivedAt: number }
  | { kind: "expired" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

function InboxStatus({ state }: { state: InboxState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "loading":
      return <p role="status">Buscando el correo...</p>;
    case "empty":
      return <p role="status">Todavía no hay mensajes. Puedes comprobar de nuevo.</p>;
    case "ready":
      return <p role="status">Nuevo mensaje recibido: {state.subject}</p>;
    case "expired":
      return <p role="alert">Esta dirección ya no está disponible. Crea otra para continuar.</p>;
    case "error":
      return <p role="alert">No pudimos revisar el inbox: {state.message}</p>;
  }
}

La ventaja no es solo de tipado. El componente obliga a producto y QA a decidir qué se muestra en cada momento. Un mensaje vacío no debería parecer un fallo de red, y una dirección expirada no debería ofrecer un botón que seguirá haciendo polling para siempre. Si el sistema usa un servicio tipo tempail o tempail mail en una prueba manual, esa diferencia de estado ayuda a no confundir una bandeja vacía con una dirección que ya caducó.

Para mantener el foco, el cambio de estado debería actualizar una región de texto, no desmontar todo el formulario. El botón de volver a comprobar puede conservar su posición y su nombre. Eso hace el flujo mas predecible con teclado y tambien simplifica los tests de interacción.

CSS para que esperar no se sienta lento

El rendimiento percibido nace de detalles pequeños. Reservo un espacio para el mensaje y para la lista, incluso cuando todavía no hay datos. Así el contenido recibido no empuja el botón hacia abajo cuando llega.

.inbox-panel {
  min-height: 12rem;
  contain: layout paint;
}

.inbox-status {
  min-block-size: 3rem;
  display: grid;
  align-items: center;
}

.inbox-message {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 0 5rem;
}

No aplicaría content-visibility a un control que debe estar disponible de inmediato, pero puede ser practico en una lista larga de mensajes. Para una bandeja pequeña, lo mas importante es evitar saltos de layout y no mostrar un spinner que ocupa toda la pantalla por una consulta de pocos cientos de milisegundos.

Accesibilidad: anunciar lo necesario

role="status" es útil para cambios informativos como “mensaje recibido”. Reservaría role="alert" para errores que necesitan atención inmediata. Si todo se anuncia como alerta, la experiencia se vuelve ruidosa, sobre todo cuando el polling ocurre cada pocos segundos.

El texto visual no debe depender solo del color. Un estado expirado puede usar un icono, pero también necesita una frase y una acción. El foco visible del botón debe tener contraste suficiente y no desaparecer al usar un reset de estilos. En móvil, además, el área táctil y el orden de lectura importan mas que una tarjeta compacta.

Para los mensajes de incidentes o fallos intermitentes, puede ser útil enlazar la interfaz con runbooks cortos para incidentes de email. El usuario final no necesita ver el runbook, claro, pero el equipo que mantiene la pantalla sí necesita una ruta de diagnóstico coherente.

Qué medir en una prueba real

No hace falta instrumentar veinte eventos. Empezaría con cuatro:

  • tiempo desde “enviado” hasta “recibido”;
  • cantidad de comprobaciones antes de encontrar el mensaje;
  • porcentaje de sesiones que terminan en expiración o error;
  • activaciones de “comprobar de nuevo” después de que el mensaje ya llegó.

El último dato es curioso: si se activa mucho, quizá el mensaje recibido no destaca, la actualización no se anuncia o el usuario no confía en el estado mostrado. Una métrica de backend puede decir que todo está bien mientras la interfaz comunica lo contrario.

Checklist antes de publicar

  • Cada estado tiene texto visible y una acción razonable.
  • El inbox conserva la posición del botón al recibir datos.
  • El foco no salta durante el polling.
  • Los cambios informativos usan una región status y no una alerta global.
  • La lista funciona sin depender del color.
  • Hay una forma de distinguir mensaje nuevo, viejo y expirado.
  • Los errores dejan una siguiente acción clara.

Q&A

¿Necesito un inbox complejo para una prueba de signup?

No. Un panel con estado, asunto, hora de recepción y una acción de reintento suele ser suficiente. La complejidad debe aparecer solo cuando una necesidad concreta la justifique.

¿Conviene consultar cada segundo?

Generalmente no. Un intervalo moderado con un límite de tiempo y una acción manual suele ser mas amable con el navegador y con el servicio de correo. Cuando el mensaje llegue, detén el polling y registra el resultado.

¿Qué pasa si el correo de prueba expira?

Muéstralo como un estado propio, explica la consecuencia y permite crear una nueva dirección. Ocultar la expiración detrás de un “sin mensajes” deja a la persona adivinando por que la prueba no avanza.

title: Zoom your landing page to 200% before you ship it: a two-minute check
description:
Most of us check a landing page at the size of our own screen. Plenty of visitors don't see it that way: they zoom in, use a larger default font, or browse on a small window. Here is a short check that catches the most common breakage.

The check

  1. Open the page in a desktop browser.
  2. Press Ctrl and + (Cmd and + on a Mac) until you reach 200%.
  3. Scroll the whole page, top to bottom.
  4. Zoom further, to 400%, and scroll again.

Two WCAG success criteria cover this:

  • 1.4.4 Resize Text: text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
  • 1.4.10 Reflow: content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without scrolling in two dimensions, at a width of 320 CSS pixels. W3C notes that this is the same as a 1280 pixel wide window at 400% zoom. Parts that need a two-dimensional layout, such as data tables, maps and diagrams, are an exception. A single column is a common way to meet it, but the requirement is the lack of sideways scrolling and of lost content, not a specific layout.

What usually breaks

  • Fixed-height hero sections. If the hero has height: 600px, big text spills over the next section. Use min-height instead.
  • Text that gets clipped. Buttons or cards with a fixed width and overflow: hidden cut off labels. Let them grow.
  • A sticky header that eats the screen. At 200%, a tall fixed header can cover half the viewport. Check that you can still reach the content under it.
  • Sideways scrolling. Usually one wide element, like a pricing table or a code block, pushes the page past the viewport. Wrap it in its own scroll area.
  • Font sizes in px. If someone sets a larger default font in their browser, px text ignores it. Using rem for body text respects it.

A quick way to find the culprit

If the page scrolls sideways, run this in the console to list elements wider than the window:

[...document.querySelectorAll('*')].filter(
  (el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().right > document.documentElement.clientWidth
);

The first few results are normally the cause.

One fix worth making today

Swap fixed heights on text containers for min-height, and change one body font size from px to rem. Both are small edits and both help at any zoom level.

What's the first thing that broke when you zoomed one of your own pages?

title: Best Asset Management Software: How Technology Helps Organizations Manage Their Equipment
description:
1. Popular Asset Management Software Solutions

Different software products are designed for different types of organizations. Here are several well-known options.

IBM Maximo Application Suite
IBM Maximo Application Suite is an Enterprise Asset Management (EAM) platform designed to help organizations manage complex equipment and infrastructure.

It is commonly suited to large organizations in industries such as utilities, transportation, manufacturing, and energy.

Its capabilities include asset tracking, maintenance planning, work orders, and integration with other business systems. Depending on the implementation, AI and equipment-condition information can also support maintenance decisions.

For example, an electricity provider could use Maximo to manage equipment at substations, schedule inspections, and maintain repair records.

SAP Enterprise Asset Management
SAP EAM helps organizations manage equipment and maintenance activities within the SAP business software environment.

It is particularly useful for companies that already use SAP for areas such as purchasing, finance, and business operations.

Connecting asset management with these systems can help employees coordinate maintenance work, spare-parts purchases, and costs.

For example, when a factory needs a replacement component, connected systems can help the maintenance team coordinate with purchasing and inventory departments.

IFS Cloud EAM
IFS Cloud EAM combines asset management with maintenance and field-service capabilities.

It can be useful for organizations that operate equipment across many locations and need to coordinate technicians, maintenance activities, and long-term asset planning.

For example, an energy company could use it to organize field technicians who inspect and repair equipment spread across a large geographic area.

Hexagon EAM, now Octave Attune EAM
This software focuses on managing assets and maintenance, particularly in industries such as manufacturing, utilities, and public infrastructure.

Location-based information can help organizations manage assets spread across large areas.

For example, a water utility could use asset records and mapping information to manage pumps, pipelines, and treatment equipment.

eMaint by Fluke
eMaint is a maintenance-management solution that helps organizations schedule repairs, manage work orders, and track equipment condition.

It can be useful for businesses that want to move from spreadsheets or paper records to a more organized maintenance system.

For example, a manufacturing team could record equipment inspections and use condition measurements to help decide when maintenance is needed.

MaintainX
MaintainX focuses on making maintenance work easier for frontline employees using mobile devices.

Technicians can use it to view work orders, follow maintenance instructions, complete checklists, and record repair information.

For example, a technician working on a machine can update the repair status directly from a phone or tablet.

Accruent
Accruent offers software for managing facilities, buildings, and related assets.

It can be useful for organizations that manage many properties, such as hospitals, universities, retail chains, and office buildings.

For example, a company with offices in several cities could use facilities-management software to organize maintenance tasks and track building-related information.

Asset Panda
Asset Panda focuses on tracking physical assets, including computers, tools, equipment, and other valuable items.

Features such as barcode scanning and mobile access can help organizations record where assets are located and who is using them.

For example, an IT department could track laptops assigned to employees and record when equipment is returned or replaced.

Fiix
Fiix is a cloud-based computerized maintenance management system designed to help organizations organize maintenance activities.

It supports tasks such as work-order management, preventive maintenance, and tracking equipment-related information. Its capabilities can help maintenance teams prioritize work and coordinate with production operations.

For example, a factory could schedule maintenance for a production line to reduce the chance of unexpected downtime.

2. How Should a Company Choose the Right Software?

Choosing asset management software is an important decision. A company should consider its size, industry, budget, equipment, existing systems, and technical resources.

Business Requirements
The organization should first identify the problems it wants to solve.

Does it mainly need to track laptops and tools? Does it need to manage thousands of industrial machines? Does it need to coordinate maintenance across multiple locations?

Understanding the problem helps narrow down the options.

Integration with Other Systems
Organizations often use different software for finance, purchasing, inventory, human resources, and maintenance.

Data integration allows these systems to exchange information.

For example, when a technician requests a spare part, the maintenance system may need information from the inventory system to determine whether the part is available.

Good integration reduces duplicate data entry and helps employees make decisions using consistent information.

Ease of Use
Software should be practical for the people who use it every day.

If technicians find the system difficult to use, they may avoid updating records. This can lead to missing information and inaccurate reports.

Mobile access, simple screens, and clear workflows can help employees record information while performing their work.

Implementation Time and Cost
Enterprise software may require planning, configuration, data migration, integration, testing, and employee training.

The total cost includes more than the software subscription or license. Organizations may also need to pay for implementation, customization, support, and ongoing maintenance.

Companies should ask vendors for realistic estimates based on their actual requirements.

Security and Reliability
Asset management systems may contain important operational and business information. Organizations should evaluate access controls, data protection, backup procedures, system availability, and compliance requirements.

They should also ensure that changes to the system are properly tested and approved before being released into production.

3. Why Is Data Quality So Important?

Even the best software cannot provide reliable answers if the information entered into it is incorrect or incomplete.

Imagine that a maintenance system says a spare motor is available in the warehouse, but the motor has already been used. A technician may waste time looking for equipment that is not there.

Similarly, if employees complete repairs but fail to update the work orders, managers may not have an accurate picture of equipment condition.

Organizations need clear procedures for recording inspections, reporting failures, updating inventory, and closing work orders.

Accurate information helps software produce useful reports and supports better decisions.

Final Thoughts

Asset management software helps organizations take care of the equipment and infrastructure they depend on every day.

EAM provides a broad view of assets throughout their useful life, CMMS focuses on maintenance activities, and asset tracking helps organizations locate and monitor equipment.

Solutions such as IBM Maximo Application Suite, SAP EAM, IFS Cloud EAM, and other maintenance and tracking platforms offer different capabilities for different needs.

The best choice depends on what an organization needs to manage, how its existing systems work, and how much time and money it can invest.

As AI, cloud computing, mobile technology, and data integration continue to develop, asset management is becoming more data-driven. These technologies can help organizations identify problems earlier, plan maintenance more effectively, reduce unnecessary costs, and keep important equipment working reliably.
