title: What Amazon buying DuckDB's makers means for Aurora users
description:
Amazon has acquired DuckLabs, the Amsterdam-based company behind the analytical database DuckDB, InfoQ reports. The first product result is already live. According to InfoQ, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL can now use DuckDB to run a single query across your live database rows and historical data stored in Amazon S3. The processing happens inside Aurora, and there is no extra fee: you pay only for the additional Aurora compute and the S3 requests those queries generate. That pricing and placement decides whether this story touches your bills and your pipelines.

The background you need

Databases do two broadly different jobs.

Transactional work, often called OLTP, is many small reads and writes: insert an order, update a user, fetch one profile. PostgreSQL is built for this. It stores each row's fields together, so grabbing or changing one record is fast.

Analytical work, often called OLAP, is the opposite. You scan millions of rows but only a few columns, as in total revenue by month for the last three years. Engines built for this store each column together. They read only the columns a query needs and process values in large batches. Running that kind of query on a row store works, but it is usually slow and expensive.

DuckDB is an open-source analytical database with that column-oriented design. Unlike most databases, it is built to run in-process. It lives inside another program instead of running as a separate server you connect to. People often describe it as SQLite for analytics. According to InfoQ, its creators are Hannes Mühleisen and Mark Raasveldt, who co-founded DuckLabs. A non-profit, the DuckDB Foundation, oversees the project.

Aurora PostgreSQL is AWS's managed database service that is compatible with PostgreSQL. Your app talks to it like normal Postgres.

Some data lake vocabulary appears in the report without definitions:

  • Amazon S3 is object storage. Many teams move older data there because it is cheap to keep.
  • Parquet is a columnar file format, the on-disk version of the column-oriented idea above.
  • Apache Iceberg is a table format. It adds a metadata layer over a pile of Parquet files so they behave like one table, with a schema and a history of changes.
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog is a registry that records which tables exist and where their files live.
  • S3 Tables is an S3 offering designed specifically for storing Iceberg tables.

Finally, ETL (extract, transform, load) means copying data out of your app database into an analytics store. Reverse ETL goes the other way: it pushes data from the analytics side back into operational systems. According to InfoQ, AWS principal solutions architect Esra Kayabali describes the old approach this way: teams that needed recent Aurora data and historical S3 data together often built reverse ETL pipelines. Those pipelines duplicated data, raised infrastructure costs, and needed ongoing work to stay in sync.

Here is an analogy. Your current stock list sits at the shop counter and your archive sits in a warehouse across town. To answer a question that spans both, you used to pay a courier to keep copying boxes back to the counter. Now the clerk at the counter can read the warehouse shelves directly. The analogy breaks in two places. First, the clerk is still the same person, so the reading uses Aurora's own compute and is not free labor. Second, nothing gets copied, so the archive is only as current as whatever you have already written to S3.

What actually changed

These parts are new, according to InfoQ:

  • The acquisition. DuckLabs joins AWS. Mühleisen and Raasveldt will continue to lead the team and the open-source project's technical direction.
  • A DuckDB-powered feature in Aurora PostgreSQL. One query can combine live operational data with Iceberg tables managed through AWS Glue Data Catalog, plus Parquet and Iceberg data in S3 and S3 Tables. InfoQ says processing stays within Aurora, without additional network hops or ETL pipelines.
  • Availability and price. The feature is in all commercial regions and AWS GovCloud (US) at no additional charge. You pay for the incremental Aurora compute and S3 requests your queries create.

These parts were already true and stay true:

  • The license. DuckDB and the rest of what DuckLabs calls its Duck Stack, including DuckLake and Quack, remain free and open source under the MIT license. The DuckDB Foundation keeps supervising the projects.
  • The relationship. It is not new. In a post on Werner Vogels's blog, AWS distinguished engineer Andy Warfield writes that contact began while the S3 team was building S3 Tables. He says the teams collaborated for roughly two years, exploring AWS Lambda as a way to launch DuckDB queries quickly. They also smoothed integrations with AWS services through DuckDB's ATTACH and CONNECT commands.

So DuckDB could already reach AWS data from the outside. What changed is that DuckDB now runs inside a managed AWS database as a feature you can use from Postgres.

What it means if you deploy and run apps

The lever is simple. The analytical work now runs on your Aurora compute, and AWS charges no separate fee for the feature. That changes where your cost and risk sit.

Pipelines you might delete. You may run a scheduled job that copies S3 history into Postgres tables just so you can join it with live data. That job is now a candidate for retirement. You would stop maintaining sync code and stop storing the same data twice. Test with your real queries before you remove anything.

Costs move, they do not vanish. The pipeline's compute and duplicate storage go away. In their place you pay Aurora compute for each analytical query, plus S3 request charges. Analytical scans can be heavy. S3 request counts also tend to grow with the number of files a query touches, so data split into many small files can cost more to read.

Watch your database load. These queries run in the same service that serves your app. Before you point dashboards or reports at your primary instance, check the AWS documentation for where these queries can run. Then watch CPU and latency while you test.

If you use DuckDB on its own, in scripts, notebooks, or CI, InfoQ reports that the license and foundation oversight stay as they were. Community reaction was positive but cautious. One Reddit commenter quoted by InfoQ wrote: "I hope this doesn't slow the pace of innovation they have been doing". Release pace is worth watching.

AWS's broader pitch is about data size and AI agents. AWS technology VP Mai-Lan Tomsen Bukovec argues that DuckDB targets the majority of queries, which she says often run on 1 terabyte of data or less. She also argues that it suits AI agents that run many small exploratory queries. That is AWS's framing, not an independent measurement.

What to watch next: InfoQ calls Aurora PostgreSQL the first service to get a user-facing DuckDB feature. Expect announcements for other AWS services, though the report names none.

No additional charge does not mean free. According to InfoQ, you still pay for the extra Aurora compute and the S3 requests each query generates. Run a few of your real analytical queries on a test instance and check the bill and the instance metrics before you move production reports to it.

What we don't know yet

  • The deal terms. InfoQ's report does not give a price or financial terms.
  • Performance. The report includes no benchmarks for Aurora with DuckDB against a pipeline or a separate warehouse.
  • The details of use. The report does not say how you enable the feature, which Aurora PostgreSQL versions support it, or whether it can write to Iceberg tables as well as read them.
  • Isolation. It is unclear how analytical queries are kept from slowing transactional traffic on the same cluster.
  • Other engines. The report mentions only Aurora PostgreSQL. It says nothing about Aurora MySQL or standard RDS for PostgreSQL.
  • Long-term direction. The current assurances cover licensing and foundation oversight. How AWS priorities will shape DuckDB's roadmap over time is still an open question.

title: Frontend Monitoring: The Complete Guide to Observability That Actually Works
description:
Frontend monitoring is not a luxury. It is the difference between knowing your application works and guessing it does. Your backend can return perfect 200 responses while users on mid-range phones stare at frozen screens, broken forms, and silent failures that never generate a support ticket. This guide covers what frontend monitoring actually is, why it matters for revenue and SEO, the tools worth your time, and how to avoid the privacy traps that turn observability into a liability.

What Frontend Monitoring Really Means

Frontend monitoring is the practice of observing how your application behaves inside real users' browsers: how fast pages load, how stable the layout remains, whether interactions respond promptly, and where errors occur before anyone complains. It spans three distinct disciplines that are often conflated but serve different purposes.

Performance monitoring tracks speed and responsiveness. The industry standard is Google's Core Web Vitals: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, target under 2.5 seconds), INP (Interaction to Next Paint, target under 200 milliseconds), and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, target under 0.1) . These thresholds are not arbitrary. Google's research drew on human-computer interaction studies showing that users perceive delays beyond roughly one second as a loss of immediate responsiveness, and the 2.5-second LCP threshold was validated against real-world Chrome data as consistently achievable for well-optimized sites .

Error tracking captures unhandled exceptions, Promise rejections, and client-side failures with readable stack traces. The critical caveat that most teams learn the hard way: frameworks like Next.js intentionally swallow errors inside error boundaries and try/catch blocks. If you do not explicitly report those errors, they never reach your dashboard.

Session replay records what users actually did before an error occurred. It is invaluable for UX debugging, but it carries privacy risks that must be configured before deployment, not after.

Why This Matters More Than You Think

The business case is straightforward. Users who encounter a slow or broken page rarely return. Without frontend monitoring, teams typically learn about problems only after users complain or abandon the product. With it, regressions surface immediately after deployment, and historical data lets you pinpoint exactly which change caused a metric to degrade.

There is a direct SEO consequence as well. Google's core ranking systems evaluate Core Web Vitals, and Google explicitly states that good scores alone do not guarantee top rankings, but they contribute to success in competitive queries where multiple pages offer equally helpful content . Google evaluates field data from real users at the 75th percentile, meaning you must optimize for the slowest quarter of your audience, not the median . A site that looks fast on your developer machine can fail for a meaningful portion of actual visitors.

There is also a compounding operational cost. A real case study from Supabase illustrates the failure mode perfectly: their frontend Sentry project accumulated roughly 475,000 weekly events of pure noise from a single rethrown user-cancellation bug, browser extension injections, and expired captchas. When an actual frontend outage occurred, not a single alert fired because the signal was buried under noise. After implementing client-side filtering and fixing the root cause, weekly crashes dropped from over 2,000 to 32, and five high-impact bugs were discovered and fixed, unblocking approximately 6,300 users . The lesson is clear: monitoring without discipline is worse than no monitoring at all.

The Tool Landscape: What Each One Is Actually For

Sentry

Sentry remains the industry standard for error tracking with precise stack traces. Its strengths are framework support (including automatic instrumentation for Next.js Server Actions and React Server Components), source map uploads during build, and a genuinely usable free tier. It has expanded into performance monitoring and session replay, but its core identity is exception diagnosis. For solo developers through mid-size teams, Sentry is the correct starting point .

Datadog

Datadog is a full observability platform connecting frontend, backend, infrastructure, and logs in one place. Its distributed tracing is powerful for microservice architectures: a single user action touching three services appears as one connected trace. However, it is expensive, has a steep learning curve, and is overkill for a simple Next.js application on Vercel. Datadog earns its cost when you have a dedicated platform team, run Kubernetes, or need compliance-grade log retention .

LogRocket

LogRocket centers the user session as the debugging record. It is the right choice when your first question after an error is "what did the user do before this happened?" rather than "what exception was thrown?" Pricing follows captured sessions, not error volume, which means a session-heavy product needs to forecast session counts even if its crash rate is low . Error tracking depth is shallower than Sentry.

New Relic

New Relic sits between Sentry and Datadog in complexity. It offers frontend error monitoring, backend performance tracing, and infrastructure monitoring with a real free tier (100 GB per month ingest). Its strongest feature is browser agent performance monitoring, capturing real user timing data across DNS lookup, connection, first byte, and DOM processing. It is worth evaluating when you need backend tracing but find Datadog's pricing difficult to justify .

Bugsnag

Bugsnag does one thing and does it well: error monitoring with clean grouping, filtering, and alerting. No session replay, no performance dashboards, no infrastructure metrics. For teams that find Sentry's dashboard overwhelming, Bugsnag is a focused alternative. Pick whichever dashboard your team will actually open .

A Decision Framework That Actually Helps

Stop reading comparison tables and ask one question: what is your biggest risk right now?

If you do not know what errors users are hitting, start with Sentry. Its free tier is sufficient for most early-stage products.

If users complain about slowness but you lack data, prioritize Real User Monitoring and Core Web Vitals tracking. RUM captures performance from actual user interactions across devices, networks, and geographies, while synthetic monitoring runs scheduled tests in controlled environments . Both matter, but RUM reflects what real users experience.

If product teams ask what users are actually doing, evaluate LogRocket or Sentry's session replay.

If you are running Kubernetes with a dedicated platform team, Datadog becomes worth its cost.

For a solo developer or side project, Sentry's free tier plus Vercel Analytics covers everything you genuinely need at zero cost .

The Privacy Trap Nobody Mentions Early Enough

Monitoring tools serialize exception data, breadcrumbs, and network events. A careless configuration can ship access tokens, session cookies, or personal data directly to a third-party backend. The beforeSend and beforeBreadcrumb hooks exist specifically to strip sensitive fields before transmission. Client-side scrubbing is a stronger guarantee than relying on server-side filtering alone, especially under GDPR. If you enable session replay, mask inputs by default and unmask only what is explicitly safe.

The Supabase case study reinforces this at the architectural level: they implemented filtering directly in the SDK rather than relying on Sentry-side data filters. Events filtered client-side never leave the browser, so they do not count against quota and do not pollute the project at all. The filter configuration lives in version control, reviewed like any other code change . Treat monitoring configuration as production code, not a set-and-forget setting.

Ready to Stop Guessing?

Install Sentry's free tier on your frontend this week. It takes under ten minutes, and the first real error you catch before a user reports it will justify the effort. If you are already running monitoring, audit your configuration today: confirm source maps are uploading, confirm PII is being scrubbed client-side, and confirm your error boundaries are actually reporting. The gap between a monitored application and a correctly monitored one is exactly where production incidents hide.

title: Optimizing Frontend Performance and SEO for Local Trade Services Web Apps
description:
When developers build websites for local service businesses—such as painters, contractors, or renovation experts—the requirements might seem simple at first glance: show the services, display a gallery, and provide a contact form.

However, from an engineering perspective, local service platforms are a demanding use case for modern frontend architecture. They face unique technical challenges:

Mobile-first users on poor connections: High bounce rates occur if heavy media asset bundles delay rendering on cellular networks.

Aggressive Core Web Vitals targets: Google’s local ranking algorithms heavily penalize slow LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) and high CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift).

Location-based entity resolution: Search engines need well-structured JSON-LD data to link physical service areas to digital routes.

In this article, we’ll look at how modern frontend patterns—from image optimization strategies to server-side rendering (SSR) and dynamic schema injection—can turn a local service site into a high-performance web asset.

1. Asset Optimization Strategy for High-Res Media

Local trade sites rely heavily on high-resolution "before & after" image galleries and project portfolios to establish trust. If unoptimized, these assets destroy performance metrics.

Technical Implementation:
Next-Gen Formats: Convert standard PNG/JPEG uploads to AVIF and WebP dynamically via build tools or image CDNs.

Responsive Source Sets: Serve tailored image dimensions based on viewport width using the tag or framework-level image components.

Explicit Dimensions: Always set width and height attributes to reserve layout space and eliminate Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) during image loading.

 <picture>
  <source srcset="renovated-interior-800.avif 800w, renovated-interior-1200.avif 1200w" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="renovated-interior-800.webp 800w, renovated-interior-1200.webp 1200w" type="image/webp">
  <img src="renovated-interior-800.jpg" width="800" height="600" alt="Professional painting and interior wall renovation in Stuttgart" loading="lazy">
</picture>

2. Geo-Localized Schema Markup & Entity Matching

Search engines parse local intent by matching physical service capabilities with structured microdata. For localized trade services (such as painting, plastering, or facade renovation), implementing the HousePainter or LocalBusiness schema via JSON-LD is essential.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "HousePainter",
  "name": "Malerexperten Stuttgart",
  "url": "https://malerexperten-stuttgart.de/",
  "areaServed": {
    "@type": "City",
    "name": "Stuttgart"
  },
  "knowsAbout": [
    "Malerarbeiten",
    "Fassadensanierung",
    "Innenanstrich",
    "Tapezierarbeiten"
  ]
}

By dynamically injecting structured data corresponding to specific routes, search crawlers can instantly identify geographic service boundaries without relying on unstructured text parsing alone.

3. Server-First Rendering for Instant Parsing

Single-Page Application (SPA) architectures built strictly on Client-Side Rendering (CSR) often introduce indexing latency. Search crawlers must execute client-side JavaScript before discovering local content and internal links.

For local service applications, adopting Server-Side Rendering (SSR) or Static Site Generation (SSG) ensures:

Time-to-First-Byte (TTFB) & Initial Render Speed: Pre-rendered HTML allows bots to crawl content on the initial request.

Low Interactivity Latency (INP): Minimizing client-side JS bundle execution keeps the main thread clear for quick user interactions (such as requesting a quote or tapping a phone link).

For regional trade and engineering platforms—such as specialized painting services like Malerexperten Stuttgart in Germany or Alfa Malerei in Austria—serving static or pre-rendered HTML guarantees both rapid indexation and optimal performance for local mobile visitors.

4. Route Architecture & Internal Link Graph

A clean URL and route hierarchy is critical for both user experience and search engine discovery.

Route Design Best Practices:
Avoid Hash Fragments & Query Strings: Avoid URLs like /services?type=painting&city=stuttgart.

Explicit Hierarchical Slugs: Use clear, semantic route structures such as /malerarbeiten-stuttgart/ or /leistungen/fassadensanierung/.

Internal Cross-Linking: Build an internal graph connecting related services (e.g., linking interior painting directly to plastering and wall prep) to pass topical authority throughout the application.

Conclusion

Building a web app for local trade services isn't just about static web design—it's a technical discipline. By applying modern frontend optimizations (AVIF/WebP assets, strict layout reservation, pre-rendered HTML, and JSON-LD entity markup), developers can build web applications that load instantly and achieve maximum visibility in local search ecosystems.

Key Resources
Google Web.dev – Core Web Vitals Optimization

Schema.org – HousePainter & LocalBusiness Specifications

Malerexperten Stuttgart – Professional Painting & Renovation Services

title: How to Choose Colors for a Website: A Practical Guide
description:
Choosing colors for a website can be harder than it looks. A color palette needs to feel consistent, keep text readable, and support the purpose of the design.

Here is a simple process you can use for your next project.

  1. Start with a Primary Color

Choose one color that represents the overall mood of your website.

For example:

Blue can feel dependable and professional.

Green can suggest growth or nature.

Orange can create a sense of energy.

Purple can give a design a creative feel.

These are common associations, not fixed rules. The right choice depends on your audience and context.

  1. Build a Small Color Palette

You do not need dozens of colors. Start with a few practical roles:

Primary: The main brand or interface color.

Secondary: A supporting color for variety.

Background: A color that keeps the layout comfortable to read.

Text: A color with strong contrast against the background.

Accent: A color for important actions or selected elements.

A limited palette is usually easier to apply consistently across buttons, cards, headings, and backgrounds.

  1. Check Contrast and Readability

A color combination may look attractive but still make text difficult to read.

Check the contrast between text and its background, especially for small text and buttons. WCAG guidance generally recommends a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

Do not rely on color alone to communicate information. Use labels, icons, or other visual cues when necessary.

  1. Test Colors Together

View your colors in context rather than judging each swatch separately. Try them on a sample button, a heading, and a card.

You can use a color palette tool to explore combinations, compare shades, and refine your choices before applying them to a full design.

For a quick starting point, explore Clicktoolset and its color tools.

  1. Keep the Palette Consistent

Once you settle on a palette, reuse the same colors for the same purposes. For example, keep primary buttons consistent and reserve accent colors for elements that deserve attention.

Documenting your colors as HEX values also makes it easier to reuse them in CSS:

:root {
  --color-primary: #2563EB;
  --color-secondary: #14B8A6;
  --color-background: #F8FAFC;
  --color-text: #1E293B;
  --color-accent: #F59E0B;
}

These values are only an example. Test your actual combinations for contrast and suitability before using them in a project.

Final Thoughts

A useful website palette does not have to be complicated. Start with a primary color, add a few supporting roles, check readability, and test the result in a real layout.

A small, consistent palette is often easier to maintain than a collection of unrelated colors.

title: React Next.js Avatar Files: CORS, Private Buckets, and a Reversible Upload Boundary
description:
Short answer: for an e-commerce avatar flow, use a browser direct upload only when the deployed React or Next.js origin already works with the storage provider's CORS behavior. If that is uncertain, upload through the backend. Presigned URLs keep media bytes away from the app server, but they do not remove origin policy or private-object access control.

The migration decision is separate from the upload decision. Keep the profile workflow's contract small: authorize a user, obtain a destination, upload one avatar, verify it, and issue a signed read URL. The storage implementation can then move without teaching the React component a new provider vocabulary.

Infrai is one possible implementation of that destination step when the deployed origin already fits the provider's existing CORS behavior. Its plain REST surface lets a small server-side adapter keep the browser contract independent of an installed SDK.

What should a private avatar upload contract guarantee?

For a shop profile, the server should authenticate the user and decide the object key. The browser sends bytes to a presigned destination. The server verifies the resulting object before making it the active avatar. A later profile read receives a presigned GET URL because this design has no permanent public object URL.

The bucket stays private. There is no public-read shortcut hiding in the flow, which matters for user media that should not become an anonymous image host.

React owns file selection and progress. Next.js owns authorization, key naming, and completion state. Storage owns the bytes. Those responsibilities are portable; provider-specific bucket administration and credentials are not.

A successful presign response is not a successful upload. Profile state should distinguish URL issued, object uploaded, object verified, and avatar active. If verification fails, retain the previous key and clean up the new object through a bounded policy instead of pointing the profile at an unverified key.

For an avatar-sized file, one PUT is easier to reason about. Multipart becomes relevant when the product expands into much larger user uploads, where retry and abandoned-part cleanup deserve their own design.

Should React and Next.js use browser direct upload for private object storage?

The browser test comes first. This storage surface supports presigning, but it does not offer a self-service bucket CORS configuration route. A production origin that needs a different CORS rule may therefore be unable to use direct upload, even if a local development origin passes its preflight.

That is a capability boundary, not a mysterious frontend problem. Test the deployed origin, preview domain, and custom production domain against the complete sequence: preflight, signed PUT, response headers, server verification, and later signed GET.

Test the real origin.

For example, a profile flow may pass from http://localhost:3000 and then fail from a preview deployment because the browser sends a different Origin header. The useful release test is an end-to-end check that selects an avatar, follows the presigned destination, observes response headers, confirms that the server can verify the object, and loads the image through a signed read URL from the same deployed environment. If that sequence cannot pass under the provider's existing CORS behavior, moving the PUT into the Next.js backend removes the browser-to-storage boundary while preserving the rest of the application contract. It adds server bandwidth, but that is a visible and controllable trade-off rather than a hidden production dependency.

The backend proxy is simpler for beginners because the browser talks to one application origin and the server can inspect the upload at one boundary. Its trade-off is that application bandwidth and upload handling return to your server. Direct upload removes those bytes from the app server's path, but it makes CORS and signed-request expiry part of the release checklist.

The security checks remain yours either way. Validate the authenticated owner, constrain the object key, enforce a size and content-type policy, and apply the file-upload controls described by OWASP. Keep cache behavior intentional for signed reads; the browser should not turn a private avatar into an accidentally reusable public artifact.

Which option keeps the storage migration reversible?

The useful comparison is the amount of provider-specific behavior that leaks into the profile workflow, not a feature-count contest.

Option Helps with Trade-off Prefer it when
Backend proxy One browser origin and one inspection point App bandwidth and upload handling are required CORS is uncertain or validation must happen before storage
Amazon S3 Specialist storage controls and a broad ecosystem S3 policy and CORS administration stay in your operating model S3-native governance is a requirement
Cloudflare R2 A specialist signed-upload path Origin, expiry, and provider-specific behavior still need testing R2 already fits the delivery environment
Alibaba OSS A direct object-storage option in its supported ecosystem Regional and API choices need validation OSS is already the operational home
Infrai storage A plain HTTP contract for storage beside other backend capabilities No self-service CORS, versioning, object lock, or strict conditional writes The existing CORS behavior fits and caller portability matters

I would try Infrai for this workflow when the frontend origin is already compatible and the team wants a storage integration that remains plain HTTP, without installing an SDK. Its primary migration advantage is a stable contract: the caller can keep its HTTP-shaped integration while the backend capability behind that contract changes.

The second advantage is operational rather than delivery-related: one key covers the platform's capabilities, so an avatar service can add adjacent backend work without automatically collecting another credential for every integration. Infrai documents 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which reduces credential and integration sprawl when the same e-commerce application grows beyond storage. That does not make it the right storage specialist for every workload.

The discovery surface is public and needs no key, and documented capabilities ship runnable examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, the backend team can inspect the current presign schema before wiring its adapter rather than building against an imagined request shape.

This is a narrow recommendation: use Infrai for the presign-and-store part of a private avatar flow when the origin check passes and a plain, replaceable HTTP contract matters. Use a specialist when the missing controls are the actual requirement.

How can a Next.js server keep the critical path provider-neutral?

The provider call belongs behind an authenticated server route. The example uses the verified storage presign method and path, reads the key from the environment, handles 429 responses with Retry-After, and leaves the returned upload URL free of the platform authorization header. Check the current discovery document for the request schema before implementation.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


API_BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def presign_avatar(bucket, content_type):
    key = f"avatars/{uuid.uuid4()}.webp"
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}
    payload = {"key": key, "content_type": content_type, "acl": "private"}

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            f"{API_BASE}/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=20,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}"
            )
        return key, response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit did not clear")


object_key, presign_result = presign_avatar(
    "private-avatars", "image/webp"
)
print(object_key, presign_result)

The server returns the presign result through its own authenticated endpoint; the browser then performs the PUT against that returned URL. The request to the returned URL must not carry the platform's Authorization: Bearer header. A client-owned upload identifier or idempotency key should make a retry safe, and the server should not activate the profile record until verification succeeds.

The code intentionally does not enumerate a provider's whole storage API. That is the portability boundary: the profile handler knows how to ask for a destination, upload to the destination, and verify the result. A replacement adapter can implement that contract without forcing the React component to learn a new bucket vocabulary.

When is the backend proxy the better answer?

Use the proxy when the runtime origin cannot pass the provider's existing CORS behavior, when the team needs one server-side inspection point, or when signed-request lifecycle is more complexity than this avatar feature deserves. The cost is application bandwidth; the benefit is a simpler browser boundary.

Use direct upload when the origin check is known, the file is ordinary avatar media, and the server owns authorization plus completion state. Do not use this storage shape for public permanent links, static-site hosting, object version recovery, object lock, strict If-Match concurrency, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud batch migration. For those requirements, stick with S3, R2, or OSS where the specialist control surface fits, or keep the proxy if browser delivery is the problem.

Lifecycle cleanup also has limits: the shortest lifecycle period is one day, abandoned multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not a server-side searchable index beyond prefix filtering. Your mileage may vary across deployment origins. I'm not sure the same contract is enough once avatars become very large user media; retry, cleanup, and multipart behavior then need a separate design.

Small contract. Clear boundary.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the avatar presign guide against the deployed origin and current request schema.

References

  • Infrai storage discovery
  • AWS S3 presigned URL uploads
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • MDN Cache-Control response header

Further reading

  • Storage object discovery

title: AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity
description:
AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity

The failure class, not just the identifier

CVE-2026-107282 is one entry in a batch of fixes published for AsyncHttpClient (AHC), the Java library that a large share of JVM services use to make outbound HTTP calls. The batch matters more than any single item because every entry in it has the same shape: the client decides who it is, or who it is talking to, from state that was computed for a different request. The result is a library that is diligent about authentication and still sends credentials to the wrong place.
The headline issue, affecting versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1, concerns cross-host request replay. When AHC re-issues a request against a different host, it updates the current request object but leaves the target request and the associated proxy context pointing at the original host. Path, Host header, Authorization credentials, or a cleartext body computed for host A can therefore be transmitted to host B.

Why that is a credential disclosure rather than a cosmetic bug

Consider a service that talks to an internal API and, after a redirect or a retry against a different endpoint, replays a request. The Authorization header was minted for the first host. The second host may be a third-party service, a different tenant's endpoint, or an attacker-controlled redirect target. Because the client decided the request was a replay, from its point of view nothing unusual happened; from the receiving end, a valid bearer token for an unrelated system just arrived in plaintext or in a header the receiver can read.
The same reasoning applies to the body. A replayed POST whose payload was assembled for the original destination can carry internal identifiers, query fragments or credentials to a host that was never meant to see them. In a microservice mesh where dozens of internal services trust bearer tokens issued by a shared issuer, a single misplaced header is enough to move laterally.
The practical lesson is about the object model, not about HTTP. Replay is inherently a copy operation, and every field of the copy has to be re-derived for the new destination. When one field is treated as immutable context, the copy is incomplete, and the incompleteness is invisible to any test that only checks whether the retry succeeded.

The rest of the batch

CVE-2026-107281 is arguably the more interesting sibling. The HTTP/1.1 connection pool key excludes the authenticated principal when connection-oriented NTLM or Negotiate authentication is in use, in versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1. A pooled connection that was established under one identity can therefore be handed to a different identity. Connection reuse is the entire point of a pool, and NTLM authenticates the connection rather than each request, so the substitution is not visible at the request layer. Any multi-tenant service that authenticates to a downstream system with NTLM through a shared client instance is exposed, and the failure is silent on both ends.
CVE-2026-107283, rated Low, is a cryptographic hygiene defect: Realm.Builder generates the HTTP Digest client nonce with ThreadLocalRandom rather than a cryptographically secure source, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. A predictable nonce weakens the replay protection that Digest was designed to provide, which makes an unrelated credential-exposure bug worse rather than better.
CVE-2026-107284, also Low, concerns WebSocketHandler.upgrade: a handshake whose Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or invalid is aborted, but the handler continues into pipeline installation. Failing to stop on a failed validation is exactly the pattern that turns a validation routine into a formality.
CVE-2026-107285, Medium at 5.9, involves proxy authentication on WebSocket requests tunnelled through CONNECT, where NettyRequestFactory.newNettyRequest and requestUri decide whether to attach proxy credentials, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. The details differ from the cross-host replay case, the reasoning does not: a decision about credentials is made from context that does not describe the request actually being sent.
A related defect in a different Java client shows how common the shape is. CVE-2026-107314 describes pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC driver, in versions 42.7.11 through 42.7.13: when the requireAuth connection property excludes every authentication method the driver knows, for example by listing them all with negation, the driver enforces nothing and accepts any method the server offers. A configuration intended to restrict authentication produces no restriction at all. The score is 5.9 and the consequence is a downgrade to whatever the server proposes.

What to do

Upgrade. The AHC fixes are in 3.0.13 and 2.16.1 for the replay and pool-key issues, and in 3.0.12 and 2.16.1 for the proxy and WebSocket items, so the practical target is the newest build in the line you maintain. Because the library is a transitive dependency in most projects, the version that matters is the one resolved into the final artifact, not the one you typed.
Inventories should be resolved dependency trees, not dependency files. Ask the build for the effective version of org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client in every deployable, and rerun the query after a framework upgrade, because spring and cloud libraries routinely pin the version for you.
If NTLM or Negotiate authentication to a downstream system is in play, treat CVE-2026-107281 as the priority. It is the item that can cross an identity boundary inside your own infrastructure without any external redirect, and it will not appear in a request log that only records that a 200 was returned.
Review your own use of copies. Where your code builds a request for one destination and then reuses it for another, verify that the URI, Host header, credentials and body are all recomputed. The library fix closes the library's path; application-level copies have the same failure mode.
Rotate where exposure was possible. Any deployment that ran an affected version between the release of the fix and the upgrade may have delivered a credential to a host that should never have received it, and rotating is cheaper than reasoning about whether it did.

title: Heuristic Evaluation Playbook for Product Teams
description:
• How heuristic evaluation protects your release schedule
  • Preparing the team and scope: pick heuristics and tasks
  • A rigorous, step‑by‑step usability checklist for reviewers
  • Synthesis and prioritization: severity, reporting, and alignment
  • Actionable templates and a ready-to-run heuristic audit protocol

Heuristic evaluation is the fastest, highest-leverage way to surface UX debt before it becomes customer-facing. When you structure that inspection around Nielsen’s 10 heuristics and a disciplined, timeboxed process, the exercise turns guesswork into concrete, fixable usability issues.

The symptoms are familiar: teams patch UI problems reactively, support tickets spike for the same flows, analytics show drop-offs but not the “why,” and designers iterate blind because there’s no common method to classify severity. That pattern wastes engineering cycles and creates recurring regressions that manual QA keeps catching — but never fully eliminating.

How heuristic evaluation protects your release schedule

Heuristic evaluation buys you early detection at low cost. Expert reviewers inspect flows against a compact set of principles, so you catch both obvious breakages (missing confirmation, broken links) and subtle design failures (poor error messaging, inconsistent affordances) before you reach user testing or a production rollout. The method is fast, repeatable, and scales with scope: run a focused sweep on a single task or a broader UX audit across a product surface.

Why QA and product teams should treat it like a gate:

  • It reduces late discovery of UX regressions that become expensive to rework during a release freeze.
  • It complements exploratory testing: findings feed reproducible test cases for manual and regression suites.
  • It clarifies what to fix first by mapping issues to business-impacting flows (checkout, onboarding, admin tasks).

Important: Always pair a heuristic evaluation with a defined task (e.g., “complete checkout with a promo code”) and the relevant user profile. Heuristics are context-dependent; scope keeps them actionable.

Sources for the practice and rationale appear in the Nielsen guidance and government UX playbooks.

Preparing the team and scope: pick heuristics and tasks

Preparation makes or breaks the outcome. Use this short checklist before any evaluation.

Who to involve

  • 3–5 experienced evaluators is the classic recommendation for heuristic evaluations. This gives a high finding yield while keeping cost low.
  • When the domain or user base is diverse or the site is complex, be prepared to increase evaluators or run multiple segmented sweeps; research shows larger samples can be necessary for complex web tasks.
  • Mix roles when possible: one UX researcher/designer, one QA/exploratory tester, and one product engineer give complementary perspectives.

Which heuristics to use

  • Start with Jakob Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics as your canonical set. Use domain-specific addenda for accessibility, safety-critical flows, or localized interfaces.
  • For regulated or safety-critical products, introduce domain heuristics (e.g., safety checks, clear escalation paths) alongside Nielsen’s list.

Scope and artifacts to prepare

  • Define: user persona, device type, task scenario, environment (logged-in state, test data).
  • Provide: test accounts, credentials, variations (guest vs. signed-in), relevant analytics slices or crash reports.
  • Provide a standard evaluation sheet (spreadsheet, workbook, or Miro board) so findings are recorded uniformly.

Training and timeboxing

  • Run a 20–30 minute calibration/practice round with a simple app to align reviewers on what constitutes a heuristic violation.
  • Timebox independent evaluations to ~1–2 hours per evaluator for a single task or a focused section; longer sessions drop signal-to-noise.

A rigorous, step‑by‑step usability checklist for reviewers

This is the operational usability checklist you can hand an evaluator. Use numbered steps and concrete acceptance criteria.

  1. Context setup (10–15 min)

    • Confirm persona, device, network speed, and the task expected. Record analytics slices if available.
    • Open the evaluation sheet and note the scope and the heuristic set (Nielsen heuristics).

  2. Walkthrough #1 — familiarization (10–15 min)

    • Perform the task once to learn the flow. Don’t annotate yet; learn the edge cases and expected system responses.

  3. Walkthrough #2 — heuristic pass (45–90 min)

    • For each screen/interaction, ask: which heuristic does this element relate to? Log one problem per row with a screenshot. Use this per-heuristic checklist:
      • Visibility of system status — Are loading states visible? Do actions provide immediate feedback?
      • Match to the real world — Does language match user mental models? Any jargon?
      • User control and freedom — Can users undo or exit quickly? Are confirmations clear?
      • Consistency & standards — Are similar actions labelled or styled consistently across pages?
      • Error prevention — Are forms validated proactively? Do confirmations prevent destructive actions?
      • Recognition vs recall — Are key items visible or hidden behind multiple layers?
      • Flexibility & efficiency — Are accelerators available for power users (shortcuts, saved defaults)?
      • Aesthetic & minimalist design — Is content noisy? Does the layout obscure primary actions?
      • Help diagnose & recover from errors — Are error messages actionable and specific?
      • Help & documentation — Is help discoverable when needed? Is it task-focused?

  4. Problem capture (for each issue)

    • Required fields: ID, Title, Flow, Page/Screen, Heuristic, Description, Repro steps, Screenshot, Estimated frequency (1–5), Severity (0–4), Suggested fix (brief), Owner, Estimated effort (T-shirt or days). Use the CSV/JSON templates below.

  5. Severity and evidence

    • Rate problems on frequency, impact on task performance, and persistence (recurring vs one-off). Record these factors separately when possible to justify prioritization.

  6. Repeat for each task segment

    • When scope includes multiple user journeys, repeat steps 1–5 for each flow.

  7. Independent finish then consolidation

    • Submit files but don’t share evaluations with other reviewers until all are done. This avoids groupthink.

Quick red‑flags to watch for (examples you can scan in 5 minutes)

  • Missing confirmation after destructive actions.
  • Form fields that fail silently.
  • Hidden primary navigation behind a hamburger icon with no indication.
  • Multiple CTA styles on the same page.
  • Error messages that show raw codes (e.g., "ERR_502").

Table: Selected heuristics → quick checks

Heuristic Quick checks Red flag
Visibility of system status spinner/progress, success messages No feedback after submit
Consistency & standards consistent labels/styles Same action uses different verbs
Recognition vs recall visible options, clear defaults Important menu items hidden
Error recovery inline errors, suggested fixes Generic "something went wrong"

[Caveat: this mapping is derived from Nielsen’s heuristics and practical QA patterns.]

id,title,flow,page_or_screen,heuristic,severity(0-4),frequency(1-5),repro_steps,screenshot,suggested_fix,owner,effort_days
HE-001,No save confirmation,Profile>Edit,Profile>Save,Visibility of system status,3,4,"Edit name -> Save -> no confirmation","/screenshots/HE-001.png","Add toast confirmation & spinner",product,0.5

{
  "id": "HE-001",
  "title": "No save confirmation",
  "flow": "Profile > Edit",
  "heuristic": "Visibility of system status",
  "severity": 3,
  "frequency": 4,
  "repro_steps": ["Edit profile", "Change name", "Click Save"],
  "screenshot": "/screenshots/HE-001.png",
  "suggested_fix": "Add toast confirmation and spinner",
  "owner": "product",
  "effort_est_days": 0.5
}

Synthesis and prioritization: severity, reporting, and alignment

A disciplined synthesis converts a long list of findings into a prioritized to-do list that engineering will act on.

Severity scale (common, 0–4)
| Score | Label | What it means | Action |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 0 | Not a problem | No usability issue identified | No action |
| 1 | Cosmetic | Little/no effect on task performance | Fix if time allows |
| 2 | Minor | Causes occasional confusion/delay | Schedule in backlog |
| 3 | Major | Frequently blocks or frustrates users | High priority fix |
| 4 | Catastrophic | Prevents completion of critical tasks | Fix before release |

This 0–4 scale and the contributing factors (frequency, impact, persistence) are standard in heuristic workflows.

Aggregation and prioritization protocol

  1. Consolidate issues (affinity cluster) and remove duplicates. Note how many evaluators found each problem.
  2. Compute a mean severity across evaluators and list reproducibility (always/sometimes/rare). Use the reproducibility and frequency estimate to re-weight severity for prioritization.
  3. Add an effort estimate and compute a simple priority score, for example: PriorityScore = MeanSeverity * (Frequency / 5) / EffortDays. Use this as a sorting heuristic, not as an absolute decision.
  4. Present a triage board with three buckets: Critical (fix before release), High (next sprint), Backlog (research / low ROI).

Reporting deliverables (minimum)

  • Consolidated issue tracker (CSV/JSON) with screenshots and repro steps.
  • Priority matrix (severity × effort).
  • UX map showing problem clusters by flow (visual).
  • A 1–2 page executive summary linking top issues to metrics (drop-off, support volume, conversions).

Meeting choreography for alignment (30–60 minutes)

  • Quick readout of top 5 issues (1 minute each).
  • Assign owners and effort bands.
  • Lock in which issues must be triaged into the next sprint and which require user research before changing.

Important: Don’t treat heuristic evaluation as the only signal. Use it to triage design debt; validate contentious fixes with targeted user testing or telemetry after remediation.

Actionable templates and a ready-to-run heuristic audit protocol

Use this deployable protocol for a focused 2‑day sweep on a single user journey.

Example schedule (compressed)

  • Day 0 — Kickoff (30–45 min): scope, heuristics, roles, practice round.
  • Day 1 — Independent evaluations (1–2 hours each per evaluator): each evaluator completes the workbook and logs issues.
  • Day 2 AM — Consolidation and affinity mapping (60–90 min): cluster duplicates and compute mean severities.
  • Day 2 PM — Prioritization and handoff (60–90 min): create tickets, assign owners, decide critical fixes.

Minimum artifacts to deliver at close

  • heuristic-findings.csv (template above)
  • priority-matrix.xlsx (severity × effort, ranked)
  • A one-page readout mapping top 3 issues to business impact (e.g., funnel step, estimated lost conversions, or support cost).

A short, practical triage template (use in your sprint planning)

  • Tag each issue with: fix-by (release), sprint (number), owner (team), risk (high/med/low), notes (research needed: yes/no).

When documenting, use clear language in tickets: state the offending element, the heuristic violated, steps to reproduce, and an example of a desirable outcome (a one-liner recommendation). That makes it easier for engineers to scope work and for product to prioritize.

Table: Sample trade-off guidance for triage
| Category | Action |
|---|---|
| Severity 4 + Low Effort | Stop release; fix immediately |
| Severity 3 + Low Effort | Prioritize in next sprint |
| Severity 3 + High Effort | Split into research + incremental fixes |
| Severity 1–2 | Document and batch as design debt |

Practical QA integration points

  • Turn reproducible heuristic findings into manual test cases for regression suites.
  • Use exploratory test sessions to validate severity and repro rate across real user data.
  • Track UX debt in JIRA or your backlog with a ux:heuristic label and link to the consolidated evidence artifact.

Closing thought
Treat heuristic evaluation as a repeatable quality gate: run small, frequent sweeps aligned to your most important journeys, translate findings into prioritized work, and measure whether the number of critical heuristic violations drops release-to-release. The discipline converts subjective impressions into objective, actionable UX fixes that save engineering time and protect your metrics.

Sources:
How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation — Nielsen Norman Group - Step-by-step process, recommended team size (3–5 evaluators), timeboxing guidance, and the NN/g workbook used for documentation and consolidation.

10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design — Nielsen Norman Group - Canonical list of the 10 heuristics with examples and tips used throughout the checklist.

ISO 9241-11:2018 — Usability: Definitions and concepts - Usability definition (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction) and the emphasis on context of use.

Reading 20: Heuristic Evaluation — MIT course material - Severity rating guidance and contributing factors (frequency, impact, persistence) used to justify the 0–4 scale and aggregation approach.

Refining the Test Phase of Usability Evaluation: How Many Subjects Is Enough? — Robert A. Virzi (1992) - Empirical study that supports small-sample discovery rates (4–5 subjects) in specific contexts.

Testing web sites: Five Users Is Nowhere Near Enough — Jared Spool & Will Schroeder (CHI 2001) - Evidence that complex web tasks may require larger samples or segmented testing; useful as a counterpoint on sample-size assumptions.

Heuristic evaluation — 18F Guides - Government guidance on running heuristics, including a recommended 3–5 person team and practical documentation notes.

How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation — Maze guide - Practical checklist and template suggestions for capturing issues and linking them to tasks.

title: Flutter vs. React + Capacitor in 2026: Which Stack Saves More Time & Budget for Your Business App?
description:
If you are a founder or business owner planning to build a cross-platform mobile app for iOS and Android in 2026, you will immediately face a critical technical decision: Should we build it in Flutter, or use a Web-to-Mobile stack like React + Capacitor?

Pick the wrong stack for your specific use case, and you can easily add 4 to 6 extra weeks to your development timeline.

At VanzaLabs, we don't treat technology choices like a religion. In fact, we recently built and shipped two production B2B mobile apps to Google Play—one written in Flutter (FormGrid: Forms & Sheets) and the other in React 19 + Tailwind CSS 4 + Capacitor 8 (Vanza: Invoices & Contracts).

Here is a practical, business-focused guide on when to use each stack—based on real production trade-offs.

When Flutter Is the Unbeatable Choice
We chose Flutter for FormGrid, our mobile workspace for creating and managing Google Forms™ and Google Sheets™ in the field.

Choose Flutter for your business app if:

You need 60/120fps native scrolling and gesture fluidity: Flutter renders its own UI via Impeller/Skia rather than relying on a browser WebView. When users scroll through hundreds of spreadsheet rows or switch between tabs rapidly, it feels indistinguishable from a native iOS/Android app.
Deep OS & Hardware Integration: Receiving shared files directly from other mobile apps (Share Intents), background isolates, and native OAuth flows are rock-solid in Flutter's ecosystem.
Mobile-First Product: If 90% of your users will interact with your product strictly on smartphones and tablets rather than a desktop web dashboard, Flutter delivers a superior mobile UX.
When React 19 + Capacitor 8 Cuts Development Time in Half
For our second product, Vanza: Invoices & Contracts (an offline PDF generator for contractors, freelancers, and SMBs), we intentionally chose React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and Capacitor 8.

Why didn't we use Flutter here? Because the core of an invoicing and contract app is document layout, dynamic multi-step forms, and complex print formatting.

Choose React + Capacitor for your business app if:

You need both a Web App AND a Mobile App from a single codebase: With React + Capacitor, 95% of your web application code runs natively inside an iOS/Android shell with full access to native APIs (filesystem, camera, share sheet, in-app purchases via RevenueCat). For a startup on a tight budget, this saves 35–45% compared to building a web app and mobile app separately.
Heavy Document, Table, or PDF Rendering: Designing 12 customizable invoice/contract themes with dynamic line-item tables, automatic tax/discount math, and canvas finger signatures was dramatically faster using HTML/CSS Flexbox & Grid + jsPDF than writing low-level PDF layout code in Dart.
Rich Offline Local Storage with IndexedDB: Using Dexie.js over IndexedDB allowed us to build a 100% offline client and service catalog database that works seamlessly in basements and construction sites without internet.
Side-by-Side Decision Matrix for Founders
Time to Market (Web + Mobile combined): React + Capacitor wins (1 shared codebase).
UI/Animation Smoothness on Budget Phones: Flutter wins.
Complex Forms, Dashboards & PDF Generation: React + Capacitor wins.
In-App Subscriptions (RevenueCat) & Offline Support: Tie — both work great in production.
Need Help Choosing the Right Architecture for Your MVP?
At VanzaLabs, our senior engineering team builds production-ready Web and Mobile MVPs in 3 to 8 weeks using both Flutter and React / Next.js / Capacitor—depending on what gives your business the fastest path to revenue and the lowest maintenance cost.

We also help growing companies automate manual workflows by integrating CRMs, ERPs, payment gateways, and custom AI agents.

title: Solid Glass Adds an AI UI Theme to shadcn/ui Projects
description:
Solid Glass is a public GitHub project that packages a glass-inspired design system for AI applications as a stylesheet intended to work with shadcn/ui. For developers building chat and agent interfaces, its practical proposition is narrow but useful: the stylesheet targets the data-slot attributes and classes that existing shadcn/ui components already carry, so adoption is presented as a theme integration rather than a component rewrite. Source: Solid Glass repository

A theme layer, not an AI framework

The project describes its visual treatment as sitting between flat design and “liquid glass”: surfaces retain outlines, borders, highlights and shadows, while avoiding the highly transparent treatment that can interfere with text legibility. Its stated design goals are tactility, precision, physicality and materiality; for interfaces with streaming responses, agent tasks and pending human decisions, it argues that neutral surfaces and reserved use of colour and motion help keep the UI calm and readable. Source: Solid Glass repository

The core distribution is one CSS file. The repository says it defines colours, three glass thicknesses, a state and motion, while also defining shadcn/ui’s variable names. It supports light and dark modes, although the project describes dark mode as the intended material treatment. Source: Solid Glass repository

Installation begins from a shadcn/ui project using React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 and Base UI components. Developers add the deeplethe/solid-glass/solid-glass stylesheet through the shadcn CLI, import it after Tailwind and shadcn styles, and remove the :root and .dark colour variables created by shadcn initialization because Solid Glass defines variables with the same names. Source: Solid Glass repository

Components for agent-facing screens

Beyond the theme, the project supplies installable components including status-glyph, panel, tag, dot-loader, turn-status, composer, tool-steps, diff-view, ask-card, context-ring, task-notice and reasoning. The README positions these around an agent workflow: showing activity, accepting a prompt, rendering tool steps and diffs, asking for user input, and displaying context usage. Source: Solid Glass repository

The repository also includes complete screen-level “Blocks,” including an agent-workspace, plus a Create page that exposes controls for thickness, tint, chart colour, type, radius, rim and blur and produces corresponding CSS variable changes. Source: Solid Glass repository

The compatibility trade-off

Analysis: Solid Glass’s most consequential choice is to treat shadcn/ui as the compatibility surface rather than create another self-contained component ecosystem. That should reduce initial adoption cost for teams already on the shadcn stack, because the theme is designed around existing slots and classes. It also leaves an unresolved maintenance question: the approach depends on those structural conventions remaining stable enough for a stylesheet to keep selecting the intended parts. The repository notes that some displayed shadcn/ui components differ slightly from stock versions, while saying the stylesheet does not depend on those differences. Source: Solid Glass repository

This is therefore best read as a focused UI layer, not evidence of a broader agent runtime or application framework. Its value will depend less on the glass treatment itself than on whether its component conventions fit a team’s existing shadcn/ui codebase and the information density of its AI workflows. The repository is licensed under MIT and includes contribution, code-of-conduct and security-policy materials. Source: Solid Glass repository

title: I ran 50 orders at 1 unit of stock. Here’s what stopped the oversell.
description:
Last week I built a small grocery-style order system to learn how event-driven services handle the classic problem: two customers click “buy” on the last item at the same time.

A caveat first. I built this in about 24 hours using AI coding agents (Cursor), and I directed the design. I’m writing this after going back through the code to understand why it works, which is a different thing from writing every line myself. If you’re after a hand-coded reference, this isn’t one. If you want to see how these patterns fit together and how I tested them, read on.

What it is

Three Spring Boot services (order, inventory, payment), each with its own PostgreSQL database, talking only through Kafka. There’s no central coordinator. Each service reacts to events and publishes its own, which is called a choreographed saga. A Next.js storefront sits on top, and an optional ELK stack lets me trace any order by its ID.

Happy path: an order goes PENDING, then RESERVED, then CONFIRMED. If stock runs out or the payment is declined, the order goes to CANCELLED and any reserved stock is released through a compensation event.

The problem

Writing to your database and publishing to Kafka are two separate operations. If the service crashes between them, you either have an order nobody hears about or an event for an order that doesn’t exist.

The three things that handle it

Transactional outbox. The order service writes the order and the event into the same database transaction. A separate step then publishes the event to Kafka. Either both are saved or neither is.
Idempotent consumers. Kafka can deliver a message more than once. Each consumer records the events it has processed (a processed_events table), so a duplicate does nothing the second time.
Atomic stock updates plus per-order keys. Stock is decremented in a single atomic update, so two orders can’t both read “1 left.” Events for one order use that order’s ID as the Kafka key, which keeps them in order.

The test

I wrote a k6 script that resets one item to a stock of 1, then fires 50 concurrent orders at it, one per virtual user. Afterward it checks that available stock never went below zero and that confirmed orders didn’t exceed the starting stock.

On my MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 16 GB), all 50 requests were accepted. After the saga settled, exactly one order was confirmed and stock sat at 0. The whole run, including setup and waiting for outcomes, took about 6.8 seconds. The other orders are designed to end up CANCELLED. [check your database and put the real count here]

What this does and doesn’t prove

It’s a correctness test, not a performance benchmark. It shows the system doesn’t oversell under a burst of 50 on a laptop. It says nothing about throughput at scale, and I haven’t run a long soak test. Payments are simulated too: a token of ok succeeds and fail declines.

What surprised me

[one or two honest sentences: something you learned or got wrong when you traced the code, e.g. what you expected the outbox to do versus what it actually does]

Try it

Everything runs with docker compose up --build. The repo has the architecture notes, the acceptance scenarios, and the benchmark results:

ArnavPoswal15 / orderflow-platform

Event-driven order platform: Spring Boot microservices + Kafka choreographed saga, transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, Redis, PostgreSQL, Next.js storefront, ELK, k6 load test

Orderflow Platform

Event-driven order platform for grocery-style orders: order, inventory, and payment services each own a database and coordinate through Kafka using a choreographed saga (no central orchestrator).

Status: Phases 1–7 complete (saga, storefront, ops, ELK observability, k6 proof load test, GitHub Actions CI, demo docs).
