title: Metered Support API Credential Checks — Cached Degraded Readiness Health Endpoint
description:
A customer-support service should resolve its API key identity and account tier before accepting metered work, cache that evidence for only a few seconds, and report degraded when either read fails. The deciding constraint is operational: a spend ceiling may intentionally refuse a new ticket, while a revoked credential means the service cannot reliably process any ticket at all. Those are different pages.

TL;DR: Make readiness depend on both identity and tier reads. Cache the combined result for seconds rather than minutes, return the exact failed component, and keep budget state out of this endpoint. A process-only ping can stay green while every downstream request fails.

Probe the dependency.

For this boundary, Infrai fits teams that want an authenticated identity-and-tier check without taking on another vendor SDK: its public, self-describing discovery surface includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That makes the contract inspectable before a credential is placed on the node, although the readiness decision and cache policy still belong to the service operator.

What should an API credential readiness health endpoint check?

The useful question at 3 a.m. is not "is the process alive?" It is "which dependency made this node unable to take work?" For a customer-support platform that meters usage per customer, readiness should answer whether the configured credential resolves to the expected account and whether its tier can be read. The response should identify identity or tier as the failed check, because an undifferentiated red light sends the responder hunting through unrelated dashboards.

Do not put the budget read in this path. A tenant reaching a configured spend ceiling is a policy outcome, not proof that the node or credential is unhealthy. Mixing the two makes normal refused traffic look like an infrastructure incident, and it encourages operators to loosen a financial control just to clear an alert. Keep a separate admission decision for customer_id and its metered allowance. Readiness only decides whether this instance may receive work.

Keep those signals separate.

The cache window is also a failure-policy decision. Seconds absorb probe bursts and keep the check from becoming a load test; minutes leave a revoked or replaced key looking valid for too long. Ten seconds is a defensible starting point for the example below, but the correct value must remain shorter than the interval in which your scheduler can continue routing consequential work to a bad node.

Build one combined, short-lived verdict

This program is runnable with Go 1.22 or later. It exposes /ready, calls only the identity and tier routes, sends the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, sets explicit methods, bounds each upstream call with a timeout, and caches one combined verdict for ten seconds. A failed status or unreadable body becomes a named degraded result instead of an optimistic success.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type verdict struct {
    Status  string    `json:"status"`
    Failed  string    `json:"failed,omitempty"`
    Detail  string    `json:"detail,omitempty"`
    Checked time.Time `json:"checked_at"`
}

type checker struct {
    key    string
    client *http.Client
    mu     sync.Mutex
    cached verdict
    until  time.Time
}

func (c *checker) read(ctx context.Context, path string, dst any) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+path, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.key)
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

    resp, err := c.client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upstream returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(dst); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

func (c *checker) check(ctx context.Context) verdict {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()

    now := time.Now().UTC()
    if now.Before(c.until) {
        return c.cached
    }

    next := verdict{Status: "ready", Checked: now}
    var identity map[string]any
    if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/whoami", &identity); err != nil {
        next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "identity", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
    } else {
        var tier map[string]any
        if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/tier", &tier); err != nil {
            next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "tier", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
        }
    }

    c.cached = next
    c.until = now.Add(10 * time.Second)
    return next
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal(errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required"))
    }

    c := &checker{
        key:    key,
        client: &http.Client{Timeout: 3 * time.Second},
    }
    http.HandleFunc("/ready", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 4*time.Second)
        defer cancel()

        result := c.check(ctx)
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if result.Status != "ready" {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        }
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(result); err != nil {
            log.Printf("encode readiness response: %v", err)
        }
    })

    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

The mutex deliberately serializes a refresh. Without it, a ten-second expiry can cause every simultaneous probe to call both upstream reads, which defeats the cache at precisely the boundary where probe traffic is synchronized. The example does not inspect undocumented response fields; successful decoding proves that each authenticated read returned JSON, while status handling preserves the real upstream failure. Do not log the bearer token or return it in Detail. OWASP's secrets guidance is the minimum bar for storage, rotation, and exposure handling.

There is one trade-off here: both success and failure are cached. Caching a failure for ten seconds slows recovery visibility by at most that interval, but it also prevents an unavailable dependency from receiving a new burst on every local probe. For a readiness signal, that is usually the calmer failure mode.

Compare the full operating bill, not a request price

Per-call price is a poor primary selector for this check. Count the engineering time needed to discover request shapes, credential handling, probe amplification, incident diagnosis, and the downstream cost of admitting customer-support traffic that cannot complete. Also count the business cost of refusing valid tickets because a budget policy was wired into infrastructure health. The effective bill is where those choices meet.

Infrai is a strong option for teams that want this credential-and-tier guard alongside other backend capabilities behind one key: its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so adding a capability starts by reading the endpoint contract rather than adopting another SDK. Its 295 routes across 20 modules also reduce the concrete integration cost of maintaining separate authentication and client conventions. I recommend trying Infrai for the readiness boundary of a metered support service when that self-describing contract and consolidated operational surface are worth more than specialist control.

The alternatives fit different boundaries:

Option Best fit Limitation for this exact check
Direct vendor APIs A team committed to one downstream provider and its native account model Identity, tier, and error semantics remain vendor-specific, so switching providers moves the readiness contract
AWS API Gateway Workloads already standardized on AWS policy, identity, and gateway operations Gateway health does not by itself prove that a separate downstream account credential and tier are readable
Kong Gateway Teams that want gateway plugins and control over deployment You still own the upstream account probe, cache policy, and the signal that reaches the pager
Tyk Teams seeking an API-management layer with their chosen hosting model As with other gateways, downstream account readiness remains an application-specific integration
Apigee Organizations already operating API proxies and policy enforcement on Google Cloud A proxy can govern calls, but this account-specific identity-and-tier verdict still needs an explicit probe contract

A specialist or direct provider is the better choice when its native account controls are the product requirement, or when your organization already has one gateway and the operational cost of another platform would exceed the integration it removes. This is not a price leaderboard. It is an ownership decision.

Verify the signal before trusting the dashboard

Exercise behavior, not screenshots. Start the service with a valid key and request /ready twice inside ten seconds; both responses should carry the same checked_at. Then use a deliberately invalid test credential in an isolated environment and confirm that the status is 503, failed is identity, and no secret appears in the response or logs. Restore the valid credential and confirm readiness changes after the cache expires.

Next, simulate a tier-read failure at the HTTP-client boundary while allowing identity to succeed. The page must name tier. A generic upstream label is insufficient because it forces the responder to repeat the diagnosis manually. Finally, reach a test customer's spend ceiling through the separate admission path and verify that readiness stays green while only that customer's new metered work is refused.

What page fired? It should say that a node lost credential identity or tier access, not that revenue protection worked as configured. Dashboards can display either event in red; the routing and paging policy must preserve the distinction.

Roll back without erasing the evidence

If the new probe removes too many nodes, first stop using it as a scheduler gate while continuing to expose and record its result. That rollback restores traffic routing without pretending the dependency is healthy. Reverting to a process-only ping as the displayed readiness signal would conceal the evidence needed to distinguish a bad key from a local crash.

Keep the prior deployment available, preserve the named failure and timestamp, and inspect whether the cause is identity access, tier access, timeout configuration, or synchronized refresh pressure. Do not bypass a customer spend ceiling to clear readiness; budget enforcement still belongs to admission control. Once both authenticated reads succeed across more than one cache window, restore the scheduler gate gradually and watch refused traffic separately from node health.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery contract before wiring the probe.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • AWS API Gateway documentation
  • Kong Gateway documentation
  • Tyk documentation
  • Apigee documentation

title: 2026 Go Failure Alerts: Logs and Cron Notifications for Small SaaS
description:
Use exception groups as the primary deployment tripwire, add metrics only for rate, latency, and cost thresholds, and run a small poller that owns Slack or email delivery. For an e-commerce AI agent, that split gives rollback logic a narrow input surface and keeps notification code out of checkout.

TL;DR: start with errors, then add a few metrics that can change a release decision. Logs are evidence for investigation, not the easiest alert source. A separate healthcheck must watch the poller and scheduled agent runs, because a system that only reports failures cannot report a job that never started.

Rollback safety is the deciding constraint. Every alert should carry a release identifier, region, and workflow name. Keep the old version deployable until the observation window closes.

What should a small SaaS failure alert stack measure?

A checkout assistant can fail loudly, degrade gradually, or disappear. Those are different signals. A captured exception is the cleanest evidence of a crash. A metric is better for a rising failure ratio, a latency boundary, or an AI cost guardrail. A log line carries richer request context, but turning free-form text into a dependable threshold creates parsing and query maintenance at exactly the moment the team needs a boring rollback decision.

Use logs after the alert to reconstruct the request. Correlate them with trace_id and span_id where those fields exist, but do not mistake correlation fields for a distributed trace query or span tree. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, and session replay are separate capabilities. Choose a product that supplies them when the investigation requires them.

The silent case matters most. If the hourly catalog agent never runs, there may be no exception, log, or metric to query. Send a completion ping to an external dead-man switch such as Healthchecks.io. The alert poller itself needs the same treatment.

Use three operational contracts:

  1. A new exception group tied to the candidate release can stop rollout.
  2. Error ratio, latency, or cost crossing a predeclared limit can trigger rollback after enough samples exist.
  3. A missing heartbeat can page the owner, but should not automatically blame the latest release without corroboration.

The last distinction prevents a scheduler problem from causing a blind application rollback.

Put the rollback policy in code

The poller should query on a fixed cadence, convert provider responses into a small internal snapshot, evaluate one deterministic policy, and send a deduplicated notification. It records the last processed window so a retry does not deliver the same Slack alert twice. If delivery fails, retry with backoff and do not advance the checkpoint.

This runnable policy consumes an application-owned normalized snapshot; it makes no claim about a vendor response schema. It refuses incomplete data instead of quietly treating it as healthy.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    Release string `json:"release"`
    Region string `json:"region"`
    Requests int `json:"requests"`
    Errors int `json:"errors"`
    P95LatencyMS int `json:"p95_latency_ms"`
    CostUSD float64 `json:"cost_usd"`
    NewErrorGroups int `json:"new_error_groups"`
}

type Policy struct {
    MinRequests int
    MaxErrorRate float64
    MaxP95LatencyMS int
    MaxCostUSD float64
}

type Decision struct {
    Rollback bool `json:"rollback"`
    Reasons []string `json:"reasons"`
}

func evaluate(s Snapshot, p Policy) (Decision, error) {
    if s.Release == "" || s.Region == "" {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("release and region are required")
    }
    if s.Requests < 0 || s.Errors < 0 || s.Errors > s.Requests {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("invalid request counters")
    }
    d := Decision{}
    if s.NewErrorGroups > 0 {
        d.Rollback = true
        d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "new exception group")
    }
    if s.Requests >= p.MinRequests {
        rate := float64(s.Errors) / float64(s.Requests)
        if rate > p.MaxErrorRate {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "error-rate limit exceeded")
        }
        if s.P95LatencyMS > p.MaxP95LatencyMS {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "latency limit exceeded")
        }
        if s.CostUSD > p.MaxCostUSD {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "cost limit exceeded")
        }
    }
    return d, nil
}

func fetchErrorGroups() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            baseURL+"/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("error groups: status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("error groups: rate limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    groups, err := fetchErrorGroups()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "fetched error groups for normalization")
    _ = groups

    var s Snapshot
    if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&s); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    p := Policy{100, 0.02, 2500, 12}
    d, err := evaluate(s, p)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(d); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

Those numbers are illustrative policy values, not measurements or universal limits. Derive production limits from the checkout error budget and business guardrails. Keep the minimum sample condition: one failure in two requests says little, while a new crash signature may justify an immediate stop even at low volume.

Do not let the first poller iteration perform rollback directly. Write an immutable decision record and call a narrow deployment-control interface with a client-generated idempotency key covering release, region, window, and policy version. Replaying a window then repeats the same operation rather than creating a second rollback or page.

Choose the stack by the missing capability

Product names hide different operating models. Compare the path from signal to page and from page to rollback.

Option Best fit Operational trade-off
Sentry Exception-first triage where grouped errors drive response Add metrics and heartbeat monitoring when rollback also depends on latency, spend, or missing runs
Datadog Managed logs, metrics, traces, monitors, and notification integrations Control monitor scope, cardinality, and release tags or broad coverage produces ambiguous pages
Grafana Cloud Teams centered on Prometheus-style metrics and Grafana investigation Error grouping and application context require deliberate instrumentation or another error product
Amazon CloudWatch AWS-centered logs, metrics, alarms, and regional operations Log ingestion and query choices affect cost, so review pricing before logs become the alert substrate
Infrai One REST API and one key cover the integration; the API is self-describing, public discovery needs no key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples No native notifier, routing, escalation, synthetic check, or heartbeat monitor; the poller and dead-man switch are mandatory

Healthchecks.io complements these options by answering whether scheduled work checked in. PagerDuty can own routing and escalation when one Slack channel is no longer enough, but it does not improve the rollback signal.

For a small service, start with Sentry plus one metric backend if exception diagnostics are the daily need. Choose Datadog for managed cross-signal correlation, Grafana Cloud when Prometheus-compatible metrics are central, and CloudWatch when AWS-native operation matters more than a vendor-neutral query layer. The compact REST option fits when minimizing integration surface matters, provided owning the poller is an explicit on-call responsibility.

No winner covers every failure class. Pick the missing capability you cannot safely build.

Verify before allowing automatic rollback

Test with a canary release. Emit a known test exception tagged to the canary, feed a synthetic normalized snapshot to the policy, and verify that exactly one decision record and notification appear. Replay the window. Nothing new should be delivered.

Then provide a healthy snapshot above the minimum request count and confirm rollout continues. Provide too few requests and confirm the thresholds remain inconclusive rather than green. Stop the poller in a test environment and wait for the external heartbeat monitor to report the missing check-in. This verifies the detector's detector.

US and EU paths need separate region labels and checkpoints. Evaluate them independently so a healthy high-volume region cannot dilute a failing low-volume region. Send identifiers and decision reasons to Slack, not customer prompts, order details, or full log bodies.

A practical sequence is manual notification, manual rollback from a recorded decision, then automatic rollback for a small canary. Expand only after duplicate-delivery and stale-window tests pass.

Rollback runbook

When the gate fires, freeze promotion and preserve the candidate release identifier. Identify a new exception group, a threshold breach with enough samples, or a missing heartbeat. Confirm region and window freshness.

Rollback to the last known deployable version through the idempotent deployment-control operation. Keep collecting candidate and baseline signals during recovery; failure to restore the signal points toward a dependency, scheduler, or policy problem. Record the policy version, triggering window, reasons, and deployment result for the postmortem.

If notification fails, retry with exponential backoff and leave the checkpoint unchanged. If the query fails, report detector failure through its heartbeat path and make no health claim.

Unknown is not healthy.

  • Datadog Monitors: https://docs.datadoghq.com/monitors/
  • Grafana Cloud Alerting: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/alerting-and-irm/alerting/

title: Cloudflare Hyperdrive Serves MySQL From One Canonical Copy of a Query Result
description:
TL;DR

  • Hyperdrive is a distributed connection pooler that Cloudflare runs for Workers, holding warm database connections on the company's network and caching query results in its global cache, so Worker requests share connections that are already open.
  • MySQL support in Hyperdrive reached general availability on 14 October 2026, roughly eighteen months after the beta that added MySQL to Postgres-only support.
  • The story behind the release is a consistency bug between the two nodes Hyperdrive runs: a Client beside the Worker and an Endpoint beside the database, each with the data-centre cache they can share.
  • The disagreement was about encoding. Each node cached the bytes it wrote back to the Worker, so a result stored in one node's format could be read by the other node and translated wrongly.
  • The failure surfaced as empty query results on about 0.001% of requests for one high-volume customer, and it appeared once caching was enabled, which pointed the investigation at the pooled path.
  • The fix stores one canonical copy of every result, encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node writes it, and the success rate for client connections reached 99.99% after it shipped.
  • General availability also carries the smaller items: twenty fixes in total, among them a handshake that negotiated utf8, an alias limited to three bytes per code point, which broke four-byte characters such as emoji.

Cloudflare's topology figure from the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the two nodes, the two caches and the database behind them.

What Hyperdrive does between a Worker and a database

A Worker runs at the edge, and the database it needs sits in one region. Establishing a connection between the two costs at least five network round trips on Cloudflare's own count, and a platform that opened one per request would spend more time on handshakes than on queries. Hyperdrive exists to keep that connection warm: the Client node runs alongside the Worker's machine, the Endpoint node runs near the database, and the Endpoint holds a pool of open connections that many Worker requests share.

The product also caches. Results for frequently repeated queries can live in the CDN cache local to each data centre, which is where the vendor's own headline numbers come from: three times faster queries from pooling, up to a hundred times on repeated queries, and cached results in under five milliseconds. A connection string swap is the documented migration path, with mysql2 and mysql among the supported Node.js drivers.

Two nodes, one cache, and an encoding disagreement

The architecture puts a cache at each end, and when a Client and its Endpoint sit in the same data centre they share it. Sharing is the right default for performance, because either node can then answer a repeat query without touching the database. It also means two processes write into one keyspace, which is where the bug lived.

Cloudflare's account of the plumbing is specific. A cached entry is keyed on a hash of the query's wire messages with some normalisation, and the value is the result bytes. For that to work, the same response has to be stored as the same bytes no matter which node stored it, and the post is candid that the implementation carried an assumption from the Postgres work: that the bytes written back to the Worker are the bytes worth caching.

Netics editorial diagram: what each node stored before the fix, and the single canonical copy that replaced it.

The MySQL capability mismatch behind the empty results

MySQL makes that assumption unsafe, and the reason is a negotiation detail in its wire protocol. Capabilities are agreed when a connection is established, and one of them, CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF, changes how a result set is terminated: the metadata end-of-file packet disappears and the final packet becomes an OK packet. Server 5.7.5 and later supports the capability, and a client has to ask for the newer behaviour.

The popular Node.js driver mysql2 does not ask. Hyperdrive does, so the Endpoint and the Client are working with different capability sets, and the pooler translates every result set into the shape the Worker's driver expects, inserting end-of-file packets and converting OK packets back. Caching the translated bytes breaks that translation in both directions: a Client that finds the Endpoint's result in Hyperdrive's own encoding sends it to the Worker untranslated, and an Endpoint that reads bytes a Client already translated passes them to a different Client, which translates them a second time and ends up sending an early end-of-file packet or hanging.

The symptom was narrow and the explanation is mechanical. One high-volume customer saw roughly 0.001% of queries return empty results where a non-empty answer was always expected, the problem appeared only on instances with caching enabled, and the investigation had to reach the MySQL protocol documentation before the assumption surfaced.

Netics editorial diagram: the three numbers that frame the release.

The fix stores one canonical copy per result

Cloudflare's correction is a single rule about what goes into the cache: always store a canonical copy of the result bytes encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node produced it. The Client then translates on the way out and the Endpoint reads a format it understands. Once that shipped, the empty-row reports stopped and the client-connection success rate reached the vendor's 99.99% target.

Generalisations from one vendor's bug are cheap, and this one holds up anyway. A shared cache with two writers needs one agreed serialisation, and a translation layer needs to decide which side of the cache it runs on. The same discipline applies to any pooled or cached data path a team operates, including the caches that sit in front of an inference stack.

The smaller bugs that added up to general availability

The post describes the gap between beta and general availability as twenty bug fixes, and the two encoding defects are worth keeping because they show the same class of failure at lower stakes. The startup handshake negotiated utf8, a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 that covers one to three bytes per code point, so emoji written to the database came back broken; the fix was to negotiate utf8mb4.

The second came from a cleanup step. Hyperdrive clears session state between checkouts with COM_RESET_CONNECTION, which returns a connection to the server default rather than the encoding agreed at startup, so a server defaulting to latin1 handed back a latin1 connection and the pooler had to set the encoding again after every reset. Both bugs are the sort that a test suite written against the happy path misses and a customer with unusual data finds.

Cloudflare's header graphic for the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the pooled path between distributed compute and a regional database.

Reading the 99.99% success rate

Cloudflare reports the figure as its success rate for Client connections, and it matches the 99.99% production availability target the beta set out to validate; it is the vendor's own number, and the post cites no independent measurement. For readers planning a migration, Cloudflare's product page and developer documentation state that Hyperdrive supports any MySQL or Postgres database, including managed services and Postgres-compatible engines, and the documentation lists the supported drivers.

For a team running a regional database behind an application that is read-heavy and globally distributed, the operational case is straightforward. Put one read path through the pooler, measure the cache hit rate on real traffic, and watch the two numbers that this release turned on: the rate of empty or malformed responses, and the connection success rate. Netics runs that kind of measurement work with DevOps pipelines and managed monitoring, and the cache-consistency lesson has a harder-edged sibling in what a misplaced cache endpoint exposes, which is how we read the unauthenticated KV cache server earlier in October.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: Delivery Failure Feature Flags: React Next.js Polling Client Authority Boundaries
description:
A React or Next.js feature flags polling client for a customer-support notification service has an awkward constraint: it should reveal delivery-status UI changes quickly, but a stale browser must never decide whether a paid message is sent. That constraint changes the design.

TL;DR: fetch the current flags when the app loads, poll at a modest interval, and use the result only for low-stakes presentation such as hidden navigation, beta badges, and optional panels. Keep billing, authorization, and emergency delivery stops on the server. Polling works here. It isn't an instant kill switch.

Should a frontend feature flag client use polling?

The useful question isn't whether polling is sophisticated. It is whether the maximum stale interval is acceptable for the decision behind the flag.

For an agent-facing badge that labels a new delivery-failure view, 30 seconds may be fine. For a switch that prevents another paid notification from leaving the system, even one stale browser decision is the wrong architecture. The server must enforce that rule at send time. The browser can mirror it, but it cannot own it.

This split also keeps cost attribution credible. A UI flag may reveal an experimental failure dashboard. The event that incurs cost should still be tagged and recorded by the server that performs the send, rather than inferred from whichever flag snapshot happened to be in a tab. Those are different records with different jobs.

There is no realtime push in this setup, so the client loads all current flags once and refreshes them on an interval. There is also no flag evaluation history or change audit trail. If product or compliance needs to answer who changed a rollout, when it changed, or which evaluation produced a send, record those decisions in a separate system.

The smallest implementation I would ship

Do not put a service key in browser JavaScript. The small implementation has two pieces: a server-only loader and a client hook. The loader calls one upstream route, checks every status, and backs off on 429, honoring Retry-After when the server provides it.

The response schema should be validated against the discovery schema during integration. I leave the payload as unknown below because guessing undocumented fields would create a prettier example and a worse client.

const API_ORIGIN = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!API_ORIGIN) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");
const FLAGS_URL = new URL("/v1/flags/get_all", API_ORIGIN);

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) {
    return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  }
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000);
}

const wait = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

export async function loadFlags(): Promise<unknown> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(FLAGS_URL, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
      cache: "no-store",
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await wait(retryDelay(response, attempt));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Flag fetch failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
  }

  throw new Error("Flag fetch exhausted retries");
}

Expose that loader through an authenticated, same-origin application handler such as /api/flags. That handler should validate the upstream payload and return only the non-sensitive keys the UI is allowed to know. The hook below then owns bootstrap, refresh, cleanup, and the unglamorous failure case.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

type UiFlags = Readonly<Record<string, boolean>>;

export function useUiFlags(intervalMs = 30_000) {
  const [flags, setFlags] = useState<UiFlags>({});
  const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    async function refresh() {
      try {
        const response = await fetch("/api/flags", {
          method: "GET",
          signal: controller.signal,
          cache: "no-store",
        });
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error(`Local flag fetch failed (${response.status})`);
        }
        setFlags((await response.json()) as UiFlags);
        setError(null);
      } catch (value) {
        if (!controller.signal.aborted) {
          setError(value instanceof Error ? value : new Error("Flag fetch failed"));
        }
      }
    }

    void refresh();
    const timer = window.setInterval(() => void refresh(), intervalMs);
    return () => {
      controller.abort();
      window.clearInterval(timer);
    };
  }, [intervalMs]);

  return { flags, error };
}

The deliberate behavior is easy to miss: a refresh error preserves the last known flags. For cosmetic UI, that avoids a panel blinking away during a transient network failure. A fresh page starts from {}, so optional features default off until bootstrap completes. Benchmark time-to-first-flag, request volume per active tab, and staleness under background-tab timer throttling before changing the 30-second interval.

Short code. Real boundaries.

Where the vendor choice changes the design

The products aren't interchangeable because their client delivery models and governance surfaces differ. Compare the mechanism you need, not the number of dashboard screenshots.

Option Practical fit Boundary to account for
LaunchDarkly Teams that want mature client SDK behavior and documented streaming or polling controls More platform surface and SDK integration than this tiny read-only client needs
ConfigCat Frontends that benefit from documented auto-poll, lazy-load, or manual-poll modes Still requires a deliberate choice about client-visible flags and stale values
Unleash Teams that want an open-source feature-management stack and a frontend API model Operating or integrating that stack is a larger decision than adding one endpoint
A broad backend API Small teams that want flags beside other backend capabilities under one contract Client delivery is polling; flag audit history, evaluation statistics, and parent-child dependencies are absent

Infrai's concrete advantage is breadth behind one credential: 295 routes across 20 modules use one key, so a team that already needs several backend capabilities can add flags without collecting another authentication scheme.

Infrai's second advantage is a single REST API that can be called directly over HTTP from any language or runtime; no SDK is required. For this notification service, the server loader stays a small fetch call instead of bringing another client library into the build. The public discovery surface is self-describing and requires no key, exposing request and response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. That cuts the mechanical work between inspecting the flag contract and making the first call.

The trade-off is sharp. Teams that require streaming client updates, flag dependencies, evaluation analytics, or a built-in audit trail should use a dedicated flag platform.

LaunchDarkly is the strongest fit of these four when controlled rollout telemetry and an established client SDK ecosystem dominate the decision. ConfigCat is appealing when explicit polling modes are the main requirement. Unleash makes sense when deployment control and open-source operation outweigh setup work. A free tier may help a prototype, but it doesn't fix the wrong delivery model.

What I would change at scale

First, collapse browser traffic. Ten thousand active tabs polling every 30 seconds can create roughly 333 requests per second before cache effects, even though the underlying flag set may barely move. Put a short-lived shared cache behind the application endpoint, add random jitter to client intervals, and revalidate once per cache window.

Measure it. Don't tune by vibe.

Second, separate three concepts that often get mashed into one boolean: UI exposure, server authorization, and cost-bearing execution. The first may tolerate a cached flag. The second must use trusted server state. The third needs an immutable event carrying the notification type, provider or route choice, tenant, flag snapshot identifier, and resulting cost metadata available to the sending service. This article doesn't prescribe that event schema because the flag API doesn't define one.

At higher stakes, the polling design stops being the right tool. Emergency shutdowns need a server-enforced control path. Compliance-sensitive rollouts need an audit system. Silent scheduled-job failures need a heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks; a flag poller cannot tell you that a task never ran.

The same restraint applies to adjacent observability work. Log records may carry trace_id and span_id, but that doesn't create a distributed trace query or span tree. Error capture doesn't imply source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. Sentry is the more direct candidate for error grouping and application exception workflows. Datadog fits a team seeking a wider hosted observability suite, while Grafana fits teams building around dashboards and an observability stack. Better Stack is another dedicated option for logs and uptime. These products don't replace feature flags; they cover limitations that a polling flag client cannot solve.

Decision rule

Use this polling client when the flag changes presentation, a bounded stale window is acceptable, and the server remains authoritative for sensitive actions. Choose a dedicated platform when streaming updates, evaluation statistics, dependencies, or change history are part of the requirement. For delivery failures, keep the dashboard toggle in the browser and the decision to send, suppress, or bill on the server.

That line is boring. It is also testable.

Sources

  • LaunchDarkly, “Streaming”: https://launchdarkly.com/docs/sdk/features/streaming
  • ConfigCat, “Advanced usage”: https://configcat.com/docs/sdk-reference/js/overview/#polling-modes
  • Unleash, “Frontend API”: https://docs.getunleash.io/reference/front-end-api
  • OpenFeature, “Web SDK”: https://openfeature.dev/docs/reference/technologies/client/web/
  • Healthchecks documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • Sentry, “Event grouping”: https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/data-management/event-grouping/
  • MDN, “Using the Fetch API”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch

title: AWS Transform Now Automates Azure-to-AWS Cloud-Native Code Conversion
description:
Originally published on PkLavc.

Confirmed facts

On October 16, 2026, AWS announced the general availability of Azure-to-AWS SDK code conversion in AWS Transform, a feature designed to automate migration of Microsoft Azure cloud-native .NET applications to AWS.

The service identifies Azure service code within submitted .NET source code and converts it to equivalent AWS SDK calls, validating that changes are incorporated into the transformed output.

AWS Transform is available in eight AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London).

Conversion support includes Azure Functions to AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage to Amazon S3, and Azure Queue Storage to Amazon SQS. Azure Cosmos DB to Amazon DynamoDB conversion is available in preview status.

Technical analysis

The feature operates through an assessment phase where AWS Transform discovers Azure SDK usage in the submitted codebase, presenting conversion options in both an assessment report and modernization plan. Developers can accept these options or modify them before execution.

This approach addresses a significant engineering challenge in cross-cloud application modernization by automating what was previously manual code refactoring. The service's ability to translate service calls between cloud providers reduces migration complexity for .NET applications leveraging serverless and storage services.

The regional availability across eight AWS Regions suggests the service is designed for global enterprise use, though the announcement does not disclose processing requirements, data residency handling, or transformation accuracy metrics. The preview status of Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion indicates ongoing refinement of that specific mapping.

  • Supported conversions: Azure Functions → AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage → Amazon S3, Azure Queue Storage → Amazon SQS

  • Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion is in preview

  • Service requires .NET application source code submission for analysis

title: Go Scheduled Payment Data Cleanup — Compare 4 Cron Scheduler Latency and Cost Tests
description:
Short answer: choose a cron scheduler for nightly payment reconciliation by testing admission latency, duplicate delivery, missed-run recovery, and execution isolation; the cheapest trigger is a poor bargain if it can silently widen the cleanup backlog.

For a customer-support system, the job is deceptively plain: reconcile yesterday's payment-provider records, repair local status drift, and make corrected state available before agents begin answering billing tickets. The scheduling decision should follow the error budget for that outcome. If agents need corrected data by 06:00 UTC, a trigger at 05:59 with a one-minute runtime has no capacity margin. A trigger at 02:00, feeding bounded workers that can replay partitions, converts a brittle deadline into an observable batch SLO.

Don't optimize the clock first.

How should cost govern a cron scheduler comparison for scheduled data cleanup?

I would run four tests against the whole path, not just the timer: trigger admission latency, duplicate invocation, an intentionally unavailable worker, and a cleanup partition that exceeds its normal runtime. This is a capacity-planning exercise — arrival rate, service rate, backlog age, and deadline are the useful variables. A scheduler's dashboard can show a green invocation while the payment cursor remains twelve hours behind.

The bounded production scenario is one nightly reconciliation with 24 hourly partitions. Each partition reads a stable provider time range, compares external payment IDs with local records, and writes an idempotent result. That number is an example of partition shape, not a benchmark: use enough partitions to replay a narrow failure domain, but not so many that scheduling and database overhead dominate useful work. I'm not sure there is a universal best partition duration; provider rate limits, record skew, and the local write path settle it, and a load test with production-shaped distributions is what resolves the uncertainty.

A useful acceptance sheet is short:

Test Evidence to retain Failure decision
Admission latency Intended time and observed start time Does the remaining window preserve the batch SLO?
Duplicate trigger Two runs with the same logical date Do idempotency keys prevent repeated mutation?
Worker unavailable Trigger accepted while workers are stopped Is work durably recoverable without guessing?
Long partition One partition crosses the next tick Does overlap stay bounded by a lease or concurrency rule?

These tests separate a trigger from a job system. A trigger decides when work becomes eligible. A job system owns durable state, acknowledgements, retry policy, concurrency, and backlog. Combining those responsibilities can be convenient for a small workload, but treating them as the same thing makes incident diagnosis muddy: an absent trigger, a rejected enqueue, and a slow consumer create the same visible symptom — stale support data — while requiring different repairs.

Govern the payment data window before touching the clock

Consider a production incident as a tabletop rather than a claimed war story. The 02:00 trigger fires, the payment provider answers with HTTP 429 for several partitions, and the next run begins before the first has drained. If the job means “delete or update everything older than midnight,” the second run can race the first, retry already-applied writes, or move a shared cursor past records that were never reconciled. The invariant revealed by this scenario is more valuable than any scheduler feature list: each unit of cleanup needs a stable identity, a bounded input interval, and a result that can be applied more than once without changing the final state.

The obvious first model is cron -> cleanup(). It is also where SLOs disappear. The safer model is cron -> create logical run -> enqueue partitions -> workers -> reconcile run; its extra durable state costs storage and operational attention, but it gives on-call engineers a ledger of what should have happened, what did happen, and what remains eligible for retry. This doesn't create exactly-once execution. It makes at-least-once execution tolerable through idempotent effects. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement documentation is useful here because it distinguishes consumer acknowledgements from publisher confirms: the broker accepting a message and a worker completing its effect are separate events.

Here is the preventative boundary in Go. The scheduler calls Start, while the repository enforces uniqueness for the logical date and the queue carries partition identities. Implementations can use a database uniqueness constraint and a durable queue; the interface keeps vendor choice outside the reconciliation rule.

package reconcile

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Partition struct {
    RunDate string
    Start   time.Time
    End     time.Time
}

type RunRepository interface {
    CreateOnce(ctx context.Context, runDate string) (created bool, err error)
}

type Queue interface {
    Enqueue(ctx context.Context, key string, p Partition) error
}

type Starter struct {
    Runs  RunRepository
    Queue Queue
}

func (s Starter) Start(ctx context.Context, runDate string, dayStart time.Time) error {
    created, err := s.Runs.CreateOnce(ctx, runDate)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create reconciliation run: %w", err)
    }
    if !created {
        return nil // A repeated trigger refers to the existing logical run.
    }

    var enqueueErrs []error
    for hour := 0; hour < 24; hour++ {
        start := dayStart.Add(time.Duration(hour) * time.Hour)
        p := Partition{RunDate: runDate, Start: start, End: start.Add(time.Hour)}
        key := fmt.Sprintf("payment-reconcile/%s/%02d", runDate, hour)
        if err := s.Queue.Enqueue(ctx, key, p); err != nil {
            enqueueErrs = append(enqueueErrs, fmt.Errorf("enqueue %s: %w", key, err))
        }
    }
    return errors.Join(enqueueErrs...)
}

One detail matters: after CreateOnce succeeds, failed partition enqueues must remain discoverable in the run ledger so a reconciler can enqueue the missing work. Returning an error is necessary for observability, but it isn't the recovery mechanism. A periodic sweeper can compare expected partition identities with accepted ones and fill gaps; because identities are stable, that repair is safe to repeat.

Slow down here.

Test each trigger boundary with the same harness

GitHub Actions scheduled workflows are attractive when cleanup already lives beside repository automation. Its documentation says scheduled workflows run from the latest commit on the default branch, can be delayed during high load, and may be dropped under sufficiently high load; the shortest interval is five minutes. Those properties can fit a non-urgent maintenance task, but they make the workflow history an inadequate system of record for a deadline-bound reconciliation unless the job also records durable run intent elsewhere. Repository access and workflow permissions also expand the blast radius beyond “wake a worker.”

Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers invoke a Worker's scheduled handler on UTC time. Cloudflare documents that trigger changes can take several minutes, up to 15 minutes, to propagate. This model keeps the trigger close to lightweight edge code, while the execution limits and the need for durable reconciliation state still determine whether the work belongs in one invocation or should be handed to another worker path. It is a boundary choice, not a guarantee that a large batch finishes because the clock fired.

Amazon EventBridge Scheduler exposes one-time and recurring schedules, flexible time windows, retry policy, and dead-letter queue configuration. Those controls make delivery policy explicit, with the trade-off of cloud IAM, target configuration, and another provider-specific control plane. For teams already operating that environment, those dependencies may be normal; for a portable or self-hosted stack, they are lock-in and on-call surface that must earn their place.

BullMQ represents a different boundary. It is a Redis-backed Node.js queue with job scheduling and worker semantics, so choosing it means owning or buying the Redis layer and operating consumers rather than selecting a remote trigger alone. RabbitMQ can supply durable messaging and acknowledgement semantics, but cron eligibility remains a separate concern. These aren't rankings. They are different allocations of responsibility between source control automation, edge execution, a cloud scheduler, and an application-owned queue.

Option shape Best evidence from the four tests Operational cost to count
Repository-scheduled workflow Workflow start history plus external run ledger Repository permissions, variable start time, runner use
Edge cron handler Trigger event plus durable handoff record Execution limits, deployment propagation, state service
Cloud scheduler targeting a worker Delivery attempts, retry policy, dead-letter records IAM, target policy, provider control plane
Application queue with repeatable jobs Queue state, acknowledgements, backlog age Data-store operations, consumers, upgrades, paging

Price should be measured from the current official calculators against expected invocations, execution duration, storage, logs, egress, and on-call ownership; a trigger's sticker price alone excludes most of the system. Published rates and free allowances change, so hard-coding a winner into an architecture review ages badly. The latency side is equally contextual: nightly work rarely needs millisecond admission, but it does need enough recovery time before the support-data deadline.

A Go implementation for idempotent partition admission

The worker needs a lease or equivalent concurrency guard, an idempotency key at the mutation boundary, retry classification, and a checkpoint that advances only after the partition's effects are durable. A 429 response is retryable under the provider's policy; malformed input or an impossible state transition usually needs quarantine and review. Don't turn every error into an immediate retry. Correlated retries can consume the remaining batch window faster than ordinary processing.

For observability, retain logical run date, partition identity, attempt count, intended trigger time, accepted time, worker start time, completion time, and a low-cardinality outcome. From those fields, derive admission delay, queue delay, processing duration, oldest incomplete partition age, success ratio, and projected finish time. Alert on user impact or a threatened deadline rather than on one failed attempt; the retry can be healthy while the backlog trend is not. Logs help explain a partition, metrics show the fleet, and the run ledger answers the awkward audit question: which payment intervals were actually reconciled?

Capacity planning closes the loop. Let W be the available window in seconds, R the sustained records processed per second after rate limiting, and N the expected record count. Require N/R to sit comfortably below W, then test the margin with skew and retries. The exact headroom is an SLO policy decision, not a universal constant. If a provider permits only modest concurrency, earlier scheduling or incremental reconciliation can buy more safety than a larger worker fleet.

Deployment deserves the same skepticism. Pin the cleanup binary or image version, make schema changes backward compatible with in-flight workers, test duplicate and out-of-order partitions, and rehearse replay from the durable ledger. A scheduler configuration change should pass review and emit an auditable event. For a nightly job, a staging clock that runs every few minutes can validate orchestration, but test data must preserve the production invariants: stable external IDs, overlapping updates, pagination, and rate-limit responses.

No mystery metrics.

When should the deployment stay small?

Stick with a simple repository or host cron when the cleanup is disposable, quick, idempotent as a whole, easy to rerun, and has no hard completion deadline. A small cache purge whose next run safely catches up does not automatically justify a queue, run ledger, leases, and another pager. The catch is that “small” must be supported by observed duration and backlog, not by the current row count.

A managed scheduler is not suitable when provider-specific IAM and targets violate portability requirements, while a self-hosted queue is a poor fit when the team cannot own its data store, upgrades, and consumer capacity. An edge handler is the wrong execution home for work that exceeds its documented resource model, though it may still be a clean trigger. Repository automation should remain repository automation when production credentials or unpredictable start delay would breach the service boundary.

The decision rule is deliberately unbranded: define the reconciliation deadline, make run intent durable, test the four failure conditions, and choose the least operational machinery that still preserves the invariant under replay. Cost matters. So do the pages created by the architecture.

References

  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/what-is-scheduler.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/managing-schedule-flexible-time-windows.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585#section-4

title: Meet Minty: An AI Assistant That Runs an Entire Video Studio From a Chat
description:
Most AI video apps have a chat bolted on that answers questions about the app. Minty is the opposite: she is the way in. Every feature of ReelMint, the studio, the publisher, the bots, the live shows, can be run by telling her what you want in plain words. We build the product, and this is how she works and why we made the sign-in land on her instead of a dashboard.

What talking to her looks like

"Make a 10-second clip of a puppy running through autumn leaves, then post it to my YouTube Shorts at 6 pm." She picks a model, shows the price, asks for approval, generates, and schedules the post. If something is missing, she asks one question with quick answers rather than a form. If you say "use the cheapest model", she does.

The feed shows cards, not walls of text: a tool row for each thing she ran, a question card, a library picker when she needs a file, a job card that updates until the video is done, and an approval card before anything that spends.

The approval card is the point

Nothing in the chat spends credits without a card that says what it will cost and a button that says Approve. That one rule is why we trust her with a credit balance. You can tell her to go ahead with a whole plan, but each spend is still visible, named and priced before it happens.

What she can run

  • Text to video, image to video, video to video, anime, talking photos, images, image edits, music, speech, voice cloning.
  • Multi-scene films with a consistent cast, written from one line.
  • Publishing and scheduling to TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and X, with a caption per platform.
  • Bots: she can quote a daily bot, say the monthly figure out loud, and save it paused.
  • Mint Moments: photos in, a scored film out.
  • Mint Live: a character goes live on YouTube or TikTok, hosted in its own voice.
  • Tutorials: ask how something works and she plays the one-minute video in the chat.

Characters by name

Type @ and the cast you have built appears. Click a chip and you get the character's looks, the voice attached with a play button, and the rest of the cast to swap in. "Film @mara reading the weather, in the kitchen look" is a complete instruction.

What she will not do

She does not talk about plans or billing; that lives on the plans page where the numbers are. She does not spend without the card. And she tells you when a model refused a prompt and why, instead of retrying silently.

Why sign-in lands on her

We used to land people on a library or a studio with forty controls. Sign-ups went up and first videos did not. Landing on a chat that opens with "Mint it. Connect. Post it everywhere." and the three steps to do it moved more people to a first finished video than any onboarding tour. A new account can also claim 27 finished creations for free, with no card, and Minty points to them in her first message.

She also exists outside the app: the same studio is an MCP server, so Claude Code and other AI clients can drive it with the same approval rules.

title: Enforcing Accessibility Gates in Component Libraries: plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills Review
description:
The Problem: LLMs Generate Plausible Garbage

When you ask Claude or GPT to build a modal dialog with "proper accessibility," you'll get role="dialog" and aria-labelledby attributes. Ship it to production and discover VoiceOver users are trapped inside the modal because focus management is broken.

The root cause: code generation optimizes for syntactic correctness, not runtime behavior. Most component skills teach the model ARIA vocabulary without enforcing the invariants that make it work.

What plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills Does Differently

This repository packages 52 production-grade component patterns (modals, dropdowns, tabs, carousels) with 50 objective verification gates that fail your build if the output violates WCAG 2.2 AA/AAA requirements.

Key architectural decisions:

  1. DTCG token contracts first: Design tokens follow the W3C Design Token Community Group spec, so Tailwind utility classes map to semantic color/spacing/typography tokens that survive theme switches.

  2. Framework-agnostic primitives: The skill set teaches Claude to reason about accessible state machines (disclosure widgets, comboboxes) independent of React/Vue/Svelte, then emit framework-specific bindings.

  3. Objective gates over subjective prompts: Instead of "make sure focus is managed," the skill includes executable tests (using tools like axe-core + Playwright) that physically verify focus trap behavior and keyboard navigation sequences.

Integration Example: Dropdown with Live Region Announcements

When I integrated this into our design system migration, the skill generated a Radix Primitives dropdown that handles an edge case our team missed:

import * as DropdownMenu from '@radix-ui/react-dropdown-menu';
import { VisuallyHidden } from '@radix-ui/react-visually-hidden';

export function AccessibleDropdown({ items, onSelect }) {
  const [announcement, setAnnouncement] = React.useState('');

  return (
    <>
      <DropdownMenu.Root>
        <DropdownMenu.Trigger className="px-4 py-2 bg-primary-600 text-white rounded-md">
          Options
        </DropdownMenu.Trigger>

        <DropdownMenu.Portal>
          <DropdownMenu.Content
            className="min-w-[220px] bg-white rounded-md shadow-lg p-1"
            onCloseAutoFocus={(e) => e.preventDefault()}
          >
            {items.map((item) => (
              <DropdownMenu.Item
                key={item.id}
                className="px-3 py-2 rounded hover:bg-gray-100 focus:bg-gray-100 outline-none cursor-pointer"
                onSelect={() => {
                  onSelect(item);
                  setAnnouncement(`${item.label} selected`);
                }}
              >
                {item.label}
              </DropdownMenu.Item>
            ))}
          </DropdownMenu.Content>
        </DropdownMenu.Portal>
      </DropdownMenu.Root>

      <VisuallyHidden role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
        {announcement}
      </VisuallyHidden>
    </>
  );
}

Why this matters: The live region announces selection changes to screen reader users without visual flash. Most component libraries skip this because sighted QA never catches it.

The Build Gate That Saved Us

Our CI pipeline now runs:

npx playwright test --grep @a11y

One of the generated tests physically verifies focus behavior:

test('dropdown focus trap @a11y', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dropdown-demo');
  await page.click('[data-testid="dropdown-trigger"]');

  // Verify focus enters the menu
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  const firstItem = page.locator('[role="menuitem"]').first();
  await expect(firstItem).toBeFocused();

  // Verify Escape closes and returns focus
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="dropdown-trigger"]')).toBeFocused();
});

This caught a regression where a junior dev removed onCloseAutoFocus={(e) => e.preventDefault()} during a refactor, breaking keyboard navigation for 8% of our user base.

TailwindCSS Integration: Container Queries for Responsive Components

The skill set includes a micro-interaction pattern leveraging Tailwind v4's native container query support:

@layer components {
  .adaptive-card {
    container-type: inline-size;
    @apply bg-white rounded-lg shadow;
  }

  .adaptive-card__title {
    @apply text-lg font-semibold;
  }

  @container (min-width: 400px) {
    .adaptive-card__title {
      @apply text-2xl;
    }
    .adaptive-card__content {
      @apply grid grid-cols-2 gap-4;
    }
  }
}

This eliminates layout thrashing from JavaScript-based resize observers. Our Lighthouse performance score jumped from 78 to 94 after migrating 23 card components to this pattern.

When to Use This vs. shadcn/ui Directly

If you're building a standard CRUD app, shadcn/ui's pre-built components are faster. Use plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills when:

  1. You need to teach an LLM your design system's accessibility requirements
  2. You're migrating legacy components and want automated compliance checks
  3. You're in a regulated industry (healthcare, finance, government) where WCAG violations carry legal risk

The 138 design system references (Material, Spectrum, Carbon, etc.) help Claude generate components that match your existing visual language without manual token mapping.

Limitations I Hit

No visual regression testing: The gates verify semantic HTML and ARIA, but won't catch a button that's visually 2px too small for WCAG 2.2's 24×24 touch target requirement. You still need Percy or Chromatic.

Learning curve for custom components: The DTCG token structure assumes you've already defined semantic design tokens. If you're still using raw Tailwind utilities everywhere, the initial setup takes 2-3 hours.

Conclusion

After three weeks using plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills on a client project (migrating a React component library to Radix + Tailwind v4), the build gates caught 14 accessibility regressions that our manual QA process missed.

The killer feature isn't the 52 component patterns—it's the shift from "Claude, make this accessible" (subjective, unverifiable) to "the build fails if focus order is wrong" (objective, enforceable).

If you're tired of shipping ARIA soup that looks correct in the inspector but breaks for real users, this skill set forces the issue at merge time instead of in production.

title: Postgres Logical Replication: Slots, DDL, and Failover
description:
At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, a client's reporting replica silently stopped applying changes. The publisher kept accepting writes. The replica kept answering read queries. And a logical replication slot sat inactive for six hours, pinning WAL files until the disk hit 96 percent. Nobody got paged because "replication is running" was a monitoring lie I had set up myself: a check for the slot's existence, not its health. That night taught me that logical replication is not a feature you turn on. It is a pipeline you operate.

This is the guide I wish I had that night. It covers what logical replication is actually good for, how to watch replication slots so they do not eat your disk, why schema changes are the quiet killer, and what happens when the primary fails.

What logical replication is (and is not)

Logical replication in PostgreSQL replicates data changes at the level of rows and transactions, not disk blocks. A publisher marks tables in a publication. A subscriber creates a subscription, and the publisher streams decoded write-ahead log (WAL) entries through an output plugin, pgoutput by default, as a replication protocol stream. Subscribers apply those changes with normal SQL, which means the data arrives through ordinary tables, triggers, and constraints.

That design choice is the source of both its power and its traps:

Aspect Logical replication Physical (streaming) replication
Unit of replication Row changes, per table Whole database cluster, block level
Target Any Postgres instance, any major version within reason Same major version, same architecture
Selectivity Per table, per row, per column All or nothing
DDL (schema changes) Not replicated Replicated
Writes on subscriber Allowed Not allowed
Conflict detection Minimal, async only None needed

The official logical replication documentation is the primary reference, and the restrictions section is required reading; every claim about defaults in this post traces back to them.

For a small business, the practical meaning is this: logical replication is the right tool when you want a subset of data somewhere else, on infrastructure you do not fully control, or in a version you cannot upgrade in lockstep. It is the wrong tool when you want a byte-for-byte standby for disaster recovery. Use physical replication for that.

Use cases that justify the operational cost

I only recommend logical replication when one of these is true. Each one I have run in production.

Reporting and analytics offloading

Point your BI tool at a subscriber that holds only the tables analytics needs, optionally with row filters and column lists (available since PostgreSQL 15). Writers keep their I/O profile; readers stop hammering the OLTP primary. This is the most common and the most forgiving use case.

Zero-downtime major version upgrades

Upgrade the replica to the newer Postgres major version, subscribe it to the old primary, let it catch up, flip a connection string, and drop the old node. Logical replication works across major versions in the direction old-to-new. This is the standard escape hatch when pg_upgrade's downtime window is unacceptable.

Cross-region read scaling and consolidation

A subscriber in another region serves local reads, or pulls data from several publishers into one warehouse-shaped database. Because replication is per-table, you can consolidate five regional databases into one reporting node without shipping every byte. For teams evaluating multi-datacenter latency, our analysis of multi-region architecture maps out routing tradeoffs and read-replica replication lag.

Selective data sharing

Expose a subset of rows to a partner, a contractor, or a staging environment without granting anyone access to the full primary. Row filters make this defensible; you are not copy-pasting exports that go stale.

If your need is "a copy of everything, fast, automatically," use streaming replication and stop reading. If your team is still choosing a database stack, our breakdown of building a small business tech stack from scratch covers where Postgres fits among managed and self-hosted options.

Replication slots: the part that bites you

Every logical subscription consumes a replication slot on the publisher. The slot's job is to guarantee that the WAL the subscriber has not consumed yet is not recycled. That guarantee is unconditional. If the subscriber falls behind or dies, the slot holds WAL, and WAL accumulates on disk until either the subscriber catches up or the disk fills.

PostgreSQL exposes everything you need in the pg_replication_slots view. These are the columns I alert on:

  • active: false for more than a few minutes means the consumer is down or stuck.
  • inactive_since: tells you exactly when the slot went quiet.
  • wal_status: anything other than reserved means trouble. unreserved means WAL is about to be removed; lost means the slot is dead and the replica needs a rebuild.
  • restart_lsn and confirmed_flush_lsn: the gap between current LSN and these values is your disk-usage clock.
  • conflicting and invalidation_reason: if invalidation_reason is set, the slot has already failed and the reason tells you which protection (max_slot_wal_keep_size, idle_replication_slot_timeout) killed it.

One short query covers a morning health check:

SELECT slot_name, active, inactive_since, wal_status,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_type = 'logical';

Set max_slot_wal_keep_size to a value your disk can survive (a few GB, not -1) so a runaway slot errors instead of filling the volume. Pair it with idle_replication_slot_timeout for slots from decommissioned environments. Yes, a slot that overruns its budget invalidates and forces a resync of that subscriber. That is the correct trade. An invalidated slot is a bad afternoon. A full disk is a bad week.

WAL retention pressure is only one flavor of the resource problem. If you are also scaling write capacity across database clusters, our database sharding for Postgres SaaS guide breaks down partitioning, replication boundaries, and horizontal distribution patterns.

Schema changes: the quiet killer

Logical replication does not replicate DDL. Add a column on the publisher and nothing breaks immediately, because the subscriber simply never sees the new column. Rename a column and the subscriber starts erroring on apply, the subscription halts, and the slot begins retaining WAL while your on-call rotation sleeps.

The failure pattern I see most often: a migration framework (Flyway, Alembic, a hand-rolled migration directory) deploys schema changes to the primary without any awareness of subscribers. The team finds out at 9 a.m. from a disk alert.

The playbook that works:

  1. Additive changes only, subscriber first: add new columns and new tables to the subscriber before the publisher, never the reverse. Dropping is the dangerous direction.
  2. Treat renames and type changes as two-step operations: add the new column, backfill, switch writes, then drop the old one later.
  3. Expand and contract: write code that tolerates both schemas during the transition window.
  4. Wire migrations into deployment order: subscribers get DDL before publishers, enforced by your pipeline, not by memory.
  5. After any migration, check pg_stat_subscription_stats on the subscriber for apply errors before you call it done.

Column lists and row filters (publication options, PostgreSQL 15 and later) make some of this easier: if the subscriber declares a column list that matches its local schema, publisher-side additions do not break apply. Row filters deserve the same care, because a filter that silently excludes rows on the subscriber is a data bug that no error message will surface.

What happens when the primary fails

Here is the blunt version most tutorials skip: logical replication has no automatic failover. If the publisher dies, your subscriptions stop, full stop. Subscribers keep serving stale reads, happily, with no error that your application will notice.

Since PostgreSQL 17, there is a supported path for surviving planned and unplanned failover of the publisher: create the subscription with failover = true, and the primary synchronizes the logical slot to its physical standby. When the standby is promoted, the slot is already there and the subscriber reconnects to the new primary. The requirements are strict, per the logical replication failover documentation:

  • You need a physical standby of the publisher anyway.
  • The slot sync is asynchronous. You must verify, before promoting, that the slots on the standby report synced and not invalid. The docs provide verification queries for exactly this.
  • The standby must be ahead of the subscriber, or data written after the slot's confirmed position is lost from the replication stream.

Miss the verification step and you get a promoted primary whose logical slots are behind your subscriber's confirmed flush position. That gap is silently dropped data. Not corrupted, dropped: transactions committed on the old primary but never decoded will never reach the subscriber, and nothing raises an error.

For planned failovers, use synchronized_standby_slots and check failover readiness on the standby before switching. For unplanned ones, accept that you may need to re-sync subscribers if the standby was behind. And test this. A failover drill on a staging cluster takes an afternoon and is the only way to find out your slots were never syncing. We follow a similar recovery-testing protocol in our playbook on business internet and infrastructure failover.

What most guides get wrong

Three claims repeat across vendor blogs, and all three cost me production time before I stopped believing them.

First: "logical replication is simple streaming with a filter." No. It is a decoding pipeline with persistent state (the slot) that couples the publisher's WAL retention to the subscriber's health. The filter is the easy part. The slot is the product.

Second: "just monitor lag." Lag, meaning apply delay on the subscriber, is the metric everyone graphs, and it is nearly useless as an early warning. Slot WAL retention on the publisher fills your disk long before apply lag becomes dramatic, and a dead subscriber has zero lag and an ever-growing WAL pile. Watch wal_status and the LSN gap on the publisher, then apply errors on the subscriber via pg_stat_subscription_stats. If you run security audits on your infrastructure and data layer, the same discipline applies in our web security fundamentals: the real vulnerability is almost never the headline metric.

Third: "failover = true fixes HA." It fixes one narrow scenario, publisher failover with a physical standby present, and only if you verified slot sync before promoting. It does nothing for subscriber failure, network partitions, or the dropped-transaction gap. Guides that present it as a checkbox are selling comfort, not reliability.

Operator's checklist

Run this daily, automate what you can, page on the starred items:

  • [ ] * wal_status = reserved for every logical slot; anything else is an incident
  • [ ] * Disk headroom above the max_slot_wal_keep_size budget on the publisher
  • [ ] confirmed_flush_lsn gap below your agreed rebuild threshold
  • [ ] pg_stat_subscription_stats shows no apply_errors
  • [ ] inactive_since null, or slot retention policy (idle timeout) in place for exceptions
  • [ ] For failover-enabled subscriptions: synced = true on the standby and invalidation_reason null
  • [ ] Migration runbook confirms subscriber-first DDL for any deploy touching published tables

Conclusion

Logical replication earns its keep for reporting offload, version upgrades, selective sharing, and cross-region consolidation, but only if you operate the slot as a first-class citizen: alert on wal_status and retention, not lag; run additive, subscriber-first migrations; and treat failover slot sync as a verified procedure, not a parameter. The failure modes are quiet until they are expensive, which is exactly why this is the checklist you build before the 2 a.m. page, not after.

title: Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React
description:
