description: "A practical engineering guide to Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."

In modern software development, Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Websocket Protocol Handshakes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Broadcasting Cursor Positions And Canvas Events: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Operational Transformation Basics: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Managing Reconnects: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: WebSocket protocol handshakes, broadcasting cursor positions and canvas events, operational transformation basics, and managing reconnects."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Working with S3 Object Tags in Buckets: SET, MERGE and CLEAR
description:
A practical walkthrough for keeping Amazon S3 objects organized without changing what is inside the files.

Object tags are easy to overlook when you are busy uploading and moving files around S3. But once a bucket starts filling up, a few consistent labels can make objects easier to organize and manage. The part that matters is how you update them: replacing a tag set is not the same as adding a tag to what is already there.

I used Buckets by Serverless Creed to explore three useful actions—SET, MERGE and CLEAR—and checked the results in the AWS S3 console. I also compared the downloaded files with their original SHA-256 hashes to make sure the contents stayed exactly the same.

A quick look at object tags

An S3 object tag is a key-value pair attached to an object. For example, env=test, team=intern or phase=review can describe where a file belongs or how it is used. These are separate from the file itself and from ordinary user-defined object metadata. S3 allows up to ten tags per object.

Tags can be useful for organizing data and for AWS features that are configured to use them, including lifecycle rules and some access-control policies. That is why updating tags deserves a little more care than simply changing a filename.

Start with a small sample folder

I worked with a handful of harmless text files in a private S3 bucket:

  docs/readme.txt
  b.txt
  c.txt
  control.txt

The files were small enough to inspect easily. The bulk operations shown below target only b.txt and c.txt. I left control.txt with a separate control=keep tag so there was always an object to compare against the ones being updated.

The sample files as they appear in the Buckets object browser.

SET: replace the existing tags

SET is the option to choose when an object needs a completely new tag set. In Buckets, select the files, open the bulk tagging action and choose Set (replace). For this example, I entered team=intern.

The important word is replace: tags that were on the object before, but are not included in the new set, will be removed. Before applying the change, the dialog shows the exact object keys being updated. It is worth reading that list rather than assuming every visible folder or file is included.

SET preview in Buckets, with the new team tag and the exact object list.

The operation completes and Buckets displays the update result.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for SET.

I then opened the object details in AWS. The tag panel showed one tag, team=intern, which is the state I expected after a replacement.

AWS S3 shows the new tag set after SET.

MERGE: add a tag without losing the others

MERGE is more useful when the existing labels should stay. I kept team=intern, switched to Merge, and entered a new tag: phase=review. I left the remove-keys field empty.

That should leave both tags on the objects. If a tag key already exists, MERGE updates that key; keys not mentioned are preserved. This is usually a safer option for incremental changes than rebuilding the full tag list by hand.

MERGE adds phase=review while preserving the other tag keys.

The MERGE action completes successfully.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for MERGE.

The AWS object details now displayed both team=intern and phase=review. Checking the entire tag list is useful here: seeing only the new key would not prove that the earlier one survived.

Both team and phase are visible in the AWS object-tag panel.

CLEAR: remove tags, not the object

CLEAR does exactly what the name suggests: it removes the object’s tag set. In Buckets, choose Clear all after selecting the intended files. The confirmation makes the scope explicit and warns that tag-dependent lifecycle rules or policies may no longer match.

This is the step where I would be most careful in a real bucket. Clearing tags does not delete a file, but tags may be used by other AWS configurations. Always check the objects listed in the confirmation before proceeding.

CLEAR warns about removing all tags and shows the affected object keys.

Buckets confirms that the tag-removal operation completed.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for CLEAR.

Afterward, the AWS object details showed Tags (0). The AWS object details still identified b.txt; the wider Buckets capture also shows readme.txt remaining in the browser after tag removal. That distinction is important: removing tags is not the same thing as deleting objects.

The S3 tag section is empty after CLEAR.

A wider view of the Buckets object browser after tag removal.

The AWS object details page still shows the file and its empty tag set.

Independent verification and SHA-256 integrity checking

I kept control.txt out of the tagging changes. Its control=keep tag was still there at the end, which was a quick check that the untouched object had retained its original tag.

The control object keeps its original tag.

For file contents, I recorded SHA-256 hashes of the original text files before uploading them. After the tagging sequence, I downloaded the S3 objects into a separate folder and compared them with that original hash list. Run the check from the download folder, with the original hash list one directory above it:

shasum -a 256 -c ../original-hashes.txt

All four downloaded files match their original SHA-256 hashes.

The output was:

docs/readme.txt: OK
b.txt: OK
c.txt: OK
control.txt: OK

The AWS Console screenshot lists CRC64NVME as its stored checksum function. The SHA-256 verification here is a separate local comparison of the downloaded bytes against the original files.

All four checks returned OK. That gives two independent views of the outcome: the AWS Console shows how the tags changed, and the hash check shows that the downloaded file bytes matched the originals.

A few habits worth keeping

Three things made this workflow straightforward. First, use SET only when replacing the full tag set is intentional; use MERGE when existing labels should remain. Second, review the exact object list before any bulk operation, especially when folders and nested files are involved. Third, check the resulting tags in S3 rather than relying on a success message alone.

For a small example like this, the difference between SET, MERGE and CLEAR is easy to see. On a busy bucket, choosing the right operation—and verifying the final state—can save a lot of confusion later.

title: Go's database/sql Has Been Ports and Adapters Since Go 1. Read Its Driver Port
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Drop one line from a Go service's import block and sql.Open answers with sql: unknown driver "postgres" (forgotten import?). The standard library guesses your bug for you. The missing line is import _ "github.com/lib/pq", and that underscore is the visible end of a ports-and-adapters design that has sat in Go's standard library since the language hit 1.0.

The package was exp/sql until the weekly snapshot of 2012-01-20 renamed it to database/sql, and it shipped in Go 1 on 28 March 2012. Alistair Cockburn had written up the ports and adapters pattern in 2005, with the stated intent of letting an application be "developed and tested in isolation from its eventual run-time devices and databases". Fourteen years after Go 1, database/sql is still a clean blueprint of that idea, plus one design decision you should not copy.

The core owns the port

Start with who defines what. The interfaces live in database/sql/driver, and the package doc opens with: "Package driver defines interfaces to be implemented by database drivers as used by package sql." The consumer writes the contract. Postgres, MySQL and SQLite authors implement it.

That is the rule the Go wiki's Code Review Comments gives for every interface: "Go interfaces generally belong in the package that uses values of the interface type, not the package that implements those values." database/sql follows it to the letter. Here is the required surface, abridged from the package docs:

// database/sql/driver (abridged)
type Driver interface {
    Open(name string) (Conn, error)
}

type Conn interface {
    Prepare(query string) (Stmt, error)
    Close() error
    Begin() (Tx, error) // deprecated
}

type Stmt interface {
    Close() error
    NumInput() int
    Exec(args []Value) (Result, error)  // deprecated
    Query(args []Value) (Rows, error)   // deprecated
}

type Rows interface {
    Columns() []string
    Close() error
    Next(dest []Value) error
}

That is small on purpose. The design goals document that sits in the package directory lists a clear split between the driver layer and the user-facing layer, type conversion handled mostly in the sql package so drivers deal with fewer types, and optional interfaces for special cases or faster paths. Your application code never touches driver.Conn. It talks to *sql.DB, *sql.Rows and *sql.Tx, which are concrete types the core controls.


The core defines one socket. Every database driver is a plug shaped to fit it.

Adapters plug themselves in

Each driver is an adapter, and it registers itself. This is the whole init in lib/pq's conn.go:

func init() {
    sql.Register("postgres", &Driver{})
}

go-sql-driver/mysql does the same with sql.Register(driverName, &MySQLDriver{}), and its package comment tells you to use it via import _ "github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql". The official Go database tutorial explains why the underscore is there: if you never call a function from the driver package directly, you need a blank import so the package still loads.

import (
    "database/sql"

    _ "github.com/lib/pq"
)

func open(dsn string) (*sql.DB, error) {
    return sql.Open("postgres", dsn)
}

The blank import runs init, init writes into a map inside database/sql, and sql.Open looks the name up in that map. Your code depends only on the port. The adapter is a line in your import block. The SQLDrivers wiki page lists roughly 60 adapters built this way, from pgx to modernc.org/sqlite, and marks the ones that pass a shared compatibility test suite.

Optional interfaces: capabilities without a fat port

Here is the part worth borrowing first. The required port stayed tiny, but the protocol grew a lot after 2012: context cancellation, named parameters, session resets, connection validation. The Go team did not add those methods to driver.Conn, which would have broken every driver. They added separate, optional interfaces and let the core detect them at runtime.

Go 1.8 brought QueryerContext, ExecerContext, ConnBeginTx and Pinger. Go 1.9 brought NamedValueChecker. Go 1.10 brought Connector, DriverContext and SessionResetter. Go 1.15 brought Validator. An old driver that implements none of them still compiles and still works.

The detection is a type assertion with a fallback. A simplified sketch of what queryDC in sql.go does:

// simplified sketch of database/sql's queryDC
queryerCtx, ok := dc.ci.(driver.QueryerContext)
var queryer driver.Queryer
if !ok {
    queryer, ok = dc.ci.(driver.Queryer)
}
if ok {
    rows, err := ctxDriverQuery(ctx, queryerCtx,
        queryer, query, args)
    if err != driver.ErrSkip {
        return rows, err // adapter handled it
    }
}
// fallback: Prepare, Query, Close the statement

The driver package docs spell out the chain: if a Conn implements neither QueryerContext nor Queryer, DB.Query prepares the statement, runs it, and closes it. And driver.ErrSkip, whose message reads "driver: skip fast-path; continue as if unimplemented", lets an adapter say "I have this capability, but not for this particular call."

Argument checking follows the same idea. According to convert.go, the core looks for NamedValueChecker on the statement first, then on the connection, and falls back to the statement's column converter or its own default checker when neither exists or when the checker returns ErrSkip. pgx's stdlib adapter implements CheckNamedValue, ResetSession and QueryContext. A smaller driver can skip all three and still get correct behaviour from the core.

That gives you a port that can grow for a decade without a breaking change.

The pool lives in the core

The other half of the design is what adapters do not have to write. The sql.OpenDB doc comment says the returned DB "maintains its own pool of idle connections". The DB struct in that same file holds freeConn, connRequests, maxOpen, maxLifetime and maxIdleTime. Idle connections default to defaultMaxIdleConns = 2, and SetMaxOpenConns documents that "The default is 0 (unlimited)."

No driver reimplements pooling, lifetimes or waiting for a free connection. The adapter contributes hooks the core calls at the right moment. If a Conn implements Validator, the driver docs say IsValid runs before the connection goes back to the pool. If it implements SessionResetter, ResetSession runs before reuse. And driver.ErrBadConn tells the core to retry on a fresh connection, with a warning not to return it if the server might already have done the work.

Policy in the core, mechanism in the adapter. When you design your own ports, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking and pooling belong on the core side for the same reason: otherwise every adapter writes its own slightly different version.

The half you should not copy: a global registry

Now the part that breaks the hexagonal rules. In sql.go, the registry is a package-level map behind a mutex:

var driversMu sync.RWMutex
var drivers = make(map[string]driver.Driver)

Adapters are wired by import side effects into global state, not by an explicit composition root, which Mark Seemann describes as "a (preferably) unique location in an application where modules are composed together." Three costs follow from that.

First, the wiring fails at runtime, not compile time. That is the error from the top of this post: the message has to guess at the forgotten import because the compiler never sees the dependency.

Second, names collide globally. Register panics with sql: Register called twice for driver on a duplicate name. pgx works around that in its init: it registers "pgx" only if sql.Drivers() does not already contain it, and always registers "pgx/v5".

Third, the map is now hard to change. The comment above it in sql.go says it should be an internal detail, but that other packages reach into it via linkname, and asks that its type signature not change.


Side-effect registration on the left, an explicit composition root on the right.

Go 1.10 gave you the exit. sql.OpenDB takes a driver.Connector value instead of a name string, so main hands the adapter to the core directly:

// pgx is github.com/jackc/pgx/v5
// stdlib is github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib (pgx's adapter)
cfg, err := pgx.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
db := sql.OpenDB(stdlib.GetConnector(*cfg))

MySQL has the same shape through mysql.NewConnector, which the Go tutorial uses as its example. Importing the package still runs its init, so the registry entry still exists, but your code no longer depends on a magic string or on import order.

Apply the good half to your own ports

Take the three habits that aged well and leave the registry behind. Say a billing service sends notifications. The service package owns the port, a richer capability is optional, and there is always a fallback:

package billing

// Sender is the port. billing owns it.
type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, m Message) error
}

// BatchSender is optional. Detected, never required.
type BatchSender interface {
    SendBatch(ctx context.Context, ms []Message) error
}

func (s *Service) notifyAll(
    ctx context.Context, ms []Message,
) error {
    if bs, ok := s.sender.(BatchSender); ok {
        return bs.SendBatch(ctx, ms)
    }
    for _, m := range ms {
        if err := s.sender.Send(ctx, m); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

Retries and rate limits go in Service, not in each adapter, the same way sql.DB owns the pool. And the wiring happens in one visible place:

func main() {
    db := mustOpenDB()
    repo := postgres.NewInvoiceRepo(db)
    sender := smtp.NewSender(loadSMTPConfig())
    svc := billing.NewService(repo, sender)
    runHTTP(svc)
}

No init, no name strings, no blank imports. If you forget an adapter, the code does not compile. For tests, pass a fake Sender into NewService, which is exactly the isolation Cockburn's 2005 write-up was after.

Next time you type import _ for a database driver, read it as the stdlib showing you the pattern, and the one place it cut a corner. Wire your own adapters in main.

If this was useful

database/sql gets the port and the capability detection right, and gets the wiring wrong. Hexagonal Architecture in Go works through both halves for your own services: where ports live in the package layout, how persistence adapters stay behind them, and how to build a composition root in main that the compiler can check. If the billing example above looks like the direction you want your codebase to go, that book is the long version of it.

title: 'useMemo' Hook in React
description:
When building React applications, components can re-render many times. During re-rendering, some calculations may run again even when the data has not changed. To avoid unnecessary calculations, React provides a Hook called useMemo.

What is useMemo?

useMemo is a React Hook that remembers, or caches, the result of a calculation. React can reuse the previous result when its dependencies have not changed.

For example:

import { useMemo } from "react";

const result = useMemo(() => {
  return number * number;
}, [number]);

Here, number is the dependency. If its value stays the same, React can reuse the cached result instead of recalculating it.

Why Do We Need useMemo?

Imagine a college application that displays student results. The application filters thousands of student records to find students who scored above 80 marks.

const topStudents = useMemo(() => {
  return students.filter(
    student => student.marks >= 80
  );
}, [students]);

Here, React can reuse the filtered student list when the students dependency remains unchanged. If the student data changes, React recalculates the list.

Understanding the Dependency Array

The dependency array tells React which values the calculation depends on.

const total = useMemo(
  () => price * quantity,
  [price, quantity]
);

If either price or quantity changes, React recalculates the total. If neither changes, React can reuse the previous result.

When Should We Use useMemo?

We can use useMemo when performing expensive calculations, filtering large datasets, sorting records, or processing complex data.

However, we should not use it for every small calculation. For simple operations, using useMemo may add unnecessary complexity without providing much benefit.

It is also important to understand that useMemo does not prevent a component from re-rendering. It only helps avoid unnecessary recalculations.

Conclusion

useMemo is a useful React Hook for improving performance when calculations are expensive. It caches a calculation result between renders and recalculates it when its dependencies change.

title: My Q4 model said True where BF16 said False, so I diffed them layer by layer
description:
Qwen3-0.6B in BF16 reads this:

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return

and puts 97.9% on False. The Q4_K_M quant of the same model puts 79.1% on True.

That's one token out of 1,282 I scored. Across the whole text, Q4_K_M changes the top token at 11.6% of positions, its mean KL from BF16 is 0.067, and perplexity goes from 7.83 to 8.53. Those numbers tell you the quant drifted. They don't tell you where: which tokens, which layers, which block inside a layer, or whether the weights are even the main cause compared with the KV cache or the batch size.

I built heterodyne to answer that.

zaydmulani09 / heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, and move activations between them to test which layers, and which attention or MLP blocks, carry the divergence. Local, CPU, no API keys.

heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, then move activations between them to test which layers' divergence actually reaches the output.

A quantized GGUF, a quantized KV cache, a different batch size, a fine-tune: each changes what your model says, and the usual answer to "how much, and where?" is one aggregate number. heterodyne runs two configurations of llama.cpp (two arms: a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers) on identical tokens and shows:

  • where the outputs differ: exact full-vocabulary KL(A‖B) and top-1 changes at every position, next to a measured numerical floor;
  • where inside the network the difference appears: the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • which layers carry it to the output: activation transplants that write one arm's residual stream into the other, layer by layer, in llama.cpp's own numerics;
  • attention or MLP…
View on GitHub

Why not the usual interpretability tools

TransformerLens, nnsight and the rest run PyTorch. But on CPU, llama.cpp quantizes the activations to 8 bits before every quantized matrix multiply. A PyTorch model with dequantized weights is a different model from the GGUF you actually run. And llama.cpp's own llama-perplexity --kl-divergence reports aggregates only.

So heterodyne works inside llama.cpp, in the same kernels you deploy.

Two arms, same tokens

An arm is a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers: K and V cache types, flash attention, ubatch size. heterodyne runs arm A and arm B on identical tokens, chunk by chunk, and records:

  • exact KL(A‖B) over the full vocabulary at every position, summed in f64 from raw logits, plus every top-1 change and how confident it was;
  • a numerical floor: arm A re-run with an odd batch split, as a yardstick for how big harmless differences get on this machine;
  • the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • transplants (next section);
  • optionally, every combination of the settings that differ, to attribute the change to one of them.

Everything is saved as an experiment file with provenance (GGUF hashes, llama.cpp commit, build flags) and an integrity hash. heterodyne verify re-runs it and compares every stored number exactly.

The hook

llama.cpp's scheduler accepts an eval callback, cb_eval. When it's set, the scheduler asks for each graph node "do you want this tensor?" and, if you say yes, computes everything up to that node, synchronizes, and hands you the data before anything downstream runs.

A small C++ shim uses that moment to either copy the tensor out or overwrite it. Every consumer of a node comes after it in topological order, so an overwrite is seen by everything downstream. Tensors are addressed by graph name: l_out-N is the residual stream after layer N, ffn_inp-N the residual between layer N's attention and its MLP. The shim counts rows per ubatch and checks that every row of every hooked tensor was seen, so a missing name is an error, not silent zeros. Rust only sees structs I define, so a llama.cpp update can't silently shift a field under the FFI.

Transplants

Denoise: run B, but write A's l_out-N into it, and measure KL(A‖patched B). Noise: the reverse. Do it at every layer and you get a curve. For Q4_K_M vs BF16:

layer   0      4      8      12     16     20     24     26     27
KL    0.062  0.052  0.038  0.029  0.021  0.013  0.006  0.004  0.0013

It falls steadily over all 28 layers: no single layer carries the divergence. The 0.0013 left after the last layer is what the final norm and output head add on their own.

At the is_prime token, writing BF16's residual into Q4_K_M brings that token's KL from 0.48 after layer 6 down to 0.04 after layer 9, and writing Q4_K_M's residual into BF16 reproduces the flip from about layer 12. At that token, the decisive difference forms in layers 6 to 12.

New: attention or MLP?

The obvious way to split a layer is to write A's MLP output into B. The problem: that also erases the MLP's reaction to every difference upstream, so a block with identical weights in both arms can still look responsible.

So heterodyne restores A's whole residual at two points per layer, after attention (ffn_inp-N) and after the MLP (l_out-N), and takes the steps between consecutive points. Attention's share at layer N is the KL with A restored at the layer's input minus the KL with A restored after attention; the MLP's is the next step. The steps telescope: summed over all layers they equal the untouched KL minus what's left after the last layer, so nothing is counted twice.

There's a check with a known answer. If two arms differ only in K-cache type, only attention reads the K cache, so every MLP step must be exactly zero. The tests check that bitwise, and it holds on Qwen3 too.

12 chunks, 1,282 scored positions, 95% intervals over chunks:

attention MLP
restoring BF16 in Q4_K_M (of 0.067) removes 0.030 (0.019–0.041) removes 0.036 (0.024–0.048)
injecting Q4_K_M into BF16 adds 0.026 (0.021–0.031) adds 0.040 (0.028–0.051)

Restoring BF16, the paired difference is 0.006 (−0.011 to 0.022): it spans zero, and attention's part ranges from 20% to 82% across chunks, so on this text the two can't be told apart. Injecting Q4_K_M, the MLPs add more (0.014, 0.005 to 0.023). The largest single step is layer 0's attention, but llama.cpp doesn't name layer 0's input, so that bar also holds any difference in the token embeddings. A few steps are negative (layer 2's attention, −0.0014): restoring that block alone left Q4_K_M further from BF16.

It costs two more passes per layer per chunk; the 12-chunk run took 29 minutes on a laptop i7-1355U.

Other things it turned up

All on Qwen3-0.6B, same text, same laptop:

B mean KL top-1 changed perplexity (BF16: 7.83)
Q8_0 0.0022 2.2% 7.83
UD-Q4_K_XL 0.058 11.3% 8.33
Q4_K_M 0.067 11.6% 8.53
Q3_K_M 0.214 20.8% 9.47
Q2_K 0.780 36.3% 16.75
  • The KV cache matters more than you'd think. Same Q8_0 file twice, B with a q8_0 K and V cache: KL 0.0038. That's further than quantizing the weights from BF16 to Q8_0 (0.0022).
  • llama.cpp's CPU path isn't batch-invariant at every size. With flash attention off, Q4_K_M output was bitwise identical at ubatch sizes that are multiples of 4 and changed at others (ubatch 63: 4.7% of top tokens). The repacked K-quant matmul quantizes activation rows in groups of 4 and sends the remainder down a separate path. That's why heterodyne's numerical floor uses an odd split.

What this is and isn't

  • One small model, one text, one machine. Intervals are 95% t-intervals with a cluster-robust standard error over chunks, because tokens within a chunk are correlated.
  • Transplants are interventions on your input. They say where restoring one model's activations removes the divergence on that text, not which block's weights quantize worse in general.
  • CPU only. GPU kernels compute differently, and nothing here says anything about them yet.

Try it

Grab a binary from the releases (Linux, Windows, macOS arm64) and run:

heterodyne serve --models ~/models

or from the command line:

heterodyne diff --a Qwen3-0.6B-BF16.gguf --b Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --text-file examples/corpus.txt --chunk 128 --max-chunks 12 --components

The experiment files behind every number here are in examples/. If you run it on a bigger model or different prompts, I'd love to see what you get.

title: Your AI Agent Needs a Face: Building Animated AI Assistants for Web Apps
description:
AI agents can think, plan, and respond. But can your users actually tell what they're doing? Let's explore how interactive animation, Rive, and React can make AI assistants feel more responsive, expressive, and human-friendly.

AI agents are becoming a familiar part of modern web applications.

They're answering customer questions, helping users complete tasks, generating content, analyzing data, and automating entire workflows.

But there's one thing many AI interfaces still have in common.

They look like a chat box.

You type a message, wait for a response, and watch a few dots animate while the AI processes your request.

That works.

But what if your AI assistant could communicate what it's doing through movement, expressions, and real-time reactions?

Imagine an assistant that:

  • Welcomes users when they open the application.
  • Listens attentively while someone speaks.
  • Shows a thoughtful expression while generating a response.
  • Moves its mouth naturally when speaking.
  • Celebrates when a task is completed.
  • Reacts gently when something goes wrong.

This is where interactive AI characters and animated mascots can make a difference.

And tools like Rive make it possible to build these experiences for production web applications.

Let's explore how.

1. The Problem With Traditional AI Chat Interfaces

Most AI-powered products have a similar interaction pattern:

User Input → Loading Indicator → AI Response

From a technical perspective, that's completely reasonable.

But from a user experience perspective, there's often a communication gap.

Consider a voice AI assistant.

When a user finishes speaking, they might wonder:

  • Did the assistant hear me?
  • Is it processing my request?
  • Is it about to respond?
  • Has something gone wrong?

A loading spinner communicates activity, but it doesn't necessarily communicate which activity is happening.

An animated AI character can offer an additional layer of visual feedback.

For example:

AI Activity Visual Behavior
Ready Natural breathing, blinking
Listening Attentive eyes, subtle head movement
Thinking Thoughtful expression, slower motion
Speaking Mouth animation, facial movement
Success Smile, small celebration
Error Concerned or reassuring expression

These behaviors can help users understand the current interaction without repeatedly reading status messages.

Of course, animation should support clear text and accessibility features, not replace them.

The goal isn't to make an AI system pretend to be human.

It's to make its interface easier to understand.

2. What Is an Interactive AI Mascot?

An interactive AI mascot is an animated character that responds to events from an application.

Unlike a traditional GIF or looping video, its behavior can change dynamically.

For example, your application might send a status update:

activity = "thinking"

The mascot responds by switching into a thinking animation.

When the AI starts speaking:

activity = "speaking"

The character transitions into a speaking state.

These transitions are driven by application logic rather than a fixed video timeline.

An interactive mascot might also receive additional information:

  • Emotion or response tone
  • Audio intensity
  • Mouth shape or viseme
  • Cursor position
  • User interaction events
  • Task completion events

This creates opportunities for more expressive interfaces without relying on prerecorded videos for every possible interaction.

3. Why Use Rive for AI Character Animation?

Rive is a real-time interactive animation tool designed for applications, websites, and games.

It's particularly useful when visual elements need to respond to changing application state.

With Rive, designers can build animated characters and define how different animations interact.

Developers can then connect the animation system to their application through supported runtimes.

For an AI assistant, several Rive capabilities are especially useful.

State Machines

State machines manage how animations transition between behaviors.

For example:

Idle → Listening → Thinking → Speaking → Idle

But real AI interactions aren't always linear.

A user might interrupt an assistant while it's speaking.

A network request could fail during thinking.

Or a user might close the voice interface entirely.

A well-designed state machine can account for these situations.

Data Binding

Rive Data Binding allows application data to influence visual properties and animation behavior.

You can expose values such as activity, emotion, or audio level and connect them to your character's animation system.

This creates a useful separation between application logic and character animation.

Reusable Character Rigs

A reusable rig lets one character support different behaviors and expressions without requiring a completely separate design for every state.

Runtime Integration

Rive supports web and mobile development workflows, making it suitable for interactive experiences across different platforms.

The important advantage isn't simply that Rive can animate a character.

It's that the animation can respond to the product.

4. Designing the AI Assistant's Behavior System

Before animating a character, define what your AI assistant actually needs to communicate.

For a conversational web assistant, I would typically start with six core activities.

Idle

The character is available but isn't currently interacting.

Possible movements:

  • Subtle breathing
  • Natural blinking
  • Small head movements
  • Occasional eye movement

Good idle animation should make the character feel present without distracting users from the interface.

Listening

The assistant is receiving user input.

Possible movements:

  • Attentive eye expression
  • Slight head tilt
  • Gentle reactive movement
  • Subtle response to microphone activity

Avoid exaggerated movement that could suggest the assistant is speaking when it's actually listening.

Thinking

The assistant is processing a request.

Possible movements:

  • Thoughtful facial expression
  • Slow eye movement
  • Gentle head movement
  • Controlled looping animation

Thinking animations should communicate progress without implying the AI has a particular internal emotion.

Speaking

The assistant is delivering a response.

Possible movements:

  • Mouth animation
  • Facial expressions
  • Natural head movement
  • Small gestures
  • Audio-reactive animation

For voice applications, you can go beyond a simple open-and-close mouth animation.

More on that shortly.

Success

The assistant completes a task.

Possible movements:

  • Smile
  • Celebration gesture
  • Small jump
  • Positive facial expression

Success reactions work well when used selectively.

Celebrating after every basic message quickly becomes repetitive.

Error

Something goes wrong.

Possible movements:

  • Concerned expression
  • Small apologetic gesture
  • Return to a calm resting pose

The animation should complement an actionable error message explaining what happened.

5. Connecting an AI Agent to an Animated Character

Here's a simple architecture for connecting an AI agent to an interactive Rive character.

              USER
               |
               v
        React Application
               |
               v
        AI Agent Controller
               |
       +-------+--------+
       |                |
       v                v
  AI Backend       UI Activity
  / Voice API       Controller
       |                |
       |                v
       |           Rive Runtime
       |                |
       +--------------->|
                        v
                Animated Mascot

The important principle is to separate the responsibilities.

AI backend: Processes requests and generates responses.

Application controller: Determines the current interaction activity.

Rive animation system: Displays the visual response.

This separation keeps your character animation independent from whichever AI provider your application uses.

Whether the backend is powered by OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, or another model, the visual interface can respond through the same normalized activity system.

6. A Simple React Activity Controller

Let's start by defining the possible activities.

type AgentActivity =
  | "idle"
  | "listening"
  | "thinking"
  | "speaking"
  | "success"
  | "error";

Now create a small React component that manages the application-side state.

import { useState } from "react";

type AgentActivity =
  | "idle"
  | "listening"
  | "thinking"
  | "speaking"
  | "success"
  | "error";

export default function AgentDemo() {
  const [activity, setActivity] =
    useState<AgentActivity>("idle");

  const activities: AgentActivity[] = [
    "idle",
    "listening",
    "thinking",
    "speaking",
    "success",
    "error",
  ];

  return (
    <main>
      <h2>AI Assistant</h2>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        Current activity: {activity}
      </p>

      <div className="agent-preview">
        {/* Mount your Rive character here */}
      </div>

      <div className="controls">
        {activities.map((nextActivity) => (
          <button
            key={nextActivity}
            onClick={() => setActivity(nextActivity)}
          >
            {nextActivity}
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>
    </main>
  );
}

This is an application-state demo, not yet a complete Rive integration.

The next step is to connect activity to a Rive View Model property through the appropriate React runtime API.

For example, your Rive project could expose an enum property named activity with the same six values.

Your integration would then follow this flow:

React activity changes
         |
         v
Update Rive View Model
         |
         v
Rive State Machine
         |
         v
Character transitions

In modern Rive workflows, Data Binding is a useful approach for this connection.

The exact integration code depends on your chosen runtime version and exported Rive file. See the official Rive runtime documentation for the current API.

7. Making Your AI Assistant Speak Naturally

One of the most interesting challenges in conversational AI animation is lip synchronization.

A basic speaking animation might repeatedly open and close the character's mouth.

That can work for a simple chatbot.

But voice AI products can benefit from more expressive mouth movement.

There are two common approaches.

Audio-Level Animation

Use the current audio amplitude to influence how much the mouth opens.

Conceptually:

const mouthOpen = Math.min(
  Math.max(audioLevel, 0),
  1
);

Then provide mouthOpen to the Rive character.

The animation system can use this value to control mouth movement.

This approach is relatively simple, but it doesn't accurately reproduce individual speech sounds.

Viseme-Based Lip Sync

Visemes represent visual mouth shapes associated with speech sounds.

A speech system capable of providing viseme information can send these values to the animation layer.

For example:

type Viseme = 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;

Your Rive character could support six simplified mouth shapes.

As the voice system produces timed viseme data, the animation controller updates the mouth shape accordingly.

Text-to-Speech System
         |
         v
Timed Viseme Events
         |
         v
Animation Controller
         |
         v
Rive Mouth Shapes

For accurate lip sync, timing matters as much as the mouth shapes themselves.

Your developer needs to coordinate the animation with actual audio playback rather than assuming that generated text and sound will arrive simultaneously.

Not every voice API provides viseme events, so the implementation depends on the audio system you're using.

8. Making the Character React to Emotion

An AI assistant doesn't necessarily need a different full-body animation for every response tone.

Instead, emotion can often be designed as an additional control layer.

For example:

type AgentEmotion =
  | "neutral"
  | "happy"
  | "empathetic"
  | "concerned"
  | "surprised";

Your activity and emotion controls can work independently.

Example:

Activity: Speaking
Emotion: Happy

The character speaks with a positive expression.

Another example:

Activity: Listening
Emotion: Concerned

The character listens attentively with a more serious facial expression.

This modular approach can reduce duplicated animation work.

However, avoid assuming that an AI model's tone classification perfectly represents the user's emotional state.

Use expressions conservatively, especially in sensitive applications such as healthcare, financial assistance, or mental health support.

9. Designing Transitions That Don't Break

This is where interactive animation becomes a real engineering problem.

Consider the following situation:

Your character is speaking.

The user interrupts.

Your application immediately switches to listening.

What should happen to the character's mouth, hands, and facial expression?

If the animation system isn't designed carefully, you might see:

  • A mouth frozen open
  • Sudden head movement
  • Hands snapping into the wrong pose
  • Conflicting animations
  • Unexpected idle transitions

The solution is to define clear transition rules and ownership of animation properties.

For example:

Transition Expected Behavior
Idle → Listening Smooth attentive movement
Listening → Thinking Gradual pose transition
Thinking → Speaking Begin speaking posture
Speaking → Listening Stop lip sync and reset mouth
Any state → Error Interrupt safely
Success → Idle Complete reaction, return to rest

For some characters, a single activity enum is sufficient.

For more advanced systems, separate layers for body movement, facial expressions, and mouth animation may provide greater flexibility.

The best architecture depends on the character and product requirements.

10. Don't Forget Performance and Accessibility

An animated AI assistant should improve the experience, not make the application harder to use.

Before shipping, consider the following.

Performance

Keep artwork and animation systems as efficient as possible.

Test your Rive file on the actual devices and browsers your users will use.

Pay attention to unnecessary redraws, heavy assets, and complex layered animations.

Reduced Motion

Respect users who prefer reduced motion.

Your application should offer a calmer version of the character or a static alternative when appropriate.

Accessibility

Animation alone shouldn't communicate critical information.

If the agent is listening, thinking, or reporting an error, provide accessible status information as well.

For example, use appropriate status messages for screen-reader users without announcing every decorative animation transition.

User Control

Allow users to minimize or disable the animated assistant.

A helpful mascot shouldn't become an obstacle.

11. Where Animated AI Assistants Make Sense

Interactive AI characters aren't appropriate for every product.

But they can be particularly useful when the application benefits from ongoing visual communication.

Potential use cases include:

AI coaching platforms: A companion that welcomes users, listens, and provides encouragement.

Language learning applications: A speaking character with expressive mouth movement and positive feedback.

Voice AI interfaces: A visual indicator for listening, thinking, and speaking.

Educational applications: Interactive tutors that guide students through tasks.

Product onboarding: Friendly characters that explain features and celebrate completed steps.

Virtual pets and gamified apps: Characters that reflect progress, rewards, and activity.

Customer support interfaces: An optional visual assistant that communicates its current activity.

In each case, the design should be driven by the user's needs rather than adding a mascot simply because it's visually appealing.

12. How I Approach Rive AI Mascot Projects

As a freelance Rive animator, I focus on building interactive character systems that designers and developers can actually use in production.

For AI companion projects, my workflow generally includes:

  1. Understanding the application's interactions and required character behaviors.
  2. Planning the character rig and animation states.
  3. Building expressive idle, listening, thinking, speaking, and reaction animations.
  4. Creating and testing the state machine.
  5. Defining runtime-facing inputs or Data Binding properties.
  6. Testing transitions, interruption behavior, and animation loops.
  7. Delivering the Rive assets with clear integration guidance.

For more advanced projects, this can also include lip-sync mouth shapes, audio-reactive animation, gaze tracking, emotions, and reusable character systems.

The goal is to create something that looks good but also behaves reliably inside the application.

Final Thoughts: Give Your AI Agent a Better Interface

AI agents are becoming increasingly capable.

But the interface connecting those systems to users still matters.

A thoughtfully animated character can make an AI product feel more responsive, approachable, and easier to understand.

It doesn't need exaggerated expressions or constant movement.

Sometimes a natural blink, an attentive listening pose, or a smooth transition into speaking is enough.

The best AI mascot isn't the one that moves the most. It's the one that communicates the right thing at the right moment.

And with tools like Rive, these experiences can become part of a real web application's interaction system rather than remaining a decorative animation.

Need an Interactive Rive Animator for Your AI Project?

I'm Praneeth Kawya Thathsara, a freelance Rive animator specializing in interactive mascots, AI character animation, state machines, lip sync, and developer-ready animation systems.

I work with startups, designers, and development teams building interactive experiences for websites, mobile applications, and AI-powered products.

If you're creating an AI agent, voice assistant, AI coach, or interactive mascot, I'd be happy to help bring the character to life.

Explore my work: RiveAnimator.com

Interactive AI mascot services: MascotEngine.com

Email: riveanimator@gmail.com

Let's build an AI character that doesn't just animate — it interacts.

title: A Green Test Suite Can Still Hide a Broken PR: 5 Questions to Ask Before Merging
description:
AI coding assistants can write implementation code and tests in minutes. The problem is that both can look correct while the behavior that matters remains untested.

A passing test suite is useful evidence, but it isn't proof that a change is correct.

I've been thinking about this problem while building a Java-focused, AI-powered pull request reviewer. These are five questions I believe developers should ask before approving a PR, especially when AI helped write the code or its tests.

1. What behavior is this test actually verifying?

Start with the expected behavior, not the number of assertions.

Imagine a service that should reject a payment when the account has insufficient funds. A test might call the service and verify that it returns a response.

But what if the test never checks whether the payment was rejected?

The test can execute successfully without verifying the important business rule.

Ask yourself:

  • What behavior should this test protect?
  • What result would prove that behavior?
  • Would the test fail if the behavior were broken?

If you cannot answer these questions, the test may provide less confidence than its green status suggests.

2. Could this test pass without checking anything meaningful?

Consider this JUnit example:

java
@test
void shouldRejectInvalidPayment() {
paymentService.processPayment(invalidPayment);

assertTrue(true);

}

The test passes as long as execution reaches the assertion. It doesn't establish that the payment was rejected.

A more meaningful test would verify the expected outcome, using the appropriate assertion for the application's behavior.

For example, if the contract requires an exception:

java
@test
void shouldRejectInvalidPayment() {
assertThrows(
InvalidPaymentException.class,
() -> paymentService.processPayment(invalidPayment)
);
}

This is only an illustration. The correct assertion depends on the actual application contract.

The important principle is simple: an assertion should verify the behavior the test claims to protect.

3. Are mocks hiding the behavior we need to verify?

Mocks are valuable when testing dependencies, failure conditions, and isolated units of code. But excessive mocking can make a test appear meaningful while avoiding the behavior that matters.

Suppose a test claims to verify that an order is saved correctly, but it mocks the repository and only verifies that save() was called.

That may establish that a method was invoked. It doesn't necessarily establish that the order was persisted correctly or that the resulting state is correct.

Before approving a heavily mocked test, ask:

  • Is the test checking an outcome or just an interaction?
  • Is the mocked dependency the behavior being tested?
  • Would an incorrect implementation still satisfy the assertions?
  • Should an integration test verify the real interaction between components?

Don't remove mocks indiscriminately. Choose the test boundary that matches the behavior you're trying to protect.

4. Does the test cover the change described in the PR?

A PR can change behavior without changing the test that originally covered it.

For example, a developer might change the conditions under which a user can access a resource. The existing test may still verify the successful access path while failing to check the newly introduced restriction.

Compare the change with the tests:

  • Which behavior changed?
  • Which existing tests exercise that behavior?
  • What new failure scenario could the change introduce?
  • Are the expected outcomes explicit?

This is also where repository context matters. The affected behavior might involve callers or related files that aren't part of the diff.

A reviewer should consider those relationships rather than treating each changed line as an isolated unit.

5. Would the test catch a deliberately broken implementation?

This is a useful thought experiment.

Imagine the implementation contains a defect that violates the requirement. Would the test fail?

If the answer is no, the test may not protect that requirement.

Mutation testing takes this idea further by making deliberate changes to the implementation and checking whether the tests detect them. It can provide stronger evidence than simply counting assertions, although it has its own limitations and costs.

You don't need a full mutation-testing setup to start asking the question during code review. But actually running tests against controlled mutations is a separate validation step, not something a normal passing test run proves.

The practical takeaway

Before merging a PR, especially one produced with AI assistance, ask:

  1. Does the test verify the intended behavior?
  2. Could it pass without a meaningful assertion?
  3. Are mocks hiding the behavior that matters?
  4. Do the tests cover the changed behavior and relevant regression scenarios?
  5. Would the tests detect a broken implementation?

These checks won't guarantee that every defect is caught. They can, however, help identify tests that create confidence without providing enough evidence.

AI can help write code and tests faster. The review process still needs to establish what those tests actually prove.

Disclosure: I'm building CodeGuard AI, a self-hosted AI-powered pull request reviewer for GitHub. It reviews PR changes alongside repository context and supports custom team review rules. It does not currently run mutation testing or guarantee detection of every weak test assertion.

Learn more about CodeGuard AI

title: Easy Full Stack Authentication and Login in the Style of Spring
description:
Three requests leave your app just as its access token expires. If each refreshes independently, the first exchange can invalidate the refresh token the other two are about to use. A login feature becomes a race between requests.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

This week's security work joins the Codename One client and backend around those transitions. The client can coordinate renewal, the server can rotate tokens, and tests can verify what happens after a real request is refused.

Put the access rule beside the route

The backend has Spring-style security chains under com.codename1.backend.security. A chain chooses which requests it handles, then authenticates and authorizes them. This excerpt from the security guide example protects an API using JWT scopes:

@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) {
    http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders:read")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .sessionManagement(session ->
            session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}

Configure the trusted issuer and the audience your API expects. The guide's configuration keys include cn1.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri and cn1.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences. Audience checking is optional unless configured, so set it deliberately when several services share an issuer.

A backend with no SecurityFilterChain bean has no security layer. Adding a dependency does not secure the routes. A stateless chain also has no CSRF filter unless you request one. Session-based browser applications have a different threat model and need the corresponding session and CSRF configuration.

Method rules such as @PreAuthorize are compiled into checks. They can apply to self-calls and private methods because the build weaves them into the method, rather than relying on calls passing through a runtime proxy. The expression language is a supported subset; ACLs, @PostAuthorize and arbitrary expression evaluation are outside it.

Give the client one owner for renewal

Register an installed app as a public OAuth client with an exact redirect URI and PKCE. A client secret embedded in an app would not remain secret. After configuring OidcClient, install an authorizer for the API base URL:

OidcRequestAuthorizer authorizer =
        new OidcRequestAuthorizer(client).install("https://api.example.com/v1");
authorizer.addSignInRequiredListener((source, reason) -> showSignIn());
authorizer.load().ready(saved -> {
    if (saved == null) {
        showSignIn();
    } else {
        showNotes();
    }
});

This is an application excerpt: client is configured with your provider and token store; showSignIn() and showNotes() are your UI methods. Use SecureStorageTokenStore for platform-protected persistence. Plain storage fallback is an explicit option, not something the app should silently enable to make an error disappear.

The authorizer matches the scheme, host and port, then whole path segments. /v1 includes /v1/notes, but not /v10. It covers ordinary ConnectionRequest calls, the REST builder and generated clients through the network layer.

Renewal starts before expiry by default. Requests queued during the exchange wait for its result. If a token-bearing request receives 401, the authorizer can refresh and retry it once; the caller receives the eventual response. A refused refresh ends the session, clears stored tokens and calls the sign-in listener. If your request writes a body from a stream, verify that your implementation can supply it again before depending on a retry.

For redirects followed by Codename One, the token is removed outside the registered origin or path. The current iOS port lets the system follow redirects before application code sees them. Keep protected API redirects within hosts you control; do not infer that every transport has the same redirect interception point.

Choose the state your deployment can share

The backend includes form login, HTTP Basic, API keys, JWT resource servers, OAuth login and authorization-server support. MFA includes TOTP and recovery codes; passkey endpoints use WebAuthn. These are separate mechanisms with separate configuration, not one switch that makes every deployment secure.

Several instances cannot share an in-memory token repository or rate limiter. Declare the database-backed stores when that is your deployment shape. cn1.security.schema.enabled=true belongs in the module's build-time application.properties; it registers the security migrations. It creates tables, but does not select JDBC stores for you.

Refresh tokens and one-use codes must be consumed atomically. Otherwise two instances can both accept the same secret. The JDBC implementations use conditional database operations and their affected-row counts for those decisions. TOTP secrets are sealed under the configured encryption key; password hashes and one-use recovery codes have their own storage rules.

The packaged server links the mechanisms its chains reach. A token-verifying API need not carry login pages and a password store. That is a useful consequence of explicit configuration and dead-code removal, although it does not reduce the need to review the rules you enabled.

Test the failure after the successful login

The end-to-end client tests connect to the HelloCodenameOne backend. BackendTokenRefreshTest deliberately replaces an access token with one the server did not sign. It checks that the generated client receives one successful response after renewal, that the refresh token rotates, and that reusing a spent refresh token ends the session.

That proves more than a mock that always supplies an authenticated user. It exercises the client's networking and token state together with the server's token endpoint and protected route.

Test layer What it can establish What it does not establish
Backend MockMvc and mock identities Route and method authorization decisions A provider login or signature verification when identity is injected
Native client integration tests Requests, token exchange, renewal and denial against the backend Every external identity provider or device sign-in surface
Browser-specific tests Browser networking and credential APIs, including the virtual-authenticator vault test Passing the native credential/redirect harness unchanged
Port test matrix The declared cases on each supported target Every security mechanism on every port

The credential/redirect tests explicitly report a browser skip because the browser owns those cookies and redirects. A green port suite must be read with those skips. WebAuthn PRF bridge coverage uses Chromium's virtual authenticator; it is not a claim that every hardware authenticator supports that extension.

SAML, LDAP, opaque-token introspection and several authorization-server extensions are outside this release. The backend security guide and client identity guide specify the supported surface. PR #5961 connects those pieces; tomorrow we will look at the migrations underneath their persistent stores.

Discussion

Which failure is hardest to reproduce in your sign-in flow: renewal, revocation, or returning from the provider?

title: css-ghost: find and delete orphaned CSS selectors with zero config
description:
You've been there. You rename a component, move a file, or quietly migrate from one styling approach to another – and the old CSS stays behind. Nobody complains, the build doesn't break, and the dead selectors quietly accumulate.

css-ghost is a small Node.js CLI tool I built to solve that problem. Point it at a folder and it tells you every CSS class defined in your style files that isn't referenced anywhere in your components.

What it does

css-ghost scans your style files (.css, .module.css, .scss, .sass, .less, MUI makeStyles, vanilla-extract), extracts every class selector, then cross-references them against every component file it can find (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, .vue, .svelte).

Anything defined but never actually used gets reported as an orphan – with its line number and the full CSS rule printed inline, so you can see what it does before deciding to delete it.

It also catches orphaned CSS custom properties (--my-token: value defined but never consumed via var(--my-token) anywhere in the codebase), reported in a separate 🔮 section.

Run it now

No install required:

npx css-ghost ./src

Or install globally for repeated use:

npm install -g css-ghost
css-ghost ./src

Interactive folder picker

Run css-ghost with no arguments and an interactive directory picker opens. Navigate with ↑↓ (or j/k), press Enter or → to go into a folder, ← to go back up, [a] to add the current directory to the scan, then [d] when done:

css-ghost

Useful when you're not sure which subfolder to target, or want to scan multiple directories in one pass.

Dynamic class detection

If a component accesses classes dynamically – styles[variable], styles[\${variant}] – css-ghost can't resolve the class name statically. Rather than silently skip those files or report false positives, it flags them with a ⚠️ warning per file:

✅ src/components/Alert/Alert.module.css

   ⚠️  Dynamic class references detected – results may be incomplete.
   Dynamic references in: src/components/Alert.jsx

   👻 .hidden (line 30)
      .hidden { display: none; }

All statically resolvable patterns are still analysed: string literals, ternaries, cx({ active: isOn }) object keys, array literals, and both branches of ternaries.

Deleting orphans

Once you're happy with the report, pass --delete to remove every flagged selector from its source file:

css-ghost ./src --delete

css-ghost prints the full report first, lists what it's about to delete, then asks for confirmation. Pass --yes to skip the prompt in CI:

css-ghost ./src --delete --yes

Tip: commit or stash first. There's no undo.

Other useful flags

Flag What it does
--ghost-trail Show the last git commit that touched each orphan
--strict Exit with code 1 when orphans exist (CI / pre-commit)
--install-hook ./src Write a pre-commit hook that blocks commits with orphans
--output <path> Custom path for the markdown report
--ai Append a plain-English AI summary (needs free OpenRouter key)

Ghost trail

Pass --ghost-trail to fetch the last git commit that changed each orphan's occurrence count:

css-ghost ./src --ghost-trail

   👻 .iconRight (line 28)
      🕵️  b5c6efb · Roland Levy · 3 weeks ago – "Refactor Button component"
      .iconRight {
        margin-left: 6px;
      }

Handy for tracking down when and why a class went dead.

Pre-commit hook 

css-ghost --install-hook ./src

Writes .git/hooks/pre-commit (executable, chmod 755) that blocks commits whenever orphaned selectors exist. Remove it with rm .git/hooks/pre-commit.

How is it different from PurgeCSS?

PurgeCSS is a build-time bundler – it hooks into webpack or PostCSS to strip unused CSS from your production output. It's designed for frameworks like Tailwind or Bootstrap where you use a fraction of the utility classes.

css-ghost is a source code auditor – it finds dead selectors in your actual codebase, with no build step and no config file.

PurgeCSS css-ghost
Works on source files ❌ Build output only ✅
Zero config, no build step ❌ ✅
CSS custom property orphans ❌ ✅
Git history per orphan ❌ ✅
Pre-commit hook ❌ ✅
Deletes dead code for you ❌ ✅
Safe with dynamic classes ❌ Silently removes them ✅ Flags with ⚠️

The two tools are complementary – PurgeCSS for trimming framework output at build time, css-ghost for auditing your own hand-written CSS throughout development.

The source is on GitHub and the package is on npm. PRs and issues welcome.

title: Building a liquid glass card with CSS
description:
A glass card can look great over a gradient and become unreadable the moment you put real content behind it. The blur is only one part of the effect. Tint, edge highlights and the backdrop matter just as much.

I built GradientDeck, formerly Gradienty.codes. Its liquid glass tool lets you adjust those pieces visually. Here’s a smaller, standalone CSS version you can use without the generator.

Start with something behind the glass

A flat background gives the filter very little to work with. This example uses two radial gradients so you can actually see the material.

<div class="scene">
  <article class="glass">
    <div class="glass-content">
      <h2>Make room for the good stuff.</h2>
      <p>A small glass card, built with plain CSS.</p>
    </div>
  </article>
</div>

.scene {
  min-height: 28rem;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  padding: 2rem;
  background:
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 20% 25%, #0d9488, transparent 60%),
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 80% 75%, #7c3aed, transparent 60%),
    #0f172a;
}

.glass {
  position: relative;
  width: min(100%, 24rem);
  box-sizing: border-box;
  padding: 2rem;
  border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 24%);
  border-radius: 1.75rem;
  background: #172033;
  color: #fff;
  box-shadow:
    0 20px 70px rgb(0 0 0 / 24%),
    inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 35%),
    inset 0 -1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 8%);
}

@supports ((backdrop-filter: blur(1px)) or
           (-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1px))) {
  .glass {
    background: rgb(15 23 42 / 48%);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
    backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
  }
}

.glass-content {
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1;
}

.glass h2 { margin: 0 0 0.75rem; }
.glass p { margin: 0; line-height: 1.6; }

The card starts with a solid background. Browsers that support backdrop filtering get the translucent version through @supports.

Add a highlight without washing out the text

The thin border defines the silhouette. The inset shadows catch the upper and lower edges. A separate highlight layer adds a little sheen:

.glass::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  border-radius: inherit;
  pointer-events: none;
  background: linear-gradient(
    135deg,
    rgb(255 255 255 / 14%),
    transparent 45%
  );
}

Keep the highlight subtle. A bright white overlay across the entire card quickly makes the surface look cloudy.

Tune it in this order

  1. Backdrop: put the card over the actual page or image you plan to use.
  2. Tint: increase the background alpha until the text is comfortable to read.
  3. Blur: soften distracting detail without losing all the color behind it.
  4. Highlights: add enough light to define the edges.

A blur value alone won’t guarantee readable text. Check the card over both the brightest and busiest parts of the background, especially if content scrolls underneath it.

When nothing seems to blur

First, check that the card’s background is translucent and that there is something behind it.

Then inspect its ancestors. A parent with opacity below 1, a filter, a mask or its own backdrop filter can limit which pixels the child samples. Nested glass panels are a common place to encounter this. MDN explains the behavior in its backdrop-filter reference.

Use an alpha background color to make the surface translucent. Setting opacity on the whole card also fades its text and children.

Give people a solid option

Where the browser exposes the reduced-transparency preference, you can honor it with an opaque surface:

@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .glass {
    background: #172033;
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: none;
    backdrop-filter: none;
  }

  .glass::before { display: none; }
}

This also removes the decorative highlight. It doesn’t replace checking contrast in the default design.

For performance, start with one filtered surface. Avoid animating the blur radius, and be cautious about adding several overlapping blur layers to every card in a scrolling list. Check the result on the devices your readers actually use.

Try the settings visually

GradientDeck’s liquid glass generator has 20 presets, editable material controls and CSS and Tailwind CSS v4 exports. It’s free and doesn’t require an account. You can also preview the glass over an image from your device.

The example above recreates a glass-like appearance with CSS; it doesn’t implement optical refraction. Start simple, put it over your real UI, and let readability decide how transparent it should be.
